license: Original collection text: MIT. Linked works retain their own licenses.

resources.name: REA — Reverse Engineer Anything
resources.description: The upstream CLI and MCP server for evidence-based investigations of shipped software and runtime behavior.
requirements: rea-agents 6.5.0 was the published npm version at review time.
Node.js ^22.19.0 || ^24.11.0 || >=26.0.0; additional tools depend on the target.

resources.name: Official reverse-engineer-anything skill
resources.description: Target routing, connection recovery and evidence practices for agents using REA.
requirements: Installing the skill provides instructions; it does not by itself register MCP or install analysis engines.
Use the connected server's actual tool schemas; repository main may be ahead of an installed release.

resources.name: Installation and client setup
resources.description: Reviewed setup plans, client registration, provider prerequisites and scoped readiness checks.
requirements: Supported Node.js and npm.
Setup previews client configuration changes; native engines have separate prerequisites.

resources.name: CLI and Evidence
resources.description: CLI workflows for saving Evidence and projecting smaller views from completed analysis.
requirements: Installed REA CLI or an explicitly pinned package runner.
CLI processes are separate; retain result files for later operations.

resources.name: MCP contracts and generated catalog
resources.description: Canonical tool contracts, provider discovery and Evidence semantics for integration authors.
requirements: A compatible MCP client for live use.
Discover the live catalog before relying on tools documented on main.

resources.name: Native binary investigation
resources.description: Locate a function, inspect instructions and pseudocode, and follow references with a selected native provider.
requirements: A target binary and a configured supported provider such as Ghidra, Hopper or IDA.
Host, architecture and provider support are scoped separately; pseudocode is not original source.

resources.name: Cross-layer JavaScript application workflows
resources.description: Trace features and compare authenticated JavaScript application graphs while preserving static-analysis limits.
requirements: Evidence from analyze_javascript_application or supported runtime reconciliation.
No native engine is required for the static JavaScript path; keep the complete parent Evidence.

resources.name: Static Android APK analysis
resources.description: Inspect Android package identity, classes, methods and references through REA's JADX integration.
requirements: Full JDK 17 or newer and caller-supplied jadx-headless-mcp 0.7.1 with the documented digest check.
Linux requires a procps-compatible ps for provider process ownership.

resources.name: Managed-code analysis
resources.description: Read PE/CLI metadata and CIL, compare managed members and inspect declared native boundaries without loading the assembly.
requirements: A supported PE/CLI assembly; no native engine is required for metadata/CIL inspection.
NativeAOT, IL2CPP and packaged single-file deployments have different boundaries.

resources.name: Historical web network captures
resources.description: Inspect saved web captures offline; recorded URLs are not fetched and no proxy is started.
requirements: A supported existing capture and an explicit format selection.
PCAP/TShark workflows are separate and have different host/tool requirements.

resources.name: Firmware analysis
resources.description: Inspect firmware regions with Binwalk and explicitly extract with Unblob, retaining tool and artifact identity.
requirements: Caller-supplied Binwalk 3.1.x for inspection; Unblob 26.6.x for extraction.
The documented verification scope is Linux x64; extraction needs a new caller-selected output directory.

resources.name: Recorded packet capture inspection
resources.description: Select TShark fields, display filters and decode-as rules over an existing network, USB or Bluetooth capture, and look up installed field names. It does not capture traffic, open an interface or control a device.
requirements: Caller-supplied TShark 4.x on Linux with util-linux prlimit; macOS and Windows hosts are refused before inspection. Listed in the rea-agents 6.5.0 release notes.

Dissector output describes the selected recording, not verified device behavior. Upstream fixtures are generated Ethernet/UDP/DNS and Bluetooth HCI PCAPs and do not cover PCAPNG, USB, BLE ATT or physical capture.

resources.name: Packet capture summaries
resources.description: Summarize a saved pcap or pcapng file’s endpoints, DNS questions and addresses, TLS SNI, protocol stacks and HTTP URIs into paged Evidence views. It does not capture traffic or fetch recorded targets.
requirements: Caller-supplied Wireshark 4.x tshark and capinfos. Capture inspection needs Linux with util-linux prlimit or Windows Job Objects; macOS reports a capability gap. Listed in the rea-agents 6.5.0 release notes.

Upstream’s current verification used Linux, Node 24.18.0 and Wireshark 4.0.17; actual Windows execution is unverified. Summaries do not establish decrypted payloads, process identity or the absence of unrecorded traffic.

resources.name: Recorded signal decoding
resources.description: Run caller-chosen sigrok protocol decoders, such as UART or I2C, over an existing logic-signal recording and keep annotation text with sample ranges. It does not acquire samples or communicate with hardware.
requirements: Caller-supplied sigrok-cli 0.7.2 with libsigrokdecode on Linux, plus util-linux prlimit; macOS and Windows are refused. Listed in the rea-agents 6.5.0 release notes.

The caller supplies decoder stacks, channel names and settings such as baud rate. Upstream’s fixture is a synthesized 9600-baud UART VCD and does not cover other formats, decoders or physical acquisition.

resources.name: Browser observation guide
resources.description: Follow a user-triggered export request in the supplied Notes browser example and connect it to the downloaded result.
requirements: A user-owned Chrome-family browser, loopback CDP connection and explicitly allowed origins.
The recorded upstream example used a separate controller to click.

resources.name: Aegis: trace a login-code calculation
resources.description: An official APK investigation follows TOTP methods in Aegis and publishes artifact identities and selected Evidence.
requirements: Upstream case: Aegis 3.4.3, REA 6.1.0, jadx-headless-mcp 0.7.1 and OpenJDK 21 on Linux x64.
Use the matching official APK for reproduction.

resources.name: DownUnderCTF: masked-squares flag checker
resources.description: An official educational challenge investigation connects binary checks to equations and records an original-program validation.
requirements: Upstream case: public DownUnderCTF 2023 challenge, REA 4.1.0 and Ghidra 12.1.4 on Linux x64.
Target hash and source revision are documented; author-reported execution.

resources.name: DX-Ball: reconstruct sound panning
resources.description: Recover one sound-pan function from instructions and constants; upstream cites 3,205 cases and a 63-byte match.
requirements: The matching DX-Ball 1.07 executable and the documented native-analysis environment.
The cited reconstruction checks concern one function.

resources.name: Notion: trace the clipboard bridge
resources.description: Trace a packaged Electron clipboard path using REA findings and separate source inspection; the dynamic wrapper remains a stated limit.
requirements: Upstream case uses Notion Desktop 7.6.1 packaged JavaScript and REA 4.1.0.
The full clipboard route was not automatically paired or observed as a desktop execution.

resources.name: TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring helper
resources.description: Inspect a 16-bit PC-98 DOS helper and relate its angle calculation to a pinned reconstruction and historical compiler checks.
requirements: The matching original TH04 MAIN.EXE and the documented Ghidra DOS load profile.
The showcase covers one helper.

resources.name: JavaScript and Electron: follow a CSV export
resources.description: A source-owned Notes fixture teaches the renderer, preload, IPC and CSV path with linked analysis evidence.
requirements: Supported Node.js and REA; no native engine is required for this static fixture.
The fixture is source-owned teaching material, not an installed Electron distribution.

resources.name: rea-playbook
resources.description: An Electron practice target, Evidence extractor and MCP probe; offline fixture mode is distinguished from real REA analysis.
requirements: README pins the real-analysis path to rea-agents 6.3.0 and lists supported Node.js versions.
The offline demo reads bundled results without running REA.

resources.name: dsh-mcp-rea
resources.description: A community MCP bridge presents a smaller selected tool surface and forwards explicit commands to the REA CLI.
requirements: Requires REA and the relevant analysis providers; distributed as a local bundle rather than a public npm package.
Use the documented REA_ENTRY mode for direct execution; PATH fallback invokes a shell.

resources.name: rea-jev
resources.description: A Claude Code plugin adds Jev-based routing and evidence checks around a pinned REA MCP integration.
requirements: Claude Code, supported Node.js and the plugin's documented macOS/Linux environment.
Optional Jev service credentials enable external model calls; excerpts may be sent to that service.
Hooks fail open on provider failure; they are not a security guarantee.

resources.name: rea-lab
resources.description: A Windows REA/Ghidra lab with seeded challenges, published studies, upstream contributions and recorded limitations.
requirements: The documented environment uses Windows 11, REA 6.4.0 and Ghidra 12.1.4.
Study results are author-reported and task/model-specific.
Code and documentation use different licenses; inspect the relevant repository notices.

resources.name: rea-casebook
resources.description: A Claude Code mod collects received REA Evidence, tracks unknowns and records findings that cite delivered evidence IDs.
requirements: README requires Claude Code 2.1.296 or newer and an MCP server registered under the name rea.
Developed with REA 6.4.0 and Ghidra 12.1 on Windows.

resources.name: PicoPrint: LX-D02 printer investigation
resources.description: The author describes REA-assisted Android investigation followed by separate Hermes decompilation to support a Windows BLE printer.
requirements: Project README lists Windows 10/11, Bluetooth LE, an LX-D02 printer and Go 1.25+ to build.
REA's stated role was readiness/device discovery and investigation framing; hermes-dec handled Hermes v98.
Author-reported results.

resources.name: Awesome Reverse Engineering
resources.description: A task-oriented reverse-engineering resource list by REA's maintainer, useful for broader tools and foundations.
requirements: Individual tools retain their own requirements and licenses.

resources.name: Awesome REA Cases
resources.description: A bilingual collection of REA and other AI-assisted reverse engineering cases, with source links and explicit distinctions between reported and reproduced outcomes.
requirements: A discovery index; review each case's original source, redistribution rights, and evidence status before reproducing it.

resources.name: ReaCut: video-editor reconstruction
resources.description: An independent video editor whose authors document REA-assisted investigation of Jianying/CapCut behavior and project formats. The public implementation includes a local timeline, FFmpeg export and an experimental, lossy draft importer.
requirements: The v0.5.0 preview reports macOS Apple Silicon testing; Windows/Linux builds still need device validation. The macOS package is ad-hoc signed and not notarized.
The experimental importer is documented against controlled Jianying 11.0.12922 drafts. Basic conversions are lossy: effects, keyframes and styles can be lost, and projects cannot be written back.
REA supports the reported research workflow but is not a runtime dependency. The project uses its own code and format; MIT source and bundled third-party components retain separate licenses.

resources.name: open-appleremote: Siri Remote protocol reconstruction
resources.description: Reconstructs first-generation Siri Remote Bluetooth reports for Linux, decoding buttons, touch and tvOS-style gestures. The Python implementation and protocol notes distinguish measured behavior, historical reports and inferred meanings.
requirements: Package 0.1.0; live use requires Linux, BlueZ, Python 3.8+ and access to the device’s hidraw interface. The core uses the Python standard library.
Project hardware checks cover A1962 with BlueZ 5.72 and Linux 6.17. A1513 is expected but untested; second- and third-generation Siri Remotes are unsupported.

The virtual keyboard has not been hardware-tested. Voice is unreleased and checked with synthetic or recorded frames, not live use in this package; it additionally needs libopus and HCI-monitor privileges.
Protocol notes label measured, previously reported and guessed facts. The public sample does not reproduce every claim from the larger unpublished capture.
MIT-licensed repository.

resources.name: GAMEKB-K17: reconstructing a macropad configuration protocol
resources.description: Implements the vendor HID configuration protocol for the GAMEKB-K17/HCY-K017 macropad. It writes key mappings, firmware macros and RGB settings, then reads them back; protocol notes separate tested commands from unconfirmed observations and other-device findings.
requirements: Package 3.0.0 requires Python 3.11+ and hidapi; the optional editor uses tkinter. Hardware identity is USB 0816:0220.
Windows is project-tested; other hidapi platforms are untested. Linux configuration requires suitable device permissions.
The documented scope includes 18 remappable controls and up to 16 firmware macros. The volume dial is fixed in firmware.
Read-back verification and interruption ordering are project claims backed by protocol documentation.
MIT license. The reviewed primary files establish reverse engineering of the vendor WebHID configurator.

resources.name: CF632BLE: a local client from scale-protocol research
resources.description: Reimplements the CF632BLE scale’s BLE protocol and body-composition calculations from research on the vendor’s Unique Health Android app. A static Web Bluetooth client receives measurements, manages device profiles and keeps its history in browser storage.
requirements: Requires the CF632BLE hardware and a Chromium browser supporting Web Bluetooth in a secure context. Firefox and Safari/iOS cannot connect to the scale through this app.
The SvelteKit/Vite application builds with npm and a static adapter. Its documented measurement path has no application server or vendor backend dependency.
Single-user browser storage is localStorage. The Device tab can explicitly write device profiles and settings; local history and scale memory are different stores.
The reviewed README and package manifest give no project license, and no root LICENSE file was present at the pinned commit.
Device compatibility and formula accuracy are project claims.

resources.name: zee-rp: reconstructing supported Axure RP 11 document operations
resources.description: Reads and rewrites supported native Axure RP 11 documents through a binary-record codec, reference-aware cloning and constrained interaction writers. CLI and MCP interfaces expose inspected edits while keeping offline structure checks separate from native application acceptance.
requirements: Package 0.1.1 requires Node.js 18+; MCP additionally uses the optional SDK dependency. Native creation needs the user’s Axure blank template and compatible libraries.
Recorded native acceptance uses macOS arm64 and Axure RP 11.0.0.4137. Linux CI covers public core checks; native GUI jobs require macOS and Accessibility permission.
Unsupported document forms, external references and interaction expressions may be rejected. Numbered lists and true native merged table cells are not supported.

Release evidence separates public/generated tests from historical assertions needing an unpublished exact fixture pack. One GUI sample checked load/save/close/reopen, not preview behavior or manual editing; newly synchronized features still need native acceptance.
Authored code/docs are MIT; Axure, its libraries and third-party assets are separate.

resources.name: Super Mario 64 DS: matching decompilation with relocation checks
resources.description: Reconstructs Super Mario 64 DS functions as C/C++ and permitted assembly primitives, comparing compiled output with a user-supplied cartridge dump. Independent relocation-destination checks strengthen the matching gate; integration into the PC port is tracked separately.
requirements: Requires the user’s cartridge dump, the pinned mwccarm matching compiler, its separate linker/setup and Python tooling such as ndspy, Capstone and pyelftools.
The pinned README reports 11,389/11,389 matched functions, including 108 byte-exact assembly primitives, but only 10,957 linked into the PC port. These counters describe different gates.

The same README retains older near-finished prose, and port/README.md describes a historical smoke-build stage. Treat matching and port-playability statements as source-specific reports, not a verified complete playable port.
Agent-assisted matching is documented, together with source review and relocation checks.
The repository has an MIT license; original game data and external compiler rights remain separate.

resources.name: GoldenEye 007: an agent-assisted native port from a decompilation
resources.description: Builds a native PC port on the existing GoldenEye 007 decompilation, with a host platform layer and assets extracted from the user’s ROM. The project documents agent collaboration, rendering comparisons, playtest scope and unresolved platform support.
requirements: The reviewed v0.5.0 documentation supports Windows 10/11 x64 and x86-64 Linux/Steam Deck with glibc 2.31+; both need OpenGL 3.0 drivers. macOS and ARM builds remain planned, despite the broader repository About description.
Release packages require the user’s US NTSC-U ROM; PAL and Japanese releases are not yet supported. This is a native port from decompiled source, not static binary recompilation.
Source builds need CMake 3.16+, C/C++, SDL2, zlib, OpenGL, Python 3 and the documented asset-extraction tools.
v0.5.0 playtests were campaign spot-checks and multiplayer sessions; the full Agent-difficulty campaign was last reported end-to-end at v0.4.0.

MIT covers original port/build/tooling/docs work only. NOTICE states inherited n64decomp/007 material has no explicit upstream license, and vendored components have separate terms; the MIT file is not a blanket grant over all contents.

resources.name: ssbu-recomp: static recompilation with explicit mode limits
resources.description: Translates Super Smash Bros. Ultimate 13.0.4 AArch64 code ahead of time and supplies a Windows runtime with Vulkan/OpenGL rendering. It also reconstructs selected fighter scripts as editable C++ and compares translated/source behavior through differential and deterministic tests.
requirements: Running requires Windows 10/11 x64, a Vulkan 1.3-capable GPU and the user’s own 13.0.4 game dump. Linux and Steam Deck support have not started.

Building requires Python 3.10+ with the documented packages, LLVM/clang 9.0.0 (8.0.0 is also documented as working), MSVC/Windows SDK, SDL3, Vulkan headers, glslang and reference tooling. Music needs libopus; movies need Media Foundation, VP9 Video Extensions and Web Media Extensions 2.x, with Media Feature Pack additionally required on Windows N.
Only some modes have reported play coverage. Adventure maps/fights and several multiplayer modes are untested; online is unavailable. Physical controllers are not yet confirmed.
The author credits Claude agents. Reported frame rates, differential equivalence and selected fighter match traces.
The README grants GPL version 3 or later. The public repository supplies tools/runtime rather than the game dump, keys or assets; game-derived output is a separate requirement.

resources.name: KartPad: platform integration for a Mario Kart Wii recompilation
resources.description: Builds Apple and Android integration around WiiCompiled’s ahead-of-time translation of Mario Kart Wii, with native graphics, input and optional Retro Rewind support. Its status and rights documents distinguish platform acceptance, unresolved device defects and game-content requirements.
requirements: Requires user-supplied supported PAL RMCP01 revision 0 game data. Retro Rewind 6.13.3 needs matching separately obtained content and a compatible compiled profile in the reviewed 0.8.3 build.

Android targets ARM64/Vulkan on Android 9+; iPhone/iPad require iOS/iPadOS 16+. The README documents a PadMint/source route for Apple Silicon macOS 14+, while the pinned status table still labels Mac experimental. tvOS 17+ is also an experimental preview.
Physical-device and emulator checks cover specific builds and devices. Missing graphics, freezes, controller and performance problems remain on some hardware.
Substantial AI assistance is disclosed without an audited generated-code percentage.

KartPad-owned work is GPL-3.0-only, with upstream component terms retained. RIGHTS_AND_LICENSES separates software obligations from game-derived logic and assets; GPL does not relicense Mario Kart Wii.

resources.name: BattleShip: an AI-assisted Super Smash Bros. native port
resources.description: Ports the existing Super Smash Bros. N64 decompilation using libultraship and Torch. The author’s earlier README describes agent-built graphics/audio comparison tools and differential debugging against emulator behavior, rather than claiming AI recovered the game from a cartridge without prior community work.
requirements: Requires the user’s own Super Smash Bros. N64 dump matching a documented hash: US NTSC-U v1.0 (NALE) or Japanese v1.0 (NALJ). Each region is a separate build; Torch extracts assets locally during a source build or on a packaged build’s first run.

The README lists native Windows, Linux, Apple Silicon macOS and Android builds; native C mods and the GameCube adapter driver are desktop-only. BUILDING.md covers desktop source builds with Git/submodules, CMake and Python 3, plus Ninja on Linux/macOS or Visual Studio 2022 and the Windows SDK on Windows.

The author reports developing the port alone with Claude until v0.3-beta and says it is no longer a pure AI project, crediting community testing, fixes and features; these statements are self-reported.

The LICENSE grants MIT only to port-specific code, build scripts, tools and docs. The decomp submodule and decomp-derived files defer to the upstream decompilation, which publishes no explicit license; libultraship/Torch, bundled fonts and controller mappings keep their own terms; game rights are separate.

resources.name: Agent decompilation: a byte-matching retrospective
resources.description: Maurice Heumann describes replacing plausible-looking agent output with compiler-based checks of reconstructed functions, relocations, data and types. The retrospective reports 99% function presence and 83% of all functions byte-exact, while keeping the reconstruction code private.
requirements: Author retrospective dated 2026-10-09; the reviewed article leaves the game unnamed.
The project uses the original compiler and binary as references; no public implementation or reproducible artifact is supplied.
Coverage figures and runtime success are author-reported.
A documented case study.

resources.name: Snowboard Kids 2: an LLM-assisted N64 matching decompilation
resources.description: A public matching decompilation of the N64 game Snowboard Kids 2, begun in 2024 with community decompilation tools. The author’s dated posts document Claude, Codex and GLM workflows, including headless one-shot loops, similarity-based function scheduling and hook-guarded, hash-checked builds, through a reported complete function match.
requirements: Building needs the user’s own big-endian Snowboard Kids 2 ROM, make, Python 3, MIPS binutils and the toolchain installed by make setup; the README reports testing only on x86 Debian/Ubuntu and macOS. It states the repository has no game assets or assembly, although the reviewed tree tracks menu-sprite PNG and palette files under assets/.

Progress figures are author-reported. The 2026-02-16 post describes matched code rising from about 25% to 58% with one-shot loops, then to about 75%, with 124 functions left; the 2026-05-17 post reports every function matched. The 2025-11-27 post’s 79% figure was a projection.

Byte-matching C is not documented or idiomatic source. The 2026-05-17 post notes remaining __asm__ coercions, many generated names and structures still needing cleanup, and graphics/audio assets mostly handled as binary blobs; the 2026-02-16 post describes brittle agent matches.

Agent assistance is not quantified beyond the posts. The 2026-05-17 post dates the first commit to September 2024 and credits four named N64 decomp community members with significant contributions, especially across the final ten functions; the 2025-11-04 post describes a human-led loop. The work relies on community tools such as splat, m2c, decomp.me, asm-differ and decomp-permuter.
No license file is present at the reviewed commit. The June 2026 Snowboard Kids 2: Recompiled release and the August 2026 decompilation of the original Snowboard Kids are separate projects.

resources.name: awesome-rea (yibie): verification-focused projects and practice reports
resources.description: Organizes AI-assisted game decompilation, native ports, static recompilation and tooling around stated acceptance checks, alongside a separate track of practitioner write-ups and discussions. Useful for finding primary reports and comparing how projects define correctness.
requirements: Project entries describe acceptance mechanisms; the separate discussion track does not require public code or an acceptance test.
The reviewed snapshot has an intentionally empty console/firmware category.
Collection summaries can lag primary repositories, including platform support, progress and license scope; follow the linked project sources before relying on a claim.
The collection LICENSE declares CC0 1.0 Universal. Linked projects and source articles retain their own rights and license conditions.
An independent community collection.

resources.name: cooler-lcd: a Thermalright display protocol implementation
resources.description: Implements a USB picture-transfer driver for Thermalright Vision cooler displays, with a Rust dashboard replacing the vendor display application. The documented protocol sends a header and JPEG frames, with periodic resends to prevent the device reverting to its logo.
requirements: Package 0.1.0 uses Rust edition 2024 and targets the 480×480 USB 87ad:70db display family.
Its documented environment is Linux with udev/systemd and Omarchy integration. Hyprland supplies away/lock state; NVIDIA telemetry uses NVML, and individual screens need their own optional services.
The driver cites TRCC Linux reverse-engineering notes for its 64-byte frame header and JPEG payload, with one-second keepalive resends.
Only one process can own the display at once; the vendor TRCC application must relinquish it.
MIT-licensed code. Optional traffic/map feeds and other external services retain their own terms.

resources.name: IsaacRecomp: translating Flash game bytecode to native C++
resources.description: Translates The Binding of Isaac’s Flash AVM1 bytecode into C++ functions and supplies a native rendering/input runtime. The project reads graphics and audio from the user’s original game and documents deterministic input, headless runs and screenshot regression checks.
requirements: Requires the user’s original Steam Isaac.exe; Wrath of the Lamb and Eternal Edition depend on the corresponding game version. This is ahead-of-time translation, not recovery of the original authored ActionScript project.

Documented targets include 64-bit Windows/Linux, Android 7.0+ on 64-bit ARM and Switch homebrew. Source builds use CMake/Ninja and SDL2/OpenGL 3.3 or ES 3.0; mobile/console builds have separate SDK/toolchain requirements.
The author credits AI assistance and reports 30 Hz game logic with higher-rate interpolated rendering.
Reported regression tests compare deterministic logic and screenshots across engine revisions.

MIT covers the authored engine, tools, build files and docs only. LICENSE explicitly excludes gen/, gen720/, patch1080/ and patch720/ translated game-code directories; third-party and original-game rights remain separate.

resources.name: Virtual Desktop Streamer: rehosting the platform layer on Linux
resources.description: An author-reported Claude Code and REA workflow replaces the macOS streamer’s capture, encoding, audio and input layer with Linux implementations while reusing vendor protocol libraries. The documented result targets desktop streaming and video playback, not Windows-only VR game streaming.
requirements: Requires the official macOS Virtual Desktop installer for proprietary libraries and the user’s Virtual Desktop headset application. It is not a complete protocol reimplementation or an official vendor port.

The build uses .NET 8. Linux runtime dependencies include GStreamer 1.16+, PulseAudio/PipeWire, X11 or an appropriate Wayland portal, OpenSSL 1.1 or 3 and uinput access; video-file playback additionally needs FFmpeg 7.

Published testing used a simulated headset, mock portal and container networking. No real headset, real Wi-Fi or GPU encoder was available; internet matchmaking and same-address network changes were untested.
The scroll fix was checked at device/libinput level without directly observing the receiving X11 app.
MIT applies to this repository’s code only. Vendor libraries remain proprietary; the project limits redistribution of packages containing them and does not grant rights to the headset application.

resources.name: Open Claude UI: REA-informed interface reference components
resources.description: Publishes React components, motion helpers and design-system notes derived from the author’s reported REA investigation of Claude Desktop. It is useful as an interface-reconstruction case, with version-specific observations rather than proof of a complete assistant application or backend clone.
requirements: Package 1.0.0 declares React/React DOM 18+, Framer Motion 10+ and lucide-react 0.280+ peer dependencies; its development setup uses TypeScript 5.5 and Framer Motion 11.
Versioned analysis explicitly targets Claude Desktop v2.37337.1 and reports REA v6.5.0.
The package exposes build/typecheck and a component preview; production-grade or high-fidelity wording remains the author’s assertion.
UI component examples do not supply Claude model access, account services or a recovered complete desktop application. Native desktop effects require their own host integration.

MIT repository license. The asset policy documents system-font fallbacks and synthesized audio instead of bundled proprietary font/audio files; it does not grant rights in upstream Claude assets or branding.

resources.name: Nanolathe: a documented Total Annihilation engine reimplementation
resources.description: Reimplements a Total Annihilation-compatible strategy-game engine in Go, with public file-format research and separate gameplay profiles. It distinguishes intended retail 3.1 behavior from community-patch research and deliberate modern changes, and separates synthetic checks from tests requiring original game data.
requirements: Native use requires the user’s installed Total Annihilation HPI archives. The reference installation includes Core Contingency, Battle Tactics and patch 3.1; other combinations remain under testing.
The pinned source requires Go 1.27.1 or newer and Ebitengine 2.10.5. Native targets include Windows, macOS 13+ and Linux with graphical/audio libraries; the browser build remains experimental.
The project is beta. Modern rules intentionally change behavior, while Strict 3.1 expresses a compatibility aim.
Synthetic tests run without retail assets; the separate retail tier requires an installed game.

Original engine code is MIT; original game assets and dependency licenses are separate. The publication note describes curated integration snapshots, omitted raw research and unresolved attribution questions.

resources.name: PlxNative: reconstructing a native webOS media-client interface
resources.description: An unofficial Plex client built after the author investigated LG webOS native media interfaces with Ghidra and coding agents. It draws its own Rust/OpenGL interface and uses the television’s decoder, with documented host, simulator and real-device test tiers.
requirements: Requires a Plex account/server and a compatible LG TV. The baseline is webOS 4.0+, with explicitly documented 3.4.3/3.9.3 exceptions; the latter needs a newer source build than prebuilt v0.8.0.
Developer Mode normally needs no root but requires renewal. Some k5lp/k3lp devices cannot play under its sandbox, and k6hp crashes remain unresolved.
Product builds need macOS (x86_64 or arm64) or arm64 Linux, the webOS NDK, the pinned Rust toolchain and CMake. The desktop simulator has a different host/setup path.

The scope is movies and TV shows, excluding music, photos, live TV and DVR. Selected relay/encrypted-server paths lack end-to-end viewing tests; timing and playback results remain author/device-specific.
GPL-3.0-or-later for project code, with separate brand and third-party terms including bundled FFmpeg.

resources.name: TH08: exact-source reconstruction and separately tested ports
resources.description: Reconstructs the original Japanese Touhou 8 version 1.00d against its binary and original compiler, then adapts the recovered code for other platforms. Source presence, strict function matching, whole-executable identity and playable-port checks are recorded as different milestones.
requirements: Exact checks require the user’s original Japanese TH08 1.00d executable and Visual C++ .NET 2002 toolchain. Ledgers and analysis helpers need Python 3.11+; Linux/macOS toolchain setup also needs Wine and msiextract. Playable products still need original game data.
The pinned main README reports source for 1,107 authored functions and strict acceptance of 1,106, with whole-executable identity still in progress.
The VC7 i386 runtime checkpoint is distinct from a redistributable modern Windows release; macOS remains in progress. Exact normal-build checks and bugfix playtests have different purposes.
A historical oracle accepted instruction bytes while missing wrong floating-literal data. The linked issue/PR records later data-reference checks.
MIT covers repository code/docs, not the original game. Historical source lineage and agent contributions retain their attribution.

resources.name: Dinosaur runner: recovering one acceleration rule
resources.description: REA’s documented teaching case inspects the HTTP t-rex-runner edition and reconstructs its speed-update rule. A separate controlled original-game check and a new demonstration compare update counts, including the floating-point step that crosses the nominal speed threshold.
requirements: The recorded target is wayou’s HTTP browser edition at the cited revision, not chrome://dino/. Source and observation hashes identify that edition.
After read-only inspection, a separate Playwright controller disabled future scheduling and obstacles to call the original update function under controlled conditions.
The reconstructed claim is limited to acceleration. Drawing, jumping, collisions and controls in the teaching game are newly authored, not independently recovered original gameplay.
Public result tables and code document the author’s checks. The cited original-source excerpts retain Chromium attribution and BSD-3-Clause terms.

resources.name: Windows Calculator: reconstructing percentage rules
resources.description: REA’s case traces the installed Windows Calculator model DLL to explain different percentage behavior for multiplication/division and other operations. An analyst-selected function is interpreted against public Microsoft source and demonstrated with fixed browser examples.
requirements: The documented target is Calculator 11.2508.4.0 x64. The public source commit is an interpretation cross-check, not an identified build commit for that installed DLL.
Function selection was analyst-assisted.
This reconstructs a bounded arithmetic rule, not the Calculator application. Public Microsoft source is MIT-licensed; access and rights to the installed target remain separate.

resources.name: Feishu: an author-reported isolated second app instance
resources.description: The author reports using Codex and REA analysis to adapt a separate macOS Feishu copy with its own application identity, data directory and single-instance lock. The account describes local signing and separation checks while retaining the original app unchanged.
requirements: The report targets Feishu 8.1.17 with REA 6.5.0 on the author’s Mac; reported elapsed times and isolation results.
The modified copy is locally signed and has automatic updates disabled. The article does not publish a redistributable replacement app or original-source reconstruction.
The author attributes some architecture tracing directly to Codex and cites prior feishu-clone work.
Original hash/signature and process/data separation checks are author-reported.

resources.name: Zelda 64: Recompiled — a native Majora’s Mask port without a full source decompilation
resources.description: Uses N64Recomp to translate Majora’s Mask into a native application and RT64 for rendering. The project separates static recompilation from source decompilation while reusing decompilation headers and selected functions for patches and enhancements.
requirements: The reviewed build accepts the US Nintendo 64 Majora’s Mask ROM supplied by the user; game assets are not included. Ocarina of Time remains planned, and this is not an emulator for arbitrary ROMs.

Runtime graphics require Direct3D 12.0 with Shader Model 6, Vulkan 1.2, or Metal Argument Buffers Tier 2. x86-64 needs SSE4.1; the README lists macOS 13.0+ with Apple Silicon or a 7th-generation Intel CPU.

Source builds additionally require submodules, CMake 3.20+, C++20 tooling, N64Recomp/RSPRecomp and the specified decompressed ROM. The build guide lists SDL2 and platform dependencies; ordinary play uses the standard ROM.
The project documents high-frame-rate, widescreen, camera and save enhancements, plus overlay and cutscene issues. These are project claims.
GPLv3 project license; original game content and dependencies retain separate terms. The team states that it does not use generative AI and bans contributions using GenAI tooling in any capacity.

resources.name: OpenGOAL: recovering GOAL code and rebuilding the Jak games
resources.description: Reconstructs readable GOAL code from the original Jak binaries and compiles it with a new GOAL compiler for modern PCs. Its workflow combines a specialized decompiler, manually supplied type information, asset extraction and an interactive development runtime.
requirements: Requires the user’s original PS2 game copy and extracted assets. The README covers retail PAL, NTSC and NTSC-J editions, including Greatest Hits, and excludes later PS3/PS4/PS5 releases.
The pinned README reports Jak 1 as complete, Jak 2 as beta with remaining issues, and substantial work still needed for Jak 3.

The supported runtime is x86-64 on Windows, Linux and macOS. The macOS guide requires Rosetta 2 on Apple Silicon and lists macOS Sequoia; native ARM64 builds are experimental and unsupported. No mobile release is planned.

Development uses C++20, CMake, NASM and platform libraries, then the project’s asset-extraction and GOAL compilation steps. The documented task commands need the corresponding task runner; runtime code editing is a development feature.
ISC license for project work; original game assets and third-party components retain their own rights.

resources.name: LEGO Island: source reconstruction with separately reported exact rebuilds
resources.description: Reconstructs the English LEGO Island 1.1 source for its original 32-bit Windows target. The project distinguishes function-comparison reports, ReproBit’s reported byte-identical retail rebuilds and ordinary developer builds; its modern portable adaptation is a separate repository.
requirements: Exact verification requires the user’s matching English 1.1 CONFIG.EXE, ISLE.EXE and LEGO1.DLL, the original Visual C++ 4.2 toolchain, Python 3.11+, Git and ReproBit; Linux/macOS also need Wine.
The pinned README reports a cold rebuild matching all three retail binaries byte for byte.
The ordinary CMake path is for development and is not the release-verification path. This repository targets 32-bit Windows only; cross-platform and Web support belongs to isle-portable.
Running the rebuilt executables still requires the original installed game data and the documented data paths. The README notes that d3drm.dll may also be needed on newer Windows systems.
The repository carries the LGPLv3 license; original game data and toolchain rights remain separate.

resources.name: Snowball War: a bounded REA-assisted minigame reconstruction
resources.description: The author uses REA’s Ghidra workflow to investigate the DOS Ski or Die binary, document Snowball War rules and rebuild that one minigame in Rust with SDL2. The public notes distinguish recovered tables and mechanics from approximations and deliberate presentation changes.
requirements: Requires the user’s matching DOS/EGA game files and Python 3 for asset extraction. The Linux build uses Rust stable (author-tested with 1.93), Cargo and SDL2 development libraries; Cargo.toml specifies the SDL2 binding 0.37.
The reported analysis used Ghidra 12.1.4 and JDK 21 through the REA CLI after unpacking EXEPACK. Caller-supplied function/code seeds are assertions.

Only Snowball War is reconstructed. Other events and the original engine are excluded; menus are new, and the close-up animation is deliberately restricted to the fort zone rather than reproducing every original placement.
The frame rate is approximated at 35 Hz, the original PRNG was not recovered, pause/exit keys are approximations, and audio playback is missing.
The pinned LICENSE.md and Cargo.toml offer MIT OR Apache-2.0, while the README’s license sentence mentions MIT only. Original art/audio must be extracted separately.

resources.name: SpaceCadetPinball: decompiled game logic adapted to SDL2
resources.description: Converts the reverse-engineered Space Cadet pinball game into compilable C++ for desktop platforms. The README identifies the Windows XP executable and public PDB, a Full Tilt executable, and the work of recovering structures, naming variables and adapting the decompiled routines.
requirements: Requires original game resources supplied separately. The project supports resource data from Windows and Full Tilt editions; its releases do not supply those assets.
The main project targets desktop Windows, Linux and macOS. Its list of console, mobile and browser ports points to separate projects.
Source builds require C++11, CMake, SDL2 and SDL2_mixer. The README gives Visual Studio, GCC/Clang and Xcode build paths, including x86_64 or arm64 selection on macOS.
The README reports that all subroutines were decompiled and converted to C++. Full Tilt feature work and possible support for its other two tables remain separate plans.
MIT license for this repository; original game resources and dependencies retain their own terms.

As checked on 2026-10-20, the latest release is Release_2.1.0 (2023-10-16); the reviewed 2024-08-21 commit is still the master head and GitHub’s last recorded push, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

resources.name: Super Mario 64: ROM reconstruction with explicit comparison gates
resources.description: Reconstructs Super Mario 64 source for Japanese, North American, European, Shindou and iQue releases. Its build files distinguish original-ROM hash comparison from nonmatching or modified configurations, while source naming and documentation remain ongoing.
requirements: Requires the user’s matching original ROM for asset extraction. The five target releases are separate.

The documented build uses GNU make, Python 3.6+, MIPS binutils, pkgconf and host development tools. Windows instructions use WSL/Linux; macOS instructions require an appropriate MIPS toolchain and newer GNU make.
The Makefile normally checks the output ROM’s SHA-1 against the selected reference. NON_MATCHING, a non-N64 target or nonstandard configurations disable comparison.
The pinned Jenkins configuration explicitly sets COMPARE=0 for iQue and enhancement builds.
The repository carries CC0-1.0; original Nintendo content and any separate third-party rights are not supplied by that declaration.

As checked on 2026-10-20, the reviewed 2023-08-17 commit is still the master head and GitHub’s last recorded push was 2024-02-04; the only GitHub releases are 2019 qemu-irix helper binaries, not game builds, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

resources.name: Unleashed Recompiled: translating Xbox 360 game code and shaders
resources.description: Builds an unofficial Sonic Unleashed PC port by statically recompiling Xbox 360 PowerPC code with XenonRecomp and Xenos shaders with XenosRecomp. The port adds modern display and modding options while documenting original-engine limits and remaining compatibility issues.
requirements: Requires the user’s US or EU Xbox 360 game files and the title update; the Japanese release and PS3 files are unsupported by the reviewed installation guide. DLC is optional, and the project does not provide game assets.

The README’s Windows/Linux baseline includes an AVX-capable CPU, 8 GB RAM and Direct3D 12.0 with Shader Model 6 or Vulkan 1.2 graphics. It lists Windows 10 version 1909 and a modern Linux distribution such as Ubuntu 22.04.

Source builds require submodules, CMake 3.20+, C++20 tooling, vcpkg with VCPKG_ROOT configured, and matching executable/update/shader inputs. At the same revision, BUILDING.md documents Xcode 16.3+ and macOS presets while the README says macOS is not on the roadmap.
High-frame-rate gameplay glitches, loading stutters and ultrawide cutscene issues remain documented. Mods replacing the original executable or shaders are unsupported.
GPLv3 project license, with separate original-game and dependency terms. This is static recompilation.

resources.name: OpenMW: replacing Morrowind’s engine while reusing original content
resources.description: Provides an independent engine for playing Morrowind and an alternative editor, OpenMW-CS. It loads original game content through its own runtime and documents script and mod compatibility differences; it is an engine replacement rather than a recovered Bethesda source tree.
requirements: Playing Morrowind requires the user’s original game data, including Morrowind.esm and the installation settings. Tribunal and Bloodmoon are optional expansions; the installation guide recommends both for best results. OpenMW-CS can also support separately authored projects.
The pinned README and build files identify version 0.52.0; this is a source-snapshot identifier. The README lists Windows 10+, macOS 14.8+ and Linux, with no 32-bit support.

The source configuration uses CMake 3.16+, C++20, SDL2 2.26+, OpenSceneGraph 3.6.5+, Boost 1.70+ and OpenAL; launcher/editor/wizard builds use Qt6. Additional dependencies depend on enabled components.

The project reports the main quests as completable, but warns about side quests and mods that depend on original-engine quirks. Example Suite integration tests and the separate Morrowind-content test setup cover selected behavior.
The official GitHub mirror points to the main GitLab project. GPLv3 covers project code, with separate font/dependency terms and original-game data rights.

resources.name: REDRIVER2: reconstructing Driver 2 through a PlayStation compatibility layer
resources.description: Translates reverse-engineered Driver 2 MIPS routines into C/C++ and uses Psy-X/Psy-Cross to adapt PlayStation interfaces for desktop systems. The project documents symbol-assisted Ghidra/IDA work alongside intentional bug fixes and gameplay changes.
requirements: Requires the user’s copies of both Driver 2 discs. The pinned installation wiki lists English PAL EU and NTSC US revisions 1.0/1.1; other languages remain planned.

Documented play paths cover Windows and Linux; installation converts disc video/audio using Java. Linux runtime instructions list SDL2 and OpenAL; original game content is not supplied by the project.
Source builds use submodules, Premake5 and a C++ toolchain. The Windows guide uses Visual Studio 2022; Linux builds link SDL2, OpenAL, OpenGL and libjpeg.

The README reports a playable reconstruction but explicitly excludes the memory-card menu from its decompilation claim. Original bugs and some gameplay are deliberately changed; [D], [T] and [A] annotations distinguish decompiled, tested and altered code.
MIT license for project code; original game data and third-party components retain their own rights.

resources.name: PhotoCraft: editor workflow reconstruction and PSD round-trip boundaries
resources.description: The authors describe this Rust image editor as a clean-room reimplementation of Photoshop-style workflows. Its document engine, UI and automation interfaces share editing commands, while the source distinguishes PSD editor round trips from byte preservation in the standalone file codec.
requirements: The pinned workspace identifies version 0.9.0 and declares Rust 1.95+ for source builds with Cargo. Native and WebAssembly paths have platform-specific dependencies; optional font inputs and reference documents are separate.
This is an implemented document/compositing engine and editing interface, not merely a screenshot mockup.

The editor-level corpus tests compare rendering before and after export/reimport. Separate PSD codec tests compare bytes for parseable files, with a named malformed-file exception. Editor saves are explicitly not byte-identical to their inputs.

The project remains alpha and distinguishes menu-command coverage from behavioral fidelity. Its dated parity assessment retains gaps in PSD exchange, typography, professional workflows, performance and plug-in compatibility.

Project code is MIT OR Apache-2.0, subject to NOTICE; fonts, artwork and other assets retain separate terms. ArtCraft branding is excluded; published modified versions must remove it, apart from contribution-only forks.

resources.name: WordCraft: document workflow reconstruction and bounded DOCX compatibility
resources.description: The authors describe WordCraft as a clean-room Rust implementation of familiar Microsoft Word workflows. It provides its own document model, layout engine and DOCX reader/writer, with desktop and browser interfaces; source tests exercise selected editing and file-preservation behavior.
requirements: The pinned workspace identifies version 0.7.0 and declares Rust 1.95+ with Cargo. The documented browser build uses Trunk; native builds and faithful layout require the relevant platform dependencies and fonts.
The outcome is a document-engine and interaction implementation. CLI/MCP and control-channel support are automation surfaces.

The reviewed DOCX tests use constructed documents and specification-based XML fixtures to check modeled properties and passthrough parts. The dated assessment against Word for Mac 16.113.4 explicitly says real-world side-by-side file/page comparisons were not performed in that assessment pass.

The project is alpha. File fidelity, page layout, advanced typography, stability and ecosystem compatibility remain limited; ribbon-command counts and author readiness estimates are not acceptance-test pass rates.
Code is MIT OR Apache-2.0 with NOTICE obligations; fonts and other assets retain separate rights, and ArtCraft branding has separate restricted terms. Clean-room is the authors’ characterization.

resources.name: GridCraft: spreadsheet workflow reconstruction and XLSX round-trip limits
resources.description: The authors describe GridCraft as a clean-room Rust implementation of Excel-style spreadsheet workflows. A workbook model, formula parser and dependency-driven recalculation are connected to XLSX I/O and a shared editing-command layer for desktop, browser and automation interfaces.
requirements: The pinned workspace identifies version 0.7.0 and declares Rust 1.90+ with Cargo. Browser builds use Trunk and wasm32-unknown-unknown; native Linux CI lists X11/Wayland, GTK, fontconfig/FreeType and graphics dependencies. Fonts and input workbooks are separate.
Reviewed XLSX tests construct workbooks and OOXML packages, compare modeled values after writing and reading, and check selected unmodeled parts and relationships.

Calculation tests use expected values for selected formulas, dependency changes and spilled arrays. The dated assessment against Excel for Mac 16.113.4 records the absence of Excel-computed conformance oracles.
The project remains alpha. File fidelity, advanced workflows, performance and ecosystem compatibility remain bounded, and the README documents graphics-driver startup issues.

Code is MIT OR Apache-2.0 with NOTICE obligations; optional fonts and ArtCraft branding have separate terms. Published modified versions must remove the ArtCraft marks, except contribution-only forks. Clean-room is the authors’ characterization.

resources.name: DeckCraft: presentation workflow reconstruction and bounded PPTX interchange
resources.description: The authors describe DeckCraft as a clean-room Rust implementation of PowerPoint-style presentation workflows. Its slide model, rendering and command layers support desktop/browser editing and PPTX interchange; reviewed source tests check constructed decks and selected preserved package parts.
requirements: The pinned workspace identifies version 0.7.0 and declares Rust 1.95+ with Cargo. Linux source builds need ALSA headers and display/window dependencies; the browser path uses Trunk and wasm32-unknown-unknown. Optional craft-fonts inputs affect rendering, with system-font fallback documented.

The reviewed PPTX corpus is authored in code, not collected from PowerPoint. Tests check retained text and content-part counts after saving, then part names and text after another save. Separate tests preserve selected XML metadata.

The dated assessment against PowerPoint for Mac 16.113.4 explicitly says rendering fidelity, performance against PowerPoint and end-to-end workflows with real users’ decks were not measured in that assessment. Feature breadth and readiness percentages are checklist counts or author estimates.
The project is alpha and has documented file-exchange, presentation-workflow, stability and ecosystem gaps. Source snapshots and older assessment rows differ.

Code is MIT OR Apache-2.0 with NOTICE obligations. Fonts/icons retain separate terms, and NOTICE lists the Symphonia audio decoder under MPL-2.0. ArtCraft marks have restricted terms and must be removed from published modified versions except contribution-only forks. Clean-room remains author-attributed.

resources.name: DevilutionX: porting Diablo’s reconstructed engine
resources.description: Builds a modern Diablo and Hellfire port on the Devilution reconstruction, with platform support, bug fixes and optional quality-of-life features. The project documents the original symbol-assisted reconstruction and includes selected dungeon-generation and saved-game regression checks.
requirements: Full Diablo play requires the user’s original DIABDAT.MPQ. Hellfire additionally needs hellfire.mpq, hfmonk.mpq, hfmusic.mpq and hfvoice.mpq. The separately offered spawn.mpq supports only the shareware portion; source availability does not supply rights to original game content.

The pinned source identifies 1.6.0-dev and requires CMake 3.22 and C++23. SDL2 is the default, with separate SDL1/SDL3 options; build documentation lists platform-dependent libraries and packaging steps.
The background describes Devilution’s use of PlayStation debug symbols, assertion strings, compiler information and assembly comparisons.

The reviewed timedemo test replays a warrior’s level-1-to-2 session and compares saved hero state; it skips without MPQ data and explicitly selects shareware mode. Separate dungeon tests compare seeded fixtures. These are bounded regression checks.

The root LICENSE.md declares Sustainable Use License 1.0: use/modification is limited to internal business purposes, non-commercial use or personal use, while distribution must be free and non-commercial. Components and original game data retain separate terms.
The same snapshot retains conflicting Public Domain wording in the Windows package README and Unlicense metadata in the Apple bundle configuration.

resources.name: ThinkPad IMX471: recovering camera tuning for Linux
resources.description: Recovers selected camera-tuning structures from an Intel Windows driver package and uses them to repair Linux image capture on one ThinkPad model. Public CPFF/AIQB parsers, kernel patches and libcamera changes accompany the author’s Claude-assisted investigation and bounded before/after measurements.
requirements: The reviewed target is a Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 (Aura Edition), with a Sony IMX471 sensor behind Intel IPU7. The author tested Fedora 44 kernel 7.2.8 and a libcamera 0.7.1 backport. The published kernel package omits BTF/debug information and is described as a test kernel, not a daily-driver recommendation.

The Python 3 analysis tools use NumPy and assume a 1928x1088 RG10 stream with a 3904-byte stride. Some scripts embed the author’s local layout and need path adaptation. Repeating the tuning analysis requires the corresponding vendor driver-package data or device captures.

The author’s controlled low-light comparison holds 400 frames for convergence and reports frame brightness rising from 31.1 to 90.9. The test record describes crop-selection, colour-bar and analogue-gain checks on the affected device. Its 46/46 v4l2-compliance passes occurred before and after the crop fix, so that pass count alone did not detect the defect.

The work adds three kernel fixes plus lens-shading and white-balance-statistics changes to an existing Linux driver and software ISP. Low-light blue remains about 17% short, an 18.8 ms exposure ceiling is not fixed here, and the second IR camera is outside scope. It does not recover the entire Windows driver, emulate the laptop or establish compatibility across camera models.

The dated investigation includes corrected and withdrawn hypotheses. The patch cover letter attributes Claude assistance and hardware checking to the author. The later blog reports submission/review activity.

No top-level project license is present at the pinned revision. Newly added libcamera implementation files in the patch declare LGPL-2.1-or-later, and the tuning-data section declares CC0-1.0; these are component notices, not a blanket license for every script or vendor-derived input. Existing kernel/libcamera code and vendor materials retain their separate terms.

resources.name: Ledger Reborn: an independent accounting app informed by QuickBooks study
resources.description: The maintainer reports using REA and Ghidra to study selected QuickBooks Desktop for Mac behavior, then independently implements a local accounting application. Its Python/SQLite engine persists double-entry journals, invoices, inventory and payments, while public synthetic fixtures test bounded accounting and rollback behavior.
requirements: The reviewed release is 2026.10.12-preview.1. The local browser edition needs Python 3.11+; the accounting core uses the standard library and SQLite. Native desktop builds use pywebview 6.2.1, PyInstaller 6.22.3 and Pillow 12.3.0, built on the target OS; Windows additionally needs the separately installed WebView2 runtime.

The maintainer identifies QuickBooks Desktop for Mac 2024 Trial, version 23.1.13.962 R14 Trial, as the investigation target. REA 6.4.0 with Ghidra, NIB decoding and selected runtime observations informed inventory arithmetic, budget signs, reconciliation paths and layouts. The Python/SQLite engine and frontend are independently written, not recovered Intuit source.

Public synthetic fixtures contain frozen, independently specified integer-cent expectations. Reviewed tests compare reports and check atomic rollback of invalid journals, bills and inventory operations. These are implementation checks.

The separate original-software comparison reportedly matched three official-sample reports account-by-account to the cent. The vendor sample company and exports are not public here, so that result remains author-reported.

The preview is single-user, local and USD-only. Payroll, tax filing, live bank/payment services, multicurrency and complete QuickBooks migration are outside the implementation. Its cash-basis output is a defined management cash view.

MIT covers the authored application; vendor inputs and bundled runtime dependencies keep separate terms. The preview is not Developer ID-signed or notarized on macOS and lacks Windows publisher signing. Package smoke tests and selected native-window observations have separate scopes.

resources.name: rauchg.com: rebuilding an RSC blog from captured Flight output
resources.description: Documents a website-rebuild-skill case that decodes browser-delivered React Server Component Flight streams, reconstructs a buildable Next project and compares its output with a captured site. The reported rauchg.com campaign uses route-tree comparison and module-reference mapping; the new server source is inferred from observable output.
requirements: The documented rauchg.com snapshot used Next 16.1.1, Turbopack and React 19 canary. The tooling requires Node.js 22+ and a local Chrome/Chromium for comparison; some stages invoke version-pinned external tools. Repeating the method needs an authorized target snapshot and a separately built reconstruction, not just the skill repository.

Flight decoding exposes delivered element trees, route state and client-module references. The reconstructed server-component source is explicitly an inference from that output; flight-to-mdx also needs site-specific shape/link adaptations.

The author reports 18/18 routes passing a Flight semantic gate and a runtime sweep for this case. The gate compares normalized trees and enforces a global module-ID bijection. It normalizes build-hash namespaces and selected encoding differences; configured prop/class exclusions can omit registered fields or subtrees.
The gate does not check CSS, so layout, fonts and rendered pixels need separate comparisons. Public synthetic self-tests include changed-text rejection and rejection of a one-to-many module mapping.

The method explicitly leaves unobserved error responses, database/write paths, server caches, dynamic-image generator source and unlinked routes unresolved. The author also notes possible model-training familiarity with a nominally blind target.

MIT applies to the skill and tooling, not to reconstructed websites, their scripts, fonts or other assets. The source documents separate authorization/publication decisions and private, noindex output defaults.

resources.name: NJFE: a Soulear camera protocol bridge for desktop inspection
resources.description: Reuses otoscope's reverse-engineered i4season/Soulear protocol in an ESP32-C3 bridge and Python desktop viewer. The author credits Claude Code for implementation and reports streaming one Hopefox Find T to a Windows PC, with recording, orientation and LED controls.
requirements: Input is the camera’s Wi-Fi i4season/Soulear UDP traffic. An ESP32-C3 SuperMini with a 0.42-inch, 72×40 SSD1306 OLED reassembles JPEG frames and sends them with accelerometer data over custom USB CDC serial to the viewer. It is not a UVC webcam, the camera’s USB port is charge-only, and no vendor firmware or full app source is recovered.

Builds with PlatformIO espressif32 6.11.0, Arduino core 2.0.17 and U8g2 ^2.35.30; the desktop tools need Python with Tkinter, pyserial >=3.5, opencv-python >=4.8, NumPy >=1.24 and Pillow >=12.3.0. Only Windows testing is reported.
Packet format, commands, frame assembly and rotation logic are credited to rbeilvert/otoscope, which reverse engineered Soulear’s libWifiCamera.so; NJFE does not pin the borrowed revision.
Results come from a single HKV41B-firmware Hopefox Find T (480×480 JPEG at about 17 fps). The --test N mode needs the hardware and there is no offline conformance suite.

The camera network is open: the bridge accepts unauthenticated UDP that can inject images or replies, serial access is trusted and recordings are unencrypted. It is an inspection tool, not a medical device.
GPL-3.0-or-later, with protocol code and roll calculation derived from GPL otoscope; third-party libraries keep their licenses, and no rights to vendor software or images are granted.

resources.name: BaoCut Slides: adapting an interactive web editor
resources.description: Documents BaoCut’s interactive slide editor, whose author says the implementation draws on Claude Slides. It adds a local deck store, HTML/CSS compiler and annotation-to-agent bridge for browser and desktop hosts; the design reports a Web-flow check, without establishing original backend recovery or full behavioral parity.
requirements: The pinned Slides component is an editor runtime, a restricted HTML/CSS slide compiler and a new BaoCut host; decks are a v4 deck.json index with per-slide HTML and local assets.

Needs Node.js >=22.12.0, npm workspace dependencies, the apps/slides-editor build and a BaoCut Runtime/host; the runtime declares React ^19.3.0 and patched PptxGenJS 3.12.0. Full BaoCut builds add Rust/Cargo, CMake and C++ tools, with full Xcode/Metal for Apple Silicon inference. Agent-made decks need Codex CLI, Claude Code or another configured engine under its own terms.

Single-user and file-backed, with per-file conflict checks but no whole-batch rollback. Shared rooms/presence, share links, persistent comment threads and sending to Google Drive/Slides are out of scope; PPTX/PDF downloads remain P1.
End-to-end validation covers only the Web annotation flow, not Electron; the published tests use fakes and no comparison with the original.

BaoCut Community License 1.0 is source-available: personal/internal use and content creation are allowed; commercializing the code or commercial hosting needs a separate license. PptxGenJS (MIT) and mediabunny (MPL-2.0) keep their terms; no reuse rights are shown for Claude material or the bundled icon font, slated for replacement.
Use independently authorized slide content.

resources.name: Pocket Tasks: reconstructing task state and persistence
resources.description: A teaching case with disclosed prior source access carries a REA-assisted investigation of a small command-line app into a separate Node implementation. It preserves observed task editing, persistence and selection behavior, then compares scoped outputs against fixed expectations and captured reference sessions.
requirements: Pocket Tasks 1.0.0 is an authored local command-line app, not a commercial app or native-binary benchmark. The Node.js 20+ candidate implements nine commands and schema-1 JSON storage with only the standard library and disposable local stores; there is no GUI or network backend.

The REA excerpt identifies the target bytes but keeps semantic coverage unknown, with 230 semantic unknowns; it is not a canonical Evidence bundle, and the later Node validator does not repeat the REA session.
The author saw the target source, scenarios, tests and prior answers before implementing.

Reported 16/16 checker sessions (12 scenarios) and 10/10 replays (seven scenarios) overlap; expectations are hand-authored, and the report keeps humanReview=pending, reaTrial=unverified and independentEvaluation=false.

Six recorded hashes and the oracle digest match the reviewed source, but the TASK.md packet hash matches an earlier wording-only revision, so the packet is historical evidence. A restricted-Windows attempt (five passes, four failures) preceded nine passes with unchanged code.

Limits: 64 commands and 65,536 UTF-8 bytes per invocation, 32 tasks and 80 UTF-16 code units per title. Concurrent writers, crash durability, filesystem races, UI, hidden backends and production performance are outside the parity claim. MIT covers the authored example only.

resources.name: Open Scrantic: reconstructing the Johnny Castaway screensaver engine
resources.description: Reconstructs the Johnny Castaway screensaver engine in Rust, with author-disclosed REA and Claude Code use. It reads original files to run recovered animation scripts and calendar-based story state on modern desktops; documented deviations and limited tests stop short of complete behavioral equivalence.
requirements: Reviewed at v0.3.0: this is a Windows 3.1 screensaver-engine reconstruction, not a game port. The author reports recovering formats and TTM/ADS script semantics from disassembly, with human-directed REA/Claude Code work and comparisons against the original.

Builds pin Rust 1.99.1; Cargo declares minimum Rust 1.99 and edition 2024. The project targets Windows, macOS and Linux using winit, softbuffer and rodio. Linux builds also require ALSA development headers and pkg-config.

Runtime requires separately obtained SCRANTIC.SCR, RESOURCE.MAP and RESOURCE.001 beside the executable. README sizes and SHA-256 values identify the expected original files; the loader instead checks known executable strings/layout, not whole-file hashes. Arbitrary original builds are unsupported. Options and story state use SCRANTIC.INI, saved on normal exit.

Deliberate differences include full-frame redraw, potentially one-pixel line/ellipse differences, bounded final-scene selection and a fixed two-second title display. Optional dedithering and softened audio default off. The original settings dialog and password feature are absent, as are unused animated-palette, 256-color and ADS-variable features.

The headless test runs 6,000 steps and requires three completed scenes, without original-frame comparison. Data-dependent tests silently return when OPEN_SCRANTIC_DATA is unset; other tests cover parsing and arithmetic. CI checks formatting, lint, three-platform builds and --version, not cargo test or original-data playback. Snapshot output supports inspection, not an automated original-output oracle.

MIT covers project source, not original executable content, art, scripts or sounds, which users must supply with appropriate authorization. The author describes independent, non-commercial interoperability without Sierra/Dynamix endorsement.

resources.name: Eleven
resources.description: An agent-first desktop reverse-engineering app that opens Mach-O, ELF and PE binaries, Android packages and GPU kernels, and lets any Agent Client Protocol agent read code, rename functions, add notes and propose patches in a shared window. Native code is decompiled by Ghidra through a bundled REA build, with Rizin and jadx as alternative engines. It is a workbench around existing engines, not a new decompiler or a reconstruction case.
requirements: Reviewed version 0.1.9 (release dated 2026-10-16) targets macOS 14+ on Apple Silicon, Windows x64 and Linux x64. The documented macOS and Windows installers pipe a remote script into the shell; macOS builds are not notarized, so the installer clears the download quarantine. Users supply the apps, binaries or APKs they analyze.

Native analysis uses Ghidra 12.x with Java 21 through REA, or Rizin for faster opening; first-run setup downloads missing engines or reuses local copies, and Ghidra is not bundled. Android packages need jadx, with apktool optional for smali. Building from source needs Bun, Node 20+, Ghidra, a JDK and a REA 6.x checkout; the release workflow builds REA from the Zfinix/rea fork’s feat/set-code-type branch rather than an upstream release.

Agents connect over the Agent Client Protocol, including the README’s Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor and Copilot options; model access, cost and data handling follow the chosen agent. Agents receive Eleven’s own MCP server and an eleven-rea proxy that passes REA tools through but redirects REA’s name, comment, bookmark and code-type writes into Eleven’s project. Per-tool Allow/Ask/Never permissions and privacy prompts are settings.

Byte patches are written to a copy, agent patches arrive as suggestions, and project changes are logged with their author and can be undone. CI at the reviewed commit runs typechecks on Ubuntu and macOS; the Ghidra-backed test suite is a separate local script.

Eleven is Apache-2.0; the bundled REA and Node.js keep their MIT and other licenses, and agent logos remain their owners’ trademarks. The tool grants no rights to analyze, patch or redistribute third-party software, and its outputs are agent-assisted analysis.

resources.name: Flutter build identification
resources.description: Identifies a Flutter APK’s Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance, then inspects one ABI’s AOT snapshot sections, through REA’s pure-parsing CLI and MCP tools. The string-pool output is a bounded byte-pattern projection of package and SDK URIs, not deserialized Dart classes or recovered source.
requirements: Reviewed on main as rea-agents 6.7.0, which declares Node ^22.19.0, ^24.11.0 or 26+. identify-flutter-build and inspect-dart-aot (MCP identify_flutter_build and inspect_dart_aot) parse a caller-supplied APK’s libapp.so and libflutter.so without an engine, external tool, execution or network lookup. Inputs are copied into an owned read-only snapshot, with documented bounds such as 2 GiB per APK and 256 MiB per library.

REA performs no hash-to-SDK lookup; mapping a snapshot hash to a Dart release needs an external dataset such as reFlutter’s. Complete structural coverage currently requires the FullAOT kind of the supported Dart 2.14 snapshot layout, and other kinds are kept with partial coverage. Typed class and function recovery needs an SDK-specific parser, and class-like tokens include incidental matches.

The documented verifier runs both tools through the compiled CLI and stdio MCP on the Flutter Gallery 2.9.2 release APK against a pinned expectations file: one agreeing snapshot hash on all three ABIs, engine labels and URI counts. A plain aapt2-built APK checks negative detection. The guide reports the Gallery workflow and 147 focused tests passing on macOS 14.8.9 x86-64 and Windows 11 x64 guests.

In merged PR #1582, an independent reviewer reports that hashes, ELF sections and package lists matched readelf/strings checks on three F-Droid apps, PocketDhamma, Flutter McSweepy and cone, on pre-merge heads, with a non-Flutter control not detected; the thread records fixes for gaps found. These checks cover build identity and structure. REA declares MIT; analysed APKs keep their own licenses.

resources.name: Static HarmonyOS package inventory
resources.description: Inventories HarmonyOS HAP, HSP and App Pack files through REA’s hardened ZIP reader and projects an execution-free application graph: component paths, IDs and hashes, Stage/FA packaging hints, runtime-family hints and path-based native-bridge hypotheses. Every claim rests on path presence; manifests, Ark bytecode, resources and signatures are not decoded or verified.
requirements: Reviewed on main as rea-agents 6.7.0, which declares Node ^22.19.0, ^24.11.0 or 26+. No HarmonyOS SDK, toolchain or engine is needed: inspect-artifact produces the inventory and project-harmony-application-graph (MCP project_harmony_application_graph) projects it, with CLI and MCP sharing one workflow. .hap, .hsp and ZIP-verified root .app inputs are recognized; .har shared libraries are deferred because the suffix also names HTTP Archive JSON.

Outputs are path-presence claims: Stage is inferred only from module.json and FA only from config.json, App Pack children are listed without recursive inventory, encrypted or unavailable entries make coverage partial, and N-API bridge entries are hypotheses. Manifest semantics, Ark bytecode contents and versions, resource resolution, signing verification and observed native boundaries stay listed as limitations, and inventories that cannot be authenticated fail closed.

The verification lane downloads a SHA-256-pinned harmony-next-pipeline 1.0.1 HAP from an MIT-licensed source repository into an ignored directory and checks inventory authenticity, projection determinism, Stage path hints, exact component sets, complete coverage and CLI/MCP parity. The fixture’s compiler/SDK versions and reproducible build are not established, and the lane does not complete the pinned-toolchain acceptance in roadmap issue #1431.

REA declares MIT. Analysed packages keep their own licenses, and the guide says the fixture’s bundled component licenses were not independently audited; the downloaded artifact is not redistributed. Merged PR #1447 introduced this increment.

resources.name: MIPS ELF analysis through Ghidra
resources.description: Documents REA’s Ghidra lane for MIPS ELF executables, relocatable objects and MIPS16 shared images, including a pinned 32-bit language for recordless legacy firmware executables that Ghidra would otherwise import as 64-bit. Admission is bounded by declared header and ABI-record facts, and verification compares source-owned fixtures with independent readelf output rather than executing or rehosting firmware.
requirements: Needs a caller-installed Ghidra and compatible JDK on a supported Linux or macOS host; Windows Ghidra P0 does not admit MIPS, and Hopper/IDA gain no MIPS support. The lane does not execute MIPS code or rehost firmware. The standard profile admits ELF32 executables and relocatable objects declaring o32 and MIPS32r2; MIPS16 shared images have a separate bounded profile. ELF64, n32/n64, microMIPS, machine variants, FP64, NAN2008 and PSP PRX are refused.

Merged PR #1898, for issue #1620, admits recordless legacy ELF32 executables with EF_MIPS_ARCH_32 or 32R2, an unspecified ABI field and an inspected absence of ABI-flags records. It pins MIPS:<LE|BE>:32:default and checks the language Ghidra reports after import. o32 is recorded as an analysis assumption, not a declared fact, and floating-point ABI semantics stay unverified.

Optional real-provider lanes need caller-supplied Clang with MIPS targets, LLD, GNU readelf or MIPS cross-binutils, and Ghidra. They build source-owned fixtures in both byte orders without executing them, comparing instruction bytes, symbols, languages and relocations with independent readelf facts. The guide states that pseudocode presence and decoding agreement do not establish runtime, delay-slot or complete floating-point semantics.

The issue author reports gating a local patch on four real MIPS32 LE firmware ELFs whose function entries matched separate 32-bit Ghidra exports, and 400 of 5,250 functions lost on one image under auto-selection; those files are not public. A PR reviewer tested header-edited OpenWrt kernels and BusyBox builds with Capstone cross-checks and found no unedited public recordless file.
