REA declares MIT. Ghidra, compilers, binutils and analysed firmware keep their own terms, and the firmware behind the author’s results is not supplied.

resources.name: PSP static ELF analysis through Ghidra
resources.description: Documents REA’s bounded Ghidra profile for static PSP ELF executables, which leaves Allegrex instructions, PSP loading and calling conventions to a caller-installed ghidra-allegrex extension while reusing REA’s CLI, MCP, Evidence and snapshot workflows. It admits one PSPSDK header and ABI declaration on Linux x64 and verifies selected static facts on a self-built fixture, not commercial games or PRX modules.
requirements: The initial profile runs on a Linux x64 host and admits little-endian ELF32 executables with the PSPSDK declaration e_flags 0x10a23001 and an inspected version-0 ABI-flags record matching the documented single-float Allegrex declarations. PRX, relocatable or shared images, PBP/ISO/CSO containers, emulation and live overlays are out of scope; missing or different declarations are refused, and file names do not identify a target.

Install a compatible ghidra-allegrex extension inside the selected Ghidra distribution; REA never downloads, installs, rebuilds or vendors it, and fingerprints its files before launch. The published compatibility pairing is Ghidra 12.1.3, extension v21.4, PSPDEV v20261001 and JDK 21. Missing prerequisites return PSP_EXTENSION_UNAVAILABLE without fallback.

Verification uses the real MIPS verifier’s PSP mode with caller-supplied PSPDEV tools. A maintained fixture built from tests/conformance/psp is analysed without execution and checked against PSP GNU tool observations: known functions, a direct call, an immediate, BITREV, a global word, snapshot reopening and an A-B-A target switch. Merged PR #1599 reports a passing real-Ghidra run on an earlier contribution head and says the final head was not freshly revalidated by that run.

These are selected static facts; the extension does not fully model VFPU prefix effects. No commercial game data is used or reconstructed, and issue #1330 remains open. REA declares MIT; ghidra-allegrex, Ghidra, PSPDEV and analysed executables keep their own terms.

resources.name: Touhou reconstructions: an agent-driven method across three games
resources.description: An essay published on REA’s site, with pinned evidence notes, describes one author’s agent-driven reconstructions of TH08, TH095 and TH04. It dates milestones from public commits and progress ledgers, separates exact-comparison and playable-build oracles, and documents a TH08 check that missed wrong floating-literal data. Project results remain author-reported, and REA is credited with supplying analysis evidence, not the reconstructions themselves.
requirements: The evidence notes, checked on 10 October 2026, treat three separate projects: a continuation of GensokyoClub’s TH08 1.00d reconstruction, a TH095 1.02a reconstruction started from zero confirmed functions, and a PC-98 TH04 reconstruction crediting ReC98. Milestone intervals use public commit timestamps and measure recorded spacing.

Pinned ledgers report 1,106 of 1,107 TH08 functions accepted, 696 exact TH095 functions out of 697 confirmed, and 661 exact TH04 functions out of 663 reviewed candidates, each under its own definitions; the notes warn against cross-game rates or whole-executable completion percentages. TH08 Linux and Web ports, a playable TH095 Windows i386 build and four TH04 DOS products are recorded milestones. TH04 play results rest on the maintainer’s manual observations, and its 64-bit port is in development.

In TH08, an instruction-byte comparison accepted source using 0.0 where the original executable used 128.0, because it did not check the referenced literal data. TH08 PRs #11 and #13 added literal-data checks and corrected twelve more stale references among 1,548 audited.

The essay and notes supply no game files, compilers or builds; each project’s repository documents its own original-game and toolchain requirements, and game rights stay with their owners. GensokyoClub’s TH08 history keeps its attribution and license.

REA is described as supplying analysis evidence to agents; the projects also used their own analysis bridges and tooling. The author presents the method and its industrial analogy as an account and argument.

resources.name: TicTacToe-AI: a bounded REA-fork reconstruction of one game method
resources.description: The author’s REA fork, posted as rea-engine and since renamed RE-Agent, decompiles the shipped .NET executable of the GPL-licensed TicTacToe-AI game, recompiles the recovered C# and resources, and repairs one decompiler error against the original IL. A differential probe runs original and rebuilt code on all 19,683 board assignments for one status method and compares six form renders. The report passes only that method; the whole game remains partial.
requirements: The reviewed develop commit (2026-10-15) reports Feature PASS for CheckGameStatus over its declared 3^9 board domain and PARTIAL for the whole game. AI move selection and RNG, menus, timing and sound are unverified, the executables are not byte-identical, and raw terminal captures differ by one carriage return. The posts’ “byte for byte” wording applies to structured board records and six render PNGs.

The input is the published TicTacToe-AI executable from tatlead’s GPL-3.0 repository, identified by SHA-256 in the report. The repository redistributes it with the GPL text and a source archive kept for license compliance; the statement that this source was not consulted during reconstruction is author-reported.

The fork needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24.11+; recovery uses ilspycmd plus a host Roslyn compiler and Mono references, with script defaults pointing at Homebrew paths on macOS. Verification needs a local X11 display and Mono/libgdiplus. The recorded run used macOS 15.3.1 on ARM64 with Xvfb, so both renders come from the same Mono runtime rather than native Windows.

Scripts recover a fresh replica, then a probe executes the original and rebuilt assemblies, compares return values and indicator bytes for every board, and captures Form.DrawToBitmap images after button sequences. The current result JSON records zero board-record mismatches and terminalBytesEqual false.

The fork is MIT with morluto’s REA copyright retained and lists optional engines such as Ghidra and Frida under their own licenses; the game and its reconstruction carry GPL-3.0 obligations. Fork-specific code is not part of upstream REA releases, and the repository was renamed after the posts, whose rea-engine link now redirects to RE-Agent.

resources.name: REA in Claude Code: an isolated static-analysis A/B trial
resources.description: A Japanese field report connects REA 6.4.0 to Claude Code in a separate project directory, denies 43 of its 170 tools and common shell launch forms, and compares REA-enabled and REA-disabled runs on two real tasks: an Electron terminal’s packaged files and a saved HAR capture. Both arms answered correctly, while the REA arm took up to 2.00× the time and 1.67× the API-equivalent cost. It is an analysis-evaluation and safety-configuration case, not a reconstruction.
requirements: The article by keigoly was published on Zenn on 2026-10-14 (JST). It pins REA 6.4.0 from the rea-agents package and runs it with a checksum-verified official Node.js 24.21.0 placed inside the project, because the host’s Homebrew Node 25.8.1 is outside REA’s supported range. All trials used non-interactive claude -p with Claude Opus 5.5 and permission prompts bypassed; the Claude Code version is not stated.

Isolation is configuration, not a sandbox: REA is enabled only through a project-local .mcp.json, a generated deny list blocks 43 tools selected from effect metadata, and Bash prefix rules block common package-runner launches. The author states that deny rules are a fence rather than isolation, that other invocation forms bypass the prefix rules, and that prompt injection through analysis output was not tested.

The tasks were MIT-licensed Orca terminal v1.4.224 (128 MB of distributed Electron files) and a 2.5 MB HAR from an unnamed venue website; answers were checked against Orca’s public source and the HAR data. The author excluded DRM or license circumvention, online multiplayer games, business or customer data and malware from scope.

Each condition ran once (n=1), the REA arm was told to prefer REA tools, parallel processes make timings approximate, and only static JavaScript/web work with one model was tested; an interrupted run was excluded and repeated. One REA analysis result exceeded the 10 MB MCP response limit. Scripts and JSONL logs are excerpted rather than published.

The author reports that REA helped with extraction, such as asar unpacking and HAR element extraction, while grep and small scripts carried code reading in both arms. Nothing was reconstructed: the HAR task identified an existing request path. Native binaries and APKs are deferred to a planned second step; Orca, the venue site, REA and the model service keep their own terms.

resources.name: NativeAOT metadata recovery with Ghidra
resources.description: Recovers .NET 8 NativeAOT metadata from x64 PE executables during REA’s Ghidra analysis: MethodTable relationships, virtual slots and frozen strings from RTR 9.1 data, through a built-in read-only parser or an optional headless adapter that annotates the Ghidra database. Generated names, inferred prototypes and recovered native pseudocode stay separate from the unknown original C# names, fields and source.
requirements: Reviewed on main as rea-agents 6.7.0, which declares Node ^22.19.0, ^24.11.0 or 26+. Bring your own Ghidra and JDK; the guide’s Windows check used Ghidra 12.1.4 and JDK 21. The built-in parser handles x64 PE32+ with .NET 8 RTR 9.1 metadata and needs a unique RTR header and exactly one DEHYDRATED_DATA row; other RTR versions and PE architectures are reported as unsupported or partial. Ordinary PE/CLI or ReadyToRun assemblies belong to REA’s managed-code tools instead.

The optional adapter is built from a clean pinned checkout of Washi1337/ghidra-nativeaot with existing git, javac and jar; REA records the JAR’s SHA-256, copies it and rechecks the digest before loading, and JARs run inside Ghidra, so supply a trusted build. It annotates within an ephemeral Program transaction and never changes the original executable. It is unavailable on Windows Ghidra P0, where database tools do not see rehydrated bytes and slot targets come from the parser report.

Outputs include MethodTable addresses, base types, interfaces, virtual slots and frozen strings, within documented local limits such as 128 MiB of captured PE bytes and 4 MiB of report JSON; rows beyond the report budget are omitted with partial coverage. Type identification uses upstream heuristics and prototypes remain inferences. Pseudocode is recovered native logic, not original C# source, and original class/member names and custom field layouts stay unknown.

Verification uses benign source-built .NET 8.0.22 fixtures with independent compiler/linker-symbol and directory-byte oracles, plus stripped and negative inputs; fixtures are never executed, and building them needs .NET SDK 8.0.416 and platform NativeAOT tools. The real MCP lane runs only on Linux x64 with the adapter. Windows-host behavior was checked manually once on Windows 11 x64 without the JAR against the fixture oracle and linker map; no CI lane repeats that check.

REA declares MIT. The parser’s hydration semantics are adapted from Washi1337/ghidra-nativeaot (MIT, with its notice shipped under licenses/) and cross-checked against .NET’s MethodTable.h. Analysed executables keep their own licenses. Merged PR #748 introduced the integration and issue #744 records the request and its closure.

resources.name: UltraSunnyMoon: a partial, REA-led Pokémon Ultra Sun reconstruction
resources.description: The author uses a pinned REA build with Ghidra to analyze a user-supplied Pokémon Ultra Sun base executable, rebuild it byte for byte from split objects, and swap in two small compiled C runtime routines. Both replacements are behavior-tested but nonmatching and every other byte stays original; one recorded input movie drives the original and hybrid builds to the same bedroom movement in the Azahar emulator. Retail compiler identity, exact matching, module loading and broader gameplay remain open.
requirements: README reports that the original and combined rebuilt games reproduce controllable bedroom gameplay, that both C replacements are behavior-tested but nonmatching, and that no completion percentage is claimed. STATUS.md (updated 2026-10-12) lists an unchanged main executable and one CRO module rebuilt byte for byte, the integrated __aeabi_vec_ctor_nocookie_nodtor helper and a 36-byte startup BSS clearer. The hybrid builds still contain mostly original code and assets and need a 3DS runtime; a native PC port is a later phase.

Requires the user’s own Ultra Sun base version 0 container (title 00040000001b5000, product code CTR-P-A2AA) kept locally; the v1.2 update stays a separate comparison input. TARGET.md records the author’s base container SHA-256 3bb3b4eb0d17f18875d8b847c871dc97a172beeda03ce99e59e62a78ed5c1a53 and notes that these hashes identify the supplied dumps, not every copy. Retail containers, extracted code, raw REA dossiers, game frames and emulator logs stay in ignored private directories.

SETUP.md uses Ubuntu WSL on Windows with Node.js 22, Python 3, GCC and readelf. Its bootstrap builds REA from source revision 7ae3c50a9d49c480035855de9fcc4484befacd92 (package version 6.4.0) and runs it with Ghidra 12.1.4 and Temurin JDK 21, with Capstone 5.0.7 as an independent decoder. Rebuilds use a pinned 3DS Decomp Pipeline revision, the C replacements were compiled with Ubuntu’s gcc-arm-none-eabi (GCC 10.3.1), and runtime checks use Azahar 2126.2 and its RPC interface.

The project reports independent byte checks of the unchanged rebuilds, isolated behavior tests and live RPC readbacks for the replaced routines, and 60 passing source-owned tests. Runtime evidence is a bounded startup, setup and bedroom comparison under one input movie; routine execution counts, battles, overworld coverage, full-movie completion and timing determinism remain unverified. The tests use source-owned fixtures, not retail bytes.

README directs agent-accessible analysis through REA and Ghidra and requires AI-assisted reconstructions to be reviewed against binary evidence; AGENTS.md and HANDOFF.md are written for continuing agent sessions, and RUNTIME.md records frame review by an independent reviewing agent. The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none; it describes itself as an independent fan project unaffiliated with Nintendo, Game Freak or The Pokémon Company.

resources.name: Reversed with AI
resources.description: A moderated website directory of AI-assisted reverse-engineering projects across games, firmware, file formats, APIs and protocols, apps and legacy software. Each entry links to its primary source and records the author-reported model, tools, time, cost and outcome, with four checks for public source, reproduction steps, real-hardware testing and third-party confirmation.
requirements: Reviewed as a live website on 2026-10-18, when the homepage reported 180 projects, 100 marked Works, 12 guides and 166 tools, and the sitemap listed 180 project pages. The site has no pinned revision or public source repository, so entries, counts and labels can change after this review.

Entries record target, model, tools, time, cost, outcome (Works, Partial or Research), a 1–5 human-effort scale and four reproducibility checks. The About page says figures are reported by authors, not measured by the site, and unknown fields are marked Not reported; a Works label is the author’s claim. A Reproducible badge needs Works plus public source and repro steps, with real-hardware or third-party confirmation for firmware and devices.

The policy lists interoperability, preservation, modding that does not bypass DRM or anti-cheat, legacy-software recovery, format, protocol and API documentation, the user’s own devices, CTFs and defensive malware analysis without live samples. It declines DRM, licence-check and anti-cheat bypasses, online cheats, leaked source, live malware samples and weaponised exploits. The site says it hosts no binaries or code and accepts takedown requests.

The maintainer, smyaseen (@whyamas on X), reviews every submission; sponsored placements are labelled, and the site says sponsors do not affect listings or order. Its guides include a third-party REA setup guide updated 2026-10-14, but the directory covers many tools beyond REA and is not an official REA resource. The reviewed pages show a copyright notice and no reuse license for directory content.

resources.name: REA plugin for Hermes Agent
resources.description: Nous Research’s Hermes Agent plugin package for REA. One catalog install registers REA’s MCP server, pinned to rea-agents 6.4.0 and launched through npx over stdio, with REA’s workflow skill adapted for Hermes and a separate crash-triage skill. About 170 REA tools stay behind Hermes’ on-demand tool search, and the adapted skill asks before tools that run programs, drive apps or change a connected Android device.
requirements: plugin.json declares 0.1.0 under MIT. Hermes’ catalog lists it as an official Nous Research plugin for Hermes 0.22.0+, installed with hermes plugins install rea and hermes plugins enable rea; it is not published by REA. Requires Node.js 22.19+, 24.11+ or 26+ with npx, not 23 or 25. A later rea-agents setup for Hermes replaces the pinned server entry.

Static JavaScript/ASAR, package, Go/Rust, PE, .NET and HAR analysis needs nothing else. Core-dump and ELF-layout tools need a Python with pwntools 4.15.0, pyelftools 0.33 and Unicorn 2.1.2 set in Hermes’ .env. Native decompilation needs Ghidra with a JDK, Hopper or IDA; Android needs JADX and Java; firmware and captures need Binwalk/Unblob, TShark, sigrok or WABT.

Only the adapted skill asks: Hermes itself does not prompt before REA tools that run PTY commands, drive apps, change Android devices or overwrite files; skip them in unattended runs. Analyze untrusted programs in a prepared environment.

In the README’s WinSCP 6.7 test the GUI import took 663 seconds under a 1000-second call budget, an author observation rather than a guarantee. Ghidra’s startup deadline is 900 seconds, while each call keeps Hermes’ 300-second MCP default.

Hermes v0.22.2 installs the package; the per-server call budget needs v0.23.0. The about-170-tool and 460 KB schema figures describe REA 6.4.0. REA’s MIT notice is included and the crash-triage workflow credits crashlens (MIT); external engines and targets keep their own terms.

resources.name: crashlens
resources.description: A crash-triage tool that turns Linux core dumps, runtime panics, exception traces and sanitizer reports into Markdown bug reports naming the crash type, the first frame in the user’s code and a stable signature. Its core-dump path calls the REA CLI to read the recorded crash and the binary layout, and can ask REA’s Ghidra provider for pseudocode of stripped functions; a Claude Code plugin bundles a skill and read-only MCP tools. It is a debugging integration around REA, not a reconstruction case, and its diagnostic accuracy remains author-reported.
requirements: Package 0.1.0 and plugin 0.2.0 are an early prototype. Panic, trace and ASan/LSan/UBSan text inputs need only Node.js 22.19+ or 24.11+. Core dumps need Linux x86-64, Python 3, rea-agents and a pwntools environment named by REA_PWNTOOLS_PYTHON; gdb, objdump and Ghidra 12.1.x with JDK 21 are optional. Windows minidumps and macOS crash reports remain roadmap items.

Supply the core dump and the exact binary that crashed; crashlens compares GNU build IDs and warns on a mismatch. rea-agents 6.4.0 or later is an optional peer dependency, and the author describes only a pinned 6.4.0 as compatible.

The plugin’s MCP server defines four read-only tools, analyze_failure, analyze_core_dump, decompile_function and analyze_crash_folder. Pseudocode is decompiler output, and crash types are heuristics with a stated confidence.

The analyzed program is not executed; gdb runs with script auto-loading and debuginfod disabled. The optional --ai flag sends the report, including code snippets and log lines, to the Anthropic API; the local web app binds 127.0.0.1 behind a session token. Core dumps can hold secrets, and reports include local paths and register values.
CI runs typechecks and unit tests on Node 22 and 24 plus an end-to-end NULL-dereference check with the latest rea-agents; the six-of-seven root-cause claim has no published transcripts.
MIT, using MIT-licensed REA through its public CLI; Ghidra, the Anthropic API and analyzed programs keep their own terms.

resources.name: Dinosaur runner: an REA-inspected speed rule rebuilt with Codex
resources.description: The author uses REA’s MCP browser tools to passively capture the JavaScript loaded by wayou’s open-source T-Rex Runner page, then has Codex rebuild its acceleration rule in one self-contained HTML5 Canvas game. The report identifies the captured script by SHA-256 and separates verified source facts from reconstruction choices; only the speed rule is claimed, not full gameplay equivalence.
requirements: The target is wayou’s open-source, Chromium-derived T-Rex Runner page, not chrome://dino/ or hidden proprietary code; the investigation read JavaScript the browser had already loaded. Only the acceleration rule is reconstructed: start at 6 and add 0.001 per eligible update while below 13, with no elapsed-time factor. Artwork, physics, obstacles and scoring are new or simplified, and the intro, ducking, audio and narrow-screen speed reduction are omitted.

README and the report record REA MCP list_browser_targets and inspect_web_page calls over a local Chrome DevTools Protocol endpoint, with no navigation, clicks or page evaluation; Codex handled analysis, implementation and tests. Evidence IDs and excerpts come from the author’s REA results, but the full evidence bundle is not published and the live upstream script may change.

Playing needs only a browser: dino-demo.html is self-contained, with no external assets, packages or build step, and a GitHub Pages copy is linked. The embedded tests run from the page’s Run speed tests button, the browser console or the documented Node.js harness with mocked DOM, Canvas and animation-frame interfaces.

The author reports 67 of 67 embedded tests passing (15 unit, 52 integration), ten rejected in-memory mutations and seven owner-reported manual browser checks on 2026-10-13 without browser or OS details. Floating-point results such as the extra step past 13 at update 7,001 were measured in the reconstruction, not sampled from the original. There is no CI or cross-browser coverage.

The project is MIT-licensed; short original-source excerpts keep the Chromium BSD-style header, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md reproduces the upstream BSD-3-Clause terms. This third-party repository is separate from REA’s own dinosaur-speed teaching case.

resources.name: Screen Studio: an author-reported REA study of auto-zoom rules
resources.description: The author reports using REA to map Screen Studio’s Electron package, reading six auto-zoom and cursor rules from its obfuscated code with Claude Code’s help, and having Claude Code write an independent recorder and renderer from those rules. The article describes the commands, evidence, a cursor-alignment check and the clone’s gaps; neither the clone nor the decoded code is published.
requirements: The 2026-10-13 article targets the macOS Screen Studio app’s app.asar with REA’s JavaScript application analyzer, run from the command line on the author’s Mac with a supported Node.js version and Xcode Command Line Tools; it names neither the REA nor the Screen Studio version. The author reports a 101-second run producing a 124 MB evidence file over 3,695 files, using an integrity policy that records, rather than stops on, 25 bundled native programs whose fingerprints no longer matched.

The relevant code was obfuscated. The author says REA’s source-recovery command was unavailable on macOS, so Claude Code wrote a separate script to make it readable; that step is the agent’s work, not REA output. The decoded code is deliberately unpublished.

From the six rules, Claude Code reportedly wrote about 1,300 lines from scratch: a Swift ScreenCaptureKit recorder that logs cursor positions separately, and a Remotion renderer. The author reports 60 fps capture without dropped frames and a 22-second clip rendered in about 50 seconds on an M4 Pro, and says a redrawn cursor overlaid on a recording of the system cursor matched in most frames, with one fast-motion frame off by a few pixels.

The author lists gaps: no graphical editor, three cursor types, simplified motion blur, no typing zoom or click sounds, and camera and microphone code that has not been tested with a real camera; the clone is far from replacing Screen Studio. Its source is unpublished.
The author says the clone uses no Screen Studio code or assets and advises reading a product’s user agreement first.

resources.name: Claude Code background lab: an REA-informed reimplementation of a desktop animation
resources.description: Reimplements the glyph-wind background of the Claude desktop app’s Claude Code New session view as an offline WebGL2 page with a 38-slider control panel. The author reports a static REA investigation of the desktop shell and its remote web bundle, followed by a newly written renderer that reuses recovered timing and layout values. It shares the original’s visual vocabulary and interaction model but is not a pixel-identical extraction.
requirements: The reviewed pin is the repository’s single public commit, dated 16 October 2026. PROVENANCE.md reports that the study targeted Claude desktop 2.37337.1, began with REA’s analyze_javascript_application, traced the shell’s remote page to the background module and stayed static: Claude was not launched or inspected at runtime. It records SHA-256 hashes of the retained ASAR and the decoded module and lists local REA evidence IDs whose archives are not published.

The public edition reuses recovered factual parameters, including 6.5 × 13 CSS-pixel cells, a nominal 9 px font, a 3 s entrance delay and fade-in, a 4 s wind reveal, a 500 ms focus fade-out and 42–64 px/s wind speeds. Its shaders, noise field, random generator, glyph sequences and single-pass instanced rendering are newly written. The author states that an earlier private prototype used extracted source and a bundled font.

Running it needs only a WebGL2 browser opening index.html, or a local static server where the browser restricts local files; there is no Canvas2D fallback, and system monospace fonts change glyph metrics. Development needs Python 3 and Node.js 18+, with no third-party runtime or build dependencies.

CI runs six Node tests of deterministic helpers, rebuilds the offline page, checks that it is current and runs a release check for offline output, syntax, local links and excluded extracted assets and local paths. VALIDATION.md reports manual Chrome-on-macOS checks of rendering and controls, but not a browser-verified settings import, runtime testing of Claude or a pixel comparison with the original. The reference recording’s remote build, seed, theme and font are unknown.

MIT covers the original code and documentation. The repository states that it distributes no recovered Anthropic source, shaders, fonts, ASAR files, screenshots of the original, recordings or account data, and that its license grants no rights in Anthropic’s software, fonts or trademarks. It is unofficial and unaffiliated with Anthropic; REA is credited as the investigation tool rather than bundled, and the author also credits AI-assisted development.

resources.name: DX-Ball: an REA-guided function-level reconstruction with Codex
resources.description: The author has Codex use REA’s Ghidra tools to inspect the English DX-Ball 1.07 executable and recover it as typed C/C++, then compiles each function with the original-era Visual C++ 4.0 and compares it byte for byte with the original after mapping relocations. The same source also builds a MinGW Windows game and a portable core library. Exact reconstruction is still in progress; REA’s separate sound-pan showcase covers just one function.
requirements: README marks exact reconstruction as in progress, to be followed by a playable Visual C++ 4.0 build and later platform ports. Generated PROGRESS.md counts 553 provisional function candidates, 475 with source, 395 byte-exact (85,106 exact code bytes) and 249 with scoped semantic acceptance, and says both Windows builds completed recorded original-board campaigns under Wine. A separate 50-board restored-CRT attempt on October 17 ended at its time limit without a full pass.

Supply the English v1.07 Windows archive identified in config/target.toml; the importer verifies the archive and DXBALL.EXE hashes and puts the executable and assets in the git-ignored original/ directory. README points to a third-party download site for that archive; the repository does not establish its distribution rights.

The documented host is Linux x86-64 with Git, Python 3.11+, Node.js 22.19.0, 32-bit Wine, Xvfb, CMake, Ninja and GCC or Clang, plus i686 MinGW for Windows cross-builds. Bootstrap scripts fetch a hash-pinned JDK, Ghidra and a Visual C++ 4.0 compiler from a third-party archive repository. The REA lock file pins rea-agents 6.5.0 with Ghidra 12.1.4, while docs/REA.md still names 6.4.0; the Codex goal workflow needs Codex 0.128.0 or newer.

An exact unit has zero differences across the whole function after COFF relocations are mapped to original functions, imports and data, with literal data also checked; match-units.toml records the inputs needed to replay each unit. Differential tests run original x86 routines under Unicorn emulation against the compiled maintained C, and public CI builds the portable source, validates recorded evidence and compiles the Windows adapter without game resources. All results are project-reported.

MIT covers repository code; the original game, credited to Michael P. Welch with 3D graphics by Seumas McNally, is supplied separately and keeps its own rights, as do the downloaded compiler and tools. REA use is documented through saved responses and a worked projectile-list example, but agent effectiveness is not independently measured.

resources.name: re2ds: a native Nintendo DS engine for Resident Evil 2
resources.description: Reimplements Resident Evil 2’s PS1 game rules in a native Nintendo DS engine, with converters that turn data from the user’s own disc into DS formats. A helper wraps the PS1 executable as an ELF for REA’s Ghidra lane, analysis notes name the PS1 functions and tables each part follows, and the Reddit post linking it credits REA and Claude Code. Leon’s disc 1 is reported playable, while Claire’s disc, most enemy types and some menus remain unfinished.
requirements: The reviewed commit targets the PAL PS1 release (SLES-00972), disc 1 with Leon. README reports all 125 disc 1 rooms, a script interpreter covering every opcode used on that disc, zombies, the lower-screen status menu, sound, voices, the opening movies and typewriter saves; it lists the map and files, other enemy types, the remaining movies and Claire’s disc as missing. It is a native engine, not an emulator, a matching decompilation or a complete port.

Requires the user’s own Resident Evil 2 PAL disc 1 as a .bin/.cue dump, of which only Track 1 is used; local conversion produces about 290 MB of DS data. The repository states that it contains no game data and that the generated build/, nitrofiles/ and re2ds.nds outputs contain Capcom data that must never be committed or shared.

Building uses devkitARM and libnds (devkitPro nds-dev), Python 3, FFmpeg with its development libraries, a C compiler and pkg-config. Windows builds run in WSL Ubuntu, and make falls back to devkitPro’s Docker image when no local devkitARM is found. The README plays the ROM in melonDS, needs DLDI SD-card setup for saves and shows a photo captioned as running on a Nintendo DSi XL.

Host tests compile the platform-independent script, enemy and cutscene code for a PC and run it against the user’s converted data; the script test reports unknown opcodes, and scd_disasm.py --check validates jump targets across rooms. Analysis notes cite PS1 addresses and mark observed versus assumed behavior. psxexe_to_elf.py wraps the executable and symbol lists as a MIPS ELF accepted by REA’s Ghidra lane; Claude Code use is stated only in the Reddit post.

No license file is present at the reviewed commit. The README credits the MIT-licensed OpenBiohazard2 reimplementation’s file-format work and script opcode table as the starting point for several converters. Capcom’s game data, movies and audio stay outside the repository and retain their own rights.

resources.name: REA Workspace Template
resources.description: A clone-first Chinese workspace template for analyzing one target per workspace with REA from Claude Code or Codex. It ships project-level REA MCP settings, agent rules that require CONFIRMED/GUESS labels with evidence locations, seven task prompts and standard-library scripts that hash imported originals, stage writable copies and strip values from HAR captures. It organizes analysis rather than performing it, and its acceptance run used only synthetic samples.
requirements: The reviewed pin is the repository’s only commit, dated 2026-10-17. It needs Git, Python 3.11+, Node.js with npm, and Claude Code or Codex; README installs rea-agents 6.4.0, the version it was validated with, and the bundled .mcp.json and .codex/config.toml both start a locally installed rea --mcp. The template supplies no REA program, decompiler or model configuration, and it adapts workflow ideas from a third-party post.

Engines are separate: APK DEX work needs JADX and a full JDK, native targets need a Ghidra, Hopper or IDA provider configured through REA’s installation guide, and commercial engines need their own licenses; source, JS/Electron and saved-HAR workflows need no native decompiler. The prompts cover source mapping, API reconstruction from a sanitized HAR to OpenAPI 3.1 and a TypeScript client, JavaScript, native binaries (at most 30 functions per round), APKs, unknown file formats and session handoff.

scripts/workspace.py copies one target into a Git-ignored target/ directory without running it, records SHA-256 baselines, sets files to 0444, rejects symlinks and special files, and creates a writable work/ copy; verify reports changed, added or missing files. sanitize_har.py rebuilds a structural HAR copy, removing header values, cookies, URL credentials and query strings and replacing JSON values with placeholders. README warns that hosts, paths and field names can still identify users and need manual review.

docs/VALIDATION.md (2026-10-17) reports 12 passing standard-library tests, a healthy rea mcp doctor run listing 170 tools, and REA static analysis of a synthetic JavaScript app and a synthetic HAR with Node 24.18.0 and Python 3.12.7. It lists client MCP connection after restart, real APK and native targets, real-HAR anonymization and runtime work as unverified, and its smoke-test outputs are not committed.

README states that the Claude Code permission rules, read-only file modes and SHA-256 baselines are not an isolation boundary, and recommends read-only mounts and controlled networking where strong isolation is needed. AGENTS.md defaults to static analysis and reserves running samples, connecting devices and contacting target services for authorized tasks. The repository has no license file, so reuse terms are unstated; REA, analysis engines, clients and targets keep their own terms.

resources.name: REA Reconstruction Companion
resources.description: A third-party Agent Skill that works alongside REA’s own skill to turn reverse-engineering evidence into scoped requirements, design, staged implementation and validation, from one feature or format to a whole app. An optional installer can add a marked routing block to the user’s REA SKILL.md so that relevant reconstruction requests load both skills. Its bundled evaluation kit consists of source-exposed, maintainer-authored examples with literal oracles, not a model benchmark.
requirements: The reviewed pin is package version 1.3.27; the repository was created on 2026-10-15, and a v1.3.27 release followed on 2026-10-18. The core is plain-Markdown Agent Skills instructions with reference guides. It supplies no analysis engine and expects REA tools or supplied REA evidence for actual investigation. README documents Codex and Claude Code installation; other agents can use an explicit skills directory.

The installer and the optional weekly update helper need Node.js 20+ and only its standard library; release building needs Python 3.10+. With --integration on, the installer edits the selected REA SKILL.md between marked comments and keeps backups, while off leaves REA untouched. README warns that REA 6.5.0’s doctor reports the edited skill as stale, and that rea setup or rea update can remove the block.

The instructions forbid actions that could add charges, treat recovered target material as untrusted evidence, and require observations, inferences, unknowns and design choices to stay separate. These are instructions to the host agent, not enforcement: README says they do not override client policies, grant tool permissions or guarantee model compliance.

CI runs the installer, package-integrity and evaluation-harness tests on Windows, macOS and Linux with Node 20, 22 and 24, then builds and verifies a release archive. The evaluation kit supplies fixtures such as Pocket Tasks, a 5,120-byte .NET Parcel.exe built from included source, a browser app and file formats, with literal oracles and human-review rubrics. Its examples are disclosed as source-exposed and same-agent; no live model trial, independent evaluation or cross-host certification is recorded.

Original code, instructions, tests and documentation are MIT, and a small Wycheproof test-data subset is Apache-2.0. No REA code is bundled; REA, target applications and model hosts keep their own terms.

resources.name: Show Your Work: a measured dissection of REA's evidence architecture
resources.description: An unofficial field study that reads REA's source and then drives the running server through 1,012 recorded calls across 27 artifact classes, measuring its content-addressed Evidence records, revision-chained unknown ledger, typed refusals, cold starts and response limits. The author maps those mechanisms onto vulnerability-research agents as an argument for not overclaiming. It evaluates REA's tool surface; it is not a reconstruction or a vulnerability finding.
requirements: Published 2026-10-18 on the author's HackThe4O4 blog under the byline Noflag, who calls it unofficial, not peer-reviewed and unaffiliated with REA's maintainers, and says the official source wins where they disagree. The main study used the published rea-agents 6.5.0 package for 993 of the 1,012 calls; 19 calls comparing two deep providers ran a build of commit fe2a398dd, 286 commits later.

All runs used one Debian-derived Linux VM (4 vCPU, 7.9 GB RAM) with operator-supplied engines, including a headless Ghidra 12.x decompiler, GDB, Rizin, a packet dissector, firmware tools, headless Chromium and Electron; the Android device was a container sharing the host kernel. The decompiler startup deadline was raised to 1,200 s, and macOS-only tools, a GUI-attached disassembler's cursor tools and an unlicensed commercial Java decompiler could not be exercised.

The author reports calling all 207 advertised tools, 178 with at least one success, and 454 Evidence-bearing replies. Oversized replies were refused with a retained-Evidence pointer, but a 10.1 MiB request dropped the connection without a reply. Decompiler cold starts ranged from 14 s to 827 s, and two schema switches cut the default 3.09 MB tool catalog to 215 KB.

Timings come from one lightly loaded VM and are offered as orders of magnitude. The calls came from the author's scripted campaign driver acting as an informed caller, and the article names no analyzed targets. The security-agent mapping is presented as argument, not a built system. Per-call records, campaign files and scripts are described as accompanying the research but are not linked from the page.

This evaluates REA's evidence model and tool surface; no reconstruction, exploit or vulnerability is reported. The page states no license; REA, the third-party engines and the analyzed artifacts keep their own terms.

resources.name: Notes CSV export: an author-reported REA check of reconstruction oracles
resources.description: A Chinese article breaks three versions of a Python CSV exporter that reproduces the Notes teaching app shipped with REA. It shows that a simple export-and-read-back test passes all three, while byte comparisons against the official JavaScript formatter on 215 fixed inputs catch each one. The author also connects REA 6.5.0 over MCP, reruns its JavaScript analysis and checks that an edited evidence record is rejected on import; this is a study of acceptance checks, not a new reconstruction.
requirements: The 2026-10-16 article by @superfang119 follows the author’s earlier walkthrough, in which a Python reimplementation of the Notes app’s CSV export reportedly matched the original byte for byte on 215 inputs. It used Windows, Node 22.19.0 and rea-agents 6.5.0 through a temporary stdio client that listed 207 tools; the JavaScript analysis returned 6 files, 32 nodes and 45 edges. The author notes that this static graph locates the export path.

The frozen byte contract quotes every title, doubles inner quotes and ends lines and the file with LF, for safe-integer ids and string titles. Each mutant changes one rule: quoting only when needed, leaving inner quotes unescaped, or dropping the final LF. A one-note read-back test passed all three. Against references from running the official JavaScript formatter on 15 fixed edge cases and 200 seeded inputs, the baseline matched 215/215 and the mutants differed on 26, 166 and 215 inputs.

Changing one evidence field from 6 to 999 while keeping its evidence_id made the same REA server reject the import with evidence_integrity_mismatch and leave session evidence unchanged; the author adds that this detects tampering but cannot show an interpretation is correct. The article also cites, without rerunning it, a TH08 project fix in which a comparator missed a 128.0 constant written as 0.0.

Analysis and implementation ran in the same Codex context, so the author states this is not clean-room separation, and the handoff prompts offered are proposals rather than a tested protocol. Scripts, mutants and outputs are not published; the three probes do not cover permissions, write failures, concurrency or the full interface. The target is REA’s own teaching sample, not a third-party product.

resources.name: Windows loader: static malware analysis with REA and Codex
resources.description: Fedele Mantuano reports using Codex with REA in an offline Docker lab to statically analyze a public Windows malware sample without executing it. The article separates behavior supported by the extracted JavaScript bundle from claims that would depend on remote components that were never obtained, and reclassifies a suspected infostealer as a loader. It is a defensive analysis case built on an author-reviewed agent report, not a reconstruction or a dynamic detonation.
requirements: The Code Geeks article by Fedele Mantuano is dated 2026-10-18, with an Italian version, and reports an analysis performed on 2026-10-17. Codex was asked to use REA on one Windows x64 executable obtained from MalwareBazaar and to write a Markdown report on files, processes, persistence, network destinations, updates, defensive indicators and limits. The agent’s technical report, artifacts and code references are not published; the author offers further details privately.

Analysis ran in a Linux/amd64 Docker Desktop container with REA 6.5.0 and Node 24.22.0, no network, a read-only root filesystem and sample mount, an unprivileged user and dropped capabilities. Neither the sample nor extracted code was executed, and Wine was not used; the author notes that Codex still communicated with its model service while the container was offline. The appendix separately documents a macOS Apple Silicon setup of REA 6.5.0, Ghidra 12.1.4, Temurin JDK 25.0.4.1 and Node.js 24.21.0 connected to Codex over MCP with the REA skill; it was not repeated on a clean Mac or tested on other hosts.

After initial PE inspection, work focused on a JavaScript bundle extracted from the executable’s embedded Bun runtime; the roughly 98 MB native executable was not fully decompiled. The author reports analyst-written decoders for the bundle’s layered string obfuscation, run without evaluating the sample’s code, and spot checks of hashes, the extraction range and decoded tables, partly against an independent Python implementation. These checks support specific findings.

The author reclassifies the suspected infostealer as a loader: its code supports host and screenshot collection, encrypted reporting, download and in-memory loading of further components, and server changes through fixed fallbacks and a remote lookup, with no DGA found in the bundle. Those further components were not obtained, so mining, credential theft, persistence and execution on a victim system remain unestablished, and one reported initialization inconsistency is left for dynamic verification. The article’s threat-intelligence pipeline is a proposed use, not an implemented or measured one.

Handling live malware needs an isolated lab and the analyst’s own authorization. The article credits REA, Ghidra and Codex together and relies on an agent-written report reviewed by the author. The pinned blog repository has no license file; REA, Ghidra, Codex and the model service keep their own terms.

resources.name: Horizon: a Rust rewrite of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 with REA bytecode queries
resources.description: Rewrites Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 as a native Rust client, dedicated server and launcher that prepare their resources from the user’s own copy of the game. Contributors are told to read the vanilla code first, and tools/rea_vanilla.py runs a pinned REA release with a headless JADX engine over the shipped client and server jars to inspect classes, methods and callers. Differential harnesses run Java oracles against the real game and Rust probes against Horizon; README reports all 281 passing, which covers only what they compare.
requirements: The repository was created on 2026-10-03, and the reviewed main snapshot (2026-10-19) follows the date-tagged release v2026.10.19.12. README reports a playable client on Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows with vanilla world generation, mobs and their AI, villagers, raids, redstone, every command, Anvil saves and joining vanilla servers, and its own audit of 2026-10-13 scores every subsystem complete. Listed known issues include unsupported online-mode servers, skin and pack-icon gaps, unwired creative hotbar keys and missing attribute lines in tooltips.

Needs Minecraft: Java Edition installed with the official launcher and 26.3 played once, plus the 26.3 server jar for the first preparation; research-lock.json pins the client and server jar SHA-1 checksums. horizon-prepare (Python 3.10+ and JDK 25) builds resources from that copy into the gitignored .local/ directory. README says Horizon never downloads game files and never publishes decompiled source or prepared resources, and tools/check_public_tree.py rejects them in commits.

Players install through the Horizon launcher for Linux x86-64, macOS Apple Silicon or Windows x64, which also starts a dedicated server that needs no Java; rendering needs Vulkan on Linux and Windows. Source builds need Rust 1.90+, Python 3.10+, JDK 25 and, on Linux, the ALSA and udev headers; development and the vanilla harnesses run on Linux. tools/rea_vanilla.py needs Node.js 22.19+ and Java 17+, runs rea-agents 6.4.0 through npx unless that version is installed, and downloads jadx-headless-mcp 0.7.1 checked by SHA-256.

Each tools/test_*_parity.py harness drives the same inputs through a Java oracle under mods/horizon running the vanilla code and through a Rust probe, then compares the outputs; README says 100% means 100% of what the harnesses compare, not proof that nothing else differs. CI runs the Python and cargo tests on GitHub-hosted Linux runners and the vanilla harnesses on a self-hosted runner holding the maintainer’s copy of the game.

LICENSE applies MIT to the project’s original work; dependencies, including the wgpu-hal copy under third_party/, keep their own licences, and README says Minecraft code and assets belong to Mojang and Microsoft under the Minecraft EULA and that the project is not affiliated with them. docs/parity-workflow.md describes agents working in parallel worktrees behind a shared gate, and horizon-ctl exposes the game to AI agents as a CLI and MCP server. REA’s documented role is limited to the bytecode queries in CONTRIBUTING.md and tools/rea_vanilla.py.

resources.name: Untangle: a browser rebuild from REA and Ghidra evidence
resources.description: An author-documented REA/Ghidra investigation of the shipped Untangle Windows binary produces a single-page playable rebuild and a claim-by-claim grading receipt. The report separates frozen findings, a later source-code answer key and a prior-knowledge audit.
requirements: The recorded run uses REA 6.3.0, Ghidra 12.1.4 and Windows 11 against puzzles version 20260923.616da16; the rebuild is available as a browser page.
The reported 52/54 correct claims and L3 seed fidelity are the author's grading results; ten names absent from REA output indicate possible prior-knowledge contamination.
The 72 MB evidence export is omitted; its hash is retained. The README documents a pre-publication history rewrite and maps old commit hashes to new ones.
Original puzzle binary and source retain Simon Tatham and contributors' MIT license.

resources.name: Sofa TV Browser: a remote-friendly BrowseHere alternative
resources.description: An Android TV browser follows BrowseHere's remote-control interaction design with its own implementation. The author reports using REA to inspect the BrowseHere APK and Claude to build Sofa; the repository documents APK releases, screenshots and current feature limits.
requirements: Android 7.0+ with Android System WebView; APKs are linked from GitHub releases. Source builds need the documented JDK/Android SDK or Nix environment.
The author's REA attribution is in the linked Reddit report, rather than a published REA evidence bundle; this is an author-reported mixed workflow.
Tabs, reader mode, phone typing, translations and user scripts are listed as missing or planned. DRM playback and frame-rate switching depend on the TV and WebView.
GPL-3.0-only; the README states that BrowseHere code, assets and text are not included. Third-party components retain their own notices.

resources.name: OpenBSD netcat: static REA and Ghidra investigation
resources.description: A REA/Ghidra report studies the Ubuntu netcat-openbsd 1.234-1 ELF binary and publishes evidence envelopes, decompiled functions and a function inventory. Its output is a static investigation, rather than a rebuilt netcat application.
requirements: Reproducing the documented analysis needs the target package binary, REA, Ghidra 12.1.x and JDK 21; the README records additional pwntools tooling.
The author explicitly reports no target execution or dynamic analysis. Function roles remain inferred, and compiler inlining or hot/cold splitting obscures boundaries.
Upstream netcat.c was consulted for function naming; recovered pseudocode is not an independently reconstructed or behaviorally validated program.
Analysis and documentation use MIT; upstream BSD attribution is retained in NOTICE.

resources.name: FastView-REA: a Rust reconstruction of Fast View 5
resources.description: A Rust desktop reconstruction of Mekhanotronika Fast View 5 uses REA and Ghidra research to reproduce oscillogram analysis and relay-characteristic views. The project publishes behavioral specifications, factual indexes, screenshots and cross-platform builds, with explicit format and visual-fidelity gaps.
requirements: Source builds need the documented Rust toolchain; release archives target Linux, Windows and macOS. Linux needs GTK 3 and a Wayland or X11 session.
The README attributes the reverse engineering to REA and Ghidra 12.1.3. Its behavioral-identity and validation statements are author-reported.
Native .sto input lacks a supplied sample, and the egui interface is not pixel-identical to original GDI/MFC rendering; original bitmaps are replaced.
Reconstruction code offers MIT or Apache-2.0. Embedded fonts and Intel-derived trigonometry keep separate licenses; the bundled FastView.fvb characteristic data remains original-vendor data.

resources.name: OpenBattlefield2: an unfinished Refractor 2 engine reimplementation
resources.description: A C++20 reimplementation of Battlefield 2’s Refractor 2 engine reads original game data and documents menu rendering, level loading and server interoperability. Published crosshair research cites REA/Ghidra evidence IDs and binary addresses; major gameplay systems remain unfinished.
requirements: Requires an owned Battlefield 2 1.5 installation, CMake 3.24+, Ninja, a C++20 compiler and SDL3; the Flash menu additionally needs Rust and Ruffle.
Published crosshair research cites REA Evidence IDs; CLAUDE.md describes the mixed REA/Ghidra workflow and its payload and temporary-project limitations.
macOS arm64 is the primary platform; the Windows preset is kept building but is not exercised. Tests needing game files can pass with a note when those files are absent.
Ammunition/reloading, recoil, projectiles, audio, driving and full commander/squad interaction remain unfinished; this is an engine research project, not a complete game port.
MIT covers the project code; no original Battlefield 2 game content is redistributed.

resources.name: keen-clone: a Commander Keen 1 C/SDL2 port
resources.description: A native Linux and browser port of Commander Keen Episode One is documented as a function-by-function REA/Ghidra reconstruction of KEEN1.EXE. Published analysis artifacts accompany the C/SDL2 game; the scope is the first episode, rather than the entire series.
requirements: Native builds need a C compiler, make and SDL2 development files, plus the user's Keen 1 data files including KEEN1.EXE; the README lists v1.1 and shareware v1.31.

Browser builds require Emscripten and supplied game data; the documented web packaging is restricted to the shareware episode. Browser shortcuts and per-origin IndexedDB storage differ from the native host.
The repository lists decompilation/disassembly, a call graph and raw REA output as analysis artifacts. It does not provide an independent behavioral-parity or full-playthrough evaluation.
No project license file was present in the reviewed root. Commander Keen and its original data retain their owners' rights; public source access supplies no additional reuse grant.

resources.name: samp-client-re: a partial SA-MP client reconstruction
resources.description: A documented REA/Ghidra investigation maps SA-MP 0.3.DL-R1 client subsystems to a new C++ DLL, loader and smoke-test executable. The result is an architectural reconstruction with explicitly unresolved network and graphics behavior, not an established retail-compatible client.
requirements: The README reports a Windows/MinGW x64 build and a GTA-independent smoke executable; actual GTA: San Andreas use requires a separate 32-bit toolchain/build.
The architecture table attributes addresses and recovered procedures to REA/Ghidra 12.1.4; names inferred from the stripped binary remain analyst interpretations.
Full RCON/RPC handling, the default-port wire format and the exact Present trampoline are marked unknown/TODO. The archive parser is described as behavior-equivalent, not a complete decryptor.
No project license file was present in the reviewed root. Original GTA and SA-MP components remain separate prerequisites with their own rights.

resources.name: Desktop Games Nostalgia: a macOS and browser port
resources.description: A Swift/macOS and JavaScript/browser port recreates the Desktop Games screen-smashing toy from a captured image. The author documents Claude and REA/Ghidra work on the Peter interpreter, a decompiled program tree and extracted assets, with explicit visual differences and no project license.
requirements: Native use requires macOS 14+; Screen Recording access captures one screen image, while wallpaper mode is available without it. The browser version uses a simulated desktop and needs a mouse/keyboard.
The README attributes interpreter analysis to REA/Ghidra and the port to Claude Code; extracted images/sounds are included upstream. The effects alter an image, not the real desktop files.
True-color rendering and translucent sprite shadows differ from the original palette renderer. The browser cannot capture the actual desktop; no independent parity measurements are supplied.
The author explicitly provides no project license and retains Gemtree credit for original design/art/sound. Desktop decoration and other upstream assets retain their separate rights.

resources.name: GunZRs: a Rust reimplementation of GunZ: The Duel
resources.description: A Rust/Bevy port reads GunZ: The Duel files from the user's installation and provides native releases, browser build tooling, screenshots and a documented REA/Ghidra investigation framework. Its LAN protocol and inferred movement behavior remain distinct from retail-server compatibility and proven gameplay parity.
requirements: Requires the user's GunZ: The Duel installation; no original game files are included. Native downloads target Linux/Windows, with Linux builds requiring the documented system libraries; WebGPU needs localhost or HTTPS and packs built from the user's data.
The README documents REA/Ghidra use for static questions about retail files.
LAN uses the port's own protocol and does not connect to retail servers; several round/quest/Blitzkrieg modes are not played over LAN. Movement constants and some content choices are inferred.
The project says gameplay has been exercised on Linux. Code is Apache-2.0, bundled fonts retain OFL terms, and original game files remain separately owned.

resources.name: MXQ PRO RK3229: an Android firmware investigation and Linux repurposing
resources.description: An owner documents identifying an RK3229 TV box, investigating its stock Android ROM and repurposing it with a userspace gamepad driver and Armbian. REA assisted ADB inventory and Android-provider routing; APK analysis and device changes are reported as a mixed workflow, not firmware reconstruction.
requirements: Requires an owned, correctly identified RK3228/RK3229-class board and its matching firmware/backups; the MXQ PRO sales label alone does not identify the hardware.
The author limits REA's role to device inventory and the Android provider pointer; JADX and separate host/device tools perform other parts of the work.
The report covers one unit and describes replacing its stock system. Partition layout, board support and boot behavior are device-specific.
Large/proprietary images, system APKs and decompiled third-party source are excluded upstream. A project-wide license grant is not stated in the reviewed README.

resources.name: iCSee LocalMod: a stock-firmware camera control extension
resources.description: An owner-authorized XM530V200 camera case uses REA/Ghidra to investigate native Sofia command handlers, then adds local control and Home Assistant integration while preserving stock drivers and recording. The source-only extension documents separate static, emulated-protocol and physical-device evidence.
requirements: Tested only on one XM530V200 / IPG-X2-WQ-BL unit. There is no universal image or public flash installer; source builds need a compatible ARM toolchain and matching Dropbear crypto library.

The documented investigation used REA 6.8.0 and Ghidra 12.1.4. Binary addresses are specific to the analyzed Sofia build; the project is stock firmware with additions, not OpenIPC or a full DVRIP implementation.
The owner reports physical PTZ/LED/audio and restart/SD-recording checks. QEMU tests use fake backends.

The local bridge uses the existing device account over plain HTTP; the route-removal guard is not a firewall. Original additions are MIT, while stock firmware/drivers and third-party components retain their own rights.

resources.name: App X-Ray
resources.description: Builds evidence-linked HTML/JSON reports, summary cards and diffs from REA analysis of app packages, native build metadata and model files. Its component and configuration findings come from static inputs; they are not observed runtime traffic, a complete security audit or reconstructed software.
requirements: README requires Node.js 22+; supported inputs include Electron/app.asar/source folders, APKs, Go/Rust executables and listed model formats. REA analysis requirements vary with the input.

Rules see literal values and metadata; runtime-generated addresses are missed. A detected setting or dependency does not prove runtime behavior or exploitability, and unsupported/obfuscated inputs can leave unknowns.
The public gallery uses open-source app snapshots. Report-derived REA-Bench answers reuse those reports as their reference.
Code is MIT; bundled Inter fonts retain SIL OFL 1.1. Reports omit target app code, and upstream software/model rights remain separate.

resources.name: DiskLens: a WinDirStat-derived disk usage analyzer
resources.description: A Rust/Tauri disk analyzer combines REA/Ghidra investigation of WinDirStat 2.5.0 with source-code ports of its treemap and color handling. Its documentation distinguishes binary-confirmed findings from source-derived algorithms and leaves several file actions and Windows integrations untested.
requirements: Requires Windows 10/11, Rust MSVC/Visual Studio build tools and Node.js for source builds; Mica styling needs Windows 11.
REA/Ghidra cross-checked the installed WinDirStat binary, while much algorithm work used its public source.

The author reports engine tests and drive scans, but new file-action routes, cleanup integrations and several dialogs are untested in the app. Fast MFT scanning is absent and hard links are counted repeatedly.
README states GPL-3.0-or-later for DiskLens and credits GPL-2.0-or-later WinDirStat code ports; third-party components keep separate licenses.

resources.name: SoundConnect Desktop: a Windows client reusing a reviewed headset engine
resources.description: A Windows Sony-headphone client adopts existing libmdr/libmdr-bt engine DLLs after a documented REA-assisted binary inventory and source review. The desktop interface is modeled on Sound Connect, while protocol implementation and device support are inherited rather than newly reconstructed.
requirements: Requires Windows 10/11 and compatible Bluetooth headphones. Source builds need Node 24, pnpm 10, Rust MSVC and pinned engine DLLs or their Visual Studio/CMake build environment.
REA inspected upstream PE resources, strings and provenance before engine adoption.

Only WH-1000XM4 hardware is reported tested; other models rely on upstream support. Concurrent phone-app control, XM4 paired-device mutations and 360 Reality Audio setup are unsupported; the installer is unsigned.
MIT covers the app and credited engine; Sony identification images retain Sony rights.

resources.name: rec-rs: an OBS-informed Rust recorder for macOS
resources.description: A macOS recorder is informed by OBS architecture research using REA package inspection, platform tools and public source references. It offers screen/camera recording and streaming with a deliberately smaller scene/source feature set; the research notes record unavailable native-analysis providers.
requirements: Universal releases target macOS 15+; building needs the documented Rust/macOS toolchain. Screen, microphone and camera capture depend on the relevant system permissions.
REA 6.4.0 plist/signature inspection succeeded, but native analyze/layout operations failed or were unavailable; notes also studied OBS source and used separate macOS inspection tools.
No free scene-layout editor, transitions, application/multi-display capture or audio filters; output is 8-bit SDR and the webcam overlay is baked in. Region capture is CLI-only.
The README supplies self-test/soak tooling; YouTube HEVC streaming was checked only against a local server.
Code is documented as MIT OR Apache-2.0; the author states that original OBS code/assets are not included.

resources.name: Sketch: a Paper-shell-informed native Rust canvas
resources.description: A Rust canvas models Paper-like editing behavior after REA investigation of the Paper Desktop shell. The hosted editor was not recovered: research separates observed shell integration from inferred editor features, and the new geometric document model differs from Paper HTML/CSS.
requirements: Requires Rust 1.95+ for source builds; macOS releases target 11+, Linux uses the documented graphics libraries and XDG portal for file dialogs.
Research targeted licensed Paper Desktop 0.5.15. The hosted editor was absent from the bundle; several editor-level capabilities were inferred from shell integration or the implementation brief.
No HTML/CSS document model, CSS/code export, rotation or complex-script shaping; several blend, clipping and SVG-import behaviors are approximations.
Linux window tests used Xvfb; macOS smoke evidence is narrower than complete input/menu/Intel testing.
Code is MIT OR Apache-2.0; Inter fonts retain SIL OFL 1.1 and bundled agent skills have separate notices.

resources.name: Terminal: a Rust terminal informed by TradingView chart research
resources.description: An independent Rust market interface uses REA browser-scenario research on public logged-out TradingView chart interactions. The notes retain observed/documented/inferred/unknown labels; the result supplies its own chart engine and data providers rather than recovering TradingView or Bloomberg server software.
requirements: Source builds need Rust and the documented platform graphics setup. Data can use an offline sample or external providers; brokerage connectivity is optional and requires the user's own provider/account setup.
REA captured browser scenarios from a public logged-out chart. Login-only behavior, some pointer gestures and unavailable interactions remain unknown.
Scanned disclosure PDFs are not OCR-processed; unofficial data endpoints are rate-limited and upstream filing-use terms still apply.
No project-wide license was identified in the reviewed root/README; repository access does not grant rights to external market data.

resources.name: Awesome Malware Analysis
resources.description: A long-running single-README list of malware analysis tools and resources, grouped into 17 top-level sections covering open-source threat intelligence, detection and classification, online scanners and sandboxes, document and shellcode analysis, deobfuscation, debugging and reverse engineering, network, memory forensics, Windows artifacts, plus books and other references. Each entry is a name linked to an external tool or resource with a short description. The repository also keeps a Simplified Chinese translation of the list.
requirements: The reviewed README, last committed 2026-05-30, links roughly 428 entries across 17 top-level sections; it is a list of pointers, and one tool can appear under several sections.

Entries give a name, an external link and a one-line description, and state no license, platform or maintenance status. Links point to varied destinations including project pages, vendors and online services.

A Malware Collection section links out to external malware corpora, sample feeds and honeypots; the list itself hosts no samples, and following those links means handling live malware, which requires an isolated environment and appropriate authorization.
The list text is licensed CC BY 4.0; linked tools and resources keep their own licenses and terms. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: Awesome Connected Things Security
resources.description: A single-README list of security-research references for IoT, embedded, industrial and automotive systems, organized into sections on hardware attacks, wireless protocols (BLE, Zigbee/Z-Wave, LoRa, Matter/Thread, cellular, NFC/RFID, Wi-Fi, USB), firmware security including extraction, static and dynamic analysis and secure boot, network and web protocols, cloud backends, mobile apps, and industrial and automotive topics. Each entry links out to an external tool, talk, paper, write-up or course with a short note. The README reports 900+ resources.
requirements: The README, last committed 2026-10-16, links roughly 979 entries and states 900+ resources; it is a list of pointers, and one entry can fit several sections.
Entries give a name, an external link and a short note, and state no license, platform or maintenance status.

The list is oriented toward security research and exploitation, with sections such as hardware attacks, memory extraction, side-channel and fault injection, firmware extraction and secure-boot bypasses. Hardware and radio work needs physical access, appropriate equipment and authorization.
The list text is released under CC0-1.0; linked tools and resources keep their own licenses and terms. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: Awesome CAN Bus
resources.description: A single-README list of CAN bus tools, hardware and resources for automotive and embedded work, grouped into sections for reverse-engineering tools, test equipment and simulators, higher-layer protocols (OBD-II, UDS, ISO-TP, J1939, J2534), general and Linux utilities, CAN database formats (DBC, KCD) with converters, and hardware for ARM, Arduino, ESP32, single-board computers and FPGA cores. Each entry links out to an external project or resource with a short description.
requirements: The README, last committed 2026-08-07, links roughly 260 entries across its sections; it is a list of pointers, and one project can appear under several sections.
Entries give a name, an external link and a short description, and state no license, platform or maintenance status.

CAN bus analysis and the listed hardware need physical access to a vehicle or bus and appropriate interface hardware; the list covers the CAN protocol and higher-layer automotive protocols as its subject.
The list text is released under CC0-1.0; linked projects and resources keep their own licenses and terms. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: Awesome CAN ID
resources.description: A single-README list that gathers links to CAN message identifier and payload decodings in one place, grouped by vehicle make and model under about 30 car brands and brand groups plus BMW, Ducati and KTM motorcycles. Its links lead to DBC files, decoding spreadsheets, wiki pages, sniffing notes and small libraries maintained elsewhere, after a Common section of general databases such as comma.ai’s opendbc and the OpenGarages CAN ID references.
requirements: The README, last changed by a merge on 2026-08-12, holds 148 links under 57 headings, the Common section and make, model and brand-group headings; the Acura, Lotus, Peugeot, DS, SAAB, Porsche and Seat headings are still empty. About 107 links go to GitHub and the rest to Google spreadsheets, wikis, forums and blog posts, several of them in Russian; two already point to Web Archive copies.

Entries give only the make or model, a link and a short note such as a model year, ECU or bus name. They state no license, verification status or coverage. Applying the decodings means reading traffic on a vehicle bus with suitable interface hardware.

Repository CI runs only awesome-lint. The list text is dedicated under CC0-1.0; linked databases, documents and code keep their own licenses and terms. Its footnotes point to the same maintainer’s CAN bus and LIN bus tool lists. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: Does reverse engineering need a bigger model? General and specialist models in Touhou reconstruction
resources.description: An essay on REA’s site by N0zoM1z0 (13 October 2026) uses dated Touhou reconstruction commits to ask whether exact function matching needs a larger general model, a compiler-specialist model or better retrieval. It walks through TH09, TH095, TH04 and TH08 cases where later GPT-6-series sessions closed stubborn matches, and the TH08 audit that found accepted functions with wrong floating constants. Specialist and reinforcement-learning comparisons are proposed as future experiments; no trained specialist was evaluated.
requirements: The essay and its notes supply no game files, compilers or builds; each linked Touhou repository documents its own requirements.
The essay is dated 13 October 2026. Its examples are function-level comparisons recorded in linked TH09, TH095, TH04 and TH08 commits.

Later sessions inherited earlier source, diagnostics and failed experiments, so the before-and-after closures are not controlled estimates of model-size effects. The notes treat gpt-web as a changing label that does not identify a run’s model, per-run reasoning effort and budgets are not uniformly recorded, and the GPT-6-Luna-max closure is presented as a discovery across model tiers, not a measured smaller-model advantage.

The TH08 example comes from commit a393f400 (2 September), which target-checks every VC7 floating-literal relocation; the follow-up audits 1,548 relocations and corrects 12 stale rows in five accepted units. The essay’s concern that a reward built on the old check could reinforce wrong source is stated as an inference: the notes record no actual RL exploit or trained model doing so.
Game rights stay with their owners.

resources.name: Awesome REA: Reverse Engineer Anything with AI (AIshihzong)
resources.description: An unofficial, bilingual awesome list of what AI agents have reverse-engineered and rebuilt, tagged by whether each case's own sources show that REA was used. It gathers REA's official resources and showcases; community cases in games, apps, hardware and protocols, and security evaluations; the wider wave of AI reverse engineering and clean-room rebuilds without confirmed REA; plugins, guides and research, related MCP tools, other lists and press; and a section on legal questions and controversy.
requirements: Started 2026-10-13, with 50 commits on six days through 2026-10-26. At the commit of that day the English README, mirrored in Simplified Chinese, has about 110 one-line entries, with separate pages that index projects by the app they replace, check each "built with REA" claim, list new additions and collect X posts and press. The README says figures were checked on 2026-10-21 and partly refreshed on 2026-10-26, and warns that numbers move weekly.

Tags separate cases whose README, author's post or official showcase says REA was used (REA) from AI reverse engineering with other or unnamed tools (AI-RE), clean-room rewrites without reverse-engineering evidence (Rebuild) and unverified claims (Claim?). Claim checks are the maintainer's reading of public sources; the claim page says X posts could not be opened when it was checked. A short evidence section summarises two third-party controlled comparisons of REA, rea-lab and leanrea.

It links this collection among its other lists, and it names other REA case trackers such as awesome-REA-cases. A daily workflow searches GitHub and posts candidates to an issue, but entries are added by hand, and a validator checks entries against the rules stated in the list's CONTRIBUTING.md.

The README calls the list unofficial. It excludes mirrors, pure forks and projects mainly aimed at bypassing licensing, copying paid features or distributing copyrighted assets, and accepts takedown requests. The list is released under CC0-1.0.

resources.name: AI Rebuilds
resources.description: A website and GitHub list of 81 projects that rebuild existing software or games without the original source: AI-built clean-room apps such as the ArtCraft suite, software rewritten with coding agents, AI-assisted game decompilations, game engine reimplementations, human-led decompilations and ports, clean-room classics such as Wine and ReactOS, and tools for rebuilders. Each entry says what it rebuilds and carries a method label and an AI-involvement label, and the site can be searched, filtered and sorted by stars or recent activity. A separate guide describes a clean-room rebuild workflow with REA.
requirements: At commit 8092b23, data/projects.json (list updated 2026-10-29, GitHub figures refreshed 2026-11-02) holds 81 projects in seven categories and generates both the README and ai-rebuilds.com.

Method labels are clean-room, reimplementation, decompilation, recompilation, port, rewrite or tool. AI labels (built, assisted, none or unknown) follow each project's own description, and 49 entries are labelled with no AI involvement. A weekly workflow refreshes stars, last-push dates, archive status and licences from the GitHub API and checks links. Entries may not distribute the original's code, binaries, ROMs or assets; the site hosts no software and takes fix and removal requests.

REA is listed first among 13 tools, and only the DX-Ball entry is described as using it. The site's third-party guide “Rebuild something with REA” covers installing rea-agents, choosing REA tools by input type, a two-agent clean-room split and checks against the original; its Node.js minimums (22.19+, 24.11+ or 26+) are older than the 22.23.4+, 24.22.1+ or 26.12.1+ that REA's README now requires.

MIT for the code and the list; the LICENSE excludes original games, their code and assets. Descriptions are the site's own, and the lists it drew entries from are credited, among them CC BY-SA 4.0 and CC0 lists.

resources.name: REA & AI RE Tools Guide (unofficial)
resources.description: An unofficial, independently run guide to installing REA and connecting it to coding agents, in 32 pages: install paths for npx, npm and Bun including Windows, MCP setup for Claude Code and Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf and Gemini CLI, a config generator for 24 clients, Ghidra, IDA and JADX provider setup, and troubleshooting pages that match exact error text to upstream REA issues. Several pages record the author's own runs, such as Android APK analysis through headless JADX on rea-agents 6.5.0 and a Claude Code setup re-test on 6.8.0. The site also compares REA with Ghidra, IDA and other reverse-engineering MCP servers and documents look-alike REA copies.
requirements: Reviewed as a live website on 2026-11-02, when its sitemap listed 32 pages. There is no public source repository or pinned revision; each page dates the check of the commands it restates (2026-10-13 to 2026-10-27 on the reviewed pages). The home page named rea-agents 6.8.0 and Node.js 22.23.4+, 24.22.1+ or 26.12.1+, matching npm and REA's README at review.
