Tested pages state their platform and versions: Android APK analysis on Debian 13 with rea-agents 6.5.0, JDK 21 and jadx-headless-mcp 0.7.1 on an F-Droid APK, and Claude Code setup re-run on rea-agents 6.8.0. The Gemini CLI page scanned REA's tool schemas on 6.5.0 and 6.7.0 but sent no request to Gemini, and the Windows page draws on REA's documentation and issue reports.

Every page calls the site an independent community guide not affiliated with the REA project and names rea.tools and morluto/rea as authoritative; its fake-copies page lists only morluto/rea, rea.tools and the rea-agents npm package as official. The pages carry no ads or affiliate links and load Cloudflare Web Analytics.
The pages state no license for the guide's own text. REA is MIT; commercial engines it can drive, such as IDA Pro and Hopper, need their own licenses.

resources.name: sh23ds: a native 3DS reconstruction of Silent Hill 2
resources.description: sh23ds rebuilds Silent Hill 2: Director's Cut as a native C engine for Nintendo 3DS using the player's PC game data. Game logic, camera, lighting and events were reconstructed from the PC executable; the research notes report analysis with Ghidra and REA. The author reports a complete playthrough in Azahar, while real-console testing and some PC behaviors remain unfinished.
requirements: A 3DS or 2DS running Luma3DS, a copy of Silent Hill 2: Director's Cut for PC and about 1.8 GB of SD-card space are required.
DSP firmware must be dumped once with DSP1 for sound.
The build is in development; the author reports little testing on real consoles and remaining behavior and rendering gaps.
GPL-3.0 license; bundled third-party code keeps its own licenses.

resources.name: Hex-Rays IDA MCP
resources.description: Official Hex-Rays MCP server for agent access to IDA databases, with headless operation and optional GUI integration.
requirements: IDA 9.4+ with idalib, Python 3.11+, Git and uv; the GUI plugin is optional for headless use.

resources.name: GhidraMCP
resources.description: Ghidra extension and MCP bridge exposing decompilation, symbol navigation and renaming to agents, with GUI and headless modes.
requirements: Match the extension to the documented Ghidra release; Python 3.10+ for the bridge, with additional PyGhidra requirements for headless mode.

resources.name: Binary Ninja MCP (official)
resources.description: Binary Ninja's own MCP interface exposes functions, symbols, disassembly, intermediate languages and decompiled text to agents.
requirements: First shipped in stable Binary Ninja 6.0 (2026-09-03). The GUI server uses HTTP and is included in every edition, Free included; headless stdio binaryninja_mcp requires Commercial or Ultimate on macOS/Linux and is not yet in native Windows packages, where upstream suggests the Linux build under WSL.

resources.name: Binary Ninja MCP (fosdickio)
resources.description: Community Binary Ninja plugin and bridge for MCP clients, including workflows that switch among multiple open binaries.
requirements: Binary Ninja, Python 3.12+ and an MCP client; install the plugin separately from the client bridge.

resources.name: IDA Pro MCP (mrexodia)
resources.description: Community IDA integration useful for existing setups and migration context; its maintainer now recommends the official Hex-Rays MCP server.
requirements: IDA Pro rather than IDA Free, Python 3.11+ and an MCP client; consult the upstream migration notice before choosing a new setup.

resources.name: Radare2 MCP Server
resources.description: Native radare2 MCP server offering binary-analysis tools, reusable sessions and configurable read-only access.
requirements: A compatible radare2 build and r2pm, plus an MCP client; advanced HTTP session features depend on the radare2 ABI.

resources.name: r2ai
resources.description: AI plugins inside radare2 for function explanations, naming suggestions and model-assisted decompilation using local or remote models.
requirements: radare2 with the matching r2ai/decai plugins; configure a local model or the credentials required by the selected remote provider.

resources.name: DAILA
resources.description: Decompiler-independent AI assistant for function summaries and naming across IDA, Ghidra, Binary Ninja and angr-management.
requirements: A supported decompiler and dailalib; configure a model backend. Ghidra requires the documented PyGhidra setup.

resources.name: RevEng.AI Ghidra Plugin
resources.description: Connects Ghidra to RevEng.AI for function similarity, recovered names, AI explanations and agent-assisted annotation.
requirements: A compatible Ghidra/Java build and a RevEng.AI API key; creating service-side analysis uploads the selected binary.

resources.name: JADX-AI-MCP
resources.description: JADX plugin paired with a Python MCP server to inspect decompiled Android classes, resources, cross-references and debugger context.
requirements: JADX with the plugin and the separate JADX MCP Server component; upstream lists Java 11+ and Python 3.10+.

resources.name: apktool-mcp-server
resources.description: Python MCP server that drives a local Apktool install so agents can decode APKs; list, read, search and edit smali and resource files; read AndroidManifest.xml and apktool.yml; and rebuild the project.
requirements: Apktool must be installed and available on PATH. Reviewed release: V3.0.2, published 2026-07-02 and identical to the default branch at review. Run it with uv; the README and script header state Python 3.10+, while pyproject.toml declares >=3.13. Apache-2.0.

MCP is served over stdio by default, or over streamable HTTP on port 8652 with --http. The README lists 13 tools; the reviewed script also registers health_check, analyze_project_structure and get_workspace_info. Project paths must stay inside the workspace directory (apktool_mcp_server_workspace by default).
modify_smali_file, modify_resource_file, clean_project and build_apk change the decoded project, so work on copies; the modify tools keep timestamped backups by default.

resources.name: frida-mcp (yfe404)
resources.description: Frida MCP server with persistent instrumentation sessions, runtime inspection and Android static-to-dynamic navigation.
requirements: Node.js 20+, Frida 17 and an accessible target; on-device operations require the documented device/frida-server setup.
The README’s License heading names MIT, but the pinned commit has no LICENSE file and package.json has no license field; the declaration appears only in the README.

resources.name: Super Trouper
resources.description: Single-binary Frida MCP server for discovering devices, managing process sessions and loading instrumentation scripts.
requirements: Published host binaries target macOS/Linux; target connectivity must support Frida. Source builds need Go, CGO and a matching Frida Core DevKit.

resources.name: LLDB MCP
resources.description: LLDB's official MCP interface gives agents debugger sessions and commands for breakpoints, memory inspection and stepping.
requirements: An LLDB distribution/build containing lldb-mcp and a compatible stdio MCP client; debug-target access follows the host platform's requirements.

resources.name: Claude Reverse Engineering Skill
resources.description: Community agent skill for triage, headless exports and evidence-based RE reports; explicitly documents workflows with REA and other MCP servers.
requirements: An Agent Skills-compatible client and Python 3.8+ for bundled scripts; analysis engines and MCP servers are configured separately.

resources.name: SpecterOps Reverse Engineering Skills
resources.description: Focused Binary Ninja and Ghidra analysis skills that describe MCP tool use, analysis recipes and annotation practices.
requirements: Configure the chosen Binary Ninja or Ghidra MCP integration separately; the skill package does not install or wrap those servers.

resources.name: Ghidra
resources.description: Open-source analysis suite for disassembly, decompilation, graphs and Java/Python automation across executable formats.
requirements: An official Ghidra release and its required JDK; extension and script compatibility must match the installed release.

resources.name: radare2
resources.description: Scriptable command-line framework for inspecting, disassembling, debugging and modifying binaries across many architectures.
requirements: Use the release/build for your host; decompilers and other optional functionality may require separate plugins.

resources.name: Cutter
resources.description: Rizin-powered graphical reverse-engineering workspace with extensible views and Ghidra decompiler integration.
requirements: Desktop builds are available for Linux, macOS and Windows; use plugins compatible with the selected Cutter release.

resources.name: Frida
resources.description: Dynamic instrumentation toolkit for observing and scripting the behavior of live native and managed processes.
requirements: Host bindings or CLI tools and a supported target setup; mobile/server/Gadget and signing requirements vary by platform.

resources.name: JADX
resources.description: Dex-to-Java decompiler with CLI/GUI navigation, resource decoding and cross-reference search for Android packages.
requirements: 64-bit Java 11+ unless using a bundled runtime; decompilation can be incomplete and should be checked against bytecode.

resources.name: Apktool
resources.description: Decodes Android resources and smali into a project-like tree and can rebuild modified packages.
requirements: A supported Java runtime and the release-specific launcher; rebuilding is distinct from recovering original Java source.

resources.name: Androguard
resources.description: Python toolkit for APK/DEX metadata, bytecode and reference analysis; the v5 source branch also documents agent skills and MCP.
requirements: Version-sensitive: the reviewed README distinguishes the v5 source tree from PyPI 4.1.4; v5 extras require additional Rust/Python components.

resources.name: ILSpy
resources.description: .NET assembly browser and C# decompiler with whole-project export, metadata inspection and a scriptable command-line frontend.
requirements: Choose a desktop or ILSpyCmd release and its matching .NET runtime; frontend and operating-system support are release-dependent.

resources.name: dnSpyEx
resources.description: Community continuation of dnSpy for debugging and editing .NET assemblies without the original source.
requirements: Windows desktop workflow; Unity debugging requires the companion runtime setup documented by the project.

resources.name: @electron/asar
resources.description: Electron's archive tool lists and extracts ASAR contents so packaged JavaScript and application assets can be inspected.
requirements: The reviewed release requires Node.js 22.12+.

resources.name: webcrack
resources.description: Improves JavaScript readability by reversing supported obfuscation patterns and unpacking webpack/Browserify bundles.
requirements: The reviewed README specifies Node.js 22 or 24; results depend on the obfuscator/bundler patterns present in the input.

resources.name: humanify
resources.description: Rename identifiers in minified JavaScript with LLM-suggested names, applied through scope-aware AST rewriting so the program structure stays unchanged. The new names are model suggestions, not recovered original identifiers.
requirements: Reviewed release: v3.1.1, published 2026-07-29. Version 3 is a single Rust binary with release builds for macOS arm64/x64, Linux x64/arm64 and Windows x64; source builds use cargo install. MIT-licensed.

Select a provider preset: OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, OpenRouter and Requesty need an API key, while Ollama runs a local model. humanify makes one model call per identifier with surrounding code context (500 characters by default); hosted modes send that context to the selected provider, and cost and rate limits scale with the identifier count.

Each run processes one JavaScript file and renames identifiers only: it does not unbundle webpack output or remove control-flow obfuscation, and upstream suggests running webcrack first. Name quality depends on the model; upstream describes local models as slower and less accurate than hosted providers.

resources.name: WABT
resources.description: WebAssembly tools for binary-to-text conversion, section inspection, validation, interpretation and C translation.
requirements: Select a release supporting the module's WebAssembly features; optional proposals may require explicit flags.

resources.name: wasm-tools
resources.description: Bytecode Alliance CLI and Rust libraries for inspecting WebAssembly modules, metadata, components and WIT interfaces.
requirements: Use prebuilt release artifacts or a Rust toolchain; proposal/component support depends on the selected release.

resources.name: Binwalk
resources.description: Identifies embedded formats and optionally extracts their contents, with entropy analysis for firmware triage.
requirements: The current v3 implementation is Rust-based; extraction needs the appropriate external tools or the documented container environment.

resources.name: unblob
resources.description: Recursively extracts archives and filesystems from binary blobs while reporting chunk boundaries and unknown regions.
requirements: Python package plus external extractors, or the bundled Docker image; check the project's dependency inventory for the formats needed.

resources.name: Ghidra Firmware Utilities
resources.description: Ghidra loaders and helpers for PCI option ROMs, UEFI firmware volumes, Intel flash descriptors and coreboot images.
requirements: The reviewed build instructions require Ghidra 12.0+ and JDK 21+; build against the same Ghidra/JRE environment used for analysis.

resources.name: Qiling
resources.description: Python emulation framework that adds OS, filesystem and API behavior around CPU emulation for instrumented binary analysis.
requirements: A supported Python environment and the target's required root filesystem/libraries; emulation coverage varies by platform.

resources.name: Unicorn Engine
resources.description: Multi-architecture CPU emulator for executing selected instruction ranges with register, memory and hook control.
requirements: Use a supported binding and explicitly supply the CPU state and memory model; it is a CPU emulator rather than a complete OS environment.

resources.name: angr
resources.description: Python binary-analysis framework combining control-flow recovery, symbolic execution, data-flow analysis and decompilation.
requirements: A compatible Python 3 environment; useful results require an appropriate model of program inputs, state and external functions.

resources.name: LIEF
resources.description: Library for structured parsing and modification of executable formats including ELF, PE and Mach-O.
requirements: C++, Python or Rust integration; check the distinction between core and extended features for the selected distribution.

resources.name: Capstone
resources.description: Disassembly library with architecture-neutral APIs and instruction details for custom binary-analysis pipelines.
requirements: Select a library/binding release supporting the target ISA and mode; the next branch can differ from stable releases.

resources.name: ImHex
resources.description: Hex editor with a binary-pattern language, structured data inspection and visual tools for understanding file formats.
requirements: Desktop build or web edition; some data sources and features depend on the platform and selected build.

resources.name: x64dbg
resources.description: Windows binary debugger with disassembly, memory views and plugins for analyzing programs without source code.
requirements: Windows; choose x32dbg or x64dbg according to the executable's architecture.

resources.name: GDB
resources.description: Native and remote debugger for controlling execution and inspecting live or crashed program state.
requirements: A GDB build supporting the target architecture and a permitted local process, core dump, simulator or remote debug endpoint.

resources.name: rr
resources.description: Records process execution and replays it under GDB, enabling repeatable inspection and reverse execution.
requirements: Linux with supported CPU performance counters; VM use depends on counter virtualization and the project's hardware requirements.

resources.name: Diaphora
resources.description: IDA-based binary diffing that matches functions and transfers names, comments and types between analyzed versions.
requirements: IDA with Python 3 support; richer pseudocode and microcode comparisons depend on the corresponding decompiler capabilities.

resources.name: BinDiff
resources.description: Compares disassembled binaries to find matching functions and changed code across versions.
requirements: Requires a separate supported disassembler/export pipeline; upstream documents IDA Pro, Binary Ninja and Ghidra configurations.

resources.name: Detect It Easy
resources.description: Format-aware file identification and static inspection using parsers, signatures and programmable heuristics.
requirements: Use the project-linked DIE-engine releases for the host platform; identification results require analyst interpretation.

resources.name: OpenSecurityTraining2
resources.description: Free self-paced security courses with learning paths for reverse engineering, firmware and systems foundations.
requirements: Browser access; choose classes according to their published prerequisites and lab requirements.

resources.name: pwn.college: Reverse Engineering
resources.description: Hands-on reverse-engineering module covering functions, data access, static tools and dynamic tools with hosted exercises.
requirements: Browser access and the platform's account/environment setup for interactive challenges.

resources.name: Reverse Engineering for Beginners
resources.description: Dennis Yurichev's free book on understanding compiled programs and assembly, available in multiple languages.
requirements: A browser or PDF reader; use the toolchains relevant to the exercises being followed.

resources.name: The Official Radare2 Book
resources.description: Official practical reference for radare2 analysis, disassembly, scripting, debugging and related plugins.
requirements: Upstream lists radare2 5.8.x as the minimum and recommends a current release for following the examples.

resources.name: RenderDoc
resources.description: Inspect frame captures, draw calls, shaders, and graphics resources in your own game or graphics application.
requirements: Supported graphics API and replay platform; upstream supports captures of your own, open-source, or free projects. Metal is not supported.

resources.name: AssetRipper
resources.description: Analyze Unity game files, inspect asset dependencies, and convert supported assets into Unity project formats.
requirements: Unity 3.5.0–6000.4.X coverage varies by version; GPL-3.0 open-source edition, with separate premium features.

resources.name: Cpp2IL
resources.description: Recover managed representations from Unity IL2CPP builds using binary and metadata analysis; reconstruction remains a work in progress.
requirements: Compatible Unity build and metadata; current development branch is a major rewrite and primarily targets .NET 9.0.

resources.name: Il2CppDumper
resources.description: Recover IL2CPP metadata and dummy assemblies, and generate helper scripts for native analysis tools; method code is not restored.
requirements: Matching IL2CPP executable and global-metadata.dat; documented Unity support is 5.3–2022.2.

As checked on 2026-10-20, the latest release is v6.7.46 (2024-07-06) and the master head is a same-day commit, four commits after the reviewed one with the README unchanged; GitHub’s last recorded push was 2024-08-18, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

resources.name: RenderDoc MCP
resources.description: Expose existing RenderDoc captures to an agent for bounded frame, pipeline, resource, and shader inspection.
requirements: Windows and replayable .rdc capture; maintainer baseline is RenderDoc 1.43. Optional native Python backend needs a source-built binding.

resources.name: Chrome DevTools MCP
resources.description: Connect an agent to Chrome for live page inspection, network debugging, and performance traces.
requirements: Supported Node.js LTS, Chrome, and an MCP client; selected browser profile and target must be available locally.

resources.name: mitmproxy
resources.description: Inspect and record HTTP traffic with an interactive proxy, web interface, or scriptable command-line tools.
requirements: Configure the client proxy; HTTPS inspection requires the appropriate local trust configuration. Saved captures and live interception are distinct workflows.

resources.name: Playwright MCP
resources.description: Drive browser interactions through structured accessibility snapshots to investigate reproducible web behavior.
requirements: Node.js 18+ and an MCP client; the upstream also offers a separate CLI-and-skills approach for coding agents.

resources.name: Burp Suite MCP Server
resources.description: PortSwigger's Burp Suite extension serves an MCP endpoint, plus a packaged stdio proxy, so agents can query proxy HTTP and WebSocket history, send HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 requests, and open Repeater or Intruder tabs.
requirements: Requires Burp Suite, proprietary PortSwigger software under its own EULA: Professional is a paid subscription, while Community Edition is free under separate Community terms. The extension's GPL-3.0 license does not cover Burp. The extension manifest lists both editions as supported.

Reviewed release: v1.3.0, published 2026-05-26 with a prebuilt burp-mcp-all.jar and also listed in the BApp Store. Source builds use Gradle and need Java and the jar command on PATH; the reviewed build targets a Java 21 toolchain.

The SSE server listens on 127.0.0.1:9876 by default; stdio-only clients use the packaged proxy JAR. Approval prompts for sending HTTP requests and for reading HTTP history, WebSocket history and Organizer items are on by default. Config-editing tools are opt-in, and exported options filter credentials by default.

Scanner-issue and Collaborator tools are registered only in Burp Suite Professional. Data returned to the MCP client is handled by that client's model provider. The default branch was seven commits ahead of v1.3.0 at review, with the same registered tool set.

resources.name: Wakaru
resources.description: Recover readable modules from shipped JavaScript bundles by reversing recognized minifier and transpiler patterns. Supports bundle splitting and modern-syntax recovery for inspecting production frontend code.
requirements: The npm CLI declares Node.js >=16; standalone v1.14.0 binaries are published for macOS arm64, Linux arm64/x64, and Windows arm64/x64.

Provide supported JavaScript bundles or source maps. Original identifiers may be unrecoverable without maps; heavy control-flow or VM obfuscation requires other tooling. Package/version inventory is explicitly still in development.

resources.name: Spectral
resources.description: Analyze captured application HTTP traffic with an LLM to generate MCP tools, OpenAPI 3.1 specifications, or GraphQL schemas. Generated tools call the observed API directly after capture and authentication setup.
requirements: Python >=3.11; capture through the Chrome extension or MITM proxy, and configure a supported LLM provider or local Ollama endpoint.
The reviewed v0.11.0 workflow depends on captured traffic and valid application authentication. Analysis and automatic repair use the configured LLM.

resources.name: jsdeob-workbench
resources.description: Inspect JavaScript ASTs and variable scopes while building visual chains of Babel transforms. Save analysis projects and reusable plugins to iteratively simplify obfuscated scripts.
requirements: Run from source with Node.js and npm; the documented default standalone build targets Windows. No GitHub release was available at review time.

Built-in transforms may need sample-specific scripts, and deeply nested input can overflow the stack. Its optional evaluation helper executes code and should be used in a local sandbox, as upstream explicitly advises.
No license was found at the pinned commit: the repository root has no LICENSE file, and neither the README nor package.json declares one. Public source availability is not a reuse grant.

resources.name: UndertaleModTool
resources.description: Browse and modify supported GameMaker data files, extract assets, and decompile or compile GML VM code. Includes room editing, scripted changes, a CLI, and the reusable UndertaleModLib library.
requirements: Supply a supported game data file such as data.win, game.ios, or game.unx. Stable 0.9.2.0 provides a 64-bit Windows GUI and CLI packages for Windows, Ubuntu, and macOS.

GML VM code editing excludes YYC, and some language features remain unsupported. Building the reviewed source requires the .NET 10 SDK or later and recursive submodules; the GUI build requires Windows.

resources.name: frida-il2cpp-bridge
resources.description: Inspect IL2CPP classes, methods, and fields in a live process, and trace or intercept method calls without supplying global-metadata.dat. Complements static IL2CPP dumpers with runtime observation.
requirements: Requires Frida access to a running IL2CPP application and the npm module. The current bundled CLI needs Python 3.12+ (inferred from its typing.override import) and Frida tooling.

The reviewed README states Unity 5.3.0–6000.3.x support. Android and Linux are the platforms upstream tests; Windows, iOS, and macOS are listed as supported with explicit warnings of possible breakage. Latest release at review: v0.14.0.

resources.name: objdiff
resources.description: Compare functions and data in reference and rebuilt object files to guide matching decompilation. Displays instruction-level differences, demangles C++ symbols, and can rebuild when source files change.
requirements: Provide reference and rebuilt object files. Project integration and automatic rebuilding use objdiff.json plus a working toolchain and build command; direct CLI comparisons can use file paths.

v3.8.2 provides GUI binaries for Windows/Linux x86_64 and macOS arm64/x86_64, with additional CLI targets. Building from source requires Rust. Supported architectures include ARM, ARM64, MIPS, PowerPC, SuperH, and x86/x86_64.

resources.name: decomp-permuter
resources.description: Randomly or systematically permutes one C function, recompiling each variant and scoring it against a target object file to search for matching compiler output. PERM macros specify manual alternatives, and the optional permuter@home mode distributes runs to other workers.
requirements: Each input directory needs a single-function .c file, the target .o, a project-specific compile script and a settings .toml; import.py can generate them for configured Make or Ninja projects. The README lists MIPS (IDO, possibly GCC), PowerPC and ARM32 assembly.

Requires Python 3 and toml; pynacl and Levenshtein are optional. permuter@home needs access granted by an existing network member, supports a limited compiler list and does not run on native Windows; workers also need Docker.

A zero score means the scored disassembly matches. The README warns that random passes often find nonsensical changes, so a human must still choose readable, non-overfitted code; the tool does not recover names, types or semantics.
MIT license. No packaged release; last commit at review: 2026-10-06.

resources.name: asm-differ
resources.description: Diffs original and rebuilt assembly for one function or ROM address to guide matching decompilation; its watch mode can rerun make when sources change. The README describes it as decomp.me’s default diff viewer and points to objdiff as a modern alternative.
requirements: Each project needs a diff_settings.py naming the original and rebuilt images and linker map; object-file mode compares against references in an expected/ directory. Requires Python 3 with colorama, watchdog, levenshtein and cxxfilt, plus an objdump for the target.

The README lists MIPS, PPC, AArch64, ARM32, SH2, SH4, m68k and limited x86. Install it as a submodule, by copying diff.py or with pip from Git; there is no packaged release. Last commit at review: 2026-09-06.
Released under the Unlicense. It shows instruction-level differences only and does not recover names, types or semantics.

resources.name: UE Explorer
resources.description: Explore Unreal packages through class, property, and dependency trees; decompile and export UnrealScript classes, inspect bytecode, and examine structured binary data.
requirements: Windows application built on .NET Framework 4.8; provide supported Unreal Engine 1, 2/2.5, or 3 packages. Latest stable release at review: 1.6.2.

UE2X and UE4/5 are not generally supported; only limited experimental parsing of loose UE4 .uasset containers is documented. Game-specific engine modifications can affect compatibility; older 1.6-and-earlier builds require decompressed packages.

resources.name: GARbro
resources.description: Browse recognized visual-novel resource archives as folders, preview their contents, and extract images or audio with conversion to common formats.
requirements: Requires Windows and .NET Framework 4.6 or newer; archive browsing and conversion depend on the supported game/format list. Encrypted archives may require credentials or a recognized game selection.

Latest GitHub release at review remains v1.5.44 (2019-03-31). As checked on 2026-10-20, the reviewed 2023-10-27 commit is still the master head, GitHub’s last recorded push was 2024-07-08, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

resources.name: Mobile Security Framework (MobSF)
resources.description: Inspect mobile application packages with static analysis and supported-device dynamic testing, including runtime behavior and network traffic, through a web interface and APIs.
requirements: The documented container setup recommends Docker 20.10+; dynamic analysis additionally needs a supported device or emulator accessible from the container.
Android dynamic analysis is documented for rooted Android 4.1–11, up to API 30; Android 12+ is not supported by that workflow.
iOS dynamic analysis uses Corellium or a jailbroken device; the physical-device route is marked beta.

resources.name: objection
resources.description: Explore running Android and iOS apps with a Frida-backed command interface for inspecting app storage, memory, runtime objects, and instrumented behavior.
requirements: Current package metadata requires Python 3.11+ and Frida 16+; this supersedes the older Python minimum still shown in the installation wiki.

The target must support the documented Frida attachment or patched-app workflow. Android patching requires Android build tools and Apktool 2.9.0+; iOS patching requires the documented Xcode and signing tools.

resources.name: Grapefruit
resources.description: Inspect and hook running iOS and Android apps from a Frida-based web interface, with method and crypto-API hooks, filesystem and SQLite browsers, iOS keychain and UI-hierarchy views, and HTTP capture from common networking libraries.
requirements: Requires a Frida server running on the target device, set up through Frida's iOS or Android guides; the reviewed release works with Frida 16 or 17 (default 17).

Reviewed release: v1.1.2 (npm package igf), published 2026-03-30. The npm package requires Node.js >=22.18.0 and is not compatible with bunx; prebuilt binaries cover macOS arm64/x64, Linux x64 and Windows x64. The server binds to localhost port 31337 by default; the default-branch README warns that it has no built-in authentication.

Optional AI features, including hook-script generation, use an LLM configured through LLM_* environment variables: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as local Ollama. Prompts are sent to the configured endpoint.

Upstream deliberately ships no Frida-detection, certificate-pinning or jailbreak/root-detection bypasses and suggests combining it with dedicated bypass tooling for authorized assessments. The default branch was 47 commits ahead of v1.1.2 and adds Dart AOT snapshot exploration that the release README does not list. MIT-licensed.

resources.name: r2frida
resources.description: Use radare2 commands and Frida instrumentation together to inspect local or remote process memory, symbols, classes, and runtime calls on desktop and mobile targets.
requirements: Install with r2pm or use a plugin build matching the radare2 major/minor ABI; the reviewed README reports CI against radare2 6.2.2 and git master.
Mobile or remote operation needs a reachable Frida target, such as frida-server over USB or TCP. The plugin bundles the host Frida library; separate host frida-tools are not required.

resources.name: EMBA
resources.description: Extract firmware, combine static checks with emulation-based analysis, inventory software components, and generate web reports and SBOMs for further investigation.
requirements: Upstream recommends an x86-64 Kali Linux VM and the default Docker mode; Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 is also listed. Native ARM execution is not supported.
Documented resource guidance is at least 16 GB RAM, 8 CPU cores recommended, and 30–100 GB free disk space; larger firmware or more parallel workers need more resources.
Install the external dependencies through the project installer. Emulation can execute firmware content; upstream reserves developer mode for development, and findings still require interpretation.

resources.name: Firmware Analysis and Comparison Tool (FACT)
resources.description: Unpack and analyze firmware through an extensible platform whose web interface and HTTP API make component contents and analysis results searchable and comparable across samples.
requirements: The reviewed installer supports Debian 13 and Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04; Kali support is experimental. The README lists Python 3.10–3.14.
Minimum documented resources are 4 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, and about 10 GB for installation, plus storage for unpacked firmware and results.
The standalone FACT_docker distribution is marked unmaintained; use the documented local or Vagrant setup. Some analysis plugins have separate licenses.

resources.name: OFRAK
resources.description: Recursively identify, unpack, analyze, modify, and repack firmware and binary formats using a resource-tree GUI and Python API, with optional disassembler backends.
requirements: The PyPI installation guide requires Python 3.9+ and format-specific external tools; macOS also needs cmake and libmagic, avoiding the documented libmagic 5.47 regression.
Docker builds require BuildKit; Docker 23+ enables it by default. Analysis backends such as Ghidra or Binary Ninja have their own installation and licensing requirements.
OFRAK uses its own Community License for personal and educational use; commercial users should review the separate Pro or Enterprise licensing terms.

resources.name: FirmAE
resources.description: Emulate router and IP-camera firmware to inspect network services and runtime behavior, with automated emulation checks and separate analysis, run, and debugging modes.
requirements: The README documents Ubuntu 20.04 as the tested host; prepare the recursive source checkout, downloaded dependencies, initialized database, and a supported firmware image.
The installer configures QEMU, PostgreSQL, extraction tools, and other host packages; documented run modes require elevated privileges. Docker orchestration is also provided.
Successful emulation depends on the firmware image; upstream benchmark results are not a guarantee for an untested device or newer host distribution.

resources.name: LLM4Decompile (EMNLP 2024)
resources.description: Research on direct binary decompilation and refinement of Ghidra output with language models. Evaluates re-executability on HumanEval and ExeBench; useful for distinguishing readable output from functional recovery.
requirements: EMNLP 2024 paper. Results are author-reported for the evaluated models and benchmarks.

resources.name: DecompileBench (Findings of ACL 2025)
resources.description: A benchmark combining functions from real programs, runtime-aware validation, and LLM-assisted assessment of decompiled-code usability. Helps separate functional correctness from perceived understandability when comparing decompilers.
requirements: Findings of ACL 2025 paper. LLM-as-judge assessments and runtime correctness measure different properties.

resources.name: ReSym (CCS 2024)
resources.description: Combines language models and program analysis to recover variable and user-defined data-structure symbols from stripped binaries. The authors provide training, inference, evaluation, and posterior-reasoning artifacts.
requirements: CCS 2024 paper with author-provided artifacts.

resources.name: LASRecomp: Link’s Awakening static recompilation
resources.description: A native desktop reconstruction of the 2019 Switch version of Link’s Awakening using static recompilation. The author attributes most code, tooling and reverse-engineering work to Claude Code with human direction and review.
requirements: Users must supply their own legally obtained v1.0.0 game files; the repository and release builds omit Nintendo game code, assets and fonts.
Release requirements include macOS 15+ on Apple Silicon or Windows 10+/Linux on x86-64; the x86-64 paths need AVX2 and Vulkan 1.3. Linux ARM remains experimental and untested on hardware.
Beta status includes documented crashes and rendering defects. AI involvement is author-reported.

resources.name: Godot RE Tools
resources.description: Recover supported Godot project files, GDScript and imported resources from exported games. Includes PCK inspection and extraction, script decompilation, and resource conversion for examining and rebuilding project structure.
requirements: Supports Godot 2.x, 3.x and 4.x project decompilation; release builds are available for Windows, macOS and Linux. Edit recovered projects with the original game's Godot version.
Encrypted inputs require the corresponding key. Godot 2.x model conversion and GDNative/GDExtension script recovery are not supported.
The tool is MIT-licensed. Building current source additionally requires the documented Godot fork, rustup and .NET 10 SDK.

resources.name: UE4SS
resources.description: Inspect Unreal Engine games at runtime through live UObject property views, reflected C++ header dumps, property mappings and actor dumps. Lua and C++ APIs support experiments while reconstructing game structures.
requirements: Targets Win64 Unreal Engine games; compatibility is game-dependent and may require custom signatures or configuration.

The development README targets UE 4.7–5.8, while the latest stable tag is v3.0.1 from 2024. Match documentation to the chosen build rather than assuming the stable release has every development feature.
MIT-licensed. Current source builds require the documented C++23, Rust and CMake toolchains plus Epic-authorized Unreal submodule access; Linux cross-compilation produces Windows binaries.

resources.name: FModel
resources.description: Explore Unreal Engine game archives with CUE4Parse-backed package and property inspection, asset previews and export. The 2026 summer release adds USD world export for reconstructing supported scene content.
requirements: Windows x64 and the .NET 10 Desktop Runtime or later; provide supported Unreal Engine game archives. Encrypted archives require the appropriate AES key.
World export in the reviewed aug-2026 release is USD-only; sockets and attachments may be positioned incorrectly.
GPL-3.0-licensed project; bundled dependencies have their own notices.

resources.name: Blutter
resources.description: Analyze Flutter Android ARM64 AOT binaries using the matching Dart runtime. Produces annotated assembly, object-pool dumps and a target-specific Frida script template for investigating compiled Dart application logic.
requirements: Provide extracted Android ARM64 libraries, including libapp.so and the Flutter engine; only recent Dart versions are supported. Direct APK/IPA input and iOS binary reading remain TODOs.
Requires Python 3 and a C++20-capable toolchain such as GCC 13+ or Clang 16+, with the documented native dependencies. The wrapper may download and compile matching Dart sources.
Linux is recommended; Windows and macOS setup is documented. MIT-licensed. Obfuscated applications can still have missing functions, and this is not a complete Dart source decompiler.

resources.name: hermes-dec
resources.description: Parse, disassemble and partially decompile React Native Hermes bytecode bundles. Makes HBC headers and instructions inspectable and emits pseudocode for understanding compiled application logic.
requirements: Current package metadata requires Python 3.10+; the application uses the Python standard library. Supply an extracted Hermes HBC bundle, not a plain-text minified JavaScript bundle.
Decompiler output is not executable JavaScript: loop and conditional structure reconstruction is incomplete. Bytecode compatibility depends on the supported opcode definitions.
The tool is AGPL-3.0-or-later, distinct from the Hermes VM's license.

resources.name: Recaf
resources.description: Inspect and modify compiled JVM applications with integrated decompilers, bytecode assembly, reference search, mappings and deobfuscation tools. The reviewed 4.0 preview also provides basic read-only Android bytecode inspection.
requirements: Requires JDK 22+ and JavaFX 22+; the recommended launcher downloads compatible JavaFX artifacts. Select a build matching the operating system and CPU.
The 4.0.0-alpha GitHub release is explicitly a preview despite being listed as a regular release. Its Android support is read-only; do not assume JVM editing features apply to Android.
MIT-licensed. Provide compiled application inputs; recovered decompiled text is an analysis view, not guaranteed original source.

resources.name: Kaitai Struct
resources.description: Turn documented binary layouts into reusable parsers for files and network packets. A .ksy specification can be inspected with visualizers and compiled to multiple languages, helping preserve reverse-engineered format knowledge in interoperable implementations.
requirements: Provide a .ksy specification or adapt an existing format description; Kaitai generates parsers from that description rather than discovering unknown protocol semantics automatically.
The stable 0.11 universal compiler runs on Linux, macOS and Windows with Java 8+; Java 21 LTS is recommended. Generated parsers also need the selected language's Kaitai runtime.

Compiler and visualizer are GPL-3.0-or-later; runtimes have separate licenses, including MIT and Apache-2.0. Compiler licensing does not impose its license on input specifications or generated output.

resources.name: Wireshark
resources.description: Inspect captured application and device traffic as decoded protocol fields, with filtering and shared GUI/TShark dissection. Custom dissectors let an analyst encode newly understood packet formats and compare protocol implementations.
requirements: Use a supported Windows, macOS or Linux/Unix build and a compatible capture file. Live capture additionally needs a supported interface, capture driver and appropriate capture permissions.
Media support depends on the operating system and hardware. Custom formats need an appropriate dissector; packet inspection does not automatically recover a peer's full implementation.
Distributed under GNU GPLv2, with additional component notices. The GitLab repository is upstream; GitHub is its official read-only mirror.

resources.name: PulseView
resources.description: Examine captured logic and analog waveforms with sigrok's graphical frontend. Protocol decoders and decoder stacking expose bus messages and higher-level device operations, making hardware communication traces useful for firmware and interoperability investigations.
requirements: Supply a supported recorded trace, or use a compatible logic analyzer/oscilloscope with the needed device access. Device support is narrower than the whole sigrok suite; PulseView is not the multimeter frontend.

Protocol decoding requires libsigrokdecode and operates on logic signals; analog captures need suitable conversion. The reviewed source accepts Qt 5.3+ or Qt 6.2+, libsigrokcxx 0.5.2+ and libsigrokdecode 0.5.2+.
GPL-3.0-or-later. GitHub is the official mirror. Development snapshots and packaged releases may differ.

resources.name: UEFITool
resources.description: Parse UEFI firmware images into an inspectable tree and check their structure. Companion UEFIExtract and UEFIFind tools extract parsed contents and locate patterns, supporting analysis of firmware components and vendor formats.
requirements: Provide a compatible firmware image. A75 has Windows, macOS, Linux and FreeBSD builds; building the GUI requires a C++ compiler and Qt5 or Qt6.
The current new engine does not rebuild images. Editing requires the explicitly outdated, unsupported 0.28 old engine.
A75 still disables AMD image parsing. Some vendor update containers are unsupported or may parse incorrectly. The project uses the BSD-2-Clause license.

resources.name: Browser Reverse Engineering Toolkit
resources.description: Capture browser-session evidence, crawl websites in a persistent Chromium session, and generate offline architecture/API reports plus OpenAPI, SDK and mock-server drafts from saved captures.
requirements: Manual capture needs access to the target browser session. Crawling requires Node.js/npm, Playwright and its Chromium browser; the reviewed package declares Playwright ^1.44.0 but no Node engines minimum.
The Node.js reconstructor processes saved captures offline. The toolkit is experimental; generated architecture, OpenAPI, SDK and mock-server outputs need review.

Browser-side capture cannot read HttpOnly cookies or bypass authorization. Request hooks see traffic only after installation; source-map references are hints, and true screenshots require browser automation.
Authenticated captures may contain sensitive data. MIT-licensed.

resources.name: screenshot-to-code
resources.description: Generate HTML/CSS, Tailwind, React, Vue, Bootstrap or Ionic front-end code from screenshots, mockups, Figma designs or screen recordings with multimodal models; an optional headless-browser preview lets the model check its rendered output. The result is a visual reconstruction of the interface, not recovered original source or backend behavior.
requirements: Self-host the MIT-licensed repository: a FastAPI backend managed with Poetry (Python ^3.10) and a React/Vite frontend run with pnpm, or both through Docker Compose. No GitHub release or tag existed at review.

At least one OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini API key is required, and inputs are processed by the selected providers. Gemini is required for video mode and handles asset extraction; a Replicate key is optional but recommended upstream for image generation, editing and background removal. The self-check preview needs Playwright's Chromium.
The README reports no fidelity or accuracy figures. Generated code needs review and cannot recover backend logic, APIs or data that the input does not show.

resources.name: nibkit
resources.description: Decode compiled iOS/macOS interface archives into object trees, Outlet/Action connections, custom classes and navigation relationships. Exports JSON or Mermaid diagrams and exposes read-only inspection commands through MCP.
requirements: Supply supported .nib/.storyboardc files, an .app/directory, or an .ipa for automatic extraction. The reviewed README lists NIBArchive coder versions 9, 10 and 11 plus older binary-plist/NSKeyedArchive formats.

Source builds require Go 1.22 or later according to go.mod. The README states a standard-library-only implementation and advertises darwin/linux arm64/amd64 prebuilt binaries with no runtime dependencies; a Windows release was not verified.
Recovery concerns compiled interface structure and wiring. Format documentation is based on reverse-engineered observations. MIT-licensed.

resources.name: PSP Web Recomp
resources.description: Translate PSP MIPS executables into C++ and WebAssembly, backed by a PSP high-level emulation runtime and WebGL2 renderer. Native tracing, frame capture and audio tools support investigating missing behavior during game porting.
requirements: Provide an image of a game you own and a compatible executable decrypter. Builds need Git, CMake, Ninja, C++20, Python 3, PSPRecomp and Emscripten. Linux is the documented tested build host; macOS is untested.

Author demonstrations cover two Ready at Dawn titles sharing an engine. Other games can require missing HLE calls or graphics features. Movies are skipped, and encrypted saves from a PSP or PPSSPP do not yet load.
Threaded browser hosting requires cross-origin isolation headers and HTTP Range support. The optional native runner also requires EGL/OpenGL ES development headers.
Upstream states that game data is not included and asks users not to redistribute generated game C++ or WebAssembly. Project code uses MIT; the bundled ATRAC decoder retains LGPL-2.1-or-later.

resources.name: N64: Recompiled
resources.description: Statically recompiles N64 MIPS binaries into C functions from symbol metadata, emitting function lookups and relocation macros so a runtime can handle statically linked and relocatable overlays. The output needs a runtime such as N64ModernRuntime; the repository also includes RSP microcode and mod tooling.
requirements: The README documents an ELF as the metadata source, most easily produced from an existing disassembly or decompilation; the reviewed source also accepts a symbols file plus ROM, which the README does not yet describe. A TOML file sets inputs, stubs, skips and instruction patches; full option documentation is not available.

Build N64Recomp from a recursive clone with CMake 3.20+ and a C++20 compiler. The only GitHub release (2025-05-04) packages the separate Recomp Mod Tool, not the recompiler. Last commit at review: 2026-05-27.
Testing has mostly covered old MIPS compilers (GCC 2.7.2, IDO) and modern clang; modern MIPS GCC output may need specific flags, and relocation support for TLB-mapped code is still planned.
MIT-licensed tool; submodules keep their own licenses. It ships no game code or assets. Downstream recompilations such as Zelda 64: Recompiled are separate projects.

resources.name: XenonRecomp
resources.description: Converts Xbox 360 PowerPC executables into C++ that can be compiled for other platforms, with the XenonAnalyse companion detecting jump tables and function boundaries. Output is a literal instruction translation rather than decompiled code and needs a runtime that the project does not supply.
requirements: A per-game TOML file supplies the XEX (plus an optional title-update XEXP), output directory, jump-table file and addresses of register save/restore and setjmp/longjmp functions; some function boundaries may need manual entries. Jump-table detection targets Sonic Unleashed patterns and may need changes for other games.

The README disclaimer states that no runtime is provided and that making a game work is the user’s responsibility. MMIO is unimplemented, exceptions are unsupported, and some PPC instruction variants are missing.

Building needs a recursive clone, CMake 3.20+ and Clang 18+; other compilers are untested and not recommended, including for generated output. There is no GitHub release; last commit at review: 2025-08-04.
MIT-licensed project code; submodules keep their own licenses. It ships no game code or assets.

resources.name: AOTopsy
resources.description: Statically inspect Flutter/Dart AOT libapp.so files to recover available metadata, class structures, call edges and pseudocode without embedding a Dart VM or compiling a matching SDK. Supports ARM64 and x86_64 analysis paths.
requirements: Source builds require Go 1.25.4 according to go.mod (README says 1.25+). Supply a supported libapp.so AOT snapshot; the reviewed README models Dart 2.10–3.13. JIT snapshots are outside scope.

Ghidra/IDA integration is ARM64-only. Most instance-field names and local/captured variable names are removed from release builds; polymorphic dispatch and virtual-call reachability remain limited. Reconstructed Dart output is not guaranteed original or behaviorally equivalent source.

Unbounded --all decompilation can need about 64 GB RAM; use targeted or capped analysis. Accuracy and syntax measurements are author-reported, and the nonredistributable ground-truth corpus tests do not run in public CI.
BSD-3-Clause. AOTopsy credits the original unflutter project and its authors; Dart SDK-derived tables retain their own notices.

resources.name: hbctool
resources.description: Disassemble and reassemble supported React Native Hermes bytecode bundles through HASM files, enabling bytecode inspection and editing for the explicitly supported legacy HBC versions.
requirements: The reviewed package metadata is 0.1.5 and classified Alpha; it declares Python ^3.6 and docopt ^0.6.2. As checked on 2026-10-20, v0.1.5 is the latest tag and PyPI release (uploaded 2021-09-17) and there are no GitHub releases; the reviewed 2023-04-10 commit is still the main head, GitHub’s last recorded push was 2023-12-10, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.
README support is limited to HBC versions 59, 62, 74 and 76. Supply a compatible Hermes bytecode bundle.
This is a bytecode assembler/disassembler, not complete original-JavaScript recovery. Overflow patching is listed as future work. MIT-licensed.

resources.name: LSX II Volume Fixer: reconstructing volume behavior
resources.description: Uses measured USB-volume behavior and a macOS audio proxy to map volume keys to a KEF LSX II’s LAN control. The project reports more even steps while forwarding USB audio; the speaker firmware is unchanged.
requirements: Requires an LSX II connected by USB and on the same LAN, macOS 14+, Xcode Command Line Tools and administrator installation. The author reports testing on macOS 27; only LSX II is tested.
Builds from source with ad-hoc signing; Windows support is only proposed. MIT source is available.
The volume curve, latency and audio claims are author-reported.

resources.name: ArkWeb: a two-game movement and collision experiment
resources.description: Runs Spider-Man Remastered and Arkham Knight together, streaming Gotham collision into Spider-Man’s physics world and compositing his rendered frame into Arkham. This experimental runtime bridge is not a recovered standalone game or new engine.
requirements: Requires owned Steam copies of both games, Spider-Man 4.0630 specifically, Windows 10 x64, an Xbox-style controller and hardware able to run both games simultaneously.
Build prerequisites include Visual Studio 2019 C++ tools, Windows 10 SDK and Python 3.12 dependencies. Collision gaps, clipping, lighting and combat-pose limitations remain.
End-to-end operation is project-reported. AI setup/documentation collaboration is visible. Public source has no repository-wide license found in the reviewed tree; game files are not supplied.

resources.name: hw-harness: scanner USB protocol investigation
resources.description: Documents an author-reported scanner investigation comparing vendor-driver USB control transfers with Linux-driver traces to infer initialization, timing and resolution parameters. The released harness organizes reference capture and comparison; it does not automatically recover a complete protocol specification.
requirements: Developed on Fedora with libvirt/KVM and a Windows 11 Pro guest running the vendor driver. The documented USB case uses a Plustek scanner with device ID 07b3:1825; physical hardware is required.

USB passthrough, host-side usbmon capture, appropriate host privileges and a matching Linux-side operation are needed for comparable traces. The harness supplies capture/control tooling rather than an automatic protocol decoder.

The generic harness was published after the original bespoke investigation. Its separate MIPI camera example inspects configuration, ACPI and calibration data rather than using the scanner’s USB capture path.
Hardware outcomes and Claude involvement are author-reported.
The pinned harness code is MIT-licensed. Vendor software and driver dependencies remain separate inputs.

resources.name: Netzob
resources.description: Model communication protocols and infer message layouts from traces, with configured active learning for protocol state machines. Python APIs expose message fields, symbols and automata for parsing, traffic generation and fuzzing.
requirements: The upstream README requires Python 3.8+; the reviewed release metadata lists Linux x86/x64. Source builds need native build tools, Python headers, libpcap/libffi development libraries and the documented Graph::Easy dependency.

Latest PyPI release at review: 2.0.0, uploaded 2023-01-08. The reviewed source head identifies itself as 2.0.1.dev0, not a newer stable release. Its build pins Cython 0.29.32 and older dependencies including NumPy 1.24.1. As checked on 2026-10-20, the reviewed 2023-01-08 commit is still the master head and GitHub’s latest release is also 2.0.0; GitHub’s last recorded push was 2024-04-18, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

Provide representative raw/PCAP messages and analyst-selected models or symbols. Active grammar learning requires input/output symbols, a communication channel and target process control. The current inference documentation is explicitly unfinished.
GPL-3.0-or-later in the reviewed source notices; documentation uses CC-BY-SA. Inference and generated models require analyst validation.

resources.name: Scapy
resources.description: Script packet dissection, construction, request/reply matching and capture-file analysis in Python. Custom packet fields and layer bindings let analysts encode understood wire formats and investigate protocol behavior.
requirements: Reviewed stable release: 2.8.0, published 2026-10-02. Its package metadata requires Python >=3.7,<4; upstream says the 2.8 major version is the last to support Python 3.7 and 3.8. Use release-matched documentation rather than older cached version pages.

Linux, macOS and BSD have documented platform support; Windows requires Npcap. Live capture or packet transmission needs suitable interfaces and privileges. Offline capture analysis is a separate workflow, and libpcap requirements vary by platform and feature.

Optional features have additional dependencies, such as cryptography for cryptographic functionality and plotting tools for visual reports. Unknown formats require suitable custom Packet/Field definitions and bindings; dissection does not automatically infer complete protocol semantics or peer implementations.
GPL-2.0-only in the reviewed package metadata, with dependency and capture-driver licenses separate. The 2.8.0 release notes describe security fixes.

resources.name: Universal Radio Hacker (URH)
resources.description: Demodulate and decode signals captured with software-defined radios, with automatic modulation-parameter detection and customizable decodings. Analysts assign protocol fields and message types by hand or review rule-based automatic field inference; a fuzzer targets stateless protocols and a simulator supports stateful exchanges.
requirements: GitHub marks the repository archived and read-only since 2026-03-29. The last release is v2.10.0, published 2025-12-17 with a Windows x64 installer and a macOS DMG; PyPI 2.10.0 requires Python >=3.9.

Install options are the Windows installer, the macOS DMG (macOS 13+ recommended) or Homebrew, pipx on Linux (recommended, with precompiled native extensions), distribution packages and the Docker image. Source installs need Python 3.9+ and setuptools, and build C++ extensions.

Recording and sending need a supported SDR with a native or external backend; several listed devices are receive-only. Non-root Linux access requires the documented udev rules, and native support from distribution packages needs the SDR -dev packages installed first.
GPL-3.0. Automatic field inference gives the analyst a rule-based starting point. Fuzzing and simulation transmit through a TX-capable SDR.

resources.name: SavvyCAN
resources.description: Capture or load CAN bus traffic and investigate frames with sniffer, graphing, file-comparison and ISO-TP/UDS decoding views; loaded or analyst-edited DBC files map raw bytes to named signals. Separate custom-sender, fuzzing and UDS-scan windows transmit frames on a live bus.
requirements: Latest GitHub release: V220, published 2025-05-09, with Linux AppImage, Windows x64 and macOS builds; the README says the current macOS build appears to need macOS 10.15+. The project site's binary links and changelog end at V208 (2022) and are not V220 release notes. Its continuous build follows the newest commit without stability promises.
Source builds need Qt 5.14+ with QtSerialBus support; a Qt 6 work-in-progress branch is described as beta quality. The interface needs at least a 1024x768 display.

Live capture uses GVRET-firmware boards such as the recommended CANDue, or Qt SerialBus drivers including SocketCAN, Vector, PEAK and TinyCAN. Loading the listed log formats needs no capture device; CANDump/Kayak, PCAN Viewer and Wireshark SocketCAN PCAP support is read-only.

MIT. Fuzzing and UDS scanning send frames to connected vehicles or devices, and the fuzzing help warns this can cause unsafe behavior. Signal meanings come from DBC definitions or analyst work rather than automatic recovery.

resources.name: AALpy
resources.description: General-purpose Python automata-learning library that infers deterministic, non-deterministic, stochastic and pushdown models of black-box systems from active queries or passive traces. Its README links a separate Bluetooth Low Energy study whose repository reports learned connection and legacy-pairing state machines; message formats are not inferred.
requirements: Latest PyPI release: 1.6.2, uploaded 2026-08-03, requiring Python >=3.6. The reviewed master branch identifies itself as unreleased 2.0.0 and requires Python 3.10+; upstream says 1.6.2 is the last release for older Python versions.

Active learning needs a user-written system-under-learning adapter, an input alphabet and an equivalence oracle; passive learning needs traces in the documented format. Learned models are bounded by the chosen alphabet, abstraction and oracle.
pydot is the only Python dependency; visualizing models needs Graphviz on the PATH. MIT-licensed.

The ble-learning study repository is separate: it needs an nRF52840 dongle or development kit flashed with the supplied SweynTooth-derived firmware, Python 3.9 and its listed libraries, and it has no repository license file.

resources.name: Glasgow Interface Explorer
resources.description: Use FPGA-based open hardware and Python applets to read and write SPI flash, I2C EEPROM and parallel memory chips, determine JTAG pinouts, debug supported processors and analyze UART, SPI and QSPI transactions on physical devices.
requirements: Requires Glasgow hardware, bought pre-assembled or built from the open design, plus physical access and correct wiring to the target; some targets need external power. The manual lists its features as working with a revC board, except the analyzer2 logic-analyzer applet, which is currently revD0+ only.

Windows has self-contained MSI installers for Windows 7 SP1 or newer (Windows 7 also needs update KB4457144). Other platforms use the documented git and pipx source install with Python >=3.13,<3.16; Linux also needs the supplied udev rules. The repository has no tagged releases, and the package metadata marks the software as alpha.

Dual-licensed 0BSD or Apache-2.0. The built-in cycle-accurate logic analyzer for debugging applets is documented as temporarily removed pending internal architecture improvements. Applets cover the documented interfaces and memory or processor families; the target interface and parameters must still be identified, and Glasgow does not extract firmware automatically.

resources.name: Penguin
resources.description: Rehost embedded Linux firmware from an extracted root filesystem using a generated, editable configuration of emulation transformations, then refine it through a guest root shell, forwarded network services and recorded dynamic-analysis output.
requirements: Reviewed release: v3.1.21, published 2026-10-06 and tagged at the reviewed commit. Install by pulling the rehosting/penguin container from Docker Hub and installing its penguin wrapper script; source and Nix builds are documented separately.

Input is a root-filesystem tarball with permissions and ownership preserved, made with the bundled fw2tar or by hand. Penguin uses whole-system emulation with a replacement kernel selected for the detected architecture; it does not reproduce the original device faithfully or recover source code. Failed rehostings are refined by editing the configuration and rerunning.

The BAR 2025 workshop paper, co-located with NDSS, reports author-run results on 13,649 embedded Linux images from 69 vendors, with working rehostings for 75% more firmware than the prior state of the art. That evaluation predates this release.
GPL-2.0-or-later; the README also carries a U.S. Government rights notice. Findings from the emulated system need analyst interpretation.

resources.name: pyghidra-mcp
resources.description: PyGhidra-based MCP server that analyzes every binary in a Ghidra project and exposes decompilation, cross-references, call graphs, symbol and string search, indexed semantic code search, and renaming, typing and comment edits. A separate HTTP CLI client and an optional mode driving a Ghidra GUI it launches are included.
requirements: Reviewed release: v0.2.7, published 2026-09-25, with package metadata requiring Python >=3.10. The README describes the project as beta and under active development; main has later, unreleased MCP Python SDK 2 changes.

Outside the published container image, install Ghidra separately and point GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR at it. Semantic search uses a local ChromaDB index built in the background, so it can lag behind decompilation on large projects; ChromaDB and GZF artifacts are stored beside the Ghidra project.

The CLI client and GUI mode require the streamable HTTP transport; GUI mode launches Ghidra in-process and cannot attach to an already-running Ghidra. Import, delete, rename, type and comment tools change the project.
Apache-2.0.

resources.name: GoReSym
resources.description: Recover Go build metadata, function names and address ranges, source file and line tables, embedded types and strings from Go binaries, including stripped and some malformed unpacked samples. JSON output can be imported into IDA Pro with the included IDAPython script.
requirements: Reviewed release: v3.4.1, published 2026-09-14 and tagged at the reviewed commit, with prebuilt Linux, macOS and Windows archives; source builds need a recent Go toolchain.

Documented support covers ARM64 and Intel x86/x64 Mach-O, ELF and PE binaries in either endianness; pclntab parsing and moduledata location need Go 1.2+, and type parsing Go 1.5+. Some stripped binaries need a manual version override, and type parsing fails if that version is wrong.
MIT. Output is runtime and symbol metadata, not original source or decompiled code. The README's write-up link now redirects to a generic Mandiant page; the article is on the Google Cloud blog.

resources.name: rev.ng
resources.description: Open-source decompilation pipeline that lifts x86-64, AArch64, i386, ARM and MIPS code with QEMU, runs LLVM-based analyses and emits C designed to be valid and recompilable. Data layout analysis infers structures from pointer use; an editable YAML model and Python or TypeScript wrappers support automation. Its VSCode-based UI is a separate closed-beta product, with commercial plans announced.
requirements: Runs only on Linux x86-64; the docs suggest WSL on Windows and Docker on macOS, using linux/amd64 on Apple Silicon. The user installer downloads the current master distributable and the repository has no tagged releases, so this entry pins the reviewed develop-branch commit.

Developer setups use the orchestra package manager with binary archives or source builds. Scripting connects to a GraphQL API, locally or over the network; QEMU serves only as a lifter and code is not emulated.

GPL-2.0 as a whole because it depends on GPLv2 components such as QEMU; individual files are MIT-licensed. The rev.ng site describes the decompilation pipeline as Free Software. The UI is in closed beta, with free cloud use planned for public projects and commercial plans for private projects and a fully offline version.
Valid, recompilable C is a stated design goal; inferred types and names need analyst review.

resources.name: LeanREA
resources.description: An independent agent skill that routes application and binary investigations through ordinary command-line tools. It supplies batched triage recipes, targeted source/disassembly reading and explicit seen/inferred/unknown evidence labels, accompanied by a small author-reported comparison against an REA MCP workflow.
requirements: A plain-text skill for a shell-capable agent; it installs no analysis engine or decompiler and needs no REA MCP server. Manual installation needs a compatible skill client, the optional npx route Node.js/npm. Recipes need their own tools, such as ripgrep, jq, Go, Electron asar tooling or Xcode command-line tools; DecompileAll.java is not bundled.

The author’s benchmark used Claude Code 2.1.301, Sonnet 5.5 and macOS arm64 on Notion 7.35.1 app.asar, mac_utils.node and a gh binary built with Go 1.27.1, against rea-agents 6.5.0 over MCP. Reproducing it needs those locally obtained targets, Python 3, Node/npm, macOS tools and model access.

Across 12 runs per arm, LeanREA scores 74/75 checks to REA’s 75/75 at lower time, cost and turn counts; these are author records, and the no-skill arm’s correction from 66/75 to 67/75 rests on an unpublished answer.

Ground truth is hand-written regex keys, not behavioral-equivalence tests. Transcripts, target hashes and the resolved model ID (the default is the mutable sonnet alias) are unpublished, and the arms ran concurrently.
The 400.7k-token figure is a separate all-tools context probe, not the comparison setup. Native analysis engines and Android were not tested, and REA also offers a CLI.
MIT for the skill and benchmark code, crediting REA’s code and documentation and disclaiming affiliation; external tools, model services and targets keep their own terms.

resources.name: UU Remote on Linux: an unofficial protocol implementation
resources.description: Implements an unofficial native Linux host for NetEase UU Remote, using protocol behavior the maintainer says was recovered from official-client traffic and shipped programs. The Rust implementation connects selected desktop, input and auxiliary-tool channels to Linux services; an additional Linux viewer remains experimental. The author attributes development to Claude and Codex, without establishing REA use.
requirements: Reviewed version 0.2.8 implements selected protocol formats and session behavior in native Rust with small C components, without Wine or bundled NetEase binaries. The additional Linux viewer is experimental. Cargo.toml declares GPL-3.0-or-later; dependencies and official clients/services retain separate terms. This is not recovered vendor source or a replacement cloud backend.

The host needs Linux, stable Rust, a C toolchain, pkg-config, X11 development libraries and FFmpeg. GTK3 supports graphical login; the optional viewer also needs SDL2. Wayland/portal builds require additional libraries and authorized desktop access. Dependencies vary by feature.

UU cloud services remain required; the host and experimental viewer interoperate with supported official clients and hosts. Account connections use the user’s own authorized account; experimental remote assistance requires an explicitly enabled host and recipient-provided connection details. The project is unaffiliated with NetEase.

Public parsing and initialization code has synthetic checks for malformed inputs, capability replies and echo correlation. Local/virtual WebRTC peers test pending-desktop responses, independent tool connections and session isolation. These are implementation checks.

The README reports real-machine GNOME/X11 use and selected GNOME Wayland checks; other desktop coverage is largely virtual-machine based. Its viewer acceptance matrix is explicitly partial, with different official-host coverage for clipboard, audio, codecs and keyboards. These remain author-reported observations.

Wayland remains experimental, with single-screen and resolution/recovery limits. Multi-monitor switching is under development; HDR, privacy-screen mode, microphone forwarding and the Linux pre-login screen are unsupported. Restrictive-network relay behavior is not thoroughly tested.

resources.name: Perfect Dark: matching Nintendo 64 decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs Perfect Dark’s Nintendo 64 code with a documented matching-ROM build. The project combines reconstructed source with assets from a user-supplied original ROM, then checks version-specific artifact hashes. It is a reproducible-build research case, distinct from the separate native PC port; matching results remain project-reported here.
requirements: The reviewed GitHub repository mirrors Ryan Dwyer’s GitLab project. README describes a complete matching decompilation; six build targets cover NTSC beta, NTSC 1.0/final, PAL beta/final and Japanese final, with ntsc-final as default. This reconstructs an N64 ROM, not a Windows/Linux/macOS game executable or the separate Perfect Dark PC port.

Supply an independently authorized original ROM in non-byteswapped .z64 form, with header 0x80371240, named for the selected ROMID. make extract reads assets and comparison segments from that ROM; final builds also reuse extracted boot code. Existing extracted files are not overwritten, so modified inputs can invalidate matching results.

The documented host setup is Linux: GNU Make, host C/C++ tools, Python 3, MIPS binutils/GCC, armips, Capstone development files and the listed 32-bit libc headers. Initialize the pinned ido-static-recomp submodule. Matching mode reconstructs IDO 5.3 and 7.1 compiler tools from its IRIX inputs; optional GCC builds are nonmatching and limited to ntsc-1.0/ntsc-final.

After building, make test runs quiet MD5 verification against the selected version’s checksum manifest, including the final ROM and intermediate artifacts. The README also documents comparing base/built ROM hashes. The mutable status page reports all six versions complete/matching.

The repository declares MIT for source; original ROMs and extracted game assets retain separate rights. Compiler components have their own terms, including the submodule’s SGI notice for IDO 5.3; the project’s MIT declaration does not replace them.

resources.name: TCLimate: reconstructing selected TCL Home cloud controls
resources.description: Implements selected TCL Home air-conditioner controls and electricity reporting in a native macOS menu-bar app. It adapts earlier community protocol work and documents an Android-module investigation to recover a separate statistics request. Reported validation checks cloud state, not independent physical operation or complete device equivalence.
requirements: Reviewed v0.1.6 beta requires macOS 14+, internet access and a TCL account with already-paired ACs. Building needs Swift 6.0+, Xcode Command Line Tools and a persistent signing certificate for the packaged app. Pairing still uses TCL Home; local LAN control and direct Google sign-in are absent.

The protocol implementation credits nemesa’s MIT-licensed Home Assistant integration. The electricity API was reportedly identified through Android Flutter-module inspection and a successful request capture; original packages, captures and detailed investigation logs are not included in the repository.

Source guards commands using reported model/state fields, restricts target temperature to whole degrees from 16–30°C, and checks reported state after sending. Unsuccessful confirmation is marked. Extra controls depend on available fields and modes.

Author validation covers a Pakistan account and two Split AC-1 units: authentication, discovery, reported state, power, temperature and daily electricity. Modes, fan, airflow and other optional controls lack physical validation; other regions/models remain unverified.

Energy parsing preserves genuine zeros, excludes invalid readings and leaves missing days as gaps; a seven-day total requires all seven readings. No persistent energy history or cost estimate is implemented. Offline tests are reported but absent from the reviewed tree/package targets.

MIT covers project code, with attribution retained for the earlier integration. Official services and third-party material retain separate terms. This is an unofficial cloud-dependent client, not recovered TCL source or firmware; APIs may change independently of the app.

resources.name: Universal Modder
resources.description: Packages agent skills, three role briefs, a Python CLI and preconfigured fal MCP settings for modding PC games the user owns. Its reverse-engineering guidance sends managed, native and data-format work to external decompilers and debuggers, and requires a round-trip check before a reverse-engineered file format is used; one worked example ships an Age of Empires II sprite writer built this way. It is a modding toolkit with agent-written field notes, not a game decompilation, and its example results remain project-reported.
requirements: Package 0.2.0 ships twelve skills, three subagent role files, the um CLI and fal MCP settings for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, VS Code/Copilot, Cursor and OpenCode. Hosts need Git, Python 3.10+ and ffmpeg (uv recommended; Blender only for 3D-to-sprite rendering); Windows capture, input and launch run natively or from WSL.

Start from a game installation you own; no game files, ROMs or decompiled code are supplied, and decompiles and extracted assets stay out of the repository. Asset generation needs a fal API key or browser sign-in; ComfyUI is a local image alternative and Sprixen a separate paid API. Tools such as ILSpy, Cpp2IL, Ghidra, IDA, Cheat Engine, Frida and RenderDoc are installed separately.
The AoE2 DE .sld writer’s 0.9/255 mean error on a stock sprite, its September 2026 in-game test and a Terraria movement port’s 99.9% velocity match are author results.
CI checks the toolkit (tests, CLI help, index and a publish lint blocking game files, decompiled code and secrets). Field notes are agent-written with self-declared verification.

Rules limit work to owned games offline or on self-hosted servers and refuse injection into anti-cheat-protected online clients, cheats against other players, and DRM, anti-cheat or ownership-check bypasses. Code is MIT with fonts under the SIL OFL; generated assets follow fal and model terms, and games and tools keep theirs.

resources.name: Browserbase plugin: re-hosting Claude in Chrome’s browser bridge
