resources.description: Stands in for the Claude in Chrome extension side of Claude Code’s local browser bridge and runs the requested actions in Browserbase cloud browsers. The author’s thread describes the reverse-engineered framing, a 4-byte little-endian length before each JSON tool call, and the plugin maps 17 named tools onto Stagehand/CDP operations. It is an archived interoperability shim with several placeholder tools, not recovered Anthropic code or a verified equivalent of the extension.
requirements: The reviewed main branch is archived, and its commits are dated 2025-12-27. A SessionStart hook launches a Node forwarding server that moves any existing claude-mcp-browser-bridge-<user> socket in the temporary directory aside and listens in its place. Messages carry a 4-byte little-endian length plus JSON; only the execute_tool method is accepted, with 17 named tool handlers and errors for anything else.

Requires Claude Code with plugin support, the Claude in Chrome extension, Node.js 18+, the Browserbase SDK and Stagehand npm packages, and a Browserbase API key and project ID. As written, the start hook looks for the extension only under the macOS Chrome profile directory and stops when it is missing, so other hosts fail that check.

Navigation, input, screenshots, page reading, form filling and JavaScript run through Stagehand on cloud sessions; console and network reads rely on the plugin’s own listeners and page-injected tracking. update_plan only echoes the submitted plan, shortcuts return an empty list or a placeholder, and image upload and GIF export are placeholders. The author’s thread counts 19 extension tools; the reviewed dispatcher names 17.

The protocol account comes from the author’s X thread, not Anthropic documentation, and no captures or comparisons against the real extension are published. package.json declares Node test scripts, but the reviewed tree has no tests directory. The undocumented local interface may change with Claude Code or extension updates.

README states MIT, but the reviewed tree has no LICENSE file and GitHub detects no license. Claude Code, the Claude in Chrome extension and Browserbase services keep their own terms, and browsed pages are processed on Browserbase infrastructure.

resources.name: Visor: an independent Ray-Ban Meta glasses client
resources.description: Implements an Android replacement for the Meta AI companion app that speaks the Ray-Ban Meta glasses’ own Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct protocol, imports media, exposes settings and answers “Hey Meta” with a model the user chooses. The project wiki documents the link layers, encryption, services and Meta-side ownership steps, and lists 153 open questions. Testing is on real glasses rather than test suites, so behavior beyond the stated model and firmware remains unverified.
requirements: Reviewed just after release v1.3.1 (2026-10-18). README targets Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) tested on firmware 72387580077200100; other Meta glasses are untested. It needs an Android 10+ phone, a Meta account using password or email-code login (passkeys do not work) and, for the assistant, an Anthropic or OpenAI-compatible API key. The glasses accept one session at a time, so Visor and the Meta AI app displace each other.

Setup makes Visor the glasses’ owner app through Meta’s login and ownership-receipt services, so it still depends on a Meta account and Meta servers for setup, frame style and language packs. Source builds need three client tokens from the official Meta AI app, which the repository does not include; without them the app builds but login and ownership fail. Release builds read them from CI secrets.

Building needs JDK 21 and the Android SDK with platform 37. CI builds a debug APK with Gradle, and tagged releases publish a signed APK with a SHA-256 file; README lists the release certificate fingerprint. Modules separate wire format and ciphers, transport, session, identity, media, settings and the assistant, which stands in for Meta’s server with Claude or an OpenAI-compatible model.

There are no test suites: CONTRIBUTING asks for hardware trials and wire.log excerpts for protocol changes, and CLAUDE.md says the app works on real glasses as of 2026-10-05. The wiki marks unconfirmed facts and lists open questions, including unread payloads and model-specific values; CLAUDE.md also refers to a desktop Python client snapshot that the repository does not contain.

Visor is AGPL-3.0 and states it is unaffiliated with Meta or EssilorLuxottica; Meta’s services, app tokens, firmware and trademarks keep their own terms. CONTRIBUTING forbids getting unsigned software past the glasses’ signature checks. Claude is one selectable assistant backend, and the repository’s CLAUDE.md is a contributor guide.

resources.name: Super Mario Sunshine: a native PC port from an AI-assisted decompilation
resources.description: Builds a native PC port of Super Mario Sunshine’s North American release from a pinned matching-decompilation fork, adding a host platform layer for graphics, disc, audio, input and OS services. The fork’s README says AI was used extensively to reconstruct and match its code; the port documents scripted regression hashes and lockstep comparisons with retail captures. Functions that do not yet match can still behave differently from retail, and the game must come from the user’s own disc image.
requirements: Targets only the North American GMSE01 Rev 0 release. README reports the 32-bit Linux and macOS builds as playable, 64-bit Linux as playable but still being tested stage by stage, and 64-bit Windows as booting under Wine with native runtime checks. macOS builds x86_64, run under Rosetta 2 on Apple Silicon, because native arm64 cannot map game memory below 4 GiB.

Requires the user’s own GMSE01 Rev 0 disc image as .iso, .gcm or Dolphin .ciso; the port reads models, textures, levels, music and movies from it at run time and ships no game data. Given the image, the build also makes a standalone executable containing the game’s files, which README says must not be shared. Optional language, texture and HD-cutscene packs are separate.

build.sh and run.sh drive CMake, Python 3, patch, SDL2 and a host compiler: Ubuntu/Debian multilib GCC for the default 32-bit Linux build, Homebrew LLVM clang targeting x86_64 on macOS, or MSYS2 MINGW64 GCC on Windows. The decomp submodule is pinned to sms-english 967436b; PC-only changes are patches applied to copies of its sources, and the separate decomp build to a matching mario.dol uses its own GameCube toolchain.

At that pin, the fork’s PROGRESS.md reports, as of 2026-09-27, 99.57% fuzzy, 72.94% byte-perfect and 33.18% source-linked code, with 12,002 of 12,904 functions matching and a byte-identical rebuilt DOL that still links extracted objects for unfinished code; its README gives slightly higher 2026-09-29 figures. The port compiles the decomp’s 588 game, JSystem and THPPlayer units, so non-matching functions can still diverge from retail. It reports scripted headless runs hashed against a baseline and compared between 32- and 64-bit builds, lockstep tracing against retail Dolphin captures and qemu-ppc checks of math routines.

The port is MIT-licensed (SoftwareAura LLC) and the decomp fork is CC0-1.0; the game and the user’s disc contents keep separate rights. AI involvement is stated by the fork’s README and agent guides, which describe Claude and Codex orchestrators.

resources.name: Majora’s Mask: matching US N64 decompilation
resources.description: Recreates a C source base for The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask from information in the game and static or dynamic analysis, then rebuilds the US Nintendo 64 ROM. The build takes assets and assembly from a user-supplied ROM and checks the output against stored MD5 checksums. The team states it will not produce a PC port; the separately curated Zelda 64: Recompiled only credits it for headers and some functions.
requirements: README calls this a work-in-progress decompilation whose codebase may still change drastically, and warns that some parts of the ROM may not yet be shiftable, so modifications can be difficult. Only N64 US 1.0 is supported; the Makefile also lists a WIP N64 Japan 1.1 target with checksum comparison disabled. Majora’s Mask 3D is out of scope, and the output is an N64 ROM, not a PC executable.

Supply your own US Majora’s Mask ROM as the base ROM; .z64, .n64 and .v64 byte orders are accepted. The repository includes no game assets or assembly: the build decompresses the supplied ROM and derives files, assets and disassembled code and data from it before compiling a ROM and a compressed ROM.

The documented host is Linux, native or under WSL or a VM, with Debian or Ubuntu recommended: Git, build-essential, MIPS binutils, curl, Python 3 with pip and venv, libpng and libxml2. macOS and Docker have separate guides. The default compiler is a static recompilation of IDO 5.3 and 7.1 that the tools Makefile downloads from decompals/ido-static-recomp; GCC and NON_MATCHING builds turn the checksum comparison off.

A default build checks both ROMs against stored MD5 values and prints OK or FAILED; FAILED means a bad base ROM or non-matching code. CI builds the US version in matching mode and Japan 1.1 as non-matching, using base ROMs from the project’s build container. The project’s mutable progress badge read 100% at review while the README still says WIP.

The reviewed tree has no top-level license file and GitHub detects no license, so source reuse terms are unstated; ROM contents and derived assets keep their own rights. The README forbids contributions from anyone who has ever accessed leaked Nintendo 64 SDK, libultra or Zelda 64 source.

resources.name: wine-uwp: running packaged Windows Store apps on a patched Wine
resources.description: Extends Wine 11.17 so that signed MSIX Store apps, with Shapr3D as the main target, install and run on Linux without their source or symbols. About 49,000 changed lines add a DirectComposition implementation, composition swap chains and an app-model host, while Microsoft’s own XAML and app-model DLLs, harvested from a Windows 11 image on the user’s machine, run unmodified. The author says Claude did most of the reverse engineering and code; app support is uneven and checked by a project regression suite.
requirements: README’s app table reports Shapr3D sketching, modelling, menus, cloud sync, sign-in and STL/PDF export; Solitaire playable; Media Player playing audio from its own UI; Calculator fully working; Feedback Hub interactive; and Camera only reaching its own error page. Shapr3D for Linux (58d9173) packages this same pinned wine-uwp commit as a beta AppImage and Flatpak; it is unofficial and not affiliated with Shapr3D.

Needs the user’s own app package (.msix or .msixbundle, or Shapr3D’s .appinstaller, from which setup downloads about 1.8 GB) and Windows components extracted from Microsoft’s free Windows 11 evaluation ISO or another Windows 11 image. Neither the repositories nor the release packages contain them, and a commit hook refuses Windows binaries. Shapr3D also needs an account and a browser sign-in.

Building copies the vendored wine/ files over the Wine 11.17 source, then runs autoreconf, configure with --enable-archs=x86_64 and make; the WinRT stand-in shims build with clang-cl and lld-link against Windows SDK headers fetched by xwin. Shapr3D for Linux needs 64-bit Linux with glibc 2.38+, working Vulkan drivers and about 11 GB free during setup, and its releases build with flatpak-builder on the freedesktop 25.08 SDK.

regress.sh requires Calculator to stay pixel-identical to a committed baseline and other apps to come up on a private Xvfb display; release.sh smoke-tests that an empty setup reaches Shapr3D’s first screen. The Findings logs record failed approaches as well as fixes. These checks are project-reported.

Neither repository has a top-level license file, and GitHub detects none. The vendored Wine files carry LGPL-2.1-or-later headers and the setup app’s Cargo manifest declares the same; the shims and investigation tools state no license. Harvested Microsoft components and Store apps keep their own terms, and the plan notes that a distributable product would need clean-room replacements for them. The author’s X posts disclose heavy Claude assistance.

resources.name: DLSSNR-AMD: reimplementing DLSS 5 neural rendering for RDNA4
resources.description: Reimplements the neural-rendering network of NVIDIA’s DLSS 5 library as Vulkan compute shaders for AMD RX 9000 (RDNA4) cards and supplies it to games through an NGX-compatible core and ReShade or Vulkan-layer routes. The weights are not distributed: installers extract them, hash-checked, from the user’s own nvngx_dlssnr.dll 310.9.16 or 310.8.0. The project compares its output with NVIDIA’s DLL on an RTX 5090 and reports close, not bit-identical, pictures.
requirements: The reviewed 0.0.x main targets RX 9000 cards because the network needs RDNA4 FP8 matrix instructions, reached through VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix; README says it was tested only on an RX 9070 XT. Linux under Steam/Proton with Mesa 26.2+ is the main version; Windows is an experimental preview tested with AMD Software 26.9.2, slower by default and closer to Linux with precompiled ACO machine code. OpenGL games are unsupported, and README warns against online games with anti-cheat.

Requires the user’s own nvngx_dlssnr.dll, version 310.9.16 (both models) or 310.8.0 (the old model only); other versions are refused, and a model file is written only when every extracted entry matches a known hash. README says packages containing the model must not be shared. The optional int4-mixed network derives its weights at install from the user’s model and project calibration tables, which THIRD_PARTY.md says hold no weight values.

The documented build runs on Ubuntu 24.04 with git, curl, Python 3, CMake, Ninja, MinGW-w64 and multilib g++; fetch_deps.sh pins third-party components, including glslang 16.5.0 for reproducible SPIR-V, and the Windows DLLs are cross-compiled. Games reach the network through an NGX core loaded by OptiScaler-NR, for DirectX 11/12 titles with an upscaler option, or through ReShade-based routes that estimate motion from the picture.

For the 310.9.16 model, the verification notes report single-frame PSNR of 49.15–50.59 dB and SSIM of about 0.997 against NVIDIA’s unmodified DLL on an RTX 5090, plus short moving sequences, from one Tomb Raider (2013) frame and its downscales; the 310.8.0 comparison reports 45.56–49.06 dB. These are project measurements on one AMD card.

MIT covers the repository’s code; third-party components keep their own licenses, including GPL-3.0 OptiScaler-NR shipped as released. NVIDIA’s DLL and weights remain NVIDIA’s, and the project states it is not affiliated with NVIDIA or AMD. The repository does not describe how the network structure was recovered; its CLAUDE.md addresses coding assistants.

resources.name: Breath of the Wild: per-function matching decompilation of the Switch executable
resources.description: Reimplements part of Breath of the Wild’s Switch v1.5.0 main executable in C++ and checks each function against the original machine code. The project calls itself a hybrid decompilation/reimplementation: it contains no assets, its ELF holds only reimplemented functions and cannot run the game, and porting is an explicit non-goal.
requirements: README calls this an experimental work-in-progress decompilation of Switch v1.5.0. The About page scopes it to the main executable (game code and most statically linked libraries), excluding RomFS assets, dynamically linked SDK libraries, libcurl, NEX and most of Havok. Functions are matched individually rather than placed at original addresses, so this is not a whole-executable matching build, a playable game or a port.

Setup needs the user’s own main NSO executable from the Switch release. The pinned setup script verifies its hash, uses 1.5.0 directly and converts listed 1.6.0 or 1.9.0 executables to 1.5.0 with a project-hosted patch; RomFS and other game content are not used. The About page says the project is useless to anyone who does not own the game.

The installation guide assumes Linux (native or WSL) or macOS and lists Python 3, Ninja, CMake, ccache, xdelta3, Clang and a Rust toolchain; the pinned CMakeLists requires CMake 3.30. Setup fetches Clang 4.0.1 for game code and installs tools/check. Submodules supply sead, agl, EventFlow, NintendoSDK headers and the shared nx-decomp-tools; the decompiling guide works from Hex-Rays or Ghidra output.

tools/check diffs each listed function against the original executable, and data/uking_functions.csv records its status. At the pinned commit that list marks 32,079 of 113,490 functions matching, 514 non-matching, 7,601 work in progress, 6,270 library and 67,026 not decompiled; the mutable botw.link badges showed 17.493% by size and 30.398% by function on review.

The pinned tree has no root license file and GitHub detects none, so no reuse license is stated; submodules and Nintendo content keep their own terms, and the About page calls the work a legal gray zone. AGENTS.md sets disclosure and human-review rules for AI-assisted contributions.

resources.name: Skyward Sword: Wii decompilation with hash-checked relinking
resources.description: Reconstructs C++ source for The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword’s Wii main.dol and REL modules, starting from the user’s NTSC-U 1.0 (SOUE01) disc files. Objects marked matching are compiled from source and linked with objects split from the original, and the result is checked against SHA-1 hashes; the repository ships no assets or assembly and is not a port.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress Wii decompilation whose only supported version is SOUE01 (NTSC-U 1.0); configure.py also lists SOUP01, but the pinned tree has configuration only for SOUE01. The output is a rebuilt main.dol and REL set for the Wii, not a PC executable or port.

Building needs the user’s own SOUE01 game: README names sys/main.dol and files/rels.arc from its data partition as the only required files. The repository contains no game assets or assembly; decomp-toolkit splits the user’s files into objects locally, using the input hash and split tables in config/SOUE01.

Builds run natively on Windows with Python and ninja, or on Linux/macOS with ninja and the automatically downloaded wibo wrapper. configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.7.1, objdiff v3.4.1, binutils 2.42-1 and a 20250812 compiler bundle, selecting Metrowerks Wii/1.5 for most code and Wii/1.3 for most NW4R code; objdiff compares individual objects during development.

The default ninja target links source-built objects only for units marked Matching (493 in configure.py; 536 remain NonMatching) and uses the original extracted object for the rest, then checks main.dol and 636 RELs against build.sha1. A passing check shows output identity. decomp.dev’s report for the pinned commit lists 27.89% of code bytes and 33,940 of 76,968 functions matched; CI uses a private container holding game files.
The repository carries CC0-1.0; that dedication does not cover Nintendo’s game, its files or the downloaded compilers.

resources.name: 2 Ship 2 Harkinian: a native Majora’s Mask port built on the decompilation
resources.description: Builds native Windows, Linux and macOS versions of The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask from an adapted copy of the zeldaret/mm decompilation, with libultraship reimplementing N64 SDK functions. Game data comes from a user-supplied ROM and is packed into an archive that custom asset packs can override. It targets a playable PC port with enhancements, not a byte-identical ROM.
requirements: The reviewed develop commit follows release 5.0.1 (2026-08-25), published as Windows, Linux and macOS archives; nightly CI builds are for playtesting and may have bugs and crashes. The repository’s decomp_diff.py describes its game sources as changed decompilation code compared with the official zeldaret/mm repository. Rendering uses DirectX 11, OpenGL or Metal.

No copyrighted assets are included: supply a supported copy of Majora’s Mask. The docs list SHA-1 hashes for NTSC-U 1.0 and NTSC-U GC versions. Built-in extraction turns the supplied game into an mm.o2r archive; custom .o2r or .otr packs go in a mods folder, and the README notes that fast64 does not fully support MM.

Source builds need the libultraship, OTRExporter and ZAPDTR submodules plus CMake. Windows uses Visual Studio 2022 with the v143 toolset, Python 3 and at least 8 GB of RAM; the Linux lists include GCC or Clang, Ninja, SDL2, libzip, spdlog, tinyxml2 and Opus/Vorbis libraries; macOS needs Xcode tools with SDL2, libpng, GLEW, Ninja, CMake, nlohmann-json and libzip.

The README and build guide report no matching, checksum or fidelity checks for the port; the release notes list tweaks and bug fixes. Enhancement and randomizer code changes behavior relative to the original game.
The repository is CC0 1.0, and the libultraship submodule is MIT; game content from the user’s copy keeps its own rights, and the README says the project does not condone piracy.

resources.name: Ship of Harkinian: a native Ocarina of Time port built on the decompilation
resources.description: Builds Ocarina of Time as a native PC application from the OoT decompilation’s source, with libultraship standing in for the N64 libultra SDK and DirectX 11, OpenGL or Metal rendering. No game assets are shipped: they are converted from the user’s supported ROM into an .o2r archive, and the port adds save states, alternate and custom assets and other enhancements.
requirements: README presents Ship of Harkinian as built on libultraship and dependent on source from the OoT decompilation project; the soh/src tree carries that decomp-derived game code. The output is a modified native port (CMake project version 9.3.0) with added features, not a matching ROM build or a byte-for-byte reconstruction.

Play requires a legally acquired, supported Ocarina of Time ROM; docs/supportedHashes.json lists 19 SHA-1 entries covering PAL, NTSC (US/JP), GameCube, Master Quest and debug variants. Copyrighted assets are not included and are converted from that ROM into oot.o2r or oot-mq.o2r; prebuilt releases still need the ROM.

README documents Windows, Linux (AppImage) and macOS releases with DirectX 11, OpenGL or Metal; CMake also has Nintendo Switch and CafeOS (Wii U) branches. Source builds need CMake 3.26+, Python 3, Git and the libultraship and Torch submodules, plus Visual Studio 2022 (v143) on Windows or the listed distribution packages and minimum GCC/Clang versions on Linux.
The reviewed CI workflow builds Windows, macOS and Linux packages and generates soh.o2r; it runs no gameplay or fidelity comparison against the original game.

The pinned tree has no root license file and GitHub detects none; the randomizer’s 3drando component carries its own license, the submodules are separate repositories and Nintendo content keeps its own rights. README says the project does not condone piracy.

resources.name: The Minish Cap: a GBA decompilation targeting five ROMs
resources.description: Recreates a C source base for The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap from information in the game and static or dynamic analysis, building five Game Boy Advance ROMs: USA, EU, JP and two demos. Each version takes its assets from a user-supplied original ROM, and normal builds check the output’s SHA-1 hash. The project remains a work in progress, and some parts of the ROM may not yet be shiftable.
requirements: README calls this a WIP decompilation whose codebase can still change drastically, and warns that some parts of the ROM may not yet be shiftable, so modifications can be difficult. Its targets are tmc.gba (USA, the default), tmc_eu.gba, tmc_jp.gba, tmc_demo_usa.gba and tmc_demo_jp.gba. The output is a GBA ROM, not a native PC port.
The repository includes no game assets. Each version to be built needs its own original base ROM matching the SHA-1 listed in INSTALL.md; the build derives its assets from that ROM.

Builds run on Linux, on macOS with the Xcode command line tools (GNU make and sed are recommended), or on Windows through WSL, WSL2 or Cygwin. They need build-essential, Git, Python 3 with pip and pycparser, CMake, libpng, an arm-none-eabi-gcc toolchain (standalone or devkitPro gba-dev) and pret’s separate agbcc compiler installed into the tree.

COMPARE runs the SHA-1 check for normal builds and is off for CUSTOM builds, which INSTALL.md requires after modifying the game. The Jenkins pipeline builds all five versions with ROMs held on its build agent and publishes progress from the USA map file. For the reviewed commit, the matching log counts all 647,908 USA code bytes as source by the script’s own rules, which also count asm/src, asm/lib and libc objects, but only 238,628 of 13,933,140 data bytes.
The reviewed tree has no license file and GitHub detects no license, so reuse terms for the source are unstated; original ROMs, derived assets and agbcc keep their own terms.

resources.name: Ocarina of Time: decompilation with MD5-checked ROM builds for 16 versions
resources.description: Recreates a C source base for Ocarina of Time that rebuilds 16 Nintendo 64, GameCube and iQue Player ROM versions, using information from the game and static and dynamic analysis. Assets come from the user’s own ROM and each default build is checked against that version’s MD5; README states the project is not producing a PC port and still calls the repository a work in progress.
requirements: README describes recreating a source base from scratch using information inside the game and static and/or dynamic analysis, and states that it is not producing a PC port. It builds 16 N64, GameCube and iQue Player ROM versions (default gc-eu-mq-dbg); some ROM parts may not yet be shiftable, so modding can be difficult.

Each build needs the user’s own base ROM for the chosen version, matching an MD5 listed in README; the repository includes no game assets and extracts them from that ROM during setup. Native ports such as Ship of Harkinian, and recompilation projects, are separate from this repository’s output.

README documents Linux or WSL builds, with separate macOS and Docker guides, needing Git, build-essential, curl, Python 3.10+ with pip and venv, libxml2 and a MIPS binutils toolchain. N64 and GameCube code builds with IDO 7.1 and 5.3 through ido-static-recomp; iQue builds also use EGCS for some files, and an optional GCC build is non-matching.

With the default COMPARE=1, make checks the built ROM’s MD5 against the version’s checksum file and prints OK or FAILED; NON_MATCHING=1 or COMPILER=gcc turns the check off. GitHub Actions, using a private container holding the base ROMs, reported all 16 version builds successful for the pinned commit, and the mutable progress badge read 100% on review.
The pinned tree has no license file and GitHub detects none, so no reuse license is stated; Nintendo content and compiler components keep their own terms.

resources.name: BaoCut Design: porting reconstructed canvas and design-system editors
resources.description: Documents BaoCut’s design-canvas and design-system editors, which the project says it ported 1:1 from TypeScript reconstructions of Claude Design’s editors and hosts in agent sessions with annotation and export. Its runtime notes record identifier fixes checked against the original scripts and a structural comparison matching 19,111 of 20,463 canvas main-page functions. Unreviewed differences, the unpublished reconstruction record and reuse rights remain open; no hosted-backend recovery is claimed.
requirements: The source reconstructions (src/design-type, src/design-system-type) and their evidence are unpublished, and no original release is named.

BaoCut shims replace the globalThis.claude host interface, the parent-origin allowlist is empty, analytics are off, and rooms, sampling and hosted design-system installs are dropped. System fonts replace Anthropic Sans, but the Anthropicons icon font is still inlined with an unconfirmed license and slated for replacement; use independently authorized content.

Needs Node.js >=22.12.0, npm workspace dependencies and the apps/design-editor and apps/design-system-editor builds; the canvas keeps React 18.3.1 beside React 19, with Babel standalone 7.29.0. Full builds add Rust, CMake and platform tools; agent-made designs use a configured local agent CLI such as Codex.

BaoCut Community License 1.0 is source-available: personal, internal and content-creation use only; commercializing BaoCut or its code needs a separate license. Third-party notices give no reuse rights in the reconstructed Claude Design code or the icon font.

resources.name: Project Arwing: Star Fox recompiled from a matching disassembly
resources.description: Disassembles Star Fox’s 65816 and SuperFX code from runtime coverage and recursive descent, reassembles it into the original ROM, then translates it statically to C on a from-scratch SNES runtime for Windows, macOS and Linux. Code never reached in recorded sessions, and RAM code that no longer matches the ROM, falls back to an interpreter; the README reports identical per-frame hashes for both paths. The generated C is a mechanical translation rather than hand-decompiled source, and results remain project-reported.
requirements: README reports a byte-identical ROM rebuild, 34,472 65816 and 14,577 SuperFX instructions, and 99.4% CPU / 100% SuperFX dispatches running recompiled over 20k gameplay frames. It lists the intro, title, training, Corneria and other levels reached by random play as playable. Labels are auto-generated, unreached code remains data run by the interpreter, and audio was checked only indirectly, not against hardware.

Supply your own Star Fox (USA) (Rev 2) ROM matching the SHA-1 in README; other revisions and regions are untested. Graphics, models and music are extracted from it at build time. The source build expects a headerless image, while the installer strips a 512-byte copier header. No game data is included.

Releases target Windows x64, macOS 11+ (not notarized) and Linux x86_64/ARM64 AppImages. Source builds need Python (3.10+ on Windows) with Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools, Xcode command-line tools and SDL2, or gcc, SDL2, FreeType and DejaVu fonts; tools/build.py chains extraction, assembly, recompilation and compilation.

tools/build.py compares the reassembled ROM’s SHA-1 but only warns on a mismatch. The documented contributor check diffs --hashlog output from recompiled and --interp runs. CI assembles and recompiles without a ROM, zero-filling data.

MIT covers tools/, src/, installer/, res/ and the build scripts; LICENSE excludes asm/, a disassembly of Nintendo's Star Fox code, and anything extracted from a ROM. This is an unofficial fan project unaffiliated with Nintendo.

resources.name: Project Arwing (2): Star Fox 2 recompiled from a matching disassembly
resources.description: Rebuilds Star Fox 2 from a coverage-seeded 65816 and SuperFX disassembly that reassembles to the original ROM, then translates it statically to C for native Windows, macOS and Linux builds. Unreached code and RAM code that differs from the ROM run through an interpreter, and the README reports identical per-frame hashes against interpreted runs. It accepts the SNES Classic release image, not the 1995 prototypes; results remain project-reported.
requirements: README reports a byte-identical ROM rebuild, 66,520 65816 and 23,186 SuperFX instructions, and 99.7% CPU / 100% SuperFX dispatches running recompiled over 20k gameplay frames, listing intro, title, menus, map and missions as playable. Labels are auto-generated, unreached code stays as interpreted data, and audio was checked only indirectly. README says Smooth mode removes slowdown but, unlike the Star Fox project, adds no interpolated 60 fps frames yet.

Supply your own Star Fox 2 ROM from the SNES Classic / Mini release, matching the SHA-1 in README; the 1995 prototypes will not work. Graphics, models and music are extracted from it at build time, and battery saves are written beside the rebuilt ROM. No game data is included.

Releases target Windows x64, macOS 11+ (not notarized) and Linux x86_64/ARM64 AppImages. Source builds need Python (3.10+ on Windows) with Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools, Xcode command-line tools and SDL2, or gcc, SDL2, FreeType and DejaVu fonts; tools/build.py chains extraction, assembly, recompilation and compilation.

tools/build.py compares the reassembled ROM’s SHA-1 but only warns on a mismatch, and the documented contributor check diffs --hashlog output from recompiled and --interp runs. HD 3D hooks one of several projection routines and recovers sub-pixel positions for about 66–90% of vertices.

MIT covers tools/, src/, installer/, res/ and the build scripts; LICENSE excludes asm/, a disassembly of Nintendo's Star Fox 2 code, and anything extracted from a ROM. This is an unofficial fan project unaffiliated with Nintendo.

resources.name: Little Planet: Sonic CD recompiled from a matching disassembly
resources.description: Disassembles every executable file on the Sonic CD disc from runtime coverage and recursive descent, reassembles them byte-identically, and translates the code statically to C on a from-scratch Mega-CD runtime that replaces the BIOS with a high-level implementation. Recompiled blocks run only where memory still holds the code they came from, and a script compares 96 stage runs frame by frame against the interpreter. The project also patches in widescreen and per-zone saves; results remain project-reported.
requirements: README reports that all 112 executable files reassemble byte-identically to the Japanese release, that 622k instructions recompile into 22,897 blocks, and that boot, gameplay, audio and bit-exact save states work. The disassembly is code only; graphics, sound and level data stay on the user’s disc. True16:9 widescreen and saves after every zone patch the game’s own programs, so those options depart from the original game.

Supply your own Sonic CD disc image (cue/bin, iso, ccd/img/sub, chd, or cue with compressed audio). The Japanese G-6021 release, identified by a data-track SHA-1 in README, is the tested one; other releases boot but are untested. No BIOS dump is needed, and no disc data is included.

Releases target Windows x64 (installer or portable zip), macOS 11+ (not notarized) and Linux x86_64/ARM64 AppImages. Source builds need Python (3.10+ on Windows) and SDL3, with Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools, Xcode command-line tools or gcc/g++. The optional remastered opening also needs a separately built FFmpeg and a fetched video.

README documents tools/decomp.sh for extracting the disc, reassembling asm/ and comparing each file; tests/rc_check.sh compares per-frame RAM and CPU-PC hashes of recompiled and --interp runs across 96 scripted stages. README also reports SingleStepTests results: all 1.6M Z80 cases, and all 1M 68000 cases apart from some undocumented DIVS/ASR and address-error cases. CI tests only a homebrew test disc.

MIT covers the runtime, tools and installer. third_party/ code, the bundled LGPL 2.1 FFmpeg and LuanUP’s remastered opening, included with permission, keep their own terms, and nothing extracted from a disc is covered. The reviewed LICENSE’s exclusion note names Star Fox 2 rather than Sonic CD. The project is unofficial, unaffiliated with Sega.

resources.name: vf2-decomp: differentially validated Virtua Fighter 2 recovery
resources.description: Recovers Virtua Fighter 2 Version 2.1’s Sega Model 2A i960 program into portable, non-matching C17, accepting each recovered path only when it matches a reference i960 executor at controlled boundaries. The repository adds ROM validation, i960 and 68000 analysis tools, a bounded Model 2A hardware model and snapshot-based differential runners. README states that it is not yet a playable port; match flow, combat, physics, AI, rasterization and much of the audio remain open.
requirements: README describes a clean-room, non-matching recovery whose native runtime preserves CPU, frame, counter and mutable-memory state through repeated scheduler and gameplay dispatches, including a 1,270,824-instruction post-scheduler corridor with no interpreted instructions. It explicitly does not claim complete decompilation, a playable executable, full Model 2/TGP emulation, SCSP DSP audio or every gameplay branch. Unverified paths fail closed with VF2_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED.

ROM-backed analysis and differential tests need a user-supplied, legally obtained copy of the supported arcade ROM set. config/vf2_v22_roms.csv records only filenames, sizes and hashes, and vf2rom verifies the set. The repository contains no Sega game data, and contributors must not commit ROMs or reconstructed region images.

Builds use CMake with a C17 compiler and warnings treated as errors, plus an optional sanitizer configuration. STATUS lists GCC/Clang CI, and README names native Windows MSVC as the canonical agent workflow. Setting VF2_ROM_DIR enables the ROM-backed CTest targets; otherwise only ROM-independent tests run.

The vf2i960 native-dispatch commands run the recorded differential milestones, and vf2cycles advances recovered C and the reference executor from a shared snapshot, stopping in strict mode at the first unsupported block, reference failure or state mismatch. STATUS reports MATCH for the third through sixth dispatches. CI runs only ROM-independent tests, so the ROM-backed results remain project-reported.

BSD-3-Clause covers the project’s code; MAME and public Intel i960 documentation serve as cross-references, not included source. docs/LEGAL.md discloses 301 original Sega symbol names, taken from a later Model 2 port DLL, as non-clean-room naming, and an untracked Sonic The Fighters disassembly is used only as a navigation aid. AGENTS.md addresses coding agents.

resources.name: z2rs: an incremental Rust reconstruction of Zelda II checked against an emulator
resources.description: Rebuilds Zelda II: The Adventure of Link (NES) in Rust for desktop, browser and Android by replacing the game’s 6502 routines one at a time. A built-in interpreter still runs the user’s ROM and hands ported routines to Rust, while a verifier compares RAM, sprites, palette and frames with a reference emulator. It is a behavioral, clean-room-style reconstruction guided by a community disassembly, not a decompilation or a finished standalone engine.
requirements: The reviewed commit is release v0.5.2 (2026-10-10), with Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon) and Windows archives plus an Android 8.0+ APK; z2rs.com hosts the browser build. PROVENANCE.md says it is not yet a standalone reimplementation: ported routines register in trap tables and the rest of the ROM is interpreted. The pinned ports.toml still marks all 2,960 routines unported.

Only the No-Intro USA dump is accepted, identified by the hash of the ROM body without its 16-byte iNES header (CRC32 BA322865). Graphics, maps, text and music are read from that ROM at run time, and nothing from the game is in the repository. Co-op, widescreen, HD packs, the randomizer and other enhancements are optional additions; Android lacks online co-op, the randomizer and enhancements.

Source builds need stable Rust; the browser build adds the wasm32-unknown-unknown target and wasm-pack, Android adds the SDK, NDK and cargo-ndk, and the default desktop netplay feature needs a C compiler. Release archives are not code-signed. Online co-op uses a public signalling server by default, and the desktop build shows Discord presence unless it is turned off.

z2-verify runs the ROM in tetanes-core 0.15 beside z2rs with identical input and compares RAM, battery WRAM, sprite OAM, palette and framebuffer after every frame, with two documented edge allowances for that emulator. Long tests replay TASVideos movies downloaded separately, and ROM-dependent tests skip without their inputs. The reviewed workflow only packages releases; no published verification results were found.

The sole maintainer releases the code under MIT; vendored matchbox_socket is MIT OR Apache-2.0, and the game itself is not covered. Routine layout comes from the CC0 FiendsOfTheElements/z2disassembly submodule and Data Crystal notes; the project describes one maintainer working from that material, not a two-team clean room, and publishes only a snapshot of earlier private history.

resources.name: sm64ex: an enhanced Super Mario 64 PC port from the decompilation
resources.description: Builds native Super Mario 64 executables from decompiled source, extending the sm64-port fork of the n64decomp reconstruction with renderer, input, camera, save-format and external-data options. Game assets are extracted from the user’s own ROM at build time. It is a non-matching enhanced port, not a byte-identical ROM reconstruction.
requirements: The reviewed nightly branch (last pushed 2024-12-17) describes itself as a fork of sm64-port/sm64-port, which GitHub records as a fork of n64decomp/sm64, the separately catalogued ROM reconstruction. The Makefile builds PC targets only: it defines NON_MATCHING and AVOID_UB and forces COMPARE to 0.

Supply an original Super Mario 64 ROM named baserom.<version>.z64 for each version built (us by default, jp or eu); extract_assets.py compares its SHA-1 with the bundled reference before extracting assets. The sh (Shindou) option skips extraction and is labelled experimental in the Makefile and broken in the wiki option table; a 2020 known-issues page reports buggy EU text and missing EU audio.

The README defers building to the wiki, whose pages cover Linux (Python 3.6+, SDL2, GLEW, host GCC toolchain), Windows through MSYS2, FreeBSD, Raspberry Pi and an Emscripten/WebGL target; cross-compiling for Windows from Linux or WSL needs MXE, and OSX_BUILD enables macOS fixes. Renderers are OpenGL 2.1, OpenGL 1.3, Direct3D 11 and Direct3D 12, the DirectX ones only on Windows.

The Jenkinsfile builds us, eu and jp and rebuilds us after each enhancement patch, all with comparison disabled. Options such as disabled draw distance, analog camera, texture fixes and cheats intentionally change behavior, and the wiki notes the draw-distance option may affect gameplay.

GitHub detects no repository license and the reviewed tree has no root license file; bundled tools carry their own licenses, and the src/pc notice reproduces an n64-fast3d-engine license that forbids binary redistribution. Original Nintendo content is not supplied, and the README forbids uploading copyrighted assets.

resources.name: Ghostship: a libultraship native port of Super Mario 64
resources.description: Builds Super Mario 64 as a native PC, Switch and Android program by compiling decompilation-style game source against the libultraship platform library. A bundled extractor converts the user’s US or Japanese ROM into an O2R archive at first launch or build time. The project ships modern renderers, configuration menus and mod-archive loading, not a matching ROM.
requirements: The reviewed develop branch declares version 3.0.0, matching the latest “Alfa” release. Its src tree keeps the audio, engine, game, goddard and menu layout of the n64decomp/sm64 reconstruction, with port code under src/port.

Supply your own Super Mario 64 ROM in .z64 byte order: the README accepts only the US and Japanese releases and lists their SHA-1 values. PC releases convert it to sm64.o2r; the Switch build reuses an O2R generated on PC, and the Android app checks the ROM hash and converts it on the device. No game data is bundled.

Source builds use CMake with the libultraship and Torch submodules: Visual Studio 2022 with the v143 toolset, Python 3 and CMake on Windows, or GCC/Clang, Ninja, SDL2, libzip and the listed libraries on Linux. Renderers are DirectX 11, OpenGL, Metal and Vulkan where drivers allow. The building guide still names sf64.o2r and 2s2h.elf from other Harbour Masters ports.

GitHub Actions workflows build Windows, macOS, Linux, Switch and web packages. The README calls CI builds playtest-only and warns of bugs and crashes. No matching, regression or original-hardware comparison result is published.

The root LICENSE.md is MIT (2026, Lywx) for the project’s own code. Submodules keep their own terms, and Nintendo’s code-derived content and ROM assets are not licensed by it; the README says it does not condone piracy.

resources.name: Super Mario Sunshine: an in-progress matching GameCube decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs Super Mario Sunshine’s C++ source so that the original Metrowerks compiler reproduces byte-identical object files for four GameCube releases and the Switch 3D All-Stars build. The target binary comes from the user’s own disc image, and objdiff compares rebuilt objects function by function. The work is incomplete, and the repository publishes contribution rules for AI agents alongside its human workflow.
requirements: The README calls this a work-in-progress decompilation. configure.py defaults to GMSJ01 (JPN Rev 0) and also targets GMSP01, GMSE01, GMSJ01 Rev 1 and the GMSP01_NX build from Super Mario 3D All-Stars. Only objects marked Matching are linked by default; --non-matching links equivalent or modded objects. For GMSJ01 at the reviewed commit, decomp.dev reported 49.51% of code decompiled and 18.42% fully linked.

Copy your own disc image for each version into orig/<version>. ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ and TGC images are accepted, and the repository says it contains no game assets or assembly. The GMSJ01 symbol configuration is generated from the mario.MAP linker map found on that disc; the CI workflow notes that GMSE01 has no MAP file and skips symbol-order checks for it.

Builds need Python and Ninja on Windows, macOS or Linux; the build fetches decomp-toolkit, binutils and retro Metrowerks compilers (GC 1.2.5 for most code), and runs them through the wibo wrapper on macOS and Linux. objdiff compares rebuilt objects with those extracted from the original DOL, and each version’s build.sha1 records the target DOL hash.

AGENTS.md requires ninja baseline and changes_all regression reports for all five versions, each still reporting its DOL as OK. CI builds every version in a build container that supplies the original files and checks symbol order for changed units. These are project-reported checks and progress figures.

AGENTS.md, symlinked as CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md, sets workflows for AI agents. It bars unsupervised agents from MSL, MetroTRK, THPPlayer, Dolphin SDK and JSystem code and defers hard judgment calls to humans, but it does not quantify agent-written code. The repository declares CC0-1.0; Nintendo’s game, disc contents and the downloaded compilers keep separate rights.

resources.name: Dusklight: a native Twilight Princess port built on the decompilation
resources.description: Reimplements Twilight Princess as a native application for desktop and mobile platforms, building on the zeldaret/tp decompilation and the Aurora GameCube/Wii compatibility layer. It runs from the user’s own disc image with no bundled assets and aims to stay accurate to the original while adding options, enhancements and mods.
requirements: README calls Dusklight a reverse-engineered reimplementation that aims to be as accurate as possible while adding options, enhancements and tools. It is based on the zeldaret/tp decompilation, which README says is matching only for GameCube, so Wii discs still show the GameCube HUD and other GameCube specifics. This is a modified port, not a matching rebuild of the original executable.

No copyrighted assets are provided: the user supplies a dump of their own disc, and README says every commercial disc except the Korean Wii release is supported. The executable reads ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO and GCZ images directly.

Runtime needs a GPU with D3D12, Vulkan 1.1+ or Metal; D3D11 and Android OpenGL ES are best-effort without full accuracy or performance. The pinned tree has Windows, Linux, macOS, iOS, tvOS and Android platform folders, and CI builds Linux, macOS, iOS, Android and Windows targets. Source builds need CMake 3.25+, Python 3, the listed per-OS toolchains and recursive submodules, including Aurora.
The CI workflow builds packages but runs no comparison against the original game. Accuracy and enhancement claims are project-reported.

LICENSE.md is CC0-1.0; it does not cover Nintendo’s game or disc content, and submodules such as Aurora and the randomizer mod are separate repositories. README says the project does not accept primarily AI-generated contributions and warns of unaffiliated sites spreading AI-generated misinformation.

resources.name: Metaforce: a Metroid Prime engine reimplementation rebuilt on the decompilation
resources.description: Started in 2015 as a reverse-engineered reimplementation of the Metroid Prime engine, Metaforce has been rewritten on top of the PrimeDecomp matching decompilation. Its native app compiles that game code as non-matching C++ for desktop and mobile through the Aurora GameCube compatibility layer and loads a user-selected disc image. The README says builds are unavailable while the rewrite stabilizes.
requirements: README dates development to June 2015 by Cirrus and Antidote and says the project was recently rewritten on the PrimeDecomp matching decompilation; builds are unavailable while it stabilizes, although CI builds Windows, Linux, Apple and Android packages. The only GitHub release is a 2015 prerelease, so none corresponds to the rewrite. This is separate from Odrannnn/MetroidPrimePort, another native port built from PrimeDecomp.

The repository ships no game files; its orig/ version folders hold only placeholders. At startup the app takes or asks for a Metroid Prime disc image (ISO, GCM, CISO, GCZ, RVZ, WIA or TGC). CMake compiles the native target with TARGET_PC, NONMATCHING and VERSION=1, and configure.py names version 1 as the default GM8E01_00 (NTSC-U v1.088) build; the README lists no supported disc revisions.

Building needs CMake 3.25+, Python 3 and a recursive clone with the aurora, borealis and musyx submodules; Windows uses Visual Studio 2019 with the Clang and clang-cl components, macOS needs Xcode 11.5+, and Linux needs the listed Ubuntu, Arch or Fedora packages. README platforms are Windows 10+ (D3D12, Vulkan or D3D11), macOS 10.15+ (Metal), Linux (Vulkan), Android (Vulkan or OpenGL ES) and iOS (Metal); Android also needs SDK Platform 37, the NDK and JDK 17+.

configure.py still records per-object matching status across ten disc versions for the separate GameCube build, but CI ignores those files and builds only native packages. The reviewed sources publish no fidelity or gameplay checks for the native app.
Metaforce contributors’ code is MIT, and a separate LICENSE.decomp carries CC0 1.0; the reviewed files do not say which directories each covers. Disc content keeps its own rights.

resources.name: Super Mario Sunshine (USA): an AI-assisted matching decompilation fork
resources.description: Extends the doldecomp Super Mario Sunshine decompilation to the North American GMSE01 release. The README says AI was used extensively, and the repository’s agent rules, work order and progress files describe batch-based Claude and Codex orchestration. Its rebuilt DOL is reported byte-identical, but unfinished objects are still linked from code extracted from the user’s disc.
requirements: This hobby fork of doldecomp/sms targets GMSE01 (USA Rev 0). The README says it began when upstream’s Japanese decompilation was about 38% matched, and PROGRESS.md names upstream ab00c3c9 as its base. GMSJ01 and GMSP01 configs remain, but the README marks PAL as slightly broken and AGENTS.md says neither can be built or regression-tested in this clone.

Supply your own North American Rev 0 disc image in orig/GMSE01 (ISO, RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ or TGC). The GMSE01 build notes record the required extracted-DOL SHA-1. Those notes say the initial symbols came from a community-hosted marioUS.map that is not on the US disc, while AGENTS.md calls the US map a real map shipped on the disc.

Builds use Python 3 and Ninja on Windows, macOS (with Wine Crossover) or Linux (wibo on x86, Wine elsewhere), plus the pinned decomp-toolkit and Metrowerks tools. The output is build/GMSE01/mario.dol, checked against the extracted original. Playing it still needs the original disc image in Dolphin; a separate native PC port uses this fork as its decompilation submodule.

The README (2026-09-29) reports 99.60% fuzzy, 73.65% byte-perfect and 34.79% source-linked code, with 12,052 of 12,904 functions exact and 542 of 732 objects linked; PROGRESS.md (2026-09-27) gives slightly lower figures. The fork’s CI matrix builds only GMSJ01, so GMSE01 results are locally reported.

AGENTS.md, symlinked as CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md, lifts upstream’s ban on autonomous library work. It requires agents to work only from the binary, the linker map and the repository, and forbids fakematches and leaked SDK sources. The repository keeps CC0-1.0, while Nintendo content and the compilers keep separate rights.

resources.name: Donkey Kong 64: Recompiled — an N64Recomp native port
resources.description: Uses N64Recomp to statically recompile the US Nintendo 64 release of Donkey Kong 64 into a native port, with RT64 as the renderer. The port is not built from decompiled source, but borrows headers and some functions from the in-progress DK64 decompilation for patches and enhancements. Its recompiler configuration reads a checked-in symbol dump and the ROM rather than a decompilation ELF.
requirements: Plays only the user’s US Nintendo 64 Donkey Kong 64 ROM; other dump formats of that ROM are converted to .z64. The repository and releases contain no game assets, it is not an emulator for other ROMs, and the README describes modding and other-language support as future work.

Release v1.0.3 (2026-09-30) ships Windows, Linux x64/ARM64, Flatpak x64 and macOS ARM64 archives. The README requires a Direct3D 12.0 (Shader Model 6) or Vulkan 1.2 GPU and an AVX-capable CPU, and lists Intel GPUs on Linux, the prebuilt Linux binary on some distributions, and overlay software as known problems.

Source builds need a recursive clone, CMake and Ninja with Clang (Visual Studio 2022 with Clang and vcpkg curl on Windows), separately built N64Recomp and RSPRecomp, and a decompressed copy of the NTSC-U 1.0 ROM matching the SHA-1 in BUILDING.md; play still uses the standard ROM.

The README reports high-frame-rate, widescreen and input-lag improvements alongside cutscene edge quirks at very wide aspect ratios. It publishes no equivalence or gameplay test; pinned-commit CI only builds the port, with extra inputs from a secret-configured checkout.
GPLv3 project license; the original game, the decompilation submodule and other dependencies keep separate terms. CONTRIBUTING.md forbids AI-generated code contributions.

resources.name: Twilight Princess: a decompilation with fully matching GameCube code
resources.description: Reconstructs Twilight Princess source that compiles back to binaries identical to the originals, building GameCube, Wii and Nvidia Shield releases from one codebase through conditional compilation. README reports the GameCube code as completely matching but not every translation unit linked yet, with Debug and Wii alignment ongoing; the repository ships no assets or assembly and will not produce a port.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress decompilation with ten listed targets: three GameCube releases (GZ2E01, GZ2P01, GZ2J01), five Wii builds including a kiosk demo, and two Nvidia Shield China builds. Output is the original platform’s executable and REL modules; README states the project will not produce a PC or other port, and Dusklight is a separate project built on this code.

Building needs the user’s own disc image of the chosen version in a supported format (ISO/GCM, RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ or TGC), which can be deleted after the first build. The repository contains no game assets or assembly; decomp-toolkit splits the original locally.

Builds run natively on Windows with Python and ninja, or on Linux/macOS with ninja and the automatically downloaded wibo wrapper. configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.8.0, objdiff v3.6.1, binutils 2.42-1 and a 20251118 compiler bundle, selecting Metrowerks compiler versions per target and library; objdiff provides per-object diffing.

The default build links source-built objects for units marked complete and original extracted objects for the rest, then checks the output against each version’s build.sha1 (758 entries for GZ2E01). decomp.dev’s reports for the pinned commit list 100% of code matched for all three GameCube versions, with 2,583 of 2,608 units complete, against 54.47% for ShieldD and 47.06% for Wii RZDE01_00. CI runs in a private container holding game files.
LICENSE.md is CC0-1.0; it does not cover Nintendo’s game, disc content or the downloaded compilers.

resources.name: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night: matching decompilation across PlayStation, PSP and Saturn builds
resources.description: Recreates C source for Castlevania: Symphony of the Night from its PlayStation, PSP and Saturn binaries, aiming for code that compiles byte for byte to the original game files. The work-in-progress build combines decompiled code with assets and assembly extracted from a user-supplied disc image, then checks per-version SHA-1 hashes. Native PC experiments in the same tree are documented as unfinished and are not a released port.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress matching decompilation of four builds: us (PlayStation SLUS-00067, the reference), hd (an unreleased Japanese PS1 build found in Castlevania: Dracula X Chronicles data), pspeu (the European Dracula X Chronicles release) and saturn (the externally developed Saturn port). The Build wiki notes that some non-matching functions remain behind a NON_MATCHING macro and are not guaranteed to be functionally equivalent. README links mutable progress pages on sotn.xee.dev and decomp.dev.

The repository includes no game assets and none of the assembly needed to compile; README requires a prior copy of the game. The Build wiki asks for an unmodified US PlayStation disc as BIN/CUE, while the pinned Makefile reads both PSP-derived builds from a European Dracula X Chronicles ISO and the Saturn build from a Saturn BIN/CUE, each placed under disks/ with a version-specific name.

The Build wiki is tested against Ubuntu 24.04 LTS in CI and also covers Windows through WSL 2 and Arch-based distributions; a Dockerfile provides an Ubuntu Noble environment. Builds need Go, Rust, Python 3.12+, MIPS and SH binutils, a MIPS GCC, ninja and submodule tools such as m2c, maspsx, asm-differ, mipsmatch and decomp-permuter. Project-hosted prebuilt archives, including cc1-psx, mwccpsp, a Cygnus 2.7 toolchain and wibo, are checked against SHA-256 files; the Saturn build also uses dosemu.

Unless SKIP_CHECK is set, the pinned build code hashes its outputs against config/check.<version>.sha, which lists main.exe, DRA.BIN, RIC.BIN and stage and overlay files for us and shorter lists for hd, pspeu and saturn. The wiki still names a make check step that the pinned Makefile does not define. These checks compare file identity for the supplied version.

The Makefile also accepts a pc version and src/pc holds native-port code, but the PC Port wiki page says no working end-to-end port based on the decompilation exists yet. The repository declares AGPL-3.0, while disc images, extracted assets and assembly, and the downloaded compilers keep separate rights. CONTRIBUTING allows coding-agent assistance only for changes contributors can justify and operate manually and requires commits and pull requests without autonomous tooling.

resources.name: LEGO Island, portable: a multi-platform port of the decompiled source
resources.description: Adapts the LEGO Island decompilation into a portable build for desktop, mobile, console, DOS and Web targets. Windows-only subsystems are replaced with SDL3, miniaudio, iniparser and a custom Direct3D Retained Mode re-implementation, while core gameplay is meant to stay unchanged. It ports reconstructed source rather than checking byte-identical binaries, so it is distinct from the exact-rebuild decompilation case.
requirements: README describes a portable version of English LEGO Island 1.1 built on isledecomp/isle, aiming at platform independence without gameplay changes or rewrites for their own sake, and the contributor guide accepts LEGO1 changes mainly when they serve platform compatibility. Light modding goes through extensions, which in the reviewed tree include multiplayer, a third-person camera and asset loaders. The status table lists Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, DOS, Web, iOS, Android, Xbox One, PlayStation Vita, Nintendo Switch and Nintendo 3DS.

An existing copy of LEGO Island is required. The guided installer asks for the retail CD-ROM or a disc image made from it and says any 1.0 or 1.1 retail version in any language works; its optional HD audio pack is limited to English 1.1. The installer describes the isle.pizza Web build as streaming the game without a local disc.

Builds use CMake 3.25+ with a C++17 compiler; by default CMake fetches SDL3 and iniparser, and libsmacker and miniaudio are submodules. README points to the CI workflow instead of a separate build guide; that workflow uses MSVC, MinGW, macOS/Linux toolchains and platform SDKs such as Emscripten, devkitPro, VitaSDK, DJGPP and Android, and the desktop settings tool needs Qt 6. Release downloads are continuous builds of master, which README warns may regress.

CI checks formatting and configures, builds and packages each platform target; it does not run the game or compare its behavior with the original. The per-platform status entries are CI badges. Kaitai Struct descriptions document save, animation, world-database and texture formats.

The repository carries LGPL-3.0; bundled and fetched third-party libraries keep their own terms, and the original game data, LEGO trademarks and the bitmaps the installer takes from the original setup program retain separate rights.

resources.name: c1: a C port of PlayStation Crash Bandicoot
resources.description: Ports the original PlayStation Crash Bandicoot game code to C function by function; its coding standard labels functions with the addresses of their original implementations. Only the PC build, using OpenGL, SDL2 and FluidSynth, currently works; it loads asset files from the user’s game disc and is only partially playable.
requirements: The README reports the code as 100% ported but functionality at 78%. The tracked issue list includes crashes in several levels, incorrect camera and collision behavior, broken demo mode and title states, and behavior that changes under compiler optimization; the PlayStation (Psy-Q) build does not work.

Running needs the NSD/NSF asset files from the user’s own Crash Bandicoot disc; the repository ships no game data and the README does not name a supported disc region or version. The game boots into the title sequence unless a constant is changed and the code recompiled.

Only 32-bit x86 executables are supported, built with GNU Make and a 32-bit GNU toolchain (multilib GCC/G++ on 64-bit hosts) against OpenGL 2.0+, SDL2 and FluidSynth (cimgui is bundled). Compilation has been tested only on Ubuntu/Debian; there are no releases, and the last commit at review is 2024-01-22.
No byte-matching, equivalence or automated gameplay check is published. The repository has no license file, so reuse rights are unspecified, and the original game retains its own rights.

resources.name: Metroid Prime Port: an AI-assisted native port of the PrimeDecomp decompilation
resources.description: Compiles the PrimeDecomp decompilation of Metroid Prime’s game and engine code as native C++20 for Linux, Windows and Android, with an experimental macOS build. Aurora supplies the GameCube SDK compatibility layer and rendering, and the port reads a user-supplied disc image at run time. The author states that parts were written with AI coding assistants under their oversight.
requirements: The reviewed port-branch commit is 16 commits after release v0.29.0 (2026-10-17), which ships Windows, Linux tarball, AppImage, Flatpak, Android and macOS arm64 packages; the macOS build is experimental and has not been played on a real Mac. The repository forks PrimeDecomp/prime and adds widescreen, uncapped frame rate, controls, save conversion, a randomizer and an Archipelago client. It does not link the separate DolRecomp recompilation experiment, and its decomp/ GameCube build is not used by the port.

No game content is included: supply a GameCube USA 1.00, 1.01 or 1.02 (GM8E01) or PAL (GM8P01) disc image as .iso, .gcm, .rvz, .wbfs, .ciso or .nkit. Japanese, Korean, Wii Trilogy and Remastered releases are not run as the base game; an experimental importer can read models and effects from the user’s own Remastered dump.

Builds need CMake 3.25+, Ninja, a C++20 compiler and a C23-capable C compiler for MusyX; Windows uses clang-cl from LLVM in an MSVC developer environment, and Android builds through Gradle. Configuring downloads about a dozen SHA-256-checked dependencies; Linux links several statically and then needs only OpenSSL 3 and the C/C++ runtime. The macOS app is ad-hoc signed and not notarized.

CI builds and runs the disc-free CTest port suite on Linux with GCC 14 and Clang 18 for pushes and pull requests; Windows and macOS workflows run weekly or by hand, and the Windows job also checks that the package reaches main and reports the missing disc. Opt-in real-disc smoke drivers cover lifecycle, mouse, area-reload and world-jump scenarios, with results reported by the author. The 1.00 sequence-break option restores named script locks, not missing 1.00 geometry.

MIT covers only the project’s platform layer, scripts, tests, tools and docs. NOTICE says the game code in src/ and include/, the decompiled Dolphin SDK and the config/ symbol data derive from the retail executable, remain with their owners and are outside that grant, and that no game assets may be packaged; vendored and fetched components keep their own licenses. AI coding assistance is author-disclosed.

resources.name: The Wind Waker: a GameCube decompilation with hash-checked relinking
resources.description: Reconstructs source for The Wind Waker’s GameCube executable and REL modules across the USA/Korea, PAL and Japanese releases and a Japanese kiosk demo. Matched units are compiled from source and linked with objects split from the user’s disc, then checked against per-version SHA-1 hashes; the repository ships no assets or assembly and covers the GameCube game, not the HD remaster.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress GameCube decompilation supporting every GameCube version: GZLE01 (USA Rev 0 and Korea Rev 48), GZLP01 (PAL), GZLJ01 (Japan) and the D44J01 Japanese kiosk demo. Output is the original executable and REL modules, not a port.

Building needs the user’s own disc image of the chosen version in a supported format (ISO/GCM, RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ or TGC), which can be deleted after the first build. The repository contains no game assets or assembly; decomp-toolkit splits the original locally.

Builds run natively on Windows with Python and ninja, or on Linux/macOS with ninja and the automatically downloaded wibo wrapper. configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.8.3, objdiff v3.7.3, binutils 2.42-1 and a 20251118 compiler bundle; README also describes a shared Ghidra project as an aid whose output is not accurate enough to copy directly.

The default build links source-built objects only for units marked complete, uses original extracted objects for the rest and checks the result against the version’s build.sha1 (415–417 entries per version). decomp.dev’s reports for the pinned commit list 79.58% of GZLE01 code (32,968 of 39,324 functions) matched, 78.38–78.65% for the other retail versions and 74.08% for the demo. CI runs in a private container holding game files.
The repository carries CC0-1.0, which does not cover Nintendo’s game, disc content or the downloaded compilers. CONTRIBUTING.md rejects primarily AI-generated pull requests.

resources.name: Sonic Mania: a game-code decompilation for the RSDKv5 engine
resources.description: Reconstructs Sonic Mania’s game code in C and builds it with the separately decompiled RSDKv5 or RSDKv5U engine for Windows, Linux, Switch and Android. Assets must come from an official Sonic Mania (Plus) release; the project adds a mod loader and can build several retail versions. Its license describes the code as mostly functionally the same as the original, not byte-matching.
requirements: The repository describes itself as a complete decompilation of Sonic Mania (2017); its license says it also contains original code and that most code is expected to be functionally the same. It adds a built-in mod loader and API and can build 1.00 (console launch), 1.03 (PC launch) and 1.06 (Plus update) variants. The reviewed commit is 15 commits after release v1.1.1 (2025-11-01).

It does not run without assets from an official Sonic Mania (Plus) release for Windows (Steam or Epic Games Store), Switch, PS4 or Xbox One; the Netflix Games version is not supported. By default it builds with the bundled RSDKv5 engine submodule at revision 3 (RSDKv5U) and game version 6, the last Steam release; with WITH_RSDK off it builds only the game code, and RETRO_DISABLE_PLUS is to be enabled for distribution builds.

Clone recursively, because GitHub’s source ZIPs omit the required submodules. CMake builds use Visual Studio with vcpkg (libtheora, libogg, GLEW, GLFW3, SDL2) on Windows, build tools with GLEW, GLFW and libtheora development packages on Linux, devkitPro packages for Switch, and the engine repository’s instructions for Android. GL builds need a user-made shader mod for videos and filters.

CI builds Windows x86 and x64 and Linux binaries against both the RSDKv5 and RSDKv5U configurations. The project publishes no comparison with the original binaries, and its FAQ says bugs present in official releases will mostly not be fixed.

The custom Sonic Mania Decompilation Source Code License v1 allows copying, modification and distribution only for non-commercial use, requires stating that the code is not the distributor’s, forbids distributing game assets other than unique modded ones, and binds forks to the same terms. Sega’s game and assets keep their own rights.

resources.name: MediEvil Recomp: a PlayStation static recompilation to C#
resources.description: Statically recompiles the North American PlayStation release of MediEvil into C# with the RecompOne recompiler and runtime. The runtime stands in for BIOS, GPU, CD-ROM and other hardware services, and project patches change rendering, widescreen and terrain behavior. README stresses that this is a recompilation, not a decompilation, and labels it an open beta.
requirements: The reviewed tree targets the North American PlayStation release (SCUS-942.27); config/MediEvil.json lists the main executable and its overlays for RecompOne to translate. README calls this an open beta in which things will break, with stable 1.0 unreleased. The v0.2b changelog replaces the PGXP renderer with a native floating-point rendering patch and adds widescreen fixes and an automatic updater.

Requires a legally owned North American MediEvil disc in bin/cue or CHD form; README and disc/README.md name the two track .bin files and the .cue expected in disc/. The project does not supply game files. RecompOne states that its runtime needs no BIOS or other Sony files, only the game files.

Building needs Git with the pinned RecompOne and ShaderMod submodules and the .NET 10 SDK. Windows batch scripts or a manual RecompOne run against config/MediEvil.json generate the game code, which is then compiled as a .NET 10 application. Running needs the .NET 10 runtime, OpenAL and an OpenGL 2.1 GPU; v0.2b release packages cover Windows x64/arm64, macOS x64/arm64 and Linux x64.

The build workflow recompiles and compiles the project using disc inputs from a separate access-restricted repository, then uploads the build; it does not run the game or compare behavior with the original. README credits references from an unnamed decompilation for function names and patches.

MediEvilRecomp has no license file in the reviewed tree, so its reuse terms are unstated; the RecompOne submodule declares MIT. Original game content, including the executable code the recompiler translates, retains separate rights. Both READMEs state that no AI was used to write the code and that AI-generated contributions are rejected.

resources.name: Crash Bandicoot 2 Recompiled: a PSXRecomp native build
resources.description: A Windows launcher that uses the PSXRecomp recompiler and runtime to translate the user’s Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back disc to C and compile it locally, so the game runs as native code with an emulated PlayStation hardware layer. The repository holds the launcher, a patched vendored runtime and a long bring-up log; it distributes no game code or data.
requirements: Needs a disc image the user owns of the North American release (serial SCUS-94154), as .cue/.bin or .chd; the launcher checks tracks, sectors and boot serial and hashes the image. No PlayStation BIOS is required because MIT-licensed OpenBIOS is included, and locally generated files derived from the disc must not be redistributed.

Release v0.9.6 (2026-10-08) is a 64-bit Windows 10+ bundle; a first build takes about 3 GB of disk space and five to twenty minutes. Source use needs Python 3.11+ with PySide6 and the PSXRecomp MinGW-w64 Clang toolchain; the notes say MSVC is unsupported, and 59 runtime patches are kept in tuning/patches.

The README calls the game completable from start to finish but a work-in-progress preview with minor sound and graphical issues. Streamed level-code overlays are compiled natively when possible and otherwise fall back to a MIPS interpreter; the opt-in 60 FPS mode runs the emulated CPU at 200% and is not verified across the whole game.
Published checks are launcher settings and UI smoke tests, scenario scripts and a harness comparing its own Direct3D 12 and OpenGL renderers.

There is no top-level license file. The README lists PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 for PSXRecomp, MIT for OpenBIOS, zlib for SDL3 and LGPLv3 for Qt/PySide6; the game and its trademarks belong to their owners.

resources.name: Petari: a matching Super Mario Galaxy decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs Super Mario Galaxy’s Wii code as C++ that rebuilds, object by object, against main.dol files extracted from the user’s own Japanese, North American, PAL or Korean disc. Matched objects are linked from source and checked with objdiff and a target hash. The project describes itself as a work in progress, separate from any PC port, and says it does not accept AI-generated decompilation.
requirements: configure.py targets RMGJ01, RMGE01, RMGP01 and RMGK01, defaulting to the Korean RMGK01 build. Only objects marked Matching are linked unless --non-matching is used. For the reviewed commit, decomp.dev reported 100.00% of RMGK01 code decompiled with 68.75% fully linked, and 99.70% decompiled for the other three versions, with 55.61–58.17% linked. These figures are project-tracker results.

Extract your own copy of the game for the chosen region with Dolphin into orig/RMG<region>01; only sys/main.dol is needed. The repository says it contains no game assets or assembly. Each version’s config records the expected DOL SHA-1 in config.yml and build.sha1.

Builds need Python and Ninja on Windows, macOS or Linux; wibo runs the Windows tools on macOS and Linux. configure.py pins Metrowerks compiler packages from the GC 2.7–3.0a5.2 and Wii 1.0 families. The GitHub Actions workflow builds all four versions in a build container its comments call private.

CONTRIBUTING.md requires 1:1 matching for objects marked as decompiled, objdiff checks and a successful link. Every non-matching function in a pull request must link a decomp.me scratch, and decompiler output must not be copied directly. The README credits doldecomp bte, zeldaret tp (JSystem) and ogws as sources of code and headers.

The README states that AI or LLMs played no role in the decompilation and limits permitted AI use to cleanup, formatting, documentation and naming. That is a project statement. The repository declares CC0-1.0, while Nintendo content, extracted files and toolchains keep separate rights. The separate AstroCore PC port mentioned in the README has no public source here.

resources.name: Wind Waker HD Recomp: a native port by static recompilation of the Wii U game
resources.description: Statically recompiles The Wind Waker HD’s Wii U PowerPC code to C ahead of time, reimplements the Cafe OS libraries the game uses and implements GX2 graphics on Metal or Vulkan, producing native macOS, Linux, Windows and Android builds without a Cemu runtime. All game code and data are generated locally from the user’s own dump; an experimental macOS-only build can instead run functions from the separate ZeldaWWHDDecomp/wwhd decompilation.
requirements: README describes a static recompilation of the USA or European Wii U release (version 0, without the update) and reports the game playable from start to finish on macOS, Windows, Linux and Android. Known gaps include unimplemented geometry shaders and rectangle primitives and no controller rumble on macOS; true 60 fps is experimental. Unlike source decompilations such as zeldaret/tww, the default build runs machine-translated game code.

Needs the user’s own, legally obtained game: a .wud/.wux disc image with its disc key and the Wii U common key, a Cemu .wua archive, or an extracted game folder. Setup checks code/cking.rpx against the SHA-256 of each supported version. The repository and releases contain no game code, assets or keys, and the locally generated code and caches must not be redistributed.

Releases target Apple Silicon macOS 14+, Windows 10 1903+ or 11 on x86-64 or arm64, and glibc 2.35+ Linux on x86-64 or arm64, with Vulkan 1.3 (or 1.1/1.2 with VK_KHR_dynamic_rendering) where Vulkan is used; Android arm64 builds the game on the phone. First setup translates and compiles the code locally with a downloaded compiler (llvm-mingw on Windows, zig on Linux) or Apple’s command-line tools. Source builds need CMake 3.20+ and Python 3.

Reported checks are side-by-side rendering comparison with Cemu, players completing the game and, for the decompiled path, tools/verify’s function-by-function comparison of hand-written C++ with the recompiled original on generated and recorded inputs. The experimental decomp build (macOS, USA game only) runs 22,705 verified functions in 862 units at the pinned submodule. All results are project-reported.

Project code is MPL-2.0; vendored Cemu code is MPL-2.0, while metal-cpp, {fmt}, Dear ImGui, zstd and the AppImage runtime components keep their own licenses, and the game remains Nintendo’s property. README calls it an unofficial fan project.

resources.name: Castlevania 64: Recompiled — a beta static-recompilation port
resources.description: Uses N64Recomp to statically recompile the US 1.0 Nintendo 64 release of Castlevania into a native PC port rendered with RT64. Game-specific C patches build against headers from a separate Castlevania 64 decompilation. A beta release tagged at the reviewed commit reports a working build with known issues, while the README there still describes an unfinished project.
