requirements: The AppStream metadata describes Castlevania 64: Recompiled as an N64: Recompiled static recompilation into a native port using RT64 for rendering. The v0.5.0 beta release, tagged at the reviewed commit, calls itself a working build and lists known issues: Banjo Recomp assets still to be replaced, texture scrolls that do not animate above 30 FPS, and glitches in some looping animations. At the same commit the README still says the WIP recomp does not build, and BUILDING.md only says WIP.

The metadata says the original game is required. The launcher accepts a single entry, the US 1.0 release (game ID cv64.us.1.0) identified by a fixed ROM hash, and cv64.toml configures the NTSC 1.0 recompilation from a decompressed ELF plus an overlay list. CI copies that ELF and a decompressed ROM from a private repository through secrets; neither is in the public tree.

The CMake project needs CMake 3.20+, C++20 and the N64Recomp and RSPRecomp tools; the workflow pins an N64Recomp commit and builds Linux x64 and ARM64 AppImages, an x64 Flatpak, Windows and macOS targets. Patches compile as MIPS code with clang and ld.lld against headers from the k64ret/cv64 decompilation submodule, with symbol dumps from CV64Syms and submodules for N64ModernRuntime, RecompFrontend and RT64. Several sources and functions still carry Banjo names.
GitHub check runs recorded for the reviewed commit report successful builds on those platforms. No matching, test or performance results are documented.
COPYING is GPLv3 and the metadata declares GPL-3.0+; the original ROM and the dependencies keep their own terms.

resources.name: RSDKv5 Decompilation: reconstructing Retro Engine v5 and v5U
resources.description: Reconstructs the Retro Engine (RSDK) v5 and v5 Ultimate runtime, the engine that runs Sonic Mania’s game code, and builds it for Windows, Linux, Switch and Android. RSDKv5U can also run RSDKv3 and RSDKv4 games such as Sonic CD and Sonic 1 & 2. The project adds a mod loader, a shader compiler and extra Windows backends, and ships no game data.
requirements: The repository describes itself as a complete decompilation of Retro Engine v5 and v5Ultimate; its license says it also contains original code and that most code is meant to be functionally the same as the specified RSDK version. RETRO_REVISION defaults to 3 (RSDKv5U). The reviewed commit is 13 commits after release v1.1.1 (2025-11-01).

Neither game data nor game logic ships here. The engine loads data files from an official RSDKv5(U) game such as Sonic Mania (Plus), and game code comes from a separate project linked as Game, such as the Sonic Mania decompilation, which also bundles this engine. The FAQ covers Sonic Origins data files, which lack the games’ music and sound effects, and notes that release builds block the Origins Plus characters.

Clone recursively, because GitHub’s source ZIPs omit the required submodules. CMake builds use Visual Studio with vcpkg on Windows, GLEW, GLFW and libtheora development packages on Linux, devkitPro packages for Switch, and a separate Android guide; community forks for WebAssembly, New 3DS, Wii U, Wii and Vita are listed as possibly WIP or outdated. The default Windows DirectX backends support only XInput controllers, and GL builds need a user-made shader mod for videos and filters.

CI builds Windows x86 and x64, Linux and Android binaries. The project publishes no comparison with the original engine binaries, and the FAQ says bugs present in official releases will mostly not be fixed.

The custom RSDKv5(U) Decompilation Source Code License v2.1 requires any distributed prebuilt executable to have DLC disabled by default, forbids commercial use and distributing game assets other than unique modded ones, requires crediting Evening Star and the decompilation authors Rubberduckycooly and chuliRMG, and binds forks to the same terms. The README says Evening Star owns the Retro Engine.

resources.name: C2C: hybrid recompilation and hand decompilation of Crash Bandicoot 2
resources.description: An early reverse-engineering effort on PlayStation Crash Bandicoot 2 that converts the engine’s MIPS machine code directly into a very large C file and runs it against a modified PCSX-R emulator library for hardware I/O. Translated functions are meant to be decompiled by hand and moved into ordinary C, gradually replacing the mechanical translation.
requirements: Running needs the user’s own PAL Crash Bandicoot 2 disc as a raw BIN image with full sector headers and that disc’s SCES_009.67 executable, plus third-party PlayStation emulator GPU, SPU and two gamepad plugins and a 128 KB memory-card file; the repository ships no game data.

Windows only: the main program builds under Cygwin with GNU Make, GCC and SDL2, the emulator library needs Microsoft Visual C++ 2005 or later, and the optional C# disassembler needs Visual C# 2005 or later. Development ran on the develop branch from January to April 2015, and there are no releases. As checked on 2026-10-20, GitHub’s last recorded push was 2020-09-30, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

The README warns that the software is not intended for regular use and reports no playability status. Its translator does little decompiling and does not resolve indirect branches or jump tables, so code regions must be listed by hand; docs/FUNCTIONS.md names 18 of 818 listed function entry points.
No matching or equivalence check is published. The repository has no license file; the PCSX-R-derived emulator sources carry GPL-2.0-or-later headers, and the original game retains its own rights.

resources.name: MediEvil decompilation: an early checksum-gated PlayStation project
resources.description: Decompiles the US PlayStation release of MediEvil toward C source that rebuilds its main executable, game executable and 26 overlays. splat splits the user's own disc files, and the default build compares all 28 outputs with SHA-1 checksums. README describes the project as a work in progress and publishes no progress figure.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress decompilation of the US PlayStation MediEvil 1, with MediEvil 2 left for later. The Makefile targets SCUS_942.27, MEDIEVIL.EXE and 26 overlay binaries. In the reviewed tree most functions are still included as split assembly through INCLUDE_ASM rather than written in C, README's progress section is a placeholder, and the pinned commit dates from 2026-02-23.

Requires files from the user's own US MediEvil disc in disk/; the splat configuration expects SCUS_942.27 with a fixed SHA-1, and make extract splits the executables and overlays from those files. The repository supplies no game files.

The build expects a Linux-style host: GNU make, mipsel-linux-gnu binutils, Python 3 with the listed packages such as spimdisasm and rabbitizer, and the splat, m2c, maspsx and asm-differ submodules. C files go through a bundled PlayStation GCC 2.8.1 cc1 binary and maspsx. README points contributors to wiki pages for setup, the rebase workflow and the decompilation process.

make all builds every binary and runs sha1sum against config/medievil.check.sha; CI runs extraction and that check using disc files from an access-restricted repository. A passing check shows that the assembled outputs match those checksums.

The repository declares MIT; original game content, the bundled compiler binaries and the PSY-Q headers and data in the tree retain their own terms. The project is separate from the MediEvil Recomp static recompilation.

resources.name: Conker's Bad Fur Day: Recompiled — an N64Recomp native port
resources.description: Statically recompiles the US Nintendo 64 release of Conker’s Bad Fur Day with N64Recomp into a native Windows, Linux and macOS port on N64ModernRuntime and RT64. Function names and boundaries come from a vendored, still mostly assembly decompilation, while the recompiled code is taken from the user’s ROM so unmatched decompiled C cannot change behavior. The author reports heavy use of Claude Code across the project.
requirements: Requires the user’s US ROM in big-endian .z64 form with the SHA-1 listed in the README; the repository and release packages contain no game data. ROM hacks that change only assets are accepted, while hacks that change code and other regions’ ROMs are refused.

Release V0.1.6 (2026-10-13) packages Windows, Linux and macOS builds plus a mods archive. Rendering uses Direct3D 12 or Vulkan on Windows, Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS; Linux builds are tested on Ubuntu 24.04, and the unsigned macOS release targets Apple Silicon with macOS 15 or later.

Source builds need a recursive clone, Git and Python 3 plus Visual Studio 2022+ on Windows, CMake, Ninja, Clang and SDL2 on Linux, or full Xcode and Homebrew on macOS, in a path without an apostrophe. N64Recomp and RSPRecomp run from a committed symbol file; regenerating it with the optional decompilation build also needs IDO and MIPS binutils.

The README reports the game played through to the end, with a widescreen pause-background issue; a macOS play-through is not yet confirmed and Intel Macs are untried. Decompiled C must rebuild the ROM’s code byte for byte, and the port is checked by play and by comparison with the original in an emulator; names are marked as guesses.

The author reports heavy Claude Code use for the recompilation setup, tool patches, host application, mods and decompiled functions. Own code is MIT, but builds including GPLv3 N64ModernRuntime are distributed under GPLv3, an RT64 patch is GPL-2.0-or-later, and the game is not covered.

resources.name: ProjectCane: a native PC port of Sly Cooper and the Thievius Raccoonus
resources.description: Rebuilds the NTSC PlayStation 2 release of Sly Cooper and the Thievius Raccoonus as a native C++ game for Windows and Linux, running on data extracted from the player's own disc image. The README reports the full game as playable while work continues on accuracy and remaining differences from the original. It does not describe its reverse-engineering method or relate the port to the separate sly1 decompilation.
requirements: README describes a complete, playable native port of the NTSC release for Windows and Linux, including Steam Deck, that began as a map viewer; the Beta 0.4.1 release is tagged one commit before the reviewed revision. Work is said to continue on accuracy, performance, controller support, platform compatibility and remaining differences from the PS2 release. The repository description says the port was rebuilt through reverse engineering, but the README gives no method, symbol source or comparison with the original.

No original game data is included. Players supply their own NTSC disc image, which the bundled extractor identifies by the serial SCUS-97198, and the extracted Worlds and Cutscenes directories must sit beside the executable. The Beta 0.4.1 notes say game data must be extracted again after that update.

Windows builds use Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ desktop workload, plus the .NET 9 SDK for the Avalonia-based extractor, or CMake presets. Linux builds need CMake 3.22+, Ninja, a C++20 compiler, pkg-config and FFmpeg development libraries; CMake fetches GLFW 3.4 and SDL2, and graphics use OpenGL through glad with Dear ImGui. Portable AppImages are built in Docker against an Ubuntu 22.04 / glibc 2.35 baseline.
No automated tests, matching checks or side-by-side comparisons are documented, so playability and fidelity remain project claims.

No license file is present, so reuse terms for the source are unstated; Sly Cooper names and assets belong to their owners, and the README disclaims affiliation with Sony Interactive Entertainment and Sucker Punch Productions. The README also asks for Sly 2 or Sly 3 debug builds with symbols to support future ports.

resources.name: Firefighter: a decompiled DOS game ported to Rust
resources.description: Eric S. Raymond’s terminal port of Firefighter, Eben Sprinsock’s 1985 DOS shareware game. The project history says ChatGPT 5.5 decompiled the DOS binary to Borland Pascal and translated it to Rust, after which Raymond modernized the interface and corrected a scoring mismatch. Unchanged gameplay is the author’s statement; the intermediate Pascal and any comparison runs are not published.
requirements: The reviewed 1.2.0 release (2026-06-08) is a Rust terminal game for Unix-like systems: a 25×25 forest-fire board with easy, medium and hard modes, an optional RNG seed and mouse cursor movement. It needs a UTF-8 ANSI terminal of at least 80×25 with alternate-screen and raw-mode input; mouse movement also needs mouse reporting.

Build with Cargo (crossterm and rand); the Makefile wraps cargo build, installs the binary and renders the manual page with Asciidoctor. Building or playing the port needs no original DOS binary or game data; the history page links an Internet Archive copy of the shareware original.

The history lists the recovery steps: decompiling the DOS binary to Borland Pascal with ChatGPT 5.5, translating that to Rust, then adding interface changes, a seed option and a fix for per-difficulty maximum scores that did not match the score computation. The decompiled Pascal, prompts and original binary are not in the repository.

Verification is limited to make check (cargo check and clippy) and a few unit tests for option parsing, the display test pattern and maximum-score consistency. No comparison with the original program is published; unchanged gameplay logic is the author’s claim.

COPYING is BSD-2-Clause, and source headers name Raymond and Sprinsock as joint copyright holders; the README says the port is released with the original author’s permission. The shareware original keeps its own rights.

resources.name: flipper-telink: replacement firmware for Tuya Zigbee remotes
resources.description: A Flipper Zero app that bit-bangs Telink’s SWire debug interface to dump and reflash TLSR825x Zigbee devices, with static-analysis notes on the dumps and freshly written firmware for two of them. For Tuya TS0044/TS0046 scene remotes, the notes trace the stock ~500 ms single-click delay to a double-click window; the replacement firmware drops that window while presenting the stock model IDs to Zigbee2MQTT. The latest Zigbee build is marked unverified for pairing, actions and battery reporting.
requirements: Hardware: a Flipper Zero on Unleashed firmware (the notes name API 87.8; apps built with the official SDK will not load), wired to the target’s SWS pin, ground and 3.3 V. The flasher app builds with ufbt and a project-local SDK; the firmware builds with the Telink Zigbee+BLE SDK in a Docker tc32 toolchain and, once installed, updates over BLE OTA.

Inputs are the user’s own devices and their flash dumps. dumps/ publishes sanitized stock images of four devices, with Zigbee network state and Tuya credentials blanked by tools/sanitize_dump.py; raw dumps stay private. Stock firmware rights stay with its vendors, and the repository states no terms for these images.

The TS0044/TS0046 notes derive GPIO roles from the factory JSON config and trace a single click through a 300 ms double-click window plus event-queue, debounce and wake overhead, citing code addresses in the dump. Disassembly uses an included TC32 disassembler built from a third-party opcode table; the TS0046 application image is reported byte-identical to the TS0044 one apart from factory data.

Replacement firmware v00.14 sends short presses on release and holds after 1 s, identifies as the stock TS0044/TS0046 to Zigbee2MQTT and keeps a BLE service mode for OTA. The progress table records hardware checks for earlier versions; v00.14 was flashed to a TS0046, but pairing, actions and battery reporting in Zigbee2MQTT are marked unverified. The separate ZG-226Z alarm firmware is documented as built but not yet run on hardware.

The repository has no top-level license. Firmware directories carry a permissive notice for build files taken from pvvx/BZdevice and the Telink SDK’s Apache-2.0 license, and the notes credit pvvx’s SWire work. The README calls the project highly vibe-coded; the author’s post credits a pi agent running GLM-5.3.

resources.name: Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days: native PC port built on a matching decompilation
resources.description: Compiles the C of the khdays-decomp matching decompilation for Windows x64 and supplies a native platform layer for the Nintendo DS hardware, SDK services and sound driver. README reports the whole game running without an ARM interpreter; its rendering, controls, mod support and network multiplayer are the port’s own additions. This is a decompilation-based port, distinct from the byte-matching DS reconstruction it builds on.
requirements: Reviewed version 0.1.2 is labelled work in progress. README reports the title, Story Mode, Mission Mode, combat, the shop and save round-trips running natively; builds exist only for Windows x64, with Linux, macOS, Windows on ARM and Switch listed as planned. The pinned khdays-decomp submodule (a2b0478) reports all 306 EU YKGP modules byte-identical; the port compiles that C after build-time rewriting and does not reproduce the DS binary.

Supply your own European Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days ROM (game code YKGP); the tools check it against a single supported-ROM entry before preparing local game data. Optional HD screens, videos and menus are generated from the player’s own KINGDOM HEARTS HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX and HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue copies. The repository includes no ROM, assets, SDK files or game binaries.

Building needs Windows, Visual Studio 2026 with the C++ workload, CMake, Ninja, Python 3.11+ and pycparser; running needs a Direct3D 12 or Vulkan GPU. Build preparation rewrites game pointers as DS-address references and repairs ARM calling-convention gaps from a ROM-derived Ghidra ABI table; cases it cannot repair mechanically stop at named KHDAYS_ABI_GAP points.

Reported checks are ctest suites (MSVC static analysis, short libFuzzer runs, GPU renders compared with the port’s software DS engines, a DeSmuME savestate comparison) and scripted regression walks through Mission Mode, Story Mode, saving and multiplayer. Tests needing player data are skipped without it, and CI builds only the format library on Windows and Linux. Internet play is reported tried through the maintainer’s server, local-network play between two PCs not yet.

The port declares MIT; its third-party notices record the decompilation as CC0 1.0 and list SDL3 (zlib), Lua, Dear ImGui and other components under their own terms. No repository license applies to the original game or material extracted from it. README states that AI-assisted coding tools were used.

resources.name: ico-pc: a native ICO port compiled from the PS2 decompilation
resources.description: Compiles the decompiled C of the PlayStation 2 game ICO natively for Windows, Linux, Android, iPhone and Apple-silicon Macs, with host code standing in for the PS2 hardware and Sony libraries. No PS2 code is interpreted or recompiled, and the program reads the player's PAL disc image on first start. It is a native port of a separately byte-matched decompilation, with documented divergences and optional enhancements.
requirements: README describes a port of the PAL PS2 release (SCES-50760). The architecture guide says the game's decompiled C under ico2/ is compiled for the host, while port/ replaces the EE kernel, GS/VU1 rendering, SPU2 audio, disc, pad and memory-card services. Its platform table, current at release v0.7.10, lists 64-bit Windows 10/11, x86-64 and arm64 Linux, Steam Deck, Android 10+, iPhone through LiveContainer and Apple-silicon macOS 12+; the maintainer reports not testing the iPhone and Mac builds.

Requires the player's own PAL ICO disc image (SCES-50760) as .iso, .chd or .bin/.cue; other regions and editions are unsupported. Building needs no disc image, but the first run copies the game's files, about 1 GB, into the ico.o2r archive and loads the data tables from it. The legal notes exclude disc data, boot ELFs, assets and data tables from the repository and downloads.

Builds use CMake presets with Ninja. The Linux quickstart targets Debian 13 or Ubuntu 24.04 with gcc 14 (gcc 13 also builds), Python 3 and a fetch script that downloads about 1.6 GB of pinned toolchains and dependencies, among them llvm-mingw, mingw-w64 gcc, SDL3, Vulkan components and DXC. Rendering uses Vulkan, Direct3D 12 on Windows, or MoltenVK on Apple platforms.

CI runs hygiene and audit checks, builds and runs ctest on x86-64 and arm64 Linux, cross-builds Windows and packages Android, iPhone and macOS; disc-dependent tests skip without the player's image. The divergence list documents known differences from the PS2 and states that no test compares a run with the PS2. The upstream decompilation separately reports byte-identical PAL and Japanese boot ELFs, with most read-only data still taken from the disc.

README and LICENSE apply MIT only to the project's own code, scripts and documentation, granting no rights in the game, its data or Sony and Team Ico trademarks; third-party code is listed separately. The LICENSE notice says building requires a disc image, unlike the build guide.

resources.name: Sly Cooper and the Thievius Raccoonus: matching PlayStation 2 decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs source code for SCUS_971.98, the NTSC-U PlayStation 2 executable of Sly Cooper and the Thievius Raccoonus, as a work-in-progress matching decompilation. Functions not yet matched are still assembled from code split out of the user's own executable, and the build checks the linked ELF's SHA-1. The result runs in PCSX2 with the original disc for assets; it is not a native PC port.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress decompilation of the NTSC-U executable SCUS_971.98 (SHA-1 prefix 57dc305d) that aims to decompile the game engine to matching source. Its FAQ says the project has built a matching ELF since July 2024 and still aims to match 100% of functions. Engine, Splice scripting-engine and data progress are reported on decomp.dev.

The repository contains no game assets or original code. Users supply SCUS_971.98 from their own legally obtained disc, or an NTSC-U ISO for the quickstart script. Running the build requires PCSX2 2.0, the user's game ISO for assets and a BIOS from the user's own PS2.

Builds run on Debian-based Linux or WSL, with a Distrobox guide for other distributions. They need Python 3.9+ with the listed packages, MIPS binutils, Ninja, and Wine or wibo to run the downloaded ee-gcc 2.95.2 SN (ProDG) compiler archive. configure.py splits the ELF with splat, inserts split assembly in place of non-matching functions and links the executable; objdiff, decomp.me and CodeMatcher support matching, the last currently against the May 19, 2002 prototype.

By default the build checks out/SCUS_971.98 against config/checksum.sha1; --skip-checksum is documented for intentional code changes, whose output may not boot. CI downloads the original ELF through a repository secret and runs this check on main, and the check run recorded for the reviewed commit succeeded. This verifies byte identity of one executable.

The repository is dedicated under CC0 1.0; the original game, extracted assembly and data, and the ProDG compiler and SCE runtime library keep separate rights. CONTRIBUTING takes mangled function names from the May 2002 prototype's debug symbols.

resources.name: Pokémon Emerald: a matching Game Boy Advance decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs Pokémon Emerald for the Game Boy Advance as buildable C source, with game scripts and data kept as assembler directives. The default agbcc build produces pokeemerald.gba, and make compare checks it against the SHA-1 of the original English ROM; an optional modern-GCC build is not hash-checked. Graphics and audio sources are committed in the tree, so the documented build reads no base ROM.
requirements: README describes a decompilation of Pokémon Emerald that builds a single ROM, pokeemerald.gba; the Makefile sets game code BPEE, revision 0, and CI builds the English version. Most game code is C, while startup code, part of the m4a sound library and the GameCube multiboot library remain assembly files, and three multiboot programs (berry fix, Colosseum, e-Reader) are included as prebuilt .gba binaries. The output is a GBA ROM, not a native PC port.

The documented build reads no original ROM: graphics, audio samples and map data are committed as PNG, WAV/AIF and JSON files and converted by bundled tools. rom.sha1 records the target English release as SHA-1 f3ae088181bf583e55daf962a92bb46f4f1d07b7, and README links that ROM’s No-Intro record.

INSTALL.md covers Windows (WSL1 recommended; msys2 or Cygwin), macOS and Linux. On Debian/Ubuntu it lists build-essential, binutils-arm-none-eabi, git and libpng-dev; the matching build also needs pret/agbcc built and installed into the tree. make modern instead uses devkitARM’s arm-none-eabi-gcc and writes pokeemerald_modern.gba.

make compare runs a SHA-1 check of the built ROM against rom.sha1 and reports pokeemerald.gba: OK on a match; the Makefile notes that comparison only makes sense for non-modern builds. CI builds with COMPARE=1 and also builds the modern target. These checks establish byte identity for this one release.

The repository has no top-level license file and GitHub detects none; license files cover only some bundled tools, and agbcc’s GCC sources carry GPL v2. The original game’s code, graphics and audio remain subject to their rights holders.

resources.name: Paper Mario: matching Nintendo 64 decompilation for four releases
resources.description: Reconstructs Paper Mario’s Nintendo 64 code as C source that rebuilds the US, Japanese, PAL and iQue ROMs. The build takes assets and comparison inputs from a user-supplied original ROM, then checks each output against a recorded SHA-1. Mutable project reports list no remaining nonmatching functions, while the README still calls the decompilation work in progress; it is distinct from the PaperBoat native port.
requirements: README calls this a work-in-progress decompilation that builds US, JP, PAL and iQue ROMs, each with a listed SHA-1. For the reviewed commit, papermar.io’s mutable progress CSVs list zero nonmatching functions for all four versions (12,679 for US), and its US page announces 100% for US, PAL and iQue. The output is an N64 ROM, not a native PC executable; HarbourMasters’ PaperBoat port is a separate project.

At least one independently obtained original ROM matching a listed SHA-1 is required, supplied as that version’s baserom.z64; the Nix route expects all four. configure splits assets from those ROMs, and neither ROMs nor extracted assets are distributed with the source.

SETUP.md supports Linux, macOS, WSL 2 and Nix. The build uses a Python configure script with ninja, pigment64 from cargo, host MIPS binutils/GCC/cpp, and downloaded compiler builds: project GCC/binutils, GCC 2.7.2, EGCS and statically recompiled IDO 5.3. configure refuses a matching iQue build on macOS because EGCS is unavailable there.

A matching build ends with sha1sum checks against each version’s checksum.sha1, reporting “papermario.z64: OK”. --non-matching, --modern-gcc and --shift builds skip that check, so they are not matching results. Jenkins builds all four versions plus a shiftable US build and publishes the progress reports.

The reviewed tree has no top-level license file and GitHub detects none, so no reuse grant is established for the source. Original ROMs and extracted assets retain separate rights, and downloaded compilers carry their own terms.

resources.name: Budokai Tenkaichi 3: a native PC port built on a matching decompilation
resources.description: Compiles the decompiled code of Dragon Ball Z: Budokai Tenkaichi 3 (PS2, USA release SLUS-21678) for PC on a new renderer, sound, input and platform layer rather than an emulator. The game code comes from the separate BT3-Decompiled matching decompilation, and the game's data is read from the user's own disc image. The README reports the full game loop and experimental online play and says AI helped make the project; these results remain project-reported.
requirements: README describes a native PC port of the PS2 USA release, not an emulator: the game's code from BT3-Decompiled sits in src/ and include/ with PC changes behind #ifdef PORT, on a new platform layer with Vulkan and OpenGL 3.3 renderers, sound and input. It reports the whole game loop working (boot, movies, menus, saves, fights, split screen), plus experimental online play with rollback through a Cloudflare Worker matchmaking service whose source is included; the 32-bit Linux build has no rollback. The port log in docs/port records what is and is not verified.

Supply your own disc image of the unmodified USA release (SLUS-21678) as an .iso. The setup and install.py read the game's data from it and check SHA-1 digests of the extracted main program (SLUS_216.78) and menu program (BIN/DBZP.BIN); a patched or damaged image is rejected. The repository carries the built-in data tables as shapes without values (port/data), which the program fills from the disc at start; no game data is distributed.

Releases target 64-bit x86 Linux (glibc 2.35 or newer) and Windows 10/11 with Vulkan, falling back to OpenGL; Apple Silicon macOS is experimental and source-only. On Linux, install.py checks gcc/g++, clang with its Python bindings for the 64-bit pointer rewriting, glslc and SDL3, then reads the disc, builds the program and runs the game's demo fight headless as a self-test. Linux and Windows release archives are built in a Docker container (clang/LLVM, SDL3, mingw-w64) without any disc input.

The BT3-Decompiled README reports 99.92% of the main program's game code and 99.97% of the menu program in matching C, with both rebuilt binaries byte-identical; Sony SDK and CRI libraries are out of scope. The port log reports a replay recorded in PCSX2 matching console health values at sampled ticks and the final clock, while an early entry still noted differing fighter state words; macOS is reported to match the Linux state on every demo frame. These remain project-reported.

The port's own code is AGPL-3.0-only after commit 06e4671 and MIT up to and including it; bundled libraries keep their own terms. README states that the game code in src/ and include/ belongs to the game's rights holders, and BT3-Decompiled's CC0 1.0 dedication covers only its own reconstruction work. README says the project was made with AI help, and the docs carry working rules for parallel decompilation agents.

resources.name: D2R Mobile: rehosting Diablo II: Resurrected’s Switch program on Apple devices
resources.description: Runs the Nintendo Switch release’s own aarch64 program natively on iPhone, iPad and Apple silicon Macs, rewriting only instructions that depend on the Horizon kernel and supplying its system services and the NVN graphics API on Metal. Shaders are translated offline from the user’s files, and the project adds its own touch interface and endgame features. It is a rehosting compatibility layer, not a decompilation or recompiled source.
requirements: Targets only the Switch release with the Reign of the Warlock expansion at 1.0.34.0 (PC 3.3.94012); the rewrite rules stop on other versions. README reports iPhone/iPad builds for A14/M1 or later (iOS 26, or iOS 18–25 via an older-API build) and native Apple silicon Mac builds; A16-and-earlier devices need an extra texture pack, Apple TV is a community developer preview, and Intel Macs, A13-and-earlier chips and online play are unsupported.

Supply your own Switch program files (ExeFS main, sdk and subsdk0) and RomFS update data for that version; the rewritten program, translated shaders and on-device resource folder are generated locally from them. The repository holds no game code, art, text or shaders, but records shader interface tables, graphics-API names and about 800 main-program addresses, itemized in docs/DERIVED.md.

The main route is a full build on an Apple silicon Mac with Xcode, the Python environment that setup.sh prepares and an Apple signing account; a no-Xcode route packages a prebuilt shell on Windows, with Linux packaging and sideloading-tool signing reported unverified. Shader translation bundles Ryujinx’s translator, and SPIRV-Cross emits Metal source.

dm/verify documents structural checks and Unicorn-based equivalence tests for every rewrite site, which need only the user’s files, plus unit tests. Save, tick-state and screenshot gates compare against ground-truth recordings from a patched Ryujinx; those recordings and driver scripts are not shipped, so these gates cannot be rerun from the repository. README reports a 44-device closed beta and dated iPhone 17 Pro Max measurements.

The project declares MIT; bundled third-party code keeps its own license (the Ryujinx translator MIT, deko3d-derived code zlib, FLIP BSD 3-Clause). Seven offline-play rewrites come from a community patch whose authorship and license are unknown. Blizzard and Nintendo retain their rights in the game.

resources.name: Ratchet & Clank: a matching PS2 decompilation with a documented agent workflow
resources.description: Reconstructs C source for SCES_509.16, the PAL v2.00 PlayStation 2 executable of Ratchet & Clank (2002), with every function linked at its retail address. Functions not yet decompiled are still built from disassembly generated from the user's own executable, and the build audits functions, layout and the whole image against retail. The project documents an LLM-agent matching workflow and written build-fidelity rules for what counts as a match.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress matching decompilation of SCES_509.16 (PAL v2.00) within the OpenRAC initiative; matched code is then refactored toward readable C++, with matching builds as regression tests. BUILD_FIDELITY.md records 3,591 matched functions as of 2026-10-07, and live progress is published on openrac.dev and bytematch.dev. The repository description names native PC reimplementation as a later goal; no port is part of this repository.

No game assets, retail executables or disassembly are included. Users supply SCES_509.16 from their own disc image, checked against the SHA-1 in README and LEGAL.md, and tools/setup_asm.sh generates the disassembly locally. LEGAL.md says the repository will not build a runnable game for anyone who does not own and dump a copy. Credited sibling projects, such as the Lombyte NTSC decompilation and the ReRAC PC port, are references.

Linux and macOS builds run in a prebuilt Wine container under Docker or Podman; Windows builds use Git Bash and Python 3.10+ natively, with a short repository path. Both clone community mirrors of SN Systems ProDG for PS2 3.01 and the SCE PS2 SDK 2.4. Game code compiles with ProDG GCC 2.95.3 and Sony SDK objects with EE-GCC 2.9-ee-991111; GNU as is used together with listed tools that model the original ps2eeas assembler and linker behaviour.

tools/build_sn.sh rebuilds from scratch, audits each decompiled function's bytes and address against retail, and compares every loaded section, allowing differences only inside known near-miss C functions; level code is checked per function. The image therefore matches retail outside in-progress functions rather than as a whole. CI enforces the build-fidelity list.

AGENT_WORKFLOW.md describes a lead model directing tiers of worker models whose candidates a strict match tool accepts or rejects; a Claude Code worker definition is committed, and a Ghidra MCP container serves decompilation to agents. Project code is GPLv3; reconstructed libraries and third-party components keep their own licenses, and the game and toolchains keep separate rights. CONTRIBUTING bans Sony SDK source and leaked material, and LEGAL.md reports that movie code derived from an SDK sample was reverted to assembly on 2026-09-30.

resources.name: Banjo: Recompiled — an N64Recomp Banjo-Kazooie native port
resources.description: Uses N64Recomp to statically recompile the US 1.0 Nintendo 64 release of Banjo-Kazooie into a native port on N64ModernRuntime, rendered by RT64 and extended with mod support. Like Zelda 64: Recompiled, it is not built from decompiled source; a symbols repository generated from the Banjo-Kazooie decompilation supplies function names for locating code in the ROM and writing patches.
requirements: Plays only the user’s US 1.0 Nintendo 64 Banjo-Kazooie ROM, loading assets from it at startup; other dump formats of that ROM are converted to .z64. The repository and releases contain no game assets, and it is not an emulator for other ROMs; the game is changed through mods instead.

Release v1.0.2 (2026-07-31) ships Windows, macOS, Linux x64/ARM64 and Flatpak x64 builds. Runtime graphics need Direct3D 12.0 with Shader Model 6, Vulkan 1.2 or Metal Argument Buffers Tier 2; x86-64 CPUs need SSE4.1, and Macs need macOS 13.0+ with Apple Silicon or a 7th-generation Intel CPU.

Source builds need a recursive clone, CMake and Ninja with Clang (Visual Studio 2022 with Clang plus make on Windows), separately built N64Recomp and RSPRecomp, the BanjoRecompSyms submodule and a decompressed copy of the NTSC-U 1.0 ROM matching the SHA-1 in BUILDING.md; play uses the standard ROM.

The README reports faithful audio, intact N64 effects, widescreen, high frame rates, note saving and fixed duplicate Mumbo token IDs, and lists overlay software as a known problem. It publishes no equivalence or gameplay test; pinned-commit CI only builds the port.
GPLv3 project license; the original game, the decompilation and other dependencies keep separate terms. The team states that it does not use generative AI and bans GenAI-assisted contributions.

resources.name: Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen: a matching Game Boy Advance decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs the English Game Boy Advance releases of Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen as buildable C source, with game scripts and data kept as assembler directives. Default agbcc builds produce six ROM images, covering both games' 1.0 and 1.1 releases and two variants labeled switch, each checked against its own SHA-1 manifest. Graphics and audio sources are committed in the tree, so the documented build reads no base ROM.
requirements: README describes a decompilation of English FireRed and LeafGreen that builds six ROM images: each game’s original and rev1 releases plus variants named _switch, which config.mk builds as revision 10. INSTALL.md documents make, make leafgreen and the rev1 targets; the Makefile adds the _switch targets. Most code is C, while startup code, part of the m4a sound library and the GameCube multiboot library remain assembly, and three multiboot programs are included as prebuilt .gba binaries. The outputs are GBA ROMs, not a native PC port.

The documented build reads no original ROM: graphics, audio samples and map data are committed as PNG, WAV/AIF and JSON files and converted by bundled tools. Six .sha1 manifests name the target images (for example pokefirered.gba, SHA-1 41cb23d8dccc8ebd7c649cd8fbb58eeace6e2fdc), and README links each image’s No-Intro record. The contributor helper compare.sh hex-diffs the output against a baserom.gba only when one is present.

INSTALL.md covers Windows (WSL1 recommended; msys2 or Cygwin), macOS and Linux. On Debian/Ubuntu it lists build-essential, binutils-arm-none-eabi, git and libpng-dev; the matching builds also need pret/agbcc built and installed into the tree. make modern and the matching *_modern targets use devkitARM’s arm-none-eabi-gcc, and a TOOLCHAIN variable selects another ARM toolchain.

make compare and the compare_* targets check each built image against its .sha1 manifest; config.mk notes that comparison only makes sense for non-modern builds. CI compares all six images and also builds the modern target. docs/bugs_and_glitches.md lists original-game bugs that the optional BUGFIX and UBFIX defines change, so those builds intentionally diverge. These checks establish byte identity for the listed images.

The repository has no top-level license file and GitHub detects none; license files cover only some bundled tools, and agbcc’s GCC sources carry GPL v2. The original games’ code, graphics and audio remain subject to their rights holders.

resources.name: PaperBoat: a native Paper Mario port built on the decompilation
resources.description: Compiles Paper Mario decompilation sources, credited to the pmret and Paper Mario DX projects, into a native US-version application on libultraship. Torch converts the user’s own ROM into a local asset archive, and the port adds rendering backends, enhancements and archive-based mods. Desktop releases are published, while Android, iOS and web builds are documented on the development branch.
requirements: The reviewed develop snapshot follows release 1.0.3 (2026-10-11), whose packages cover Windows, Linux and macOS. CMake compiles the decompilation’s game C sources for VERSION_US with port code replacing the N64 boot and most OS layers. This is a native port that deliberately adds enhancements and fixes, not a matching ROM build or a static recompilation.

Requires the user’s US Paper Mario ROM with the SHA-1 listed in the README; config.yml carries recipes for that hash only, and the README states no copyrighted assets are included. Torch generates the pm64.o2r game archive on the user’s machine or device; that archive never ships with the app.

Source builds need the Torch and libultraship submodules, CMake 3.24+, Ninja and C99/C++20 compilers. Windows uses Visual Studio 2022 with clang-cl, because plain MSVC cl.exe is unsupported for the C99 decompilation sources. Renderers are DirectX 11, OpenGL and Metal. Android arm64-v8a, iOS 16.3+ and Emscripten builds are documented, with scripting and native mods disabled there.

The CI workflow builds Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and web artifacts and checks package contents; the platform guide states CI never touches a ROM, and its named desktop check script is absent from the reviewed tree. Nightly builds are labeled playtest-only with expected bugs and crashes. No gameplay-equivalence or performance results are reported.

The repository carries CC0-1.0 text, but GitHub detects no license for the credited pmret and Paper Mario DX repositories, and submodules have separate terms; the CC0 file is not treated as a grant over inherited code or game content. The README says AI-assisted pull requests are accepted under a HarbourMasters policy.

resources.name: Halo 2: an agent-assisted matching decompilation of an LTCG Xbox build
resources.description: A work-in-progress matching decompilation of Halo 2 for the original Xbox: contributors write C and C++ that the period compiler, building the whole program with link-time code generation, must turn back into the retail executable's bytes function by function. The README reports just under half of the game-function bytes matched and leaves a native port for a later stage. It discloses that much of the maintainer's work runs in Claude and Codex coding-agent lanes.
requirements: README targets the retail disc build's default.xbe (internal name halo2ship.exe, linked 2004-09-28, XDK 5849, Visual C++ 7.1 with /LTCG), identified by SHA-256. At the reviewed commit it reports 9,115 of 11,321 game functions matched (46.90% of game-function bytes; 35.59% of all in-scope bytes). Decompilation and readability work are in progress and a native port is a later stage, so the project produces no playable or ported build.

Supply the retail default.xbe from a copy you are entitled to use, and the XDK 5849 development toolchain, yourself; neither is provided, and the maintainers will not help obtain the SDK. README says byte-for-byte checking currently depends on that original compiler, which no open-source toolchain can yet reproduce; analysis and documentation need neither. The repository holds no game assets, disc images or leaked material.

The tools are Python (requirements-dev.txt, with capstone for the checker). tools/build.py builds the whole game as one LTCG image with each source file's flags; tools/check.py compares every marked function with the retail bytes apart from relocated address fields, writes matched/near/todo status to config/functions.csv and exits nonzero while any function differs. Public CI runs the Python tests, whose retail and SDK tests skip without those local inputs, and exports the decomp.dev report from the committed CSV.

Match counts come from the project's checker; tools/masked.py lists differences the address masking can hide, such as nearby float constants and strings. PROVENANCE.md reports that earlier names drew on sources its policy forbids (third-party names derived from unreleased 2003 linker maps, and an internal 2007 debug build); those were removed or renamed with match status unchanged, while the derivation of names that follow the Halo CE decompilation is still under review.

Contributors' own work is CC0 1.0; LEGAL.md states this places no Halo 2 code, content or trademarks in the public domain, and the project is unaffiliated with Microsoft, Bungie or 343 Industries. README says much of the maintainer's decompilation runs in automated lanes driven by Claude and Codex, with each batch reviewed and checked before it lands, and it offers contributors a prompt for AI coding agents.

resources.name: DiabloWeb: a WebAssembly browser port built on Devilution
resources.description: Runs Diablo in web browsers by compiling a stripped-down fork of Devilution, the community reconstruction of the game’s original source, to WebAssembly behind a React front end. The fork removes the Storm, DiabloUI, DirectX and Windows dependencies and reworks event handling for the browser. It is a port built on a reconstruction and reports no matching or behavior-equivalence checks of its own.
requirements: Reviewed diabloweb 1.0.39 at its last commit (May 2022). Prebuilt WebAssembly modules for the retail and shareware builds, and an MPQ compressor, are committed; their C/C++ source is the separate d07RiV/devilution fork. That fork’s README says many parts of the code were modified, correct behavior is not guaranteed and network play was broken; diabloweb carries WebSocket and WebRTC client modules.

The full game needs the user’s own DIABDAT.MPQ from an original copy (the page points to the GOG release); the shareware SPAWN.MPQ runs the free demo. Data files are selected or dropped in the browser, saves are kept in IndexedDB and can be downloaded or uploaded as .sv files, and the app can optionally compress the MPQ locally. Neither repository includes retail game data.

The front end is a webpack/React project built with Node.js. Rebuilding the WebAssembly modules requires Emscripten and the fork’s node build.js; the fork can also build a Windows app in Visual Studio 2017. README says the hosted page serves the shareware SPAWN.MPQ; local runs need it placed in the public folder.
Neither README reports tests, matching results or comparisons with the original executable, and the reviewed front-end tree has no test files. Reported playability rests on the hosted deployment.

diabloweb has no license file. The fork ships Unlicense text, yet its README limits the source to non-commercial use; current upstream Devilution uses the Sustainable Use License 1.0, and Blizzard retains its rights in Diablo and its data.

resources.name: pokered: a matching Pokémon Red and Blue disassembly
resources.description: Reconstructs the Game Boy games Pokémon Red and Blue as RGBDS assembly, with graphics and data kept as editable source files. One tree builds the USA/Europe Red and Blue ROMs, a Blue debug build and patches for the Virtual Console releases, each checked against a recorded SHA-1. It is a full disassembly rather than a decompilation into a higher-level language.
requirements: README says the disassembly builds Pokemon Red (UE), Pokemon Blue (UE), the BLUEMONS.GB debug build and two Virtual Console patch files, listing a SHA-1 for each. Code, text, maps and audio are RGBDS assembly, and graphics are PNG files converted during the build; Virtual Console patches come from separate VC builds and patch templates.

The build reads no original ROM: every input is in the repository, so the outputs are rebuilt from source rather than combined with extracted assets. The repository therefore carries the game's text, graphics and data in source form.

INSTALL.md covers Linux distributions, macOS with Homebrew, Windows through WSL (or Cygwin on older Windows) and Termux. The build needs make, gcc or clang, git and rgbds 1.0.4, which the repository pins; helper tools under tools/ handle graphics conversion, compression and patch generation.

make compare builds every target and runs sha1sum against roms.sha1. pret's CI does this on Linux and macOS with rgbds 1.0.4 and fails when the build leaves uncommitted changes, while forks only build. Matching hashes show identical output bytes.
The repository has no license file, so reuse terms for the disassembly are unstated, and the original game's content remains its rights holders'. rgbds is a separate project with its own terms.

resources.name: Lighthouse: a Banjo-Kazooie PC port built on the decompilation
resources.description: A native Windows, Linux and macOS port of Banjo-Kazooie that compiles game C sources, many tagged with their Banjo-Kazooie decompilation file paths, against libultraship, a reimplementation of the N64 SDK. Torch extracts the user’s ROM into an asset archive, and the port adds Anchor multiplayer, romhack and language-pack support and a randomizer. Unlike Banjo: Recompiled, it builds from decompiled source rather than statically recompiling the ROM’s code.
requirements: Requires a supported retail ROM in .z64 form, identified by SHA-1 in the README: US 1.0, US 1.1, Japanese or PAL. It is extracted into a local bk.o2r archive; other regions can be added as language packs, and romhacks need the US 1.0 base. The repository includes no copyrighted game assets.
Release 1.1.0 “Hatteras Alfa” (2026-08-17) ships Windows x64, Linux and macOS archives. Rendering backends are DirectX 11 (Windows default), OpenGL on all platforms and Metal (macOS default).

Source builds need the libultraship and Torch submodules and CMake, plus Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC v143), Python 3 and at least 8 GB RAM on Windows, GCC or Clang with Ninja and the listed SDL2, libzip, tinyxml2, spdlog, Boost and Vorbis packages on Linux, or Xcode and the listed packages on macOS. Build targets extract bk.o2r from the ROM and package port assets as lighthouse.o2r.
The README publishes no matching or fidelity checks. Most supported romhacks are not fully tested, and CI nightly builds are for playtesting and may crash.

The repository is dedicated under CC0 1.0; submodules keep their own licenses, and the game is not covered. The README discloses AI assistance for information gathering and accepts AI-assisted pull requests under the HarbourMasters policy.

resources.name: Lost Odyssey Recomp: statically recompiling an Xbox 360 RPG into native ports
resources.description: Translates Lost Odyssey’s Xbox 360 PowerPC executable with patched XenonRecomp tooling and runs the generated code on a native runtime that renders through Direct3D 12, Vulkan or Metal. Windows, Linux, macOS and Android packages import the user’s own disc data. The maintainer documents development with Claude Code and Codex CLI and records each release separately from validation and acceptance.
requirements: The reviewed main snapshot follows v1.0.4 (2026-10-18), packaged for Windows x64 with AVX, Linux x64 AppImage/Flatpak, macOS 15+ on Apple Silicon and 64-bit Android 8.0+ with Vulkan. STATUS.md and ROADMAP.md record each release as published but not accepted by the maintainer. This is static recompilation of the shipped executable, not recovered authored source or a general Xbox 360 emulator.

Players import data from one supported four-disc set, Asian multilingual or USA/Europe (Title ID 4D5307FA); Disc 1 is required, DLC is optional, and other regions, title updates and modified XEX files are unsupported. Source builds use the Asian multilingual Disc 1 default.xex, LO.fpi and resource archives, and BUILDING.md still calls four-disc integration incomplete. Game data and generated code are kept out of the repository.

Builds need submodules including XenonRecomp, XenosRecomp, plume and SDL 3, with project patches applied, plus Python 3.11+, CMake 3.28+, Ninja and Clang: clang-cl with Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools on Windows 10 1803+, or Clang/LLD with a Vulkan driver on Linux. tools/ppc_codegen.py regenerates the guest sources locally before the runtime build.

STATUS.md separates implementation, validation, acceptance and release; for example, v1.0.4’s save fix passed a logic review, a CPU fixture and a Release link but was not run in-game. Upscaler and rendering checks name bounded fixtures and GPUs. The workflow guide states that a release does not mean the game was completed start to finish.

GPL-3.0 covers project code; Lost Odyssey and its assets belong to their owners, and dependencies such as the Xenia FFmpeg fork, DXC, optional DLSS/FSR/XeSS SDKs and Android GPU drivers keep their own terms. docs/AI_WORKFLOW.md says one maintainer used Claude Code as the main session with Codex CLI and subagents; Ghidra scripts and a third-party reverse-engineering skill are referenced.

resources.name: Super Smash Bros. Melee: a matching GameCube decompilation with a shiftable build
resources.description: A matching decompilation of Super Smash Bros. Melee's US 1.02 release (GALE01) that rebuilds main.dol from C with the original Metrowerks compilers and checks it against the retail SHA-1. decomp.dev reports the code fully decompiled and linked at the reviewed commit, and the README says current work is mostly naming and cleanup. Because the build can be shifted, a separate non-matching mode lets modders add code to a DOL run with their own disc dump.
requirements: README describes a matching decompilation that builds the US 1.02 main.dol (game ID GALE01) with SHA-1 08e0bf20134dfcb260699671004527b2d6bb1a45, the digest config/GALE01/build.sha1 checks. decomp.dev reports 100.00% decompiled and 100.00% fully linked for this commit, and README says most effort now goes to naming and cleanup. The output is a GameCube DOL, not a PC executable; the CMake library and DWARF packages CI also builds are not documented as a playable port.

Supply main.dol from your own GALE01 disc; the repository's orig/GALE01 folders hold only placeholders. The README's modding path needs the whole disc dumped to a folder, enables configure.py --non-matching with new objects marked Equivalent, and runs the rebuilt DOL in Dolphin. Such modified builds are not byte-identical to retail.

Host tools are Python and ninja on Windows (native tooling recommended), macOS (Game Porting Toolkit runs the Windows compilers) or Linux (WiBo on x86, Wine elsewhere). configure.py sets up decomp-toolkit, sjiswrap and the Metrowerks GC/1.2.5 and GC/1.1p1 compilers with the GC/1.3.2 linker; objdiff diffs objects and tools/decomp.py drafts functions with m2c. CI builds link, test and debug modes in a build container that provides the original files, plus a Nix matching build.

Matching rests on the linked DOL's SHA-1 and objdiff's per-unit report; CI's check_complete.py warns when a unit matches fully but is not yet marked complete. The 100% figures are decomp.dev's report for this commit.

No repository-wide licence file is present at the reviewed commit and GitHub detects none; bundled tools under tools/ carry their own licences, and the game, its DOL and assets keep their rights holders' terms. CONTRIBUTING.md says using AI to match functions is acceptable and frequently practiced, while asking contributors not to let AI name struct fields or global identifiers or attempt data-section matches.

resources.name: pokecrystal: a matching Pokémon Crystal disassembly
resources.description: Reconstructs the Game Boy Color game Pokémon Crystal as RGBDS assembly, with graphics, maps and data stored as editable sources. One tree builds the international 1.0 and 1.1 releases, the Australian release, two debug builds and a Virtual Console patch, each checked against a recorded SHA-1. Companion documentation covers script command formats and known bugs in the original game.
requirements: README lists six outputs with SHA-1s: Crystal (UE) 1.0 and 1.1, the Australian release, two debug builds and the CGBBYTE1.784 Virtual Console patch. Version differences are selected with assembler defines such as _CRYSTAL11 and _CRYSTAL_AU, and plain make builds only the 1.0 ROM. The Japanese release is not among the listed targets.

The build reads no original ROM: code, text, maps, audio, PNG graphics and other data are in the repository, including the mobile library code linked into the ROM. The repository therefore carries the game's content in source form. Packaging the Virtual Console patch into an installable title is outside the project's scope.

INSTALL.md covers Linux distributions, macOS with Homebrew, Windows through WSL (or Cygwin on older Windows) and Termux. The build needs make, gcc or clang, git and rgbds 1.0.4, which the repository pins; FAQ.md notes that rgbds releases before 1.0.0 fail.

make compare builds every target and runs sha1sum against roms.sha1. pret's CI does this on Linux and macOS with rgbds 1.0.4 and fails when the build leaves uncommitted changes, while forks only build. Bug and design-flaw notes describe fixes as optional diffs, since the matching build keeps the original behavior.
The repository has no license file, so reuse terms for the disassembly are unstated, and the original game's content remains its rights holders'. rgbds is a separate project with its own terms.

resources.name: Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver: a work-in-progress, checksum-matched DS disassembly
resources.description: Rebuilds the US Nintendo DS releases of Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver from a work-in-progress disassembly in which part of the code has been decompiled to C. Each default build checks the ARM9 and ARM7 binaries, the filesystem and the complete ROM against per-game SHA-1 manifests. README warns that, because decompilation is incomplete, edits that change code or data layout can crash the game.
requirements: README calls this a work-in-progress disassembly of the US releases; it warns that symbol names and code structure can change, and that edits altering the size or layout of any function or data structure can crash the game because the ROM is not fully decompiled. At the reviewed commit asm/ still holds 283 assembly files beside 406 C files in src/, and CONTRIBUTING.md describes NONMATCHING C kept beside the inline-assembly versions used for matching builds. Outputs are pokeheartgold.us.nds and pokesoulsilver.us.nds, not a PC port.

The documented build reads no original ROM: the DS filesystem’s graphics, model, text and data files are committed under files/. The target images are identified by SHA-1 (HeartGold 4fcded0e2713dc03929845de631d0932ea2b5a37, SoulSilver f8dc38ea20c17541a43b58c5e6d18c1732c7e582), and README links their No-Intro records. Only the contributor asmdiff tool refers to a user-supplied base ROM.

INSTALL.md covers WSL2 (recommended), WSL1, MSYS2, macOS and Debian, Arch and Fedora Linux; packages include an ARM GCC toolchain, bison, flex, Ninja, Python 3, libpng and 32-bit libc, and macOS also needs Wine. The Makefile clones Meson 1.12.0 and downloads the metroskrew 0.1.3 release, which its repository describes as a relinked Linux port of the proprietary Windows Metrowerks ARM compiler; Meson fetches pinned NitroSDK, NitroSystem, NitroDWC, NitroWiFi and libvct subprojects. make builds HeartGold and make soulsilver builds SoulSilver.

make runs Meson tests after building that check the ARM9 main binary, ARM7 binary, filesystem and complete ROM against SHA-1 manifests; the Makefile tells modders they may drop that check after their first build. CI builds and checks both games and runs a progress calculation on pushes. Matching hashes establish identity for these two US images.

The repository has no top-level license file and GitHub detects none; some bundled tools carry their own licenses, and the metroskrew and ntrtwl SDK repositories declare no license on GitHub. SDK libraries and original game content remain subject to their rights holders. CONTRIBUTING.md prohibits LLM-generated contributions apart from narrow, disclosed exceptions.

resources.name: FFTARecomp: static recompilation of Final Fantasy Tactics Advance
resources.description: Recompiles the user’s Final Fantasy Tactics Advance (USA) Game Boy Advance ROM ahead of time into native code for Windows, Linux and Steam Deck, building on JRickey’s gba-recomp toolkit. ARM and Thumb code is translated to C and compiled locally, while a Rust runtime models the console’s graphics, sound, DMA, timers and BIOS calls. The port adds widescreen, zoom, fast-forward and remappable controls.
requirements: Reviewed source follows the v2.0 release (2026-10-13) and is labelled a work in progress. README targets Windows 10/11, Linux and Steam Deck; its recomp manifest also lists Android and calls the game fully playable from start to finish. Without a C compiler the recompiler falls back to an interpreter, which upstream keeps for self-modifying code and as a differential-testing oracle. Known issues include brief sprite silhouettes in the first level and a gamepad that may go undetected on first launch.

Supply your own Final Fantasy Tactics Advance (USA) ROM, serial AFXE; the project manifest records the expected SHA-1. No console BIOS is needed, because BIOS calls are high-level emulated. The installer recompiles the game on the user’s PC, and the project excludes ROMs, saves, memory dumps and generated game C from its uploads.

Building from source needs Rust and Windows PowerShell (build-all.ps1). A C compiler is also a runtime requirement: the recompiler emits C11 and links a per-title library. The Windows installer downloads the w64devkit 2.10.0 GCC toolchain, and Linux release builds use Zig as a build-only cross compiler.

A dated release audit (2026-10-12) reports clean source-upload scans, 26 passing input-configuration and menu tests and successful Windows and Linux release builds, and leaves physical-controller behavior unmeasured. README cites no hardware or emulator comparison results.

FFTARecomp changes are MIT and retain upstream gba-recomp notices (MIT OR Apache-2.0); gamedb.sqlite function metadata is CC0 1.0, and w64devkit tools keep their GPL-family licenses. Square Enix and Nintendo retain their game rights. Upstream gba-recomp describes itself as AI-assisted.

resources.name: SymphonyRecomp: a RecompOne static recompilation of Symphony of the Night
resources.description: Statically recompiles the North American PlayStation release of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night into C# with BlackLabelHQ’s RecompOne, whose runtime simulates the BIOS, memory-mapped I/O, GPU and CD-ROM so the game runs natively without a console BIOS. Per-overlay function maps and patches add widescreen, quality-of-life, randomizer and cheat features. References from the SOTN decompilation help name functions, but the project stresses that it is a recompilation, not a decompilation.
requirements: Requires the user’s own North American disc (serial SLUS-00067) as a two-track BIN/CUE set or CHD with fixed file names; other-language discs are described only as future sources for a language switcher. The repository contains no game data, and RecompOne needs no BIOS or other Sony components.

Release v0.5.1b (2026-08-19) ships Windows x64/ARM64, macOS ARM64/x64 and Linux x64 builds; Linux ARM64 was dropped in 0.5b. Source-build prerequisites list an OpenGL 2.1+ GPU, .NET 10, OpenAL and Git, and the changelog calls the OpenGL 2.1 path experimental with bitmasking problems. Game code is generated by running the RecompOne submodule against config/sotn.json.
The README calls this an open beta that may contain game-breaking bugs, and 1.0 has not been released. No equivalence or automated gameplay test is published.
SymphonyRecomp has no license file, so reuse terms are unspecified; the pinned RecompOne recompiler and runtime are MIT-licensed, and the game retains its own rights.

resources.name: The Two Towers Recompiled: an original Xbox static-recompilation port
resources.description: Statically recompiles the x86 code of The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers (Xbox, USA, 2002) into C with the bundled xboxrecomp toolkit, producing native Windows, Linux and experimental macOS builds. The recompiled sources are generated locally from the player's own default.xbe, and game data comes from their disc image or extracted folder. README reports the game as fully playable, with visual, frame-rate and mod issues listed.
requirements: README for v1.9.2 calls the port a fully playable work in progress and recommends 60 FPS; unlocked frame rates and widescreen are experimental. Downloads cover 64-bit Windows 7 SP1 to 11, x86-64 Linux with glibc 2.27+, and macOS 10.15+ on Intel or through Rosetta 2, with the macOS build not yet tested on a Mac. Known issues include stretched character shadows, lighting glitches, Vulkan black screens and several problems with the bundled extra-heroes mod.

Players need their own USA Xbox disc image or extracted game folder, and no game data is included. generate.py checks the retail default.xbe against a fixed SHA-256, then runs the xboxrecomp pipeline (XBE parsing, disassembly, function identification, ABI analysis, naming and recompilation) to write the C sources locally, so no recompiled code is committed. A separately distributed GameCube high-resolution texture pack is optional and not part of the release.

The repository vendors the xboxrecomp 0.12.0 static-recompilation toolkit, which translates an XBE's x86 code into C, and CHANGES.md lists the fixes made to it for this game. The game project builds with CMake 3.20+ and C11 under MSVC, MinGW or Clang/GCC; Linux uses SDL2 with OpenGL loaded at run time, and the renderer options are Direct3D 11, Vulkan through DXVK or OpenGL. The README at this revision has no build section; generate.py only says to build with CMake afterwards.

Testing reported for 1.9.2 covers menus, level loading and fonts in several languages under Wine and on Linux with OpenGL, and states that the Windows, Linux and macOS builds compile. No automated tests or CI runs are recorded for the reviewed commit.

LICENSE.txt applies MIT to the port's own code (twotowers/ and generate.py); the vendored xboxrecomp keeps MIT plus LGPL-2.1-or-later for parts taken from xemu. The license adds that the release's game program contains code mechanically translated from the original executable, which it does not cover and which remains the rights holders' property.

resources.name: Melee Unlocked: a Windows source port and static recompilation of Melee
resources.description: A beta Windows build of Super Smash Bros. Melee (NTSC 1.02) with two engines: a source port that compiles the doldecomp decompilation as a native library, and a static recompilation that translates the retail DOL's PowerPC code and Slippi's Gecko codes into C++. Both run on a native runtime with Direct3D rendering, unlocked display rates and natively implemented Slippi rollback play. The user's own ISO supplies all game data, and the README says the work was AI-assisted.
requirements: README describes a beta Windows build with two engines chosen in the launcher. The Source Port compiles doldecomp/melee (a submodule pinned at 039c4bf plus a tracked native patch) into melee_game.dll on a native runtime with Direct3D 12/11 rendering, a mixer and direct controller input. The Static Recomp uses the project's Python recompiler to translate the retail DOL's PowerPC code and Slippi's Gecko codes ahead of time into C++, over HLE of the GameCube SDK. Game logic stays at 60 Hz while the display interpolates from animation data; VERSION and the latest release are 0.8.99, though README still names 0.8.76.

Supply your own Melee NTSC 1.02 ISO: the game reads its data from it, and the from-source build takes the retail main.dol from it as the recompiler's input. Nothing from the disc is committed or shipped. Online play needs a Slippi account through the Slippi Launcher; the optional DLSS 5 path needs NVIDIA's separately supplied runtime and model.

Windows 10/11 only. The Static Recomp build uses Python, CMake and the Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools (play.bat can install them with winget). The Source Port additionally needs MinGW-w64 GCC 14 or newer with Ninja for the game DLL, an MSVC-built host, and the same guest-translation step; it pins the doldecomp/melee and encounter/aurora submodules and applies its patch with a checking script.

README lists CTest unit tests, a validator requiring 2,400 simulation checkpoints to match across headless, hidden, threaded and authored rendering, and a two-instance Slippi match that must log no DESYNC. docs/replay-validation.md compares replays frame by frame in eight Slippi post-frame fields; PORT_COMPLETION.md makes resolving a differing replay byte a precondition for claiming deterministic online compatibility. These are project-reported.

GPL-3.0-or-later from 0.8.5 (GPL-2.0-or-later through 0.8.1); NOTICE lists code ported from Dolphin, Slippi Ishiiruka and Slippi, bundled components with their own licences, and a GPL section 7 permission for NVIDIA and Intel SDKs. Melee belongs to Nintendo and HAL Laboratory, and the project is unaffiliated with the Slippi team. README says it was developed with Fable 5.1 and GPT 6 Astra, and PORT_COMPLETION.md names Fable and Codex working branches.

resources.name: pokeruby: a matching Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs the Game Boy Advance games Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire as C source built with pret's agbcc compiler, alongside assembly data scripts and editable graphics. Matching builds cover the English 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 revisions, debug builds and the first German editions, each checked against a stored SHA-1. A separate modern-GCC target is not expected to match.
requirements: README still calls the project a disassembly and lists hashes for English pokeruby.gba and pokesapphire.gba; INSTALL.md adds 1.1/1.2 revision targets, 1.0-only debug targets and first-edition German builds, and the tree holds 14 SHA-1 files. No asm/ directory remains in the reviewed tree: game code is C under src/, apart from handwritten startup and library assembly and functions marked NONMATCHING whose matching builds keep inline assembly. The contributor guide still describes the earlier asm-to-C workflow.

The build reads no original ROM: code, scripts, text, graphics and sound sources are in the repository, so the repository carries the game's content in source form. German builds need a setup script before compiling and a teardown script before any English build.

INSTALL.md lists Linux, macOS with Xcode Command Line Tools, and Windows through WSL or the devkitPro MSYS2 environment, plus build-essential, git, libpng and devkitARM. pret's agbcc must be cloned, built and installed into the tree; make modern uses devkitARM's arm-none-eabi-gcc instead, and other toolchains can be set with TOOLCHAIN.

With COMPARE=1 the Makefile checks the selected build against its SHA-1 file. The GitHub Actions workflow compares the English 1.0/1.1/1.2 Ruby and Sapphire builds and German first-edition variants, then compiles the NONMATCHING sources and the modern target without comparison; README's build badge still points to Travis CI. Matching hashes show identical ROM bytes.
No license file is present, so reuse terms are unstated; the original game's content remains its rights holders', and agbcc and devkitPro components keep their own terms.

resources.name: Vandal Hearts: native PC port built on matching decompilations
resources.description: Builds on shao113’s matching decompilation of PlayStation Vandal Hearts, adds a Japanese matching tree, and carries both through to a native Windows and Linux port. SDL2, OpenGL or Metal and OpenAL backends replace the console’s GPU, GTE, CD-ROM/XA, SPU, MDEC and pad interfaces, and one executable runs the USA, Asia and Japan discs. The matching builds are still checked on every change; PC-only features such as Tactical Mode and HD packs are opt-in.
requirements: Reviewed source follows v2.1.0 (2026-08-31). README reports every non-PsyQ function decompiled, with make check confirming byte-identical rebuilds of the US SLUS_004.47 and, since 2.0.0, the Japanese SLPM_860.07 by MD5, and full playthroughs through the endgame on Windows and Linux. macOS is a community-supported experimental build tested through the first battle; its full-playthrough and notarisation validation are pending.

Supply your own raw .bin disc image of the USA (SLUS-00447), Asia (SCPS-45183) or Japan (SLPM-86007) release; the port verifies and auto-detects each disc. The matching build also needs the original executable as its MD5 reference and locally sourced proprietary PsyQ SDK files (README lists ASPSX 2.21 and LIB34.ZIP by MD5). The kanji font, in-game text and static data segment are generated from the user’s copy, not committed.

The port builds with Make or CMake against SDL2, OpenAL, OpenGL (Metal on macOS), libwebp, libav and Python 3; Windows binaries are cross-compiled from Linux with MinGW-w64, and Linux ships as an AppImage. The matching build uses splat, maspsx, decompals’ GCC 2.5.7/2.6.3 frontends and MIPS binutils, and needs a Linux host because those frontends are 32-bit Linux executables.

Project-reported checks include make check for both regions, AddressSanitizer and UBSan sweeps that fixed seven latent out-of-bounds bugs, audio/visual fidelity validated against BizHawk, and a software rasterizer reported 99.84–99.99% pixel-exact against DuckStation VRAM captures. The known-issues list places remaining defects in the port’s rendering and backend layer.

GPL-2.0 covers only the project’s original port code, tooling and documentation. The decompiled game code, derived from shao113’s unlicensed decompilation, and the reconstructed data tables are Konami’s and are not licensed by the project; pre-built releases embed part of the game-derived data segment and a BIOS-derived font. The repository keeps its setup recipe in Claude Code skill files.

resources.name: Pokémon Platinum: a checksum-matched Nintendo DS decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs the US Nintendo DS release of Pokémon Platinum as C source that rebuilds revision 1 by default and revision 0 on request. The default make target runs Meson checks of the code binaries, filesystem and complete ROM against SHA-1 manifests. README still calls the project work in progress; its contributing guide says the code is entirely C but much of it remains obfuscated, leaving documentation and tooling as the main work.
requirements: README calls this a WIP decompilation of US Pokémon Platinum. CONTRIBUTING.md states that the repository is 100% C code, although much of it is obfuscated, so current work is mainly documentation and tooling; at the reviewed commit asm/ holds only macro includes beside 1,013 C files in src/. Outputs are pokeplatinum.us.nds ROM images, not a PC port.

The documented build reads no original ROM: graphics, sound, text and data sources, including some prebuilt data, are committed under res/. Revision 1, the default, has SHA-1 0862ec35b24de5c7e2dcb88c9eea0873110d755c; ROM_REVISION=0 builds revision 0, SHA-1 ce81046eda7d232513069519cb2085349896dec7, which INSTALL.md describes as the original North American retail version with a GTS level-range display error that a later shipment patched. README links both No-Intro records.

INSTALL.md covers WSL2 (recommended), WSL1, MSYS2, macOS and Debian, Arch and Fedora Linux; packages include an ARM GCC toolchain, bison, flex, Ninja, Python 3, libpng and 32-bit libc, and macOS also needs Wine. The Makefile clones Meson 1.12.0 and downloads the metroskrew 0.1.3 release, which its repository describes as a relinked Linux port of the proprietary Windows Metrowerks ARM compiler; Meson fetches pinned NitroSDK, NitroSystem, NitroDWC, NitroWiFi and libvct subprojects. make debug builds a GDB-enabled ROM, for which INSTALL.md points to an overlay-aware binutils-gdb fork.

make runs Meson tests that check shared, revision-specific and ARM7 binaries, the filesystem and the complete ROM against SHA-1 manifests; make rom skips the checksum when code is modified. CI installs metroskrew and runs make check for the default revision.

The repository has no top-level license file and GitHub detects none; some bundled tools carry their own licenses, and the metroskrew and ntrtwl SDK repositories declare no license on GitHub. SDK libraries and original game content remain subject to their rights holders.

resources.name: Saints Reborn: a ReXGlue static recompilation of Saints Row
resources.description: An unofficial native Windows port of Saints Row (Xbox 360, 2006) that statically recompiles the game's PowerPC executable to C++ for x86-64 with the ReXGlue SDK, which also reimplements the console's kernel, GPU (on Direct3D 12), audio and input. A recompiler manifest, game-specific function overrides and an SDK patch make the result run, and each user builds it locally from their own disc. The README reports the game fully playable with built-in co-op and lists known issues.
requirements: README describes a static recompilation, not a decompilation or an emulator: the ReXGlue SDK, pinned at v0.10.0 (commit c94f5eb) and patched by patches/rexglue-sdk.patch, translates every PowerPC function in default.xex to C++. config/saintsrow_manifest.toml adds ABI helpers, 19 functions reached only through vtables and two mid-function hooks, and project/src overrides rendering (predicated tiling), audio, kernel-object and occlusion-query behaviour. README reports the game fully playable from start to finish, with co-op over LAN, direct IP or a join code, an optional 60 FPS mod and a mod loader; known issues include texture flicker in the character creator.

Supply your own Saints Row (Xbox 360) disc as an .iso, or a game folder containing default.xex and packfiles. Only the disc version the port was made with is supported: setup compares default.xex with one known SHA-1 for the World disc release and warns otherwise, because the hooks use fixed addresses. The repository contains no game code, data, recompiled output or executables, and its legal notice forbids using it to distribute them.

Windows 10/11 (64-bit) with a Direct3D 12 GPU, about 15 GB of disk space and 16 GB of RAM. Setup downloads a portable clang, CMake, Ninja and Microsoft's C++ headers and libraries (about 1.5 GB) and builds the game locally in 10–60 minutes; the older setup.bat path needs Visual Studio 2022 with its Clang and CMake components, plus Git. README lists Linux (through Proton) as coming soon, although BUILDING.md already describes Setup as working on Windows and Linux.

Playability and the known-issue list are the author's reports. The only CI workflow builds the setup application; the repository's tests cover co-op, modding and map tools, and no automated comparison of recompiled behaviour against the console is documented.

Project code is Apache-2.0 with a NOTICE that redistributors must keep, crediting Saints Reborn by Whompay.
