resources.description: Translates the PlayStation game’s MIPS code to C with a pinned psxrecomp fork and builds Windows and Linux programs on its hardware-modelling runtime, with a launcher and a game-specific plugin. Without patching game code, the plugin adds 16:9 matches, 60 FPS by raising the emulated CPU clock and rescaling movement, intro skipping and unlocks. The user’s own NTSC-U disc image is required, and the measurements are author-reported.
requirements: The reviewed master branch (VERSION 1.0.0, matching the v1.0.0 release) is a static recompilation, not a decompilation: psxrecomp translates SLUS_012.27’s R3000A code into a local generated/ tree using Ghidra-derived function seeds. psxrecomp is a pinned submodule from TekRantGaming’s fork of RetroPortingToolKit/psxrecomp, whose README describes a hardware-accurate runtime with bundled OpenBIOS as the default, so a retail BIOS is not normally required. Known issues include misplaced widescreen pause-screen HUD elements and uneven experimental 120 FPS.

The user supplies The Simpsons Wrestling (PlayStation, North America, SLUS-01227) as a .cue with its .bin. game.toml records the expected data-track size and hashes; the launcher checks the disc before play and reads it in place. Building also needs that disc to generate the C code. README states that the repository holds no game code and that the download contains no game files.

Play needs 64-bit Windows 10/11 or 64-bit Linux with glibc 2.38, plus OpenGL 3.3. Windows builds use Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools, CMake, Ninja and the bundled clang-cl with ThinLTO and a committed PGO profile; Linux builds use gcc with X11, Wayland, GL, ALSA, PulseAudio and udev development packages. The launcher is a separate SDL2 program from the TRG Launcher submodule, while the runtime uses SDL3.

TECHNICAL.md reports attract-demo matches in two arenas at 1.00x speed and a steady 60 FPS on one Ryzen 7 7800X3D/RTX 4070 Ti PC, plus jump-height and walking-distance comparisons with stock timing. Linux was checked only under WSL2; the AppImage is untested on native Linux and Steam Deck. These are author measurements.

GitHub detects no license and the reviewed tree has no LICENSE file, so reuse terms for the project’s own code are not stated; the pinned psxrecomp fork carries the PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 license. The game and its trademarks remain with Fox Interactive, Activision and the other named owners. README discloses that the port was made almost entirely with Claude Code under the owner’s direction.

resources.name: OpenRCT2: an open re-implementation of RollerCoaster Tycoon 2
resources.description: Re-implements RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, originally written in x86 assembly, as a C++ engine that runs on the original game’s data. It loads RCT2 saves and scenarios, and RCT1 scenarios when those files are present, while saving to its own documented park format. Modern-platform support, interface and AI changes, higher limits and multiplayer are deliberate extensions, not reproductions of the original.
requirements: The reviewed develop snapshot follows the v0.5.6 release of 2026-10-10. The README says OpenRCT2 attempts to provide everything from RCT2 plus many improvements, and restores some RollerCoaster Tycoon mechanics, so intentional differences are part of the design. No original source is recovered.

Playing requires the user’s own RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 files; the README names Steam and GOG.com editions. Original RollerCoaster Tycoon files are optional and enable its scenarios. By default, installation downloads OpenRCT2’s own objects, title sequences, OpenSoundEffects and OpenMusic packs, and test builds also fetch replays, each pinned by SHA-256.

Source builds use CMake 3.24+ and a C++20 compiler, with wiki guides for Linux, macOS, Windows, WSL and MSYS2 MinGW and an option to force 32-bit builds. Portable builds, installers, a launcher and several Linux and BSD packages are listed for players.

CI checks formatting, builds on several platforms and runs the GoogleTest suite, including replay, RCT2 save import/export, ride-rating, pathfinding and scenario-decryption tests on project test data. These guard OpenRCT2’s own behaviour and file compatibility.
licence.txt applies GPL-3.0-or-later to OpenRCT2; original game data and purchased editions keep their own rights.

resources.name: Touhou 6: reconstructing Embodiment of Scarlet Devil 1.02h source
resources.description: Reconstructs C++ source for the Windows executable of Touhou 6: Embodiment of Scarlet Devil version 1.02h, aiming at an exact rebuild with the original Visual Studio .NET 2002 and DirectX 8 toolchain. reccmp and objdiff compare the rebuilt binary with the user’s original executable function by function. The committed progress badge reports every function implemented but 98.03% byte accuracy, so whole-binary identity is not claimed.
requirements: README states the aim of perfectly reconstructing the 1.02h source; the committed, mutable progress badge reports 100.0% implemented and 98.03% byte accuracy for TH06.EXE. README points to a separate portable branch for Linux and modern Windows. The team’s Ghidra work is exported as XML to the companion happyhavoc/th06-re repository.

Supply your own original 東方紅魔郷.exe version 1.02h matching the SHA-256 in README, copied to resources/th06.exe; reccmp checks the same hash, and the build extracts the game icon from that file. The repository contains no game executable or data; the comparison workflow fetches the original binary from a secret-configured URL.

Builds need Python 3.4+, plus msiextract and Wine outside Windows (CrossOver is suggested on macOS); aria2c is optional. scripts/create_devenv.py downloads Visual Studio .NET 2002 and the DirectX 8.0 SDK from web archives, along with ninja, objdiff, Ghidra and helper tools, and scripts/build.py generates and runs a ninja build.

Contributors diff with reccmp, which reports per-function accuracy of the rebuilt executable against the original as an HTML report. CI builds on Windows and compares an objdiff build with objects delinked from the original through Ghidra; a small munit suite reads the user’s game archive. Badge figures are project-generated.
The repository is dedicated under CC0 1.0; the original game, the downloaded Microsoft toolchain and third-party tools keep their own terms.

resources.name: BINNY
resources.description: An open-source terminal agent harness from OpenBin that runs a user-chosen hosted or local model over binary-analysis data. It reads decompiled functions, strings, imports and data from an OpenBin or OpenAPK project or a local Ghidra container run, follows triage, investigation and drafting playbooks, and saves a draft malware-analysis or vulnerability-research report for human review. It is an analysis harness with draft outputs, not a reconstruction project.
requirements: The reviewed pin follows the v0.1.0-beta.2 release of 2026-10-15. BINNY is a Go terminal program; release builds use Go 1.22 and cover Linux, macOS and Windows, and the README installers fetch scripts from openbin.ai. Startup needs an OpenBin sign-in: main.go loads the openbin CLI’s stored credentials and stops with an instruction to run openbin login when none exist. Source comments describe planned paid access whose gating is deferred during testing.

Models are bring-your-own-key, with Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, Gemini through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and Bedrock preconfigured; Ollama or LM Studio models must support tool calling and need a larger context window than Ollama’s 4k default. Analysis data comes from the user’s OpenBin or OpenAPK projects or a local file. Local decompilation and the sandbox need Docker, and the first local decompile downloads an OpenBin Ghidra worker image of about 700 MB.

The sandbox tool runs scripts in a container with no network, a read-only root and sample mount, dropped capabilities and CPU, memory and process limits. Triage labels samples with the STIX 2.1 malware vocabulary, malware and vulnerability modes change the report lens, and autonomous, supervised or collaborative modes decide when the agent stops to ask. The README treats existing reports as claims to check and saves drafts for review before publication.

The repository has Go unit tests, which the release workflow runs before cross-compiling; it publishes no benchmark, accuracy measurement or worked example report. Its README still calls the source repository private while it is public.

LICENSE is AGPL-3.0; the README states AGPL-3.0 or later. Contributors sign a CLA so OpenBin can also offer the code under a commercial licence, and the README says the OpenBin platform it talks to uses the same licence. Model services, OpenBin accounts, Ghidra and analysed samples carry their own terms.

resources.name: RKD Telemetry Extractor: decoding Race-Keeper track-day recordings
resources.description: Documents the proprietary .rkd telemetry format written by Race-Keeper “Instant Video” recorders, whose bundled player runs only on Windows, and implements matching Python and Go parsers that export GPS and IMU channels as Telemetry Overlay CSV and GPX. The author credits Claude Code with the hex-dump analysis and hypothesis testing, anchored by known car IDs, circuit location and speeds. Field meanings rest on physical cross-checks from the author’s own recordings, and several record types remain partly unknown.
requirements: The reviewed pin is Python package version 1.0.0 from February 2026. It decodes the 8-byte signature, meta header, 10-byte record headers and the configuration, GPS, accelerometer, gyroscope, periodic, timestamp and terminator records, then exports 30 Hz Telemetry Overlay CSV, roughly 5 Hz GPX and a session summary. It reads telemetry only; the .mp4 video is used as is, and OBD-II channels are unsupported because the source recordings had no scanner connected.

Users supply .rkd files from their own Race-Keeper recordings. The repository includes a truncated sample of about 50 GPS fixes from the author’s 2021 session with reference CSV and GPX output, but not the vendor player, the USB-stick contents or full recordings. Python 3.9+ and the Go toolchain use only standard libraries; README says Go 1.21+, while go.mod declares go 1.24.7.

Research notes and a session log attribute the analysis to Claude Code (claude-opus-4-6) across three February 2026 sessions plus a fourth for tests, documentation and the Go port. The README and notes give about four hours, while the log’s per-session durations total more. The JSONL transcripts are described but not published, so the dialogue cannot be checked from the repository.

Reported validation compares recorded speed with haversine-derived speed (under 1% error), checks mean vertical acceleration against 1 g, fits a gyroscope divisor of about 28 against GPS heading changes and matches altitude to circuit topography. The CRC polynomial, periodic and timer fields, two terminator fields and the exact gyroscope calibration remain unknown or empirical. CI runs Python 3.9, 3.11 and 3.13 tests with a 100% branch-coverage gate, and Go tests on Ubuntu and macOS that compare Go output with the committed Python reference CSV and GPX.

The project declares MIT and states that it is independent of and not endorsed by Race-Keeper or Trivinci Systems LLC. Decoding is limited to the hardware revision and recordings the author examined, and other devices or firmware versions may differ.

resources.name: pwndbg
resources.description: Python plug-in that loads into GDB, or runs as a REPL around LLDB, to make live program state easier to inspect. Each stop prints a context of registers, stack, call frames and annotated disassembly with recursively dereferenced pointers; commands cover memory maps, search, telescoping, heap allocators and Go values, with Capstone/Unicorn emulation and decompiler integration for IDA, Binary Ninja, Ghidra and angr-management. The README lists Linux ELF, macOS Mach-O, QEMU user/system and embedded Cortex-M or RISC-V/32 debugging.
requirements: Compatibility table: pwndbg-gdb needs Python 3.10+ and GDB 12.1+ (tested on Ubuntu 22.04/24.04); pwndbg-lldb needs Python 3.12+ and LLDB 19+, and its support is marked experimental/early-stage; qemu-user needs QEMU 8.1+ (its vFile API is needed for vmmap) and qemu-system QEMU 6.2+. Mach-O debugging on macOS uses LLDB, and qemu-user debugging is GDB only.

Release at review: 2026.09.15, published 2026-09-20, with portable archives, deb/rpm/apk/Arch packages, including macOS portable builds; the setup guide covers Linux and macOS through an install script, Homebrew, Nix, distro packages and source installs. The reviewed dev commit declares the same version.
MIT license. Decompiler integration needs the separately installed decompiler.

resources.name: Driver Recompiled: a psxrecomp setup host that builds the game locally
resources.description: Packages a psxrecomp static-recompilation project for Driver (PlayStation, USA) as a setup host: releases carry the recompiler, runtime and a recomp-ui launcher, and the player’s machine generates and compiles the game from the user’s own disc image. The repository holds configuration, Ghidra-derived function seeds and release automation rather than game code. Its documented status is thin: an operator-confirmed private build reaches gameplay, while package release gates remain open.
requirements: The reviewed main branch (VERSION 0.3.6) targets only the USA release SLUS-00842 and pins Alexbeav’s psxrecomp fork at 08ec704a and recomp-ui at be8ac1d0. FEASIBILITY.md records the status bootstrap_verified: the operator confirmed that a private promoted build reaches gameplay. No mode or feature coverage is documented, and the README notes that public v0.3.0 can relaunch the wrong executable after its first build.

The player supplies an owned disc image of Driver (USA, SLUS-00842); game.toml records the expected data-track size and hashes. Release CI packages a setup host without game C, BIOS backends, disc images or a prebuilt playable executable. The workflow says users generate OpenBIOS, with a retail BIOS optional, while FEASIBILITY.md mentions the player supplying a BIOS; generated code and the executable stay on the user’s machine.

v0.3.6 publishes packages for Windows x64, Linux x64, macOS Apple Silicon and macOS Intel, but the documentation keeps each platform claim pending exact-package setup, startup and clean-exit gates; the README describes 0.3.0 as Windows x64 only. Local builds use the psxrecomp CLI, CMake, Ninja, Python and C/C++ toolchains, with Windows on the framework’s portable toolchain route.

Reported checks are setup executable-name and source-parity tests and YAML and release-workflow audits. The README also describes boot gates and A/B comparisons against Beetle and DuckStation across the author’s ports, but the reviewed tree publishes no comparison results for this title. These are project reports.

Project-owned files are GPL-3.0-only; psxrecomp keeps PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 and recomp-ui MIT, and the GPL does not cover retail content or generated retail code. The README says the ports are developed with substantial AI assistance, with AI writing most of the code.

resources.name: Himuro: a matching Fatal Frame PS2 decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs Fatal Frame’s PS2 executable as C for the US, EU and Japanese releases, built with the original EE-GCC 2.9 toolchain and checked by SHA-1 against the user’s own executables. Committed objdiff reports list the US and EU code as fully matched and the Japanese code as partial, and a few routines still rely on assembly or byte patches. Porting to modern hardware is a stated later goal, not part of this repository.
requirements: Covers SLUS_203.88 (US), SLES_508.21 (EU) and SLPS_250.74 (JP); the output is a rebuilt PS2 ELF, not a PC port, which the README names only as a later goal. After the project’s own report-adjustment script, the committed objdiff reports list 3,437 of 3,437 US and 3,464 of 3,464 EU functions with all code and data matched, but 2,712 of 3,394 JP functions (73.64% of code). The README’s decomp.dev badges are mutable.

Copy the matching main executable from your own disc or ISO into config/<region>/; the README gives the required SHA-1 for each region. Data extraction, splitting and the expected assembly are generated locally, and no game assets are committed.

Linux is required: Python 3.8+ in a virtual environment, make, i386 libc/libstdc++ for the committed 32-bit EE-GCC 2.9-991111-01 compiler, and the decompals PS2 binutils v0.10 installed separately; objdiff-cli is also committed. Each region is extracted, configured and built separately.

The ninja build runs sha1sum against config/<region>/checksum.sha1, so a successful build reproduces the supplied executable. To reach that hash, the build rewrites selected compiler output from asm_patches.json and copies listed byte ranges from the original executable into the built file (PhotoScoreCount in US and EU, DspSpData in EU). CI only uploads the committed reports and cannot build without the executables.
MIT license for the project; Fatal Frame and its executables retain separate rights, and the committed compiler binaries keep their own terms.

resources.name: DOAXVB Native PC Port: statically recompiling Dead or Alive Xtreme Beach Volleyball
resources.description: Lifts the original Xbox executable of Dead or Alive Xtreme Beach Volleyball to C with a fork of xboxrecomp and links it with a hand-written runtime that replaces kernel imports, audio and key Direct3D 8 and DirectSound APIs. Setup builds the runner locally from the user’s USA disc image and checks generated files against hashes in an authenticated recipe; releases carry only tools and source. Rewriting game logic as readable source has so far reached only the startup thread entry.
requirements: The README calls the port fully playable as of 0.4 Beta: long player sessions covered every stage, the Casino, Hotel and Shops, saving and reloading, and a vacation’s end, the last starting from an edited save. Lighting, camera and full rendering fidelity remain incomplete, three known issues are open, and the 0.6.0 RC1 prerelease has had only macOS and Steam Deck smoke runs. Hand-written game logic covers only the startup thread entry.

Requires the user’s own USA Xbox disc image; setup extracts it, checks the XBE and stops if any recipe input or generated file differs from the recorded hashes. Generated game C, extracted files, saves and run evidence stay in an ignored private folder, and NOTICE states that the repository distributes no game, generated game code, assets or console firmware.

Windows release setup bundles Python, Capstone, Git, CMake and extract-xiso and downloads a pinned llvm-mingw clang release. macOS and Linux/SteamOS builds need CMake, Ninja, SDL3, Python with Capstone 5.0.9 and a self-built extract-xiso, with Vulkan through SDL3 and shaderc on Linux. The lifter is a pinned branch of NoRain211’s fork of sp00nznet/xboxrecomp.

Public CI checks the recipe, setup and ISO-extraction scripts with synthetic inputs and builds and runs the runtime tests on Windows without game files. The status page states that these tests do not show the game boots or plays; playability rests on owner and contributor sessions, and PlayStation pads are unconfirmed on hardware.

Original code is GPL-3.0-or-later, and NOTICE grants no rights to the game; xboxrecomp is MIT and other components keep their own licenses. The README and NOTICE state substantial use of LLMs and AI coding agents for code, reverse-engineering analysis, debugging, tests and documentation, with changes reviewed and tested.

resources.name: Elgato HDR: a userspace capture path for the Elgato 4K X’s 10-bit mode
resources.description: A native macOS app that reaches the Elgato 4K X capture card’s 10-bit P010 video mode, which the project says Apple’s built-in webcam driver does not expose to apps. A root helper detaches that driver and runs the card’s USB Video Class streaming directly through libusb, feeding a Metal HDR viewer, an HDR10 recorder and an editor. Latency figures and device coverage remain author-reported.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-13 head, after release 1.0.0 (2026-09-08). It targets an Elgato 4K X on macOS 14 or newer; the README reports building and testing on Apple Silicon only, and other Elgato cards with a P010 UVC format are untested. The HDR preview needs an HDR/EDR display. Among the 10-bit modes, 4K is limited to 30 fps by USB bandwidth.

Building needs Xcode Command Line Tools and Homebrew’s libusb: build.sh compiles the C helper against libusb, bundles the library, compiles the Swift app and signs it ad hoc, and releases are not notarized. The helper needs one administrator prompt because detaching the macOS kernel driver requires root; it exits about 20 seconds after the app quits and hands the card back to macOS.

The repository keeps the USB descriptor-dump tools used while reverse-engineering the card and a script that sweeps every capture mode; it contains no vendor firmware or driver binaries. Recordings carry fixed HDR10 mastering metadata because, per the README, the card does not pass the source’s HDMI HDR metadata over USB.

The README and the Game-mode pull request report display delays of about 48, 22 and 5 ms for the Smooth, Game and Lowest Latency modes at 1440p60 on a 120 Hz MacBook Pro, measured from USB transfer completion to display as reported by macOS; the card’s own processing comes on top, and the PR notes that the test card sent silent audio. These are author measurements.

MIT covers the project code; the bundled libusb library and captured content keep their own terms, and the project states it is not affiliated with Elgato or Corsair. An X post under the same handle credits REA with helping this latency work.

resources.name: ido-static-recomp
resources.description: Statically recompiles the IRIX MIPS programs of SGI's IDO 5.3 and 7.1 C toolchain, such as cc, cfe, uopt, ugen and as1, into native Linux, macOS and Windows executables, so matching decompilation projects can build with the original compiler code on modern hosts. It recompiles compilers, not games: it neither decompiles nor translates game code.
requirements: Building needs make and a C11/C++17 compiler (build-essential on Debian/Ubuntu, Homebrew make on macOS). make setup builds the vendored rabbitizer disassembler and the recompiler; make VERSION=5.3 or VERSION=7.1 then emits the toolchain under build/<version>/out, with RELEASE=1 for optimized builds and TARGET=universal for universal macOS binaries. Release v1.2 (2024-11-12) ships IDO 5.3 and 7.1 archives for Linux, Linux ARM, macOS and Windows; the reviewed main commit dates from 2025-07-05.

Recompiled programs expect a flattened directory beside cc, with USR_LIB and USR_INCLUDE environment overrides for the /usr/lib and /usr/include redirection. The IDO 5.3 program list includes copt, ld and strip, which the 7.1 list lacks.

Perfect Dark pins github.com/Emill/ido-static-recomp at 421e546 (per-function branch, 2021-11-03) as its tools/recomp submodule. GitHub compares that commit with this entry's pin as diverged, 87 commits ahead and 2 behind, and Emill is among the decompals contributors; neither repository is marked as a fork. Other matching decompilations, such as Majora's Mask, download builds from decompals.

The repository bundles the original IRIX compiler binaries under ido/5.3 and ido/7.1. Only ido/5.3 carries an SGI freeware notice; no license file covers the recompiler or the IDO 7.1 binaries at the reviewed commit, GitHub detects no repository license, and the vendored rabbitizer keeps its own MIT license.

resources.name: TH08 Web: a WebAssembly port built from reconstructed source
resources.description: Compiles the reconstructed C++ source of the Japanese Touhou 8 1.00d release to WebAssembly with Emscripten, adding WebGL 2 rendering, Web Audio, browser input and IndexedDB saves behind the game’s D3D8-, DirectSound- and DirectInput-shaped interfaces. Players select their own retail DAT files locally. The web build makes no binary-exact claim and is a separate port from the curated TH08 reconstruction.
requirements: README reports the game playable from title to ending in desktop browsers and recommends current Chrome; Firefox automatically uses a dedicated no-readback build, while Safari and mobile browsers are not verified. The page needs WebAssembly threads, SharedArrayBuffer, WebGL 2, Web Audio and cross-origin-isolated HTTPS. Listed remaining work includes Firefox hardware profiling, replay endurance and memory-ceiling measurement.

Select th08.dat and thbgm.dat from your own legally obtained TH08 installation. The launcher copies th08.dat into session memory and range-reads thbgm.dat; README says neither is uploaded, bundled or persisted. The repository, deployment and release v0.1.0 contain no retail data or executable, and a provenance script rejects forbidden payloads and any artifact outside the nine-file allowlist.

Local builds need Docker, Python 3 and a desktop browser: scripts/build-web-game.sh uses a digest-pinned Emscripten 6.0.8 image, and scripts/serve-web.py supplies the COOP, COEP and CORP headers a generic static server lacks. The public site is a Cloudflare Pages deployment from main, and self-hosting the release archive needs the same isolation headers.

WEB_ARCHITECTURE.md records author-run checks with user-selected retail files: a complete Lunatic Final-B route in Chromium and on an earlier Firefox bridge, a Stage 6B practice run, persistence tests showing no DAT in IndexedDB, and replay-driven pacing samples near 60 Hz under the SwiftShader and llvmpipe software renderers.

MIT covers repository code and documentation, not the original game, DAT files, music or graphics; the pinned Detours submodule keeps its own terms. README describes this repository as the web-focused fork of N0zoM1z0/th08 with its history retained.

resources.name: ipsw
resources.description: Command-line toolkit for Apple firmware research and reverse engineering. It downloads and unpacks IPSWs, OTAs and KDKs and compares builds; inspects Mach-O load commands, symbols, signatures and entitlements with ARM64 disassembly; finds symbols and cross-references in dyld shared caches, extracts dylibs and dumps Objective-C headers and Swift metadata; extracts KEXTs and compares kernelcaches; and parses IMG4, decrypts AEA archives and inspects iBoot and coprocessor firmware.
requirements: Release at review: v3.1.739, published 2026-10-16, with Linux, macOS, Windows and iOS builds plus deb, rpm, apk and Arch packages; the reviewed master commit is three cache and documentation commits ahead. Install with Homebrew (tap or core formula), snap or Scoop. The extras build (Unicorn-based dyld emulation, libusb device commands) and the Frida build are macOS only. Source builds need a C toolchain for CGO and, per the README, Go 1.26+, although go.mod declares go 1.27.

Firmware, caches and binaries are supplied by the user or fetched with the download commands. With --dec, macho disass and dyld disass send disassembly to the LLM provider chosen with --dec-llm: hosted OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini or router APIs, ACP agent CLIs, or local Ollama. The separate ipswd daemon exposes a REST API, and the README points agents to the separate ipsw-skill repository.

MIT license. The README notes that extracted dylibs can still reference metadata elsewhere in the cache, so it recommends Objective-C analysis on the cache itself. LLM decompilation output is model-generated and needs verification.

resources.name: OpenXcom: an open-source clone of X-COM: UFO Defense and Terror from the Deep
resources.description: Reimplements MicroProse’s UFO: Enemy Unknown (X-COM: UFO Defense) and X-COM: Terror from the Deep as a C++/SDL engine that runs on the user’s original game resources. Game data such as items, craft, research and missions is expressed in YAML rulesets, which also carry its standard mods and a wider modding ecosystem. It is a clone that reuses original content, not recovered MicroProse code.
requirements: The reviewed master snapshot reports version 1.0 Dev; the last tagged release is v1.0 from 2014, and a nightly workflow builds later Windows, Linux and macOS versions. It covers both games and can import saved games from the originals, while standard mods based on XcomUtil and UFOExtender add optional changes.

Requires an unmodified copy of the resources from either or both original games. For UFO these include the GEODATA, GEOGRAPH, MAPS, ROUTES, SOUND, TERRAIN, UFOGRAPH and UNITS folders, and TFTD needs a similar set. The README warns against modded copies such as XcomUtil-patched data; the Windows installer can detect Steam editions.

Building targets C++11 with CMake 3.5+, Visual C++, Xcode or a plain Makefile, against SDL 1.2, SDL_mixer, SDL_gfx 2.0.22+, SDL_image and yaml-cpp 0.5.3+. CI compiles debug builds on Linux, 32-bit Windows and macOS.
CI only compiles the code, and the repository has no automated behaviour tests.
Source headers apply GPL-3.0-or-later, and the README notes modified SDL_gfx code (LGPL) used with its author’s permission. Original game resources keep their own rights.

resources.name: Skate 3 Recomp: a native Xbox 360 recompilation through ReXGlue
resources.description: Recompiles the Xbox 360 version of Skate 3 into native Windows, Linux and macOS builds with a Skate-specific fork of the ReXGlue SDK. Since v2.0.0 a native Direct3D 12 and Vulkan renderer with ports of the game’s own material shading replaces emulation of the Xbox 360 GPU, which remains as a fallback. Game files come from the user’s disc image; the author calls the native renderer early and has not tested the game end to end.
requirements: The latest reviewed release is v2.0.2 (July 2026) for Windows, Linux and experimental Apple-silicon macOS; the README calls Windows the most tested platform. Known native-renderer issues include streaming pop-in, skater-customization rendering, Hall of Meat highlights and skate-park parity; frame-rate and power gains over the emulated renderer are author-reported.

Players choose an ISO of their own Xbox 360 copy of Skate 3 for the built-in installer, and DLC needs the user’s own package files. Source codegen reads default.xex and data/webkit/EAWebkit.xex from an extracted dump and should also be given the Title Update 3 package, whose patched executables release builds require. Retail files and generated recompilation sources are git-ignored.

Builds need CMake 3.25+, Ninja and Clang 18 or newer (Clang 20 is recommended on Ubuntu 24.04); MSVC and Apple Clang are unsupported. The pinned rexglue-sdk submodule is the author’s fork on the rexglue 0.8.0 line, holding the runtime, codegen, input, timing and both graphics backends. Vulkan SPIR-V shader binaries are committed, and macOS uses Homebrew LLVM with MoltenVK.

The reviewed tree contains no CI workflow, test suite or fidelity comparison, and the README says the game has not been played through on the native renderer. Visual-parity statements are project claims.

Neither the repository nor its GitHub metadata declares a license for the project’s code; the rexglue fork carries a Xenia-derived BSD-3-Clause notice, and Skate 3 content retains Electronic Arts’ rights.

resources.name: decomp.wtf
resources.description: A discontinued local app and MCP server that hands AI coding agents one function of a user-owned console game at a time, compiles each C attempt with the game’s period compiler and accepts it only when the linked result matches the original bytes. It can start a project from a ROM or disc image, or work inside forks of public decompilation projects listed on decomp.dev, where objdiff judges the result. Its final commit, dated 15 October 2026, marks it discontinued in response to opposition in the decompilation community; the code stays under MIT without further fixes or releases.
requirements: The reviewed pin is the discontinuation commit of the archived repository, at package version 0.10.6, which the README names as the last installable release. The author will not fix issues, review pull requests or publish releases; existing installs keep working without updates. It runs on Linux and, marked unstable, on Windows inside its own WSL 2 distribution; macOS is unsupported. It needs Python 3.12 or later, and its installer sets up uv, the app, pinned checksum-verified period compilers and the m2c draft decompiler.

Agents connect through the local decomp mcp server or a Claude Code plugin that adds a decompile skill. README lists Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity CLI, opencode, other MCP clients and a built-in loop for OpenAI-compatible APIs, including local models. Agents receive only decomp.wtf’s tools, without a shell. Users pay their own model provider; the author reports about 8 cents for a small function with Claude Code and warns that large functions take many more attempts.

Users supply their own ROM, disc image or program file. The tool contains no game code or ROMs apart from a bundled demo N64 ROM built from public-domain code and zlib. Proprietary period compilers such as IDO and CodeWarrior are installed only after the user agrees. Continuing a public decomp clones that project locally and runs its build scripts, so the README advises forking only trusted projects.

README lists GameCube, Wii and N64 as recommended and PlayStation, PlayStation 2, Game Boy Advance and DS as beta, tested mostly on homemade games. It reports imports tested on named commercial titles and exports that rebuild the input byte for byte, with GameCube and Wii files linked and checksum-checked in dtk-template projects. These remain author statements: the repository has a pytest suite but no CI workflow at the pin, publishes no game results.

The repository is MIT-licensed. Its README asks users to work only on games they own, not to circumvent copy protection, not to publish decompiled code of games whose rights they do not hold, and to follow each public project’s contribution rules, noting that many community decomps reject AI-written contributions. Nothing is sent upstream automatically. The project disclaims affiliation with the tools it builds on.

resources.name: Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection native Windows port
resources.description: Runs the PS4 Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection’s own x86-64 executables natively on Windows: a runtime supplies the PS4 system libraries and a shadPS4-derived Vulkan renderer executes the GPU work. The port adds a per-game launcher, resolution patches and modern upscaling, and its status table reports all three games playable with listed open issues. It is a compatibility-runtime port rather than a decompilation, and its results remain project-reported.
requirements: Reviewed at the commit of release v0.2.3 (2026-10-18); v0.1.0 was published on 2026-10-15. README reports Drake’s Fortune, Among Thieves and Drake’s Deception playable, with the Collection menu, game switching, saves, audio, movies and controllers working. Known issues include a Drake’s Fortune grenade-launcher fault, cropped ultrawide views, single-core GPU-command limits on slower CPUs, experimental multithreaded rendering and less play-testing for Uncharted 3. The original game code is run with local patches, not rebuilt from recovered source.

Supply your own dumped copy of the PS4 game CUSA02344, the folder holding eboot.bin and sce_sys; game update 1.02 is optional and recommended. README says no game files are in the repository or its builds, and the preparation script patches the game executables locally for resolution and update handling. The project disclaims affiliation with Sony, Naughty Dog and Bluepoint Games, and the games keep their own rights.

Play needs 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, a CPU with AVX, F16C, BMI1, MOVBE and LZCNT (Intel Haswell or newer, or any AMD Ryzen), a Vulkan 1.3 GPU and about 6 GB of free RAM, with 16 GB recommended. Local builds use an MSYS2 CLANG64 toolchain with CMake, Ninja, the Vulkan stack, SDL3, FFmpeg, Boost and other listed packages, plus a Windows Python 3.10+ with Pillow for packaging. GitHub Actions builds the Windows package on each push, and the launcher’s updater checks release SHA-256 digests.

STATUS.md records native runtime tests for fibers, services, video decoding, buffered input and clock timing, with the cause and user confirmation of individual fixes. README frame rates come from the author’s RTX 5080 and integrated Radeon tests plus one player report. The CI workflow builds and publishes packages without automated game tests.

README declares GPL v2 or later. The runtime started from FelipePrado0’s GPL-2.0 gow3_pc and the shadPS4 video core, and the TAA camera approach credits SuperMedo’s GPL v2 Uncharted port. Packages bundle third-party libraries; NVIDIA’s DLSS DLL, fetched by a build script from NVIDIA’s DLSS repository, stays under NVIDIA’s license. STATUS.md mentions REA as unable to decompile the prepared ELF on Windows.

resources.name: TH095: function-level reconstruction of Shoot the Bullet 1.02a
resources.description: Reconstructs source for the original Japanese Touhou 9.5: Shoot the Bullet 1.02a executable, accepting function exactness only through reproducible byte comparison of pinned Visual C++ .NET 2003 builds against one hash-attested target. The whole program also compiles and links into a playable Windows i386 executable, while README keeps playability, function matching and whole-executable identity as separate statuses.
requirements: Generated PROGRESS.md reports 697 confirmed authored functions among 1,880 candidates, all with source, and 696 canonically exact, covering 99.22% of confirmed authored bytes; Controller::GetInput keeps one differing byte. README lists semantic reconstruction as active and Windows x86-64, Linux and Web ports as planned, and tags the playable baseline v0.1.0-windows-i386 without release binaries.

Supply your own original Japanese 1.02a th095.exe matching the size, SHA-256 and MD5 in README, imported as resources/th095.exe; playing also needs the game’s data. README says copyrighted executables, game data and private analysis databases are not included, and public CI runs only target-independent checks.

scripts/bootstrap-tools.sh needs curl, git, sha256sum, tar, unzip, uv and Wine, then fetches checksum-pinned Ghidra 12.1.3, Temurin JDK 21, objdiff 3.8.0 and Microsoft Visual C++ .NET 2003 (13.10.3077) binaries from a third-party archive repository; reccmp 0.1.6 is also pinned. scripts/build-whole.py cold-compiles and links the production graph and refuses stubbed or force-linked images.

Exact credit requires a zero-difference COFF function comparison recorded in the match ledgers; Ghidra, IDA MCP and runtime observation count only as supporting evidence. README cites a full-game runtime video using a test-only no-death launcher plus separate normal-build tests, and RUNTIME_ISSUES.md notes those checks used 2026-09-10 source, with later semantic changes only compile- and link-validated.

MIT covers repository code and documentation, not the game or its assets; the downloaded compiler and tools keep their own terms. The repository carries coding-agent rules and skills and a GPT web Ghidra bridge; REA’s separately published Touhou essay discusses this project.

resources.name: DynamoRIO
resources.description: Runtime code manipulation system for building dynamic tools that observe or transform any part of an unmodified program while it runs. Its API and IA-32/AMD64/ARM/AArch64 instruction manipulation library allow arbitrary changes to application instructions, not only inserted callouts. The release package bundles tools including drcov for code coverage, drltrace for library-call tracing, drstrace for Windows system calls, drmemtrace instruction and memory traces and the drdisas disassembler. It is a framework for building instrumentation tools, distinct from Frida's scripting of live processes.
requirements: The README lists Windows, Linux and Android on IA-32, AMD64, ARM and AArch64 hardware; macOS support is in progress. Latest stable release at review: release_11.3.0-1, published 2025-01-11, with Windows, Linux, AArch64 Linux, ARM Linux EABIHF and ARM Android packages. Weekly cronbuild packages follow master (cronbuild-11.91.20741, published 2026-10-17, with no Android package); this entry pins the reviewed master commit.

Custom tools are written against the API, whose documentation ships in the release package and online; API samples cover memory-address, instruction and basic-block tracing and instruction counting. The README names WinAFL, the Arm Instruction Emulator, DrCCTProf, VClinic and GWPSan as external tools built on it and bundles Dr. Memory.
Primarily BSD. The drsyscall, drwrap and drutil extensions and the Dr. Memory Framework libraries are LGPL 2.1, and the drsyms extension links elfutils libraries under LGPL 3.

resources.name: LGwebOS-menubar: a native macOS remote for LG webOS TVs
resources.description: A native macOS menu-bar app that pairs with an LG webOS TV over its local encrypted WebSocket interface to launch apps, switch inputs, adjust volume and picture settings, send pointer input and cast selected media. The project credits the public Connect SDK for webOS protocol behavior and reuses PyWebOSTV’s registration manifest. Testing covers one TV on webOS 5.0.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-13 head, when the repository held only this app. By 2026-10-20 GitHub serves it as TVmenubar-MacOS, and its head README splits it into separate LG webOS 5.0 and Roku OS 15.3.4 apps. It needs macOS 14 or later, Xcode Command Line Tools with Swift 5.9 or later, and an LG webOS TV on the same network; the only tested set is an LG 50UN7310PSC on webOS 5.0, and other models and versions are unverified. Pairing must be accepted on the TV, an IPv4 address is required, and Wake-on-LAN needs the TV’s MAC address.

scripts/build.sh produces a locally signed, unnotarized app bundle. Pairing uses encrypted WebSockets on port 3001; the app pins the TV certificate after explicit approval and keeps pairing keys in Keychain. The repository ships no device addresses or pairing keys, and a privacy-check script scans files before publishing.
The offline --self-check runs preference, certificate, pointer, Home, usage, resource and loopback media tests without a TV.

The README narrows the author’s post: screen time is counted locally only while the app is connected, AirPlay support is limited to guidance for macOS Screen Mirroring, picture-setting changes depend on TV permissions, and casting depends on the TV’s codecs and DLNA service.

MIT covers the project code; the PyWebOSTV manifest keeps its MIT notice, and LG, app and console icons keep their owners’ rights. Commits credit Claude as co-author, and an X post by the same account credits REA. This is an unofficial client.

resources.name: PS2Recomp
resources.description: Experimental static recompiler that translates MIPS R5900 code from PlayStation 2 ELF executables into C++ and links it with a bundled runtime. ps2xAnalyzer or a Ghidra export script produces a per-game TOML of functions, stubs, skips and instruction patches; ps2xRecomp emits a literal instruction-by-instruction translation; ps2xRuntime and ps2xIOP supply guest memory, syscall dispatch, IOP module execution with HLE fallbacks and partial, largely stubbed GS/VU hardware. Output is not decompiled source, and getting a game to run remains per-game porting work.
requirements: Building needs CMake 3.20+ and a C++20 compiler; the README says it is tested mainly with MSVC, and some vector paths need SSE4/AVX host support. CMake fetches ELFIO, toml11, fmt, libdwarf and raylib at configure time, plus Dear ImGui when the debug UI is enabled. GitHub lists five source-only prereleases, v0.0 to v0.4 (the latest from 2026-04-05), with no binaries attached; the reviewed main commit (2026-10-14) is 36 commits after v0.4.

The user supplies the game ELF; the project ships no game code, and its project-description guidance names the original release as one the user must own. The preferred workflow exports functions from Ghidra with the bundled ExportPS2Functions.java script, while ps2_analyzer suits ELFs with debug symbols. Stub address bindings and game overrides target one exact ELF build and are not portable across games, regions or builds.
The README lists very poor VU and GS performance and partial, often stubbed hardware emulation as limitations. The tree also holds Android and PS Vita build directories and a ps2xStudio front end.
GPL-3.0; fetched dependencies keep their own licenses, and the README cites PCSX2 as a runtime reference.

resources.name: CorsixTH: an open reimplementation of Theme Hospital
resources.description: Reimplements the engine of Bullfrog’s 1997 Theme Hospital, with game logic in Lua and C++ for graphics, sound, movies and pathfinding, on top of the original game’s data files. The README reports that the full campaign can be completed, lists features that are still missing, and adds extensions such as high resolutions and a map editor. It recreates the game’s behaviour on original content rather than recovering Bullfrog source code.
requirements: The reviewed master snapshot follows the v0.70.1 release of 2026-08-28. The README lists multiplayer/LAN, AI hospitals, rats and the bonus rat level, vomit waves and the win-level video or letter as missing, and warns that some objects may glitch with walls. Custom campaigns, 4K support, the level editor and improved game logic are deliberate extensions.

Needs the user’s Theme Hospital data from the original CD, the GOG.com or EA editions, or the Theme Hospital demo, including the resource folder with ANIMS and LEVELS (sometimes named HOSP). The original graphics lack complete sets for some patient types, so enabling their regular spawning may cause anomalies.

Source builds use CMake 3.16+ with a C++17 compiler, SDL3, SDL3_mixer, Lua (or optionally LuaJIT) and zlib; FFmpeg enables in-game movies, and vcpkg manages dependencies for preset builds. The README lists builds for Windows and macOS, a Linux AppImage, Flatpak and Snap, and distribution packages for Linux and BSD.
CI runs luacheck and busted Lua unit tests on Linux, plus CMake builds with CTest on Windows.

LICENSE.txt grants MIT terms for CorsixTH and includes notices for bundled components such as Lua 5.5, LPeg and LuaFileSystem, so GitHub does not classify it as one licence. Original Theme Hospital data keeps its own rights. AGENTS.md gives instructions for AI coding agents.

resources.name: OpenRiseOfNations: a native macOS engine reimplementation
resources.description: Reimplements the Rise of Nations: Extended Edition engine as a native macOS app with a Metal renderer, a deterministic simulation, a computer opponent and a compatible BigHugeScript compiler and virtual machine, loading art, maps, rules and scripts from the user’s own Windows installation. Subsystem specifications written from Ghidra study of the symbol-bearing executable, together with JavaScript reference tools, guided a C++17 implementation built with heavy Claude Code assistance. The alpha plays tutorials and scenarios, and its bit-exactness checks remain project-reported.
requirements: The reviewed pin is version 0.1.1; releases v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 are dated 2026-10-14. README calls the C++17 engine early but playable on macOS 12+ with Metal and AppKit, covering tutorials and stock scenarios, unit control, economy, construction, combat, a computer opponent and the game’s scripts. Random maps and the skirmish setup screen, the Conquer the World campaign, multiplayer, saves and replays, garrisons, heroes and several other systems are not yet implemented.

Users must own Rise of Nations: Extended Edition and supply the Windows version’s game folder, whose Data and scenario directories provide the art, maps, rules, scripts and audio; README names SteamCMD or a copy from a Windows PC as routes. The repository and the un-notarised DMG ship no game files or original program code, with a fan-adapted main-menu logo as the stated exception. Building from source needs only Apple’s Command Line Tools and build-mac.sh.

README says the executable ships with full debug symbols, which enabled Ghidra study; about thirty specifications in docs/ describe each subsystem in paraphrase, citing original functions by name and address, and JavaScript reference tools in re/tools read the game data. README credits heavy use of Claude Code, directed and reviewed by the maintainer. STATUS.md says the reverse engineering ran as background agents that each produced a spec, while the author’s reply says he reverse-engineered in Ghidra and wrote the specs himself.

Verification is project-reported. C++ checkers compare damage on all 169,312 attacker/target pairs, prices, income and interface layouts with the reference tools, rules tables with a recorded game’s memory image and world grids across 156 stock scenarios, and a headless harness checks determinism. The simulation targets bit-identical lockstep behavior but has not yet been compared with recorded games, and rendering was checked by reading snapshots.

The engine is GPL-3.0; the menu logo is excluded, and its rights stay with the original owners. The project states that it is unaffiliated with Microsoft, Big Huge Games and SkyBox Labs. .gitignore keeps decompiler output, symbol dumps and extracted data out of the repository, although two small instruction-search outputs listing original addresses are committed under re/jobs.

resources.name: TH04: rebuilding Lotus Land Story’s four PC-98 programs from source
resources.description: Reconstructs source for the Japanese PC-98 Touhou 4: Lotus Land Story and rebuilds all four DOS programs, MAIN.EXE, OP.EXE, MAINE.EXE and ZUN.COM, with a pinned Borland toolchain under Wine. Function acceptance against the original binaries is tracked separately from emulator replays that compare inputs, RNG, object pools and video with the original game. Complete-campaign, original-timing and byte-identity goals remain open.
requirements: Generated PROGRESS.md reports 661 of 663 reviewed authored functions exact across the four artifacts and 99.97% of confirmed MAIN authored bytes, with two MAIN cases deferred. README says the rebuilt products need not reproduce the original executable bytes and that complete-game and original-timing acceptance are unfinished. A 64-bit native port on the port/modern-64 branch is reported with scoped Linux clears.

Supply your own legal copy containing the Japanese zun.hdi; the importer requires OP.EXE, MAIN.EXE, MAINE.EXE and ZUN.COM matching the sizes and SHA-256 values in README, whose provenance is marked candidate-local-attested pending an independent pristine dump. Image preparation modifies a disposable copy of that image, and original executables and assets are never committed.

Builds use Turbo C++ 4.0J, TASM 5.0 and TLINK under Wine; the bootstrapper fetches them from third-party mirrors that TOOLCHAIN.md does not treat as authoritative, and takes MS-DOS Player from a pinned ReC98 checkout. The tested host is Debian 12 x86-64 with Python 3.11. Runtime checks also need DOSBox-X 2024.03.01, Xvfb, xdotool and ImageMagick, and the Windows build entry point uses a WSL toolchain bridge.

README reports original-versus-reconstructed DOS replays agreeing on consumed input, score, RNG, nine actor pools, 22 state blocks and configured video regions across the four bundled demos and longer Stage 1–3 routes, while raw GDC timing and some post-reset input samples still differ. A 2026-10-16 audit found frozen native programs and candidate MAIN files missing from local storage, so historical replay first needs recovery. Public CI runs target-independent checks only.

MIT covers repository-authored code and documentation, not the game, its assets or third-party work; ReC98, credited as a migration input, has no license file at the pinned revision, and the Borland tools stay proprietary. The repository is organized around coding-agent handoffs; REA’s TH04 helper showcase and Touhou essay cover parts of it.

resources.name: Supermodel: initial Real3D Pro-1000 image-generator emulation
resources.description: Adds emulation of Real3D’s Pro-1000, the SCSI-attached image generator from which Sega’s Model 3 graphics hardware derives, to the Supermodel arcade emulator. It boots user-supplied Pro-1000 firmware from the SDK disc, emulates the board’s interrupt, JTAG and UART hardware, and exposes the firmware’s built-in monitor on the console. Nothing renders yet, and SCSI host communication is unimplemented.
requirements: Reviewed at merge commit 4f5d686 of pull request #343, merged 2026-10-14, which adds a CPro1000 emulator class beside the Model 3 one. The PR boots the firmware to its UART monitor and accepts console commands such as help; it states that nothing is drawn, not even the start-up logo, and that SCSI communication is the next step.

Supply the Pro-1000 firmware images p1_p4.bin and p2.bin from the SDK disc; Config/Games.xml lists their CRC32 values, and the repository does not include them. The PR says the default scene and model data sat in a SCSI ROM that the SDK lacks and would have to come from original hardware that likely no longer exists; a synthetic SCSI ROM only gets past renderer initialization.

Supermodel documents builds with GCC and Make on Windows (MSYS2, with SDL2 and SDL2_net), Linux and macOS, and a Visual Studio project; the PR adds its sources to the shared Makefile rules and that project. No Pro-1000 test or rendering comparison accompanies the change.

Source comments describe the hardware findings as reverse-engineered working hypotheses drawn from firmware disassembly, logs of unmapped accesses and UART output, embedded SCCS module strings, address cross-references, part datasheets and the SDK manuals. Some registers and the JTAG scan chain remain unknown.

Supermodel’s source headers declare GPL-3.0-or-later; the firmware, SDK material and demo databases keep their own rights. The author’s X post credits Claude with doing the reverse engineering and writing the emulation, and credits co-author Ian Curtis with the earlier SCSI-interception demos.

resources.name: Blackbox Protobuf
resources.description: NCC Group's tools for decoding and re-encoding Protocol Buffers messages without the matching .proto definition. The decoder returns the message data with an editable type definition built from best-effort guesses based on wire types; analysts can name fields, correct types and re-encode edited messages, which protoc --decode_raw cannot do. It ships as a Python library with a bbpb CLI, a Jython Burp Suite extension and a mitmproxy addon, and its README traces it to modifying messages during mobile penetration tests.
requirements: The library and CLI install from PyPI as bbpb (1.4.2, Python >=3.8,<4.0); the README calls the blackboxprotobuf PyPI package an older fork. The mitmproxy addon loads mitmproxy/bbpb.py with bbpb installed in the same environment; edited types survive restarts only with the bbpb_project_file option, and editing commands are unavailable in mitmweb.
The Burp extension needs Burp Suite configured with Jython 2.7+ and a clone with git submodule update --init. gRPC needs Burp's HTTP/2 support, and only uncompressed gRPC payloads are handled.

Field types are guessed from wire types and occasionally field content, so type definitions may need analyst correction; field names and meanings are not recovered, and a type-discovery tool is listed only as future work. .proto import and export use a partial parser that does not resolve import statements.
MIT. The default branch was last committed on 2025-03-14, the day of release v1.4.2.

resources.name: Claude Intercept
resources.description: A local man-in-the-middle proxy and dashboard that captures HTTP/S traffic from the user’s own computer and devices, stores it in SQLite and hands it to Claude Code through an /intercept skill and CLI. Exports such as API documentation and traffic summaries support investigating request patterns and undocumented endpoints. It is an agent-facing capture tool for authorized testing, not a reconstruction case, and it has no established REA connection.
requirements: The reviewed pin is package version 1.0.0, last updated 2026-06-02. It combines a Node.js proxy with a per-machine CA, a live web dashboard, local SQLite storage, a CLI and a Claude Code /intercept skill, with Markdown or JSON exports shaped for agent analysis. README asks for Node.js 22.5+, while package.json declares 22.15.0 or later; the system-proxy toggle and certificate trust are automated on macOS and GNOME/KDE Linux, and Windows needs manual configuration.

HTTPS capture requires installing and trusting the generated CA and routing a device through the proxy; README covers macOS, Linux, iOS, Android and Firefox, and warns that leaving the system proxy enabled after stopping the server breaks connectivity. README says some certificate-pinned domains fail under the proxy, and the skill states that WebSocket connections are tunneled and logged without frame parsing.

In the reviewed source the proxy and the dashboard listen on all network interfaces, and the dashboard API has no access check; README warns against running it on untrusted networks. Captures and some exports can contain account credentials and personal data, and anything passed to Claude for analysis leaves the machine under the model provider’s terms. The project limits use to devices and accounts the user owns or is explicitly permitted to test.
Tests under src/__tests__ run with node --test, but the repository has no CI workflow, and the README’s install example still uses a placeholder repository URL.

The repository is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0, a non-commercial Creative Commons license rather than a software license, so commercial use is not permitted. The reported post presents it as a Ship Systems project built with William Haesemeyer.

resources.name: Finding Jingle Town: Debugging an N64 Game without Symbols
resources.description: A walkthrough from the Snowboard Kids 2 decompilation project on attaching gdb-multiarch to the Ares emulator while the matching build still cannot carry debug information. It breaks on a function by its ELF symbol name and reads one structure byte by hand to test whether that byte selects the level overlay. A short method note on checking decompilation hypotheses at runtime, not a reconstruction result.
requirements: The post, dated 23 December 2025, asks one question: how Snowboard Kids 2 picks the level overlay on level entry. It breaks on a function that indexes 16 overlays and reads the candidate byte for Sunny Mountain, Turtle Island and Jingle Town (0, 1 and 2). Other levels and the code that sets the index are not traced.

Following it needs a Snowboard Kids 2 N64 ROM, original or rebuilt by the decompilation (the post treats them as byte-identical), and the decompilation's build/snowboardkids2.elf for function names. The post does not cover obtaining or building either.

Tools are gdb-multiarch set to mips:4000 and Ares with debugging enabled, connected through Ares's GDB remote support; an SSH reverse tunnel is optional when GDB runs on another host, as on the author's x86 Ubuntu server. The post explains that adding -g would shift sections in the absolute-address build and usually stop it booting, so structure fields are read by manual pointer arithmetic.

Results are the author's observations from one debugging session. The post calls the workflow painfully manual and reports gdbgui did not work with the setup. Its generated names have since changed: at reviewed commit 7600c79, symbol_addrs.txt names 0x8003D560 initRace and 0x800AFE8C gGameSessionContext, and the footnoted src/3E160.c is no longer in the tree.
The post describes manual debugging. The decompilation repository has no license file at the reviewed commit, and the game ROM and its content keep their own rights.

resources.name: JPCERT/CC: APK analysis and API probing on attack servers
resources.description: JPCERT/CC’s 15 October 2026 blog post on the infrastructure behind a series of unauthorized-access incidents in Japan. It reports that the attackers used AI for known-vulnerability scanning and API attacks, and that attack servers held APKs, jadx- and Blutter-related files, APK-extraction directories and an SSRF test script used to probe app APIs. It is a defender’s account of observed attacker tooling with mitigation advice, not a published AI-assisted analysis method or reproducible workflow.
requirements: The reviewed source is the Japanese-language JPCERT/CC Eyes post dated 15 October 2026; no English version was found at the corresponding URL during review. It follows JPCERT/CC’s 8 October alert about personal-data leaks reported by several organizations in Japan, and describes three investigated servers, one of which it states is not directly related to these attacks.

The post states that JPCERT/CC confirmed AI use for scanning and API attacks, but it does not name the AI system or tooling or explain how AI was applied. The roles of the SSRF script and some files are described as likely rather than confirmed. Findings are illustrated with partial file listings and one script; no samples, logs, prompts or timelines are published.

Appendix A describes Blutter as an open-source tool for analyzing the Dart AOT-compiled code in Flutter apps, and cites third-party write-ups that combine Frida, Blutter, LIEF and Capstone to recover embedded keys and request-signing logic. These are referenced examples, not JPCERT/CC’s own reproduction.

Recommended mitigations are to keep API signing keys and long-lived credentials out of apps, to authenticate and authorize users on the server rather than rely on in-app signing or obfuscation, to rate-limit and monitor API use, and to restrict SSRF-prone URL fetches and re-validate redirect destinations. The post also lists three attacker IP indicators.
The post names jadx and Blutter but no other analysis tools.

resources.name: Xenosaga I Decomp Compatibility Kit
resources.description: Checks a PS2 matching decompilation from outside its own build: the C is recompiled with a stock, unpatched ee-gcc 2.96 and assembler, then each function is byte-compared against the original and every difference is classified by its likely toolchain cause. Companion scripts export ELF symbol tables to CSV and convert them to splat symbol files. Defaults target Xenosaga Episode I; the README says the method generalises but the defaults do not.
requirements: The reviewed commit d9bb53d is the second of two commits, both made on 2026-09-25; there are no releases or tests. It holds three Python tools and symbol data for the NTSC-U Xenosaga Episode I executable SLUS_204.69 and its five overlays, built with SCE ee-gcc 2.96. Tool docstrings still refer to out/ paths and a TOOLCHAIN.md that are not in the repository.

verify_decomp.py needs a checkout of the decompilation under test, your own SLUS_204.69 and extracted originals (located through DECOMP_GAME_DIR), and an i386 root filesystem with stock ee-gcc 2.96 and ee-as run through Docker under linux/386 emulation, plus clang for preprocessing. The README points to decompme/compilers for the compiler, which is not vendored, and documents a colima and binfmt route for Apple-silicon Macs.

It compiles each C translation unit with -DSKIP_ASM, compares every defined function against the original bytes, labels differences hazard-nop, reorder, mixed, immediate or unexplained, and exits nonzero only for unexplained ones. The README warns that the mixed class masks branch and call targets, so a wrong target there is not flagged; functions whose relocations need the tested project's data layout are reported as unverifiable.

The README's case study against an anonymised PS2 matching decompilation reports 817 of 857 functions identical, 40 differences all in toolchain classes, 195 unverifiable and one compiler crash. It also reports 5,927 shared names with no address disagreements against another decompilation's symbol file. Neither result is published with its inputs.

MIT-licensed. The repository includes a 15,132-entry symbol table that its README says comes from the unstripped retail executables, but no game binaries, extracted assets or decompiled game code; the game remains its rights holders' property.

resources.name: inFAMOUS Second Son native PC port
resources.description: Runs the PS4 inFAMOUS Second Son’s own x86-64 code natively on Windows and Linux: a runtime reimplements the PS4 system libraries the game uses, and a shadPS4-derived core translates its GPU commands and shaders to Vulkan. The project reports a playable, in-development port that reaches gameplay and the first chapters, with unstable performance and remaining graphics glitches. It is a compatibility-runtime port rather than a decompilation, and its results remain project-reported.
requirements: Reviewed at the commit of release v2026.10.19-d3995fe (2026-10-19); the repository was created on 2026-10-13 and changes quickly. README marks the port playable and in development: boot, intro, gameplay up to a named early mission, saves, audio, controllers and motion-sensor substitutes work, while performance is typically 20–30 FPS on an RTX 2060, first-time shader compilation stutters and some fog, water and fire effects flicker. Full-game completion is not confirmed, and a crash on AMD Polaris GPUs under Windows remains open.

Supply your own copy of the US PS4 release CUSA00223, base game 1.00 merged with update 1.07 (about 33 GB), including the 1.07 eboot.bin and the game’s own libc and Fios2 modules; README reports that CUSA00004 also boots but is not tested in depth. No PS4 firmware modules are needed, and README states that no game code, files or art are distributed. The project disclaims affiliation with Sony Interactive Entertainment and Sucker Punch Productions.

Play needs 64-bit Windows 10 (1903+) or 11, or x86-64 Linux with glibc 2.39+, and a Vulkan 1.3 GPU, with 6 GB of VRAM recommended; CPUs lacking F16C or SSE4A get instruction emulation at start-up. Building uses a recursive clone with the listed submodules and port/build.sh, with SDL3, Vulkan, FFmpeg, FreeType, Boost, fmt, Zydis and glslang on Linux and an MSYS2 CLANG64 toolchain on Windows; the Qt launcher needs PySide6.

Evidence is play-testing, issue reports and logs: README cites Linux tests on Nobara/Fedora 44, player tests on Windows and a seven-minute RTX 2060 session with a median of 27 FPS. The CI workflow builds Linux and Windows packages for pull requests and authorized manual releases, and its Linux job runs C, Python and GPU-library unit tests without game content or automated gameplay tests.

README declares GPL-2.0 for the project and credits code from HayatoG’s earlier The Last Guardian and Gravity Rush 2 ports, gow3_pc, bloodborne_pc, shadPS4 and a fork of it, and a Shadow of the Colossus port; experimental fixes are traced to their source commits. The game and its assets keep their owners’ rights.

resources.name: xoreos: an open reimplementation of BioWare’s Aurora engine family
resources.description: Reimplements BioWare’s Aurora engine and its later derivatives as a portable C++ engine that runs on the user’s installed game data, targeting nine games from Neverwinter Nights to Dragon Age II. Resource management, many Aurora file formats, graphics and sound are in place, and every target shows partial in-game areas in a free-flying spectator mode. README states that normal gameplay is not implemented yet, so this is an early-stage engine case, not a playable replacement.
requirements: The reviewed master snapshot (2026-09-04) still reports version 0.0.6; release v0.0.6 dates from 2020-08-03, and the repository calls itself pre-pre-alpha. README targets Neverwinter Nights 1 and 2, Knights of the Old Republic I and II, Jade Empire, Sonic Chronicles: The Dark Brotherhood, The Witcher, and Dragon Age: Origins and II; the 0.0.6 notes report a partially playable KotOR tutorial and partial menus in other games.

Needs the user’s own copy of a supported game, fully installed or copied to disk; xoreos reads its resources from that directory, and the repository contains no game files. There is no launcher GUI: a game starts from the command line with its path, or with a target section that xoreos saves in its xoreos.conf configuration file.

Builds use CMake 3.1+ with C++17, or autotools, against the libraries in BUILDDEP.md, including Boost 1.53+, SDL2 2.0.4+, OpenGL 2.1+, FreeType 2, OpenAL Soft and the MAD, Vorbis, FAAD, Xvid and libvpx codecs. README points to release binaries for Windows, Mac OS X and GNU/Linux on 32- and 64-bit x86; the FAQ says mobile devices lack an OpenGL ES renderer and console ports are highly unlikely.

CI builds with autotools and CMake on Linux (GCC and Clang), macOS and Windows (MSVC) and runs the Google Test unit tests, which cover Aurora file formats and shared engine code. No comparison with the original executables is published, and per-game progress is tracked on the project wiki.

README and COPYING apply GPL-3.0-or-later; doc/ adds GPLv2, LGPL-2.1 and font licence texts for incorporated components, and the games keep their publishers’ rights. CONTRIBUTING.md forbids AI-generated code, comments and commit messages.

resources.name: Ghidra MCP Server (bethington)
resources.description: A Ghidra GUI plugin, standalone headless server and Python MCP bridge exposing a 209-tool catalog: decompilation, cross-references, renaming, typing, structures, comments and batch edits, plus P-code emulation, live debugging through Ghidra’s TraceRmi framework, shared Ghidra Server repository and version-control operations, and hash-based transfer of function documentation between binary versions. The bridge loads three tool groups on connect and lets the model search for and load the rest, while naming and type conventions are enforced in the tool layer. Its NOTICE says it began as a derivative of LaurieWired’s GhidraMCP in August 2025 and has since been substantially rewritten and extended.
requirements: The reviewed pin is the default dev branch at bridge version 7.0.0 plus unreleased changes; the README calls tagged releases stable, release candidates and main beta, and dev experimental, with tools renamed and merged freely. At review the newest published build was the 7.0.0-rc.3 pre-release of 2026-10-14, which ships the extension zip and bridge wheel, and the newest stable release was v6.0.0 of 2026-07-25. The README says the GUI plugin serves 205 of the 209 tools and the headless server 190, with the debugger tools GUI-only.

The extension loads only in the exact Ghidra version it was built for, Ghidra 12.1.4 at this pin, and needs Java 21; the bridge needs Python 3.10+, with uv recommended. Source builds use Maven 3.9+ or the committed Gradle wrapper, with install guides for Windows, Ubuntu/Debian, macOS and Arch Linux; Python Ghidra scripts need Ghidra’s optional Jython extension, and shared-server work needs a Ghidra Server version compatible with the 12.1 client. Clients connect over stdio or streamable HTTP, and a Docker Compose stack runs the headless server and bridge as two containers.

Users analyse programs imported into their own Ghidra project; the repository ships only two generated PE test fixtures for its regression tiers. Write tools change the project, and script execution, which runs arbitrary Java inside Ghidra, stays off unless GHIDRA_MCP_ALLOW_SCRIPTS is set. The HTTP server binds 127.0.0.1 without authentication by default and refuses a non-loopback bind without GHIDRA_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN, which the Docker stack always requires; GHIDRA_MCP_FILE_ROOT confines file-path endpoints to one directory.

CI builds the extension with Maven against a downloaded Ghidra, runs offline and real-Ghidra Java tests and Python unit and fake-server tests on Linux, and runs Python unit tests on Windows. docs/TESTING.md describes opt-in live tiers that import the fixtures into a running Ghidra and exercise endpoints and a debugger launch, and says the debugger tier is only partly restored. Sub-second responses, 93% fewer API calls through batching and workflows refined across hundreds of functions are the author’s claims.
Apache-2.0; NOTICE credits the original LaurieWired GhidraMCP code, whose copyright remains for any surviving portions. Ghidra, MCP clients, model services and analysed programs keep their own terms.

resources.name: librw: a re-implementation of the RenderWare Graphics engine
resources.description: Re-implements a large part of the RenderWare Graphics middleware API as a portable C++ library that reads and writes its DFF model and TXD texture files for PS2, D3D8, D3D9 and Xbox and is meant to convert them between platforms. Direct3D 9 and OpenGL backends render the scenes, while PS2 rendering works only as a test. README names rendering GTA as its use; BSP world files are not supported.
requirements: The reviewed master snapshot dates from 2026-08-26; CMake reports version 0.0.1 and the repository has no tagged releases. README calls librw a re-implementation of RenderWare graphics, “or a good part of it”: not all pre-instanced PS2 DFFs load and BSP is unsupported, and TODO lists morphing, several pipelines and PS2 rendering as open. ARCHITECTURE.MD says some design decisions follow the original RW and others are the author’s own.

As a library, librw needs no particular original files: applications hand it RenderWare DFF models and TXD texture dictionaries, such as those of the games they render. The repository ships no game data, but its demo tools include four small DFF sample models whose provenance it does not state.

Builds use premake5 (a premake5.exe is committed) or CMake 3.8+, selecting a NULL, GL3 or D3D9 platform and, for GL3 (OpenGL 2.1+ or ES 2.0+), GLFW, SDL2 or SDL3 for windowing. premake targets Windows x86/amd64, Linux x86/amd64/ARM and PS2, and the CMake files add PS2 and Nintendo Switch toolchains; a skeleton application framework with bundled Dear ImGui accompanies the demo tools.

The GitHub Actions workflow builds and packages 14 configurations: Windows D3D9, GL3 and null, macOS and Ubuntu GL3 and null, PS2 in a ps2dev container and Switch in a devkitPro container. It runs no tests, and the repository has no test suite or comparison with original RenderWare output.
LICENSE applies MIT to librw; the bundled Dear ImGui and ImGuizmo code carries its own licence files, and RenderWare itself and any game assets keep their owners’ rights.

resources.name: awesome-game-decompilations
resources.description: A single-README list of about 480 game decompilation, recompilation and disassembly projects, grouped by console from the NES and Game Boy to the Xbox 360, PC and mobile, with a large uncategorised section. Each entry is a game title linked to its project, mostly on GitHub, and entries with AI involvement are marked with a warning emoji under the maintainer’s disclosure policy.
requirements: The reviewed README, committed 2026-10-12, links 481 entries: 214 under 19 console and platform headings and 267 in an Uncategorised section kept for works in progress, while the table of contents and console index are marked under construction. One game can appear under several platforms.

Entries give only a title and a link, mostly to GitHub with a few on GitLab, Codeberg and SourceHut. They state no project type, completion or matching status, original-file requirement or license, and the list mixes decompilations, disassemblies, static recompilations and occasional reimplementations.
The README’s AI disclosure allows projects with AI involvement and marks them with ⚠️; 10 entries carried the mark at review.

The repository holds only README.md, with no license file or contribution guide, so the list states no reuse terms; linked projects and the games they reconstruct keep their own rights. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: Vineflower
resources.description: Fernflower-derived decompiler for Java and other JVM languages that continues the ForgeFlower, Fabric and Quiltflower forks, focused on output quality and modern Java, including records, sealed classes, switch expressions and pattern matching through Java 21+. Its command line takes a JAR, ZIP, folder or class file and writes a folder, an archive or console output, with multithreaded decompilation and automatic formatting. It can also be embedded as a library from Maven Central or used in IntelliJ IDEA through a plugin that replaces Fernflower, and the regular release JAR bundles three plugins, including Kotlin support and variable renaming.
requirements: Release at review: 1.12.0, published 2026-04-29 on GitHub and Maven Central (org.vineflower:vineflower). The regular JAR includes the three bundled plugins and the -slim JAR only the decompiler. The reviewed master commit is identical to that tag; pull requests target the develop branches, and develop/1.13.0 was 28 commits ahead.

The README says Vineflower 1.9+ needs Java 11 or newer and 1.11+ needs Java 17 or newer to run; the build uses a Java 17 toolchain with ./gradlew build. The IntelliJ IDEA plugin is a separate Marketplace download.

Inputs are user-supplied JAR, ZIP, folder or class files, with libraries added through -e/--add-external as classpath context. The output comparison on the project website is the project's own; decompiled code is reconstructed and is not the original source.

Apache-2.0. The README calls it a fork of JetBrains' Fernflower, MinecraftForge's ForgeFlower and FabricMC's Fernflower fork and a continuation of Quiltflower; its console entry point keeps Fernflower's org.jetbrains.java.decompiler package.

resources.name: Decompyle++ (pycdc)
resources.description: C++ disassembler and decompiler for compiled Python bytecode that aims to support bytecode from any Python version. pycdas prints the disassembly of a .pyc file, and pycdc prints reconstructed Python source to stdout with errors on stderr; both also accept raw marshalled code objects when the Python version is given on the command line. The source carries opcode tables for Python 1.0 through 3.13.
requirements: The project publishes no releases or tags, so it is built from source; the reviewed master commit dates from 2026-04-07. The README makes no per-version completeness claim. The .pyc loader recognizes bytecode up to Python 3.13 but not 3.14, and the regression suite’s compiled samples stop at 3.12: 20 of its 191 samples are for 3.10–3.12, and 39 more are kept as expected failures.

CMakeLists.txt requires CMake 3.12+ and a C++11 compiler, and GCC and Clang builds treat warnings as errors. make check runs the tests on Unix-like systems or MSYS; CI builds and tests on Ubuntu and as 32-bit Visual Studio 2022 builds on Windows, where the executables are kept only as workflow artifacts.

Input .pyc files or marshalled code objects come from the user; recovering them from packaged applications is outside the tool. The README describes no verification of decompiled output, so uncertain regions should be compared with the pycdas disassembly.
GPL-3.0. Recovered source remains subject to the rights of the original program’s owner.

resources.name: Super Mario Odyssey: per-function matching decompilation of the Switch executable
