resources.description: Reconstructs C++ source for Super Mario Odyssey’s Switch 1.0 main executable and checks each function against the original AArch64 machine code with the shared nx-decomp-tools checker. At the pinned commit its function list marks 18,996 of 74,171 functions matching. The README warns that the build is not a playable game, the repository ships no game assets, and Nintendo libraries such as sead and agl come from open-ead’s separate reconstructions.
requirements: The reviewed master pin is dated 2026-09-29. README describes a work-in-progress decompilation of Super Mario Odyssey 1.0.0 that recreates a source base from scratch and warns that it will not produce a playable game. The GitHub description says all versions, but setup.py builds only 1.0 and skips 1.0.1, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 as a to-do, and README lists cross-version comparison and 1.3.0’s different optimisation as open work. Functions are matched individually.

Setup needs the user’s own original 1.0 main NSO executable, compressed or not; setup.py accepts only two SHA-256 hashes, converts it to an ELF and checks that result’s hash too. Only the ExeFS is needed, though README notes that RomFS files help cross-reference names. The repository holds no game assets, while data/ carries the function list and address, symbol and string-literal tables for the 1.0 executable; contributors work from Hex-Rays or Ghidra output.

The documented setup is Linux, WSL or macOS, with a VS Code dev container and a Nix flake as alternatives; it needs Python 3.6+, Ninja, CMake 3.13+, ccache, llvm-objdump, a Rust toolchain and the listed Python modules. setup.py downloads prebuilt clang, ld.lld and the viking checker from the project’s tools-cache release v1.2.6, or builds them from source, and fetches LLVM 3.9.1 libc++ headers. Submodules supply open-ead’s sead, agl, eui, NintendoSDK and NEX headers, a musl build and nx-decomp-tools.

tools/check compares every function marked in data/file_list.yml with the original executable. At the pin the list marks 18,996 functions matching, 47 with minor and 252 with major differences and 54,876 not decompiled, and decomp.dev’s report for the commit gives the same 25.61% of functions, or 15.77% of code bytes. CI fetches the executable through a repository secret, builds and requires the check to pass, and separately checks that every header compiles on its own.

GitHub detects no license and the pinned root has no license file, so no reuse terms are stated; submodules and Nintendo content keep their own terms. A workflow adds an ai label to new pull requests from authors who, in its own words, usually use AI.

resources.name: Droid ASC
resources.description: Python Android decompiler that answers queries directly against an APK instead of first unpacking and indexing it. It probes compressed DEX entries in place, uses the layout that the R8 compiler’s constant relocation and instruction deduplication leave behind to search string, type, method and field references across DEX files, and for a requested class rebuilds a minimal, self-consistent DEX in memory that a bundled copy of Androguard’s decompiler turns into Java. The droidasc CLI and Tk GUI list classes, decompile single classes, decode AndroidManifest.xml and find subclasses or interface implementations; the README presents it as a lightweight back end for agents analyzing many APKs.
requirements: Latest release at review: dev-0.1.2-post2, published 2026-10-14 without binary assets and matching PyPI’s droidasc 0.1.2.post2; the reviewed main commit adds only two README notes. The project began in June 2026. The README now says it has been rewritten 1:1 in Rust as the separate rust_ASC repository, which adds full-APK decompilation and is to be updated in sync.

Install with pip install droidasc or from source. pyproject.toml requires Python 3.10+ with axml and mutf8, and CI runs the unit, integration and GUI suites and gates performance regressions on Ubuntu with Python 3.11 and 3.12. APK and DEX inputs come from the user; the README’s benchmark APKs are not in the repository, and the DEX inside the test fixture holds only AndroidX, Kotlin and Material Components library classes.

Speed and memory figures are author-reported: on Telegram X, WhatsApp, Grab and Lark APKs of 59–352 MB with 10 threads, the README reports string-reference searches 62–302× and single-class decompilation 38–304× faster than JADX while using 36–141 MB, and says JADX ran out of memory on the largest. Java output comes from the bundled Androguard decompiler, one class at a time. The README targets agent workflows but describes no MCP server; agents call the CLI or Python package.
Apache-2.0; the bundled dadguard package carries Androguard code, which is also Apache-2.0. Decompiled code keeps the rights of the app’s owner.

resources.name: APKEditor
resources.description: Command-line APK editor built on ARSCLib that decodes an APK's binary resources and DEX into editable JSON, XML or smali and rebuilds a package from them, independent of aapt and aapt2. It also merges split bundles such as XAPK, APKM and APKS, refactors obfuscated resource names, and prints package information.
requirements: Runs as a single executable JAR on a Java runtime; the Gradle build targets Java 8 source and target compatibility, and the README notes large inputs may need an increased -Xmx heap to avoid an OutOfMemoryError.

Operates on APK files the user supplies; the README documents decoding to XML source for un-obfuscated packages only, and rebuilding a package is distinct from recovering original Java source. Apache-2.0 licensed.

resources.name: avatar²
resources.description: Python framework from EURECOM's S3 group that orchestrates emulators, debuggers and physical devices for dynamic analysis of embedded firmware. An analysis script declares targets, such as a modified QEMU, PANDA, Unicorn, a gdbserver or an OpenOCD or J-Link debug probe, then a memory layout whose ranges can forward accesses from one target to another, and an execution plan. Execution and register or memory state can move between targets, so firmware can run in an emulator while its peripheral accesses go to the real device.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.4.7, uploaded to PyPI on 2022-02-10 and tagged v1.4.7; GitHub lists no release pages. The reviewed main commit, from 2024-10-23, is nine commits ahead of that tag, adding ARMv7-M interrupt forwarding and hardware-runner plugins and pinning Unicorn 2.0.1.post1.

The core installs with pip; CI tests Python 3.7-3.9 on Ubuntu 20.04. Target endpoints are separate: python -m avatar2.installer or the targets/build_*.sh scripts build the avatar-qemu fork and PANDA, with build scripts provided for Ubuntu 20.04 only, and the scripts add a restricted deb-src repository to /etc/apt/sources.list, so the README suggests a VM or container. A Dockerfile generator builds images with selected endpoints.

An analysis needs the user's own firmware image and, for hybrid setups, the physical device reachable through a gdbserver, an OpenOCD script or a Segger J-Link probe. Architecture definitions cover ARM, including Cortex-M3 and big-endian variants, MIPS and x86/x86-64. The analyst writes the memory layout, forwarding rules and execution plan in Python.
Apache-2.0; avatar-qemu and PANDA come from separate repositories with their own licenses. The README lists research publications that describe, use or extend the framework.

resources.name: cwe_checker
resources.description: Static analyzer from Fraunhofer FKIE that searches binary executables, mainly Linux and Unix ELF files, for code paths matching Common Weakness Enumeration bug classes such as buffer overflows, use-after-free and double free, NULL pointer dereferences, format strings and integer overflows. Ghidra disassembles the binary into a common intermediate representation on which its checks run, from simple heuristics to abstract-interpretation data-flow analysis, so it covers the CPU architectures Ghidra supports, including x86, ARM, MIPS and PowerPC. Warnings are printed as text or JSON, and a bundled Ghidra script annotates them in the disassembly for manual review.
requirements: Latest stable release at review: v0.9, published 2024-08-20 as a source release. Prebuilt Docker images on the GitHub container registry are tagged latest (master), stable and v0.9 and are x86 only, although the image can be built natively on ARM. The reviewed master commit is 97 commits after v0.9; CHANGES.md labels it 0.10-dev, with a rewritten P-Code extractor and support for more architectures through a Ghidra update, while the crate manifests still say 0.9.0 and the online documentation covers the stable version.

Local builds need Rust 1.82+ and a Ghidra 10.2+ installation, which make all locates when GHIDRA_PATH is omitted; the Docker image builds on a Ghidra 11.2.1 headless base, and a Nix flake is also provided. Checks are tuned through src/config.json. Analysis of Linux loadable kernel modules, which runs a subset of the checks with its own configuration, and of bare-metal binaries, which needs a per-device configuration such as the bundled STM32F407VG example, is experimental.

Each run takes one binary supplied by the user. The README warns that both false positives and false negatives are to be expected and keeps the CWE-78 OS command injection check disabled on standard runs, so warnings mark code paths for manual review rather than confirmed vulnerabilities. It is also integrated as a plugin in FACT.
LGPL-3.0; the README notice allows version 3 or later.

resources.name: jnitrace
resources.description: Frida-based dynamic-analysis tool that traces an Android app's use of the JNI API, similar to frida-trace or strace but for the Java Native Interface. It logs the JNI calls that native libraries make through the JNIEnv and JavaVM structures, with include and exclude filters, backtraces and optional JSON output for later post-processing. The tracing engine is also published as a separate jnitrace-engine library.
requirements: Installed from PyPI as jnitrace (setup.py marks version 3.3.1 and Python 3) and runs on a Linux, macOS or Windows host; building from source additionally needs Node.js.

Tracing a target needs an arm, arm64, x86 or x64 Android device running a Frida server, which the README states must provide Frida support greater than 14, with the target package already installed on the device.

Intended for apps the analyst is authorized to inspect. MIT licensed; the repository ships the tool only. The last reviewed upstream commit dates to 2023 and targets the Frida 14-era API. As checked on 2026-10-20, that 2023-04-01 commit is still the master head and the latest release is v3.3.1 from the same day; GitHub’s last recorded push was 2023-07-18, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

resources.name: FLARE-VM
resources.description: Mandiant FLARE installer that sets up and maintains a Windows virtual machine for reverse engineering and malware analysis. Its PowerShell script uses Boxstarter and Chocolatey to install packages from the separate VM-Packages feed and the Chocolatey community feed, chosen in a GUI or a custom config.xml that also sets environment paths, the taskbar layout and post-install registry, service and path settings. The reviewed default configuration lists 137 packages, among them Ghidra, IDA Free, x64dbg, dnSpyEx, capa, FLOSS, PE-sieve, FakeNet-NG and Wireshark; scripts in its virtualbox folder build, snapshot and export FLARE-VM and REMnux VMs in VirtualBox.
requirements: Needs a Windows 10 or later virtual machine with PowerShell 5+, at least 60 GB of disk and 2 GB of memory, a username without spaces or special characters and internet access. The README says FLARE-VM should only be installed on a VM and that Windows Updates, Tamper Protection and anti-malware must be disabled on it first; it recommends a snapshot before installation and host-only networking afterward. The installer checks that it is running in a VM and warns on Windows builds other than the tested 19045, 20348 and 26100.

FLARE-VM itself has no releases because its packages download tools from external URLs outside the project's control; the only release, vbox-1.0.0 (2025-08-13), holds Linux executables for some VirtualBox helper scripts, which were tested on Debian 12 with GNOME. Package updates are best effort and untested, failures of individual packages are reported to VM-Packages, and the README suggests a fresh install when updates break. The idapro.vm package needs the user's own IDA Pro installer, and optionally a license file, on the Desktop.
The scripts are Apache-2.0. Per the README's legal notice, every downloaded or installed package keeps its own license terms, which the user must review and accept; installing accepts those terms.

resources.name: B2R2
resources.description: Binary analysis framework written in F# for .NET by KAIST's SoftSec Lab. It parses ELF, PE, Mach-O and WebAssembly files, parses, disassembles and lifts instructions into its own IR, recovers control-flow graphs and assembles code; the README's feature table covers x86/x86-64, ARMv7/AArch64, MIPS, PowerPC, RISC-V, SPARC, S390 and other ISAs as well as CIL, EVM, eBPF, WebAssembly and Python bytecode. Its b2r2 launcher starts a readelf-like format scanner, a linear-sweep disassembler, a recursive-descent explorer with a web GUI, an IR and assembly REPL and an assembler.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.10.1, published 2026-06-17, with BinExplore archives for Linux, macOS and Windows on x64 and arm64; libraries such as B2R2.FrontEnd.API and the B2R2.RearEnd.Launcher .NET tool are on NuGet at 0.10.1. The reviewed main commit (2026-10-17) is 1,231 commits ahead of that tag and still declares 0.10.1.

Building needs the .NET 10 SDK or later, and the projects target net10.0. The README states that the core library has no external dependencies, while System.IO.Hashing, FSharp.Compiler.Service, FParsec, BenchmarkDotNet and Avalonia.FuncUI serve specific components; it presents the APIs as usable from F# and, in principle, other CLI languages, on Linux, macOS, Windows and other .NET platforms.

Input is a user-supplied ELF, PE, Mach-O or WebAssembly file, or a raw byte image loaded with an explicit ISA. The README's feature table gives CFG recovery a full mark only for x86, x86-64 and EVM and a half mark for the other ISAs, lists no lifting, CFG recovery or assembly for TMS320C6000, and notes that some areas are still in progress.
MIT license. The README cites the 2019 NDSS Binary Analysis Research workshop paper describing B2R2 and lists research papers that use or build on it.

resources.name: rz-ghidra
resources.description: Rizin plugin that embeds Ghidra's C++ decompiler and Sleigh disassembler, so no Java Ghidra installation is needed. Its pdg commands decompile the current function, optionally side by side with offsets or as XML or JSON, can return the output to Rizin as comments, and list the loaded Sleigh languages; config variables control formatting and can override the auto-detected Sleigh language. The decompiler draws on Rizin's loaded binary, types and comments, and an optional plugin brings it into the Cutter GUI.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.9.0, published 2026-06-21 as a source tarball, which its notes declare compatible with the Rizin v0.9.x series and which updates the Ghidra code it uses to 12.1. The reviewed dev commit, from 2026-10-12, tracks Rizin's dev branch and is 3 commits ahead of and 5 behind that release tag. The README says version numbers do not guarantee Rizin compatibility and points distributors to rz-* tags instead.

Builds with CMake against an installed Rizin after fetching the rizinorg/ghidra and pugixml submodules. The install step is required because it installs the Sleigh files; the rz-pm package sets them up automatically. The Cutter plugin needs Cutter installed from source and -DBUILD_CUTTER_PLUGIN=ON. CI builds on Debian Bullseye, Arch Linux and Windows.
Decompilation works on binaries loaded and analyzed in Rizin, for architectures whose Sleigh specifications are installed; output is Ghidra decompiler output and needs analyst review.

LGPL-3.0-or-later, which the README notes is stricter than Ghidra's own license; the decompiler sources come from the separate rizinorg/ghidra fork. Its test binaries are built from C sources in the repository.

resources.name: AsmResolver
resources.description: C# library for reading, modifying and rebuilding Portable Executable files, covering both native Windows images and images with .NET metadata. It offers three levels of abstraction: raw headers and sections (PEFile); interpreted data directories such as imports, exports, TLS, exceptions, debug data and Win32 resources (PEImage); and a System.Reflection-like model of .NET assemblies and modules with managed, native and dynamic method bodies. It also extracts files from AppHost/single-file bundles, supports ReadyToRun images and reads PDB and Portable PDB symbols without DIA, and upstream designs it to stay robust against malformed or obfuscated binaries.
requirements: Release at review: v6.0.1, published 2026-07-25 on GitHub and NuGet; the reviewed master commit is one contributing-guide commit ahead. Nightly builds come from a separate NuGet feed. Version 6.0 changed the API, and upstream publishes a guide for migrating from v5.x.

Distributed as layered NuGet packages: AsmResolver, AsmResolver.PE.File, AsmResolver.PE, AsmResolver.PE.Win32Resources, AsmResolver.DotNet, AsmResolver.DotNet.Dynamic and AsmResolver.Symbols.Pdb. The libraries target .NET Framework 3.5, 4.6.2 and 4.7.2, .NET Standard 2.0 and 2.1, .NET Core 3.1 and .NET 6, 8, 9 and 10, and the README lists Windows, Unix-like systems, Mono and NixOS. Building uses the .NET SDK; the full test suite needs additional .NET runtimes, plus Mono and Wine on macOS and Linux.

It is a library without a GUI or a C# decompiler: users write .NET code against its API and supply their own PE files or .NET assemblies. Modified or rebuilt images still have to be checked by running them.
MIT license. The test resources are purpose-built sample binaries. Robustness against malformed or obfuscated binaries is an upstream design goal.

resources.name: DecompilerServer
resources.description: Stdio MCP server built on the ICSharpCode.Decompiler engine that lets agents load managed .NET assemblies, including a Unity game's Assembly-CSharp.dll located from its game directory, then search symbols, string literals and attributes, read decompiled C# or IL, and trace callers, callees, usages and inheritance. Several assemblies stay loaded under aliases, so an agent can compare two versions structurally or diff individual method bodies, the README's example being RimWorld mod porting. Modding-oriented tools generate Harmony patch skeletons, detour stubs and transpiler anchor suggestions as text from the inspected members.
requirements: Reviewed release: v1.4.0, published 2026-10-01; its tag points at the reviewed main commit. Release assets are framework-dependent single-file executables for Windows x64, macOS arm64 and x64, and Linux x64 and arm64 that need the .NET 10 runtime; building from source needs the .NET 10 SDK. The server speaks MCP over stdio, with README setup for Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code/Copilot and Codex, and an optional script installs a locally signed build and the bundled decompiler-mcp skill for Codex on macOS.

Users supply the managed .NET assemblies to inspect, such as a game's Assembly-CSharp.dll or a third-party library; the repository contains only its own test libraries, and the README notes that native libraries do not load. Loaded aliases are registered in LocalApplicationData/DecompilerServer/contexts.json and restored on demand, and at most four contexts stay resident by default (DECOMPILER_MAX_LOADED_CONTEXTS changes the limit).

Inspection tools carry the MCP readOnlyHint annotation; loading, unloading, context selection, decompiler settings and cache tools change server state. The patch, stub and wrapper generators return source text and do not modify the loaded assemblies. Responses are compact by default; DECOMPILER_RESPONSE_MODE=extended restores the earlier response fields.
The v1.4.0 release notes report 238 passing Release tests, and the release workflow builds and runs the test suite before publishing assets; these are project-reported results. MIT.

resources.name: Gepetto
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin that sends Hex-Rays pseudocode to a hosted or local language model the user selects, to explain a function, comment it or propose new variable and function names, which the user picks from before they are applied. A chat console inside IDA also lets the model call tools that read disassembly, decompilation, cross-references, strings and types, rename and comment the database and run Python. The README warns that these general-purpose models may well be wrong and asks users to treat every result critically.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is 38 commits after the v1.5.1 release of 2025-11-19, while ida-plugin.json and pyproject.toml still declare version 1.5.0. The README requires IDA Pro 7.6 or later with the Hex-Rays decompiler. Installation uses Hex-Rays’ hcli plugin command, or copies gepetto.py and the gepetto folder into the IDA plugins directory and installs requirements.txt into IDA’s Python; pyproject.toml asks for Python 3.10+.

Each request sends the current function’s pseudocode, and in the chat console whatever the tools return, to the selected provider. Built-in providers include Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Together, Novita AI, Kluster.ai, DeepSeek and OpenRouter with the user’s own API keys, which the README notes are usually paid, plus local Ollama or LM Studio models. Further providers load as drop-in Python files or entry-point packages, which the README warns execute arbitrary code when IDA starts.

The chat console, chosen as Gepetto in IDA’s input bar, offers the model 22 tools: reading disassembly, bytes, pseudocode, cross-references, imports, symbols, strings, structures and search results; declaring C types; renaming functions, globals and local variables; setting comments; and run_python, which executes model-supplied Python inside IDA with no confirmation step. Its system prompt tells the model to carry out requested changes without asking. The Explain, Comment and Auto-rename menu actions work on one function, and Auto-rename lists the proposed names so the user selects which to apply; two actions the README does not describe, Generate C Code and Generate Python Code, save a model-written rewrite of the function to a file.

Repository tests use pytest with Hex-Rays’ idapro library and open a bundled manalyze.exe build, from the author’s Manalyze PE analyser, as a fixture; no CI workflow is published. The README’s before-and-after screenshot and its observation that renaming works better after an explanation are the author’s.

GPL-3.0 per LICENSE and ida-plugin.json; IDA Pro, the Hex-Rays decompiler and model services keep their own licences and terms. The README credits Kaspersky with initial funding and HarfangLab as the current backer.

resources.name: GhidrAssistMCP
resources.description: Ghidra extension that runs an MCP server inside Ghidra over streamable HTTP and legacy SSE, with 100 explicitly named tools (93 enabled by default) for pseudocode, disassembly, P-code, control-flow and call graphs, cross-references, strings, imports and exports, plus renaming, retyping, comments and structure inference. Since version 3.0.0 the server starts with the project manager, so agents can create, open, save and close projects and open programs before a CodeBrowser exists, while one shared server tracks whichever CodeBrowser window has focus. Six program resource templates, seven analysis prompts and a bundled script for running the server under analyzeHeadless complete the package.
requirements: Ghidra 12.0 or 12.1 Public running on Java 25 or newer; extension zips are specific to one Ghidra version. Release 3.0.0 (2026-10-09), whose tag is the reviewed commit, publishes a zip for Ghidra 12.1; installation goes through File → Install Extensions, and source builds use the bundled Gradle wrapper with Java 25 and GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR. The server listens on localhost:8080 by default, with streamable HTTP at /mcp (MCP 2025-11-25) and legacy SSE at /sse (2024-11-05); the Java MCP SDK 2.0.1, Jetty and Jackson are bundled under private package names.

Programs come from the user's own Ghidra project or imports; the extension supplies no target binaries. Headless mode runs the bundled GAMCPStartServerScript.java inside analyzeHeadless against the loaded program, with wait=true to keep the session open and a completion_file option to end it; the project lifecycle tools need the GUI project manager.

Write tools change the program or project, including names, types, comments, structures, disassembly, analysis options and saves, and read and write tools carry separate MCP annotations. import_file, export_program and the five Ghidra script tools are disabled by default; a headless agent_lab profile enables sandbox-local program export while arbitrary-path import and scripts stay disabled. The README describes no client authentication; the server rejects browser requests whose Origin header is not allowed.

The project's modernization review reports 90 passing tests in buildExtension test runs against Ghidra 12.0 and 12.1, and a live Ghidra 12.1 smoke test on 2026-10-09 that predates the four project-control tools; these are project-reported. MIT. The repository moved from jtang613/GhidrAssistMCP, and its README recommends the author's GhidrAssist client.

resources.name: dewolf
resources.description: Research decompiler from Fraunhofer FKIE, developed with Singapore's DSO National Laboratories between 2019 and 2021, that runs as a Binary Ninja plugin and starts from Binary Ninja's Medium Level IL. A pipeline of preprocessing, SSA, data-flow and control-flow stages restructures code following the DREAM/DREAM++ approach and emits C-like output. Results appear in a Binary Ninja dock widget, or decompile.py prints or writes them for a whole binary or one named function in batch use.
requirements: Release at review: v2026.7.11, published 2026-07-11 by the project's automatic release workflow; the reviewed main commit is that release, and plugin.json declares the same version and lists Windows, Linux and macOS.

Needs Python 3.10+, a separately licensed Binary Ninja (the README asks for the latest stable release, at least 3.4; plugin.json sets minimum build 4271) with its Python API installed in the same environment, and astyle for indentation; libgraph-easy-perl is needed only for ASCII graph output. The plugin is installed by cloning it into Binary Ninja's plugin folder and installing requirements.txt, which pulls the project's dewolf-logic and dewolf-idioms packages from Git.
Settings made in the Binary Ninja GUI do not apply to decompile.py, which reads a config.json in the plugin folder instead; decompiler/util/default.json lists every option.

The README calls dewolf a research prototype that is not optimized for production use and warns of bugs or decompilation failures on real-world binaries. Its tests compile C sample sources and keep GNU coreutils executables under tests/coreutils/binaries as fixtures; CI builds a Docker image around a Binary Ninja archive and license supplied from repository secrets.
LGPL-2.1 (the plugin.json notice allows any later version).

resources.name: Dembrandt
resources.description: Node.js CLI that renders a website in Playwright-driven Chromium or Firefox and reads computed styles from the DOM to extract its design system: logo, color roles with the evidence behind each pick, typography, spacing, borders, shadows, motion, breakpoints and component styles such as buttons and inputs. Results export as W3C design tokens (DTCG), Tailwind v4 or shadcn/ui themes, DESIGN.md, an HTML report or a brand-guide PDF, alongside WCAG contrast checks on real DOM pairs and a CI drift gate against a committed baseline. It also runs as an MCP server for agent clients.
requirements: Release at review: v0.39.2, published 2026-10-11 on GitHub and npm; the reviewed main commit is ten README, MCP-registry and Action-metadata commits ahead. SECURITY.md describes the project as pre-1.0, with fixes only for the latest 0.x release.

Requires Node.js 18+ and a one-time dembrandt install-browser step, because playwright-core ships no browser; Linux and CI hosts also need Playwright's system libraries, and Docker or CI containers may need --no-sandbox. The experimental --ai brand-color model needs the optional onnxruntime-node package. The MCP server starts with npx dembrandt mcp, and a separate GitHub Action wraps the drift gate.

Input is a live URL, rendered at 1920x1080 by default or 390x844 with --mobile; crawls merge several pages found from navigation links or from sitemap.xml after a robots.txt check. The README's limitations: dark mode needs --dark-mode, canvas/WebGL sites cannot be analyzed, some dynamically loaded content and hover or focus states can be missed, and JavaScript-heavy sites need hydration time. Pages behind a sign-in can be reached with the user's own cookies or an interactive login.

MIT. The README limits intended use to design systems you own or may analyze, on sites whose terms permit automated access, and asks users not to reproduce third-party brand identities, logos or trademarks. The optional --key flag uploads each run's snapshot to the vendor's hosted Dembrandt App, which is in beta.

resources.name: Android Reverse Engineering Skill
resources.description: Claude Code plugin and agent skill that drives jadx and Fernflower/Vineflower to decompile Android APK, XAPK, JAR and AAR files and document their HTTP APIs. A fingerprint pass first identifies the app's framework, HTTP stack, obfuscation level and native libraries, then shell scripts extract endpoints and authentication patterns across Retrofit, OkHttp, Volley, Ktor and Apollo/GraphQL, trace call flows from UI down to the network layer, and rebuild original Kotlin class names from the metadata R8 leaves behind. It installs through the bundled Claude Code marketplace, and its scripts also run standalone with a /decompile slash command.
requirements: A Claude Code client with plugin/skill support; install by adding SimoneAvogadro/android-reverse-engineering-skill as a marketplace and installing the android-reverse-engineering plugin, or from a local clone. The reviewed plugin manifest is version 1.5.0 on the master commit, ahead of the latest GitHub release v1.1.0 (2026-04-27).

The skill runs external tools it does not bundle: Java JDK 17+ and the jadx CLI are required, and Vineflower or Fernflower plus dex2jar are optional for better Java output; a dependency checker and an OS-detecting install helper are provided. Bash scripts are the primary path, with experimental PowerShell equivalents for Windows.

Users supply the Android packages to analyze; the repository ships no app files. Work is static decompilation, API documentation, call-flow tracing and Kotlin name recovery; the author reports roughly complete recovery of the Repository/ViewModel/UseCase classes on a typical app, which is a project-reported figure.

Apache-2.0 for the skill; the decompilers and other driven tools keep their own licenses. The README limits use to lawful purposes such as authorized security research, interoperability analysis, and malware analysis, and places responsibility on the user.

resources.name: GB Recompiled
resources.description: Static recompiler that turns Game Boy and Game Boy Color ROMs into portable C projects: it decodes and analyzes banked LR35902 code, emits C with machine-readable metadata, and links it with a shared SDL2 runtime for video, audio, input, saves and hardware timing. Jump targets that static analysis missed fall back to an interpreter. The repository also carries differential, replay and frame and audio capture tooling, plus a Pokémon Crystal port that builds native features on hooks into the exact ROM.
requirements: The README calls it an experimental recompiler and says successful code generation does not guarantee that every scene runs correctly. ACCURACY.md (generated 2026-07-13) reports 8 of 8 Blargg and 63 of 67 Mooneye test ROMs passing and states that this is not a measure of commercial-game compatibility.

Users supply their own .gb or .gbc ROMs; the repository contains no ROMs. The bundled Crystal Recompiled port is ROM-free: it requires the user's exact US/Europe Rev 1 ROM, checks its hash before writing any ROM-derived output, and keeps generated projects in ignored local or private-cache paths, and its distribution policy forbids releasing ROMs, generated C or extracted assets. That port's alpha is verified end to end only on macOS arm64.

Release v0.1.0 (2026-08-03) ships prebuilt gbrecomp archives for Linux x64, macOS Intel and Apple silicon, and Windows x64; the reviewed main commit is 13 commits ahead, last committed 2026-09-10. Building from source needs CMake 3.20+, Ninja, SDL2 development files and a C11/C++20 compiler, and generated projects build with CMake and Ninja. ANDROID.md documents a separate single-ROM APK workflow.

A CTest suite covers isolated invariants. The README notes that differential mode shares runtime devices with the interpreter, leaving SameBoy comparisons and frame, audio and state captures as separate evidence. The only GitHub workflow builds release archives and smoke-tests them with a generated fixture ROM; an optional manual job checks the Crystal port against a privately held ROM without publishing.

MIT-licensed; the vendored Dear ImGui keeps its own license. The README states no affiliation with Nintendo, and the Crystal port none with Nintendo, The Pokémon Company, Game Freak or Creatures. The README points contributors and coding agents to AGENTS.md.

resources.name: CodemerxDecompile
resources.description: Cross-platform desktop .NET decompiler maintained by the original JustDecompile creators as a continuation of their JustDecompile Engine, built with Mono.Cecil and an Avalonia UI. It loads assemblies into a tree of namespaces, types, members and resolved references, shows decompiled C#, VB.NET or IL with go-to-definition and back/forward navigation, and searches names, types, string literals and instructions. A create-project command exports an assembly as a Visual Studio 2015, 2017 or 2019 project.
requirements: Release at review: 1.5.0, published 2024-11-18, with portable archives for Windows x64 and ARM64, Linux x64 and macOS ARM64 and x64; the reviewed master commit is from the same day and was still the latest at review. The README says the macOS app is unsigned, so macOS reports it as damaged until its quarantine attribute is removed.

Source builds need the JustDecompileEngine and AvaloniaEdit Git submodules and the .NET 7 SDK: the app targets net7.0, and the release workflow publishes one build per runtime with dotnet publish. The main view uses the engine's C# 7 and Visual Basic 10 language modes.

Release builds send usage events, such as start-up, opening files, changing language, searching and creating projects, to a Matomo cloud server together with a hashed device identifier, the app version and OS details, and they query the GitHub API for newer releases; no setting to turn this off was found in the reviewed source.
AGPL-3.0 for the app and the JustDecompile Engine; Mono.Cecil and AvaloniaEdit are MIT-licensed, per the README and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md. Input is the user's own .NET assemblies.

resources.name: Reverify
resources.description: Python CLI and stdio MCP server that checks a model’s structured claims about a binary, such as bytes or typed values at an offset, strings, imports and exports, instruction mnemonics, emulation results and tested or Z3-proved equivalence, and returns VERIFIED, REFUTED or INCONCLUSIVE with the evidence the tools observed. Grounded and refuted results are kept in a per-binary ledger on disk, so a reset or later session resumes from them instead of from a summary, and a reconstruct loop has a model propose claims until an informative set verifies. A separate rollover command replaces context compaction in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or OpenCode with file hand-offs and fresh sessions.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is 25 commits after the v0.11.0 GitHub release of 2026-09-04; PyPI’s newest version is 0.10.0, and the README’s status section still describes v0.9.0. The core is pure Python with no dependencies, and pyproject.toml declares Python 3.8+. The full extra adds capstone, unicorn, lief and z3-solver, and the angr extra adds the function, call and cross-reference claims, which return INCONCLUSIVE without an engine. The toolkit also parses PE, ELF and Mach-O files, scans byte patterns, decodes Protobuf and TLV data and generates Frida hook scripts.

The verifier and benchmarks need no model. reconstruct calls an OpenAI-compatible endpoint configured by OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_MODEL, orchestrate can drive Claude through the Claude Agent SDK on a Claude Code login, and the MCP server gives any MCP client parsing, disassembly, pattern-scan, semantic, claim, ledger and checkpoint tools. Ledgers and checkpoints are written under .reverify in the working directory. Users supply the binaries to analyse; the repository holds benchmark sources and result records, not target binaries.

reverify rollover install edits the user settings of each supported CLI it finds to add hooks and switch off native compaction, keeping backups and offering uninstall. The README warns that a Claude Code or Codex session not started through its launcher can then grow without limit, and reports one session that reached 909k tokens.

The headline benchmark applies a fixed textbook push rbp; mov rbp, rsp prologue guess, not a live model, to the entry points of system binaries. BENCHMARK.md reports that guess refuted on 69 of 71 Windows 11 files and never falsely verified, and 0 false VERIFIED among 475 known-false claims on 50 Windows binaries; CI repeats both checks on Linux, Windows and macOS and fails on any false VERIFIED. The author notes that 0 of N bounds the error rate rather than proving it zero. These are project-reported results.

MIT. SECURITY.md limits use to authorised work such as malware analysis, CTF, interoperability research and software the user owns or may analyse, and excludes circumventing licensing or copy protection on software the user does not own or license.

resources.name: wxapkg
resources.description: Desktop GUI for Windows and macOS, built with Wails, that unpacks WeChat mini-program .wxapkg packages for study. It scans the mini-program package folders of local WeChat 3.x and 4.x installations, including per-user folders, or takes a file or folder the user selects; packages that the PC client stores encrypted are decrypted first. Each packaged file is written to its recorded path, with optional beautification of JSON, HTML and JavaScript.
requirements: Release at review: v2.0.0, published 2026-04-16, with a Windows x64 executable and a macOS universal app; earlier v1.x releases shipped Windows executables only. The reviewed main commit adds only a settings dialog for the default output directory after that release.
The README names Windows and macOS as the supported platforms. Building from source needs Go 1.25 as declared in go.mod, the Wails v2 CLI and npm for the Vue frontend.

Input is .wxapkg packages already on the machine, found in WeChat's package folders or selected manually. The output is the files stored in the package: the reviewed code has no WXML or WXSS decompilation step, so compiled view code stays compiled, and reading mini-program information is still an unchecked item in the README's feature list.

No license file or license declaration was found. The README disclaimer limits use to learning and researching the design ideas and principles in software, with users bearing all legal responsibility; analyze only packages you are authorized to inspect.

resources.name: React Native Decompiler
resources.description: Alpha-stage Node.js CLI that splits a React Native JavaScript bundle (index.android.bundle or main.jsbundle), an unbundled js-modules folder, or Webpack entrypoint and chunk bundles into one readable file per module. Tagger, editor and decompiler plugins working on a Babel AST undo compilation artifacts such as Babel helpers, comma-operator chains and shortened booleans, turn element calls back into JSX and can rewrite modules as ES6 imports and exports, after which ESLint and Prettier tidy the output. Modules recognized as npm packages are skipped unless requested, and one module ID can limit output to that module and its dependencies.
requirements: Latest npm release: react-native-decompiler 0.2.4, published 2023-03-31, providing the react-native-decompiler and rnd commands; the reviewed master commit is from the same day and was still the latest at review. The package declares no Node.js engine range, its publish workflow uses Node.js 12, and it pins Babel 7.12, ESLint 7 and Prettier 2. It continues Richard Fu's original repository, which is now archived.

Input is a plain-JavaScript bundle taken from the user's own React Native app, a js-modules folder, or a Webpack entrypoint bundle or chunk folder. The README states in bold that encrypted or binary bundles are not supported.

The README labels the tool alpha, and the repository has no automated tests; CI only builds and lints it. The README documents the Prettier switch as --prettier, but the source reads --noPrettier. Output is cleaned-up module code for reading, not the original project sources.
AGPL-3.0-or-later.

resources.name: DecompAI
resources.description: Gradio chat application whose LangGraph ReAct agent analyses an uploaded x86 Linux ELF binary: it lists and disassembles functions, decompiles them with Ghidra, drives radare2 and gdb, and runs shell commands and Python scripts in a privileged Kali Linux runner container. Workspaces are keyed by the binary’s SHA-256, so uploading the same file again restores the session. It came out of a school research project, and its CTF results are the authors’ own report.
requirements: The reviewed main commit of 2025-11-10 containerised the app. The repository has no tagged releases; the README points to app and runner images tagged 1.0.0 on Docker Hub. Only x86 Linux ELF binaries are supported, and QEMU-based ARM, MIPS and Windows PE support is listed as future work.

The app needs Python with the pinned requirements.txt (Gradio 5.25, LangGraph and LangChain) and Docker. docker compose builds or pulls a Kali runner image with kali-linux-headless, Ghidra 11.3.1, OpenJDK 21 and radare2 plugins, and the app controls the host Docker daemon through a mounted /var/run/docker.sock. Runner containers start with --privileged on Docker’s default network, and the Gradio interface listens on 0.0.0.0:7860 by default; the README asks maintainers to audit any added dependencies.

An OpenAI or Gemini API key and an LLM_MODEL setting go in .env. The README suggests gemini-2.5-pro or gemini-2.5-flash, while the code defaults to gpt-4o-mini; disassembly, decompiled code and tool output are sent to that provider. Users upload their own binaries. None are committed, and tests/test_disassemble.py expects a binaries/ch2.bin that the repository does not include.

The README reports validation on Root-Me CTF challenges, consistently solving difficulty-3-of-5 exercises automatically or semi-automatically, with no published runs or logs. Session data under /tmp/decompai_analysis_sessions by default is lost on reboot.

LICENSE is MIT text with an added clause requiring any use, modification or distribution to display a “Based on DecompAI” attribution, so GitHub does not recognise it as a standard licence; Ghidra, the Kali packages and model services keep their own terms. The README limits use to lawful reverse engineering, education and security research.

resources.name: dtk-template
resources.description: Project template for starting GameCube and Wii matching-decompilation repositories around decomp-toolkit. Its configure.py generates a ninja build that analyzes and splits the game's DOL and REL files from per-version config.yml, symbols.txt and splits.txt files, compiles the decompiled C/C++ with period Metrowerks compilers, relinks the result and checks it against recorded SHA-1 hashes. It also wires in objdiff for per-object diffing, progress reporting for decomp.dev and an example GitHub Actions workflow.
requirements: A scaffold rather than a finished project: users rename the GAMEID placeholders, write each version's configuration and refine symbols and splits after the initial analysis. The README says nearly all active GameCube and Wii decompilation projects use this structure. There are no releases or tags; the reviewed commit (2026-04-26) pins decomp-toolkit v1.8.3, objdiff v3.6.1, binutils 2.42-2 and the 20251118 compilers package.

Users place their own disc image or extracted game files in the ignored orig/[GAMEID] directory, and no game assets are committed. The CI guide has the game files needed for a build stored in a separate build-container repository and warns that it must stay private to avoid exposing the game's assets.

Needs Python and ninja on Windows, macOS or Linux; outside Windows a downloaded wibo wrapper runs the 32-bit Windows compilers, or a user-supplied Wine. configure.py downloads pinned decomp-toolkit, GameCube/Wii binutils, objdiff, sjiswrap and wibo releases plus a Metrowerks CodeWarrior compiler archive hosted by decomp.dev rather than by this repository.

Verification happens per project: the build compares the rebuilt DOL and REL files with the hashes in build.sha1, and objdiff and decomp.dev report per-object matching progress. The template ships no game configuration.
Released under CC0-1.0, which the README suggests replacing with the project's own license; downloaded tools keep their own licenses, and the CodeWarrior compilers are proprietary.

resources.name: hermes-decomp
resources.description: Rust decompiler and analysis toolkit for Hermes bytecode (.hbc), the compiled form React Native apps ship for the Hermes engine; the README lists HBC versions 40 to 99. Its hermes-decomp CLI shows file information, disassembles, decompiles whole bundles or single functions to JavaScript, with a slower deep mode that recovers more names, and provides a terminal UI, cross-references, call graphs, control-flow graphs, Metro module and closure views and bytecode diffing. A separate hermes-mcp server exposes the read and analysis functions as MCP tools, and the hbc-decomp crate offers them as a Rust library.
requirements: Release at review: v0.2.4, published 2026-10-01, which is the reviewed main commit. Its archives contain hermes-decomp and hermes-mcp for Linux x86_64 and ARM64, macOS ARM64 and Windows x86_64, with SHA256SUMS; the README also lists a macOS x86_64 build, which this release lacks. Source builds need Rust 1.70+, and an update command checks for or installs newer releases.

Input is a Hermes bytecode file from the user's own React Native app, not a plain-JavaScript bundle. Full-bundle decompilation writes an .hdcache file next to the input unless --no-cache is passed. hermes-mcp uses stdio by default; its HTTP transport listens on 127.0.0.1:8744 unless another host is given, and docs/MCP.md lists only read and analysis tools.

Separate CLI write commands assemble or patch bytecode and HASM; they never recompile decompiled JavaScript. USAGE.md reports full write support for HBC 96 and below, verified against the Hermes VM, while HBC 97+ files support only same-length string patches and can be checked only with a macOS helper.

CI checks formatting and Clippy, builds on each platform and runs the test suite with corpus-dependent tests skipped; the repository keeps small jsx_cycle .hbc test fixtures. Local gates compile sample snippets with hermesc toolchains that the scripts fetch or build, run the original and decompiled code under Node and compare output, with five known failures listed, and cap unparsable modules per bundle, at 211 for the one recorded bundle, so decompiled output is not always valid JavaScript.
MIT license.

resources.name: N64ModernRuntime
resources.description: Runtime for N64Recomp static recompilations and traditional source ports of N64 games, made of two libraries. ultramodern reimplements core libultra services (threads, message queues, timers, controllers, audio, RSP task handling and VI timing) and leaves controller input, audio playback and the graphics renderer, with RT64 recommended, to callbacks the host project registers. librecomp bridges N64Recomp-generated code to ultramodern and adds overlay handling, PI DMA ROM reads, and EEPROM, SRAM and Flash RAM saves.
requirements: No releases or tags at review; the README recommends including the libraries in a project's own CMake build with add_subdirectory. The reviewed main commit (2026-08-30) needs CMake 3.20+ and C++20; the README says it was developed with Clang 15, older Clang versions may not work, and recent MSVC and GCC should work but are not regularly tested. N64Recomp, miniz, xxHash and o1heap are pinned submodules.

The runtime contains no game code: the host project supplies the recompiled code, the renderer and the platform callbacks, and the user supplies the game ROM. The reviewed librecomp source checks a user-selected ROM against a per-game hash and also loads .nrm mod packages; the README does not describe either feature.
The README covers library scope only and has no compatibility list.
GPL-3.0 (COPYING); submodules keep their own licenses. CONTRIBUTING.md states that AI-generated code contributions are not accepted.

resources.name: REDscript
resources.description: Compiler and decompiler toolkit for REDscript, a statically typed, object-oriented language for writing scripts for REDengine, CD Projekt's engine used in Cyberpunk 2077. Its Rust crates parse and analyze source, generate bytecode with monomorphization of generics, decompile .redscripts bytecode bundles back into REDscript source, read and write REDengine's native binary format, and provide a drop-in replacement for CD Projekt's scc script compiler plus a C API with source mapping. The CLI exposes decompile, compile, lint and format commands; the language server and debugger live in a separate redscript-ide repository.
requirements: GitHub's latest stable release is v0.5.31 (2025-08-28), with Windows and macOS archives and standalone CLI binaries for Windows and macOS arm64. The default 1.0.x branch declares 1.0.0-preview.22, the newest prerelease (2025-09-07); the reviewed commit (2026-05-27) is 26 commits after that tag, and older lines live on the 0.5.x and 0.6.x branches. Source builds use Cargo with a Rust toolchain that supports the 2024 edition.

Installation targets the user's own Cyberpunk 2077 installation: the Windows archive is extracted into the game directory so scripts compile at game startup, with logs under r6/logs. On native macOS the game does not compile scripts at startup, so the README uses a bundled launch_modded.sh, and downloaded binaries must first be removed from quarantine. The decompiler reads a .redscripts bundle from the user's game, compilation uses one as its base, and the reviewed tree contains no game scripts or bundles.

Language documentation is on the REDmodding community wiki, and editor support for VS Code, neovim, IntelliJ IDEA, Zed and Helix is in the separate redscript-ide repository. The README states no supported game patch range.
MIT. The game's license terms are separate.

resources.name: Kong
resources.description: Command-line pipeline that runs Ghidra in-process through PyGhidra and asks Claude, OpenAI or OpenAI-compatible models to name the functions, types and parameters of a stripped binary, working bottom-up through the call graph so callers see already-named callees. It matches known library and cryptographic signatures first, sends functions whose decompilation looks obfuscated through a tool-using deobfuscation pass with z3-based simplification, applies results to the Ghidra program and exports annotated C and an analysis.json file. Its README calls it the first agentic reverse engineer; that label and its accuracy and cost figures are the author’s claims.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is 25 commits after the v0.2.2 release of 2026-03-18, which matches kong-re 0.2.2 on PyPI; those later commits add an unreleased Rust kong-ml crate and XDA model-training scripts that the README does not describe. Kong needs Python 3.11+ with uv, a local Ghidra installation and JDK 21+, which it detects or reads from GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR and JAVA_HOME. Its commands are kong setup, analyze, info and eval, with a Textual interface or --headless output.

Analysis needs an Anthropic or OpenAI API key, or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint passed with --base-url, and sends each function’s decompilation with its cross-references, strings and neighbouring signatures to that service; Kong tracks token use and estimated cost per model. Users supply the binary to analyse, and the repository ships no target binaries.

The README rates its confidence by architecture and source language: high for C and C++ on x86, x86-64, ARM and AArch64, medium or low for Go, Rust, MIPS and PowerPC, and lower as binaries grow. Obfuscation is detected by patterns in the decompiled text before the deobfuscation pass. BENCHMARKS.md reports a single run with claude-opus-4-6 on a stripped liblzma.so.5.4.1 from the backdoored XZ Utils 5.6.1 (CVE-2024-3094): 355 of 396 queued functions analysed in 15 minutes for $6.63, with the five core implant functions found at model-reported confidence of 90–95%. These are author results.

The kong eval command scores analysis.json against ground-truth source, using word-based Jaccard matching for names and signature-component scoring for types; no evaluation results are published. CI runs the pytest suite on Python 3.11 to 3.14 for pull requests.
Apache-2.0 per LICENSE and pyproject.toml; Ghidra, model services and analysed binaries keep their own terms. The README names KeygraphHQ’s Shannon web-pentesting pipeline as its inspiration.

resources.name: Spice86
resources.description: PC emulator for executing, reverse engineering and rewriting real-mode DOS programs whose source code is unavailable. While a program runs it builds a control-flow graph, and on exit it dumps memory, execution flow, Ghidra-compatible symbols and a self-contained, runnable C# project whose generated functions override the original assembly, so analysts can rewrite them function by function into readable code while the program keeps working. It also provides a GDB remote server with custom analysis commands, a built-in debugger with a C-header structure viewer, an optional HTTP memory API and an MCP server whose tools cover CPU, memory, breakpoints, CFG and device state; an optional Ghidra plugin imports the dumps.
requirements: Releases are published on NuGet (16.1.0 at review, published 2026-08-05); the GitHub release tagged latest is a rolling development prerelease built from master with debug and release archives. The reviewed master commit (2026-10-13) declares 16.1.0. The project is a C# port and continuation of the original Java Spice86. Running and building need .NET 10 on Windows, macOS or Linux; source builds use dotnet build.

The README lists 8086/8088 as fully implemented, with partial 80186, 80286 and 80386 support (no protected mode or paging, and no FPU beyond detection); 1 MB segmented memory with EMS, XMS and HMA; text, CGA, EGA, VGA and VESA VBE 1.2 graphics, with CGA and EGA best effort; a largely complete DOS 5.0 INT 21h; and Sound Blaster, OPL and Adlib Gold audio ported from DOSBox Staging, with MT-32 partial and unavailable on macOS. COMPATIBILITY.md says many programs do not run and lists tested games individually.

The analyst supplies the DOS program and its files; the emulated C: drive defaults to the program folder. Dumps go to a subfolder named by the program's SHA-256 hash, and the generated project passes the expected checksum so overrides cannot run against a different binary. The GDB server starts by default on port 10000, and the MCP HTTP server is documented as enabled by default on port 8081. The Ghidra plugin is a separate repository that needs Java 17. The README suggests LLM assistance for rewriting generated functions and points to the project's Cryogenic rewrite of Cryo's Dune as a worked example.

Apache-2.0; NOTICE credits the Aeon project, the README credits DOSBox Staging for ported sound code and as the model for CD and floppy emulation, and a prebuilt FastExpressionCompiler DLL is vendored in 3rdparty. Test resources are small DOS test programs, most with assembly sources in the repository.

resources.name: PS2 Web Recomp
resources.description: Statically recompiles PlayStation 2 games for the browser: eerecomp translates the Emotion Engine code of a game's boot executable into C++ that is compiled to WebAssembly, and a runtime emulates the rest of the console, including a high-level EE kernel, an interpreted I/O processor running the disc's IRX modules, the vector units, SPU2 sound and the Graphics Synthesizer on WebGPU compute shaders. Its port script repeats headless runs to find functions reached through pointers and vector-unit microprograms to compile ahead of time, then builds the web page and a native runner.
requirements: The README reports two titles brought up so far: the PAL Gran Turismo 4, playable from boot through races at full speed in Chrome, and God of War II from its menus into combat, which needed no game-specific code but exposed a recompiler bug and a vector-unit timing bug. It warns that another game will most likely stop at an unimplemented system call, IOP library function or GS feature, and that vector-unit results can differ from the console's in the last bit.

Users bring a disc image of a game they own; the repository contains no game code or data. The README states that the generated C++ and the built WebAssembly are translations of the game's executable that belong to its owners, asks users to keep them on their own machine and not publish them, and warns that anyone who can reach the local server can load the game.

Porting needs Git, CMake 3.20+, Ninja, a C++20 compiler (Clang preferred), Python 3 and 7-Zip for .7z images; the first run installs the Emscripten SDK and downloads wgpu-native, and the native window needs SDL2. Everything has been run on x86-64 Linux, and the scripts also build on Apple-silicon macOS; expect about 300 MB of disk per game. The page needs WebGPU, which Linux Chrome enables only behind flags (the software renderer fallback is too slow for 3D), plus cross-origin isolation headers and HTTP Range support.

There is no release, tag or CI workflow. scripts/test_vu_codegen.py exercises native and WebAssembly vector-unit code generation without a game disc, and a software GS rasterizer is kept as the reference for the GPU output. Frame rates are the author's measurements on one laptop. Last commit at review: 2026-10-19.

MIT-licensed; the MPEG decoder's VLC tables adapted from Play! keep its BSD 2-clause notice, and the README names PCSX2, Play! and the ps2sdk headers as behavior references. It states no affiliation with Sony or the games' publishers.

resources.name: shuji
resources.description: Command-line tool that writes the original JavaScript and CSS sources embedded in source maps back out as files. It reads .map files, or JavaScript and CSS files whose sourceMappingURL holds an inline Base64 or URL-encoded map or points to a map in the same folder, and can walk directories with a regular-expression filter. Output is flattened to file names by default, or keeps the map's folder structure with --preserve.
requirements: npm release at review: shuji 0.8.0, published 2023-12-04, which requires Node.js 14.15.0+; the repository publishes tags but no GitHub releases. The reviewed main commit is 139 commits ahead and unreleased: it raises the minimum to Node.js 24.12.0, which the README already states, moves linting to Oxlint and, since 2026-10-11, rejects output paths that would escape the output directory.

Install the CLI globally with npm and run it on a file or directory with -o for the output directory; the default filter only picks .map files, so -M is needed to scan .js or .css files for inline maps. Maps are read from local files only: a referenced map must sit relative to the code file, and remote maps are not fetched.

Only sources whose content is embedded in the map's sourcesContent are written; entries that list a path without content are skipped, so maps built without included sources yield nothing for them. Existing files are never overwritten, so flattened sources with the same file name are skipped unless --preserve is used.
MIT. Recovered files remain the original authors' code under their own terms.

resources.name: xboxrecomp
resources.description: Static-recompilation toolkit for original Xbox games: a Python pipeline parses a retail XBE, disassembles it, classifies library functions, recovers calling conventions and lifts every x86 function to C. The generated code is compiled in a separate game project that links the toolkit's runtime libraries, which stand in for the Xbox kernel and translate Direct3D 8, NV2A, audio and input to Direct3D 11 and Win32 APIs, or to SDL2 and OpenGL on Linux and macOS.
requirements: The README for v0.14.0 (2026-10-16, the reviewed commit) calls the toolkit title-agnostic but built against Burnout 3: Takedown, and says a first run of a recompiled game will crash and needs iterative stubbing, indirect-call fixes and runtime work for each title. The author's own ports are early: the README retires an earlier playable claim for Burnout 3, whose recompiled path reaches engine initialization, and lists Wreckless and Blood Wake as booting or scaffolded.

Users supply default.xbe and the game's data files from their own original Xbox disc image. The repository contains no game code or assets and builds only libraries, never a game executable; the generated C, often millions of lines, is written into the user's own game project created from the bundled template.

The pipeline needs Python 3.10+ with Capstone (pytest for tests); Ghidra or IDA are optional and only recover symbol names. The runtime builds with CMake 3.20+ and Visual Studio 2022 or MinGW-w64 on Windows (D3D11, XInput, XAudio2, Media Foundation), or Clang/GCC with SDL2, libepoxy and pkg-config on x86-64 and arm64 Linux and macOS, where FMV decoding is not available. The v0.14.0 release has no binary assets.

Unit tests need no game files, and several compile the lifter's output and check it against x86 definitions with paired negative controls; the README gives 812 passed and 0 skipped as a clean run. A conformance suite runs lifted C and the original instructions on a real 32-bit x86 CPU over the same inputs, with Docker images supplying GCC and MSVC under Wine on Linux and macOS. The README calls lifter coverage good but unquantified, and the repository has no CI workflow.

MIT-licensed, except the MCPX APU sources and NV2A register definitions extracted from xemu, which stay LGPL-2.1-or-later as listed in NOTICE. The README credits Claude Code for AI-assisted development.

resources.name: PCSX-Redux
resources.description: PlayStation 1 emulator forked from PCSX and built around development and reverse engineering, with an interpreter and dynamic recompiler, software and OpenGL renderers, a MIPS debugger, VRAM viewer, SPU and GPU debugging tools, and a built-in GDB server that its documentation connects to gdb, IDA Pro and Ghidra's debugger. A LuaJIT API exposes breakpoints, memory and registers, an assembler and an ISO builder, and an optional REST web server can dump RAM and VRAM. The repository also holds the OpenBIOS replacement BIOS, PS-EXE conversion and packing tools, a Psy-Q object-file converter, Ghidra scripts for exchanging symbols and overlays with the emulator, and PS1 hardware designs.
requirements: No tagged GitHub releases at review: the README links rolling development builds for Windows x64 (GUI and CLI), Linux x64 and arm64 AppImages and macOS Arm, and says the codebase is still experimental and has not reached its first stable release. Builds are 64-bit only and need a GPU and driver that can create at least an OpenGL 3.0 context; the macOS build is unsigned. The reviewed main commit is from 2026-10-19.

Source builds need a recursive clone: Visual Studio 2022 with NuGet on Windows; Docker for the AppImage, or make with clang and packages such as Capstone, FFmpeg, libuv, SDL3 and curl, on Linux; macOS Catalina or later with Xcode and Homebrew packages. OpenBIOS and other PS1 code need a mipsel-none-elf GCC toolchain, for which the repository provides install scripts.

Game discs and executables come from the user. The README presents OpenBIOS, built separately, as an alternative to the copyrighted retail BIOS, and the reviewed trees contain no retail BIOS, Psy-Q libraries or game files. The docs say most CPU debugging features need the dynarec disabled and the debugger enabled, and Ghidra debugging needs gdb-multiarch and Ghidra 10.3+. When enabled, the web server listens on port 8080 on all network interfaces by default, which the docs note makes it reachable from other machines.
GPL-2.0 for PCSX-Redux; OpenBIOS lives in the MIT-licensed nugget submodule, and LICENSES.md lists third-party libraries with their own licenses, some vendored with modifications.

resources.name: Obfuscator.io Deobfuscator
resources.description: Deobfuscator dedicated to JavaScript produced by Obfuscator.io (javascript-obfuscator), which its README says also handles most forks. Working statically on a Babel AST, it reveals strings hidden in rotated, Base64- or RC4-encoded string arrays, inlines proxy functions, simplifies objects, arithmetic and string concatenation, removes dead code and the obfuscator's anti-tamper wrappers, and reverses control-flow flattening. Its configuration is detected automatically, and the author also hosts an online version.
requirements: npm release at review: obfuscator-io-deobfuscator 1.0.6, published 2025-03-27. The reviewed main commit, merged 2026-08-09, adds unreleased improvements to string-array wrapper identification and README notes on running the CLI from source; package.json still reports 1.0.6. No GitHub releases are published.

Install the global obfuscator-io-deobfuscator CLI, which takes an input file and an optional output path, or build it from source with npm and TypeScript. It applies its Babel-based transformations repeatedly, for at most 50 passes; package.json declares no Node.js version range. An online version runs at obf-io.deobfuscate.io.

Input must be JavaScript produced by Obfuscator.io or a compatible fork; other obfuscators are out of scope, and the author's general-purpose javascript-deobfuscator covers generic patterns. The README states that it does not run untrusted code or use a sandbox; recovered strings and control flow still need checking against the original script.
The LICENSE file is Apache-2.0, while package.json and the npm metadata declare ISC.

resources.name: decomp2dbg
resources.description: Decompiler-to-debugger bridge that serves function names, global variables, stack and register variable names and decompiled code from IDA Pro, Binary Ninja, Ghidra or angr-management to GDB over an XML-RPC connection. Synced functions and globals become ordinary GDB symbols for breakpoints and memory examination, local variables appear as convenience variables, and each breakpoint stop prints the decompiled line for the current address. It works with vanilla GDB, GEF and pwndbg, and can map a shared library's symbols once its load range is supplied.
requirements: Release at review: v4.0.3, published 2026-07-14 on GitHub and PyPI; the reviewed main commit is that version bump. Package metadata requires Python 3.10+, and the README says decomp2dbg must be installed in the same Python environment as the decompiler and the debugger. The bundled installer places the decompiler plugin and sources the GDB client from the user's .gdbinit, after GEF or pwndbg are loaded; a Windows decompiler outside WSL needs the README's manual steps.

The README lists IDA Pro 9.0+, Binary Ninja 2.4+, Ghidra 12+ (started in PyGhidra mode with the plugin enabled) and angr-management 9.0+, each installed separately; decompiler access goes through the declib library. Only GDB-based debuggers are supported: LLDB and WinDbg support, struct syncing, function-type syncing and online DWARF creation are listed as unfinished.

The decompiler side starts an XML-RPC server on localhost:3662 by default; debugging from another machine or VM needs the host and port at connect time and the port reachable. One decompiler can be connected at a time, and a shared library's symbols need its base and end addresses supplied manually.

tests.py holds integration tests that drive headless Ghidra, or IDA through idalib, with GDB; CI runs only the Ghidra suites against Ghidra 12.0. The testing/binaries directory keeps sample executables, including an Ubuntu objdump build, as test fixtures. BSD-2-Clause license.

resources.name: javascript-deobfuscator
resources.description: General-purpose JavaScript deobfuscator for common obfuscation patterns, published on npm as js-deobfuscator and usable as a library or CLI. It unpacks arrays of literals and replaces references to them, removes simple, array and arithmetic proxy functions, simplifies arithmetic and string concatenation, removes dead branches, turns computed member access into static properties, renames hexadecimal identifiers such as _0xca830a and beautifies the result. The author also hosts an online version and maintains a separate deobfuscator for Obfuscator.io output.
requirements: npm release at review: js-deobfuscator 1.1.7, published 2025-07-15; the reviewed main commit is that version bump. No GitHub releases are published. The TypeScript package parses and regenerates code with the Shift parser and the author's shift-codegen fork; package.json declares no Node.js version range.

Install it locally to import as a module, or globally for the js-deobfuscator CLI, which reads an input file and writes an output file, with -m for ES modules. The library config toggles each transformation. An online version runs at deobfuscate.io.

Supply the JavaScript to analyze yourself. It handles the generic patterns listed in the README; for Obfuscator.io output the README points to the author's dedicated deobfuscator. Hexadecimal identifiers are replaced with names drawn from a bundled word list, not recovered originals, so output still needs analyst review.
The LICENSE file is Apache-2.0, while package.json and the npm metadata declare ISC.

resources.name: Il2CppInspector
resources.description: Static analysis tool for Unity IL2CPP applications that reads an IL2CPP binary with its global-metadata.dat and outputs the application's type structure and method addresses as C# stub code, .NET assembly shim DLLs for decompilers such as ILSpy and dnSpy, IDA and Ghidra Python scripts that apply symbols and types, C++ type scaffolding and JSON address maps. Three APIs, also published as a NuGet package, and a plugin SDK expose the binary metadata, .NET type model and C++ model for custom analysis. The README states that it is not a decompiler and does not recover method source code.
requirements: The README announces that development is suspended for the foreseeable future and that the author will not respond to issues or pull requests. The reviewed master commit, which added that notice, dates from 2021-11-23, 16 commits after the last release, 2021.1 (2021-01-31). The README recommends Cpp2IL instead.

Its version table marks Unity 5.3.0 through 2020.3.x (IL2CPP 16 to 27.1) as working and 2021.1 (27.2) as partial; later Unity versions are not covered. Documented inputs are ELF, PE, Mach-O, Universal Binary and PS4 FSELF images, 32- and 64-bit, for ARMv7, Thumb-2, ARMv8, x86 and x64, plus APK, AAB, XAPK, Zip and decrypted IPA packages.

The analyst supplies the IL2CPP binary and its matching global-metadata.dat; IPA executables must already be decrypted, and the README says packed, encrypted or obfuscated IL2CPP files are not its intended input. It warns that loading a packed PE file runs the DLL's entry point and initialization code, so untrusted DLLs should not be loaded and the tool should never run as administrator.

Builds use dotnet publish from a recursive clone and target .NET Core 3.1; the CLI builds for Windows, macOS and Linux, while the WPF GUI is Windows-only, and plugins are fetched separately with the get-plugins scripts. AGPL-3.0; the Bin2Object submodule and libraries such as dnlib and CxxDemangler keep their own licenses.

resources.name: whatsapp-web-reveng: documenting the legacy WhatsApp Web protocol
resources.description: Documents and reimplements the WebSocket protocol WhatsApp Web used while browser sessions mirrored a paired phone: QR pairing, Curve25519/HKDF key setup, AES/HMAC-protected binary messages, the token-based node encoding and end-to-end media encryption. A Python backend, Node.js relay and browser front end decode a logged-in session’s messages into inspectable JSON, and the README lists independent reimplementations such as Baileys and go-whatsapp. This is an older protocol generation from before WhatsApp’s 2021 multi-device architecture, not a description of current WhatsApp Web.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2024-04-22 master head, a README-only change; the backend and Node relay last changed in August 2021, the protobuf schema in March 2020, and there are no releases or tags. The README’s pairing flow has the phone supply session details such as its battery level, the phone-mirroring companion model that WhatsApp’s July 2021 engineering post says multi-device replaces. A 2022 issue reports the server answering a QR scan with an upgrade_md_prod command. As checked on 2026-10-20, the 2024-04-22 head is still GitHub’s last recorded push, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

Use needs the user’s own WhatsApp account and phone to scan the pairing code, and the backend connects to WhatsApp’s servers. The protobuf definitions come from a helper script that parses the public WhatsApp Web JavaScript bundle. The README’s task list still names growing binary-decoding errors, writing binary messages and a less technical interface as open work.

Bare-metal setup needs Node.js 8+ and Python 2.7 with websocket-client, simple-websocket-server, curve25519-donna, pycrypto (pycryptodome in requirements.txt), pyqrcode and protobuf; Windows also needs Visual C++ for Python 9.0 and a supplied header. A shell.nix (Python 2.7, Node.js 13) and a Dockerfile are provided, and npm start runs the backend, Node API and front end together. The README says the Docker version is not stable enough for production.

There is no test suite: the package.json test script only starts the components. The documented correctness checks are HMAC validation of the server’s key data and of each binary message, and an in-browser JavaScript demo prints decrypted messages after a QR scan.

MIT (LICENSE, package.json). The README states the project is unaffiliated with and not endorsed by WhatsApp, that use is at the user’s own risk, and adds a cryptography export notice; WhatsApp’s services and terms apply separately.

resources.name: E9Patch
resources.description: Static binary rewriter for x86-64 Linux ELF executables and shared objects that inserts instrumentation without control-flow recovery and writes a drop-in replacement binary, following the PLDI 2020 paper Binary Rewriting without Control Flow Recovery. The e9tool front end selects instructions with a matching language over disassembly attributes and patches them with built-in trampolines, calls into C or C++ functions compiled with e9compile.sh, or hand-written plugin trampolines; the e9patch back end accepts JSON-RPC commands so other tools can drive it. Optional modes add heuristic control-flow recovery for faster rewritten binaries or SIGILL-based fallbacks for full patch coverage.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.0.1, published 2026-06-22, with an amd64 Debian package; earlier 1.0.0 release candidates ran through rc10 (2025-04-16) before v1.0.0 on 2026-03-01. The reviewed master commit (2026-06-28) is one commit ahead of v1.0.1, fixing undefined behavior on empty trampoline template entries, and its VERSION file reads 1.0.1.

build.sh builds e9patch and e9tool after checking for gcc, g++, make, binutils, xxd, markdown and zlib headers, and suggests Debian/Ubuntu package names; Zydis and libdw are vendored under contrib. Patch functions are compiled with e9compile.sh using gcc and freestanding flags. The README targets x86_64 Linux; the source also contains PE handling and a Windows example that calls itself a proof of concept, which the guides do not document.

Input is the user's own ELF executable or shared object, and output is written to a.out or a.so by default. The guide notes that the built-in linear disassembler can mishandle binaries that mix code and data and accepts --use-disasm and --use-targets CSV files from other analyzers. The CFR mode is heuristic and less robust, and in the -100 mode a rewritten program's own attempts to install a SIGILL handler fail with ENOSYS.
GPL-3.0, with specific files such as examples/stdlib.c under MIT as stated in their preambles.

resources.name: MelonLoader
resources.description: Mod loader for Unity games on both the Mono and IL2CPP runtimes, which loads plugins and mods from folders in a locally installed game; on Windows a proxy DLL, version.dll by default, starts it with the game. For IL2CPP games its assembly generator runs Cpp2IL and Il2CppInterop to produce managed interop assemblies, and HarmonyX and MonoMod are bundled for runtime patching. Its logs can capture Unity player output and Harmony messages, and debug options provide a Mono debug server for Mono games and a wait-for-debugger option for IL2CPP games.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.7.3, published 2026-05-14, with Windows x64/x86, Linux x64 and macOS x64 archives plus Windows, Linux and macOS installers; the README also links nightly builds. The reviewed master commit (2026-10-01) declares the unreleased 0.7.4, 69 commits after v0.7.3, and its pending release notes add macOS arm64 support. The README links Linux instructions for Wine, Proton and native games, and marks Android and Oculus Quest support as work in progress.

The README lists the .NET 6.0 Desktop Runtime as a requirement for IL2CPP games, installed automatically on Windows. The installer or a manual install places MelonLoader and its proxy DLL in the user's own game folder, where the Plugins, Mods, logs and UserData/Loader.cfg configuration are created; some games need one of the alternative proxy file names. Source builds use the dotnet SDK, and the projects target Mono, Mono bleeding-edge and .NET frameworks.
