On IL2CPP games the assembly generator queries MelonLoader's remote API by game name for settings such as a Cpp2IL version, obfuscation regex or deobfuscation mapping, and the README lists Cpp2IL, Unity runtime libraries and the .NET runtime as downloaded at run time. Configuration and launch options can force offline generation, a dumper version or regeneration.

Apache-2.0; bundled libraries such as Dobby, plthook, HarmonyX, MonoMod, Mono.Cecil, AsmResolver and Il2CppInterop (LGPL-3.0) keep their own licenses, and the README says the downloaded Unity runtime libraries are subject to Unity's terms of service. Game license terms are separate.

resources.name: Rellic
resources.description: Trail of Bits implementation of the pattern-independent structuring algorithm from the No More Gotos paper, turning LLVM bitcode into goto-free C as a small, hackable decompiler back end that interoperates with LLVM and Remill. rellic-decomp translates a bitcode module to C in batch, rellic-xref serves a web interface for choosing refinement passes and linking C AST nodes to the bitcode that produced them, and rellic-headergen emits C layouts of data structures from a module's DWARF metadata. Machine code must first be lifted to bitcode by another tool; a bundled IDA script uses Anvill for that step.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.2.3, published 2023-04-04, with LLVM 15 builds: deb and tgz packages for Ubuntu 20.04 and a tgz package for macOS 11. The reviewed master commit (2025-11-03) is 13 commits ahead and comments out the AnghaBench CI cron jobs; the code commits before it date from April 2024.

The README supports Linux, tested on Ubuntu 22.04, and also documents a macOS build. Building needs CMake 3.21+, LLVM and Clang 16, Z3 4.7.1+, gflags and glog, most of which come from Trail of Bits' prebuilt cxx-common packages; scripts/build.sh downloads the rest and produces a deb package. Docker images on Docker Hub and the GitHub Package Registry are parameterized by Ubuntu and LLVM version.

Input is an LLVM bitcode module built with the same LLVM version as the decompiler. C sources can be compiled with clang -emit-llvm, but executables need a separate lifter such as Remill or Anvill. The README's examples show output whose control flow and variable types differ from the original source, and its AnghaBench 1,000-program test only checks that bitcode translates to C, not the readability or behavior of the result.
Apache-2.0 license. The roundtrip tests compile C to IR and back and check that the result builds and behaves roughly like the original. By default rellic-xref listens on all addresses, on port 80.

resources.name: ghidra-delinker-extension
resources.description: Ghidra extension that delinks a selected part of a program back into a relocatable object file. Its relocation table synthesizer analyzer reconstructs, from the Ghidra database, the relocations a linker normally discards, and its exporters write COFF (x86, x86-64), ELF (x86, x86-64, MIPS) or OMF (x86) objects with symbols and relocation tables that a toolchain can link again. The README lists binary patching through the linker, software ports, format conversion, library extraction and decompilation projects that reimplement a program one object file at a time among its uses.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.9.2, published 2026-09-26 at the reviewed commit, with separate extension archives for Ghidra 12.0.4, 12.1, 12.1.2, 12.1.3 and 12.1.4; use the archive built for the installed Ghidra release. CI builds with JDK 21.

Source builds need GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR and Gradle. Dependencies come from GitHub's Maven registry, which requires a token with read:packages, or from vendored submodules through gradle installStandaloneDeps. After installation, RelocationTableSynthesizedPlugin is enabled from Ghidra's Experimental plugin list; a bundled DelinkProgram script covers headless use.

Input is a program already loaded and analyzed in Ghidra. The README warns that synthesized relocations depend on the accuracy of the Ghidra database, so incorrect or missing information can break or miss relocations, and advises rerunning the analyzer right before each export. Only the listed format and architecture combinations are supported.

Apache-2.0. The test references are built from C sources in the repository. The README's examples link the author's blog series, including one on decompiling the PlayStation game Tenchu: Stealth Assassins.

resources.name: BepInEx
resources.description: Plugin and patching framework for Unity Mono, Unity IL2CPP and .NET Framework games such as XNA, FNA and MonoGame titles, which loads mods and analysis plugins into a locally installed game. Plugins patch methods at runtime with the bundled HarmonyX and MonoMod.RuntimeDetour, while preloader patchers rewrite managed assemblies with Mono.Cecil before the game loads them; on IL2CPP games it runs Cpp2IL and Il2CppInterop to generate interop assemblies from the game binary and global-metadata.dat. Its guides also cover configuration, logging, and debugging plugins and game assemblies with dnSpy.
requirements: Latest stable release at review: v5.4.23.5, published 2026-02-08 from the v5-lts branch, with Windows x86/x64, Linux x86/x64, macOS universal and patcher archives; the README says only Unity Mono has stable releases. The reviewed master commit (2026-10-16) declares the unreleased 6.0.0 and is 75 commits after the latest 6.x prerelease, v6.0.0-pre.2 from 2024-08-27, which ships Unity Mono, Unity IL2CPP and .NET builds; newer bleeding-edge builds are published separately. The guides note that the preloader-patcher contract changed between v5 and v6.

The README's compatibility chart lists Unity Mono on Windows, macOS and Linux, Unity IL2CPP on Windows and Linux but not macOS or ARM, and .NET/XNA games on Windows or through Mono on macOS and Linux. The master installation guide lists Windows 7–10, Linux distributions with GCC 10+, macOS 10.13+ and Unity 3 or newer. Source builds use the bundled Cake script and need .NET 6.0 or newer.

BepInEx installs into the user's own game directory: the guide identifies Unity Mono games by a Managed folder and IL2CPP games by il2cpp_data. IL2CPP interop generation reads the game's binary and global-metadata.dat and, by default, downloads managed Unity base libraries for the game's Unity version from unity.bepinex.dev; a configuration option points it to a locally placed archive instead. Some games need the documented troubleshooting steps.

LGPL-2.1 (LGPL-2.1-only in the package metadata); the libraries it uses, including UnityDoorstop, HarmonyX, MonoMod, Mono.Cecil, Cpp2IL and Il2CppInterop, keep their own licenses. Game license terms are separate from the framework's license.

resources.name: BinExport
resources.description: The exporter component of BinDiff: plugins for IDA Pro and Binary Ninja and an extension for Ghidra that write an analyzed disassembly to the Protocol Buffer format BinDiff requires. The BinExport2 schema covers instructions with their operands and expressions, basic blocks, flow graphs, the call graph, sections, strings, comments and data references; the exporter can also write a statistics text file or a text dump for debugging. Exports can be scripted through IDC or IDAPython in IDA and through a BinExport.java script that also runs in Ghidra's headless analyzer.
requirements: Latest release at review: v12-20240417-ghidra_11.0.3, published 2024-04-17, with Linux, macOS and Windows plugin archives and a Ghidra 11.0.3 extension; the release notes say its artifacts are not code-signed. The reviewed main commit is 111 commits ahead of that release, and its README requires IDA Pro 9.4 or later and drops the 8.x series, so the current README describes plugins that no release yet provides.

Requires a separately licensed IDA Pro or Binary Ninja installation, or Ghidra; Binary Ninja integration is minimal and the Ghidra extension is described as experimental. Users supply their own binaries and analysis databases, and BinDiff itself is a separate tool.

Native builds need CMake 3.20+, Boost 1.83+ (a partial copy is bundled), GCC 15 or recent Clang on Linux and macOS or Visual Studio 2022 with the Windows 11 SDK, and download Abseil, GoogleTest, Protocol Buffers and the IDA and Binary Ninja SDKs; Debian 11 is the preferred Linux build environment. The Ghidra extension builds with OpenJDK 21+, Gradle 8.7+ and Ghidra 11.0.3.
Apache-2.0. The README states that it is not an official Google product.

resources.name: Karta
resources.description: Source-code-assisted IDA Python plugin from Check Point Research that finds and matches open-source libraries compiled into large binaries and firmware. Its identifier script reports which supported libraries, such as OpenSSL, zlib, libpng and net-snmp, are present and fingerprints their versions; the matcher then uses a JSON configuration built from that library version to locate its compiled files by their original function order, match their functions and the external libc functions they call, and export selected matches as IDA names. The bundled Thumbs Up scripts improve IDA's function analysis beforehand, including ARM/Thumb separation in firmware.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.1.0, published 2021-05-18; the reviewed master commit, from 2022-03-15, adds only README and CI workflow changes. The README says the original author can no longer maintain the repository after leaving Check Point Research, citing the IDA Pro versions and regression-test requirements involved.

Requires IDA Pro 7.4 or newer with Python 3; v1.2.0 is the last release for Python 2 and older IDA versions. setup.py installs dependencies including elementals, sark, click and scikit-learn, while requirements.txt still names the old sklearn package. The scripts are loaded through IDA's script-file menu rather than installed as plugins. IDA is the only implemented disassembler backend, although the docs describe an interface for adding others.

Run the scripts on a binary that IDA has already analyzed well, and select the Windows option for Windows-compiled binaries. Matching needs a configuration for the exact library version: the repository ships configurations for OpenSSL 1.0.1j, libpng 1.2.29, libtiff 4.0.8 and zlib 1.2.3 and 1.2.11, and others are generated with karta_analyze_src.py, which also drives IDA, from the static library and object files of a library you compile yourself, following the notes in compilations/. Upstream advises backing up the binary before Thumbs Up, which makes major changes to its analysis.

MIT license. The identifier covers 15 library modules, including the closed-source Treck library, which is detected only. Matches are heuristic proposals whose matching rules differ in accuracy and are shown in different colors, so they need analyst review.

resources.name: VTIL-Core
resources.description: C++20 core of the VTIL (Virtual-machine Translation Intermediate Language) project, an intermediate language and optimizing compiler that the README describes as built for binary de-obfuscation and de-virtualization. Unlike LLVM IR, VTIL keeps the native stack, physical registers and non-SSA form, so code from register or stack machines can be lifted into it, native instructions can stay inline, and code can be emitted back at any virtual address. The library provides the IL with routines, basic blocks and serialization, a symbolic expression engine and simplifier, optimizer passes such as dead-code elimination, propagation and stack pinning, and Capstone/Keystone-based AMD64 and ARM64 disassembly and assembly helpers.
requirements: No releases or tags; the README says the repository is incomplete because the initial release is not done, and further documentation is still to come. The reviewed master commit (2026-07-27) only edits the README; the preceding code commits date from 2026-04-04 and 2026-04-05.

Build with CMake 3.16+ and a C++20 compiler: generate a Visual Studio solution on Windows, or use Ninja on Linux and macOS, where Apple Silicon builds need -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=x86_64. CMake fetches Capstone and Keystone at pinned commits, and CI builds on Windows Server 2022, Ubuntu 24.04 and macOS 14.

This is a library for analyzing virtualized or obfuscated code: the user supplies a lifter that translates the code under analysis into VTIL routines, which can then be optimized, inspected or re-emitted. The reviewed tree contains no lifter for a particular virtual machine or protector. Its Sample Routines folder holds 2020 .vtil test routines next to the small C test functions they correspond to, which commit messages describe as VMProtect tests.
BSD-3-Clause license. The fetched dependencies keep their own licenses: Capstone's BSD-style license, and Keystone's GPL-2.0 with a FOSS license exception, which matters when distributing builds.

resources.name: efiXplorer
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin and loader that automate static analysis of UEFI firmware. The plugin annotates Boot, Runtime, SMM and PEI service calls, lists the EFI protocols and known GUIDs a module installs or consumes, applies protocol interface types in the Hex-Rays decompiler, flags suspected SMM callout and GetVariable out-of-bounds write patterns for review and saves a JSON report. The efiXloader module opens a whole firmware image in one IDA database, with driver entry points, navigation between drivers and a DXE driver dependency graph.
requirements: Latest release at review: v6.3.0, published 2026-08-20 as a zip of prebuilt binaries; the reviewed master commit is two GUID-database submodule updates ahead. ida-plugin.json declares IDA 8.3 or newer on Windows x86_64, Linux x86_64 and macOS x86_64/aarch64; the plugin is listed in Hex-Rays' plugin repository and can be installed with ida-hcli.

Needs a licensed IDA Pro. Applying protocol interface types also needs the Hex-Rays decompiler, and the build instructions cover building without it. Source builds use CMake or build.py against the IDA SDK, UEFITool and GUID database submodules; a manual install copies the plugin and the guids directory into IDA's plugins folder and the loader into its loaders folder.

Input is a UEFI firmware image or individual UEFI driver the analyst already has. The wiki's feature table lists SMM services and the dependency graph for 64-bit modules only and PEI services for 32-bit only. Its loader page still says only 64-bit drivers are supported, while the v6.3.0 notes add 32-bit modules in the loader, and the wiki pages still link the earlier binarly-io repository.

GPL-3.0; ida-plugin.json declares GPL-3.0-only. Vulnerability-scanner hits are suspected findings presented for analyst review, not confirmed bugs; the authors' Black Hat Europe 2020 and EKO 2020 publications describe the approach.

resources.name: Frida Workbench for VSCode
resources.description: Unofficial Visual Studio Code extension for Frida work. A sidebar lists apps and processes on local, Apple Simulator, USB and remote devices to attach, spawn or kill, and runtime panels browse an attached process's native modules and exports and its Java and Objective-C classes, methods and protocols; selected items generate Interceptor, Objective-C or Java hook scaffolds, optionally with GitHub Copilot-inferred native signatures, and Objective-C headers or Java class stubs can be dumped. A language server completes class, selector and module names from a live target, and the extension also scaffolds Frida agent and C-module projects, script-debugging configurations, syslog streaming and Android frida-server setup.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.12.11, published 2026-09-29 as a .vsix package, whose tag is the reviewed main commit; package.json requires VS Code 1.94+. The extension is also listed on the Visual Studio Marketplace under the CodeColorist publisher. CHANGELOG.md's newest entry is v0.12.8, so later releases are not described there.

Needs Python 3.7+ with the frida-tools package; because of PEP 668 the README recommends the workspace's active virtual environment, or pipx or uv. Targets need a working Frida setup: on Android the extension can download and start frida-server, iOS USB access from Windows needs iTunes kept open, libimobiledevice is optional for SSH shells, and iOS shells require a jailbroken device.

The language server attaches to the live target named in .vscode/frida.json, which needs a device and exactly one of app, pid or process. Copilot-assisted hook generation depends on GitHub Copilot, and Objection is an optional external tool. Users supply their own devices, apps and processes.
A community project, not affiliated with the Frida team; MIT-licensed.

resources.name: ghidriff
resources.description: Command-line binary diffing engine that drives Ghidra headlessly through pyghidra: it imports and analyzes an old and a new binary, then reports added, deleted and modified functions, with patch diffing as its main use. The default VersionTrackingDiff engine combines several Ghidra Version Tracking correlators with BSim matching, alongside simpler symbol-name and structural-graph engines and a GhidraDiffEngine base class for custom differs. Results are written as JSON and Markdown with Mermaid charts and meta diffs of strings, called and calling functions and binary metadata, plus optional side-by-side HTML.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.0.0, published 2025-07-04 on GitHub and PyPI, which requires Python 3.9+ and pyghidra 2.0+. The reviewed main commit, merged 2026-05-11, is six commits ahead and still reports version 1.0.0: it requires Python 3.10+ and pyghidra 3.x, targets Ghidra 12.0.4 and logs a warning when another Ghidra or pyghidra version is running. setup.cfg classifies the package as Alpha.

Install Ghidra with a JDK supported by that release, set GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR and install the package with pip or uvx; the README covers Windows, Linux and macOS, and its x64/arm64 Docker image ships the PyPI release so Ghidra and Java need not be installed on the host. Large binaries may need a larger JVM memory share.

Supply two or more versions of the same binary, ordered oldest to newest, with an optional summary across several new versions; anything Ghidra can import and analyze can be compared, with a custom base address for firmware or bootloader images, analyzer options and GDT type archives. The supported-platforms page says native code works best, managed .NET results are mixed and native libraries must be taken out of an APK first. A preflight check stops the diff when the two programs' processor languages differ or their symbol counts differ by 4,000 or more, unless --force-diff is given. By default Ghidra's well-known PDB symbol servers are configured with a local symbol store unless --no-symbols is set.

GPL-3.0. Matching quality depends on Ghidra's analysis and decompilation. The README's use cases and the documentation site's sample diffs cover Windows and macOS system binaries obtained separately; the repository ships no target binaries.

resources.name: vmlinux-to-elf
resources.description: Rebuild an analyzable ELF with function and variable symbols from a Linux kernel image, whether a raw or compressed vmlinux, vmlinuz, zImage or bzImage blob, certain Android boot.img files or a stripped kernel ELF, by locating and decoding the embedded kallsyms symbol table. It detects the compression format, instruction set, endianness, word size, entry point and an approximate base address and writes an ELF for IDA Pro or Ghidra; a kallsyms-finder listing, a standalone decompressor and a GTK GUI are included.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.3.6, published 2026-05-20 on GitHub and PyPI; its notes include provisional support for reserializing section-stripped ELF kernels and uImage LZMA decompression. The reviewed master commit is four commits ahead, with GUI and packaging updates, and carries a 1.3.6.1 tag that has no release. PyPI classifies the project as beta.

Requires Python 3.9+ with lz4, zstandard, minilzo and peewee. The README installs the CLI and GUI with snap on Ubuntu, from the AUR, or with uv plus GTK 4, libadwaita and PyGObject development packages; Flathub provides the GUI on distributions whose libadwaita is older than 1.6.

Input is a kernel image the analyst already has; kernels built without CONFIG_KALLSYMS are not supported. The README states support for Linux 2.6.10 through 6.4 as of August 2023, raw-kernel architecture detection for MIPS, ARM, ARM64, PowerPC, SPARC, x86, x86-64, SuperH and ARC, XZ, LZMA, GZip, BZ2, LZ4, LZO and Zstd decompression, and OpenWrt's uncompressed kallsyms variant. Instruction set, bit size, file offset and base address can be overridden when detection fails.
GPL-3.0-or-later. Recovered symbols carry only the name, address and nm-style type stored in kallsyms, and the base address is a heuristic: the first text symbol address with the low 12 bits cleared.

resources.name: Ddisasm
resources.description: GrammaTech's Datalog disassembler, which turns ELF and PE binaries for x86-32, x86-64, ARM32, ARM64 and MIPS32 into the GTIRB intermediate representation. It decodes a superset of possible instructions, then applies Soufflé Datalog rules and weighted heuristics to infer code locations, symbolization and function boundaries; gtirb-pprinter turns the result into reassemblable assembly or a rebuilt binary, and the GTIRB APIs or gtirb-rewriting can modify it in between. User hint files add Datalog facts or change heuristic weights where inference goes wrong.
requirements: Latest GitHub release at review: v1.8.0, published 2023-12-14 without attached files. Later versions are distributed elsewhere: PyPI lists ddisasm 1.9.5, uploaded 2026-07-06 as a single manylinux x86_64 wheel. The reviewed main commit, from 2026-10-13, declares version 1.9.6, which its changelog marks unreleased.

Prebuilt options are the grammatech/ddisasm Docker image (stable or unstable tags), Ubuntu 20 (focal) apt packages and Windows .zip builds on GrammaTech's servers; the docs warn against mixing stable and unstable tools. Source builds need a C++17 compiler, GTIRB 1.12.1+, gtirb-pprinter 2.0.0+, Capstone 5.0.1+ (GrammaTech tests with its fork), Soufflé 2.4 built with 64-bit numbers, libehp 1.0.0+ and LIEF 0.13.2+.

Input is an ELF or PE binary; rebuilding through gtirb-pprinter invokes a compiler or assembler such as gcc. Code inference and symbolization are heuristic: --self-diagnose checks symbolization only for binaries linked with complete relocation information, and the docs call the option that replaces CFI directives with .eh_frame symbolic expressions experimental and unreliable.

AGPL-3.0; contributions require GrammaTech's contributor license agreement. GTIRB, gtirb-pprinter and gtirb-rewriting are separate projects. The README cites a USENIX Security 2020 paper and an IEEE S&P 2025 paper on the approach.

resources.name: PINCE
resources.description: Linux front end for the GNU Debugger (GDB), focused on games but usable for other reverse engineering; the name stands for “PINCE is not Cheat Engine”. It scans process memory and pointers through libmemscan into a typed address table, and its memory view adds disassembly, an on-the-fly assembler, code dissection for referenced calls, jumps and strings, function, region and instruction searches, and structure overlays, including structures generated from Mono/IL2CPP class dissection of native Linux or Wine/Proton processes. Debugging covers chained breakpoints and watchpoints, tracking of the instructions that access an address, tracing and stack traces, alongside a GDB console and the reusable libpince Python library.
requirements: Linux only. Latest release at review: v0.10.2, published 2026-09-18, whose tag is the reviewed master commit; it ships an x86_64 AppImage that the README supports on distributions as new as Ubuntu 22.04 or newer.

Local development installs run install.sh with APT, Pacman or DNF and need Python 3.11+, PyQt 6.11+ and GDB; Kubuntu 22.04+ and Arch Linux are officially supported, while Debian 12+, Fedora 35+ and openSUSE are only partially supported and not actively tested. The PINCE.sh launcher runs PINCE as root, elevating through pkexec or sudo.

Users select a running process of their own to inspect. The README states that users are responsible for their actions and asks that only this GitHub repository be trusted as a source of PINCE code or packages.
GPL-3.0-or-later (COPYING); AUTHORS lists the bundled Silk icons in media/icons under CC BY 3.0 (COPYING.CC-BY).

resources.name: uncompyle6
resources.description: Cross-version decompiler that translates Python bytecode back into equivalent Python source, accepting bytecode from Python 1.0 through 3.8 as well as some PyPy bytecode and Dropbox's Python 2.5. It disassembles code objects with the companion xdis library and parses the instruction stream into a grammar-based tree from which source is printed; it can also deparse just the fragment around a given bytecode offset, which the author's trepan debuggers use for exact location reporting. It succeeds the older decompyle, uncompyle and uncompyle2 forks.
requirements: Latest release at review: 3.9.3, published 2025-09-29 on GitHub and PyPI; the reviewed master commit is 34 commits later and reports 3.9.4.dev0. Installing from PyPI, like the master branch, is meant for running on Python 3.11+; older interpreters back to Python 2.4 use the version-specific tarballs, eggs or wheels on GitHub Releases, built from separate git branches. It depends on xdis 6.3+, spark-parser and click.

The README reports testing on bytecode from Python 1.4, 2.1–2.7 and 3.0–3.8 and later PyPy versions. Python 3 support is strongest around 3.3–3.4 and weakens further away, control flow is the biggest known problem, and the author does not intend serious work on 3.8 or 3.9, pointing to the separate decompyle3 for 3.7 and 3.8. Bytecode newer than 3.8 is not decompiled, and candidate-release magic numbers, some Python 3.6 magic variants, encrypted or custom-interpreter bytecode other than Dropbox's old 2.5, obfuscated code, Cython and MicroPython are not handled.

Input .pyc or .pyo files come from the user; it cannot decompile Py2EXE executables directly, and bytecode bundled by such packagers has to be extracted first. The --syntax-verify option checks only that the output is valid Python syntax, so the README suggests cross-checking with other uncompyle6 versions or other decompilers such as pycdc. Recovered source remains subject to the rights of the original program’s owner.
GPL-3.0-or-later per pyproject.toml, with the GPL-3.0 text in COPYING.

resources.name: ret-sync
resources.description: Reverse-Engineering Tools SYNChronization: plugins that keep IDA, Ghidra or Binary Ninja graph and decompiler views following a live WinDbg, GDB, LLDB, OllyDbg 1.10/2 or x64dbg session, rebasing addresses on the fly so ASLR does not break the mapping. Debugger commands push comments, labels, rebased addresses and command output into the disassembler database and resolve symbols from it, while disassembler hotkeys set breakpoints and step the debugger; several databases can be synced at once and the two sides may run on different hosts. A standalone Python library offers the same position syncing to custom tracing tools.
requirements: No release tracks the reviewed master commit (2026-02-15): the only GitHub release is a 2022 Binary Ninja community build, prebuilt WinDbg, OllyDbg, OllyDbg2 and x64dbg plugins come from an Azure DevOps pipeline, and ext_ghidra/dist holds per-version Ghidra extension archives, the newest for Ghidra 11.4.2. Each Ghidra archive supports only the Ghidra version in its file name; other versions are built with Gradle against a local installation.

The IDA plugin requires IDA 9.2+, with older IDA versions served by history before the ida9.2 tag; the Binary Ninja plugin needs Binary Ninja 2.2+ with Python 3 and is marked experimental; the WinDbg extension is built from a Visual Studio solution, reported working with Visual Studio 2017 and 2026; the IDA and GDB plugins need Python 2.7+ or Python 3. IDA, Binary Ninja and WinDbg are obtained separately, and users supply their own binaries and debugging targets.

The README states there is no authentication or encryption between debugger and disassembler and that self-modifying code is out of scope; its tested-versions list is older (Python 2.7/3.7, IDA 7.7, Ghidra 10.1.1, Binary Ninja 3.0, GDB 8.1, LLDB 310.2.37), and it notes GDB signal issues with multi-threaded debugging and a possible WinDbg race condition. Remote and renamed-module setups are configured through an optional .sync INI file.
GPL-3.0-or-later; the Binary Ninja plugin is MIT-licensed. ret-sync is a fork of Quarkslab's qb-sync.

resources.name: PyInstaller Extractor (pyinstxtractor)
resources.description: Single-file Python script that extracts the contents of executables built with PyInstaller, including Linux ELF builds without other tools. It locates the PyInstaller archive in the executable, reports the PyInstaller and Python versions and likely entry-point scripts, and writes out the bundled CArchive files and the modules in the PYZ archive. It fixes the headers of the extracted .pyc files so that Python bytecode decompilers such as uncompyle6 and Decompyle++ (pycdc) recognize them.
requirements: Runs under Python 2.x or 3.x and needs no PyInstaller installation. Latest release at review: 2026.07, published 2026-07-22 without attached files; it tags the reviewed master commit, whose script header still calls itself version 2.0. The README lists PyInstaller 2.0 through 6.19.0 as tested against a separate test-binary repository and supported.

Modules in the PYZ archive are extracted only when the script runs under the same Python major and minor version that built the executable; otherwise it warns and skips them, and an archive whose table of contents fails to unmarshal is skipped too. Entries that cannot be decompressed, such as those of encrypted PYZ archives, are saved unchanged with an .encrypted suffix rather than decoded.

The PyInstaller executable comes from the user, and turning the recovered bytecode into source needs a separate decompiler. Recovered code remains subject to the rights of the original program’s owner.

resources.name: Binary Analysis Platform (BAP)
resources.description: OCaml binary analysis platform from Carnegie Mellon University. Its bap command loads a program, disassembles it, lifts instructions into an architecture-neutral intermediate representation, builds the control-flow graph and runs analysis passes, while objdump, raw-loader and mc modes handle linear disassembly, raw code blobs and single encodings. The README lists x86, x86-64, ARM, MIPS and PowerPC support, an interpreter, a microexecution interpreter, a symbolic executor and the Primus Lisp language for analyses, function stubs and SMT-solver queries; analyses are written as OCaml plugins or by embedding BAP as a library, with C bindings and minimal Python support in separate repositories.
requirements: Latest stable release at review: v2.5.0, published 2022-07-11, with x86_64 Debian and RPM packages, tgz archives and sigs.zip/sigs.tar.gz signature archives; a v2.6.0-alpha development build dates from 2023-01-07. The reviewed master commit (2026-05-07) is 60 commits ahead of v2.5.0 and its opam packages carry version dev; the commit before it dates from April 2025.

The binary packages omit the OCaml development environment, so writing analyses needs a source install. The README recommends opam with OCaml 4.14.1 (opam install bap), offers a rolling testing opam repository that follows master, and also documents dune builds from a clone; the opam dependencies keep core_kernel and base below v0.16. The LLVM backend needs llvm-config (conf-bap-llvm 1.8+). The Ghidra and radare2 integrations, which the README calls experimental, and the Z3-based symbolic executor come with the bap-extra meta-package; IDA Pro integration is a separate package.

Input is a user-supplied executable, or a raw code blob opened with --loader=raw and a base address. The tree also has RISC-V, SystemZ and Thumb packages beyond the README's architecture list. Lifted output depends on per-architecture semantics coverage; the 2.5.0 changelog adds a --print-missing option to list unlifted instructions.

MIT license; contributions to the repository are accepted under MIT, while separately hosted plugins may use any license, including a proprietary one. The README names ForAllSecure Mayhem, Draper's CBAT tools and Fraunhofer FKIE's CWE Checker as projects built on BAP.

resources.name: furiousMAC Continuity
resources.description: Reverse-engineering notes and a Wireshark dissector for Apple's proprietary Continuity Bluetooth LE advertisements, continuing the authors' PETS 2019 privacy study. Per-message pages document field layouts and observed values for 14 message types, including AirDrop, Handoff, Proximity Pairing, Nearby Info and Find My, and the dissector replaces Wireshark's packet-bthci_cmd.c so captured advertisements decode into named btcommon.apple fields.
requirements: No GitHub releases; the reviewed commit, from 2025-08-29, merges a typo fix. The dissector README calls the March 2021 version for Wireshark 3.4.4 the most up to date: the 4.4.0 file contributed in 2024 ports it to build on Wireshark 4.4.0 without dissector changes and may not correctly dissect messages from the latest iOS versions. Fields the message tables mark as unknown or uncertain remain open.

On Linux and macOS, users download the Wireshark source for the matching version, replace epan/dissectors/packet-bthci_cmd.c with the project's file and build Wireshark. The repository also commits prebuilt 64-bit Windows Wireshark installers for 3.0.8 and 3.2.1, which the dissector README says are based on the original ShmooCon 2020 dissector and should not be used.

Capturing advertisements needs a BLE sniffer: HARDWARE.md recommends a Nordic nRF51 dongle with Nordic's sniffer firmware, or an Ubertooth One with the included btleshark.sh capture script. Analysis uses advertisements the analyst captures; the repository contains no sample captures.
GPL-2.0. The README credits many message types and field meanings to Celosia and Cunche's PETS 2020 paper.

resources.name: Reko
resources.description: General-purpose decompiler that loads executables or raw images, scans their machine code into a machine-independent register transfer language, groups it into procedures and decompiles them into high-level C code. The reviewed source has 64 architecture directories, from 6502, Z80 and PDP-11 to ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, RISC-V and x86, and loaders for formats including ELF, PE/MZ, Mach-O, COFF, Amiga Hunk, VMS, WebAssembly, Xbox XBE and Xbox 360 XEX. It runs as a Windows Forms GUI, a command-line client or a .NET library, and project files and scripts let users add names, types and comments.
requirements: Latest release at review: 0.12.5, published 2026-09-29, with x86 and x64 Windows MSI installers and command-line and GUI zip builds; the Reko.Decompiler.Runtime NuGet package is also at 0.12.5. The reviewed master commit, from 2026-10-14, is ten commits ahead of that release.

Requires .NET 9.0. Source builds use the .NET 9.0 SDK, or Visual Studio 2026 for IDE users, plus CMake for the NativeProxy project; the WiX toolset is needed only for MSI installers. CI builds on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS. The cross-platform Avalonia GUI is still under development, and the user guide's non-Windows instructions still mention AppVeyor builds and Mono.

Input is a binary the user has the right to decompile; the README warns that many software licenses prohibit decompilation. Raw images need the loader, architecture, base and entry addresses given explicitly. The user guide says useful decompilation usually needs the user to supply types, names and comments, and that a heuristic scan may be needed when indirect jumps or calls hide code.

GPL-2.0 (COPYING). The complete architecture and format list is on the project wiki. The repository's subjects directory holds regression samples collected from other sources together with Reko's output for them; it is test data, not part of the tool.

resources.name: Dyninst
resources.description: Binary instrumentation, analysis and modification libraries from the Paradyn project. DyninstAPI inserts and changes instrumentation in a running program, or rewrites an executable or library on disk and writes the patched copy back, through one machine-independent interface that also supports static and dynamic analysis. Separately documented components handle symbol tables, line numbers and types (SymtabAPI), instruction decoding and disassembly (InstructionAPI), parsing into blocks, functions and loops (ParseAPI), dataflow analyses such as slicing (DataFlowAPI), process control, stack walking and patching.
requirements: The CMake platform check accepts Linux, FreeBSD and Windows hosts on x86-64, 32-bit x86, AArch64, ppc64le and riscv64, plus AMD GPU code-generation targets; InstructionAPI documents x86, x86-64, ARMv8-64 and 32/64-bit PowerPC decoding. The README calls AArch64 dynamic instrumentation experimental and incomplete, and its known issues include no Windows 64-bit or Windows rewriter mode, uncaught exceptions in relocated code, a fragile Windows stack walker and a crash when parsing a binary with no functions.

Latest release at review: v13.0.0, published 2024-03-21. The reviewed master commit still declares version 13.0.0 and is 590 commits ahead of that tag; the README says the bundled v13.0.0 PDF manuals are a snapshot, so current behavior needs manuals built from source with pdflatex.

Install with Spack or build from source with CMake 3.14+ (3.19.0 is rejected), a C11/C++11 toolchain (GCC 6+), Boost 1.71+, TBB 2019.9+ and, on Unix, elfutils 0.186+; Docker containers for development are described in the docker directory. Users supply their own executables, libraries or running processes to analyze or instrument.
LGPL-2.1 (LICENSE.md). COPYRIGHT credits Barton P. Miller with contributions from LLNS, Red Hat and Bull SAS, and DataFlowAPI incorporates Rose Compiler Project code under its own copyright notice.

resources.name: goblin
resources.description: Rust crate for zero-copy, endian-aware parsing of ELF32/64, 32/64-bit Mach-O and multi-architecture fat containers, PE32/PE32+, COFF objects, Terse Executable (TE) images and Unix/BSD archives; Object::parse picks the format from its magic bytes. Parsed structures cover ELF headers, sections, symbols, dynamic entries, relocations and notes, Mach-O load commands, imports and exports, and PE imports, exports, relocations, TLS, resources, exception and unwind data, Authenticode certificates and the .NET CLR header. Feature flags can reduce it to std-free #[repr(C)] struct definitions for kernels and other no_std code.
requirements: Latest tag at review: 0.10.6 (also tagged v0.10.6) on the 2026-05-25 version-bump commit; the project publishes no GitHub releases. crates.io also lists 0.10.7, published 2026-05-28, which has no matching tag or changelog entry. The reviewed master commit (2026-08-30) still declares 0.10.6.

Used as a Cargo dependency; it needs rustc 1.85.0+ (Rust 2024 edition) and depends on plain, scroll and an optional log. Default features enable every format with std; elf32/elf64, mach32/mach64, pe32/pe64, te and archive select backends, endian_fd parses by the binary's own byte order, and Mach-O, PE and TE parsing requires alloc and endian_fd.

Input is a byte slice holding an executable, object file or archive the user supplies. goblin parses format metadata only and includes no disassembler, so code needs a separate instruction decoder. PE parse options can skip RVA resolution, attribute certificates, TLS data, resources or imports, and the changelog describes an ELF and PE permissive mode for packed, broken or malware samples.
MIT license. The README quotes a report of 100 million fuzzing runs, and the repository holds cargo-fuzz and AFL harnesses.

resources.name: mitmproxy2swagger
resources.description: Command-line tool that reverse-engineers undocumented REST APIs from captured traffic. It reads a mitmproxy flow file, or a HAR export from the browser DevTools, and generates an OpenAPI 3.0 specification describing the observed endpoints. Running it again over further captures safely merges the new data into an existing schema.
requirements: Installed from PyPI (also packaged for Arch Linux) or run via the provided Dockerfile; pyproject.toml marks version 0.15.0 and requires Python 3.12+.

Takes a mitmproxy flow file or a browser HAR export as input; the analyst captures that traffic separately, for example with mitmproxy, and supplies the API base-URL prefix. The two-pass workflow lets several captures be merged into an existing schema.

Intended for APIs and traffic the analyst is authorized to capture and analyze. The project metadata in pyproject.toml declares the MIT license; no standalone LICENSE file is present for GitHub to detect.

resources.name: opendbc
resources.description: comma.ai's repository of DBC files describing the CAN messages and signals of many car makes, with a Python library that parses and builds CAN messages from those definitions; its porting guide has contributors reverse engineer new messages from recorded drives in the cabana tool. Per-brand car ports built on it parse vehicle state, identify models from ECU firmware versions and generate openpilot's steering, gas and brake messages, while safety code for comma's panda interface restricts which messages can be sent.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.3.1, published 2026-04-22 on GitHub and PyPI; the reviewed master commit is 296 commits ahead of it. docs/CARS.md lists 406 known cars: 341 with upstream support, 14 community, 32 dashcam-only, 16 not compatible and 3 in a custom category. The README says it and that list are the project's only documentation.

The package requires Python 3.11 or 3.12 because pycapnp does not work with 3.13. From a clone, test.sh installs dependencies, builds with SCons, runs the tests and lints; the README roadmap still lists pip install opendbc as open even though PyPI carries the 0.3.x releases. For a live car, the porting guide starts with a comma four and a car-specific harness, and the DBC README connects through a panda.

New definitions come from the analyst's own recorded drives loaded in cabana, which lives in the openpilot repository; the README also points to the commaCarSegments dataset of CAN data from 300 car models. The DBC README recommends recording uncertain signal interpretations as comments, so definitions cover only what contributors have documented for each car.
MIT. The README says panda safety firmware starts with silent CAN buses and that some output modes are disabled in release firmware.

resources.name: FLOSS (FLARE Obfuscated String Solver)
resources.description: Mandiant FLARE string extractor for malware analysis that is used like strings.exe but also recovers obfuscated strings. Besides static ASCII and UTF-16LE strings it extracts stack strings, tight strings and strings decoded by functions: it heuristically identifies decoding routines, recovers their arguments through control-flow analysis, emulates them and diffs memory before and after emulation. It also extracts Go and Rust strings and accepts PE, ELF and raw 32- or 64-bit shellcode; JSON results can be turned into import scripts for IDA Pro, Ghidra, Binary Ninja, radare2 and x64dbg.
requirements: Latest release at review: v3.2.0, published 2026-10-16 as standalone Linux, macOS and Windows executables and on PyPI for Python 3.10+; it adds basic ELF support and moves the Ghidra import script to PyGhidra. The reviewed master commit has 857 commits that are not in v3.2.0, which in turn has 8 not on master: it merges the QUANTUMSTRAND preview, so the layout-aware static strings with file-structure context and tags, the HTML report and the hosted viewer described in its README have so far shipped only in quantumstrand pre-releases (latest quantumstrand-beta3, 2026-04-22). Master requires Python 3.12+ and still reports version 3.1.1.

Decoding uses static emulation with embedded FLIRT signatures to identify library functions; files above 64 MB abort deobfuscation unless --large-file is given. Shellcode is recognized by .sc32/.raw32/.sc64/.raw64 extensions or selected with -f. Source clones need Git LFS for the tag databases and signature files, and the installation guide calls the Python API unstable between releases, leaving the CLI as the stable interface.

Samples come from the analyst. v3.2.0 fixed an issue in which crafted .viv vivisect workspace files, either the sample itself or one beside it, could execute code during analysis in v3.1.1 and earlier and in the QUANTUMSTRAND pre-releases; saved workspaces now load only with FLOSS_LOAD_VIV_WORKSPACE=1. Decoded strings come only from routines that FLOSS identifies as decoders and emulates.
Apache-2.0.

resources.name: Zydis
resources.description: Lightweight C11 x86/x86-64 disassembler and code-generation library. Its decoder reports each instruction's operands, accessed CPU and FPU flags, ISA set and extension and branch type; the formatter prints Intel, MASM or AT&T syntax, and the encoder assembles instructions from encoder requests, which can also be derived from decoded instructions. ZydisDisasm and ZydisInfo command-line tools are included, and the official Rust and Python 3 bindings live in separate repositories.
requirements: Latest release at review: v4.1.1, published 2025-02-16 with no attached files; v4.1.0 (2024-02-04) carries the zydis-amalgamated single-header and single-source archives the README describes. The README says master holds the next, unreleased version without API stability guarantees; the reviewed master commit (2026-07-27) declares 5.0.0 and is 121 commits ahead of and 59 behind the v4.1.1 tag.

Build with CMake 3.10+ (the README lists Windows, macOS, Linux and the BSDs), the Meson 1.3+ build file, the maintained Visual Studio 2022 project, or the amalgamated files with any C11 compiler. A recursive clone fetches the Zycore support library from its zycore-c submodule unless a system copy is forced. The README lists Arch, Debian, Ubuntu, Homebrew, NixOS and vcpkg packages, and CMake options can disable the decoder, encoder, formatter, AVX-512 or KNC support or force minimal decoding mode.

The caller supplies code bytes and selects a 16-, 32- or 64-bit machine mode; ZydisDisasm reads a raw byte file. No executable-format loader is documented, so locating code in PE, ELF or firmware images needs another tool.

MIT license; Zycore is a separate MIT-licensed zyantific repository. The README's statements about performance, dependency-free and allocation-free operation, thread safety, testing on Windows, macOS, FreeBSD, Linux and UEFI, and use in x64dbg, Firefox and WebKit.

resources.name: Sony-PMCA-RE
resources.description: USB tool built from reverse engineering Sony digital cameras. On supported models it reads camera information and installs Android apps through the PlayMemories Camera Apps mechanism, while its firmware-updater and service-mode shells can dump firmware, run Linux commands and change settings. The repository's notes describe the app-installation exchange between the Sony app store, the browser plugin and the camera.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.18, published 2022-04-08, with Windows and macOS builds of the pmca-console command line and the more limited pmca-gui. The reviewed master commit, from 2022-08-18, is 22 commits ahead of it. On Linux the Python 3 sources run with the listed requirements and libusb; the CI builds use Python 3.6 and PyInstaller. As checked on 2026-10-20, the reviewed 2022-08-18 commit is still the master head, GitHub’s last recorded push was 2024-07-27, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

Needs a supported Sony camera connected over USB; the README links an external OpenMemories compatibility list. App installation needs a camera with PlayMemories Camera Apps support. Firmware-updater mode uses the operating system's mass-storage driver and excludes CXD90045 and CXD90057 devices, whose firmware is cryptographically signed. Service mode is console-only and needs libusb drivers on Windows; macOS mass-storage access needs Sony's camera driver.

The README calls the project an early-stage experiment based on reverse engineering and warns that it could harm the camera, with no responsibility taken. Firmware-file unpacking lives in the separate fwtool project.
MIT. The repository holds no Sony firmware or apps; the prebuilt updater payloads under updatershell/fdat are packed by pack.py from the project's own sources.

resources.name: QBDI
resources.description: Quarkslab's modular dynamic binary instrumentation (DBI) framework, which JIT-recompiles a program's basic blocks inside its own process so that an instrumentation tool can register callbacks before or after instructions, on memory reads and writes, and on VM events. The engine is a library that can start an instrumented execution anywhere in a process, scripted from C, C++, Python (PyQBDI) or Frida JavaScript. It has no preferred injection method: it bundles the LD_PRELOAD-based QBDIPreload for Linux and macOS dynamic executables and is integrated with Frida.
requirements: The README status table supports execution and memory-access information for x86-64 and x86 on Android, Linux, macOS and Windows, ARM on Android and Linux, and AArch64 on Android, Linux, macOS and iOS; iOS support is described as unstable and needs a jailbroken device. Latest release at review: v0.12.1, published 2026-01-07, with Android, iOS, macOS and Windows packages; Linux packages last appear in v0.12.0 (2025-10-14). PyQBDI 0.12.1 on PyPI requires Python 3.8+.

The reviewed dev-next commit is 12 commits ahead of v0.12.1; the README says all new work merges there and there is no scheduled release plan. Source builds need CMake 3.12+, Ninja or Make and a C++17 toolchain, and build a bundled LLVM statically because QBDI uses private LLVM APIs of one specific version; per-platform configuration scripts cover Linux, macOS, Windows (with a native Python 3 and Visual Studio) and Android NDK cross-compilation.

The README states that QBDI does not handle signals, new-thread creation or C++ exceptions. Its documentation adds that the instrumentation tool shares the target's heap and libraries, so non-reentrant code such as the heap allocator should be left to the execution broker outside the instrumentation range, and the OS loader itself cannot be instrumented. Users supply their own target programs and an injection route.

LICENSE.txt places QBDI under Apache-2.0 and lists statically linked components: LLVM (Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions), spdlog, fmtlib, Catch2, pybind11 and a GPLv3/Apache-2.0 SHA-256 implementation; GitHub could not classify the combined file.

resources.name: MEDUSA
resources.description: Modular Frida-based framework for runtime analysis of Android and iOS apps the analyst is authorized to test. From a single coordinated script it loads plug-in modules to inspect network and WebView activity, trace API calls, examine memory and cryptographic operations, monitor malware behavior, and handle protections such as SSL pinning. The README reports it ships with over 90 reusable modules.
requirements: Requires Python 3 and runs on Linux or macOS, with the README noting limited functionality on Windows; a preconfigured Dockerfile is also provided.
Instrumenting a target needs a rooted device or emulator with adb and a running Frida server; the tool operates only on apps the analyst is authorized to test.

The README reports 90+ reusable modules and an optional MCP server component; it names capabilities such as SSL-pinning handling. GPL-3.0 licensed; the repository ships the framework and its modules, no application packages.

resources.name: binsider
resources.description: Terminal user interface for inspecting ELF binaries. It shows file information and linked shared libraries in the manner of stat and ldd, browses ELF headers, notes, sections, segments, symbols, dynamic symbols and relocations much like readelf, extracts strings with an adjustable minimum length, and offers a searchable hexdump view. Optional dynamic analysis runs the binary and traces its system calls like strace, with a summary of time and call counts per system call; the interface can also be embedded as a Rust library in Ratatui applications.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.3.2, published 2026-02-01, on crates.io and as prebuilt archives for Linux (x86_64, i686, AArch64, ARM and powerpc64le, with glibc and musl variants), macOS on Intel and Apple silicon, and Windows x86_64. The release workflow enables dynamic analysis only in the x86_64 Linux builds and the AArch64 glibc build. The reviewed main commit is six commits later and adds the --syscall-number, --string-limit and --no-abbrev trace options, which the website documents but no release includes yet.

Cargo.toml requires Rust 1.88+, although the website's installation pages still give an MSRV of 1.74.1. The dynamic-analysis feature is enabled by default and can be left out with --no-default-features. The website also documents Docker, Nix, Arch Linux and Alpine Linux installation.

Input is an ELF file chosen by the user. Dynamic analysis executes that binary on the host under ptrace-based tracing, so untrusted samples should only be traced in an isolated environment; the other views read the file without running it.
Dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0.

resources.name: Reverse Engineering (mytechnotalent)
resources.description: A free, English lesson index by mytechnotalent that grows almost daily: 490 numbered lessons, most of which have learners write small programs and then debug and patch ("hack") them, across x86, x64, 32/64-bit ARM, RISC-V and AVR. Early courses start from number systems, registers, memory and the stack; later ones cover microcontroller firmware on Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2, STM32F401, ESP32-C3, ATmega328P and micro:bit boards, plus Windows, Go, Rust and WebAssembly programs. The README is a table of links; the lesson text lives in a GitBook and in the author's other repositories and PDF books.
requirements: At reviewed commit 8ae661a (pushed 2026-10-18) the README lists 490 numbered lessons in 26 courses and headlines a dated "Today's Tutorial" (Lesson 329, 18 October 2026); the default branch has received commits on most recent days. Lesson 1 describes the x86 course as starting from the basic concepts of malware reverse engineering and working up to an entry-level look at assembly, while later courses assume that grounding. The Reverse Engineering Data course (lessons 461–490) is statistics and machine-learning notebooks, not binary analysis.

No third-party target files are needed: most courses follow a write, debug, then patch pattern on programs the learner builds from the lessons. The embedded courses need physical boards (Raspberry Pi Pico and Pico 2/RP2350, STM32F401CCU6, ESP32-C3, ATmega328P, micro:bit), and the RISC-V course says it lists everything to purchase. The repository root also keeps Fritzing schematics and a few Windows MASM/Visual Studio example projects with their Debug builds.

Toolchains are set out in the linked material rather than the README, which mentions GDB in the x86 course, a Linux install lesson and PlatformIO for the ESP32-C3. Most of lessons 1–203 point to the "Reverse Engineering For Everyone!" GitBook by @mytechnotalent (built by @0xInfection); later lessons point to PDF books and lesson files in the author's separate repositories, which move independently.
The README's "Reverse Engineering Assistant" (REA) link is the author's own mytechnotalent/rea tool. The repository is Apache-2.0; linked books and repositories carry their own terms.

resources.name: Co-op Anything
resources.description: Agent playbook, skill set and stdio MCP server for adding online or split-screen co-op to single-player games the players already have installed. Agents either revive an existing co-op mod or reverse engineer the game and engine to build one, test it with in-game bots and send their notes back, while the MCP server searches a directory of 223 co-op projects and 32 open gaps, detects a game’s engine from its install folder and records the executable’s identity. Its README and reverse-engineering skill pair it with REA for native code, and two game write-ups report observations made through REA’s Ghidra lane.
requirements: The repository was created on 2026-10-16, the reviewed commit is from 2026-10-18, and there are no releases, so the playbook, directory and reported results are changing quickly. The MCP server is a Python 3.9+ script without an SDK that needs PyYAML for its directory tools; Claude Code picks it up from .mcp.json, and the playbook gives Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor settings. The same skills ship under .agents/skills and .claude/skills.

Every player needs the game installed, and the hub holds no game files or assets. AGENTS.md tells agents to work on a copied install, ask the owner before installing software or using their accounts, and pin downloads by SHA-256. Its rules allow building on existing decompilations or decompiling a game, with that code kept in the game’s own repository under the licence of what it builds on. Analysis tools such as REA, Ghidra, IDA MCP servers, Frida, Cheat Engine, BepInEx and UE4SS are installed separately, and the playbook leaves REA’s npx rea-agents setup for the owner to run before restarting the agent.

Networking guidance uses Steam relay through Valve’s free Spacewar test app, and split-screen guidance builds on Nucleus Co-op and PartyDeck. The project rules restrict it to co-op and forbid anti-cheat bypass for online services and cheating in other people’s multiplayer games.

Results are reported by the author and contributors. The README lists Deus Ex as released and Ocarina of Time as fully synced, with other games in progress; each directory entry carries a QA level, from none through player reports and automated bot tests to a verified playthrough, and the Deus Ex write-up reports automated tests with real game clients. CI only checks that DIRECTORY.md matches data/directory.yaml.

MIT for the hub; MinHook source vendored in one game experiment keeps its own licence, and linked mods, decompilations, tools and games keep their own terms. The REA connection is a documented pairing for native analysis plus reported use in game notes.

resources.name: FISSURE
resources.description: GNU Radio-based RF framework that carries a signal from survey and detection through IQ capture, inspection, conditioning, feature extraction and classification into a protocol discovery workflow. Its demodulation workspace estimates symbol rates for OOK/ASK and binary FSK recordings, and the bitstream and framing stage applies Manchester or differential decoding, sync-pattern and CRC evidence and repeated-message detection to propose message boundaries. A Qt dashboard coordinates local or remote SDR sensor nodes, a library keeps protocol and packet definitions, dissectors and archived recordings, and plugins add inspection modules such as radar pulse analysis.
requirements: Development happens on the Python3 branch, reviewed at its 2026-10-17 commit; the README calls GitHub releases periodic snapshots that may lack recent fixes, and the latest, Python3_20260921 (published 2026-09-29), is seven commits behind. The changelog shows protocol discovery being rebuilt in October 2026: Demodulation and Bitstream & Framing are new, Packet Analysis is a placeholder, and the older Bit Slicing, Dissectors and Sniffer tabs are hidden as obsolete, while the Read the Docs operation pages still describe the older tabs.

Installed by cloning the repository and running its interactive installer as a normal user, not with sudo, preferably on a clean system. The README lists DragonOS, Kali, Raspberry Pi OS and Ubuntu 20.04 to 24.04 with PyQt5 and GNU Radio 3.8 or 3.10 (Ubuntu 18.04 only on the deprecated Python2 branch), beta support for a few other distributions, Windows 11 through WSL2 and Apptainer images on Ubuntu 24.04. Testing is most extensive on Ubuntu, and flow graphs may need recompiling across GNU Radio versions.

Live capture needs a supported SDR such as a USRP, HackRF, RTL2832U, LimeSDR, bladeRF, PlutoSDR or SDRplay receiver; the README says hardware support is being migrated into the plugin architecture, so not every legacy integration works in every workflow. Offline analysis uses the analyst's own IQ or SigMF recordings.

GPL-3.0; GNU Radio out-of-tree blocks come from git submodules under their own licenses. The framework also includes transmit, packet-crafting, fuzzing and attack workflows, plus geolocation, targeting and TAK sharing for distributed operations.

resources.name: Android Unpinner
resources.description: Tool from the mitmproxy project that removes certificate pinning from an Android APK you own or are authorized to test, without a rooted device. It marks the app debuggable, touching only AndroidManifest.xml, and injects a Frida Gadget over ADB so an interception proxy can read the app's traffic, reusing HTTP Toolkit's unpinning script. It bundles the Android SDK helpers it needs and can also handle split APKs delivered as XAPK.
requirements: Installed with uv or pip and requires Python 3.10+ (pyproject version 1.0); the target device connects to a desktop over USB/ADB, and the tool bundles the adb, apksigner, zipalign and aapt2 helpers for Windows, Linux and macOS.
Patches the target APK and needs active instrumentation from the desktop each time the app launches, so rooting the device is not required; intended only for apps you own or are authorized to test.

The README states the project's own code is MIT-licensed, with no separate LICENSE file for GitHub to detect; bundled components keep their own licenses, including HTTP Toolkit's unpinning script (AGPL-3.0), the Frida gadgets (wxWindows Library Licence) and Android build/platform tools. The repository also ships HTTP Toolkit's open-source SSL-pinning demo APK (Apache-2.0) as a test target.

resources.name: cpu_rec
resources.description: Statistically recognize the CPU instruction set in an arbitrary binary file, such as an unknown firmware image, by comparing Markov-chain byte statistics with a default corpus covering dozens of architectures, from 6502 and 8051 to ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, RISC-V, x86-64 and WebAssembly. It reports a match for the whole file, then the largest chunk that matches one architecture, and shows entropy so that encrypted or compressed regions can be discounted. It runs standalone, as a Python function or as a binwalk module.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.1, published 2024-03-19 and tagged at the reviewed commit; it adds an optional pickled corpus for faster startup and LIEF as an alternative to elfesteem. There is no package: cpu_rec.py and the cpu_rec_corpus directory are copied into the same directory. As checked on 2026-10-20, nothing has been pushed since v1.1 and the repository is not archived; the README’s Development status section holds only CI badges and does not mark the project as maintained, superseded or archived.

Runs on Python 3 or Python 2; the portability workflow covers Python 3.10, PyPy 2.7 and 3.9 and GraalPy on Ubuntu and macOS. Without the lzma module the .xz corpus files must be decompressed first. Optional elfesteem or LIEF extracts the text section of ELF, PE, Mach-O or COFF files. The README reports about one minute of analysis per MB, and 1 GB of RAM to build signatures for 70 architectures, on the author's laptop.
Binwalk mode installs into binwalk's module directory and needs a binwalk that includes devttys0/binwalk pull request 241; these instructions point to the earlier Python binwalk.

Results are heuristic: the README warns that files can contain several architectures, small chunks can be misdetected, and results for data with entropy above 0.9 are probably meaningless. 78k and TriCore are left out of the default corpus for licensing reasons and can only be added from the user's own binaries.

cpu_rec.py is Apache-2.0. The README describes the default corpus as a composite of code chunks under their own licenses, mostly from Debian, BusyBox, C-Kermit and the author's own cross-compiled open-source builds, plus a few of unknown license, including an H8S binary distributed by Dell; build_default_corpus records each origin.

resources.name: iced
resources.description: x86 instruction library for 16-, 32- and 64-bit code that decodes, formats, assembles and encodes instructions, with masm, nasm, GNU AT&T and Intel XED output syntaxes. Its instruction-info API reports the registers, memory operands and RFLAGS bits an instruction reads or writes, its CPUID feature flags and control-flow type, and the encoder can re-encode decoded instructions at any address. Rust, C# (.NET) and Java implementations live in one repository, with Python, JavaScript (WebAssembly) and Lua bindings built on the Rust crate.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.21.0, published 2024-01-20, distributed as iced-x86 on crates.io, PyPI, npm and Maven Central (group io.github.icedland.iced) and as iced on NuGet. The reviewed master commit (2026-07-14) is 340 commits ahead of that tag, with no newer release, and still declares version 1.21.0.

The Rust crate needs rustc 1.64.0+, supports no_std and WebAssembly, and uses Cargo features to select the decoder, encoder, block encoder, instruction info, each formatter and the optional code assembler. The .NET library targets .NET Standard 2.0/2.1 and .NET Framework 4.5, and the Java library needs Java 8+. PyPI ships Windows, macOS and Linux wheels, and source builds need Rust and Python 3.8+; the JavaScript package is built with wasm-pack, and the Lua binding is built from source with Rust, luarocks and Lua 5.1+.

The caller supplies raw code bytes, the bitness and the instruction pointer. The reviewed documentation describes no executable-format parsing or function discovery, so a loader or format library has to locate code first. Knights Corner MVEX instructions need the mvex feature and the KNC decoder option.

MIT license. The README reports that all instructions are tested, that iced was tested against xed, gas, objdump, masm, dumpbin, nasm and ndisasm and fuzzed, and Rust throughput above 250 MB/s for decoding and 130 MB/s for decoding plus formatting in its disas-bench results.

resources.name: apk-mitm
resources.description: Command-line tool that prepares an Android APK you own or are authorized to test for HTTPS traffic inspection. It decodes the package with Apktool, adjusts the network security configuration to trust user-added certificates, disables certificate pinning, then re-encodes and signs the patched APK, so a proxy can read the app's traffic without a rooted device. App bundles supplied as .xapk or .apks are also supported.
requirements: Installed from npm as a global CLI and requires Node.js 14+ and Java 8+ per the README; patching app bundles on Linux also needs zip and unzip available.

Operates on an APK or app bundle the analyst supplies and is intended only for apps you own or are authorized to test; rooting the device is not required because the changes are applied statically before install.

The README notes the static Apktool-based approach can fail on large or complex apps and cannot address certificate pinning enforced inside native binaries such as Flutter. MIT licensed; the repository ships the tool only, no application packages.

As checked on 2026-10-20, the latest release, v1.3.0 (2024-04-21, also the latest npm version), is the reviewed commit and still the main head; GitHub’s last recorded push was 2024-07-24, the repository is not archived and the README does not mark it as maintained, superseded or archived.

resources.name: friTap
resources.description: Frida-based tool that hooks TLS libraries such as OpenSSL, BoringSSL, NSS and GnuTLS inside a running process and writes NSS key logs and decrypted payloads as PCAP, so analysts can inspect an application's encrypted traffic in Wireshark. For stripped or statically linked libraries it accepts byte patterns or offsets and can scan for renamed libraries, or it can recover TLS secrets by scanning heap memory instead of hooking. A terminal UI, a Python API and a Wireshark extcap integration wrap the same capture.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.5.2, uploaded to PyPI on 2026-09-29 and published on GitHub on 2026-10-04; the reviewed main commit is identical to that tag. The README describes Linux, Windows and Android as supported and macOS and iOS as partial and still under development, and says the Windows implementations were verified only on Windows 10.

Installed with pip as fritap on Python 3.10+. friTap 2.x requires frida 17.x and frida-tools 14.x; devices with an older frida-server need a legacy friTap line installed through the documented constraints files. Mobile apps need a frida-server running on the device, and the Android walkthrough uses a rooted phone or emulator with adb in PATH; the desktop example attaches with sudo. libpcap or Npcap is needed only for full packet capture, and live Wireshark piping works only on Linux and macOS.

Analysts name the process or app package to attach to or spawn. Coverage differs by library and platform: the README's support table marks many combinations as read/write hooks only, keys only or not yet implemented, so plaintext captures can be incomplete. Byte patterns for statically linked BoringSSL can come from the authors' separate BoringSecretHunter tool, which analyzes the user's own copy of the library.

GPL-3.0; setup.py declares GPL-3.0-only while its inline comment says GPLv3 or later. The README presents the tool for malware analysis and application privacy research and asks users to cite the authors' 2024 Forensic Science International: Digital Investigation paper on TLS key material extraction.

resources.name: hrtng
resources.description: IDA plugin published by Kaspersky that extends the Hex-Rays decompiler with tools its author collected for reverse-engineering work, including malware analysis. It decrypts strings, data and constants with built-in ciphers or in bulk through IDA's Appcall debugger feature, resolves API-name hashes, unflattens control flow and forces decompilation of obfuscated code, and recognizes library code through microcode signatures, inlined-function detection and PAT files built from an IDA database. Pseudocode helpers cover automatic renaming, retyping and enum substitution, structure creation, virtual and indirect call navigation, and patching.
requirements: Requires IDA with the Hex-Rays decompiler. The README supports only the latest IDA version; the plugin can still be compiled against IDA SDK 7.3 or later, but new features are usually not well tested on older versions. Latest release at review: v3.9.114, published 2026-09-02, with prebuilt archives for IDA 9.2, 9.3 and 9.4 plus a separate 7z archive; the reviewed master commit is one changelog fix ahead and declares 3.9.115 in ida-plugin.json.

The CI workflow builds Linux x64, macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Windows x64 binaries, and Linux ARM for IDA 9.3 and 9.4. Source builds use CMake with the Crypto++ CMake submodule and an IDA SDK whose path and version are set in src/CMakeLists.txt; the README gives manual SDK fixes for 8.5 and 9.1. The apilist.txt and literal.txt files from bin/plugins must sit beside the plugin for API-hash scanning and enum substitution.

Samples and IDA databases come from the analyst. The Appcall engine for mass decryption runs the analyzed program's own decryption routine under the selected IDA debugger, and its documentation reports testing only with the imul emulator and IDA's Remote Windows debugger. Obfuscated-code decompilation and inline detection are described as experimental.

GPL-3.0. NOTICE.txt lists bundled third-party code and its licenses, including Crypto++ 8.9.0 under the Boost Software License 1.0, used for ciphers such as RC4, AES and ChaCha20, and MIT-licensed GraphSlick and microavx code.

resources.name: Frida Mobile Interception Scripts
resources.description: A set of Frida scripts from HTTP Toolkit for inspecting a mobile app's HTTPS traffic while analysing apps you own or are authorized to test. Injected into a running Android or iOS app, they redirect its connections to an interception proxy, add a user-supplied CA certificate to the trust stores, and disable certificate pinning and transparency checks so the proxy can read the traffic. Individual scripts can also be used on their own to hook specific behaviour.
requirements: Delivered as Frida scripts injected into a target app with the Frida CLI; the README's Android workflow requires a rooted device or emulator running frida-server as root, and the iOS workflow requires a jailbroken device with Frida installed.

The analyst supplies their own interception proxy and CA certificate and edits config.js before use; the scripts are intended only for mobile apps you own or are authorized to test, not for circumventing protections on third-party software.
AGPL-3.0 licensed and funded by NLnet as part of the HTTP Toolkit project; the repository ships scripts only and no application packages.

resources.name: BinCAT
resources.description: Static binary code analysis toolkit designed for reverse engineers. Starting from a chosen address and initial state, it computes register and memory values, taint and reconstructed types, with forward and backward analysis and heap use-after-free and double-free detection; bits it cannot determine are shown as unknown. It is driven from an IDA plugin, where analysts can override values or taint, skip functions or replace instructions with NOPs before re-running, or from Python and an .ini configuration for automation.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.5, published 2025-02-25; its tag is the reviewed master commit, and the repository has had no commits since. The Linux and Windows release archives bundle the analyzer and the IDA plugin, which is installed by running install_plugin.py from IDA. The plugin requires IDA 7.4 or later with Python 3; the changelog adds IDA 8.3 support in v1.3 and IDA 9.0 support in v1.4.

The README lists x86-32, x86-64, ARMv7, ARMv8 and PowerPC as analysis targets; the changelog also records initial RISC-V and initial, incomplete ARMv7 Thumb support. The analyzer runs locally on Linux or Windows (macOS only “maybe”, per the README) or as a Flask web service in the airbusseclab/bincat Docker image that the plugin reaches through its remote URL option. Source builds need OCaml with dune, menhir, ocamlgraph, ppxlib and zarith plus Python 3; Windows builds use Cygwin and an opam mingw64 OCaml switch.

Each analysis is described by a versioned .ini file covering the program, its sections and imports, the initial register and memory state and overrides; the IDA plugin generates it from the open database, ELF core dumps can supply the initial state, and the format documentation is partial, with the parser source as its reference. Binaries to analyze come from the user; the tutorial uses the project’s own keygen-me sample.

AGPL-3.0 per the README and doc/COPYING; GitHub detects no license because there is no root license file. The OCaml code includes LGPLv2 OCaml runtime code, the plugin includes Apache-2.0 code from python-pyqt5-hexview, and a modified copy of c2newspeak is bundled. Results depend on the configured initial state, skipped functions and overrides.

resources.name: pbtk
resources.description: Recover Protobuf message definitions from compiled programs as readable .proto files. Extractors cover the Java runtimes in JAR, DEX and APK files (including ProGuard-obfuscated code), binaries that embed Protobuf reflection metadata, and web apps using the Protobuf-URL format. A GUI then binds a recovered message type to an HTTP endpoint, decodes hex-encoded captured samples into an editable field tree and resends edited messages, so analysts can relate each field to the response.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.1.3, published 2026-08-21 on GitHub and PyPI; the reviewed master commit is four commits ahead of it, adding a version display, a dependency bump and new brand colors, and carries a 1.1.3.1 tag with no GitHub release or PyPI upload. The README's 2026 notes say Java extraction now works mostly with older APKs and the Chrome-based Protobuf-URL web extractor needs an update; finishing the automatic fuzzing part is listed as forthcoming.

Requires Python 3.10+, PySide6 and the Python protobuf runtime. The README documents a snap for Ubuntu, the pbtk-git AUR package, and uv or pipx installs, and says Windows is supported. Java extraction needs a Java runtime (the Debian instructions install OpenJDK 8), and web extraction drives a Chrome or Chromium instance through websocket-client.

Analysts supply the APK, JAR, DEX or native library to analyze and, optionally, hex-encoded request samples they captured themselves with a proxy such as mitmproxy or Wireshark. Replay sends the edited messages to the live endpoint the analyst configures. Extracted .protos and endpoint definitions are stored in a .pbtk folder in the home directory (a pbtk folder under APPDATA on Windows).

GPL-3.0-or-later per pyproject.toml. The package bundles third-party executables: protoc builds, dex2jar 2.4 jars with their Apache-2.0 notice, and JAD decompiler binaries for which the repository includes no license text. Definitions recovered from minified code keep obfuscated names until the analyst renames them.

resources.name: reFlutter
resources.description: Flutter reverse-engineering framework for apps the analyst is authorized to inspect. It repacks an app with a prebuilt patched Dart engine, or instruments the app's own engine at runtime, to emit a JSONL dump of every function's name, class, library and code offset into the Dart instructions image for Frida or IDA/Ghidra work. It can also route the app's HTTPS traffic through an inspection proxy with Flutter certificate pinning disabled.
requirements: Installed from PyPI as reflutter (setup.py marks version 0.9.8 and requires Python 3.10+) and runs on Linux, Windows or macOS; the README notes a repacked APK must be re-signed and zip-aligned with an external signer before install.

The README lists support for Android arm64, arm32 and x64 and iOS arm64 across release and profile builds on the stable and beta channels, with engine coverage keyed by snapshot hash in enginehash.csv; pre-monorepo engines (<= 3.27) are built from the archived flutter/engine repository. Frida hooking and dump collection need a matching frida-server on the target device or emulator.
Intended for Flutter applications the analyst owns or is authorized to inspect. GPL-3.0 licensed; the project ships tooling and prebuilt engine assets but no application packages.

resources.name: ddc
resources.description: Rust decompiler that turns Android DEX bytecode, versions 035 to 041, from APKs, multi-dex apps and XAPK/APKS/APKM containers into Java, folding lambdas and string concatenation back into Java syntax and giving locals jadx-style names.
