By default every file also goes through a source-level cleanup pass, described as semantics-preserving, that inlines copy chains, recovers ternaries and for-each loops and drops dead stores; --fast skips it. Alongside full decompilation, 15 query subcommands return app and manifest information, resources, strings, cross-references, class hierarchies, disassembly or single classes and methods on demand, and the same queries are served over REST and MCP.
requirements: Release at review: v0.1.30, published 2026-10-18, which is the reviewed main commit. The repository was created in September 2026 and releases come quickly (v0.1.28 to v0.1.30 within eight days). Releases ship raw binaries for Linux, Windows and macOS on x86_64 and ARM64, the non-macOS builds UPX-compressed, and Homebrew, Scoop and cargo-binstall install them; source builds use stable Rust and the author's jdc-core, cure and xyz-rust crates.

Input is an APK, app container or DEX file from the user's own app; full decompilation writes an <input>-out directory next to the input by default. ddc serve and ddc http default to the listen address :8080, with no host given, and bearer-token authentication is optional; ddc mcp stdio runs as an agent subprocess.

The README reports that all 909,689 files emitted for seven benchmark APKs, and docs/validation.md that 4.08 million files from 39 apps, pass javac's parse phase; this is a syntax check only. Known limitations include erased generic types, separate d8-desugared lambda classes, timeouts on some very large R8 methods whose output can vary between runs, and desugared pattern switches; a full-classpath javac run still finds about 7,500 ddc-attributable errors across 0.91 million files, roughly twice jadx's count on the same set.
CI builds and runs cargo test on Linux, macOS and Windows. The benchmark APKs are not in the repository; its fixtures are small DEX files and one binary AndroidManifest. MIT license.

resources.name: ME Analyzer
resources.description: Parse Intel Management Engine (CS)ME, TXE and SPS firmware, Graphics System Controller firmware and their independent PMC, PCHC, PHY and option-ROM images to report family, version, release, SKU, platform, size and health status. Research options print flash partition, BPDT/IFWI and CSE layout tables, validate RSA signatures and checksums, and unpack the supported CSE and GSC code and file systems. A bundled database identifies known images and reports those not yet listed in the community firmware repositories.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.312.0 with database r378 (tag v1.312.0-r378), published 2026-09-06 at the reviewed commit, with no attached builds. The README describes the tool as the MEA.py script plus its bundled MEA.dat, Huffman.dat and FileTable.dat databases, and says MEA.dat is required to run.
Requires Python 3.7+, which the script checks at startup, and the third-party colorama, crccheck and pltable modules. The README lists Windows, Linux and macOS hosts; the script also accepts BSD.

Input is an Intel Engine, Graphics or Independent firmware image the user already has, given as files or scanned from a directory with -mass. The README lists ME 2-15, TXE 0-4, SPS 1-5, GSC 100 (DG1) and selected PMC, PCHC, PHY and OROM generations, and states that any family or version not listed is unsupported, with no plans to add others.

By default the script contacts GitHub to compare its version and database with the latest ones (-duc disables this) and copies any input that triggers a note, warning or error into a __CHECK__ folder in the output directory (-dcm disables this).
BSD-2-Clause-Patent. The README describes parsing, validation and unpacking, not rebuilding or modifying images; reported details depend on the bundled database.

resources.name: DeepExtract (DeepExtractIDA)
resources.description: IDA Pro 9.x plugin and PowerShell batch extractor that turn Windows PE files into material AI coding agents can read: a per-binary SQLite database of PE metadata, signatures, disassembly, Hex-Rays pseudocode, cross-references, strings, stack frames, loops and dangerous API calls, plus optional grouped C++ and assembly files with per-function caller, callee and string headers and JSON indexes. It runs headless over directories, file lists or the modules of a running process, or interactively on the open IDA database, keeping the analyst’s renames and comments. The agent commands that work on this output come from the separate DeepExtractRuntime project.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is the v0.9.14 release of 2026-09-12; ida-plugin.json lists IDA 9.0 to 9.3 on Windows x86-64, and the plugin installs with Hex-Rays’ hcli or runs from a clone. The README requires Windows 10 or 11 and IDA Pro 9.x, with the Pro edition for headless mode. The Hex-Rays decompiler is needed only for pseudocode and C++ output, while assembly output works from disassembly alone. pefile is vendored; the batch script also checks for Python on PATH and needs symchk.exe from the Windows SDK Debugging Tools for its default PDB download from Microsoft’s public symbol server.

Users supply the PE files, from single binaries to whole directories such as System32 or the modules loaded by a running process. The README warns that large batches can run for days and produce tens to hundreds of gigabytes. Outputs contain disassembly and decompiled code of the analysed binaries, whose own licences still apply.

The extractor calls no model. With -EnableAI, the batch extractor writes a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent, without asking the user, to clone the DeepExtractRuntime repository’s default branch into .claude and install Cursor rules and hooks; that runtime and its agents are not part of this repository.

Vtable and indirect-call resolution are labelled experimental, with stated limits such as a single vtable at object offset 0 and a short intra-procedural instruction window. Tests load IDA-independent modules such as the schema, configuration and code formatters outside IDA, and the release workflow only packages the plugin.

MIT, with the vendored pefile under its own MIT licence; IDA Pro, the Hex-Rays decompiler and the Windows SDK tools are licensed separately. The README presents the output for AI-assisted vulnerability research, reverse engineering, threat hunting and code review.

resources.name: Simplify
resources.description: Generic Android deobfuscator built on smalivm, a sandboxed Dalvik virtual machine that executes each method and records every possible register and class value along all execution paths, taking both branches when a value such as file or network input is unknown. Simplify then repeatedly applies constant propagation, dead-code removal, unreflection and peephole optimizations to the APK or DEX, which can decrypt strings and remove reflection while keeping behaviour the same; it does not rename classes or methods. smalivm can also be used as a library, and the last release adds sdbg, a step-through Smali debugger built on it.
requirements: Development is inactive: the latest release, v1.3.0 of 2020-03-30, ships simplify, smalivm and sdbg jars, and the reviewed master commit dates from 2021-05-23. The project pins smali/dexlib2 2.4.0 and, by default, builds its Android framework reference from android-25 classes, so check results on apps that use newer DEX or API features.

Run it as java -jar simplify.jar on a user-supplied APK or DEX. Building needs JDK 8, a recursive clone for the AndroidFrameworkSmali submodule of reference framework classes, and the Gradle fatjar task. Execution limits on visits, call depth and time apply per method; the README advises narrowing large apps with include and exclude patterns, and output DEX defaults to API level 15.

--remove-weak, on by default, removes code even when it has weak side effects, and --ignore-errors may lead to unexpected behaviour, so compare output with the original code. The repository includes a project-provided obfuscated example app for testing; tests ran through a Travis CI configuration using Oracle JDK 8, the repository has no GitHub Actions workflow.
Dual-licensed: GPL-3.0 for open-source use, or a commercial license that permits binary distribution without source redistribution. Android framework classes and dependencies keep their own terms.

resources.name: GDA (GJoy Dex Analyzer)
resources.description: Windows-native Dalvik decompiler and Android analysis workbench written in C++ that opens APK, DEX, ODEX, OAT, JAR, AAR and class files without installation. Besides Java and Smali views with cross-references, renaming and comments, it identifies packers, deobfuscates and decrypts strings, tracks data flow and taint, solves paths, runs rule-based malicious-behaviour, vulnerability and privacy-leak scans, and can dump device memory or hook methods with Frida. Shell and server CLI modes, Python and Java scripting and a sample malware-triage agent skill expose the same analysis to scripts and agents.
requirements: Releases are Windows-only zip archives; the latest, GDA 4.12 of 2026-04-07, adds shell and server CLI modes among fixes. The repository holds no decompiler source: the README says GDA is not an open-source project, at least in the short term, and the repository publishes the free binaries with open scripts, plugin examples, rule samples and colour themes.

The executable runs without setup. Dex-family inputs need no Java, while JAR, AAR and class files need a working Java runtime for the bundled dx tool. The README says GDA is protected with VMProtect and unpacks embedded adb, a gdump memory-dump helper and rule files into the user’s application-data folder, which some antivirus products flag; the author states it has no malicious behaviour.

The skills folder holds a gda-analyze skill in Claude Code’s format that drives a bundled GDA.exe through a Python wrapper to trace code, extract indicators and draft malware reports, plus a server-mode client and test script. Its output, like the built-in rule-based scans, needs manual confirmation.

LICENSE is Apache-2.0, and NOTICE says most of GDA is released under it, with adb and dex libraries taken from the Android SDK and AOSP; this conflicts with the README’s closed-source statement, so the binaries’ terms are unclear. Users supply the apps they analyze.

resources.name: GEF (GDB Enhanced Features)
resources.description: Single-file Python extension, gef.py, that adds dynamic-analysis commands to GDB. Each stop shows a context view of registers, stack, code, threads and call trace, and commands cover memory maps, pointer dereferencing, searching process memory for patterns, ELF and security-property information, process status and glibc heap inspection. An architecture abstraction layer covers x86-32/64, ARMv5–v7, AArch64, SPARC, MIPS and PowerPC, and gef-remote enriches remote sessions through gdbserver or the GDB stubs of qemu-user and qemu-system.
requirements: Needs GDB 10.0+ built with Python 3.10+, the baseline since GEF 2025.01 in the compatibility table, plus file, readelf, nm, ps and python3 on the host; Python 2 users are pointed to the separate gef-legacy. The README installs it by downloading gef.py, through an install script or manually, and sourcing it from the user's .gdbinit file.

Release at review: 2026.01, published 2026-02-02 without binary assets; the reviewed main commit is 12 commits ahead, adding glibc 2.42/2.43 heap support and removing unmaintained commands. More commands live in the separate GEF-Extras repository.

GEF relies on the GDB API and Linux-specific sources such as /proc/<pid>, so some features may not work on custom or hardened systems, and heap commands support only the glibc allocator. qemu mode needs a local copy of the debugged binary because QEMU's GDB stub cannot transfer files. The README aims it at exploit developers and reverse engineers.
MIT license. Tests run with pytest under the Python version GDB was built against.

resources.name: Z0FCourse Reverse Engineering
resources.description: A free English course by Z0F on reverse engineering 64-bit Windows programs, which its README pitches as taking learners from beginner to intermediate. Markdown lessons move from number systems, x64 registers, memory layout and calling conventions to x64dbg and Ghidra, then reverse small samples and an author-written DLL, recovering a Player class and calling the DLL's exports from a program of one's own. The unfinished later chapters introduce Windows internals and reverse ntdll's generic-table functions.
requirements: Reviewed at commit ee4b070 (2026-07-25). Most lessons were written in 2019–2020, and the table of contents marks Chapter 7 (Windows) and Chapter 8 (Generic Table) as work in progress; the .NET and other-architecture material promised by the setup and Before You Begin pages is not in the tree. Later commits are small fixes, formatting, refreshed PDF copies and new links. The README points to two TryHackMe rooms as an interactive version of chapters 1–6.

Chapter 1 lists a good understanding of C/C++, object-oriented programming and pointers as prerequisites and highly recommends prior x86/x64 assembly. The course needs a 64-bit Windows system, a virtual machine being optional until the malware material; setup names the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable, x64dbg (with the optional xAnalyzer plugin) and dnSpy or ILSpy as required, with Ghidra and Visual Studio highly recommended.

The target programs are the author's own and ship with their source in FilesNeeded: the Chapter 6 DLL with two host programs and debug symbols, plus a sample malware program and dropper for a chapter not yet written, which FilesNeeded marks as use-at-your-own-risk. Chapter 8 instead analyzes Windows's own ntdll.dll, which is not included. PDF copies of the chapters are also committed, and the README warns they may lag the Markdown lessons.
The repository's License.md is the AGPL-3.0 text; the FAQ adds that downloading is allowed for personal use only and defers redistribution and teaching use to the license.

resources.name: APKLab
resources.description: VS Code extension that turns the editor into an Android reverse-engineering workbench around Apktool, Jadx, smali-lsp and uber-apk-signer. It decodes an APK into resources and Smali, decompiles it to Java, gives Smali go-to-definition, references and diagnostics through a language server, and rebuilds, signs and installs the modified app. It can also generate Frida hooks for Smali methods, add a Frida gadget, prepare an app for HTTPS traffic inspection with apk-mitm and produce a Quark-Engine malware-analysis report.
requirements: The latest tag, v2.0.0, dated 2026-04-06 in the changelog, added smali-lsp, Frida hook generation and gadget injection and Apktool 3.0+ compatibility; the reviewed master commit of 2026-07-16 is five commits ahead of it. The extension is published on the VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX, and package.json requires VS Code 1.91+. The README lists Linux, macOS and WSL2, and CI also builds and tests it on Windows.

JDK 17+ is required. On first use the extension downloads the tools named in the project’s update configuration into a .apklab folder in the user’s home directory, at review Apktool 3.0.2, smali-lsp 1.5.0, uber-apk-signer 1.3.0 and Jadx 1.5.6, unless the user sets their paths. adb is optional for installing to a device, and Quark-Engine 21.01.6+ is optional for malware reports. Users supply the APKs.

CI lints and packages the extension and runs its test suite on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows against a sample open-source APK from the separate testdata repository. Jadx output can be incomplete, and rebuilt APKs are re-signed with uber-apk-signer, using the configured keystore when one is set.

AGPL-3.0; Apktool, Jadx, smali-lsp, uber-apk-signer, apk-mitm, Frida and Quark-Engine keep their own licenses. HTTPS-inspection patching and gadget injection modify the app under analysis, and the tool grants no rights to analyze, patch or redistribute third-party apps.

resources.name: Triton
resources.description: C++ library with Python bindings for dynamic binary analysis of x86, x86-64, ARM32, AArch64 and RISC-V 32/64 code. Callers process instructions one at a time, optionally with concrete register and memory values; Triton builds symbolic expressions from each instruction's semantics, tracks taint and solves path constraints through Z3 or Bitwuzla. It also synthesizes and simplifies expressions and lifts them to LLVM IR or Z3 and back, for building analysis tools, automating reverse engineering, software verification or emulating code.
requirements: The README calls Triton a part-time project that may not be fully reliable. The newest GitHub release is v0.9 from 2022-02-09, with Windows builds only; PyPI's triton-library 1.0.0rc4, first uploaded 2024-05-22 with wheels added through 2026-02-23, provides CPython 3.8–3.14 wheels for x86_64 Linux (manylinux 2.31/2.34), macOS 12 and Windows. The reviewed master commit declares version 1.0, and the dev-v1.0 branch was 22 commits ahead.

Source builds use CMake 3.20+ and need Capstone 5+. Z3 4.6+ is the default solver; Bitwuzla 0.4+, LLVM 12+ for lifting, Boost 1.68+ and libpython 3.6+ for the Python bindings are optional, and LLVM and Bitwuzla are off by default. The README also covers Windows builds and a vcpkg port maintained outside the project.

The README example processes raw instruction bytes against caller-set registers; some bundled examples load executables with LIEF and hook libc functions themselves, and the examples include CTF write-ups with their challenge binaries. CTest runs Python unit tests and per-architecture scripts that compare Triton's semantics with the Unicorn emulator; the x86 script notes that Unicorn 2.1.1 lacks some tested instructions.
Apache-2.0; Capstone, Z3, Bitwuzla, LLVM and Boost keep their own licenses. Symbolic results describe only the executed instructions and modeled state.

resources.name: PyLingual
resources.description: Research decompiler for CPython bytecode from Python 3.6 onward that pairs per-version transformer models with control-flow reconstruction. A segmentation model splits bytecode into statements, a statement model translates each into source, and templates rebuild loops, conditionals, exception handlers, with blocks and match statements. The result is recompiled with the target Python version and its control flow compared with the original bytecode, and failing segments are retried with alternative segmentations; the design is described in the IEEE S&P 2025 paper “PyLingual: Toward Perfect Decompilation of Evolving High-Level Languages”.
requirements: First release at review: v0.0.1, published 2026-09-21, whose notes report decompilation rates of about 82–87% for Python 3.6–3.12 and about 71% for 3.13–3.15 on the separate pylingual_eval_dataset; these are project-reported figures. The reviewed main commit is 67 commits later and declares version 0.1.0. The README warns that this readability-focused codebase may initially regress in control-flow accuracy compared with the hosted service.

Installed from a clone with uv tool install; pyproject.toml requires Python 3.12+ and pulls in PyTorch, Transformers, Hugging Face Hub and xdis. Per-version segmentation and statement models are downloaded from the syssec-utd Hugging Face organization at their unpinned main revision and run on CUDA when available, otherwise on CPU. Model cards differ in declared licenses: the 3.12 statement model states Apache-2.0, while its segmenter states none.

Checking a reconstruction compiles it in the target version: uv-managed interpreters cover 3.8–3.15, while 3.6 and 3.7 need pyenv or pyenv-win, which --init-pyenv can install. An optional Redis instance caches model predictions, keyed by version and normalized bytecode but not by model revision. The pylingual.io web service is a hosted alternative, so confidential .pyc files should stay with the local CLI.
GPL-3.0-only. Passing the control-flow check does not prove that the recovered source is identical to the original, and recovered code keeps the original owner’s rights.

resources.name: Star Fox 64: a complete matching Nintendo 64 decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs C source for the US 1.1 (Rev A) Nintendo 64 release of Star Fox 64 that, compiled with the IDO compiler through a static recompilation, rebuilds a ROM with the published MD5; the README badge counts all 2,951 functions as matching. Code and assets are split from the user’s own ROM at build time, and the repository contains no assets or assembly. The separately curated Starship PC port compiles this C code, while Starfox 64: Recompiled takes headers and some functions from it for its patches.
requirements: The reviewed master pin of 2026-09-28 is a clean-up commit after the July 2026 commits announcing 100% completion. README calls this a complete matching decompilation of the US 1.1 (Rev A) ROM, MD5 741a94eee093c4c8684e66b89f8685e8, and says it is not a PC port. Splat configurations and linker scripts also exist for US 1.0, Japanese and European releases, with checksum files for uncompressed Japanese and European 1.0 ROMs, but README does not document building them.

Building needs the user’s own US 1.1 Rev A ROM, placed in the project root as baserom.us.rev1.z64. README says the repository includes no assets or assembly code; make init decompresses the ROM, splits code, data and assets with splat, then builds. config.yml and assets/yaml also hold the Torch asset definitions that write starship.otr for the Starship port.

README documents Linux, natively or under WSL or a VM, with make, Git, build-essential, MIPS binutils, Python 3 with pip, libpng and the listed clang tools, or macOS with Homebrew’s coreutils, make, pkg-config and mips64-elf binutils; native Windows builds are unsupported. make toolchain downloads decompals’ ido-static-recomp build of the IDO compiler and builds the mio0 tool and Torch, while submodules add splat, asm-processor, asm-differ, m2c and Torch. A GCC build is available but defines NON_MATCHING.

With COMPARE=1 by default, the build checks the output against starfox64.us.rev1.md5, and README reads a mismatch as a bad base ROM or non-matching code. CI runs make init on the US ROM, fetched from a private repository through secrets, and a separate workflow checks formatting.
The repository carries CC0-1.0, which does not cover Nintendo’s game, the ROM or extracted assets; the IDO compiler and the submodules keep their own terms.

resources.name: Galaxy Buds Client: an unofficial manager built on Samsung’s earbud protocol
resources.description: Reimplements control of Samsung Galaxy Buds over their proprietary RFCOMM serial protocol in a cross-platform desktop and Android manager. The author reports recovering the message format by analyzing the earbuds’ binary stream and disassembling Samsung’s official Android apps, and publishes partial packet notes for the 2019 Buds and the Buds+. Beyond the official app’s settings, it exposes battery statistics, diagnostics, factory self-tests, hidden debug information and firmware flashing for supported models.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-01 master head, 72 commits after release 5.2.1 (2026-06-07). Device specifications in source cover Galaxy Buds models from the original 2019 Buds through the Buds4 series. The protocol notes say they are incomplete and point to the source for details; this is an independent client, not recovered Samsung source, and features vary by model.

Requires the user’s own Galaxy Buds paired over Bluetooth; earbud firmware and Samsung’s official apps are not part of the repository. Firmware flashing and downgrades download builds from the author’s firmware service, behind an in-app disclaimer and a model-compatibility check meant to avoid bricking. Release notes say the app can share protocol data through an on-demand crowdsourcing feature to support models the author does not own, and sends crash dumps to Sentry; both can be disabled in settings.

Builds from one solution with the .NET 10 SDK (global.json pins 10.0.300) and Avalonia, targeting Windows 10 build 19041+, macOS 12+, Linux and Android 7.0+ (API 24); Linux Bluetooth uses a bundled BlueZ D-Bus library. Release 5.2.1 attaches unsigned Windows and macOS installers and Linux x64/ARM portable binaries; the README also lists Flatpak, AUR and winget packages, and the Android version is sold on Google Play.

An NUnit test project decodes captured extended-status packets from seven models and checks message and spatial-audio parsing; the reviewed CI workflows build and publish binaries without running those tests. Protocol and feature behavior on real earbuds remains author-reported.
GPLv3 (LICENSE); the README states the project is not affiliated with or supervised by Samsung. Samsung firmware, apps and trademarks keep their own rights.

resources.name: OWASP Mobile Application Security Testing Guide (MASTG)
resources.description: OWASP’s open manual for Android and iOS app security testing and reverse engineering, published at mas.owasp.org. Chapters on platform internals, test setup and app tampering and reverse engineering sit beside modular, individually referenced tests, techniques, tool pages, knowledge articles, best practices and runnable demos, all mapped to MASVS controls and MASWE weaknesses. OWASP’s UnCrackable crackme apps serve as practice targets and examples.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-09-30 master commit. The latest release, v2.0.0 of 2026-06-30, is described as completing the refactor into modular, machine-readable components and as the first stable release of that framework, while CITATION.cff still names version 1.5.0 of 2022. The pin holds 92 v1 tests and 200 atomic tests, 167 techniques, 135 tool pages, 157 demos, 141 knowledge articles and 74 best practices.

Reading needs only a browser; OWASP’s separate mas-website workflow builds the site. Following the techniques needs a Windows, Linux or macOS host with the tools each page names, such as the Android SDK platform tools, plus test devices or emulators. The guide recommends a rooted Android test device or jailbroken iOS device for dynamic analysis, warns against using a personal device, and describes fallbacks for testers without one.

The UnCrackable apps for Android and iOS are OWASP’s own reverse-engineering challenges, used as examples throughout the guide. Sample-app pages describe third-party apps, and tool pages describe external software; both keep their own terms. Demo results are written up from the guide’s sample code, not from tests of production apps.
The repository is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, so adapted text needs attribution and the same license.

resources.name: Wino Mail: recreating Windows Mail and Calendar
resources.description: Native Windows client that aims to preserve the familiar Windows Mail and Calendar experience while rebuilding its functionality. The upstream README documents a WinUI 3 interface, mail and calendar providers, contacts, tasks and offline workflows.
requirements: Windows application from bkaankose/Wino-Mail; the README links Microsoft Store and App Installer distribution.
The repository publishes GNU GPL v3 license text for its code; this does not license the original Microsoft application or branding.
Feature coverage and preservation of the original experience are upstream goals and claims.

resources.name: Metroid Prime: the PrimeDecomp matching GameCube decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs C++ source for Metroid Prime’s GameCube executable and its NES-emulator module so that CodeWarrior builds match the originals, across the USA, Korean, PAL and Japanese releases, with early configurations for demo discs and three Wii releases. Matched units are compiled from source and linked with objects split from the user’s disc, then checked against per-version SHA-1 hashes; the repository contains no game assets or assembly. The separately curated Metaforce and Metroid Prime Port build their native ports on this code.
requirements: The reviewed main pin of 2026-10-19 updates objdiff to v3.8.2. README describes a work-in-progress decompilation supporting GM8E01_00 (USA v1.088), GM8E01_01 (USA v1.093), GM8E01_48 (Korea v1.097), GM8P01_00 (PAL v1.110), GM8J01_00 (Japan v1.111) and GM8E01_02 (USA v1.111); configure.py and CI also cover the Multi-Game Demo Disc, a Japanese demo and the Wii New Play Control and Trilogy releases. Output is the original main.dol and, for the six retail GameCube versions, the NES emulator REL, not a port; docs/metaforce.md explains how to convert code from Metaforce into matching C++98.

Building needs the user’s own disc image of the chosen version in its orig/ folder, in ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ or TGC format, which can be deleted after the first build. The repository contains no game assets or assembly; decomp-toolkit splits the original executable and its embedded data locally. CONTRIBUTING lists Metaforce, a shared Ghidra server and a symbol map from an early demo disc as references for contributors.

Builds run natively on Windows with Python and ninja; macOS needs ninja and Wine Crossover, and Linux uses ninja with the automatically downloaded wibo wrapper on x86 or Wine elsewhere. configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.8.4, objdiff v3.8.2, binutils 2.42-1, sjiswrap v1.2.2, wibo 1.0.3 and a 20251118 compiler bundle from files.decomp.dev, compiling game code with CodeWarrior GC/1.3.2, or Wii/1.0a for the Wii releases. The MusyX audio library comes from a submodule.

The default build links source-built objects only for units marked Matching, uses original extracted objects for the rest and checks main.dol and the NES REL against the version’s build.sha1. decomp.dev’s reports for the pinned commit list 93.89% of GM8E01_00 code (16,478 of 16,685 functions) and 98.47% of its data matched, with 739 of 829 units complete; the other USA and Korean releases report 92.5–93.83% of code, PAL 84.37%, Japan 82.91%, and the demo and Wii builds early figures. CI builds all eleven configurations in a container that supplies the original files.
The repository carries CC0-1.0, which does not cover Nintendo’s game, the disc content or the downloaded compilers; the vendored zlib 1.1.3 keeps its own license and MusyX is a separate repository.

resources.name: Batla 3D server emulator (2015 client)
resources.description: C# server emulator for the 2015 Steam client of Batla 3D, covering HTTP account, shop and room services and Lidgren UDP gameplay. It includes a client-assembly patcher and protocol notes that distinguish recovered client evidence from emulator rules.
requirements: Requires an owned Unity 4.6.9f1 Steam client and .NET 10 SDK. The patcher uses dnlib; strict Steam validation requires Windows x86 Steam libraries.
MIT covers the repository code; game files must come from your own installation. Client patches also change packet fields and gameplay behavior beyond the server address.
Some combat, economy and objective values are emulator policies.
The README declares this stack frozen and unsupported. The referenced Batla.UdpSmoke harness is absent from the reviewed tree.

resources.name: The Decompilation Wiki
resources.description: Community wiki explaining how decompilers work, from disassembly, lifting and control-flow recovery to type recovery, control-flow structuring, quality evaluation and neural decompilation, citing the research behind each technique. It also keeps directories of decompilers, plugins, blogs and talks, pages on applied research such as symbol recovery, code similarity and vulnerability discovery, and a table of about 240 game reconstruction projects by original platform.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-15 main commit, from which a workflow builds the site with MkDocs Material and publishes it to GitHub Pages; reading needs only a browser. The README calls the wiki early in development: it has about 30 pages, several of them short, and the neural-decompilation page was last changed in September 2024.

Listings are compiled from contributions. The decompiler directory’s 23 rows note open-source, inactive, plugin and educational status, and the program-reconstruction table lists 241 games, 39 marked completed. Cited papers are gathered in a linked Google Sheets list kept outside the repository.

Changes arrive as GitHub pull requests: listing additions should give a description link, tags and a source link, while content changes to research areas need a citation or a reasoned argument. Local previews use Python and MkDocs.
The repository is BSD-2-Clause; linked papers, tools and projects keep their own terms. The wiki was started by Zion Leonahenahe Basque and is maintained with community contributions.

resources.name: RSDKv4 Decompilation: Retro Engine v4 and the Sonic 1 & 2 (2013) menus
resources.description: Decompiles Retro Engine (RSDK) v4, the engine behind Sonic the Hedgehog and Sonic the Hedgehog 2 (2013), together with the games’ natively coded menus, and builds it for Windows, Linux and Android. The engine runs the game scripts contained in the official releases’ data files, which users must supply. The project adds a script compiler, a mod loader and an experimental online mode for Sonic 2’s 2P VS; it is the predecessor of the same group’s RSDKv5 decompilation.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-09-06 main head, 13 commits after release 1.3.3 (2025-11-02). README calls it a complete decompilation of Retro Engine v4 and the menus from Sonic 1 and 2 (2013); the licence says most code is meant to be functionally the same as the specified RSDK version. RETRO_REVISION defaults to 3 (Origins), and RETRO_ORIGINAL_CODE removes the project’s changes but, per CMake, cannot build a playable game.

It will not run without assets from an official release of Sonic 1 or Sonic 2: README names Sonic Origins on Steam, the Epic Games Store and Switch, and the now-delisted iOS and Android releases. The FAQ notes that Origins data files are packed as RSDKv5 datapacks and lack the games’ music and sound effects, and that release builds and autobuilds disable the DLC and block Origins’ Amy; the repository ships no game data.

Clone recursively, because GitHub’s source ZIPs omit the stb, tinyxml2, asio and Flatpak submodules. CMake 3.10+ builds use Visual Studio with vcpkg (GLEW, SDL2, libogg, libvorbis) on Windows, the listed GLEW, SDL2 and Ogg/Vorbis packages on Linux, and a separate Android guide; Xcode, UWP and Flatpak projects are included, while Vita, Switch, 3DS and WebAssembly ports are unofficial forks. Sonic 2’s online 2P VS needs a Python 3.8+ server that README calls a very unstable proof of concept.

CI builds Windows x86 and x64, Android and Linux binaries with the Plus DLC disabled; it runs no tests, and the project publishes no comparison with the original engine binaries. The FAQ says bugs present in official releases will mostly not be fixed.

The custom RSDKv3/v4 Decompilation Source Code License v2 requires distributed prebuilt executables to default to DLC off, forbids commercial use and distributing game assets other than unique modded ones, requires crediting the original RSDK author Christian “Taxman” Whitehead and the decompilation authors Rubberduckycooly and st×tic, and binds forks to the same terms.

resources.name: Miasm
resources.description: Python reverse-engineering framework for analyzing, modifying and generating binary programs. It reads, modifies and generates 32- and 64-bit PE and ELF files, assembles and disassembles x86, ARM, AArch64, MIPS, PowerPC, SH4, MSP430 and MeP code, and lifts it into its own intermediate language for symbolic execution, SSA and data-flow analysis, dependency graphs and expression simplification aimed at deobfuscation. Its JIT emulator runs shellcode or parts of binaries through LLVM, GCC, Clang or pure-Python backends, with Python callbacks that stand in for library functions, sandboxes with selected Windows API and Linux emulation, and dynamic symbolic execution through Z3.
requirements: PyPI’s latest release and the newest tag are 0.1.5 from 2023-04-18; GitHub releases stop at v0.1.3 from 2019. The reviewed master commit still declares 0.1.5 but is 100 commits ahead of that tag, so current code is installed from a clone with pip or taken from the project’s Docker images. CI runs the regression suite on Ubuntu with Python 3.10 and 3.13.

pyproject.toml requires Python 3.10+ with future and pyparsing, pinned to 3.3.2. Native jitter extensions are built only when a C compiler is available; otherwise installation continues without the jitter features unless MIASM_REQUIRE_JIT=1 is set. Optional extras add pycparser C-type parsing, Z3 for solver-backed dependency graphs and dynamic symbolic execution, llvmlite 0.44.0 for the LLVM backend, graphviz export and pycryptodome for Windows crypto API emulation. The README marks the LLVM backend untested on Windows.

Binaries, shellcode and memory dumps come from the analyst. The bundled Windows API emulation targets 32-bit x86, and other library effects are modeled with Python callbacks. The IDA plugins use a subset of Miasm without the jitter.
GPL-2.0-only. Lifted IR, simplified expressions and emulation results are analysis aids.

resources.name: Fernflower
resources.description: JetBrains' analytical decompiler that turns Java class files back into Java source; IntelliJ IDEA bundles it to show code when debugging or browsing class files. The standalone console decompiler takes class files, JARs, ZIPs or directories, can load library files with -e only as analysis context, and writes Java sources to an output directory. Options cover generic signatures, lambdas, inner classes, record and switch patterns, per-method time limits and renaming of ambiguous or obfuscated identifiers, optionally through a user-supplied renamer class.
requirements: No GitHub releases: the README says releases are published in the IntelliJ repository, whose java-decompiler-engine metadata listed 262.10968.63 as the latest release at review. The README describes Fernflower as part of IntelliJ Community, which takes patches as pull requests, and bugs go to JetBrains' YouTrack (subsystem Java. Decompiler. Engine).

The reviewed master commit's Gradle build (wrapper 9.1.0) compiles for Java 21 and produces fernflower.jar, or a fernflower start script with ./gradlew installDist; the README documents the java -jar fernflower.jar command line.

Inputs are user-supplied class, JAR or ZIP files; libraries passed with -e inform analysis of class and method relationships but are not decompiled. The README says most options are aimed at professional reverse engineers. Output is reconstructed Java, not the original source.

Apache-2.0 with a JetBrains NOTICE. The README credits Stiver as the original author and JetBrains as maintainer since 2014, with some ForgeFlower patches merged; Vineflower is a separately maintained fork.

resources.name: HyperDbg
resources.description: Hypervisor-assisted Windows debugger that virtualizes the running system with Intel VT-x and Extended Page Tables to debug kernel and user mode, either locally as a tracing and introspection tool or from a host attached over a serial connection to a guest virtual machine. Its events include EPT-based hidden breakpoints and hooks, memory read, write and execute monitoring without the limits of hardware debug registers, monitoring of system calls, CPUID, MSRs, I/O ports, MMIO, exceptions and interrupts, and Intel PT and LBR branch tracing. A kernel-side script engine, PDB symbol support and an SDK automate analysis.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.24, published 2026-09-22 as a single compiled ZIP; the reviewed master commit is that release. The README and FAQ name Windows as the only supported OS. The v0.24 changelog reports that the kernel modules now compile on Linux, but Linux support is still under development.

Requires an Intel x64 processor with VT-x and EPT; AMD and ARM processors are not supported, and the FAQ says most features need a 4th-generation or later Intel processor. The driver is not digitally signed, so the documented setup enables VT-x in firmware and turns off driver signature enforcement and virtualization-based security on the debugged machine. The documentation recommends a guest VM under VMware Workstation, ESXi or KVM in Debugger Mode, because local VMI Mode cannot pause or step.

Building from source needs a recursive clone, Visual Studio 2026 and current Windows SDK and WDK releases; CI builds with Visual Studio 2022 and 2026. The user supplies the drivers, programs or systems to debug, and the README recommends OpenSecurityTraining2’s Reversing with HyperDbg (Dbg3301) course for getting started.
GPL-3.0 for HyperDbg and its submodules unless a file states otherwise; dependencies keep their own licenses. The README also describes transparency features aimed at debugger detection.

resources.name: JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler (FFDec)
resources.description: Java desktop decompiler and editor for Adobe Flash SWF files. It decompiles ActionScript 1/2 and AS3 side by side with the P-code they came from, edits scripts as source (experimental) or through the assembler view, and exports or replaces images, shapes, sounds, video, fonts and texts, with SWF-to-FLA conversion, SWF-to-XML round trips and SVG or HTML5 Canvas output. It also opens SWC and ABC files, Scaleform GFx and 64-bit Iggy files, has an ActionScript debugger and deobfuscation passes for obfuscated AS3, and offers its parser and decompiler as the ffdec_lib Java library and a command line.
requirements: Latest stable release at review: 26.3.0, published 2026-09-14, with a Windows MSI, a Debian package, a macOS app and pkg, a cross-platform ZIP and separate ffdec_lib and Javadoc archives; nightly prereleases are built from the dev branch. The reviewed master commit is two commits after the version26.3.0 tag, a Chinese README update and a dependency bump.

The application needs Java 8 or later on Windows, Linux or macOS; the installation guide asks for Oracle JDK 8+ on macOS. build.properties targets Java 8, and source builds use Apache Ant or the bundled NetBeans project, with Git recommended so the build can embed the revision. The Dockerfile runs the command-line interface on an Eclipse Temurin 21 JRE, and CI runs the Ant checkstyle, build and test targets on Windows.

SWF, SWC, GFx and Iggy inputs come from the user. Video display and export rely on the vlcj and JNA libraries, debugging needs a debug Flash Player, either the standalone player launched from FFDec or a remote player in listening mode, and AS3 editing through the Flex SDK is marked unstable.

The application is GPL-3.0-or-later and the ffdec_lib library LGPL-3.0, with bundled third-party libraries under their own licenses. Decompiled scripts and extracted assets keep the rights of the SWF’s owners. The README directs bug reports to the tracker on free-decompiler.com rather than GitHub issues.

resources.name: Mizuchi
resources.description: Plugin pipeline for matching decompilation that loops over functions in an existing decomp project: m2c drafts C, decomp-permuter mutates it, Claude rewrites it through a compile-and-diff tool, and objdiff accepts a result only when the compiled object matches the target assembly. A local Decomp Atlas web app indexes matched and unmatched functions with call graphs and code embeddings, helps pick the next function and builds prompts, while HTML reports summarise each run. An optional integrator places matched C into a git worktree, checks the build and can commit, push or open a PR.
requirements: The reviewed main commit of 2026-08-17 declares package version 0.1.0; the repository has no releases or tags and is installed from source with npm on Node.js 22+. m2c and decomp-permuter are optional git submodules with setup scripts. Code embeddings need Python 3.10+ and download torch, transformers and an embedding model of about 2–3 GB, using Apple-Silicon MPS or the CPU; --skip-embeddings avoids them.

The Claude phase runs through the Claude Agent SDK and needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or cached Claude Code credentials; responses are cached locally by prompt hash. The example configuration allows 25 retries per prompt, gives the model read-only codebase tools plus compile_and_view_assembly, and accepts code only at zero instruction differences.

Mizuchi works inside a decompilation project the user already has, configured with a map file, non-matching assembly folders, a compiler shell script and the project’s period compiler. It supplies no ROMs, game assets or decompiled game code; the original files come from that project and the user’s own copies. Listed target settings include GBA, DS, 3DS, N64, GameCube, Wii, PlayStation 1/2, PSP, Switch, Saturn, Dreamcast, Win32, Android x86 and IRIX.

CI on Ubuntu runs type checks, lint, formatting and the Vitest suite and builds the CLI, using bundled agbcc and KMC GCC compiler fixtures. The README links an author post on benchmarks, and the repository publishes no match results. The integrator can push branches and open PRs with gh, and its optional AI build fix lets Claude edit files and run shell commands in the worktree, so review its output before it reaches a shared project.
MIT-licensed. m2c, decomp-permuter, objdiff, the embedding model and the compilers keep their own terms, and decompiled code inherits the target project’s rights and contribution rules.

resources.name: Kuna
resources.description: Agent-first decompiler written in Rust that began as a port of Ghidra’s C++ decompiler and SLEIGH compiler, and has since diverged with option-gated features, some ported from angr. A single self-contained kuna binary decompiles one function or exports a whole binary to C, header and assembly files, and the same engine runs in the browser through WebAssembly or as the decompiler backend inside Ghidra. The project calls itself an experiment in having LLM agents refine the decompiler; most code is agent-written and steered by regression and benchmark results.
requirements: The README calls Kuna an experiment. A scheduled workflow publishes releases daily; the latest at review, v1.906 of 2026-10-18, has kuna archives for Linux x86_64 (glibc and musl) and arm64, macOS arm64 and x86_64 and Windows x86_64, a specs archive and a Ghidra 12.1.2 extension zip. The reviewed main commit is 40 commits ahead of it, and the README’s Ghidra install step still links the older v1.157 zip.

Release binaries embed the compiled SLEIGH specs. Source builds need only a Rust toolchain, with the workspace declaring Rust 1.90+; make specs compiles the vendored Ghidra processor specs before a release-style kuna build. Users supply the binaries to analyze; the README says the browser version decompiles on the user’s machine, so the file stays local.

The Ghidra extension is version-locked to the Ghidra release in its file name and bundles Linux, macOS and Windows backends; other 12.x releases are marked unverified, and the README says not all native Ghidra features are supported yet. Headless Ghidra never loads the plugin, so the README swaps the stock decompile binary or uses a PyGhidra toggle, and reports testing that swap with Ghidra 12.1.2 and REA 3.1.0.

CI runs the 675-assertion XML regression corpus vendored from Ghidra against a checked-in baseline, Kuna’s own stage testcases, the cargo workspace suite, a spec-documentation check, CLI tests and the browser page’s modules. docs/history.md reports that the Rust port matched all 675 assertions against the untouched C++ decompiler before the C++ tree was removed. The README’s top DecBench standing and speed figures are project-reported.

Apache-2.0. NOTICE says the engine, SLEIGH compiler, processor specs and regression corpus derive from Ghidra, also Apache-2.0, and that some structuring and region-recovery code is ported from angr under BSD-2-Clause. Output can differ from stock Ghidra by design and is a reading aid.

resources.name: Bytecode Viewer
resources.description: Desktop suite for inspecting compiled Java and Android programs: drop in a class, JAR, WAR, APK, DEX, XAPK or APKM file to browse its classes and resources, with up to three decompiler or disassembler views side by side. The README lists six bundled Java decompilers (Krakatau, CFR, Procyon, FernFlower, JADX and JD-GUI), Krakatau and Smali/baksmali disassemblers and assemblers plus javap, Dex2Jar and Enjarify for APK/DEX conversion, a built-in Java compiler for editing, and static search. Java and JavaScript plugins receive every loaded class as an ASM ClassNode for jobs such as string deobfuscation or malicious-code searches.
requirements: Release at review: v2.13.2, published 2026-01-01 and re-released on 2026-01-06 with Windows APK fixes, as a single runnable JAR started with java -jar. Its notes call it an in-development version whose CLI is being rewritten and is not functional, pointing CLI users to v2.12; the reviewed master commit is ten fix commits ahead of that tag and still declares 2.13.2.

pom.xml targets Java 8 and holds the bundled JADX at 1.4.7 because newer versions need Java 11+; source builds use mvn package. Some tools call external runtimes: the Krakatau decompiler needs a configured Python 2 command and a JRE rt.jar library, and Enjarify needs Python 3. The README suggests a larger -Xmx heap for OutOfMemoryError.

Inputs are user-supplied class, JAR, ZIP, WAR, APK, DEX, XAPK or APKM files. Decompiled Java is reconstructed from bytecode rather than recovered source, and the bundled decompilers can disagree; the side-by-side views are for comparing them.
GPL-3.0 per the LICENSE file; bundled decompilers and converters keep their own licenses. The repository's Zip Slip advisory (CVE-2022-21675) affects v2.10.x and is fixed from v2.11.0.

resources.name: Binary Ninja API
resources.description: Vector 35’s public C++, Python and Rust APIs for Binary Ninja, with their documentation, examples and the open-source plugins built on them. Binary Ninja itself is a closed-source commercial application, and this repository does not contain its analysis core. The open plugins cover the x86/x86_64, ARM64, ARMv7, PowerPC, MIPS, RISC-V and MSP430 architectures, ELF, PE/COFF, Mach-O and Apple shared-cache and kernel-cache loaders, DWARF, PDB and IDB import, and Objective-C, RTTI and SVD analysis, while the examples walk the low- and medium-level intermediate languages and extend the analysis pipeline through workflows.
requirements: The dev branch tracks Binary Ninja development builds. The newest release in this repository at review is stable/6.0.10601, published 2026-09-03, whose assets are Binary Ninja Free installers; the reviewed dev commit is 165 commits ahead of it, and dev-only material such as the guide to plugin-registered MCP tools is not in that release. The README says master tracks the stable build, but master was last updated in August 2024.

The API does not run on its own: plugins and scripts load the closed-source core from an installed copy of Binary Ninja. C++ plugins must be built from the API revision named in the installation’s api_REVISION.txt, and the install_api.py script shipped with the installation adds the Python module to another interpreter. The standalone examples and other headless scripts need a license with headless API access; the plugin guide says non-commercial licenses lack headless automation and names the Commercial and Ultimate editions for it.

CMakeLists.txt requires CMake 3.28+, a 64-bit C++20 toolchain and a Python 3.12+ interpreter. UI plugins need Qt 6.8.2, which the README recommends taking from the official installer or Vector 35’s Qt build rather than Homebrew, and -DHEADLESS=ON skips them. The Rust crate declares rust-version 1.98.1.

Most of the API and documentation is MIT-licensed and the Rust API is Apache-2.0; some components carry their own license files, and contributions go through Vector 35’s CLA. These licenses cover the API layer only and do not make Binary Ninja open source. The repository’s issue tracker also serves the wider product.

resources.name: OpenRW: an open re-implementation of the Grand Theft Auto III engine
resources.description: Re-implements Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto III (2001) as a cross-platform C++ engine that runs on the data of a legitimate PC copy. It has its own loaders for the game’s RenderWare models, textures and archives, a script machine for the original mission scripts, and an optional Qt data viewer. Playability is partial: the project’s mission tracker marks six early Portland story missions as completable.
requirements: The reviewed main snapshot dates from 2025-06-18; the repository has no tagged releases and the wiki says there are no official builds, so OpenRW is built from source. The playable-missions tracker (issue #52, last updated 2024-07-24) checks six story missions, all in Portland, and notes missing AI, broken cutscenes or unimplemented opcodes for many others; the FAQ says Vice City and San Andreas are not supported yet.

README requires a legitimate copy of the original PC game, and the FAQ says the original assets cannot be distributed; the repository contains no game data. rwgame reads the game directory set in its openrw.ini configuration file, and the optional rwviewer opens objects and models from the same data.

Builds use CMake 3.8+ and a C++17 compiler against Boost (program_options and system, plus unit_test_framework for tests), OpenAL, Bullet, GLM, FFmpeg, SDL2 and OpenGL, with FreeType for the tools and Qt 5 for the viewer; Conan is an optional package manager. The FAQ names C++17 and OpenGL 3.3 Core as hard requirements, and README reports ports to Linux, macOS, Windows and several BSDs.

GitHub Actions jobs on Arch Linux, Fedora and Ubuntu and an AppVeyor Visual Studio 2017 job run a CTest script that builds the code and its Boost.Test unit suite; tests that need game data sit behind the TEST_DATA option, which that script does not enable. No comparison with the original executable is published.

README applies GPL-3.0-or-later and lists FFmpeg (LGPL-2.1 or later), Bullet and SDL 2.0 (zlib) as third-party licences; the microprofile and imgui submodules are separate projects, and the game’s own assets keep their rights.

resources.name: ReXGlue SDK
resources.description: Experimental SDK for statically recompiling Xbox 360 executables into portable C++23 that runs natively on Windows, Linux and macOS. Its rexglue CLI scaffolds a per-game CMake project and, from a TOML config, analyzes a XEX binary (import resolution, PDATA, block discovery, gap filling, jump resolution and call-target validation) before translating each PowerPC instruction into C++; a runtime derived from Xenia's emulator core, with D3D12 or Vulkan graphics, hosts the generated code. Generated functions are weak aliases that native C++ overrides or mid-function hooks can replace, so a port can be refined one function at a time.
requirements: The README cautions that the project is in early development with breaking API changes, and the wiki calls it experimental and pre-1.0, not a turnkey way to play Xbox 360 games or an alternative to Xenia. Users must specify function boundaries, implement missing kernel imports and iterate on the codegen output; unresolved calls stop generation as validation errors unless --force is passed.

Release at review: v0.10.0, published 2026-08-21, with SDK archives for Windows amd64, Linux amd64/arm64 and macOS amd64/arm64; the default main branch holds that release, while nightly prereleases are built from the development branch, 24 commits ahead. Building needs a recursive clone, CMake 3.25+, Ninja and Clang 18+ or AppleClang 16+ on a 64-bit x86_64 or ARM64 host, and other compilers are rejected; the wiki's Windows setup uses Visual Studio 2022 with its Clang toolset and its Linux setup Clang 20+ with GTK3 headers.

Each project's TOML config points at the user's own Xbox 360 XEX; the SDK ships no game code. Documentation is the GitHub wiki, last edited 2026-06-04, whose status section still describes v0.3.x and calls the graphics, audio and input backends in flux.

LICENSE is a BSD-3-Clause text that credits Xenia-derived portions (GitHub reports NOASSERTION); submodules and the bundled PowerPC binutils executables keep their own licenses. The README disclaims affiliation with Microsoft and prohibits use for piracy.

resources.name: ReAgent
resources.description: An open-source Python agent, published on PyPI as auto-re-agent, that drafts C/C++ implementations of functions in a compiled program from Ghidra evidence and has a separately configurable checker model review each draft in a bounded fix loop. A candidate is accepted only after a structural comparison with the decompile, assembly, control-flow and P-code evidence, the project’s own build, test and optional differential commands, and 11 heuristic parity signals. The README calls these gates conservative evidence, not proof of equivalence, and the tool writes candidates to an overlay rather than patching the source tree.
requirements: The reviewed pin follows the v0.4.0 release of 2026-09-09 by one documentation commit; pyproject.toml classifies the package as alpha. The re-agent CLI covers init, plan, reverse, parity, status, estimate and evidence commands, with generic-cpp, windows-x64, gta-reversed and openrct2 profiles, the last two carrying hook and stub patterns for those existing reimplementation projects. Outputs are per-function candidate code, per-call prompt and response logs, checkpoints and a knowledge graph; the README says it never commits, pushes or overwrites the original tree.

Users supply the target program, a local Ghidra project in which it is imported, and a C/C++ project whose matching function bodies candidates replace in a temporary copy; the FAQ says useful results depend on that project’s source context, types, symbols and validation commands. Evidence comes from Ghidra exports read through the author’s separate ghidra-ai-bridge, whose headless export needs PyGhidra and a local Ghidra installation; without Ghidra only source-only parity checks run. No target binary or Ghidra export is bundled, and the GTA example needs the user’s own San Andreas executable.

It needs Python 3.10 or later; CI runs the tests on Linux with Python 3.10–3.13, on Windows with 3.12 and on macOS with 3.13. At least one model provider is required: a Claude or OpenAI-compatible API key, or an authenticated local Claude Code or Codex CLI, with reverser and checker free to use different providers at the user’s cost. Build, test and runtime commands are project-owned; argument arrays run directly on Windows and POSIX, legacy string commands need /bin/sh, and their results count as acceptance evidence only after trust_configured_commands is set explicitly.

docs/validation-0.3.md reports 131 tests passing locally on Python 3.13 with Ruff and strict mypy, and CI skips tests that need a model or Ghidra. Its one reference experiment, dated 2026-09-04, generated three GTA San Andreas timer functions with Claude CLI; each is reported to have passed review in one round, compiled through the example adapter and matched the original x86 code under Unicorn on seven inputs, with all three wrong-output controls detected. The author calls these 21 matching observations.

The repository and ghidra-ai-bridge are MIT-licensed; Ghidra, model services and the analysed programs keep their own terms. The README warns that configured commands are arbitrary project-owned commands to be trusted only when the project owner controls them, and that the Ghidra integration has to be tested in the user’s own environment.

resources.name: capa
resources.description: Mandiant FLARE tool that reports what an executable can do by matching a YAML rule set against features extracted from PE, ELF and .NET files or 32/64-bit shellcode, such as API calls, imports, strings and constants. Matches are grouped into capability namespaces with ATT&CK and MBC tags, and verbose output shows the function or basic-block addresses and features behind each match, pointing analysts to code worth studying. It also reads CAPE, DRAKVUF and VMRay sandbox reports for dynamic features and can use vivisect, IDA Pro, Ghidra or Binary Ninja for analysis, with explorer plugins for IDA and Ghidra and a browser viewer for its JSON results.
requirements: Release at review: v10.0.0, published 2026-10-16, with standalone PyInstaller builds for Linux (x86_64, arm64 and a Python 3.13 variant), macOS (x86_64 and arm64) and Windows that run without installation; the reviewed master commit only syncs the rules submodule after that tag. The installation guide says the Linux build needs GLIBC 2.26+ and that macOS Gatekeeper must approve the binary on first run. The flare-capa PyPI package (10.0.0, Python 3.10+) does not include the default rules or library-identification signatures, which are passed with -r and -s.

Inputs are user-supplied PE, ELF or .NET modules, raw shellcode, CAPE, DRAKVUF or VMRay reports, BinExport2 files or saved capa feature files. The IDA Pro explorer needs IDA 7.4+ with Python 3.10+ (tested through IDA 9.0); the Ghidra backend and explorer script need Ghidra 12.0+ started through PyGhidra; the Binary Ninja backend uses a separately installed Binary Ninja.

The limitations guide states that packed or obfuscated programs, installers and packaged programs such as AutoIt give misleading or incomplete results, and that capabilities split across wrapper or child functions are not matched; capa warns when its rules detect packing or installers. Matches are rule-based indications of capability, not confirmed behavior.

Apache-2.0, as is the separate capa-rules repository. v10.0.0 fixes code execution through crafted vivisect .viv workspace files, which affected v9.4.0 and earlier; existing workspaces now load only with CAPA_LOAD_VIV_WORKSPACE=1. A recursive source clone also fetches the test-file submodule, which the installation guide warns contains many malware samples.

resources.name: Ruffle: a Rust reimplementation of Adobe Flash Player
resources.description: Reimplements Adobe Flash Player in Rust so that SWF content, from ActionScript 1/2 (AVM1) to ActionScript 3 (AVM2), runs in a native desktop player or in browsers through WebAssembly, as a self-hosted script or a browser extension. Its contributor guide says behavior comes from observing Flash Player's output or from license-compatible sources such as Adobe's open avmplus code, and forbids decompiling Flash Player, Flash Professional or Animate. Regression tests run contributor-made SWFs and compare their trace output, and optionally rendered images, with captures from the official debug Flash Player.
requirements: The README says Ruffle supports ActionScript 1, 2 and 3 pretty well but is not finished. At review, the website's compatibility page reported 99% of the AVM1 language and 82% of its API, and 90% of the AVM2 language and 82% of its API, and acknowledged graphical inaccuracies in AVM1 content. Release at review: v0.7.1, published 2026-10-07 and described as equivalent to v0.7.0 apart from extension-publishing fixes; nightly builds continue, and the reviewed master commit is 73 commits ahead.

Users supply the SWF files or the pages that embed them. Release assets cover Linux (x86_64, i686 and aarch64), macOS universal and Windows (x86 and x86_64) desktop builds, self-hosted web and browser-extension packages and a reproducible source archive; the README also points to Firefox and Chrome extensions, Flathub, npm and a separate Android project.

Building needs the latest stable Rust (the workspace uses the 2024 edition) and Java on PATH to compile the ActionScript 3 built-in classes; Linux builds need ALSA, udev, fontconfig, FreeType and OpenSSL development packages. Web builds also need the wasm32-unknown-unknown target, Node.js with npm 7+, wasm-bindgen-cli 0.2.127 and Binaryen. Bundled scanner and exporter tools bulk-parse SWFs and render PNG screenshots.

Contributors are asked to commit each test SWF with its source, and expected trace output and screenshots come from running the debug Flash Player; known failures can be marked in a test's test.toml. These tests check Ruffle's behavior on authored test files.

Dual-licensed MIT or Apache-2.0 (GitHub reports NOASSERTION); LICENSE.md lists third-party dependency licenses, and the repository includes asc.jar from the Flex SDK to compile its ActionScript classes. SWF content keeps its own rights.

resources.name: ps3recomp
resources.description: Toolkit and runtime for statically recompiling PlayStation 3 games into native executables. Python tools parse PS3 ELF and PRX files, find functions and firmware imports, and lift PPU and SPU code to C/C++; a project template links that code with a C/C++ runtime providing LV2 system calls, high-level emulation of the system libraries and RSX graphics translation to Direct3D 12, Metal or Vulkan.
requirements: The README for v0.15.0 (released 2026-10-16; the reviewed master commit is two commits ahead) reports about 93 complete and 5 partial high-level-emulated system-library modules, with media decoding and SPURS still partial. Only Windows with Direct3D 12 runs a recompiled game from this tree; macOS and Linux build the runtime and pass its tests, but no title has yet booted to gameplay there.

Users supply a decrypted ELF of the game executable (EBOOT.BIN) from their own legally obtained copy; the repository ships no keys, firmware or game files and does not decrypt retail executables. The optional firmware low-level-emulation path also needs decrypted firmware modules that the user provides. Each game is ported in its own project: the README lists The Simpsons Arcade Game and Tornado Outbreak as in game in separate repositories.

Building from source needs Python (3.10+ in the README, 3.9+ in the build guides), CMake 3.20+ and a C17/C++20 compiler (MSVC or clang-cl, GCC 12+ or Clang 15+). SDL2 is required off Windows, and FFmpeg is optional and loaded at run time for video and ATRAC3plus decoding. Releases ship prebuilt SDK bundles with the runtime library, headers and Python pipeline for Windows x64, macOS arm64 and Linux x64. Last commit at review: 2026-10-16.

CI builds the runtime and runs the lifter test suites and C unit tests on Windows, macOS arm64 and Linux, plus the Vulkan backend on lavapipe; the README states that a passing check does not mean a game ran. A lifter conformance suite checks the C emitted for single instructions against expectations derived from the PowerISA, and a regression gate compares five ports with recorded milestone logs before shared-runtime changes land.

MIT-licensed; the vendored ATRAC3/ATRAC3plus decoder taken from PPSSPP stays LGPL-2.1-or-later. The README states that the project contains no Sony code, firmware, keys or copyrighted material and that its system-library modules are written from documented behavior, with RPCS3 used as a behavioral reference rather than a code source.

resources.name: Nebula (NebulaFD)
resources.description: Work-in-progress decompiler for games made with Clickteam Fusion 2.5, with fixes for older Multimedia Fusion 1.5 files. Its .NET console app reads Windows executables, Android APKs, iOS IPAs, CCN data files and existing MFA projects, then runs plug-in tools: an MFA Parser that writes the game back out as an editable Fusion project, and an Asset Dumper for images, sounds, music, fonts, icons, shaders and packed files.
requirements: The README is a placeholder that calls itself a work in progress and documents no usage, build steps or supported formats. The latest release, september_2026_update (2026-09-28, the reviewed commit), lists fixes for Multimedia Fusion 1.5 files and Fusion 2.5 build 296 events plus experimental Android support, and notes that console-exporter detection breaks with custom exporters.

Users supply a compiled Fusion game: the console asks for a file path and picks a reader from the extension (EXE, APK, IPA, MFA, ZIP, ANM, TMP or GAM, with other files read as CCN data) or from the user's choice. The MFA Parser and Asset Dumper load as DLLs from the program's Tools folder and write to a Dumps folder.

Release archives require the .NET 6.0 Desktop Runtime, and the projects target net6.0. The only GitHub workflow compiles the solution with MSBuild on Windows and uploads the build as an artifact, and the dumper's post-build step uses the Windows robocopy command; no other platform is documented. The repository contains no test project.
There is no license file and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms are not stated. The README credits Kostya for the image bank.

resources.name: ScooterLink: reconstructing Honda RoadSync’s handlebar-button protocol
resources.description: Replaces Honda RoadSync’s Apple Music-only media control with an iOS app that pairs with a Honda PCX 2025 TFT dash over Bluetooth Low Energy and turns handlebar presses into system-wide commands for any player. The author documents the dash’s BLE services, key exchange, button registration and event bytes, reportedly worked out from the official Android app and logged traffic. Results are author-reported on one PCX125, and the protocol notes separate confirmed from unverified parts.
requirements: The reviewed commit follows the v1.2 release and changes only one README link. It targets a Honda PCX 2025 with the TFT dash and RoadSync support; README reports testing on a PCX125 2025 and calls other RoadSync models untested. Select and Back map to play/pause and Next/Previous to track changes, and the app reconnects at ignition and switches the dash to phone mode. Now-playing text, speed and volume control are unavailable, and no Android version exists.

No Honda software is needed at runtime, but RoadSync’s phone pairing must first be deleted on the dash, which keeps one phone key. The protocol was reportedly derived from the official RoadSync Android app and logged traffic; source comments cite decompiled Android app version 26.8.10 and a findings file, but the app, decompiled code, captures and that file are not in the repository.

Building needs a Mac with Xcode 16+, XcodeGen and the user’s own signing team and bundle ID; the app targets iOS 17, and the prebuilt v1.2 IPA must be sideloaded with a personal or developer Apple ID. Controlling other apps’ playback relies on Apple’s private MediaRemote framework, which README says rules out App Store distribution.

docs/PROTOCOL.md marks key exchange, per-connection validation, button registration, the phone-screen request and button events as confirmed on a real PCX125 2025, and dash drawing as unverified. A Mac-run Swift self-test checks CRC values, a simulated key exchange, validation parsing and registration and screen byte layouts. README reports that experimental colour slots and a drawn screen left the dash refusing phone mode until re-pairing, keeps that code switched off and warns never to write to the firmware-update service.

MIT covers the project code. README says the project is independent of Honda and contains no Honda code or files, only original code and a description of the Bluetooth messages written for interoperability; Honda, PCX and RoadSync remain trademarks of their owners. The author’s post credits Claude with the reverse engineering.

resources.name: Frontkick vs Rikugan: a CREBench agent comparison
resources.description: Matthieu Breuil’s Synacktiv article explains tool-calling and code-executing agent designs and describes Frontkick, a CodeAct agent that runs generated Python inside Binary Ninja. It compares Frontkick with the open-source Rikugan plugin on two CREBench cryptographic binary tasks, then attributes most of Frontkick’s advantage to a prompt that listed installed Python libraries rather than to its architecture. It is a small evaluation write-up with per-run results, not a released tool or a general benchmark finding.
requirements: The article on Synacktiv’s publications site is dated 13/10/2026. It describes Frontkick as a CodeAct agent that executes generated Python against Binary Ninja’s API, with a recipe-retrieval corpus, a single-level subagent and truncation of older turns; no download, repository or license for Frontkick is linked. Rikugan is an MIT-licensed community agent plugin for IDA Pro and Binary Ninja built on schema-validated tools, while Vector 35’s closed-source Sidekick was excluded because its internals are not accessible.

The comparison used Claude Sonnet 5.5 with CREBench’s AES-128-CBC and ChaCha20 cases in the hardcode_plain/O0 setting, supplied as stripped binaries, with four runs per case for each agent and a 1M-token budget. Each run had to identify the algorithm and key and reimplement decryption to recover the flag. The article does not state the Binary Ninja, Rikugan or Frontkick versions or publish the run transcripts it inspected.

In the published run table Frontkick fully solves six of eight runs and Rikugan none; the means are about 86 versus 31 out of 100 and about 0.60M versus 0.95M tokens, which the article summarizes as roughly half the tokens and nearly three times the score. On AES-128-CBC, Rikugan repeatedly tried a Python crypto package that was not installed and fell back to a manual implementation, whereas Frontkick’s prompt listed the installed libraries. The author therefore calls the outcome a draw driven by prompt design, and proposes a rerun with aligned prompts.
Two tasks, one model and eight runs per agent cannot support general conclusions about either agent, about tool-calling versus code-executing designs, or about other CREBench settings.

resources.name: OpenDMCUFirm: a reimplemented Wii U DMCU display firmware
resources.description: Reimplements in C the firmware of the Wii U’s DMCU, the M68HC11-compatible display microcontroller in its AMD graphics controller, which in Wii mode reads the Video Interface state and configures display output, deinterlacing, scaling and overscan. The README says the work is based on reverse engineering of the original firmware but is not a byte-for-byte matching decompilation, and calls it a work in progress. The built image replaces the stock firmware in Wii mode when loaded through the evWii plugin.
requirements: The reviewed main commit has no releases or tags. The README describes a work-in-progress reimplementation with potential issues expected; recent commits name registers and state fields, and one reports a function fully matched after a missing variable caused problems in 240p titles. link.ld warns that Nintendo’s nn_cmpt writes values into the middle of the DMCU’s ERAM and can overwrite the code.

The build uses only the project’s C sources and needs no original firmware. Running the result needs a Wii U with the Aroma plugin environment and evWii: dmcu.d.hex goes in the SD card’s wiiu folder and is loaded with evWii’s “Load DMCU Firmware from SD Card” option for Wii mode.

The compiler is GCC 3.3.6-m68hc1x-20060122 from the GNU 68HC11/12 packages. The Dockerfile sets it up on Ubuntu 24.04 from the checksum-verified Windows installer run under Wine, and a prebuilt garyodernichts/dmcubuilder image is offered; Python 3 runs hexconv.py to turn the S19 output into the DMCU hex format.
CI only builds dmcu.d.hex in that container and uploads it as an artifact. The reviewed files contain no test suite, hardware test log or comparison with the stock firmware’s behavior.

The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none; project source files state only that they are part of OpenDMCUFirm. The bundled 68HC11 and stdint headers keep their FSF GPL and BSD notices, evWii is GPL-2.0, and the original firmware keeps its own rights.

resources.name: CoD4 Rewrite: Rust/Bevy reconstruction
resources.description: A Rust/Bevy reconstruction of Call of Duty 4 multiplayer systems, using assets from a local game installation. Source covers menus, local bots, movement and combat, and connects custom relay-based netplay to the game.
requirements: Requires Windows, a Vulkan-capable GPU and an owned CoD4 patch 1.7 installation. Optional Black Ops, Modern Warfare 2 and World at War content requires their separate installations; game assets are not supplied.
Current source connects the multiplayer dependency and NetplayPlugin despite README statements that networking is pending.
Rendering and gameplay include deliberate extensions.
Cargo declares MIT OR Apache-2.0, inherited by the game and multiplayer crates. No standalone license text was found in the reviewed tree.

resources.name: libd2: Diablo II 1.14d engine-core libraries
resources.description: Zig libraries reconstructing Diablo II 1.14d seeded maps, item generation, saves, simulation rules and network formats. Selected components expose native and WebAssembly interfaces; verification notes distinguish retail map comparisons from weaker subsystem evidence.
requirements: Builds require Zig 0.16.0. These are modular engine libraries, not a complete playable client; basic generation uses embedded data and fixtures.
MIT covers the Zig source. Included Blizzard-derived binary blobs and map fixtures are expressly excluded from that grant; the repository is not asset-free.
The authors report cell-level comparisons for five Nightmare seeds and two holdouts, plus per-level CRC checks for 200 seeds at three difficulties.
The game and net packages are checked against recovered rules and packet layouts, not a live server; save, item and pathfinding checks have different depth.

resources.name: Underworld Exhumed: reconstructing Ultima Underworld I and II
resources.description: Pairs reconstructed DOS sources with native ports of Ultima Underworld I and II. The upstream documents Exhume-based byte-matching builds, routine-level comparisons and recorded-session replay against DOS.
requirements: Native ports target macOS, Windows and Linux. Playing and checking against the originals requires your own matching game files (the README targets GOG releases); byte-matching builds additionally require the documented Turbo C++ 1.01 and TASM 2.0 inputs. Native-port compilation itself does not require game data.

The MIT license covers the project’s own tools, documentation and added annotations/structure. NOTICE explicitly excludes rights in the original games and derived game code; optional MT-32 playback requires separately obtained ROMs.
Recorded sessions and routine tests provide bounded upstream evidence. Full tests require licensed inputs absent from the public repository.

resources.name: LineWars II: a portable SDL3 reconstruction
resources.description: Provides an SDL3 backend for a portable-C reconstruction of the 1994 DOS game. Its build configuration links the reconstructed engine to video, input and audio adapters; the upstream documents differential gates against original machine code.
requirements: Builds target Windows and Linux using C99, CMake 3.16+ and SDL3; the reviewed build notes specify SDL 3.4.12 built with the same compiler as the game. This is a port of the separate LineWarsII-DOS reconstruction.

The reconstructed/ported source uses PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. NOTICE reports original-author Patrick Aalto’s July 16, 2026 permission for freeware distribution of the original game material; it does not grant commercial-use permission. SDL keeps its separate zlib license.
The upstream reports renderer and menu comparisons and captured PCM levels within about 10% of its DOS reference; higher-resolution rendering changes the presentation.

resources.name: BFM-decomp: Brave Fencer Musashi matching decompilation
