requirements: README describes a C++ reimplementation of Mario Kart Wii’s physics engine aiming at perfectly accurate ghost replay. At the reviewed commit STATUS.md lists 55 time-trial ghost test cases, each marked synchronized for every frame; the latest GitHub release, 0.6 (2025-09-04), adds x86-64 Linux, macOS and Windows binaries of the simulator. Source comments name addresses in the original game, but nothing rebuilds its executable; README points to the separate riidefi/mkw matching decompilation for that.

Running needs the Race folder (the Common and course archives) from your own Mario Kart Wii disc, placed relative to the executable; the repository ships no game files, and README requires any contributed frontend not to distribute in-game assets. The committed samples are time-trial ghost files (.rkg) with per-frame .krkg reference traces that README says come from a custom vabold/mkw-sp build running the PAL release; such traces are verification data captured from the game, as is common for reconstruction projects.

README lists g++ 13.1 with C++23, ninja 1.3 and Python 3.6; configure.py generates the ninja build and compiles testCases.json into the binary suite file. CMakeLists.txt also exposes a libkinoko library target for embedding the engine in other C++23 projects. CI builds with GCC 14 on Ubuntu; the program is a command-line host with test and replay modes, and README says no GUI is planned.

kinoko test compares position, rotation, internal and external velocity, speed, acceleration, soft speed limit, race completion and checkpoint values with every .krkg frame by exact equality and reports the first desynchronized frame; kinoko replay checks whether a ghost finishes with the time in its .rkg header. CI runs the suite with runtime files fetched from a secret-configured URL and checks that STATUS.md is current. These are project-reported results.
LICENSE applies MIT (copyright vabold, 2022–2026) to the project; Mario Kart Wii and its game data keep Nintendo’s rights, and the bundled doxygen-awesome-css theme has its own license file.

resources.name: OWASP Firmware Security Testing Methodology (FSTM)
resources.description: A free English methodology, maintained by Aaron Guzman and published on GitBook, for security testing and reverse engineering embedded-device firmware. It is organized as nine stages: information gathering, obtaining firmware, analyzing the image, extracting the filesystem, static analysis of its contents, emulation, dynamic testing, runtime analysis and binary exploitation, with example commands for tools such as binwalk, unblob, FACT, EMBA, Firmwalker, QEMU and Ghidra. An October 2025 revision added C/C++ static-analysis tools, SBOM generation and a mapping to the OWASP IoT Security Verification Standard (ISVS).
requirements: Reviewed at default-branch commit ec666e8 (2025-10-05). Most of the text dates from 2019–2020, with a 2022 EMBA/EMBArk update and an October 2025 revision that refreshed tool references, removed commercial ones and added the SAST, SBOM and ISVS sections; the published GitBook includes those additions. A feature branch adding ISVS requirement mappings by stage (June 2026) was not merged at review, and a shorter 2020 Chinese translation sits on the separate zhong-wen-fstm branch.

Its stated audience is security researchers, software developers, consultants, hobbyists and information-security professionals. It is a single long reference page of procedures and commands rather than a paced course, and it points to the OWASP IoT Security Testing Guide for hardware, wireless, network and user-interface tests outside firmware.

Following it needs the firmware image or the physical device under an authorized assessment; the methodology tells testers to choose acquisition methods by project objectives and rules of engagement and to follow local laws. Some stages assume hardware debug access and a chip programmer. Tools mostly run on Linux; the README links a preconfigured EmbedOS Ubuntu VM from 2020 and, for practice, deliberately vulnerable firmware such as OWASP IoTGoat, DVRF and DVID.
Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (License.md).

resources.name: Awesome Android Reverse Engineering
resources.description: An awesome list of Android reverse-engineering training, tools and resources started in 2023 by James Stevenson, with 92 one-line entries, 16 of them starred as great and up to date. It covers courses, videos and books; static analysis and deobfuscation, networking and Frida-based instrumentation, decompilers and malware analysis tools; documentation and case studies; CTFs and crackmes; obfuscation and anti-reversing; and a short firmware and kernel section.
requirements: Reviewed at commit 0ade43d (2025-07-08). 51 of 58 commits date from 2023; a March 2025 rewrite reorganized the list and added the obfuscation and firmware sections, and the July 2025 commit removed the Cloud API section while its contents-menu entry remains.

Entries give a link and a one-line summary with no license, version or maintenance notes, and some summaries are loose; AFLSmart, for example, is described as a firmware-image fuzzer, while its own README presents an input-structure-aware greybox fuzzer. 8 of 90 unique URLs gave no response, a 404 or a 530: five linked GitHub repositories no longer exist, four of them (the ATDF, Paranoid, libhooker and Android kernel-exploits entries) added in the March 2025 rewrite, and the Houseparty case study, the Flare-On page and AndroidXref did not load.

Six entries are the maintainer's own tools and one his blog post. Burp Suite, IDA Pro, JEB and DexGuard are commercial, the Documentation section links the APKMirror and APKPure download sites, and tools for bypassing app controls, dumping memory and kernel exploitation appear as listed.

LICENSE is the MIT License (2023, James Stevenson), although the README points to a LICENSE.md that does not exist; placeholder changelog and to-do files from the repository template remain under .github. Linked tools, books and APKs keep their own terms. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: Mario Kart: Double Dash!!: a matching GameCube decompilation of the debug build
resources.description: A work-in-progress 1:1 decompilation of Mario Kart: Double Dash!! that rebuilds the GameCube main.dol of the US debug build (MarioClub_us) from C and C++ with the original Metrowerks compilers, checking it against a stored SHA-1. The build splits the binary from a user-supplied disc image, and objdiff compares objects during development. decomp.dev reported 47.09% of code matched at the reviewed commit; a European retail target is configured but marked as not working yet.
requirements: README calls this a WIP 1:1 decompilation and says only the debug version is supported: the default MarioClub_us (USA) target, whose main.dol SHA-1 config/MarioClub_us/build.sha1 records. configure.py also lists Release_eu, but its config.yml is marked as not working yet, and CI builds only MarioClub_us. The output is a GameCube DOL, not a PC executable or port.

Copy your own disc image of that build to orig/MarioClub_us; ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ and TGC images are accepted. README says the repository contains no game assets or assembly: decomp-toolkit splits the user’s DOL using the committed symbol and split tables, and during the build extracts a font, system.arc and build-time data from that DOL locally.

Builds need Python and ninja on Windows (native tooling recommended), macOS (with wine-crossover) or Linux (an automatically downloaded wibo on x86, Wine elsewhere). configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.6.2, objdiff v3.3.1, binutils 2.42-1, sjiswrap v1.2.1, wibo 0.7.0 and the 20250812 compiler bundle, using Metrowerks GC/2.6 for game, JSystem, MSL and TRK code and GC/1.2.5n for the Dolphin SDK libraries.

Objects marked Matching (518 in configure.py; 277 remain NonMatching and 13 Equivalent) are compiled from source, the rest are taken from the split DOL, and the build checks main.dol against build.sha1. CI builds MarioClub_us in a container that supplies the disc files and compilers, uploads a progress report and validates symbol order for changed C++ files. decomp.dev’s report for the pinned commit lists 1,517,644 of 3,222,748 code bytes (47.09%) and 8,695 of 15,357 functions matched, with 518 of 807 units complete.

The repository carries CC0-1.0; Nintendo’s game, disc contents and the downloaded compilers keep their own rights. README credits JSystem and SDK code reused from other decompilations, including Metroid Prime, Pikmin 2, Super Mario Galaxy, Super Mario Sunshine and Twilight Princess.

resources.name: 3S Decomp: a byte-compared PS2 decompilation of Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike
resources.description: Decompiles the PlayStation 2 executable of Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike from Street Fighter Anniversary Collection into C that period Metrowerks and EE GCC compilers rebuild, then compares the rebuilt executable word by word with the user’s original. README reports the game code fully decompiled and the CRI middleware partly so. The separate 3SX native port describes itself as this project’s continuation.
requirements: README reports the game code fully decompiled and the CRI middleware partly decompiled, with most file-system and sound functions the game uses matching; cri-progress.md checks off 497 of the 503 CRI functions it lists. At the reviewed commit, two game functions (sea_write and mlt_obj_trans_rgb_ext) and 39 of 52 CRI C files still include assembly in the PS2 build, and PS2 SDK and GCC library code is out of scope. The output is the PS2 executable, not a PC port.

Building needs THIRD_U.BIN from the user’s own copy of the game; the split configuration records its SHA-1 as cf58495054c31ad852175c66e9ca04d5094f000e, and make split derives the assembly and linker script from it. The decompiling guide also relies on the executable’s DWARF debug data, dumped with decomp-toolkit, for signatures and local variables. A separate split_cps3 target for the CPS3 arcade version needs a user-supplied arcade ROM set and has only a code-segment configuration.

The build guide covers Linux (Debian packages with i386 support, MIPS binutils, and a Python venv with splat64 0.29.0 and spimdisasm 1.35.0) and macOS through the provided Dockerfile. make setup_tools downloads Metrowerks mwccps2 3.0b38 and EE GCC 2.96 from decomp.me’s compiler releases plus the wibo loader for Windows tools; m2c, asm-differ, mwccgap and saturn-splitter are git submodules.

A successful build ends with compare_bytes.py checking the rebuilt executable against the original from offset 0x80 to 0x478A00 and printing “Files match ✅”. That check tolerates 163 listed words in about 20 game and CRI functions, attributed to register and operand swaps, assert line numbers, string encoding, a misplaced nop and a call misalignment, so equivalence is near-byte-level by the project’s own check rather than a whole-file hash. The latest commit removed the GitHub Actions workflows.

LICENSE is AGPL-3.0 for the project’s code. The original executable and game content keep their own rights; include/cri carries headers marked “CRI Middleware SDK” and “Copyright (c) … CRI-MW”, and the vendored zlib keeps its own license.

resources.name: Halo: Combat Evolved: an incremental re-implementation patched into the original Xbox executable
resources.description: A research project re-implementing the original Xbox Halo: Combat Evolved in C, one function at a time. Rewritten functions are compiled into a separate image and patched into the user’s original executable with redirects from the original implementations, so the hybrid game can be run and debugged in xemu or on an Xbox as work progresses. The project reports an early stage, and its sources document no byte-for-byte comparison with the original code.
requirements: README describes studying and creating a free, open-source re-implementation of the Xbox launch title; its current-state list reports that the patched game runs, the main loop and several more functions are re-implemented, and there is a long way to go. The linked progress page, whose data file was last modified in November 2022, reports 0.37% of the .text section’s game code across 40 functions. The last default-branch commit is dated 2023-07-07.

Supply the retail disc’s game files and the original executable version 01.10.12.2276, identified by MD5 in README and kb.json and placed as cachebeta.xbe in a halo-patched directory; tools/patch.py checks that hash. The repository includes no game executable or assets, and README says they must come from your own copy. The build writes a patched default.xbe beside them as the user’s local modified copy; the project distributes no game build.

Builds use CMake 3.16+, Python 3 with libclang, pefile and pyxbe, and either 32-bit MSVC on Windows or Clang and LLD targeting i386-pc-win32 on Linux and macOS; a Dockerfile provides an Ubuntu 22.04 build image. The result targets the original Xbox and runs in the xemu emulator or on console hardware, and the build generates a .gdbinit for debugging with GDB through xemu’s GDB server.

kb.json declares 323 original functions and 71 data items with addresses, grouped by original object file; tools/knowledge.py generates headers, thunks and an import library from it, and gen-struct-checks.py emits static size checks for types.h. CI builds only the re-implementation image (Debug and Release on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS) without original files, so it checks compilation, not behaviour.

The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms for the project’s code are not stated; src/xboxkrnl.exe.def carries a CC0-1.0 notice (2017, Stefan Schmidt). README presents the work as educational research, the progress page says it is not affiliated with Microsoft or Bungie, and the game keeps its rights holders’ terms.

resources.name: Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door: an early matching GameCube decompilation
resources.description: A work-in-progress matching decompilation of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door that targets the Japanese Rev 0 GameCube release (G8MJ01), rebuilding MarioSt.dol and 31 REL modules with the original Metrowerks compilers and checking each against a stored SHA-1. The build splits these binaries from a user-supplied disc image, and objdiff compares objects during development. decomp.dev reported 12.10% of code matched at the reviewed commit.
requirements: README lists one supported version, G8MJ01 (Rev 0, JP); configure.py defines no other version and CI builds only G8MJ01. README still carries template leftovers: its badges point at another project, its clone command names NWPlayer123/G8MJ01-dtk and one line calls G8MJ01 the USA version. The output is a GameCube DOL and REL set, not a PC port.

Copy your own G8MJ01 disc image to orig/G8MJ01; ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ and TGC images are accepted. README says the repository contains no game assets or assembly: decomp-toolkit splits main.dol and the RELs using committed symbol and split tables, and extracts the memory-card icon and banner textures from the DOL into local headers. Decompiled sources such as src/pmario_sound.c also carry game data tables reconstructed as C.

Builds need Python and ninja on Windows (native tooling recommended), macOS (with wine-crossover) or Linux (an automatically downloaded wibo on x86, Wine elsewhere). configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.8.3, objdiff v3.7.1, binutils 2.42-2, sjiswrap v1.2.2, wibo 1.1.0 and the 20260305 compiler bundle, using Metrowerks GC/2.6 for game and REL code and GC/1.2.5n for the Dolphin SDK. tools/ttydasm is a Rust helper that decodes a named event script from the linked DOL or REL outputs in build/G8MJ01.

Objects marked Matching (100 of 547 in configure.py) are compiled from source and the rest come from the split originals; the default ninja target checks the DOL and all RELs against config/G8MJ01/build.sha1 before reporting progress. CI builds G8MJ01 in a container that supplies the disc files and compilers and uploads a progress report. decomp.dev’s report for the pinned commit lists 457,800 of 3,784,980 code bytes (12.10%) and 2,029 of 9,770 functions matched, with 100 of 1,239 units complete.
The repository carries the MIT License (copyright NWPlayer123), and libs/musyx has its own MIT license; neither covers Nintendo’s game, disc contents or the downloaded compilers.

resources.name: Awesome Frida
resources.description: An awesome list of libraries, scripts, tools, talks and articles built on or about Frida, the dynamic instrumentation toolkit, started by David Weinstein in May 2016. Its 82 entries fall into libraries (about half of them NowSecure Node.js modules), script collections and projects, talks and papers, tools powered by Frida such as r2frida, objection, friTap and Fridump, videos, blog posts and community links, most with a one-line summary.
requirements: Reviewed at commit e20da3b (2026-04-10). 43 of 68 commits date from 2016–2017, most talks, videos and posts are from 2015–2017, and after the April 2023 addition of RoboDroid the only change is the April 2026 addition of rekit. Entries do not say which Frida version they target; frida-load is marked deprecated and the Lobotomy entries are struck through.

13 of 110 unique URLs gave no response or a 404, including the OSDC, ZeroNights and RMLL event pages and a three-part tutorial series, and three talk PDFs are linked as relative files that are not in the repository. Of the 57 GitHub repositories linked, 4 are archived, 2 no longer exist and 13 have not been pushed to since 2019. The README asks contributors to flag listings that are unmaintained or have had no commits for two to three years.
Several listed tools dump process memory, decrypt protected apps or log TLS keys, and two posts cover detecting Frida.

The LICENSE file is CC0 1.0. The contribution guide, adapted from the general awesome-list guidelines, refers to a code of conduct and a list-creation guide that are not in the repository. Linked projects keep their own licenses. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: 3SX: a native Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike port continuing the PS2 decompilation
resources.description: Builds Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike as native C for Windows, macOS and Linux, continuing the 3s-decomp PS2 decompilation, with SDL3 for video, input and audio and GekkoNet for rollback netplay. README stresses that it is neither a recompilation nor emulation. The port needs the player’s own PS2 game files and works toward arcade-accurate balance, which an optional Statcheck build tests against CPS3 RAM states recorded from Fightcade replays.
requirements: README calls 3SX a native port and a continuation of 3s-decomp, explicitly neither a recompilation nor emulation. At the reviewed commit the game code under src/sf33rd has no remaining INCLUDE_ASM stubs, and src/port supplies SDL3 platform, input and sound layers, including its own ADX decoder. This is a modified port: its goals include fixing balance regressions the PS2 version introduced, and the arcade-balance option is marked work in progress. The only release is a rolling pre-release rebuilt from main, and goals such as stable PC play and the arcade ROM as sole dependency remain on the 1.0 milestone.

Play requires a legally obtained PS2 copy of Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike or Street Fighter Anniversary Collection: a startup wizard reads the user’s disc image, or SF33RD.AFS from it is placed in the resources folder, and release builds compare that file with a SHA-256 in resources.c. The arcade-balance option also needs the user’s sfiii3nr1.zip CPS3 ROM set. The tree ships no game archives, but src/bin2obj carries large C data tables from the decompilation.

Prebuilt rolling releases cover Windows, macOS, and x86_64 and arm64 Linux. Source builds use CMake 3.24+ with Clang, after MSYS2 MinGW64 packages on Windows, the listed Ubuntu packages or Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS; build-deps.sh fetches and builds SDL3, SDL_net, GekkoNet, libcdio, minizip-ng and TF-PSA-Crypto. CMake and CI also carry a PSP branch built with Docker tooling.

Pull-request CI only builds the Windows, macOS, Linux and PSP targets. Arcade accuracy is checked with the optional Statcheck build: tools/fcade-replays, described as a reverse-engineering helper for Fightcade’s replay stream, downloads replays; a custom FBNeo fork records per-frame CPS3 RAM dumps; and Statcheck stops at the first mismatch in health, positions, stun, super-art meter, timer or round phase. The reviewed tree publishes no Statcheck results.

The repository carries an agent skill with a Codex interface file. It directs a coding agent to compare local functions with a CPS3 program through a read-only Ghidra MCP server, mark each function’s parity and add CPS3 behaviour behind the arcade-balance flag. LICENSE is AGPL-3.0. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES lists GPLv3+ libcdio with zlib, BSD-2-Clause, MIT and Apache-2.0 components, the game and its assets keep their own rights, and README says the project does not condone piracy.

resources.name: re4: a byte-identical decompilation of the Resident Evil 4 GameCube debug build
resources.description: Reconstructs C and C++ source for the two-disc Resident Evil 4 GameCube debug prototype (G4BE08) and rebuilds main.dol and all 114 REL overlays with the compilers the README names, checking every output against a SHA-1 list. Function names are Capcom’s own from the debug build’s Bio4.sym files, and most struct and field names are aligned from the PS2 debug build’s debug information. The project’s research log says AI agents did the matching work; byte identity is project-reported.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-02 head, under four weeks after the first commit of 2026-09-07. README calls the decompilation complete: every unit compiles to the original bytes, src/ holds about 570,000 lines of C and C++ with no assembly files, and 526 `// COMPILER-DIFF:` spots coax the compiler’s register or instruction choices without emitting code. Nearly all remaining inline assembly is in routines the vendors also wrote in assembly. The output is the debug prototype’s DOL and RELs, not a retail build or PC port.

Supply your own images of both debug discs in orig/G4BE08/: disc 1 provides main.dol and most RELs, disc 2 the four island-stage RELs, and configure.py also reads the matching Bio4 symbol files from them. The game code’s compiler is built from SN Systems’ GPL source release of its ProDG 3.9.3 GCC port, which the user also supplies. The repository contains no game assets.

The documented host is Linux with Python 3 and ninja. tools/sn-gcc/build.sh builds SN’s GCC 2.95.3 (SN BUILD v1.79) natively once with the project’s Linux-host and memory-flag patches; CRI middleware builds with Metrowerks CodeWarrior 2.4.7 and the Nintendo SDK, taken from dolsdk2004, with GC/1.2.5n. The first configure run downloads pinned decomp-toolkit, objdiff, wibo and CodeWarrior compiler releases.

A successful build should end with ninja reporting 100% matched and linked, and dtk shasum against config/G4BE08/build.sha1 should print OK for all 115 binaries; tools/bytecmp.py compares single units and tools/asmcheck.py --all counts instructions emitted from asm templates, a total changes must not alter. The repository has no CI workflow or release, so these results are project-reported.

LICENSE applies CC0 only to the project’s build scripts, tools, configuration and documentation. README and LICENSE state that the reconstructed game, SDK and middleware source in src/ and include/ remains the property of Capcom, Nintendo and CRI Middleware and is published for research and preservation only. docs/research/README.md describes its matching notes as written by the AI agents that did the matching work.

resources.name: Super Smash Bros. Brawl: an early matching Wii decompilation
resources.description: A work-in-progress matching decompilation of Super Smash Bros. Brawl that targets the USA Rev 2 Wii release (RSBE01_02), splitting main.dol and 126 REL modules from a user-supplied disc image and checking the rebuilt binaries against stored SHA-1 values. objdiff compares objects during development, and six other regional revisions are listed but commented out of the supported set. decomp.dev reported 1.27% of code matched at the reviewed commit.
requirements: README lists one supported version, RSBE01_02 (USA Rev 2), with the Japan, USA Rev 1, PAL and Korea revisions commented out; configure.py names all seven, but only RSBE01_02 has a configuration and CI builds only it. The output is a Wii main.dol and REL set, not a PC port.

Copy your own disc image to orig/RSBE01_02; ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ and TGC images are accepted. README says the repository contains no game assets or assembly: decomp-toolkit splits the DOL and RELs using committed per-module symbol and split tables, and extracts one embedded binary (HomeBtnIcon) from the DOL locally. Game headers come from the BrawlHeaders submodule (Sammi-Husky/BrawlHeaders), which README says to initialize before building.

Builds need Python and ninja on Windows (native tooling recommended), macOS (with wine-crossover) or Linux (an automatically downloaded wibo on x86, Wine elsewhere). configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.7.5, objdiff v3.4.4, binutils 2.42-1, sjiswrap v1.2.2, wibo 1.0.0 and the 20250812 compiler bundle, compiling and linking with Metrowerks GC/3.0a5.2.

Objects marked Matching (184 in configure.py; 20 remain NonMatching) are compiled from source and the rest come from the split originals; the default ninja target checks main.dol and the RELs against config/RSBE01_02/build.sha1 before reporting progress. CI builds RSBE01_02 in a container that supplies the disc files and compilers and uploads a progress report. decomp.dev’s report for the pinned commit lists 201,252 of 15,833,548 code bytes (1.27%) and 2,504 of 92,523 functions matched, with 516 of 4,415 units complete.
The repository carries CC0-1.0; Nintendo’s game, disc contents and the downloaded compilers fall outside that dedication, and the BrawlHeaders submodule declares no license on GitHub.

resources.name: re-plants-vs-zombies: decompiling and modernizing Plants vs. Zombies GOTY
resources.description: Reconstructs C++ source for Plants vs. Zombies on PopCap’s open-source SexyAppFramework, starting from an earlier community decompilation of version 0.9.9 and adding functionality reversed from the Game of the Year edition, with functions annotated by GOTY addresses. The project also modernizes the engine with current C++ and is replacing the DirectDraw and Direct3D 7 renderers with GLFW. It builds a fan executable that runs from an original game folder, aiming at a modernized, extensible game rather than an identical binary.
requirements: README describes decompiling the latest functionality of the first PvZ title and expanding the game and its engine, building on a since-deleted 0.9.9 decompilation by Miya (rspforhp) that it credits ruslan831 with archiving. Its roadmap marks x64 support and achievements as partial, the GLFW renderer and cross-platform replacements as in progress, and Zombatar and a modding API as not done. There are no releases; the last commit is dated 2026-07-11.

Playing needs the original game files from a purchased copy; README links the Steam Game of the Year Edition but names no exact executable version. The built executable is run from that game folder, and the audio code loads bass.dll or fmod.dll at runtime instead of linking a committed copy. README says the repository includes no PopCap IP beyond the open-source engine; Resources.cpp/.h reconstruct the game’s generated resource-ID tables, data derived from the game as is usual for such projects.

Builds use CMake 3.16+ and C++23. README documents Visual Studio Community, whose CMakeSettings.json has x86 and x64 MSVC configurations, or CMake with Ninja; toolchain.cmake cross-compiles with x86_64-w64-mingw32 Clang and windres. The reviewed build produces a Windows executable, and the repository has no CI workflow.

The sources document no tests, CI or comparison with the original executable; contributors annotate reversed functions and class members with their GOTY addresses. Fidelity to the original game is not measured.

LICENSE dedicates the repository under CC0 1.0. The SexyAppFramework code derives from the engine PopCap made public, but PopCap’s license text is not included; the ogg code keeps Xiph.org’s BSD-style notice, and the FMOD 3 (Firelight, 1999–2002) and BASS 2.4 (Un4seen, 1999–2022) API headers keep their vendors’ copyrights. The original game and its files keep their rights holders’ terms. README says the project does not condone piracy.

resources.name: Awesome Ghidra
resources.description: An awesome list of Ghidra scripts, plugins, extensions, learning materials and related services, kept by the Allsafe GitHub organization since December 2019. Its 49 entries comprise 36 scripts and extensions, from malware-analysis and crypto-constant finders to Go, JNI, EVM and EFI helpers, Python and Jupyter bridges, P-code emulation and patch-diff correlators; 10 books, talks and courses; and three related projects such as r2ghidra-dec and Ghidraaas, each with a one-line summary.
requirements: Reviewed at commit 9265b2f (2026-06-18). 42 of 53 commits date from 2019–2021; after that gap the maintainers merged four contributor pull requests in June 2026, adding entries such as the printf-inliner plugin, 0xdea's scripts, IDAObjcTypes and GhidrAI. Entries name no Ghidra versions, GhidrAI is the only AI-assisted entry, and no MCP server is listed.

Entries give a link and a one-line summary with no license or maintenance information. Of the 42 GitHub repositories linked, 1 is archived and 17 have not been pushed to since 2021, so each project's Ghidra compatibility must be checked at its source; only the OOAnalyzer plugin path returned a 404.

Five entries are the maintaining organization's own scripts and tools. The Materials section includes a Japanese-language practical guide, the NSA's GhidraClass course material in the Ghidra repository, conference talks and The Ghidra Book.
GitHub detects no license and the repository has no license file or contribution guide, so the list states no reuse terms; linked projects keep their own licenses.

resources.name: Sonic Advance 1 & 2: a matching GBA decompilation with widescreen ports
resources.description: Reconstructs Sonic Advance and Sonic Advance 2 for the Game Boy Advance as C that rebuilds six hash-listed ROMs with SAT-R’s agbcc fork, and compiles the same code into widescreen SDL ports for Linux, macOS and Windows plus PSP and PS2 builds. README reports Sonic Advance 2 built entirely from C with about 60 functions still non-matching. Extracted graphics, music and data are committed, so the builds read no original ROM.
requirements: README marks the project unfinished and under active development. It lists six ROM targets with SHA-1 values: Sonic Advance (Europe) and Sonic Advance 2 (USA, Europe, Japan, Japanese Virtual Console and a 2002-10-25 USA beta). README reports that SA2 builds 100% from C with about 60 non-matching functions pulled in from asm/non_matching, which at the reviewed commit holds 64 SA2, 99 SA1, 17 shared and 8 engine files, and that over 600 SA2 functions are unnamed. The Tiny Chao Garden and Collect Rings multiboot sub-games are built for matching and only partly decompiled.

The documented builds read no original ROM. The tree commits over 12,000 PNG sprite frames and tiles, 474 MIDI songs, tilemaps and other raw data, including a 191 KB data file included piecewise into the Tiny Chao Garden multiboot ROM. Port CI jobs still download a base ROM from private storage, which the Makefile does not reference.

INSTALL.md targets Linux (with WSL for Windows users) and macOS: ARM GCC and binutils, libpng, SDL2 and MinGW-w64, plus mkisofs or cdrtools for PS2. Matching GBA builds need SAT-R’s agbcc fork built and installed into the tree. Ports build with make sdl (Linux/macOS), sdl_win32 (Windows), sdl_psp (PSPDEV) and ps2 (PS2DEV) at a 426×240 widescreen resolution; README marks the Win32 OpenGL target not functional, and no GitHub release is published.

On the GBA platform, make runs a SHA-1 check of the built ROM against its listed hash. CI checks formatting, then builds and hash-checks SA2 USA, SA1 Europe and the four other SA2 variants; it also builds SDL, Win32, PSP and PS2 port targets for both games on Ubuntu and macOS, and replays a committed any% speedrun input recording through a headless SDL build. Matching applies to the GBA ROMs, not to the widescreen ports.

The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none. The extracted graphics, music and data, and the Nintendo SDK libraries rebuilt in libagbsyscall, m4a and agb_flash, keep their rights holders’ terms. README sets a strict no-LLM/no-AI policy for issues and pull requests.

resources.name: Paleblood: a functional decompilation of Bloodborne with its own runtime
resources.description: Rewrites code from Bloodborne’s PS4 executable (CUSA03173 with update 1.09) as readable C++, one function at a time, aiming at a native PC source port on a clean-room runtime of its own. It is a functional rather than matching decompilation: each replacement is hooked in, compared with the original machine code on recorded and generated inputs, and independently reviewed. Work is at an early stage: README reports 21 of 157,757 functions verified, and the game does not yet run on Paleblood’s own runtime.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-19 head, 12 days after the first commit. The generated status reports 31 functions replaced and 21 verified out of a 157,757-function Ghidra export; the project’s loader maps the executable, and its boot stops at the first unimplemented system call with 247 of 686 system imports implemented. Replacements cover parts of the frame loop and the event, kernel, input, AI, character, physics and render layers, and BB_TARGET_FPS reproduces three community frame-rate patches in code.

Requires Bloodborne CUSA03173 (EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from the user’s own PS4; the executables converted from it must match target.sha256. README says the repository holds no game code, assets, binaries, decompiler output or extracted data, a check rejects game data in the pre-commit hook and CI, and the project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools.

Development is documented on Linux with CMake 3.20+ and CTest, plus Ghidra 12.0.3 with the GhidraOrbis loader for analysis. Full game runs still use an external scaffold: third_party/bbport, the project’s fork of the GPL-2.0-or-later bloodborne_pc port, which runs the original executable natively with shadPS4-derived Vulkan rendering. CI does not fetch that submodule.

README says tools/verify.py runs the original code and a replacement side by side, comparing return values, registers, every byte written and every library call, and that deliberately wrong versions must fail; options that replace a community patch are checked against the original with that patch applied. CI builds with GCC and Clang and runs unit, harness and policy checks without game data, so verification against the game is contributor-run and project-reported.

GPL-2.0-or-later per LICENSE; the bbport scaffold has its own GPL-2.0-or-later notice, which README says grants no right in the game or its code. README calls Paleblood a fan project unaffiliated with Sony Interactive Entertainment or FromSoftware and describes the runtime as clean-room. CONTRIBUTING.md allows disclosed, verified AI-assisted work, and recent commits carry Co-Authored-By trailers naming Claude Opus 5.5 and Codex.

resources.name: Pikmin 2: a fully matched GameCube decompilation across five releases
resources.description: A fan decompilation of Pikmin 2 that rebuilds main.dol for five GameCube releases (USA retail, two USA demos, PAL and Japan) with the original Metrowerks compilers, checking each against a stored SHA-1. The build reads main.dol from the user’s own copy of each release. decomp.dev reported all code matched and fully linked for every version at the reviewed commit, and a non-matching mode builds the US DOL entirely from C++ for modding.
requirements: README still calls this a work-in-progress decompilation and lists five supported versions: GPVE01 (USA retail, the default), GPVE01_D17 and GPVE01_D18 (USA demos 17 and 18), GPVP01 (PAL) and GPVJ01 (Japan). Each has its own configuration and SHA-1 file, and CI builds all five. Outputs are GameCube DOLs, not a PC executable or port.

Each version needs main.dol from the user’s own copy of that release at orig/<version>/sys/main.dol, and decomp-toolkit checks it against the hash in that version’s config.yml before splitting. The repository commits game-derived symbol and split tables for every version; config comments say the GPVE01 symbols were generated from a pikmin2UP.MAP linker map and the Japanese and PAL tables were recovered from those DOLs using the US symbols. No disc images or extracted game files are included.

Builds need Python and ninja on Windows (native tooling recommended), macOS (with wine-crossover) or Linux (an automatically downloaded wibo on x86, Wine elsewhere). configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.7.5, objdiff v3.4.1, binutils 2.42-1, sjiswrap v1.2.2, wibo 1.0.0-beta.5 and the 20250812 compiler bundle, using Metrowerks GC/2.6 for game, JSystem and runtime code and GC/1.2.5n for the Dolphin SDK libraries.

configure.py marks 1,154 objects Matching for every supported version and one more for Japan only; none is NonMatching. The default ninja target checks the linked DOL against config/<version>/build.sha1 before reporting progress, and CI builds all five versions in a container that supplies the original files and compilers. decomp.dev’s reports for the pinned commit list 100.00% of code matched and fully linked for each version (24,957 functions and 1,153 units for GPVE01).

With --non-matching, README says the final hash check is disabled and the US DOL builds completely from C++ source that is, to the team’s knowledge, functionally equivalent, so every file can be edited for modding. The repository carries CC0-1.0 in LICENSE.MD; Nintendo’s game, its files and the downloaded compilers fall outside that dedication.

resources.name: Gran Turismo 4: an agent-assisted PS2 engine matching decompilation
resources.description: Decompiles Gran Turismo 4’s PS2 engine executable (CORE.GT4, NTSC-U v1.01) into one C or C++ source per function for Sony’s ee-gcc 2.96, matching public libraries such as newlib and Expat from their own source. The README credits AI agents (Anthropic’s Claude) driving the project’s tools with most of the matching, each function accepted only on a compiler-and-judge comparison, and reports 95.4% of functions and 83.6% of code bytes matched for an October 2026 commit. A local full build links sources at their original addresses, fills the rest from disassembly and compares SHA-1 with the user’s executable.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress matching decompilation of the engine executable only: most game logic lives in Adhoc scripts, which the separate OpenAdhoc project re-creates, and the separate GT4 Native PC port is described as not playable. The progress-branch report for commit ba5d800 (2026-10-19), which decomp.dev also shows for the reviewed commit, gives 29,551 of 30,962 functions and 83.55% of code matched, 82.08% of code linked from source and 2.13% of data placed from source; 202 hand-written assembly functions are not counted.

Supply your own Gran Turismo 4 (USA) v1.01 disc image (SCUS-97328); orig/README.md lists SHA-1 values for SCUS_973.28, CORE.GT4 and the ELF converted from it. Nothing from the game is committed, so the SHA-1 build check and the progress reports run only where those files are present, not in CI.

Documented for Linux or WSL (Ubuntu) with Python 3.11+ and rabbitizer. tools/setup_linux.sh installs MIPS binutils and 32-bit libc, downloads decomp.me’s ee-gcc 2.96 build, clones decomp-permuter and installs splat in a virtual environment; project.toml names further decomp.me compilers, including ee-gcc 2.9 for about 270 Sony SDK functions.

A function counts as matched when tools/match.py (or the agents’ tools/swarm.py) prints MATCH, and tools/build.py links every function at its original address and compares SHA-1 of the loaded segments. CI runs unit tests, an assembly-in-C policy check and layout checks and compiles every source, but cannot link or compare without the game; matching figures are author-reported.

MIT for the project’s tools, documentation and source. THIRD_PARTY.md lists matched public libraries under their own terms (Expat, newlib, GNU libio and the GCC runtime under GPL with exceptions, SGI STL headers, MT19937), which build.py --without can leave out, and records proprietary SCE-RT/Medius, Logitech and Sony SDK code as identified but not copied. Gran Turismo 4 belongs to Sony Interactive Entertainment. Agent instructions are in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and .claude/.

resources.name: Mario Kart Wii: an in-progress matching decompilation of the PAL release
resources.description: A work-in-progress matching decompilation of Mario Kart Wii that targets the PAL release (RMCP01), rebuilding main.dol and the StaticR.rel module from C and C++ with Metrowerks compilers and checking both against stored SHA-1 values. The build splits these binaries from a user-supplied disc image, and objdiff compares objects during development. The README’s progress badges point to a decomp.dev page that did not resolve at review, and the default branch was last updated in September 2025.
requirements: README lists one supported version, RMCP01 (PAL); configure.py defines no other and CI builds only RMCP01. The repository was renamed from riidefi/mkw, which README’s badges and clone command still use, and CONTRIBUTING.md and HACK.md still describe an earlier mkwutil and ppcdis build layout that the pinned tree no longer contains. The output is a Wii main.dol and StaticR.rel, not a PC port.

Copy your own RMCP01 disc image to orig/RMCP01; ISO (GCM), RVZ, WIA, WBFS, CISO, NFS, GCZ and TGC images are accepted, and config.yml records the expected SHA-1 of both binaries. README says the repository contains no game assets or assembly; decomp-toolkit splits main.dol and StaticR.rel locally using the committed, game-derived symbol and split tables.

Builds need Python and ninja on Windows (native tooling recommended), macOS (with wine-crossover) or Linux (an automatically downloaded wibo on x86, Wine elsewhere). configure.py pins decomp-toolkit v1.3.0, objdiff v2.4.0, binutils 2.42-1, sjiswrap v1.2.0, wibo 0.6.16 and the 20240706 compiler bundle, using Metrowerks Wii/0x4201_127 for the game, NW4R, EGG, RFL and MSL code and as the linker, and GC/3.0a5.2 for the Revolution SDK, TRK, DWC and GameSpy libraries.

Objects marked Matching (106 of the 213 listed in configure.py; 105 NonMatching, 2 Equivalent) are compiled from source and the rest of each binary comes from the split originals; the default ninja target checks main.dol and StaticR.rel against config/RMCP01/build.sha1 before reporting progress. CI builds RMCP01 in a private container holding the original files and uploads a progress report. decomp.dev had no report for the repository under either name at review.

The repository carries CC0-1.0; lib/gamespy keeps the GameSpy SDK’s own BSD-style license from IGN Entertainment, and Nintendo’s game, disc contents and the downloaded compilers keep their own rights.

resources.name: Pinyon Shift: a ShiftGlue static recompilation of Forza Horizon for PC
resources.description: Builds a native port of the Xbox 360 release of Forza Horizon by translating its PowerPC executable ahead of time into C++ with ShiftGlue, the author’s fork of ReXGlue, and compiling it on the player’s machine from their own disc. A renderer written for this game runs its GPU commands on Vulkan, and some translated library code, such as FMOD Ex DSP units, is replaced by independently written native code checked against the translated original. README presents it as a playable preview with rendering bugs and slowdowns.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-17 head, tagged v0.6.0; the repository was created on 2026-08-25. It holds the launcher, build tools, host code and configuration, and README says it contains no game, assets, generated translations or prebuilt executable; the v0.6.0 Windows launcher archive holds only the launcher and a source archive. This is static recompilation with native replacements, not recovered authored source.

Requires an ISO dumped from the user’s own USA retail disc (serial MS-2505, title ID 4D5309C9) or an unmodified folder extracted from it; setup checks its exact size and SHA-256 against config/supported-dumps.json and rejects unknown dumps. Owned DLC packages are verified before import, and the Rally and 1000 Club add-ons need the optional title update v4 build.

Players need Windows 10/11 x64, x86-64 Linux including SteamOS, or macOS 13+ on Apple silicon, with a Vulkan 1.3 GPU; NVIDIA is tested, while AMD and Intel are not yet qualified. The launcher installs pinned build tools and builds the game locally, which takes 20–60 minutes and about 30 GB the first time; the Windows source path needs Visual Studio 2022 C++ Build Tools 17.1+. An Android 13+ arm64 build is a developer alpha cross-compiled on the PC.

CI checks the repository boundary, runs release-tooling and host tests, builds the launchers and cross-builds the Android runtime, all without the game. Scripted render-test routes, golden frame replays and README’s performance figures, such as a 119 fps median at 1x on an RTX 4080, come from the project’s local runs.

BSD-3-Clause covers only independently authored material. docs/LEGAL.md says it grants no rights to Forza Horizon, Xbox software, ReXGlue or user-supplied content, and bars committing generated translations, hand translations of disassembly or decompiler output, and data copied from the executable. README states no affiliation with Microsoft, Xbox, Turn 10 Studios or Playground Games. CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md agent instructions bar AI attribution in commits.

resources.name: Touhou 7: reconstructing Perfect Cherry Blossom 1.00b source
resources.description: Reconstructs C++ source for the Windows executable of Touhou 7: Perfect Cherry Blossom 1.00b and its custom.exe configuration tool, built with the original Visual Studio .NET 2002 and DirectX 8 toolchain and compared function by function with the user’s originals through reccmp. The committed progress badges report th07.exe fully implemented at 99.78% accuracy and custom.exe fully matched. The README says the game should be fully playable, but a matching build trips the game’s integrity check, and the cross-platform ports live on separate branches.
requirements: README calls this a work-in-progress matching decompilation of th07.exe 1.00b and custom.exe; the committed, mutable badges report 694 of 694 th07.exe functions implemented at 99.78% accuracy, and custom.exe at 100% for both. Behaviour is meant to match the original but may differ. The portable and reallyportable branches (desktop, mobile and web ports) are separate. README credits the GensokyoClub th06 and th08 decompilations for shared types, names and code.

Supply your own th07.exe 1.00b (README gives its MD5, reccmp-project.yml its SHA-256), copied to resources/, for icon extraction and as reccmp’s comparison base; custom.exe is needed only for the configuration tool, and --no-icon builds without either. No game executable or game data files are committed; resources/csv holds the function, global, string and float tables reccmp uses.

This branch builds only for 32-bit Windows with the MSVC 2002 toolchain, run under Wine on Linux, and needs uv and ninja. scripts/download_deps.py fetches Visual Studio .NET 2002 and the DirectX 8 SDK from archive.org and EstexNT’s var_order compiler patch from a gist; scripts/build.py generates and runs the ninja build.

Contributors diff with reccmp, which reports per-function accuracy against the original as an HTML page or for one address. Because th07.exe is not yet byte-identical, README says a matching build fails the game’s integrity check and crashes after 3,999 Supervisor cycles; --no-matching disables that check. The repository has no CI; badge figures are project-generated.

CC0 1.0 for the repository; the game and the downloaded Microsoft toolchain and SDK keep their own terms. resources/svgicon.png, embedded in the progress badge, is the game’s cover artwork marked © 2003 Team Shanghai Alice, which the CC0 dedication does not cover.

resources.name: DKC1Recomp: static recompilation of Donkey Kong Country
resources.description: Statically recompiles the North American v1.0 SNES release of Donkey Kong Country into native Windows, macOS and iOS applications with a pinned fork of snesrecomp, which translates 65816 code to C and links it against a modelled SNES hardware runtime. Function boundaries, entry flag states and jump-table targets are ingested from a byte-identical community disassembly instead of discovered heuristically, and the game code is generated locally from the user’s verified ROM. Optional widescreen, CRT filters, MSU-1 music and a Dixie Kong Country variant are host-side additions to what the README calls a playable bring-up.
requirements: Reviewed at the main commit tagged v0.0.14 (2026-09-15); releases v0.0.15 to v0.0.17 (through 2026-09-19) are tagged on commits that are not on main. README reports a playable bring-up with fully statically generated game code, a headless validation host and Windows, macOS and iOS hosts. Widescreen, on by default in the desktop host, fails closed to stock output or black margins where a scene is unproven; the generated widescreen coverage report lists 252 of 256 level entrances as never observed, and the Dixie variant is not validated over the full game.

Supply your own headerless Donkey Kong Country (USA) v1.0 ROM of 4 MiB, checked against the SHA-256 in the README; other images are rejected unless a single audited data-only edit is pinned by its hash. The optional Baby Kong mod also verifies the user’s own North American DKC3 ROM in memory. README states that no ROM bytes, extracted assets or generated game code are committed; the Dixie variant embeds the hack author’s public IPS patch, which the project records as a deliberate exception applied only to the verified clean ROM.

A source build initializes the snesrecomp submodule and runs scripts/generate_snesrecomp.py against the ROM, writing C into the git-ignored generated/ directory; recomp/*.cfg holds only names, addresses and structural metadata from the GPL-3 Yoshifanatic1 disassembly. Windows builds need Windows 10/11 x64, Visual Studio 2022 C++ tools, Python 3, Git, CMake, Ninja and an OpenGL 3.3 GPU; the arm64 macOS app targets macOS 26 with CMake, Ninja and SDL2, and the iOS sideload IPA needs iOS/iPadOS 16 or newer and re-signing for the recipient’s device.

Verification is deterministic tooling rather than a matching build: a headless host with input playback, replayable flight-recorder bundles, save-state continuity checks, route recipes and regression contracts, plus C and Python model tests, many of which need the private ROM. The reviewed tree has no CI workflow; the bring-up log reports nine private boot replays and inspection of the live window for the v0.0.10 Windows host.

Project host and tooling code is MIT; the pinned snesrecomp fork is under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0, the cfg metadata keeps its GPL-3 provenance, the Windows package adds SDL 2.30.9 (zlib) and miniz 3.0.2 (MIT), and Nintendo and Rare keep their game rights. AGENTS.md sets operating rules for Codex and other coding agents working in the repository.

resources.name: San Andreas Unity: a GTA San Andreas engine reimplementation in Unity
resources.description: Reimplements the Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas engine in Unity (C#), loading the archives, RenderWare models and textures, collision, animations, audio, text and item definitions from the user’s own PC installation. README says it will not be a complete reimplementation; it focuses on gameplay features, multiplayer and a framework for extending and modding the game through C# plugins. Development has stalled: the newest commit on any branch dates from 2022-09-30.
requirements: Reviewed at the head of the default dev branch, committed 2022-09-30; no branch has a later commit, GitHub records the last push on 2023-06-16 and the latest release is v4.0 (2022-05-24), so the project appears inactive. README says it will not be a complete reimplementation and focuses on gameplay, multiplayer and a moddable framework; Docs/TODO.md still lists work such as asynchronous geometry loading and unloading distant parts of the world.

Play requires a PC installation of GTA San Andreas that the user owns: on first start the game asks for its path, and config.json points the loaders at data files such as gta.dat, the vehicle, ped and default .ide files, handling.cfg, water.dat, carcols.dat and weapon.dat. The Android build needs those PC files copied to the device, about 5 GB according to the wiki, with the audio folder optional. The repository ships no game data; the NavMeshes submodule holds a precomputed navigation mesh, which the wiki says is generated from the imported game world because the original game has none.

Development uses Unity 2020.3.26 or newer (the project file names 2020.3.26f1), a recursive clone of the MirrorLite, UnityStandardAssets, NavMeshes, NetworkDiscoveryUnity and UGameCoreUtilities submodules and the Startup scene. README reports testing on Linux, Windows, macOS and Android with both Mono and IL2CPP backends; v4.0 provides Windows and Linux archives and an Android APK. Multiplayer runs as a dedicated server, host or client, and game modes load as C# DLL plugins.

There is no CI workflow or automated test suite for the importers or gameplay, and no comparison with the original executable is published. Evidence consists of README claims that multiplayer fully works, the v4.0 release notes, screenshots and videos; Docs/Performance.md records vertex and draw-call counts for one Las Venturas view.

LICENSE is MIT with a 2015 copyright line for James King; the bundled NVorbis and Newtonsoft.Json DLLs and the submodules are separate projects under their own terms, and Rockstar’s game files keep their own rights.

resources.name: MinecraftLCE: an early-stage Minecraft: Nintendo Switch Edition decompilation
resources.description: Decompiles Minecraft: Nintendo Switch Edition v1.0.17, a Legacy Console Edition release, into C++ that is compared function by function with the original executable using a patched Clang 4.0.1 and the open-ead Switch decompilation tools. The README explains the choice of the Switch build for its matchable Clang toolchain and type information, with names ported from the symbol-bearing Wii U Edition. At the reviewed commit the function list marks about 11% of functions decompiled, most of them matching; the result cannot run the game.
requirements: README describes a work-in-progress decompilation of Minecraft: Nintendo Switch Edition v1.0.17 that cannot be used to play the game. At the reviewed commit data/mcswitch_functions.csv lists 57,972 functions: 6,279 matching, 224 non-matching and 51,469 not yet decompiled, the 11.217% that a workflow writes into the GitHub description. Matched functions are checked individually; there is no whole-executable rebuild.

Supply the main NSO executable from your own Minecraft: Nintendo Switch Edition v1.0.17 update; the Wii U Edition’s Minecraft.Client.rpx (Patch 35, v560) is recommended only for porting symbols. README says these executables will never be provided in the repository and no game assets are included.

Documented for Linux or WSL (with macOS also intended): Python 3.6+, Ninja, CMake 3.13+, ccache, llvm-objdump, libncurses5, a Rust toolchain and the listed Python modules. tools/setup.py converts the executable, downloads Clang 4.0.1 from the LLVM releases and applies the committed libc++ patches; submodules supply open-ead’s nx-decomp-tools, nnheaders and musl and the stb image library, and lib/ vendors libpng and zlib.

tools/check compares compiled functions with the original and tools/common/progress.py summarises the function list. CI lints, compiles the project without the game and publishes progress counted from the committed function list, so matching status is project-reported.

No license file is present and GitHub detects none; Minecraft belongs to Microsoft and Mojang, and vendored libraries keep their own licenses. README says Microsoft-licensed Java Edition mappings cannot be used and notes that projects whose research was not clean-room have been taken down.

resources.name: Final Fantasy VII: a matching PlayStation decompilation
resources.description: Reconstructs C source for the US PlayStation release of Final Fantasy VII, aiming for code that compiles back to the original main executable and its game overlays. The build splits the user’s disc files with splat, compiles with period cc1-psx compilers and checks every rebuilt file against its SHA-1. A native build against the PsyZ PlayStation-library replacement is compiled in CI but is not documented as a playable port.
requirements: The project describes itself as a matching decompilation of the PS1 game; config/us.yaml defines the single us version, covering SCUS_941.63 and battle, field, menu, world, minigame, magic and other overlays with 29 SHA-1 entries. Source tables such as the chocobo minigame’s arccosine table are data taken from the game, as is usual for such projects. README states no completion figure; CI uploads a progress report as a build artifact.

Supply disc 1 of Final Fantasy VII (USA) as BIN/CUE under disks/; README lists the USA Interactive Sampler CD as optional, though the reviewed config builds only us. CONTRIBUTING says the repository includes no original game data and is not a playable or standalone version. CI fetches its disc images from a private dependency repository through a secret token.

README documents Debian/Ubuntu and Arch Linux with Go, Python 3 (a venv with splat64, spimdisasm and others), ninja, 7zip, bchunk and mipsel-linux-gnu binutils and GCC; CI notes that Ubuntu 24.04’s binutils 2.42 linker does not match the game. Make downloads the cc1-psx-26 and cc1-psx-272 compiler builds from the project’s init release and checks them against committed SHA-256 files; maspsx, m2c, asm-differ and PsyZ come in as submodules, and a Dockerfile is provided.

make build ends with a ninja rule running sha1sum -c over the expected hashes of every overlay. CI on the upstream repository checks formatting, runs that build, lints for overlapping symbols and compiles the PsyZ build. These checks compare file identity for the US release.

LICENSE is AGPL-3.0; the game discs, extracted data and downloaded compilers keep separate rights. README says the decompiled code is written by humans and rejects LLM-accelerated decompilation, while allowing LLMs for tooling, permuting hard functions or hunting runtime bugs; CONTRIBUTING forbids autonomously generated pull requests and commit messages.

resources.name: Mega Man X Recompiled: a snesrecomp static recompilation
resources.description: Statically translates the 65816 CPU code of the SNES Mega Man X (USA Rev 1) to C with the snesrecomp framework; the PPU, audio, DMA and other hardware run in the framework’s runtime, and a LakeSnes-derived interpreter executes whatever the static pass cannot prove. The C is generated locally from the user’s ROM, with function names imported from community DiztinGUIsh annotations. Playable Zero, co-op and rollback netplay, X2/X3 boss weapons and adaptive widescreen are layered on top, using assets extracted locally from the user’s own sequel ROMs.
requirements: Reviewed at the main commit of release v2.2.9-alpha (2026-10-18), which offers a Windows ZIP and a Linux AppImage. The snesrecomp README lists the game as fully playable, and this README says the adaptive widescreen renderer was playtested through the ending on Windows. Execution is interpreter-first: compiled bodies replace only code the analysis proves, the rest stays interpreted, and Rockman X (Japan v1.1) is a separate variant that keeps its original view.

Supply your own Mega Man X (USA) Rev 1 ROM as .sfc or .smc, headered or not. Zero, co-op and the X3 weapons also need the user’s Mega Man X3 USA ROM, and the X2 weapons the Mega Man X2 USA ROM; their assets are extracted on the user’s machine. README states that ROMs, extracted assets and the generated src/gen C are neither committed nor in the downloads; the Saber Zero sprites and sounds from the Zashiko Mod are included with permission for non-commercial use.

Source builds clone the snesrecomp, recomp-ui and dizProjects submodules, stage the ROM and run tools/regen.sh, which emits per-bank C from recomp/bank*.cfg. CMake with Ninja and SDL3, or SDL2 as a fallback, is the maintained build: Windows 10+ through MSYS2 mingw64 with Python 3.9+ and rustup, Linux with gcc or clang, and macOS on Apple Silicon or Intel.

CI compiles ROM-free setup hosts and runs the ROM-free CTest regressions; ROM-backed state tests and a replay suite that stops at the first WRAM, co-op, camera or VRAM mismatch need the user’s ROMs. A dated coverage checkpoint reports two 12,000-frame routes matching the control build’s CPU and WRAM traces and final snapshots, without comparing audio, and the v2.2.9 release notes report Windows and Linux checks of all 28 Boss Rush pairs.

The project and the pinned snesrecomp framework are under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0; the interpreter is LakeSnes-derived (MIT), vendored dependencies keep their own licenses, and Capcom keeps its game rights. README presents the project as part of R.A.I.D. (Retro AI Development), a Discord community for AI-assisted retro reverse engineering.

resources.name: OpenSC4: an early open-source reimplementation of SimCity 4
resources.description: Reimplements SimCity 4 as a Godot project in GDScript that reads DBPF archives, region folders and city saves from the user’s own SimCity 4 installation. The code draws a region view with city thumbnails and interface elements built from the game’s UI definitions, opens a saved city’s terrain and water in 3D, and includes a DAT explorer for previewing archive subfiles. It is an early, inactive engine case without simulation gameplay, not a playable replacement.
requirements: The reviewed main snapshot (2024-03-29) only added a README and a Discord invite; the last code change dates from 2023-02-17, and the repository has no releases or tags. README describes an open source “clone” meant to use modern hardware and run on other platforms. The code covers DBPF parsing, a region view for the hard-coded Timbuktu region, a city terrain view and the DAT explorer, with no zoning, budget or growth simulation.

Needs the user’s own SimCity 4 installation: the boot screen asks for its folder and checks for SimCity 4.ini, Sound.dat, Intro.dat, SimCity_1.dat to SimCity_5.dat and EP1.dat, then reads .sc4 city saves, config.bmp and region music from that folder. .gitignore excludes SimCity 4 data, although the tree contains a “Graphics Rules.sgr.backup” text file whose header says SC4Launcher generated it.

Runs from source in the Godot editor: README’s setup is to install Godot, import the cloned project and run it, without naming a version. project.godot uses config_version 4 and the scripts call Godot 3 APIs such as yield and Directory; no export presets or packaged builds are provided.
The repository has no tests or CI workflows and publishes no comparison with SimCity 4’s behaviour or output.

GitHub detects no license and the tree has no license file; nine GDScript files carry AGPL-3.0-or-later headers for “The OpenSC4 contributors” (2023), and utils/logger.gd is MIT-licensed code from KOBUGE Games’ godot-logger. SimCity 4 and its data keep their owners’ rights.

resources.name: synchrony
resources.description: JavaScript cleaner and deobfuscator aimed mainly at output from javascript-obfuscator (obfuscator.io). It parses a script with acorn and runs a fixed pipeline of AST transformers that fold expressions, clean member accesses, remove dead branches, split sequence expressions, undo switch-based control-flow flattening and decode string arrays, re-implementing their base64 and RC4 decoders in TypeScript rather than executing the input. It ships on npm as deobfuscator with a synchrony CLI and a library API, and optional renaming replaces identifiers with generated word names rather than recovering the originals.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2.4.6, published to GitHub and to npm as deobfuscator on 2026-07-07, the same day as the reviewed master commit; the previous release, 2.4.5, dates from 2023-11-09. The README also points to a hosted web version at deobfuscate.relative.im.

Install with npm, yarn or pnpm, or from the Git repository; package.json declares no Node.js version. The CLI reads one file, writes <name>.cleaned.<ext> unless --output is given, and offers --rename, --loose parsing, --ecma-version and --sourceType. A --config file is loaded with Node's require, so it runs as code, and a custom transformer list replaces the default pipeline; two jsconfuser transformers are available only that way and are not documented in the README.

The README warns that output from old javascript-obfuscator versions will likely not deobfuscate correctly and that there is no user configuration for the automatic string decoder. The repository has no test suite, and its latest commit removed the GitHub CI configuration.
GPL-3.0-only according to package.json and LICENSE.md.

resources.name: R.E.L.I.V.E.: an Oddworld Abe’s Oddysee and Abe’s Exoddus engine reimplementation
resources.description: Reimplements the engine of Oddworld: Abe’s Oddysee and Abe’s Exoddus as an open-source replacement executable that runs from the user’s own game folder. The team decompiled the original executables and replaced their functions incrementally, using injected DLLs that hook reimplemented code into the patched retail executable, then rewrote the result into a standalone cross-platform engine. The project site says both games are playable in their entirety, with bug fixes and windowed, high-resolution and controller play.
requirements: Reviewed at the master commit of 2026-09-01 that merged the SDL3 port; the latest release is github-v1.0.9, labelled “relive stable v1.0.9” (2025-03-21), while CMake still declares project version 0.1. The project site’s FAQ says both games can be played through, over a hundred original bugs are fixed and there should be no noticeable gameplay difference from the retail version; PSX-quality music, deeper modding and an in-game level editor are listed as future work. The FAQ describes the method as decompiling the retail executable and then spending years rewriting the output into readable code.

Play requires the user’s own Abe’s Oddysee or Abe’s Exoddus installation; the FAQ names the Steam, GOG and early disc versions. The executable runs from the game folder that holds the .lvl files, and the Linux launcher scripts look for the default Steam folder or ask for that directory. The repository contains no game data files, though source files embed data tables used by the reimplemented code, such as fonts and video-decompression tables; the FAQ says the team will not provide game files.

Builds use CMake 3.10+, C++17 and SDL3 after a recursive clone of the Detours, googletest, magic_enum, jsonxx, stb, lodepng and nlohmann/json submodules; README documents Visual Studio 2022 on Windows and Ubuntu packages on Linux, and cpack produces a Debian package. MSVC builds also produce the AliveDllAE and AliveDllAO hooking DLLs, linked with Detours on 32-bit Windows. GitHub Actions builds Windows 32-bit, Windows 64-bit and Linux packages; its macOS job is commented out, although the FAQ says the games run on macOS.

The GitHub Actions workflow builds and packages without running tests. The tree has googletest unit and integration tests for the relive_api level-data tool, and the integration test reads .lvl files from hard-coded GOG install paths; older AppVeyor and Azure Pipelines configurations still invoke ctest. The FAQ reports automated replays that record a full play-through with a stable build and flag desyncs in development builds (the recorder saves input, RNG, ticks and sync points), but no replay results are published.

The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none; README only says contributions will be licensed under a GPL-compatible license, most likely MIT, in the future, so reuse terms are currently unstated. 3rdParty/DxOld carries three DirectX 7-era Direct3D headers, one with a Microsoft all-rights-reserved notice, and the submodules keep their own licenses. The FAQ disclaims affiliation with Oddworld Inhabitants, whose games keep their own rights.

resources.name: RetDec
resources.description: Avast's retargetable machine-code decompiler built on LLVM. It takes ELF, PE, Mach-O, COFF, AR, Intel HEX or raw code for 32-bit x86, ARM, MIPS, PIC32 and PowerPC or 64-bit x86-64 and ARM64, recovers functions, types and C++ class hierarchies, and emits C or a Python-like language with call and control-flow graphs.
requirements: README warns that RetDec is in limited maintenance mode: pull requests are reviewed with priority, issues get delayed reactions and are not actively solved unless they concern basic maintenance, and only very limited development continues. The latest release is v5.0 (2022-12-08); the reviewed master commit of 2026-05-26 is 81 commits ahead of it and still declares version 5.0.

Release packages cover Linux, macOS and Windows; README lists Windows 7+, Linux, macOS and experimental FreeBSD, with about 5–6 GB per installation. Source builds need a C++17 compiler (GCC 7+, Visual Studio 2017 15.7+ or full Xcode on macOS 10.15+), OpenSSL 1.1.1+, Python 3.4+ and, outside Windows, autotools; CMakeLists.txt requires CMake 3.13, not README's 3.6. The build downloads pinned Capstone, Keystone, YARA and yaramod, an Avast LLVM fork and a 2019 support package.

Input is the user's own executable, object file, archive or raw machine code. Since v5.0 the decompiler is also a set of CMake libraries for other projects, and separate retdec-idaplugin and retdec-r2plugin repositories embed it in IDA and radare2.

GitHub Actions builds Release and Debug builds on Ubuntu 22.04, Windows (MSYS2) and macOS, then runs the separate retdec-regression-tests suite. README calls nightly builds unguaranteed, with possible regressions, and Docker support community-maintained.
MIT (Avast Software). The modified PeLib keeps its zlib/libpng license, and LICENSE-THIRD-PARTY lists the other components, including Keystone used under its FOSS exception to GPLv2.

resources.name: Age of Empires Free Software Remake: a re-implementation on the original data
resources.description: Re-implements Microsoft’s Age of Empires and its Rise of Rome expansion as a cross-platform C++17 engine on SDL2 and OpenGL that loads the original game’s DRS archives and language.dll resources. README says it mimics the Windows API and the Genie engine for compatibility and reconstructs some code from the disassembly; the repository adds format notes and Python tools for inspecting the original data files. Only very basic gameplay through a multiplayer session exists so far, so it is an early engine case rather than a playable replacement.
requirements: The reviewed master snapshot (2026-09-20) sets CMake version 0.1, and the repository has no releases or tags; the user guide says no binary builds are provided. README reports only very basic gameplay and only multiplayer mode: single-player means hosting a session and adding computer players, which only gather resources until attacked. doc/reverse_engineering documents the DRS archive contents, the Windows API functions the original imports, the scenario format, civilizations and unit statistics.

Needs a legitimate copy of Age of Empires or Rise of Rome, on the CD-ROM or installed: the engine loads Border.drs, graphics.drs, Interfac.drs, sounds.drs and Terrain.drs from the data folder plus language.dll, and expects the game fonts COPRGTB.TTF and COPRGTL.TTF that the original installer adds. The repository contains no game data, and community replacement assets are not supported yet.

README lists Windows 10+, macOS Sequoia 15.7.7, Fedora 44 and Ubuntu 22+ as tested, while INSTALL still warns that Linux builds look for hard-coded legacy TTF font paths. Builds use CMake 3.11+ with C99 and C++17 against SDL2, SDL2_image, SDL2_mixer and OpenGL, plus the imgui, tracy, wepoll and miniz submodules; Windows builds use Visual Studio with vcpkg or MinGW.

GitHub Actions builds the game with Clang on Ubuntu and Fedora and runs the Google Test suite in headless mode; its tests cover networking, the protocol, the server, SDL and a UI menu rather than equivalence with the original executable. No comparison with the original game is published.

LICENSE applies Apache-2.0; the submodules and the bundled headers in game/src/external keep their own licenses. README states that all copyrighted material and trademarks belong to their respective owners and calls the work an educational non-profit project.

resources.name: God of War PS2 static recompilation: a native Windows port via PS2Recomp
resources.description: Statically recompiles the MIPS R5900 code of the NTSC-U PlayStation 2 God of War executable (SCUS-97399) to C++ with PS2Recomp and builds it as a native Windows program. Since October 2026 the port builds on Waffle565’s runtime, which replaces the PS2 hardware with native code: VU1 microprograms and, optionally, the game’s IRX modules are compiled ahead of time, and an OpenGL renderer stands in for the GS. The repository holds only the game-specific function map, recompiler configuration, overrides and runtime patches; the README reports gameplay on the opening ship level, with sustained 60 fps and a full playthrough still pending.
requirements: Reviewed at main (2026-10-18); the project has published no release. README marks the port experimental and reports boot, menus, a new game and the ship fight with HUD, native VU1 and IOP, and exact game speed. Sustained 60 fps, saves and movies with sound (so far verified only in Waffle565’s port), a full playthrough and PAL languages remain open, and an intermittent hang of the window thread is under investigation. The .recomp.json metadata still describes an earlier, not-yet-playable state, and most technical documents are in Spanish.

Requires the user’s own NTSC-U God of War disc (SCUS-97399): the build reads its SCUS_973.99 executable, and play reads the IRX modules and PAK data from the user’s disc files kept at their original sectors. README states that the repository contains no game files, IRX modules or generated C++, and .gitignore excludes disc images, the executable, IRX and PAK files and the generated directories.

Builds only on Windows 10/11 x64 with Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools (C++ workload, including CMake and Ninja), Git and Python 3, with about 20 GB free and 16 GB of RAM recommended. scripts/2_compilar.cmd clones PS2Recomp at commit c5a9d02, applies the patches in order, generates about 6,400 C++ files from the user’s executable and builds ps2EntryRunner.exe; the first build takes 20–40 minutes.

CI validates the function map and recompiler configuration, applies every patch to PS2Recomp and runs its ps2x_tests runtime suite against a known-failures list, and runs game-independent GS, VU1, pad and camera tests, plus a Windows job that links an isolated PCSX2 GS module without a GPU. Gameplay and performance figures come from the author’s runs on one Ryzen 7 5800XT and RX 5700 XT machine, recorded in docs/ESTADO.md.

The repository is GPL-3.0, matching PS2Recomp; the applied runtime comes from Waffle565’s God-Of-War-Native-Port, whose repository root has no license file, and brings PCSX2-derived code (GPL-3.0+). Sony Interactive Entertainment and Santa Monica Studio keep their game rights. AGENTS.md says several agents work on main at once, CLAUDE.md points Claude to those conventions and the status log credits fixes to Claude.

resources.name: REDasm
resources.description: Cross-platform interactive disassembler whose version 4 is a plain-C rewrite: a C17 engine library, the Qt6 GUI kept in this repository, and loader, processor and analyzer plugins loaded as shared libraries. The listing supports renaming, comments and typed data, with a synchronized control-flow graph, cross-references, string detection, a hex view, patching and saved projects. Besides PE and ELF, loaders cover retro and console formats such as DOS MZ, Win16 NE, OS/2 LE/LX, PlayStation 1, original Xbox and ZX Spectrum, with x86/x86-64, MIPS32, ARM/Thumb, ARM64, Z80 and 6502 processors.
requirements: Latest release at review: v4.0.0-beta3, published 2026-09-02, with a Linux x86_64 AppImage and a portable Windows x86_64 ZIP plus GPG-signed checksums; the reviewed master commit is 43 commits ahead of that tag. Nightly builds from master, which the README warns may be unstable, also include macOS DMGs. Version 4 is a complete rewrite still in beta; the README says version 3 was retired, and its last release, 3.0 beta 5, dates from 2021.

The README rates Windows 10+ with Visual Studio 2022 and Linux with GCC 12+ (Ubuntu 24.04/Debian 13 reference) as actively tested platforms with official binaries; FreeBSD and macOS only pass CI builds and tests, and Haiku only compiles. Source builds go through the separate workspace repository, which fetches the core, GUI, plugin and knowledge-base repositories and needs CMake 3.20, C17/C++17 compilers and Qt 6.8 LTS.

Executables and console program files are supplied by the user. The README's maturity tables rate PE, ELF and x86/x86-64 support production ready and Visual Basic 5/6 event recovery highly stable, but the DOS MZ, PS1 BIOS, Xbox, ZX Spectrum and NES (NROM only) loaders and the Z80 and 6502 processors only functional, and MSVC RTTI and exception-handling recovery work in progress. There is no decompiler yet, and extensions are written in C; a Python plugin API is on the roadmap.
GPL-3.0 for the GUI, the core and every bundled plugin; the separate knowledge-base repository of TOML signatures and type definitions is CC0-1.0.

resources.name: protobuf-inspector
resources.description: Parses Protocol Buffers blobs (proto2 or proto3) without their .proto definition and prints a colored view of the fields in wire order, trying each length-delimited chunk as a nested message, then a packed array, a string and finally a hexdump. Analysts record what they work out in a protobuf_config.py file, with field types and names, message and enum types and custom native types, until the parser no longer has to guess. Field names, zig-zag encoding, signedness and integer-versus-float choices cannot be read from the wire, and the README says guesses can be wrong, especially for small chunks.
requirements: Development is dormant: the only release, 0.2 on PyPI and tagged v0.2.0, and the reviewed master commit both date from 2020-11-24, with no later commits.
