resources.description: A table-based reading list of 71 research papers on automatic protocol reverse engineering for network protocols, from the Protocol Informatics project (2004) to NetPlier (2021). Built from three surveys and extended since, it compares each method by approach, by input (network traces or execution traces) and output (message formats, state machines or other artifacts), and by the text, binary or hybrid protocols it was evaluated on, with full references and a short table of the few papers that released code.
requirements: The reviewed README was last updated on 2024-05-22, when NetPlier and NEMETYL were added; the other changes date from November 2020 to May 2021. Its 71 papers span 2004–2021, so later protocol reverse-engineering work is not covered.

40 of the 71 overview rows still read “Please review” instead of describing the approach, several input/output rows are empty, and 29 rows of the tested-protocols table name no protocol. The tables summarize what each paper reports.

The README states that most papers do not provide their code; its source-code table lists eight projects, one only through a Web Archive copy of the Protocol Informatics page. The remaining entries are papers, with PDF links where the maintainer found one.

CSVtoREADME.py generates the README tables from tools.csv, contributions are requested as additions to tools.ods, and two further spreadsheets keep categorisations from the Duchêne et al. and Sija et al. surveys.
LICENSE is CC0-1.0, while CSVtoREADME.py carries a GPL-3.0-or-later header; the linked papers keep their publishers' terms. An independent reading list.

resources.name: REstringer
resources.description: HUMAN Security's Node.js JavaScript deobfuscator. It identifies the obfuscation type, runs matching processors for obfuscator.io, Caesar Plus and array-based patterns, then iterates 40+ AST modules that rebuild strings, resolve expressions and calls and simplify control flow; unsafe modules evaluate code in a sandbox. It works as a CLI or library.
requirements: The reviewed HumanSecurity main commit (2025-12-07) is v2.1.0 plus one README edit removing the retired REstringer.tech web tool. The author now continues the project in his fork ctrl-escp/restringer, which the npm package lists as its repository: npm 2.2.0 (2026-05-09) and 2.3.0 (2026-08-30) come from it, and at 2.3.0 its README requires Node.js 22+, makes isolated-vm optional and adds Node, Deno and Bun subprocess sandboxes, so npm installs code newer than the reviewed source.

The reviewed source needs Node.js 20+ (22+ recommended) and installs as a global CLI or a module. It depends on flast, obfuscation-detector, commander and isolated-vm 5.0.4, a native module that CI builds with Python and g++. Output goes to stdout or <input>-deob.js; -m caps iterations, and -c removes dead nodes, which README marks unsafe.

Input is an obfuscated JavaScript file or string. Safe modules transform the AST without evaluating code; unsafe modules evaluate parts of the input with eval() inside an isolated-vm sandbox to resolve expressions and calls.

GitHub Actions runs npm test on Node.js 20 and 22. Besides module and processor unit tests, the full suite deobfuscates 11 bundled obfuscated samples, among them obfuscator.io, JSFuck and Caesar Plus scripts, and compares each result with a stored expected output.
MIT, copyright 2025 HUMAN Security; the fork adds a 2026 copyright line for Ben Baryo. The repository was formerly PerimeterX/restringer, which now redirects to HumanSecurity/restringer.

resources.name: Emproof workshop: Firmware Reverse Engineering
resources.description: Slides and 14 self-contained exercises from Emproof's firmware reverse-engineering workshop at ScapyCon Automotive 2025, designed by Tim Blazytko for a technical audience with little security experience. The firmware and binary tasks move from reading ELF metadata with binutils and first steps in Ghidra or Binary Ninja, through unpacking two embedded-Linux CTF images with binwalk, to bare-metal analysis: identifying the microcontroller, toolchain and memory map of a model car's firmware ELF, and rebasing a raw STM32F103 flash dump with segments taken from the datasheet. Other tasks decrypt strings statically in a Mirai sample and trace a hardcoded AES key back to its data section.
requirements: The reviewed main commit, from 2025-09-25, ends a 14-commit history that began on 2025-09-21. It holds slides.pdf and 14 tasks, each a task.md with step-by-step questions next to a samples folder; no model solutions are included, and the two embedded-Linux tasks link an external write-up.

The README says most samples target ARMv7 (Thumb/ARM32) or AArch64, and many come with C source. A Kali Linux-based Docker image fixed to linux/arm64, emulated on x86_64 hosts, supplies binutils, binwalk, John the Ripper and armhf runtime libraries; on first use docker_run.sh installs QEMU binfmt handlers on the host through a privileged container. Ghidra and Binary Ninja Free are installed on the host, and because Binary Ninja Free lacks AArch64 support, many tasks also ship an .armv7 build.

Bare-metal tasks expect the analyst to consult the microcontroller's datasheet or reference manual; the STM32F103 task names the flash, SRAM, peripheral and system-control-space ranges to define before re-analysis. Several further tasks are crackme-style license, keygen and anti-patching exercises on the workshop's own binaries.

The workshop materials are GPL-2.0, but the README excludes three sample folders from that license and provides them for analysis and education only, without redistribution: the two embedded-Linux images, which the tasks attribute to WORMCON CTF 2021, and a Mirai botnet binary that its task describes as active malware not to be executed, stored in a password-protected archive.

resources.name: pyatv: a reverse-engineered client for Apple TV and AirPlay protocols
resources.description: Asyncio Python library and command-line tools that act as an independent client for Apple TV and AirPlay devices by reimplementing the DMAP/DACP, Media Remote Protocol, Companion Link, AirPlay and RAOP protocols, which its protocol documentation describes as reverse engineered. That page records the recovered binary formats, Zeroconf properties, the OPACK encoding, pair-setup and pair-verify exchanges and Companion commands, with some request headers taken from Wireshark captures of the iPhone Remote app, and the bundled atvproxy relays MRP, Companion and AirPlay sessions to print decrypted messages for further analysis. On this basis pyatv provides remote control, metadata with push updates, app and account switching, audio-output management and AirPlay streaming to Apple TVs, HomePods and third-party receivers.
requirements: Release at review: 0.18.0, published to GitHub and PyPI on 2026-06-19 as a tvOS-compatibility release; the reviewed master commit is the release commit, while the v0.18.0 tag points to a parallel commit that differs only in CHANGES.md and pyatv/const.py. The protocol page limits itself to what has been reverse engineered: its Companion Link section is called mostly speculation and guesses, the OPACK description is incomplete and unverified, and the MRP implementation section is still marked TBD. The acknowledgements say MRP support builds on Jean Regisser's mediaremotetv-protocol findings.

No Apple software, firmware or keys are bundled. pyatv connects to the user's own Apple TV, HomePod, AirPort Express or other AirPlay receiver on the local network; most protocols require pairing with a PIN shown on the device, and credentials and settings are kept in pyatv's storage. On tvOS 15 and later AirPlay must be set up because MRP moved into an AirPlay 2 stream, and RAOP supports only legacy pairing.

Requires Python 3.9+ and installs from PyPI or the project's container images; the installation guide lists build-essential, libssl-dev, libffi-dev and Python headers for building dependencies on Debian-style systems, and RAOP audio streaming relies on miniaudio. CI runs on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows with Python 3.9 to 3.14.

Tests are mostly unit tests, plus functional tests for DMAP, MRP, Companion, RAOP, mDNS and scanning that run against a fake device which, according to the testing guide, implements limited functionality and is only meant to be compatible with pyatv. atvproxy is described as an incubating script that depends on internal APIs.
MIT (LICENSE.md). Apple's protocols, devices and software keep their own rights; pyatv is an independent implementation.

resources.name: lisa.py
resources.description: LLDB extension that adds an MCP bridge to a debugging session, adapted from ida-pro-mcp: the plugin's mcp start command serves 18 debugger functions over local JSON-RPC, and a FastMCP stdio server generated from those functions exposes them to MCP clients such as Claude Desktop. The tools create, launch or attach to targets, step, manage breakpoints, read backtraces, variables, disassembly and memory, evaluate expressions and run arbitrary LLDB commands. The same script keeps lisa.py's earlier exploit-development helpers, including checksec, a register and stack context view, Mach-O header and load-command display, Capstone disassembly and an exploitable crash-triage command.
requirements: The default dev branch was reviewed at commit 9dd61e9 from 2025-03-29, the last of three commits that day adding the MCP integration to a 2021 rewrite of lisa.py. There are no releases or tags, the master branch still holds the 2017 version without MCP support, and the README's TODO list asks for updated manuals and more test cases.

Python 3.10+ and LLDB with Python bindings; the LLDB Python environment must also import capstone, pinned to 4.0.2 in requirements.txt, and the MCP server needs fastmcp and httpx. The README is partly out of step with the code: it names server.py, lldb_plugin.py and an lldb-mcp clone path, while the repository ships lisa.py and lldb_mcp.py, and the pyproject lldb-mcp entry point names a module that does not exist.

Load lisa.py into LLDB with command script import, run mcp start, and point the MCP client at lldb_mcp.py; the README shows a Claude Desktop configuration that runs it through uv. The plugin listens on localhost port 13338 without authentication, and the MCP server always connects to that port even if mcp start was given another. run_lldb_command passes any LLDB command through, so a connected client has full control of the debugger and the debugged process.

The helper commands parse Mach-O headers and load commands and handle x86_64 and arm64/arm64e registers; the README states no supported operating system or LLDB version. The tests directory holds small crash programs, including Objective-C and libdispatch cases, that make rtests runs through LLDB; no CI is configured.
LICENSE is Apache-2.0, but pyproject.toml declares MIT and lldb_mcp.py carries ida-pro-mcp's MIT notice.

resources.name: WireMCP
resources.description: Node.js MCP server that runs Wireshark's tshark for LLM clients, aimed in its README at threat hunting, network diagnostics and anomaly detection. Three tools capture a few seconds of live traffic and return either a fixed set of IP, port, TCP-flag and HTTP fields, tshark's protocol-hierarchy statistics or TCP conversation statistics; analyze_pcap returns IPs, ports, HTTP URLs and protocol stacks from a saved capture. The remaining tools match captured IPs against the URLhaus blocklist and scan a capture for HTTP Basic, FTP, Telnet and Kerberos credentials, beside the dissection output.
requirements: Reviewed at main commit 7f45f8b from 2025-07-09, the last of nine commits since 2025-03-28; there are no releases or tags, package.json says 1.0.0 and its test script is a placeholder. It runs with Node.js (the README recommends v16+) after npm install, finds tshark on PATH or in common install locations, and is started by the MCP client as node index.js over stdio; the README lists macOS, Windows and Linux. Each tool also has a matching prompt template.

The live-capture tools default to interface en0 for 5 seconds and need capture permissions on the host; they write temp_capture.pcap in the working directory and delete it afterwards, and packet JSON is trimmed to about 720,000 characters. The server builds tshark shell commands by inserting the interface and file-path arguments without escaping, so it should be exposed only to trusted clients.
Field sets are fixed in the code: there is no arbitrary field extraction, display filter, decode-as or protocol-preference control, and the server does not infer unknown message formats.

check_threats and check_ip_threats download the URLhaus text blocklist from abuse.ch and match IPs locally; although the README mentions multiple threat feeds, the reviewed code queries only URLhaus. The credential scan and threat checks are security heuristics, and their findings need analyst review.
MIT; Wireshark and tshark keep their own GPL terms.

resources.name: Wind Waker HD decompilation: functions verified against the recompiled Wii U game
resources.description: Decompiles the USA Wii U release of The Wind Waker HD function by function into readable C++ in zeldaret/tww’s style, and verifies each function by running it beside the original, statically recompiled from the user’s own copy, comparing return values, memory writes and calls on generated and recorded inputs, with coverage and mutation checks. README reports 28,244 of the game’s 39,713 functions verified, including 22,068 of 22,215 GameCube-derived functions. The code calls undecompiled functions by address, so it runs only inside the ZeldaWWHDRecomp port, not as a standalone game build.
requirements: README describes a hybrid decompilation of cking.rpx (USA, version 0): decompiled functions call others through their original addresses, so the tree builds no game on its own and runs only with the port’s recompiled code. It reports the HD UI decompiled, while about 11,400 generic-library functions (sead, agl, NW4F, most of JSystem, the Cafe SDK and the C runtime) are not planned. zeldaret/tww is the reference for names and structure, and the docs record HD differences for 838 units compared with the GameCube version.

Building or verifying needs the user’s own legally obtained game, extracted with the port’s tool from a disc image with its disc key and the Wii U common key. README states that the repository contains no machine code, recompiled code, game assets or keys; small data tables used by the code are included, while model data, the RPX image, recompiled output, game-derived names and recorded inputs are generated locally and git-ignored. The recommended GameCube signature checks also use zeldaret/tww built from the user’s own GameCube disc.

The harness runs inside a ZeldaWWHDRecomp checkout at the tested commit df2cf51b (v0.2.3), replacing the port’s older tools/verify. It needs Python 3, clang/clang++ with C++20 and the port’s game-extraction requirements; building the port itself is needed only for recording inputs. A full verify_all.py run is long, and some units need tens of GB of memory.

Each function runs on 10,000 generated inputs on each of two seeds, must reach nearly all basic blocks of the original and is mutation-tested; README reports the whole tree re-verified after the October 2026 readability rewrite. tools/verify/README.md says equivalence is to the recompiled code’s model of the Espresso CPU, not the console, and that timing, threading and the exact stack layout are not checked. The in-game swap-test build is not part of the release, and the repository has no CI workflow.

CC0 1.0 covers the decompiled source, tools and documentation; the game, Nintendo data and the port runtime keep their own terms. README calls it an unofficial, non-commercial fan project with no donations or paid builds. tools/verify/README.md reports pilot timings for an agent using the tools and two functions written by parallel agents.

resources.name: SiegeFX: a Dungeon Siege engine reimplementation in alpha
resources.description: A C#/.NET 10 engine loads Dungeon Siege's original archives, scripts and models, with published alpha builds and an audit/parity ledger. The project also provides SiegeSmith modding tools, while describing remaining fidelity and playthrough risks.
requirements: Requires an owned Dungeon Siege installation; Windows and Linux builds are linked. Source builds need .NET 10; Linux needs OpenGL 3.3 and internet multiplayer additionally needs OpenSSL 3.
The README calls this alpha software. It reports campaign progression to the final boss since v0.4.0, with Bink movies, interior lighting fidelity and combat balance still open.
Code is GPL-3.0-only; original game assets are not bundled. Multiplayer uses Epic Online Services under separate SDK terms.

resources.name: Legend of Legaia: a Rust port with disc-local browser tooling
resources.description: A from-scratch Rust port of the North American PlayStation Legend of Legaia includes native/browser play, asset extraction and disc patching. The author documents Ghidra/emulator research and a full-game ladder; this is a fresh implementation, not a matching decompilation or static recompilation.
requirements: Supply an owned North American SCUS-94254 disc image; browser tooling reads the image locally. Source builds require a Rust toolchain supporting edition 2024.
The README reports New Game-to-credits coverage and parity oracles, but disc-dependent tests skip and pass without LEGAIA_DISC_BIN.
Enhancements can differ from retail behavior; the README describes a retail-faithful mode. No Sony game executable, ROM or asset data is distributed.
Project code and documentation offer Unlicense or MIT; these licenses do not grant rights to the original game.

resources.name: Chrome extension source viewer (CRX Viewer)
resources.description: Browser extension and web page by Rob Wu for inspecting packaged browser extensions without installing them. On Chrome Web Store, Opera, Firefox, Thunderbird and Microsoft Edge add-on pages it adds a button that downloads the package as a zip or opens it in a viewer, and links to extension packages hosted elsewhere can be opened as well. The viewer reads CRX, NEX, XPI and ZIP files: it lists and filters files, searches content by string or regular expression, beautifies and syntax-highlights code, previews images, opens nested zips, shows per-file hashes and derives the extension ID from the package key, signature or manifest.
requirements: Version 1.7.1, committed on 2026-09-01 as the reviewed master head, is the version in all three manifests: Manifest V3 builds for Chrome 88+ and Opera 74+, and a Manifest V2 build for Firefox 115+. The repository has no tags or releases; the README links the Chrome Web Store, Opera and addons.mozilla.org listings and an online demo page that opens local files or URLs.

Store listings are the documented install route; the README gives no build instructions. make.js builds the Chrome, Opera, Firefox and web packages with shelljs and the less compiler from npm and zips them with 7z.

The extension requests tabs, storage, context-menu, downloads and declarativeContent permissions and access to Google's CRX download endpoints, and asks for optional access to all sites before fetching packages hosted elsewhere. Its Firefox build routes addons.mozilla.org requests through services.addons.mozilla.org, a workaround the source documents for Firefox's restrictions on add-ons reading some Mozilla domains and still uses for non-public XPI files such as developer submissions.
The viewer shows package contents as published: beautification only reformats code and does not reverse obfuscation. Downloaded extensions keep their authors' rights and store terms.
MPL-2.0; bundled libraries such as zip.js, Prism, js-beautify and SparkMD5 keep their own licenses.

resources.name: har-to-openapi
resources.description: TypeScript library and CLI that infers OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 documents from HAR captures of HTTP traffic, loosely based on har2openapi. Requests are grouped into one document per domain, with options to turn IDs in paths into parameters, infer query, form and JSON body schemas from observed values, and merge several captures into the same operations. Optional settings extract reusable component schemas, keep multiple redacted examples, mark fields required only when every sample contains them, attach per-field observation counts as evidence and apply an OpenAPI Overlay so hand-written names and corrections survive regeneration.
requirements: Reviewed at main commit 432e096 from 2026-09-07, tagged v3.0.1 and published to npm the same day; v3.0.0, released a day earlier, added capture merging, reusable schemas, overlays, redaction, reports and requiredness evidence. Node.js 22.19.0+ is required; it installs from npm as a library or runs as the har-to-openapi command. CI tests Node 24 and the latest Node on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Input is one or more HAR files the user records, plus optional JSON or YAML configuration and overlay files. Without --multi-spec the CLI returns only the first domain's document. --validate and --strict check the result locally, and a conversion report lists counts and diagnostics for filtered entries, parse failures and schema fallbacks.

The README states that observations describe finite captures and that a field present in every capture does not establish an API contract, so requirements should be confirmed with the API owner and recorded in an overlay. Endpoints, parameters and responses absent from the captures do not appear, and the default requiredness setting keeps the earlier legacy behavior.

Generated documents copy captured values as examples unless examples are turned off or a redact list masks them; the README presents redaction as a step before sharing, and the reviewed commit closed further redaction gaps. Convert only traffic you are authorized to capture and analyze.
MIT.

resources.name: RSDKv3 Decompilation: Sonic CD (2011) on a reconstructed Retro Engine v3
resources.description: Reconstructs Retro Engine v3, the engine behind the 2011 Sonic CD remaster, as a native C++ source port for Windows, Linux, macOS and Android. The engine runs the game's own scripts and assets from an official release, which the repository does not ship, and adds a mod loader, a settings file with remappable controls, support for the mobile versions' updated scripts and extra developer-menu debug keys. Its license describes the code as mostly functionally the same as the original rather than byte-matching; the same team's RSDKv5 decompilation is listed as a separate case.
requirements: The README calls it a complete decompilation of Retro Engine v3; its license says the repository also contains original code and that most code is meant to be functionally the same as the specified RSDK version. The RETRO_ORIGINAL_CODE option strips the custom code but, per the README and CMake file, cannot build a playable game. The reviewed commit is 19 commits after release 1.3.3 (2025-11-02), which attaches prebuilt Windows x86 and x64, Linux, macOS and Android builds of the engine.

It does not run without assets from an official Sonic CD release: the original Steam release, Sonic Origins on Steam, Epic or Switch, or the delisted iOS and Android versions. The engine loads the game's Data.rsdk datapack, and full-motion video works only with the original Steam release's video files. The FAQ notes that the Sonic Origins datafile uses the RSDKv5 datapack format and contains no music or sound effects, and that the Origins-only playable characters are blocked in release builds. The repository commits no game data or game scripts; the separate script decompilation is its own repository.

Clone recursively, because GitHub's source ZIPs omit the tinyxml2 and flatpak shared-modules submodules. CMake builds use Visual Studio with vcpkg (GLEW, SDL2, libogg, libtheora, libvorbis) on Windows, distribution packages on Linux and separate guides for macOS and Android; the tree also carries iOS, UWP and PS Vita project files that the README does not document, and the Switch and New 3DS ports are unofficial forks the project does not support.

CI builds Windows x86 and x64, Linux, macOS and Android binaries with RETRO_DISABLE_PLUS on. The project publishes no comparison with the original engine binaries; the FAQ says bugs present in official releases will mostly not be fixed and that menu buttons such as leaderboards and achievements stay unimplemented.

The custom RSDKv3/v4 Decompilation Source Code License v2 requires every prebuilt executable given to anyone to have DLC disabled by default, forbids commercial use and distributing game assets other than unique modded ones, requires crediting the original and decompilation developers, and binds forks to the same terms. It names Christian Whitehead as the original RSDK author and Rubberduckycooly and st×tic as the decompilation authors. Sega's game and assets keep their own rights.

resources.name: ICO decompilation: byte-identical PAL and Japanese PlayStation 2 boot ELFs
resources.description: Rebuilds the boot ELFs of ICO’s PAL (SCES-50760) and Japanese (SCPS-11003) PlayStation 2 discs from one source tree with the game’s original compiler versions, and checks that every loaded byte and the whole ELF file match the disc’s SHA-1. The 73 data-only archive members are generated at build time from the user’s own ELF, so most read-only data still comes from the disc rather than from source. Separate branches target the USA, Korean and August 2001 prototype builds, and the catalog’s ICO PC port is a fork of this tree.
requirements: README reports every section of both targets identical to its base ELF; .rodata is about 9.5% from source and 90.5% generated from the disc, and .data about 73% from source. The Japanese build is an earlier link of the same program, kept as VERSION_JPN blocks in the shared PAL-based tree, while kor, ntsc and aug6 are separate single-target branches not yet merged into main. The output is a PS2 boot ELF and ROM image, not a PC port.

Each target needs the user’s own disc image, the PAL .iso or the Japanese .bin/.cue, from which the build extracts the boot ELF and checks it against config/sha1sums. docs/LEGAL.md excludes disc images, boot ELFs, assets, data tables and bulk symbol or map tables from the repository, and forbids leaked SDKs and leaked source as inputs. It says the Sony runtime libraries reconstructed under sce/ were written from the shipped instructions using the SDK’s public naming, and the newlib and libgcc members follow their published source.

Builds on 64-bit Linux with 32-bit libraries and multilib gcc, Python 3, mips-linux-gnu-objcopy and network access on the first run. tools/setup.sh fetches ee-gcc 2.9-991111-01 and the SCE ee-as from decomp.me’s compiler releases, builds GNU ld 2.10 with two patches and builds a patched ps2dev dvp-as for the five VU1 microprograms; README says nothing comes from a Sony SDK.

./build.sh ends with tools/check_elf.py --gate, which compares every allocated section with the base ELF by address and requires the whole-file SHA-1 to match; progress badges and the dashboard are regenerated from the built ELF and link map. The only CI workflow publishes that dashboard, and building needs a disc that CI does not have.

MIT covers the project’s own code, scripts and documentation and grants no rights in the game, its data or Sony and Team Ico property; the toolchain components keep their GPL licences. README states the project is unaffiliated with Sony Interactive Entertainment or Team Ico.

resources.name: ESP32 Bit Pirate
resources.description: Open-source firmware that turns ESP32-S3 boards into a Bus Pirate-inspired multi-protocol hardware tool, operated from a USB serial terminal, a Wi-Fi web CLI or the M5 Cardputer's own keyboard and screen. Its modes talk to, sniff and script I2C, SPI, UART, 1-Wire, CAN and other buses, read EEPROM and flash chips, and scan for JTAG and SWD pinouts. USB adapter modes let host tools such as flashrom, OpenOCD and sigrok/PulseView use the board as an SPI programmer, debug adapter or logic analyzer.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.8, published 2026-10-11, with prebuilt images for 17 board builds that the README installs through the project's web flasher or, for M5Stack devices, M5Burner; the reviewed pioarduino branch commit is identical to that tag. Source builds use PlatformIO with the Arduino framework on a pinned pioarduino ESP32 platform, and CI runs the native unit tests.

Needs an ESP32-S3 board with at least 4 MB of flash. The README lists ESP32-S3 dev kits and M5Stack, LILYGO, Heltec, Seeed Studio, Waveshare and Unexpected Maker boards with the same feature set, warns that the default pin mapping may not match other boards, and notes that some features need additional hardware. Connected devices must run at 3.3 V or 5 V.

Analysis needs physical access and wiring to the target's buses, memory chips or debug pins; the firmware talks to and captures what it is connected to and does not interpret recovered firmware. The README also lists Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, sub-GHz, RFID and cellular modes, some of which transmit, and limits use to educational, diagnostic and interoperability testing on authorized devices.

MIT-licensed; the lib directory vendors third-party drivers under their own licenses, including GPL-2.0 for RF24. The repository holds firmware sources, board profiles, tests and images, with no target firmware.

resources.name: decode-js
resources.description: Babel-based AST processor that turns obfuscated JavaScript back into readable source, with one target selected per run: javascript-obfuscator (obfuscator.io), JS-Confuser 2.x up to its high preset, sojson and its v7 variant for jsjiami.com.v7, sojson's jjencode variant, and a generic pass for unreachable code, nested blocks and constant expressions. A second, version-aware obfuscator.io target reports the encoder era it detects and returns nothing, with a reason, rather than a half-decoded program when a string-array layer cannot be read. The JS-Confuser notes list each transform it reverses and those, such as variable renaming, that destroy information and cannot be recovered.
requirements: No releases or tags are published; the reviewed main commit of 2026-10-17 runs from source. package.json requires Node.js 26.x to match its native isolated-vm 7 dependency, whose build requirements the README asks users to check first. After npm i, the CLI runs as npm run decode -- -t <target> with optional input and output paths, or through shortcuts such as deob, deobx, dejsc, deso and desov7.

Input is a single obfuscated script, input.js by default, and the README says the file must not contain other, non-obfuscated code. Coverage depends on the obfuscator and its version: the version-aware target covers the javascript-obfuscator 2.x eras and 5.5.0, leaves 3.0.0–4.2.2 unverified and reports samples in that range as unknown, and the JS-Confuser target cannot restore RenameVariables, RenameLabels or ObjectExtraction.

Decoding evaluates parts of the input: string-array decoders and JS-Confuser runtime helpers run inside isolated-vm sandboxes, but the obfuscator, sojson and sojsonv7 targets unpack an outer eval wrapper with Node.js eval in the decoder's own process. Treat inputs as untrusted code, and check recovered strings and control flow against the original script.

CI runs the Vitest suite on Node.js 26; its fixtures pair obfuscated samples, mostly generated from included source files, with expected decodes for the JS-Confuser, obfuscator.io and sojson v7 targets. GPL-3.0-or-later per the README, LICENSE and package.json.

resources.name: NiimBlue: an independent web client for NIIMBOT label printers
resources.description: Replaces NIIMBOT's own label app with a browser client that designs labels and prints them over Web Bluetooth or Web Serial, with Android (Capacitor) and Windows (Tauri) builds of the same interface. Printer communication comes from the same author's NiimBlueLib, which the README calls the most complete implementation of the NIIMBOT protocol; the protocol is documented on the NIIMBOT Community Wiki, and owners of models that do not print are asked for a packet capture of a print made with the official app. The README says the client runs entirely in the browser and keeps label data there.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is the v2026.9.0 release of 2026-09-27; newer work lands on the dev branch, which CONTRIBUTING names as the base for pull requests. The README keeps no list of supported models and points to a NiimBlueLib issue that collects tested models; it suggests trying a different print-task version in the preview dialog when printing fails.

Needs the user's own NIIMBOT printer over Bluetooth or USB serial and a browser with the Web Bluetooth or Web Serial API, usually Chrome-based; some systems need Chrome flags enabled, Safari needs a third-party extension, and deployments other than localhost need HTTPS. No vendor app or firmware is needed to print. The optional firmware updater only flashes a .bin file the user selects.

Built with Node.js and npm from Svelte 5, Vite and Fabric.js, with @mmote/niimbluelib pinned at 0.47.0; npm run build writes static files, and the Dockerfile serves them with nginx. Releases attach the static site as niimblue-dist.zip plus an Android APK and a Windows executable, built by the repository's Gitea workflows.

The repository has no automated test suite: the Dockerfile and deployment workflow run svelte-check before building, and the Gitea workflows build and publish the site and apps. The protocol code and its tests live in the separate NiimBlueLib repository. Model support rests on user reports.

MIT (LICENSE, 2024 MultiMote); NiimBlueLib is also MIT, and its README says the work is for informational and educational purposes, is not affiliated with or endorsed by the vendor and is not meant for commercial use without the vendor's consent. CONTRIBUTING says AI-generated code is not appreciated and must be reviewed if used.

resources.name: FIRERPA (lamda)
resources.description: Client/server Android automation and dynamic-analysis platform for devices the analyst is authorized to test. An on-device server exposes UI automation, a browser-based remote desktop, HTTPS traffic capture (MITM), and bundled Frida instrumentation through one service, driven from a Python client library of 160+ APIs. The README reports it works on Android 6.0+ with or without root, maps Frida RPC to Python and JSON-RPC calls, and includes an MCP server and a natural-language agent command.
requirements: Latest release at review: v10.9, published 2026-09-27 from the default branch 10; the reviewed commit a980a38 is that release's auto-commit. The Python client requires Python 3.6+ (setup.py pins >=3.6,<3.15); the README lists Android 6.0+ targets on arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86 and x86_64, including emulators and cloud phones.

This repository holds the Python client library, the gRPC/protobuf service definitions and helper scripts; the on-device server and its Debian environment are distributed as prebuilt per-architecture release tarballs and a Magisk module, not committed to the tree. Deployment uses a one-click app (root or Shizuku), a Magisk module, manual extraction or ROM integration.

Operates only on a device the server is installed on, over a single service port with TLS and certificate-based access control; the README positions it for security testing and compliance analysis. The committed tools directory includes the project's own default MITM CA and SSH material, described in the repository as open defaults.

MIT-licensed. A DISCLAIMER.TXT requires use only for lawful study, research or authorized application analysis on a virtual or dedicated device, and states the software itself provides no capability to intrude on other applications.

resources.name: open_oura: a cloud-free Oura Ring client built on its reverse-engineered BLE protocol
resources.description: Reimplements the Bluetooth Low Energy protocol of the Oura Ring Gen 3/4/5 in Rust crates and an oura command-line client that pairs with, authenticates to and syncs a ring directly, with no Oura account or cloud service. The author reports recovering the GATT layout, packet framing and AES app-auth flow from the decompiled Android app, and porting history-event decoders and several on-device metrics, such as HRV, sleep debt and nightly temperature baselines, from Ghidra decompilations of the app's native libraries. Event bodies are stored raw in SQLite so they can be re-decoded as decoders improve.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-10-07 main head; there are no releases or tags, and the workspace version is 0.1.0. The README reports live pairing, authentication and event sync on a Ring 3 Horizon and a Ring 5, and says the client is designed for Ring 3/4/5, which share one GATT layout, packet framing and auth flow. Several event layouts are marked inferred or partly unresolved, and the algorithm status table lists the sleep, readiness and activity scores as only partly recovered. The iOS app and web dashboard built on these crates live in the separate open_health repository.

Requires the user's own ring and a host Bluetooth adapter. Auth-gated reads need the ring's 16-byte app-auth key in a key file: the pair command installs a new key on a factory-reset ring, while an app-onboarded ring's key sits in the official app's local database, and the bundled helper for exporting it needs a rooted Android phone. Sleep staging and some scores depend on Oura's proprietary on-device models, which the README says are not included and must be supplied by the user; factory-reset and other state-changing commands sit behind explicit flags.

Builds with Cargo as a Rust 2021 workspace. The oura-link crate uses btleplug for BLE by default and can be built without it so that an iOS host supplies its own CoreBluetooth transport; on macOS the terminal needs Bluetooth permission. A separate Python research bench in tools/ uses bleak and pycryptodome.

cargo test runs 88 Rust unit tests at review, covering captured-packet decoding, an AES auth known-answer vector, mock-transport authentication and sync and the ported metric functions; no CI workflow is committed. Physiological figures in the documentation, such as overnight heart rate, RMSSD and SpO2 ratios, come from the author's own rings.

MIT (LICENSE and Cargo metadata). Oura's apps, native libraries, models, firmware, decompiled output, captures and keys are kept out of the repository. A CLAUDE.md guide for coding agents is committed.

resources.name: PE-sieve
resources.description: Windows process scanner by hasherezade that finds and dumps implants in one running process: replaced or injected PE modules, shellcode, inline and IAT hooks and other in-memory patches, with the README naming Process Hollowing, Process Doppelgänging and reflective DLL injection among the techniques it detects. Options add shellcode detection by patterns or statistics, scans of thread call stacks, non-executable pages and encrypted or obfuscated content, a choice of dump mode with import-table recovery for dumped PEs, minidumps and JSON reports. It builds as an EXE, as a DLL with a small API that Python, Go and Rust bindings use, or as a static library, and is the engine behind HollowsHunter and MalUnpack.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.4.1.1, published 2025-09-13, with 32- and 64-bit EXEs and DLLs; the README also lists Chocolatey and Scoop packages. The reviewed master commit (2026-06-06) reports version 0.4.1.5, so the pinned sources may describe unreleased changes. PE-sieve runs on Windows and scans one process per run, selected by PID; the separate HollowsHunter scans many processes or the whole system.

Source builds use CMake 3.12+ (or the MinGW build script) and a recursive clone for the libpeconv, paramkit and sig_finder submodules, with an option to build an EXE, a DLL or a static library. The Python bindings in the repository and the separate Go and Rust bindings load pe-sieve32.dll or pe-sieve64.dll from PESIEVE_DIR or the current directory. Optional symbol download fetches symbols for the scanned modules.

Inputs are running processes on a machine the analyst controls, and the README describes the results as potentially malicious material collected for further analysis, so detections and dumps need review. AppVeyor builds x86 and x64 Release and Debug configurations, and its only CTest check runs pe-sieve -? and expects a version string; the GitHub workflow publishes Doxygen documentation.
BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE, 2017-2026 @hasherezade); the submodules keep their own licenses.

resources.name: oletools
resources.description: Python package by Philippe Lagadec for analyzing Microsoft OLE2 (Compound File Binary) files such as Office 97–2003 documents, MSI files and Outlook messages, as well as RTF and OpenXML documents, mainly for malware analysis, forensics and debugging. Its command-line tools detect and extract VBA and Excel 4 (XLM) macros, embedded OLE and Flash objects and DDE links (olevba, MacroRaptor, oleobj, rtfobj, pyxswf, msodde), flag characteristics common in malicious files with oleid and ftguess, and show directory entries, metadata, timestamps and sector maps with oledir, olemeta, oletimes and olemap. It is built on the same author's olefile parser.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.60.2, published 2024-07-02 on GitHub and PyPI. The reviewed master commit (2026-01-26) already sets version 0.60.3, and its README news lists 0.60.3 under 2025-05-22 with an olevba fix for a security issue with ANSI escape codes in CLI output, but no 0.60.3 tag or PyPI upload existed at review. SECURITY.md lists 0.60.x and later as supported.

Install with pip as oletools, or oletools[full] to add the optional XLMMacroDeobfuscator. Dependencies are pyparsing, olefile, easygui, colorclass and pcodedmp, plus msoffcrypto-tool for encrypted documents except on PyPy under Windows, macOS or Python 2. setup.py classifiers list Python 2.7 and 3.4 to 3.12; the GitHub workflow runs pylint -E and the unit tests on Linux, Windows and macOS with current CPython 3 and PyPy 3.9, while the older Travis configuration targets Python 2.7 to 3.8 and PyPy.

Inputs are user-supplied documents, which in malware analysis may be malicious; the unit tests use sample documents committed under tests/test-data. The README describes oleid as detecting characteristics usually found in malicious files and MacroRaptor as detecting malicious VBA macros, so results are indicators that need analyst review.

LICENSE.md applies a two-clause BSD license (copyright 2012–2025 Philippe Lagadec) to the package; olevba contains MIT-licensed code from officeparser, and the thirdparty folder keeps its own terms, including GPL-3.0 for xxxswf and public-domain oledump plugin code. The README notes that python-oletools is unrelated to BeCubed Software's OLETools.

resources.name: Binder Trace
resources.description: Frida-based terminal tool, described by its authors as "Wireshark for Binder", that intercepts the Binder IPC transactions an Android process sends and parses each message and its reply. Bundled structure files for specific Android releases map transaction codes back to AIDL interface and method names and decode parcel arguments into typed fields beside a hex dump. A frequency pane and a JSON filter file narrow the stream by interface, method or type, showing which system services an app calls and with what data.
requirements: PyPI release at review: binder-trace 1.4.1, published 2024-08-01, requiring Python 3.9+. The reviewed main commit of 2025-09-11 is one README-only commit later, correcting the frida-server steps and the listed Android versions, and is the latest activity.

Needs a rooted Android device or emulator, adb running as root and a frida-server matching the installed Frida Python package, which requirements.txt leaves unpinned. It attaches to a process by PID or name, or spawns it, and should be used on devices and apps the analyst may analyse. Clipboard copy on Linux needs xclip or xsel.

Default structure sets cover Android 9 to 14, with extra sets for 8.1 and some point releases. STRUCTURES.md explains that AIDL method numbering and parcel layouts change between builds, so results on a device whose build differs from the bundled AOSP tags can be wrong and the files may need hand-editing. Only transactions the attached process issues through libbinder's IPCThreadState::transact are captured, together with their replies.

CI runs tox with isort, black, flake8, pydocstyle and pytest across several Python versions; the tests cover argument parsing, parcel parsing and the terminal interface, not live devices. MIT licensed.

resources.name: MonkeyDev
resources.description: Based on iOSOpenDev, MonkeyDev adds a MonkeyApp project template to Xcode for instrumenting iOS apps the developer is authorized to analyze. From Xcode it injects a developer-written dylib into a supplied decrypted app, builds Objective-C or Logos (CaptainHook) hooks, and re-signs, installs and debugs the result with source-level breakpoints; optional build settings restore Objective-C symbols, export the target's Objective-C headers and enable Reveal view inspection. The current version also builds jailbreak Logos/CaptainHook tweaks and command-line tools for rootless, rootful or roothide environments.
requirements: The reviewed master commit f906af1 (last pushed 2026-10-20) documents version 4.10; the repository has no tagged release. The README reports the non-jailbreak flow verified on Apple Silicon Macs with Xcode 27.0 and an iPhone 14 Pro on iOS 18.6.2, covering build, repeat install, hooking, symbol breakpoints, header export and Reveal, and separately reports rootless tweak and command-line builds verified on device with rootful only build- and package-checked.

Installation needs a full Xcode, a native arm64 shell and Theos installed separately under the current user's home directory; it installs to /opt/MonkeyDev and registers the templates in the user's Xcode template directory without modifying Xcode.app. The repository commits prebuilt native helper binaries (its own monkeyparser and a build of class-dump) and the libsubstitute.dylib library, plus a demo app under Resource/TargetApp.app used as the built-in validation input.

Each MonkeyApp needs one target input the developer supplies: a decrypted .app or already-dumped IPA placed in the project's TargetApp folder, or the built-in demo when none is provided. The README states MonkeyDev does not decrypt apps on non-jailbroken devices. Signing requires a certificate available to the current team, a matching provisioning profile and device authorization, and the keep-bundle-ID toggle does not bypass signing entitlements.

GPL-3.0 licensed; the bundled roothide SDK under Librarys/roothide is MIT. The repository ships the Xcode templates, install/packaging scripts, the helper binaries and the demo app, and contains no third-party target application.

resources.name: Firmware Analysis Toolkit (FAT)
resources.description: Attify's firmware security toolkit, rewritten for version 2 as a Rust command-line tool built around per-image projects. It classifies unknown blobs and firmware images, extracts filesystems, inventories startup scripts, credential strings and crypto material, triages ELF binaries with radare2-based decompilation and source-to-sink taint, and inspects bare-metal MCU images, BMC flash, Edge AI model files and Android APKs. Projects can then go through preflight checks and QEMU emulation on native, FirmAE, Firmadyne or EMUX backends.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.0.1, published 2026-09-26, with archives for macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Linux x86-64 (glibc 2.35+) and ARM64 (glibc 2.39+) and Windows x86-64, plus a separate runtime-data bundle. The reviewed master commit adds unreleased BMC inspection, native JFFS2 recovery, hash-pinned BMC emulation profiles and Redfish session and process debugging. Version 2 is a rewrite; the FAT 1.x setup.sh and fat.py workflow belongs to the older release.

Source builds need Rust 1.91+ and Python 3; the installer can add system packages and builds pinned binwalk-ng 4.0.0 and Sasquatch. The Windows build covers native analysis commands only, and workflows that need Linux filesystem semantics or Unix tools run under WSL. Optional workflows need radare2 with r2ghidra, Ghidra, Joern, angr, QEMU, GDB, tmux or Docker, and FirmAE, Firmadyne and EMUX backends are configured separately; fat doctor reports what is missing.

Users supply the firmware images, extracted filesystems, binaries or APKs to analyze. The third-party notices state that the source tree and release bundles contain no firmware images, kernel or U-Boot binaries, proprietary model files or extracted device filesystems. BMC emulation profiles require an exact input SHA-256 for a named OpenBMC or ASUS BMC image, and the README warns that emulation executes untrusted vendor code.

docs/epistemics.md treats results as bounded observations: startup intent does not prove reachability, Edge AI hits do not show that a model executes, shell taint is deliberately unsound and reports weak candidates, and an emulation validator proves only what it checked in that run. Test fixtures are synthetic, including Cortex-M images built from in-repo C sources with arm-none-eabi-gcc; a prebuilt MIPS PID-1 trampoline ships with its assembly source. DEVELOPMENT.md documents local cargo tests, while the GitHub workflows build and smoke-test release archives.

FAT 2.0 is source available under FSL-1.1-ALv2, which GitHub reports as NOASSERTION: use, modification and redistribution are permitted except a commercial Competing Use, and each version also becomes available under Apache-2.0 two years after Attify first makes it available. FAT 1.x history stays MIT, the optional QEMU hook plugin source is GPL-2.0-or-later, and third-party dependencies and external assets keep their own terms. Users must be authorized to analyze their targets.

resources.name: Quark-Engine
resources.description: Rule-based engine for analysing suspicious Android apps: it loads an APK's Dalvik bytecode and checks JSON behaviour rules, each naming permissions and a pair of framework API calls, through five confidence stages, from the permission being requested and either API being called up to both calls appearing in order in one method and passing the same register. Weighted rule matches produce a threat score, with summary, detail, JSON, web, call-graph and label reports, and Quark Script exposes the analysis as a Python API that the project presents for finding vulnerabilities. The repository also ships two Claude Code skills, for running an analysis and generating a rule, and an optional LangChain agent that uses the OpenAI API.
requirements: Latest release at review: v26.10.1, published on GitHub and PyPI on 2026-10-10 and requiring Python 3.10+. The reviewed master commit of 2026-10-17 differs from it only by an added malware-family report in the documentation.

Install from PyPI, or from source with Pipenv, then run freshquark, which git-clones the separate quark-rules repository into a .quark-engine folder in the user's home directory. dextrace is the default core library, with Androguard 4.1.4 pinned, rizin and radare2 backends through optional extras plus the native tools, and a Shuriken backend; call graphs need Graphviz. The Quark Agent needs an OpenAI API key, and the Claude Code skills need Claude Code with Quark installed.

Input is one APK per run; the documentation scans directories with a shell loop or the Python API. Reports are static rule matches whose confidence counts the stages a rule passes, so coverage depends on the rule set; setup.py calls Quark an obfuscation-neglect scoring system. Suspicious samples belong in an isolated analysis environment, and the test suite downloads live malware and deliberately vulnerable APKs from a separate sample repository.

CI builds rizin 0.7.3 and radare2 5.9.0 and runs pytest with coverage on Python 3.10. The malware-family reports in the documentation are project analyses. GPL-3.0 per LICENSE and the setup.py classifier.

resources.name: Hollows Hunter
resources.description: Windows command-line memory scanner by hasherezade that runs the PE-sieve engine across many processes, or the whole system, instead of a single PID. It recognizes and dumps replaced or implanted PE modules, shellcode, hooks and other in-memory patches for further analysis, selecting processes by PID list, name list or creation time relative to the scan. Scans can repeat in a loop or, in the 64-bit build, run as an ETW listener whose INI profile chooses the triggering events.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.4.1.1, published 2025-09-13, with 32- and 64-bit executables, ZIP archives and DLL-build archives; the README also points to a Chocolatey package, and the wiki to unstable AppVeyor test builds. The reviewed master commit identifies itself as the unreleased 0.4.1.3, 37 commits later and mostly PE-sieve submodule updates.

Windows only. Source builds need a recursive clone with the pinned PE-sieve, paramkit and Microsoft krabsetw submodules, plus CMake 3.12+; AppVeyor builds x86 and x64 with Visual Studio 2019, and mingw_build.sh shows a MinGW-w64 cross-build. ETW mode works only in the 64-bit build, must run as Administrator and writes HH_ETWProfile.ini to the current directory.

It scans processes running on the analyst's own system or VM, and the repository holds no samples. Hook and patch scanning is off by default and enabled with /hooks, dumps go to the current directory unless /dir is given, and the wiki calls looped full-system scans processor-intensive. The wiki warns that detected processes are not necessarily malicious and links PE-sieve's false-positive FAQ, so reports and dumps need review; the optional /suspend and /kill responses act on live processes.

AppVeyor runs ctest after each build: the tests check that the executable starts and that scans of the clean build machine report zero suspicious processes, then run IAT, hook, thread and shellcode-pattern scans that only check the report format. The only GitHub workflow publishes Doxygen code documentation.
BSD-2-Clause, like PE-sieve; krabsetw is MIT, and the pinned paramkit commit has no license file.

resources.name: awesome-reverse-engineering (alphaSeclab)
resources.description: Large reverse-engineering link list, auto-exported in 2019 in English and Chinese, with abridged and full README versions. The full English README lists about 3,600 open-source tools and 2,300 posts and videos, grouped under Windows, Linux, Apple platforms and Android, and under tool sections for IDA, Ghidra, x64dbg, OllyDbg, WinDbg, radare2, Cuckoo, Binary Ninja and dynamic binary instrumentation. Tool rows carry a star count, language and upstream description captured at export time.
requirements: The latest master commit dates from 2019-12-31; GitHub reports a later push in 2021, but master holds no newer commit and the list has not been updated since. Its star counts, update ages and links reflect that export, so many may be out of date.

Readme_en.md and the Chinese Readme.md are abridged pages; the English one has 675 tool rows and 684 post rows. Readme_full_en.md and Readme_full.md hold the complete list, with 3,619 tool rows and 2,310 dated post rows in English. Post rows give a month, a source site and a title, and many point to Chinese forums such as Kanxue and Anquanke.
The README says the contents are auto-exported by the maintainers' system. Rows are list entries: they state no license, maintenance status or verification.
No license file is present and GitHub detects none, so the list states no reuse terms; linked projects and posts keep their own rights. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: restore-symbol
resources.description: macOS command-line tool that writes a stripped iOS app's Mach-O executable back out with a rebuilt symbol table, so a debugger such as lldb can break on and display Objective-C method names. It recovers method names and addresses from the binary's Objective-C metadata through class-dump, and can merge extra name and address pairs from a JSON file, such as the block symbols found by the bundled IDA script.
requirements: There are no releases or tags; the reviewed master commit of 2019-04-27 is the latest, and the repository has no tests or CI. The README covers Objective-C methods and blocks only and does not mention Swift symbols.

Builds on macOS with Xcode: make initializes the pinned class-dump submodule (0xced's fork) and runs xcodebuild on a project targeting macOS 10.11. The block-symbol script search_oc_block/ida_search_block.py runs inside IDA, uses Python 2 print statements and the legacy idaapi.get_inf_structure call, and writes block_symbol.json.

Input is a thin armv7 or arm64 Mach-O executable from an app the user is authorized to analyze; the tool rejects fat files with a request to thin them using lipo, and writes a new output file instead of changing the input. The README then re-signs the bundle with the user's own developer certificate and debugs it on a device with lldb. The repository contains source and a README screenshot, no app binaries.

There is no license file and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms for restore-symbol's own code are not stated; the build links the MachObjC library from the class-dump submodule, which is GPL-2.0-or-later.

resources.name: awesome-mobile-security
resources.description: A single-README list of Android and iOS application security resources, about 245 links in all, divided by platform into blogs, papers and how-tos, books, courses, tools, deliberately vulnerable lab apps, talks and miscellany. Android tools are further split into static analysis, dynamic analysis and online APK analyzers, and reverse-engineering entries such as smali/baksmali, radare2, Cutter, Bytecode Viewer, Frida and Objection sit alongside pentesting guides and vulnerability write-ups.
requirements: The reviewed README, last changed 2021-01-20, has 168 Android and 78 iOS list entries, a few of them repeated. It has not changed since, so listed versions and services date from that time; for example, it names Magisk v20.2.

Entries give a name and link, sometimes with a short note, and state no license, maintenance status, platform requirement or test result. The list mixes open-source projects, commercial and online scanning services, books, courses and conference talks, and includes rooting and jailbreak tools, so check each resource's own terms and use it only on devices and apps you are authorized to test.
The repository holds only README.md and has no license file, so the list states no reuse terms; its GitHub description says the references and tools belong to their respective owners.

resources.name: Dexcalibur (Reversense)
resources.description: Android reverse-engineering platform that combines static analysis with Frida-based dynamic instrumentation; the master branch is Reversense (Dexcalibur 2.0), a rewrite that runs as a Node.js web server for collaborative projects. Its README describes modeling an app's files, Smali and native code into one searchable representation with Radare2 integration, generating hooks for Java methods, Objective-C and native functions, and building dynamic cross-references from traces collected on attached devices. Inspector plugins in the repository observe areas such as permissions, cryptography, file-system, network and UI activity.
requirements: The latest GitHub release and npm package are still the original Dexcalibur v0.7.10 (2021-09-27, Apache-2.0 in its package metadata); the reviewed master commit (2026-10-02) declares the unreleased 2.0.0 rewrite. Its README getting-started, prerequisite and installation sections, and the installation page of the linked documentation site, are unfinished placeholders, and TESTED.md lists only a short set of basic engine, web-server, platform, device, project and ADB-bridge checks.

package.json targets Node.js on macOS, Linux and Windows (.nvmrc pins 22.14.0), and the reviewed commit adds Deno as a second runner; the documentation site says Windows is not officially supported. The README asks for a .dexcalibur settings folder in the user's home directory and names Frida 16.1.4, while package.json depends on frida ^17.6.2. MongoDB backs the project database (the Docker Compose file uses MongoDB 6.0.9), OpenID Connect with KeyCloak provides SSO, and the web UIs and device agent are built from separate reversenseorg repositories.

Analysis starts from the user's own app package and, for dynamic work, an Android device or emulator reachable over ADB with Frida. The third-party setup script downloads Android platform-tools, apktool 2.7.0, baksmali 2.5.2 and binwalk from their upstream hosts. The repository's test workspace bundles apktool.jar, OWASP's UnCrackable Level 1 training APK with its apktool-decoded files, and small ELF, Mach-O, plist and nib parser fixtures.

The 2.0 source is AGPL-3.0-only; the third-party notice covers EFF's apkeep (MIT). README features such as automated SAST/DAST scanning, device-farm management and the built-in MCP server are project-reported, and Reversense offers professional support and modules separately. Intended for apps the analyst is authorized to inspect.

resources.name: FakeNet-NG
resources.description: Mandiant FLARE's dynamic network analysis tool for malware analysts, a successor to the original Fakenet. Its Diverter redirects traffic from local processes on Windows, or from other hosts in Linux MultiHost mode, to configurable listeners that simulate DNS, HTTP and HTTPS, SMTP, FTP, TFTP, IRC, POP and raw TCP or UDP services, with process and host filters, custom responses and an option to launch a command such as a debugger on a connection. Sessions can be saved as PCAP and end with an interactive HTML report of network-based indicators grouped by process and protocol.
requirements: Latest release at review: v3.5, published 2025-04-09, as fakenet3.5.zip with a PyInstaller fakenet.exe for Windows. The reviewed master commit, 11 commits later and still versioned 3.5, adds a Windows release-build workflow, CRL generation for TLS revocation checks and SingleHost as the default NetworkMode, although the README still recommends Auto.

Module installs use Python 3.10.11 and administrator rights; Windows needs the Visual C++ build tools, and Linux needs build tools, Python and libnetfilter-queue development packages and port 53 freed from systemd-resolved, with the README's Linux steps tested on Ubuntu 24.04.2. SingleHost mode needs Windows Vista or later and is experimental on Linux, without process and host filtering; MultiHost is Linux-only, only TCP, UDP and ICMP are intercepted, and the Linux Diverter mishandles packets over 4,016 bytes.

The README recommends a controlled, isolated VM, because the tool changes the system's network settings, and says antivirus and EDR products may flag it. The repository bundles runtime helpers: WinDivert 32- and 64-bit DLLs and drivers, a small FakeNetMini.exe and other placeholder files served from defaultFiles, and TLS listener keys plus a static CA certificate and private key. The repository states no separate license for the WinDivert files, and the README notes that some dynamically loaded libraries may be LGPL; since the CA private key is public, trust that CA only inside the analysis VM.

docs/testing.md describes an interactive test/test.py suite and manual tests on Windows and Linux VMs on a host-only network; the GitHub workflow only builds the Windows PyInstaller release. FakeNet-NG itself is Apache-2.0.

resources.name: Joern
resources.description: Static code analysis platform that parses source code, JVM bytecode and executables into code property graphs held in a graph database and queried with a Scala-based language from an interactive shell or server mode. Frontends cover C/C++, Java, JavaScript, Python, Kotlin, PHP, Go, Ruby, Swift, C#, Rust and ABAP source, JVM bytecode and APK/DEX files through Soot, and binaries loaded through an embedded Ghidra, which the documentation lists as x86/x64 support. It adds a static taint-tracking engine, the joern-scan query database of vulnerability patterns, and export of AST, CFG, PDG or whole-graph views to DOT, GraphML, GraphSON or Neo4j CSV.
requirements: Release at review: v4.0.660, published 2026-10-19; the README says releases are created automatically once a day, and the reviewed master commit is three commits ahead of that tag. Each release ships joern-cli zips for Linux, macOS and Windows on x86_64 and arm64 plus joern-install.sh, and the README also documents ghcr.io/joernio/joern Docker images, with an AlmaLinux 8 variant for CPUs without SSE4.2.

The README requires JDK 21 and says other versions have not been properly tested; gcc and g++ are optional, for discovering C/C++ system headers. Source builds use sbt, with an experimental partial Bazel setup. Inputs are the user's own source trees, class, JAR, APK or DEX files, or executables.

Binary support is the ghidra2cpg frontend, built on a bundled Ghidra 12.2 package. It has specific passes for MIPS and ARM/AArch64 and routes every other processor through its x86 pass; its README notes that varargs are not handled properly. The documentation's maturity table rates C/C++ and Java very high, JavaScript, Python and x86/x64 via Ghidra high, JVM bytecode, Kotlin, PHP, Go and Swift medium, and Ruby and C# medium-low; the Rust and ABAP frontends in the reviewed tree are not rated there.

Apache-2.0; CITATION.cff still names version 2.0, released 2024-01-18. The project describes itself as a tool for vulnerability discovery and static program analysis research; query and taint results describe the generated graph, not observed runtime behavior.

resources.name: ReverserAI
resources.description: Binary Ninja plugin that suggests function names from HLIL decompiler output with a language model run locally through llama.cpp; the README says it operates entirely offline once the model is downloaded. It can rename the current function, every function still carrying a default sub_ name in call-graph post-order, or only those referencing strings and imported or library symbols. The author presents it as a research proof of concept whose only implemented task is function naming.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is the v1.2 release of 2026-05-20, and plugin.json and setup.py both declare version 1.2. It installs through Binary Ninja’s plugin manager, or by cloning into Binary Ninja’s plugins folder and installing requirements.txt (huggingface-hub, llama-cpp-python, networkx, toml, typer) and the package; setup.py asks for Python 3.10+, and plugin.json lists macOS, Windows and Linux with minimum Binary Ninja build 2487.

On first use the plugin downloads the selected GGUF model from Hugging Face: by default mistral-7b-instruct-v0.2.Q4_K_M.gguf, about 5 GB and needing about 5 GB of RAM, or a Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct quantization needing about 25 GB. Inference then runs on the local CPU or GPU, which the README describes as entirely offline. It advises at least 16 GB of RAM and 12 CPU threads and reports 20 to 30 seconds per query on CPU, or 2 to 5 seconds with GPU offload such as on Apple silicon. Model, memory mapping, CPU threads, GPU layers and seed are Binary Ninja settings that take effect after a restart.

Three Plugins → ReverserAI commands cover the naming modes: Rename Current Function, Rename All Functions, and Enhance Function Naming with Context, which limits renaming to default-named functions referencing strings or import, library or external symbols. Each request puts one function’s HLIL text into a fixed prompt asking for a name of up to 20 characters, keeps the first line of the reply and writes it to the database as the function name without a confirmation step, logging the old and new names. Functions whose decompiler output exceeds the 4,000-token context fail with a logged warning.

The README calls ReverserAI a proof of concept, notes that local models do not match cloud models, and plans code explanation, other decompilers and server-hosted inference only as future work. The examples folder ships a password-protected samples.zip of test samples, including the PowerPC stub triton_inject.bin from the Triton malware, and its README describes their results qualitatively. CI runs only ruff formatting and lint checks, a setup.py metadata check and a Python syntax parse; there are no tests.
GPL-2.0 per LICENSE; plugin.json and setup.py state version 2 or later. Binary Ninja and the downloaded model weights keep their own licences and terms.

resources.name: Speakeasy
resources.description: Mandiant's Windows malware emulation framework, which runs PE executables, DLLs, kernel drivers and raw x86/amd64 shellcode on the Unicorn CPU emulator inside a modeled Windows runtime instead of a full VM. Hand-written handlers and a signature database built from win32metadata and phnt emulate Windows API calls, process and thread behavior, the filesystem, registry and network, and each run is recorded as a structured JSON report of API events with named arguments, dropped files and optional memory snapshots. It runs from the speakeasy CLI or as a Python library, and a built-in GDB stub lets an analyst step through an emulated sample.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.0.0b9, a GitHub pre-release published 2026-10-11 that tags the reviewed master commit and moves the report format to version 5.0.0. The newest stable speakeasy-emulator on PyPI is still 1.5.11 from 2022, and pip skips pre-releases by default, so the README's plain pip install resolves to 1.5.11 unless a 2.0 beta is requested.

Requires Python 3.10+; dependencies include Unicorn 2.1.4+, pefile, Capstone and pycryptodome, and the package is marked OS independent. Source installs need a recursive clone for the win32json and phnt submodules plus two scripts that generate the API signature databases; the Dockerfile builds a Python 3.13 image that mounts samples at /sandbox. GDB sessions connect gdb-multiarch or another GDB to the stub, which the documentation warns has no authentication.

Samples come from the user. The tests use small test executables, DLLs, WDM drivers and a shellcode blob under tests/bins, and the capa-testfiles submodule of Mandiant's capa test data, which supplies Practical Malware Analysis lab samples; handle both as malware-analysis material.

The limitations page says only a curated subset of APIs has handlers: APIs emulated from signatures alone return success values without real side effects, unknown imports stop a run, and a missing file, registry key or network response can look like anti-analysis behavior, so reports need analyst interpretation. MIT licensed; the win32json, phnt and capa-testfiles submodules keep their own terms.

resources.name: iOS App Reverse Engineering
resources.description: Freely published 2015 book by snakeninny and hangcom on reverse engineering iOS apps, distributed in its repository as a 442-page English PDF. Its four parts cover the iOS filesystem and file types; OS X and on-device tools such as class-dump, Theos, Reveal, IDA, Cycript and LLDB with debugserver; an Objective-C and ARM assembly methodology for locating the code behind a feature; and four worked practices that locate the relevant code in Notes, Mail, WeChat and Messages and then extend those apps with tweaks.
requirements: A historical resource: the repository has not changed since 2015-09-17 and holds only the README, an MIT LICENSE and the PDF. The book states that its examples were done on an iPhone 5 with iOS 8.1, and its tooling chapters date from the Xcode 6 and Cydia Substrate era, so tools, file locations and app internals described there may no longer match current iOS releases.

Reading needs only a PDF reader. The practices assume an OS X host with the tools the book names and a jailbroken test device, and they examine Apple's bundled apps and WeChat as installed on that device.

The cover credits the English translation to Ziqi Wu, 0xBBC, tianqing and Fei Cheng, and the preface warns that the book may contain errors and inaccuracies. The README invites readers who find it useful to buy the paid ebook edition.
MIT license, copyright 2015 snakeninny; the apps examined in the practices keep their owners' rights.

resources.name: LazyIDA
resources.description: Single-file IDA plugin of convenience actions first written for CTF work. In the disassembly and hex views it dumps a selection as a string, hex string, C/C++ array or Python list of bytes, words, dwords or qwords and copies the result to the clipboard, shows a selection XORed with one byte, fills it with NOPs, and copies or jumps to addresses and file offsets by hotkey. With Hex-Rays it toggles a function’s return type to void, copies item names and jumps to the member function behind an obj->func call on double-click, while a heuristic scan lists printf-family calls whose format argument is not a read-only constant.
requirements: The reviewed master commit is three commits after the v1.1.0 release of 2026-01-25; LazyIDA.py now declares 1.1.1 while ida-plugin.json still says 1.1.0. The plugin is the single LazyIDA.py file, installed with Hex-Rays’ hcli plugin command or copied into the IDA plugins directory. ida-plugin.json asks for IDA 7.4 or later on Windows x86-64, Linux x86-64 and macOS x86-64 or arm64; the changelog adds IDA 9.0 and 9.2 support, and clipboard access uses PySide6 on IDA 9.2+ and PyQt5 on earlier GUI builds.

It works on whatever database the user opens in IDA and bundles no sample binaries. The Hex-Rays actions load only when a Hex-Rays decompiler initialises. The format-string scan is offered in the disassembly view only for 32- and 64-bit x86 and 32-bit ARM databases; it walks back from each call to printf-family functions in .text, .plt, .idata or .plt.got using fixed register and stack-slot conventions, so its hits are leads to check by hand, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

The README says the project was written casually about ten years ago and that several features are now outdated: return-type removal is built into IDA 7.5+, IDA’s Shift-E export can replace the dump actions, and the format-string scan should be reimplemented with the Hex-Rays API; it points users to HappyIDA instead. Multi-byte dumps decode little-endian values, and Fill with NOPs writes x86 0x90 bytes into the database whatever the architecture.
The repository has no tests or CI. MIT per LICENSE and ida-plugin.json; IDA Pro and the Hex-Rays decompiler keep their own licences.

resources.name: Tiny Tracer
resources.description: Intel Pin tool by hasherezade that traces a 32- or 64-bit program while it runs on Windows or Linux, logging API calls (with arguments and return values for watched functions), chosen local and statically linked functions, inline system calls, RDTSC, CPUID and INT instructions, and transitions between sections of the traced module, which helps find the original entry point of a packed module. It can follow code the module unpacks into new memory, disassemble selected ranges and, on Windows, flag the anti-debug and anti-VM checks a sample performs. Each run writes a .tag file of RVA;event lines that PE-bear reads natively and that the wiki shows loading into IDA Pro, Binary Ninja, x64dbg, Ghidra and Cutter to annotate code.
requirements: Release at review: 4.0, published 2026-05-28 and refactored for Intel Pin 4.x; the reviewed master commit is two commits ahead of it. Releases contain source only, because, as the release notes and installation guide explain, Pin's license does not allow distributing compiled Pin tools. Users download Pin themselves and build the tool inside Pin's source/tools tree; the README names Pin 4.2 as the version tested, Pin before 4.0 needs a pre-4.0 release with the legacy build, and Windows versions older than 8 also need the legacy build.

Windows builds use MSYS2 make with clang-cl, with Visual Studio 2019 or later optional as an editor; Linux builds use g++ and make. Both scripts produce 32- and 64-bit builds in install32_64, which holds run_me.bat with context-menu .reg files, pin_attach.bat for attaching to a running process, tiny_runner.sh for Linux, and the TinyTracer.ini, params.txt and excluded.txt settings. The README says kernel debugging must be disabled for Pin to work.

install32_64 also commits the author's prebuilt Windows helpers dll_load32.exe, dll_load64.exe, kdb_check.exe, pe_check.exe and syscall_extract.exe, whose sources are in the separate hasherezade/pe_utils repository; the README notes that Windows Defender sometimes flags kdb_check.exe, a known false positive. The anti-debug and anti-VM modes are Windows-only, and the deep anti-debug mode is documented as prone to false positives. The analyst supplies the program to trace, which executes natively under Pin.
GPL-2.0 in LICENSE.txt; Intel Pin keeps its own license. Traces cover only code that executes during the run.

resources.name: vdexExtractor
resources.description: Command-line C tool that extracts the Dex bytecode held in the Vdex containers that ART's dex2oat compiler writes beside Oat files since Android 8.0 (API 26), and by default reverts ART's dex-to-dex quickening so the output is ordinary Dex again. It can also dump the verified-dependency records stored in a Vdex file, disassemble the bytecode in a dexdump-like format and report the Android API level of a Vdex version. Android 9 and 10 Vdex files hold CompactDex, which the bundled deodex helper converts back to standard Dex through a separately built compact_dex_converter.
requirements: Inactive: the last tag is 0.6.0 (2019-12-30), there are no GitHub releases, and the reviewed master commit (2020-05-13) is seven commits past that tag. Backends exist for Vdex versions 006, 010, 019 and 021, which the README and changelog place between Android 8 (Oreo) and Android 10 (Q); there is no backend for later Vdex versions.

Build with make.sh using gcc (default) or clang on Linux or macOS, or under Cygwin on Windows; zlib development files are required, and the cross-android target uses the Android NDK's ndk-build to produce armeabi-v7a, arm64-v8a, x86 and x86_64 executables. Binaries are written under bin/; the repository commits no prebuilt executables.

Inputs are Vdex files, or directories of them, that the user takes from their own device or system image; scripts/extract-apps-from-device.sh pulls the oat, art and vdex outputs, and optionally the APKs, of installed packages over ADB, and some system app data needs root. tools/deodex/run.sh needs wget, shasum and unzip and downloads the author's prebuilt compact_dex_converter archives from OneDrive with SHA-256 checks; the API 29 converter is Linux-only, and the converter's own source builds only as an AOSP module.
Apache-2.0 (copyright CENSUS S.A.). The README notes that equivalent unquickening was contributed to AOSP's oatdump. Recovered Dex code remains subject to the rights of the app or system-image owner.

resources.name: Ponce
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin, described by its repository as the winner of the 2016 IDA plugin contest, that brings the Triton framework's taint analysis and symbolic execution into IDA's debugger for x86 and x64 programs.
