After the analyst taints or symbolizes registers, memory or inputs such as argv or a buffer read with fread, Ponce single-steps the debugged program, analyzes each instruction with Triton and renames the functions that the input influences. Its symbolic engine can solve a branch condition, or negate it and inject a satisfying input into memory, while execution snapshots restore earlier state to try that input; builds with Hex-Rays support also show the results in decompiler pseudocode.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.3.7, published 2023-06-01, with prebuilt Windows, Linux and macOS zips; the Windows zip holds Ponce.dll and Ponce64.dll builds for IDA 7.0 through 8.1, with none for later IDA releases. The README says Ponce works with any IDA version from 7.0 and that the binary built for the installed IDA version must be used. The reviewed master commit of 2025-06-06 adds only a work-in-progress CI fix after that release.

Installation copies the matching build into IDA's plugins folder; the README lists native Windows, Linux and OS X support. Source builds use CMake 3.15+, the IDA SDK for the target version (IDASDK_ROOT_DIR) and Triton, which the CI installs through vcpkg; pseudocode feedback also needs hexrays.hpp from an IDA installation that includes the Hex-Rays decompiler, otherwise -DBUILD_HEXRAYS_SUPPORT=OFF. The repository contains no SDK files, and its CI clones the SDK archives from a separate repository that is not public, so source builds rely on the user's own SDK.

Ponce analyzes a program the analyst runs under IDA's debugger, stepping one instruction at a time; the README cites about 3,000 instructions per second in the authors' tests, and common library functions such as printf are blacklisted from analysis by default. The limitations page says symbolic memory indexes can lose track of the input, Triton handles floating-point instructions poorly, and concolic execution only analyzes instructions that actually execute.
Ponce's own terms are a BSD-style license, and LICENSE also reproduces Triton's BSD and Z3's MIT licenses; GitHub does not classify the file.

resources.name: CAN Commander
resources.description: A Flipper Zero app and earlier Arduino sketches for reverse engineering CAN bus traffic, chiefly in vehicles. The current app is a UART front end for a CAN Commander ESP32 board: it streams all or filtered frames, lists unique IDs, measures message rates, tracks per-bit and per-byte changes, and runs a two-phase Auto Reverse Engineer that first calibrates out background traffic and then shows which IDs change during an action. It also decodes live signals from DBC-based profiles and reads OBD-II PIDs, the VIN and trouble codes.
requirements: The reviewed main commit of 2026-04-25 sets app version v2.3.1 (fap_version 2.3), and there are no GitHub releases. The app needs a CAN Commander board connected to the Flipper's GPIO and running ESP32 firmware v2.2 or newer. That firmware, and the converter from .dbc files to the app's .dbcprof and .injprof profiles, are offered at cancommander.com rather than in this repository.

The README lists limits such as 16 cached DBC signals, 10 tracked changed IDs on the reverse-engineering dashboard and 384 frames per replay recording, and warns that heavy traffic needs filtering and that streaming the Flipper screen during DBC decoding can exhaust RAM. A Wi-Fi TCP command line mirrors the USB command set; dedicated companion clients are described as planned.

Legacy/ keeps the earlier Arduino sketches for Arduino, ESP8266, ESP32 or RP2040 boards with an MCP2515 controller, a bundled MCP2515 library copy with an MIT notice, a JavaScript BLE companion app, OBD-II PID tables and about 80 vehicle DBC files without a stated source or license. The repository has no tests or CI.

The write, Smart Injection, Replay and Clear DTCs tools transmit on the bus and can change vehicle state; use them only on vehicles and networks you own or are authorized to test. There is no license file and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms for the project's own code are not stated.

resources.name: Frida Snippets
resources.description: A single large README that collects hand-written Frida instrumentation examples, grouped into Native, Android and iOS sections, for observing how a running app behaves. The examples show patterns such as attaching interceptors, enumerating loaded modules and classes, describing class members, tracing method arguments and return values, printing backtraces, logging SQLite queries and I/O, and scanning or dumping process memory. A scripts directory adds helper code, including Python generators that emit hook stubs from a decompiler and a frida-server install script, plus editor snippets for Sublime and Vim.
requirements: A reference collection, not an installable package: the content is the README and the scripts directory at the reviewed commit (last pushed 2024-11-29). The snippets assume a current Frida and are written for its JavaScript API with some ObjC and Java bridge calls; running any of them needs a separate, matching Frida install, which the repository does not pin.

Examples run against an app the analyst controls: Android snippets expect a device or emulator with a frida-server (the bundled install_frida_server.sh pushes one over ADB), and the iOS notes assume a jailbroken device. Scripts are standalone and uneven in quality, with several explicitly marked work-in-progress (WIP) files, and one JEB plugin that copies a generated hook to the clipboard needs JEB and xclip.
The target app comes from the user; the repository ships only example code and one demonstration GIF, no app binaries. It is intended for instrumenting software the analyst is authorized to analyze.
No license file is present and GitHub detects no license, so the examples carry no granted reuse terms and default to all rights reserved by the author.

resources.name: Sony Headphones Client: a desktop client for Sony’s headset control protocol
resources.description: Recreates part of Sony’s mobile-only Headphones app as a Windows, Linux and macOS desktop client that changes noise-cancelling, ambient-sound and virtual-sound settings over a Bluetooth RFCOMM connection to a paired headset. The author reports reverse engineering the phone app to define its control protocol, and the code rebuilds its message framing, with start and end markers, byte escaping, sequence numbers, a sum checksum and acknowledgements, together with the two set-parameter commands the client sends. Full support is reported for few models, mainly the WH-1000XM3, and the project is archived.
requirements: The reviewed master commit of 2025-07-19 is ten commits after the v1.3.2 release of 2023-04-26, adding build notes, a GCC include fix and the archival notice; CMakeLists.txt still embeds version 1.3.1. The repository is archived: the README says the app keeps working for the devices it supports and points to untested forks for others. Implemented controls are ambient sound with focus on voice, disabling noise cancelling, and the Virtual Sound VPT and sound-position presets; reading battery or current settings from the headset and the equalizer were never done, so the client only sends settings.

No Sony software or files are needed or included; the client connects over RFCOMM to the headset’s control service UUID. The README reports the WH-1000XM3 and MDR-XB950BT as fully working and the WH-1000XM4 as partial, with other models in a user report issue, and the serializer caps ambient-sound levels at the WH-1000XM3’s 19 steps. The README says the app was reverse engineered for interoperability and that only some enums and data are in the code, the rest to be obtained statically or dynamically, linking a comment on sniffing messages; no decompiled app code, captures or method notes are in the repository.

Releases provide prebuilt Windows x64, Linux x64 and macOS builds, and the Windows build needs the Microsoft VC++ Redistributable. Windows and Linux builds use CMake, a C++20 compiler and the Dear ImGui submodule, with Visual Studio 2022 and the Windows SDK on Windows and BlueZ, GLEW, GLFW, D-Bus and OpenGL development packages on Linux; macOS builds use the bundled Xcode project.
CI only builds the Linux and Windows clients with CMake and the macOS app with xcodebuild and uploads them; there are no protocol tests, and headset compatibility is user-reported.

MIT per LICENSE; the bundled Cascadia Code font is under the SIL Open Font License, and Dear ImGui keeps its own license. The README states the program is not affiliated with Sony, which keeps its rights in the app and headsets.

resources.name: Garlic
resources.description: Java and Android decompiler written in C that recovers Java source from class, JAR, WAR, DEX and APK files on multiple threads; it also prints javap- or dexdump-style class listings, converts APK and DEX files to smali, searches their strings with regular expressions and generates call graphs for DEX and APK files. Running garlic -m starts a stdio MCP server whose seven tools decompile files, dump class information, build call graphs, load them into DuckDB for SQL queries and read the extracted AndroidManifest.xml. The README reports decompiling an APK of more than 200 MB with about 190,000 classes in 12 seconds.
requirements: Latest garlic release at review: v1.8-release, published 2026-08-17, with standalone binaries for Linux x64, i686 and aarch64, macOS x64 and aarch64, and Windows win32 and win64; the reviewed main commit is 34 commits ahead of it. The later v1.8-release-thyme tag instead carries installers for Thyme, a separate paid reverse-engineering IDE presented on the repository's homepage.

Source builds use CMake 3.26+ on Linux and macOS, Zig 0.16.0+ for host and cross-compiled builds, MinGW-w64 for Windows, or the Android NDK (r21 or later, verified on r28) for an arm64-v8a binary. The MCP server needs the DuckDB CLI on PATH for its analyze, cg_import and cg_query tools. Inputs are the user's own class, JAR, WAR, DEX or APK files.

The -n native-library analysis, which the README lists as control flow, IR, imports, exports, strings and call graphs for AArch64 ELF files, comes from librosemarylib: a closed-source library committed in prebuilt form as librosemarylib.so, .dylib and .dll files under libs/ for each desktop platform and embedded into the garlic binary at build time. Without it, and on Android, -n is disabled. garlic's -l option installs a purchased license key for that library.

The repository's LICENSE is Apache-2.0; no separate terms or source are published for librosemarylib. The README reports no correctness evaluation of decompiled output, and release notes list fixes for decompilation errors and crashes on specific apps.

resources.name: DRAKVUF Sandbox
resources.description: CERT Polska’s automated black-box malware analysis system built on the DRAKVUF engine, which observes a Windows guest from the Xen hypervisor through virtual machine introspection rather than an agent installed in the guest. Samples submitted through the web interface or the CLI run in a restored snapshot, and the report covers the process tree, WinAPI, file and network activity, a PCAP, intercepted TLS keys, memory dumps, screenshots and capa-based TTP indicators. A drakrun installer builds the Windows guest, its snapshot and the VMI profile.
requirements: The reviewed master commit is the v0.21.0 release of 2026-08-19, which GitHub ships as a Python wheel; the drakvuf-sandbox package provides the drakrun CLI, web application and workers, needs Python 3.9+ and pins its dependencies, including flare-capa 7.4.0. The host needs an Intel CPU with VT-x and EPT and Debian 12 or Ubuntu 22.04 booted through GRUB into Xen 4.17+ (4.19 recommended); the getting-started guide asks for at least two cores and 8 GB of RAM, while the README says 5 GB. Xen, LibVMI and the DRAKVUF engine come from prebuilt .deb packages or source builds, Redis, dnsmasq, tcpdump and other host packages are added, and the documented installation runs as root.

Guests are Windows 10 x64 (build 2004 or later, 22H2 recommended) or Windows 7 x64, installed by drakrun install from a Windows installation ISO the user supplies and completed over VNC, then snapshotted and profiled by drakrun postinstall. The guide suggests turning off UAC and Windows Defender in the reference snapshot and adding Visual C++ and .NET runtimes, and each analysis can cut the guest’s internet access. Nested virtualization works under Xen, under KVM as experimental, and under VMware Workstation with virtualized EPT; cloud hosts, Hyper-V and VMware Fusion are unsupported.

Observations come from DRAKVUF plugins: apimon, filetracer, memdump, procmon, socketmon and tlsmon by default, with regmon, syscalls, exmon and others optional and Intel Processor Trace plugins documented as experimental. The docs warn that many plugins slow execution, that monitoring begins only after the sample process starts, and that summary observations derive from DRAKVUF output, so exact network data should be checked in the PCAP. S3 storage, a ZFS storage backend and Karton integration are optional.

Profiling injects a small drakshell shellcode agent into explorer.exe for preparation commands. The repository carries source for drakshell and other guest helpers, a 15 KB test/test.exe sample used by its sanity test, and pinned DRAKVUF and Mandiant capa-rules submodules. That test suite installs the sandbox on a VM-runner service needing project credentials, while the public workflow only builds the docs, tools, web bundle and wheel and lints the Python code. The README warns that maintaining a sandbox is difficult and bugs may reproduce only on one configuration.

LICENSE applies GPL-2.0 with the authors’ added clarifications and exceptions, including a broad reading of derivative works and a bar on combining it with plain-GPL software, so GitHub reports no standard license; DRAKVUF and the capa rules keep their own licenses, and Windows guests remain under Microsoft’s terms. It is a defensive platform for running untrusted samples in isolated guests.

resources.name: HexRaysPyTools
resources.description: IDAPython plugin for IDA Pro's Hex-Rays decompiler that helps rebuild structures and classes from pseudocode. Its structure builder collects the fields a variable accesses within one function or, with deep scan, across the functions it is passed to, marks virtual tables, resolves conflicting fields and finalizes a C declaration applied to every scanned variable; a Classes view edits classes and their virtual functions, and a graph shows how local types relate. Pseudocode helpers recast and rename across assignments and calls, propagate names, rewrite out-of-bounds pointers as CONTAINING_RECORD for a containing structure, edit function signatures, rename functions from assert strings and untangle if statements.
requirements: No commits since 2020-02-15 and no releases; the tags ida_6_8 and ida_7_2 mark older code. The README states support for IDA Pro 7.x with Python 2 or 3 and says nothing about later IDA releases; it notes that IDA 7.4 added an official implementation of its structure cross-references (Shift+X), describes Guessing Allocation as a very raw feature and marks its API as under construction.

Needs IDA Pro with the Hex-Rays decompiler. Installation copies HexRaysPyTools.py and the HexRaysPyTools directory into IDA's plugins folder; settings live in IDADIR\cfg\HexRaysPyTools.cfg, and by default the cross-references collected during decompilation are stored in the database (store_xrefs). It works on the analyst's own IDA databases and type libraries.
The repository has no license file and GitHub detects no license, so it grants no explicit reuse terms.

resources.name: Automated CAN Payload Reverse Engineering
resources.description: Research Python and R scripts that automate reverse engineering of Controller Area Network (CAN) payloads recorded from passenger vehicles, implementing the pipeline from Brent Stone's AFIT dissertation. The Python pipeline pre-processes a CAN log into per-arbitration-ID data frames, pulls out public SAE J1979 diagnostic data, runs a lexical analysis that guesses individual signal time-series boundaries, then a semantic analysis that builds a correlation matrix and hierarchically clusters related signals, with plots and a dendrogram as output. A separate R script set applies the rEDM empirical dynamic modeling package to engine-RPM, brake-pressure and vehicle-speed time series to study causal relationships.
requirements: Dissertation research code with no releases or tags; the reviewed commit dates to 2022-02-01. The README says the scripts were developed and tested on Python 3.6 and need NumPy, Pandas, scikit-learn and (for plotting) matplotlib listed in requirements.txt; the R scripts need R with the rEDM package. There is no packaging or install step, and the README says the scripts will not run immediately after cloning.

Two Python folders implement the same concept: Pipeline is the basic single-file version driven from Main.py, and Pipeline_multi-file is the more complete batch version that the README says contains bug fixes not back-ported to Pipeline. Input is a CAN capture in the bundled loggerProgram0.log delta-time/ID/DLC/hex format; an April 2020 addition also reads the can-utils log format via a -c/--can-utils argument, and other formats require editing PreProcessor.py.

The user supplies their own CAN capture. The repository bundles the author's own example data: the loggerProgram0.log vehicle capture, example pipeline output, an OBD2 PID table, and R-folder CSV time series of engine RPM, brake pressure and vehicle speed for different driving conditions, plus the author's dissertation PDF. The results are signal-boundary and clustering estimates that need analyst validation, not confirmed signal definitions.

The repository includes a GPL-3.0 LICENSE file, while the README states the code is a work of the U.S. Government not subject to copyright protection in the United States, cleared for public release (case 88ABW-2019-0910). The scripts read passive logs and perform analysis only; no device interaction or frame transmission is described.

resources.name: CAPE Sandbox (CAPEv2)
resources.description: Malware sandbox derived from Cuckoo v1 that runs samples in isolated Windows guests and records API-hook behavior, created and modified files, network traffic as PCAP, screenshots and memory dumps. Its capemon monitor adds automated unpacking, capturing injected, extracted or decompressed payloads and dumping process images, plus a debugger that YARA signatures or submission options can program with breakpoints and short instruction traces. Results are classified with YARA, Suricata and behavioral signatures, and malware configurations are extracted by parsers maintained in the separate CAPE-parsers package.
requirements: There are no releases or tags: the reviewed master commit of 2026-10-18 is a rolling snapshot, with changes recorded in changelog.md, and pyproject.toml carries the placeholder version 0.1.0. The README recommends an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS host with KVM and Python 3.10 or 3.12, and Windows 10 or Windows 11 23H2 guests running agent.py under 32-bit Python 3.7.2 or 3.8. The kvm-qemu.sh and cape2.sh installers must be edited before use, only the rooter component runs as root, and the README asks users to read every file in conf/.

Users supply the samples and their own Windows guest VMs; the repository ships no guest operating system. The Windows analyzer bundles helper binaries: the capemon.dll and capemon_x64.dll monitors and the loader.exe and loader_x64.exe loaders, built from the separate GPL-3.0 capemon repository; PPLinject and version.dll helpers whose source the reviewed files do not identify; and third-party tools under their publishers' own terms, namely Sysinternals PsExec, signtool.exe from the Windows SDK and the AutoIt3 interpreter.

CI runs ruff, the pytest suites for the core, web interface and Linux analyzer, and mypy on Ubuntu 22.04 with Python 3.10 after a recursive checkout, plus pytest for the Windows analyzer on Windows. These check the framework's code, not detection or unpacking quality, and the README warns that configuration parsers can break as malware families change. A recursive clone also fetches the CAPE-TestFiles unit-test submodule, which includes a malware folder.

LICENSE applies GPL-3.0 under a Cuckoo Foundation notice, which GitHub reports as NOASSERTION; the bundled Microsoft and AutoIt executables are not covered by it. Analysis executes malicious files, which the README places in an isolated environment.

resources.name: LuaDec
resources.description: Lua bytecode decompiler that turns compiled chunks back into Lua source, with a disassembly mode, selection of single nested functions by number and a guesser for local variable declarations that can be overridden by hand. Its -fc option recompiles each decompiled function and compares it instruction by instruction with the original. It targets Lua 5.1, marks Lua 5.2 and 5.3 support as experimental, and continues Hisham Muhammad’s LuaDec for Lua 5.0 and Zsolt Sztupak’s LuaDec51.
requirements: The reviewed master commit, the latest on the default branch, dates from 2017-01-06, and the repository has no releases or tags. A build initialises one Lua submodule from the author’s lua5 fork (branch 5.1, 5.2 or 5.3), builds that Lua, then runs make LUAVER=5.x in luadec/, which also builds the luareplace and luaopswap helpers; Visual C++ 2008 project files are included, which the README says were tested with VC 2008 and 2013. A Travis CI configuration builds each Lua version with gcc and clang but runs no tests.

Input is a chunk compiled by the matching standard Lua version, or a Lua source file compiled on the fly for testing. For bytecode from a virtual machine with a reordered opcode table, luaopswap compares that VM’s compilation of a bundled script using every opcode with a standard compilation, derives an opcode map and rewrites files to standard opcodes; luareplace swaps a nested function between two files. The -fc check reports per function whether the decompiled code recompiles to the same instructions, and the README’s own example shows failures, so output must be checked function by function.

test/ holds small Lua source cases for control-flow constructs, and test-compiled/lua-5.1 bundles compiled Lua 5.1 chunks as decompiler inputs, including files named for the Xunlei downloader, JX3 add-ons and the Defense Witches game; the repository does not state their origin or rights. ChunkSpy listers for each Lua version and Ruby comparison scripts are also included.

The README says LuaDec is free software under the same license as the original LuaDec but does not name it, the repository has no license file and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms are unclear; the Lua, LuaAssemblyTools, ilua and memwatch submodules and the bundled ChunkSpy scripts keep their own terms.

resources.name: xpcspy
resources.description: Frida-powered command-line tool that observes XPC messages exchanged between processes on iOS and macOS in both directions, for understanding how Apple-platform apps and services talk over XPC. It can spawn or attach to a target over a USB or remote Frida connection, filter the trace by direction (incoming or outgoing) and by service name with wildcards, and optionally parse the binary-plist payloads carried in XPC dictionaries, with bplist00 and bplist16 described as officially supported and bplist15 and bplist17 as experimental. A Python CLI drives a TypeScript Frida agent that is compiled to JavaScript.
requirements: Reviewed at tag v0.9.0 (the reviewed commit, last pushed 2026-05-11); the matching xpcspy 0.9.0 release was uploaded to PyPI the same day. requirements.txt pins frida ~=17.9.7 and frida-tools ~=14.8.2, so a compatible Frida must be present, and interception works only where that Frida can instrument the target: a local macOS process, or an iOS device reachable by a frida-server over USB (-U) or remotely (-R/-H).

Install with pip3 install xpcspy for the CLI. Building from source uses the Makefile: the Frida agent under agent/ is a TypeScript project compiled with frida-compile (needs Node.js and npm), then python3 setup.py sdist packages the Python tool. The package metadata credits author hot3eed and points its homepage at github.com/hot3eed/xpcspy.

The analyst chooses the process to inspect by name, PID, frontmost application or a spawned file; no sample files ship with the tool. It reads the XPC traffic of a running target for analysis and does not modify or inject messages. bplist parsing is partly experimental, and the README's TODO list notes recursive bplist deserialization and other unfinished work.
Apache-2.0.

resources.name: de4py
resources.description: Python deobfuscation and analysis toolkit with a PySide6 GUI and a CLI mode, aimed at analysts examining obfuscated or packed Python programs. It bundles deobfuscators for named Python obfuscators such as Jawbreaker, BlankOBF, PlusOBF, Wodx, Hyperion and pyobfuscate, and an AI-assisted "Onyx" engine that pairs a local Ollama LLM (default qwen2.5-coder:1.5b) with AST cleaning and pattern matching. A file analyzer detects packers such as PyInstaller, computes hashes, looks up suspicious strings and extracts metadata, while a behavior monitor and a Python-code execution shell support dynamic inspection of a target process. It has a plugin API and can be used as a library.
requirements: The reviewed main commit (2026-08-17) is 18 commits past the v3.3.2-stable release (2026-08-12) and carries the same 3.3.2 version. The README asks for Python 3.10+ and recommends Windows for full feature support, while pyproject.toml declares requires-python >=3.8. There is no PyPI package: install from source with git clone then pip install . (entry point de4py, or python -m de4py / python main.py).

Dependencies include PySide6 for the GUI, xdis, pefile and pyinstaller for the analyzers, plus requests, psutil, pycryptodome, colorama, pypresence and sentry-sdk; the project also ships a remote API client and Sentry telemetry. The optional Onyx AI engine needs a separately installed Ollama with the configured model pulled; the model and thresholds are set in the UI.

Inputs are the user's own obfuscated Python scripts or packed executables. The repository's samples directory bundles the project's own test fixtures: obfuscated Python files for each supported obfuscator and small packer-built sample executables (PyInstaller, Nuitka and py2exe outputs). No third-party application files are required.

Licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial); the README states the tool is free and open source and that any paid copies are misrepresentations, and GitHub does not classify this license. The disclaimer says the tool is for educational purposes and that software should not be deobfuscated without permission.

resources.name: FujiHack
resources.description: Research codebase for reverse engineering Fujifilm cameras so that custom code can run on them under a patched firmware. It holds ARM firmware patches, chiefly a PTP/USB debugger that adds memory read, write and execute commands, a host CLI that uploads code and dumps memory over USB, and C headers documenting Fujifilm’s RTOS API with per-model firmware addresses and function stubs. On-camera code adds POSIX, graphics and I/O wrappers over that RTOS, a video record-limit mod, button remapping and the Frontier UI and module system.
requirements: The reviewed master commit dates from 2024-08-17. Its two GitHub releases carry no files: 0.1.0, the debugger release of 2022-10-27, is marked deprecated in favour of a separate fffw project, and 0.2.0, a 2023 DOOM-port demo for the X-A2, is marked no longer supported. The README says FujiHack runs only under a patched firmware, that custom firmware is always dangerous and can damage the camera, and that recovery of bricked devices through the SoC boot ROM has not been reverse engineered. It reports the debugger patch ported to the XF1 and X-A2; model headers with firmware addresses cover ten cameras, from the Z3 and HS20EXR to the X-T4.

The repository contains no Fujifilm firmware, dumps or keys: model headers reference the vendor’s own firmware download URLs, and patching happens in the separate browser-based patcher, which the README says unpacks, injects, patches, repacks and downgrades a firmware DAT file the user selects. Helper programs in etc/, including a Unicorn emulation script, read firmware or RAM dumps the user makes from their own camera.

On-camera code is built per model with arm-none-eabi-gcc, plus rustc for a few Rust files, through make hack.bin model=<model>. The host fuji CLI needs libusb-1.0 and the camlib PTP library submodule, and its Windows build downloads the author’s libwpd DLL. A workflow that compiled the X-A2 target sits in a disabled .github/workflows_ directory, so no CI runs, and there are no tests.

GPL-3.0 per LICENSE and the README, copyright 2021–2024 Daniel C and contributors; usb/dbg.c carries another contributor’s copyright notice, and the camlib submodule keeps its own license. The README frames the work as interoperability research; Fujifilm’s firmware and trademarks remain the vendor’s.

resources.name: efiSeek
resources.description: Ghidra analyzer extension from Digital Security for individual UEFI modules, enabled by default during auto-analysis of x86 and x64 PE images with an EFI subsystem. It labels known GUIDs from a bundled database, applies UEFI types from bundled data-type archives, passes the image handle and system table from the entry point into called functions, and marks protocols located with LocateProtocol or installed with InstallProtocolInterface, protocol-notify callbacks and SMI handlers registered for software, hardware and child interrupts. Findings are also kept as JSON in the program, which a headless-mode script uses to sort SMM modules into project folders by handler type.
requirements: The repository has no releases or tags; the latest master commit, from 2022-04-26, adds compatibility with a Ghidra 10.2 development build. Open issues report that the pinned Gradle 7.4.2 wrapper does not work with Ghidra 11.2 and newer and that a PE header API change in Ghidra 12.0 causes errors; the pull requests proposing fixes were unmerged at review, so building for current Ghidra releases may need those or similar changes.

Built from source with the bundled Gradle wrapper against a Ghidra installation named by GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR; the build fetches the org.json library from Maven Central. The README then has the zip from dist copied into Ghidra's Extensions/Ghidra folder and the extension enabled, after which the analyzer is preselected when an EFI file is opened.

Input is a single UEFI module the analyst already has: the analyzer accepts only PE images with an EFI subsystem and only the x86 and x64 machine types, so modules must first be taken out of a full firmware image. It rebases the program to 0x80000000 and makes every memory block readable, writable and executable.

Apache-2.0, per LICENSE and the source headers. The repository bundles the Behemotx32.gdt and Behemotx64.gdt data-type archives and the guids-db.ini GUID database that the analyzer loads, plus the Gradle wrapper JAR. Labels and handler classifications are heuristic annotations for analyst review.

resources.name: Dwarf
resources.description: PyQt5 debugger built on Frida that attaches to or spawns processes on Android and iOS devices, the local machine or a remote Frida server. A session offers breakpoints, watchpoints, register context, backtraces and threads, a Capstone disassembly view for x86, x64, ARM and ARM64, a hex editor and panels for modules, memory ranges and memory search, while Java explorer, inspector and trace panels and an Objective-C inspector cover mobile app runtimes. User Frida scripts and Python plugins extend a session, and companion commands trace Java methods or native addresses (dwarf-trace), log syscalls from one module on arm64 (dwarf-strace) and scaffold scripting projects with Dwarf API typings (dwarf-creator).
requirements: Latest release at review: dwarf-debugger 1.1.3 on PyPI, uploaded 2022-04-09; the repository has no GitHub releases or tags. The reviewed master commit, from 2024-05-16 and the most recent at review, merges a small type fix after that release. The README still says a Dwarf 2.0 release is being worked on, and none has been published.

Installed with pip from PyPI or a master archive. setup.py accepts any Python 3 and declares Linux, Windows and macOS, depending on frida 12.8+, PyQt5 5.11.3+ (requirements.txt pins 5.13.*), Capstone 4.0.1+, requests and pyperclip. The bundled core.js agent is built from the core1 branch of the separate DwarfCore repository; the reviewed sources do not state which current Frida releases it works with.

The user supplies the apps, processes and devices to debug; the repository holds only Dwarf's own code, agent, icons and examples. Android sessions use adb and a device running frida-server: the device bar can download the latest frida-server from Frida's GitHub releases and install it with su on a rooted device, and flags devices where it finds no root access. iOS sessions use a USB-connected Frida device, local sessions spawn a given path or attach to a PID, and remote sessions use Frida's remote device.

GPL-3.0 (setup.py: GPLv3+). The README lists two known JavaTraceView display problems, and dwarf-strace handles only arm64 processes. The README pitches the tool to reverse engineers, crackers and security analysts.

resources.name: FwAnalyzer
resources.description: Rule-based checker for filesystem images taken from firmware: it reads ext2/3/4, FAT/VFAT, SquashFS and UBIFS images, cpio archives or a directory, and writes a JSON report of every file that breaks the rules in a TOML configuration. Rules cover SUID and world-writable files, allowed owners, SELinux labels and Linux capabilities, per-file metadata, content regexes, SHA-256 digests, JSON fields and external scripts such as the bundled checksec wrapper; it can also extract values such as version strings and compare the file tree or selected files with a previous run. Cruise describes it as part of a firmware security check suite, and check.py with an Android OTA unpacker runs it over each image in a firmware package.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.4.4, published 2022-10-24 without an attached binary; releases 1.4.1 to 1.4.3 attach a prebuilt Linux fwanalyzer. The reviewed master commit, from 2023-10-08, only fixes typos after that release and is the latest commit; the repository is not archived, and the Makefile still sets VERSION=1.4.1.

Built from source with Go (go.mod declares Go 1.13; the Makefile defaults GOOS to linux) through make deps and make, giving build/fwanalyzer. Each filesystem backend calls external programs: e2ls and e2cp from e2tools for ext images, mdir and mcopy from mtools for FAT, unsquashfs, ubireader_list_files from ubi_reader, and cpio. SELinux and capability data need the author's patched e2tools and squashfs-tools forks, and ext symlink handling needs e2tools' link_support branch; the Dockerfile lists the full dependency set on a golang:1.13 image.

Input is a filesystem image or unpacked directory the user already has; FwAnalyzer itself does not unpack firmware packages. check.py needs an unpacker script that maps configurations to images, and the bundled Android OTA unpacker relies on the separate extract_android_ota_payload and mkbootimg_tools projects. Findings depend entirely on the user's configuration: the devices folder supplies sample Android user-build, Android property and generic Linux root-filesystem rules, and the report lists rule offenders rather than assessed vulnerabilities.

make test runs Go unit tests, and the integration target runs test/test.py, written for Python 2, against bundled fixtures in test/: small ext2, SquashFS, UBIFS, VFAT and cpio images, hello-world ELF builds for ARM32, ARM64 and x86-64, and prebuilt e2cp and unsquashfs helper executables; make testsetup uses sudo setcap. CircleCI builds and tests inside the Docker image, while the GitHub workflow only lints with golangci-lint v1.29.
Apache-2.0, copyright Cruise LLC; the external filesystem tools keep their own licenses.

resources.name: WPeGPT
resources.description: IDA plugin, formerly WPeChatGPT and inspired by Gepetto, that sends the Hex-Rays pseudocode of a function to an OpenAI-compatible model (OpenAI, DeepSeek or another compatible endpoint) and writes the model's analysis back into IDA as comments. Interactive actions explain a function's purpose and behavior, suggest variable names, re-express small routines such as XOR decoding in Python and flag potential vulnerabilities. Version 3.0 adds WPeServer, a TCP command server inside IDA through which an external controller or the separate wpegpt-analyzer skill runs headless light, full or vulnerability-focused passes, with string classification, network-indicator extraction, function suspiciousness scoring and JSON plus Markdown reports.
requirements: Reviewed at tag v3.0 (2026-05-27), which is the reviewed main commit; the GitHub release has no attached files. Install by copying WPeGPT.py and the WPeGPT_Config folder (config.py and wpe_ai_controller.py) into IDA's plugins directory. IDA must run Python 3, and the plugin imports ida_hexrays, so a Hex-Rays decompiler for the target architecture is needed. Python dependencies are openai >= 0.27.0 and httpx.

config.py ships with empty API_KEY, API_BASE_URL and MODEL values that must be set for an OpenAI-compatible provider, plus an optional forward proxy, worker count and default analysis mode (light); the interface defaults to Chinese (ZH_CN = True). The README estimates light, full and vuln runs at roughly 2–5, 10–30 and 5–20 minutes. WPeServer binds to 127.0.0.1 on an OS-assigned port, and headless runs start from the IDA menu or the separately maintained wpegpt-analyzer skill.

Works on a binary the user opens in IDA; the repository bundles only the plugin, its configuration and screenshots. Each request sends decompiled pseudocode to the configured model provider, and automated runs send many functions, so weigh confidentiality and API cost before analyzing sensitive samples. The README calls AI results for reference only; comments and reports are model suggestions that need analyst checking.
No license file is present and GitHub detects no license, so no reuse terms are granted. IDA, the Hex-Rays decompiler and model APIs are licensed separately.

resources.name: iOSRE: iOS Reverse Engineering reference
resources.description: A community-maintained reference on iOS reverse engineering started by kpwn, built from a wiki, a curated index of public technical papers and talks, and a few environment-setup scripts. The wiki pages introduce iOS internals such as the Mach-O executable format, the XNU kernel and IOKit, the boot chain and a history of platform mitigations, while the README states the project is an early, ongoing effort and several pages remain stubs. The repository hosts notes and external links rather than any Apple firmware, device images or app binaries.
requirements: Reviewed at commit 20aff77 on the master branch; the repository was last pushed on 2018-06-30 and has not been updated since, so its iOS 8/9-era material is historical and does not track current iOS versions. The README calls the effort new and ongoing, and several wiki pages on topics such as auditing the XNU kernel, the boot ROM, the sandbox and userland subjects are still marked TODO.

The repository ships documentation and links, not target files: resources/papers/README.md is an index that links to publicly published papers and talks rather than hosting the PDFs, and no Apple firmware images, device keys or app binaries are committed. Working through the material assumes the reader supplies their own research device and Apple or third-party tooling, which the repository does not provide.

The setup scripts under resources/scripts target macOS with Xcode command-line tools and download third-party software at runtime, including Homebrew, ldid, Theos, Reveal, Hopper and class-dump, while a separate Install XPwn script builds tools on Linux through apt; each stays under its own license.
The README warns that files in the resources folder are mostly user-contributed and may be malicious and advises checking them before running; the project reports no testing or verified results.

LICENSE.txt is the author's Modified Anyone But Richard M Stallman (MABRMS) license, which GitHub cannot classify (NOASSERTION) and which permits broad reuse with the warranty disclaimer in that file; individual files may state otherwise, and the linked papers and tools keep their own terms.

resources.name: Android-Disassembler
resources.description: On-device disassembler and binary viewer for Android, built on Capstone, that opens ELF shared libraries and executables, object files, Windows PE files, .NET assemblies, dex files and APKs chosen from storage or from installed apps. It shows ELF details and symbol tables, PE import and export tables, disassembly with jump following and navigation by symbol or address, a hex view, ASCII string search and byte statistics such as entropy and chi-square tests to help tell whether data is encrypted. Analyses are kept as projects and can be exported as raw, text, JSON or database files.
requirements: Latest formal release at review: v2.1.5, published 2021-08-06 with a debug APK. A rolling Preview latest prerelease, last published 2026-03-20, carries a debug-signed APK built from the newest branch, and CI uploads a debug APK on every run. The README says maintenance has resumed but the project is still in a recovery and modernization phase; the reviewed master commit of 2026-03-22 is part of that work.

The app supports Android 5.0 (API 21) and newer, with target and compile SDK 35. Files open through the Storage Access Framework picker by default; a separate Advanced import path for raw-filesystem, root and installed-app browsing is meant for power users, and system files that need root permission can be read only on rooted phones.

Building needs initialized git submodules and Android Studio or Gradle with an Android SDK and NDK; build.gradle pins NDK 23.1.7779620 and builds the native code with CMake, and CI uses JDK 17 to run unit tests, a debug build and instrumentation UI tests on API 30 and 35 emulators. The app applies Firebase Analytics and Crashlytics, and the README's privacy note says crash reports of types such as FileCorruptedException may attach the file being analyzed to the bug-report email and upload it to the GitHub repository.

MIT license, copyright 2018 Hyeonseo Yang. The repository commits prebuilt Capstone libraries, library JARs including pecoff4j, facile, RootTools and jep, small ls helper executables for ARM and x86 in the app assets, and a Test subject files folder of sample ELF libraries and an arm-linux-androideabi-ar binary; bundled components keep their own licenses. Users supply the files they analyze.

resources.name: bddisasm
resources.description: Bitdefender’s dependency-free C decoder for x86/x64 instructions, reporting explicit and implicit operands with their access modes, CPUID feature flags, flag accesses and valid modes, and printing Intel/MASM-style text. A minimal API with a 64-byte instruction structure trades detail for speed, and the companion bdshemu library emulates basic x86/x64 code in a raw buffer to flag shellcode-like behaviour such as NOP sleds, reading the instruction pointer, self-modification, TEB/PEB access and system calls. The disasmtool command-line example decodes or emulates files and hex strings.
requirements: The reviewed master commit is the v3.1.0 release of 2026-10-14, which attaches a Linux .deb package and x86 and x64 Windows zip bundles; the README says releases newer than 2.1.4 can be checked with GitHub artifact attestations. v3.1.0 removed the Python and Rust bindings, whose directories now hold only notices that they are unsupported and must not be used in production, and the README warns that the vcpkg package may lag behind.

Builds use CMake 3.16+ with optional Ninja, tested with GCC and Clang on Linux and MSVC on Windows; a Makefile builds only the static libraries, and the Visual Studio 2019 solution with Windows SDK 10.0.18362.0 adds Windows kernel configurations that need WDK 1903. Python 3 is needed only to regenerate the instruction tables with isagenerator, and Make or MSBuild builds leave nd_vsnprintf_s and nd_memset for the integrator to supply.

The caller supplies code bytes and a 16-, 32- or 64-bit mode, optionally with vendor and feature preferences, and only Intel/MASM-style syntax is printed. No executable-format loader is documented, so code in PE, ELF or firmware images must be located with another tool. The README says bdshemu handles only basic instructions, emulates no API calls and supports memory accesses only inside the shellcode and its emulated stack, so its flags describe shellcode-like behaviour rather than a full program run.

CI builds on Linux, Windows and macOS, runs cppcheck and runs the repository’s decoder and emulator regression suites, which compare disasmtool output for bundled test byte files, many with their .asm sources, against expected results. The README also reports internal fuzzing, testing with mishegos and per-instruction speed figures.
Apache-2.0 license. The documentation says Bitdefender uses the library in Windows and Linux user mode, Windows kernel mode and its Napoca hypervisor.

resources.name: decompyle3
resources.description: Reworking of uncompyle6 by the same author that translates Python 3.7 and 3.8 bytecode, including some PyPy 3.7 and 3.8 bytecode, back into equivalent Python source; older bytecode stays with uncompyle6. It disassembles code objects with the companion xdis library, then tokenizes and parses the instruction stream with a refactored grammar into a tree from which source is printed, and it can decompile between given start and stop offsets or, through decompyle3-code, only a file's lambdas, generators and comprehensions. The README says the grammar rewrite does not by itself fix uncompyle6's control-flow problem, which the author is addressing with dominator-based analysis in a separate, non-public project.
requirements: Latest release at review: 3.9.3, published 2025-10-01 on GitHub and PyPI; the reviewed master commit, from 2026-07-21, is 18 commits later and reports 3.9.4.dev0. The README says the code runs on Python 3.7 or 3.8, whereas pyproject.toml requires Python 3.7+ with classifiers through 3.13, master CI tests under Python 3.13, and a separate python-3.7-to-3.10 branch is tested under 3.8; the 3.9.3 release also ships wheels and eggs for 3.7, 3.8 and 3.9. It depends on xdis newer than 6.2, spark-parser 1.8.9 up to but not including 1.9.2, and click; master CI installs xdis from its git repository until the next xdis release.

The README reports testing on bytecode from Python 3.7 and 3.8, and the regression suite keeps compiled 3.7 and 3.8 samples plus a few PyPy ones; the release notes state that bytecode newer than 3.8 is not decompiled. The author warns of numerous decompilation bugs and does not intend serious work on 3.8 or 3.9 until the project is better funded. Candidate-release magic numbers, PJOrion or otherwise obfuscated code, Cython and MicroPython are not handled, and pathologically long expression or statement lists are slow.

Input .pyc or .pyo files come from the user; it cannot decompile Py2EXE executables directly, and bytecode bundled by such packagers has to be extracted first. The README's --syntax-verify option appears in the reviewed CLI as --verify syntax, next to --verify run; a syntax check is meaningful only when the checking interpreter matches the bytecode version, so the README suggests cross-checking with another decompiler such as unpyc37 and with programs that test themselves, including Python's standard-library tests. Recovered source remains subject to the rights of the original program’s owner.
GPL-3.0-or-later per pyproject.toml, with the GPL-3.0 text in COPYING.

resources.name: FwHunt Community Scanner (fwhunt-scan)
resources.description: Binarly's Python scanner that checks UEFI firmware modules against FwHunt rules, the YAML detection format for known UEFI firmware vulnerabilities whose rules are kept in the separate fwhunt repository. Its rizin-based analyzer reports a PE or TE module's Boot, Runtime and PEI service calls, protocols, PPIs, GUIDs, NVRAM variables and SMI handlers, which rules combine with code patterns, strings and hex strings. The CLI analyzes or scans one module, or extracts the modules of a whole firmware image and scans them, and the same classes work as a Python library.
requirements: The repository has no GitHub releases or tags. The reviewed master commit, from 2025-05-02 and the latest at review, follows the setup.py bump to 2.3.8, the version uploaded to PyPI that day; a separate release branch publishes Docker images to GHCR tagged by commit.

Needs Python 3 (README: tested on 3.6 and above; CI runs on 3.9 to 3.13) with click, rzpipe 0.4.0, PyYAML and uefi_firmware, plus an installed rizin. The README names rizin v0.6.2, and the Dockerfile builds that release from source on a python:3.11 image. Passing an in-memory blob instead of a file path works only on Linux.

Input is a UEFI module or firmware image the user already has, plus FwHunt rule files; no rules are bundled, and the README's rules/ and test/fw.bin example paths are not in this repository. scan-firmware applies firmware-target rules to the whole image and module rules only to modules from the volumes their volume_guids name, unless --force applies them to every module; extract writes all found modules to a directory.

The only test checks GUID table lookups, and CI runs it after a flake8 syntax check. A scan reports, per rule and variant, whether a known pattern matched, printed as threat detected or not; no match does not show that a module is free of other vulnerabilities.
GPL-3.0: setup.py declares GPL-3.0 and source headers GPL-3.0+; the separate fwhunt rule repository is CC0-1.0.

resources.name: DRAKVUF
resources.description: Tamas K Lengyel's virtualization-based, agentless black-box binary analysis system: running on the Xen hypervisor through LibVMI, it traces execution in Windows and Linux guests, from kernel functions to user-mode code, without installing software inside the analyzed virtual machine. Plugins log system calls, API calls and file, registry, process, socket and memory activity, extract files from memory before they are deleted and dump process memory, while an injector starts programs in the guest without an in-guest helper. CERT Polska's separate DRAKVUF Sandbox builds an automated sandbox with a GUI on top of it.
requirements: Latest tagged release: 1.0, published 2022-12-29 with Debian and Ubuntu packages. meson.build at the reviewed main commit of 2026-09-30 declares version 1.1, and the separate drakvuf-builds repository publishes per-commit drakvuf-bundle 1.1 packages for Debian bookworm and Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 with matching Xen 4.20.1 hypervisor packages, including a build of the reviewed commit.

Needs an Intel CPU with VT-x and Extended Page Tables; the README says DRAKVUF will not work on AMD or on Intel CPUs without them. DRAKVUF runs in Xen's dom0. The project website's installation guide, last updated 2022-12-29 for Xen 4.17 and mainly tested on Ubuntu 22.04, builds Xen from the bundled submodule, sets Xen boot options, asks for a dom0 kernel of 5.11 or newer and stores guest disks on LVM; DRAKVUF itself builds with meson and ninja.

The README lists Windows 7 and 8 (32- and 64-bit), Windows 10 64-bit and Linux 2.6.x to 6.x guests; the older website guide says Linux up to 5.x. The analyst installs the guest from their own operating-system media and generates a JSON kernel profile for LibVMI, from the Windows kernel's PDB with the bundled Volatility 3 pdbconv script or from Linux kernel debug symbols with dwarf2json; extra per-module profiles, such as one for tcpip.sys, enable plugins like socketmon.

Custom license: GPL version 2 only with the author's clarifications and exceptions, which read derivative works broadly, bar combining DRAKVUF with plain-GPL software and offer alternative licenses for proprietary use; GitHub does not classify it. Xen, LibVMI, Volatility 3 and dwarf2json are git submodules under their own licenses. The README presents it mainly for malware analysis.

resources.name: ViperMonkey
resources.description: VBA parser and emulation engine, created by Philippe Lagadec and developed since 2017 mainly by Kirk Sayre and other contributors, for analyzing and deobfuscating malicious macros in Microsoft Office files such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Publisher documents, as well as VBScript files and HTA files carrying VBScript. The vmonkey command reads the macros through oletools' olevba, emulates them from their auto-run entry points or from functions the analyst names, and reports the recorded actions, such as process creation, along with optional intermediate IOCs and the files the code would write; vbashell is an interactive VBA shell. A Python API evaluates VBA snippets, walks and emulates individual code blocks, replaces functions and deobfuscates code.
requirements: Version 1.0.3, set in setup.py and vmonkey.py in 2021; there are no GitHub releases, tags or PyPI package, so it is installed from a master archive. The reviewed master commit, from 2024-04-25 and the latest at review, caps oletools at 0.60.1. The README says most development since November 2017 happens in Kirk Sayre's fork and is synchronised here regularly; at review that fork's master branch was 162 commits ahead of and 8 behind this one, with its latest commit from 2021-08-04.

Runs on Python 2.7: the README installs it under PyPy 2.7, recommended as about five times faster, or CPython 2.7, and the API tutorial uses Python 2 print statements. Dependencies are pinned for that interpreter, including pyparsing 2.2.0 because newer versions mis-parse or run out of memory on some samples, unidecode 1.2.0 and oletools 0.56.1–0.60.1, plus olefile, xlrd, xlrd2, prettytable, colorlog and colorama. Alternatively, docker/dockermonkey.sh pulls the third-party haroldogden/vipermonkey image, updates the checkouts inside it with git pull, starts headless LibreOffice, disconnects the container from the network and runs vmonkey with -s, --iocs and --jit.

The user supplies the suspicious documents or VBScript files; the repository includes no samples, and its tests are four Python modules. The README calls ViperMonkey experimental, working on some but not all maldocs, and extremely slow, recommending -s to strip useless statements. --jit converts VB loops to Python and runs them with eval, which the README flags as a security risk and suggests the Docker sandbox for; dropped files, including PE files found embedded in Office files, are written to a <file>_artifacts directory with their SHA-256 hashes reported. Results depend on how far the engine emulates VBA, Office objects and called DLLs or ActiveX objects, which the README describes as hard and incomplete.

BSD two-clause terms stated in the README and source headers, copyright 2015–2020 Philippe Lagadec; there is no license file, so GitHub detects none, and the README's exception for a thirdparty folder refers to a folder absent from the reviewed commit.

resources.name: linux-re-101
resources.description: Michal Malik’s single-README reading list for Linux reverse engineering, with about 230 links and book titles that run from quick references on system calls, ELF and processor ABIs through 101 and 201 tiers on program start-up, linking and relocations. Later sections gather material on packers and obfuscation, anti-debugging, ELF infection, kernel modules and rootkits, exploitation, crackmes, radare2 walkthroughs, detection tools and books. It is a lightly annotated link list last changed in January 2022, useful as a background syllabus rather than a maintained course.
requirements: The reviewed master commit f858da0, dated 2022-01-16, contains a single file, README.md, which calls the list a work in progress. It holds 231 bullet entries under 15 headings; the largest are Linux kernel, rootkits and LKM development (40), 101 (22) and viruses and infection techniques (20), and several articles appear in more than one section.

Entries give a title and a link, sometimes marked Optional or followed by a short remark; beyond the 101 and 201 headings they state no level, prerequisites or exercises. 148 of the 229 URLs use plain HTTP, and most dated links point to posts from 2008–2017.

The material centres on Linux ELF binaries on x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64 and MIPS, and the hands-on section mostly uses radare2, with GDB, IDA and LIEF references elsewhere. The repository supplies no labs, sample binaries or setup; crackme and challenge links lead to external archives, and readers need a Linux system plus whatever tools each linked article names.

The packer, anti-debugging, infection, rootkit and exploitation sections link offensive write-ups, rootkit source repositories and external virus collections alongside detection material; linked code and samples are third-party material with their own risks and terms.
GitHub detects no license and the repository has no license file, so the list states no reuse terms; linked articles, books and code keep their own rights. An independent learning list.

resources.name: XAPKDetector
resources.description: APK and DEX detector from hors, the author of Detect-It-Easy, that reports the build tools, libraries and protections it identifies in Android packages, using scan engines and signature databases from the Detect-It-Easy family. The Qt GUI also shows AndroidManifest.xml, MANIFEST.MF, DEX and ELF contents, strings, hex, entropy, hashes and the APK signature, and can scan whole directories. A console build runs recursive, deep, heuristic or all-types scans and writes XML, JSON, CSV or TSV results.
requirements: Latest release at review: 0.03, published 2022-03-14, with Windows portable zips (including a Windows XP build), macOS packages including a Qt 6 build, a Linux AppImage and Debian and Ubuntu packages; release_version.txt still reads 0.03. The master branch was still receiving submodule updates at review, such as new Detect-It-Easy signatures on 2026-10-19, so the source is ahead of the released binaries.

Building needs a recursive clone of 55 git submodules from the author's other repositories, including Formats, XDEX, SpecAbstract, the signatures database and Detect-It-Easy, plus Qt. docs/BUILD.md covers Docker, a Debian package build tested on Ubuntu 14.04 to 20.04, autotools and CMake, macOS with Qt 5.15.2, and Windows with Visual Studio 2019 and Qt 5.15.2 or, for Windows XP, Visual Studio 2013 and Qt 5.6.3.

Input is APK, APKS or DEX files the analyst already has; the changelog adds APKS support in 0.03. Detections are signature and heuristic identifications for analyst confirmation. The repository itself contains no tests or CI workflows.
MIT license, copyright 2020-2026 hors; the submodules are separate repositories.

resources.name: BREAD
resources.description: Injectable real-mode x86 debugger for legacy BIOS code, boot code and DOS programs on real hardware or in a virtual machine. A small 16-bit assembly stub placed in the target code installs interrupt handlers, single-steps the processor and talks over a serial line to a Linux bridge, which translates its simple packets into the GDB remote protocol so GDB can read and write memory and registers, step, continue and set one hardware breakpoint and one watchpoint at a time. A companion script turns an address–label list into a minimal ELF symbol file for GDB.
requirements: No releases are published. The reviewed master commit of 2025-10-21 fixes EIP handling in the interrupt-based mode; the previous code change, adding the symbolify tool, dates from 2023-10-19. Building needs a Linux host with GNU Make, a C compiler such as GCC, Clang or TCC, and NASM. The default build polls the UART at full CPU load, while UART_POLLING=no selects the interrupt-based mode, which is not the default because interrupts are not always enabled.

dbg.asm must be edited for each target, changing its ORG and return path and restoring any instructions replaced by the call into it, and the assembled dbg.bin then goes into the user’s own BIOS ROM image or runs as a DOS .COM program from a minimal FreeDOS or DOS boot floppy. Real hardware needs a serial connection to the Linux host. The repository ships no ROM; symbols/ami_ipm41d3.txt holds the author’s symbol names for one PCWare IPM41-D3 AMI legacy BIOS, which its header calls the author’s interpretation, not official or leaked symbols.

The README lists limits: the debugged code is unaware of the debugger, so a switch to protected mode, a changed IDT or a missing stack stops it from working, and BIOS code cannot be followed from the boot block because RAM must already be set up; a warm reboot can replay initialisation but may take a different path from a cold boot. Virtual machines need debug-register support, from a Bochs build with its x86 debugger enabled or QEMU with KVM, which the bundled qemu target uses with a floppy built from the included boot sector and debugger.

The repository has no tests or CI; the README links a demonstration video that changes the CPU name string. MIT license by Davidson Francis; firmware and programs being debugged keep their own rights.

resources.name: Mergen
resources.description: Function-level lifter that symbolically lifts one x86-64 function from a Windows PE binary into LLVM IR, then iterates LLVM and custom passes to a fixpoint so obfuscated or virtualized code reduces to simpler control flow and semantics for analysis. Its scope document lists 119 instruction handlers, two-way branches and tested jump-table shapes; README examples lift small test functions the authors protected with VMProtect and Themida, and the IR can be compiled for viewing in a decompiler.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.7, published 2026-03-29, with Windows lifter and microtest executables for the iced and Zydis decoder backends. The reviewed main commit, dated 2026-05-08, is 150 commits past the later v0.8 tag, which has no release. docs/SCOPE.md limits support to x86-64 PE files and one function per run: 32-bit x86, other formats and architectures, self-modifying code, floating-point or AVX code beyond the listed SSE2 integer instructions and whole-binary lifting are unsupported, and general-purpose decompilation is a non-goal.

The lifter takes a PE file and the target function's address, with optional --outline addresses; analysts supply their own binaries. The VMProtect check runs against local protected samples that are not committed, and the reviewed tree holds source, assembly and C test sources and documentation rather than prebuilt executables. Output is LLVM IR text plus output_diagnostics.json, which records unresolved indirect jumps and returns.

Developed and CI-tested mainly on Windows with CMake, Ninja, clang-cl using MSVC headers and libraries, LLVM 18 and Rust/Cargo for the default iced backend; the Zydis-only lane builds from a vendored Zydis 4.1.0 amalgamation, and linux-pe is a git submodule. A secondary Ubuntu 22.04 Dockerfile builds and exports a Linux lifter.

docs/SCOPE.md reports 115 of 119 handlers covered by a Unicorn-generated oracle suite, 33 semantic samples with 177 runtime cases checked under lli, golden IR hashes and Windows build lanes in CI, and says reliability on protected code varies by protection level. The README's branch example still says jumps with more than two targets are unsupported, while the newer scope document lists tested jump-table shapes. These gates cover the project's own compiled samples, not arbitrary protected software.
LICENSE is GPL-3.0; the vendored Zydis source and the submodule keep their own licenses. Lifted IR still needs analyst validation.

resources.name: readpe (formerly pev)
resources.description: Command-line toolkit, formerly named pev, for analyzing 32- and 64-bit Windows PE files. readpe prints the DOS, COFF and optional headers, sections, data directories, imports and exports, while companion tools disassemble code (pedis), hash the file, headers or sections with ssdeep and imphash among others (pehash), list and extract resources (peres), match packer signatures (pepack), flag traits such as TLS callbacks, high entropy or an unusual entry point (pescan), report ASLR, DEP/NX, SEH and stack-cookie flags and dump certificates (pesec), find strings and convert between file offsets and RVAs. Output plugins write text, CSV, XML, HTML or JSON, and the bundled libpe C library provides the parser.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.85.1, published 2025-08-29 to correct the version string reported by v0.85 (2025-08-08); only the older v0.81 and v0.82 releases attach Windows ZIP builds. The reviewed master commit, from 2026-07-08, is five commits ahead, fixing peres version output and ordinal-only imports and moving the macOS CI build to a newer OpenSSL. The README explains the rename from pev and that libpe was merged into this repository.

Built from source with make and a C compiler and needs OpenSSL development headers. On Linux, make install puts files under /usr/local, and /usr/local/lib must be registered with ldconfig so libpe.so is found; macOS builds pass Homebrew OpenSSL paths in CFLAGS and LDFLAGS, and Windows builds use Cygwin with gcc-core, binutils, make, zip and libssl-devel, where make zip also builds cpload and bundles the needed Cygwin DLLs. CI only compiles on Linux, macOS and Cygwin.

Input is a PE file the user supplies. The other tools parse it, but the Windows-only cpload loads a Control Panel (.cpl) item and sends it CPL messages for debugging, so it runs that item's code. pepack depends on the bundled userdb.txt list of PEiD-style signatures, whose header counts 3,520 entries without naming their source, and pescan and pesec report heuristic indicators and header flags rather than verdicts.

tests/run.sh runs each tool in every output format and diffs the results against an expected_outputs directory that is not in the repository; valgrind scripts and a helloworld.exe sample built from tests/samples_src with MinGW are also included. CI does not run these tests.
The tools are GPL-2.0-or-later with an OpenSSL linking exception, lib/libpe is LGPL-3.0, and the bundled udis86 disassembler keeps its BSD notice.

resources.name: sniffROM
resources.description: Python tool that reconstructs serial flash contents from passive bus captures: it parses SPI or I²C analyzer exports from Saleae Logic, recorded while a device reads and writes its own flash chip, and writes the observed data into a binary image at the original memory addresses. It recognizes more than 100 SPI flash commands from vendors such as Winbond, Macronix, Spansion and GigaDevice and currently parses 12 of them, reports manufacturer and device IDs seen in JEDEC ID reads, and can print a command summary, show a visual map of the captured address ranges and plot the timing of reads and writes.
requirements: No releases or tags; the script was last changed in July 2020. A README note added on 2023-12-07 says Saleae Logic 2 breaks the SPI analyzer export that sniffROM depends on, so it currently works only with data exported from Logic 1.x, and that it was unknown when this would be fixed.

A single Python 2 script (it uses print statements) that needs matplotlib for the data map and timing plot; the README's usage text calls it sniffROM_new.py. Input is a CSV export from Saleae Logic's SPI or I²C analyzer, with options for 2-, 3- or 4-byte SPI addresses, byte endianness and analyzing only read or only write commands.

Capturing needs a Saleae logic analyzer connected to the flash bus of a device the analyst is permitted to examine; the wiki's Getting Started page points to an external guide for the capture itself. Only data the device accessed during the capture is recovered, and unseen bytes are filled with a padding value; the wiki's boot-time SPI examples captured about 29% and 42% of the rebuilt images.

GPL-3.0 (COPYING). The repository also stores manufacturers' datasheet PDFs for the supported SPI and I²C chips and a commands.xlsx command table; the datasheets remain their vendors' documents. No firmware images or bus captures are committed.

resources.name: IDAssist
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin by Jason Tang, who also wrote GhidrAssist, that adds a dockable PySide6 panel for LLM-assisted analysis of the open database. Its tabs explain decompiled or disassembled functions with a security summary, keep persistent chats with context macros and an optional ReAct agent mode, propose function, variable and type renames for review before they are applied, and build a semantic knowledge graph of functions, calls, data flows and security traits, with retrieval over reference documents the analyst adds. Models can call built-in IDA tools or external MCP servers, and a SymGraph tab imports and publishes names, types and graph data through the hosted symgraph.ai service.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2.4.0, published 2026-09-14 as a source-only GitHub release; the reviewed master commit is one commit later and only updates model guidance. The README and getting-started guide require IDA Pro 9.0+ with its bundled Python 3.11+ and PySide6, while ida-plugin.json lists IDA 9.1–9.4, and the 2.3.0 notes report fixes for IDA 9.3 and 9.4 on Windows with Python 3.14. Hex-Rays is recommended for pseudocode, with disassembly used otherwise. It installs with Hex-Rays' hcli plugin manager, or from a release archive in the IDA plugins directory with requirements.txt installed into IDA's Python; that file adds boto3 for Bedrock, which the manifest's dependency list omits.

Analysis needs at least one configured LLM provider. The reviewed provider types cover Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and xAI API keys, OpenAI and Gemini subscription sign-in through OAuth, the local Claude Code CLI, AWS Bedrock, a LiteLLM proxy, and local Ollama, LM Studio or Open WebUI endpoints; the README's table also lists an Anthropic OAuth type that the source does not define. Explanations, chats and agent runs send pseudocode or disassembly to the active provider, so only a local or self-hosted endpoint keeps code on the machine. The documentation says chats, graphs, settings and feedback are kept in local SQLite databases in the .idapro/idassist folder of the user's home directory, with API keys encrypted in the settings database.

Programs come from the user's own IDA databases. Rename suggestions show confidence scores and are written to the IDB only for the rows the user selects. During a chat, built-in tools and external MCP servers, reached by URL over SSE or streamable HTTP or launched over stdio, can read and modify the IDB; in the Query tab, calls to tools whose names do not look read-only wait for an allow-once, allow-for-session or deny decision unless the chat accepts all tools, and this classification relies on tool-name keywords.

The SymGraph tab looks up the input binary by SHA-256 without a key, but importing, publishing and uploading need a SymGraph API key, and publishing uploads the raw binary itself when the service does not already hold it. The repository has no tests or CI workflows. MIT, per LICENSE and ida-plugin.json; IDA Pro, the Hex-Rays decompiler, model providers and SymGraph keep their own terms.

resources.name: Pawn
resources.description: Linux command-line tool from Google that reads the BIOS/UEFI firmware image out of the SPI flash of Intel-based workstations and laptops. Running as root, it identifies the chipset's LPC bridge over PCI, maps the chipset's root-complex registers through /dev/mem, and reports the flash descriptor regions and the BIOS write- and read-protection settings it finds. It then reads the flash through the SPI controller's hardware sequencing into a single image file, which the README suggests processing further with tools such as UEFITool.
requirements: Releases v0.1 and v0.2, published 2017-08-30 and 2017-09-09, each ship a Debian amd64 package with its source; the reviewed main commit, from 2026-02-17, updates dependencies and GitHub Actions and still declares version 0.2. The README states that Pawn is not an official Google product. Builds need Linux on x86_64 (FreeBSD might also work, per the README), CMake 3.31+, GCC or Clang 7+ and Ninja or Make; CMake fetches Abseil, and GoogleTest for tests, at pinned commits. CI builds and runs the unit test on Ubuntu 24.04 and keeps the binary only as a workflow artifact.

Runs as root on the machine whose firmware is read, using I/O-port access to PCI configuration space and /dev/mem. On Linux kernels newer than 4.8.4 the README requires CONFIG_IO_DEVMEM=n or booting with iomem=relaxed; the program's own error message names IO_STRICT_DEVMEM. Only Intel ICH8, ICH9 and ICH10 and 6 to 9 Series chipsets are recognized, the newest being the 9 Series whose datasheet the source cites from May 2014; the BIOS must boot from SPI flash in descriptor mode.

It always reads 16 MiB from flash address 0, so flash beyond that size is not dumped, and failed block reads are ignored; the default output name is bios_via_spi_hs.bin. The repository contains only source, build and Debian packaging files, with no firmware images; a dump is the machine vendor's firmware and keeps the vendor's rights.
Apache-2.0.

resources.name: EMBArk
resources.description: Web-based enterprise interface for the EMBA firmware security scanner, which it installs and runs as its scanning backend. In the browser, users upload firmware, configure and follow EMBA scans, open the full EMBA HTML report and a security overview per firmware, and compare results in an aggregated dashboard; results are access-controlled per user and can be archived. The current main branch adds a REST API for upload, scan status and SBOM retrieval, and an orchestrator that distributes scans to EMBA worker nodes reached over SSH.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.3, published 2025-06-24. The reviewed main commit is 941 commits ahead of it and identifies itself as 0.3-630649d1 in VERSION.txt; the REST API and worker orchestrator described here come from that branch. The installation wiki calls the software alpha and strongly recommends a virtual machine, and the README notes that the new tracking application does not work offline and that device, vendor and version tracking is not yet in every dashboard.

The README names Ubuntu 24 LTS as the only supported OS. installer.sh -d installs Docker, pipenv and EMBA and configures the MySQL and Redis containers defined in docker-compose.yml; EMBA is pinned as a git submodule (at review an EMBA commit from 2026-04-07, older than EMBA's latest releases) and runs in its Docker mode, while -s skips it. The wiki suggests 8–32+ GB RAM, 4–16+ CPUs, at least 20 GB of disk (100+ GB recommended) and an isolated network, and EMBA's own requirements also apply.

run-server.sh serves HTTP on port 80 on all interfaces under the default name embark.local, which must resolve through a hosts file or DNS; -a adds names or addresses and -b opens the admin pages beyond localhost. The installer and server script run with sudo, and the server is deployed to /var/www under a dedicated service user. API calls carry an API key in a header or query parameter, and the orchestrator scans an IP range and installs EMBA on workers using SSH credentials the user supplies.

Supply the firmware images yourself; the repository contains no firmware, and its test fixtures are EMBA result exports such as a CycloneDX SBOM and module CSV/JSON files. Scan findings come from EMBA and still need analyst interpretation. CI installs the server without EMBA and runs Django and server tests, linters, ShellCheck and CodeQL, so no firmware scan is part of it.
MIT license, copyright The AMOS Projects and Siemens Energy AG; EMBA and the tools it installs keep their own licenses.

resources.name: Frida Labs
resources.description: Eleven Android challenge apps with step-by-step write-ups for learning Frida instrumentation, progressing from setting up frida-server and hooking a Java method through calling static methods, changing fields, creating instances and hooking constructors to hooking, calling and patching native functions. The author presents them as beginner-to-intermediate exercises rather than hard CTF challenges: each app hides a flag, but the stated goal is learning Frida’s common APIs and being able to read scripts written by others.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-02-22 main commit, which adds Frida 17 workarounds to the native-hooking write-ups for challenges 0x8 to 0xB; the first write-up deploys frida-server 16.1.4. There are no releases, and the README says new challenges will be added over time.

Each challenge is a prebuilt APK committed by the author, with package names such as com.ad2001.frida0x1; the apps’ source code is not in the repository, and the solutions are Markdown write-ups with screenshots. They assume a rooted Android device or emulator, adb, frida-tools from pip and a frida-server build matching the device architecture, with jadx for the Java code and Ghidra for the native libraries; the 0xB write-up shows instruction patches for both x86 and ARM64 builds.

Flags and solution scripts are published next to each APK, so the set works as guided practice rather than an assessment. The README points to learnfrida.info and Frida CodeShare for further material.
MIT license for the repository; Frida, jadx, Ghidra and the Android tools keep their own terms.

resources.name: malware-jail
resources.description: Node.js sandbox for semi-automatic analysis of JavaScript malware: it runs a sample in Node's vm module against emulated Windows Script Host and ActiveX objects such as WScript.Shell, MSXML2.XMLHTTP, ADODB.Stream, Scripting.FileSystemObject and WMI, plus a partial browser context with selectable browser profiles. It logs the objects created and methods called, keeps every eval() argument to help deobfuscation, records requested URLs and WMI queries, and saves the files a dropper tries to write so payloads can be examined. When the run ends, the whole sandbox context is dumped to JSON for review.
requirements: There are no releases or tags, and the README says an npm package is not yet available. The reviewed master commit, from 2023-06-16, only edits the README; the last code change, adding newly analyzed malware and ADODB methods, dates from 2019-08-08. Version labels disagree: package.json says 0.18.0, the README 0.19 and jailme.js 0.20.

Requires Node.js and npm: package.json declares Node 6 or later, and the README says the tool was developed and tested on Linux with Node.js v6.6.0. npm install fetches minimist, iconv-lite, entities and sync-request, npm test runs a small tap suite for the WScript emulation, and native_test holds scripts meant to run under Windows cscript for comparison.
