Emulation covers the WScript and ActiveX features the author saw malware use and only part of the browser context, so a sample may stop early or diverge from real Windows behavior; the logs and dumps are traces for an analyst, not a verdict.

Node's vm module is not a security boundary: the README warns that sandbox-aware malware may try to escape and recommends an unprivileged Linux account or a virtualized Windows machine. By default HTTP requests are not sent and receive dummy responses; --down lets the sample contact remote servers and download payloads, while --h404 and --t404 answer every request with HTTP 404 so all remote URLs can be listed. Execution stops after 60 seconds unless -t sets another limit.

The malware folder holds real-world samples, most of them downloaded from malwr.com according to the README, with their logs and dumps. Besides scripts and HTML pages it includes two extracted Windows payload files, a .exe under malware/20171004 and a .tmp under malware/20190808, and the README states that the Angler files are not disarmed, so a clone contains live malware.
MIT, per the LICENSE file and README.

resources.name: IDAPython Embedded Toolkit
resources.description: Maddie Stone's IDAPython scripts for triaging and annotating embedded-device firmware images in IDA Pro, presented at RECON Montreal and DerbyCon in 2017. Triage scripts define code and functions from per-architecture prologue and epilogue patterns, mark address ranges as bytes, words or double words and turn unexplored bytes into strings; analysis scripts resolve memory accesses made at offsets from a known base value and add cross-references and value comments, and annotation scripts list CPU port (GPIO) use, tag functions without cross-references as possible dead code and trace where an operand is used. An Android folder adds a script that comments JNIEnv function calls in native libraries and one that decrypts the strings of ARM32 libraries packed with the WeddingCake anti-analysis wrapper.
requirements: Ten Python scripts and the slides of the two 2017 talks as PDFs, with no releases or tags; the reviewed master commit, from 2019-08-14, is the latest. The README says the scripts have only been tested on IDA Pro 6.95, with IDA 7.0 testing in progress, and runs each one separately through File > Script file in an open IDA database with IDAPython. Most use Python 2 print statements and pre-7.0 IDC calls such as MakeCode, MakeComm, MakeStr and AskAddr; jni_translate.py, added in 2019, uses Python 3-compatible print calls but still calls idc.MakeComm.

The user supplies the firmware image or Android native library and its IDA database, and enters address ranges, regular expressions or base values at prompts or in each script's user-defined section. Processor-specific syntax is chosen from IDA's processor name: define_code_functions.py covers 8051, PIC18, Mitsubishi M32R, TI TMS320C28x and AVR, and find_mem_accesses.py only 8051, while identify_port_use_locations.py ships one active PIC18 pattern with commented 8051 alternatives. Unsupported processors stop with an error until the analyst adds patterns, and find_mem_accesses.py cannot create references into segments that do not yet exist.

Several scripts rewrite the database: define_data_as_types.py first undefines the range, overwriting code or strings there, and WeddingCake_decrypt.py overwrites encrypted strings with their decrypted contents and needs JNI_OnLoad defined and exported. The WeddingCake files accompany Maddie Stone's Black Hat USA 2018 talk on that packer.

MIT, copyright 2017 Maddie Stone, in LICENSE; the README's copyright notice instead names The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, and the Android README and WeddingCake script carry a Google LLC 2018 copyright line without separate license terms.

resources.name: osx & ios re 101
resources.description: A single-README reading list for macOS (OS X) and iOS reverse engineering, kept by Michal Malik from 2015 to 2019 and labelled a work in progress. Its 98 entries in nine sections run from must-read blogs and Mach-O, ABI and system-call references through Mach-O basics, malware, anti-debugging and obfuscation write-ups, kernel, sandbox and jailbreak research, kernel-extension development and kernel debugging, and forensics and monitoring material, to crackmes and six books. Entries are bare links or titles, mostly with no annotation.
requirements: The reviewed commit, from 2019-12-19 and the latest, closes a history of 69 commits that began on 2015-07-13. Most linked material targets OS X 10.x and iOS 8–10 era internals, such as El Capitan kernels and iOS 9 and 10 jailbreak analyses, and the list predates current macOS and iOS releases and Apple silicon Macs. A December 2019 commit replaced some broken and outdated links.

No target files are supplied or needed by the list itself; the linked tutorials and crackmes bring their own samples, and the books are listed by title only. Following the material assumes a Mac or iOS device and the tools each article uses, such as LLDB, Hopper, and VMware Fusion or VirtualBox for kernel debugging.

The list mixes analysis tutorials with malware infection, rootkit, privilege-escalation and jailbreak write-ups. The repository contains only README.md and no license file, so the list states no reuse terms, and linked works keep their own rights.

resources.name: gxpc
resources.description: macOS command-line XPC sniffer, inspired by xpcspy, that injects a Frida agent into an attached or newly spawned process and logs the XPC messages it sends and receives, labelled with the libxpc function, connection name, peer PID and process name. The agent recursively converts xpc_object_t dictionaries, arrays and scalar values into readable output and decodes binary-plist payloads, while a Go host built on frida-go selects a local, USB or remote Frida device, filters connections by name or PID and can save the trace to a file. It observes how Apple-platform apps and services communicate over XPC and does not alter or inject messages.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.2.1, published 2025-08-12, with macOS x86_64 and arm64 archives that GoReleaser links against the Frida 17.2.16 core devkit; the reviewed main commit adds only a cobra dependency bump (2025-09-02). Installing with go install instead needs Go, cgo and the Frida devkit set up as frida-go documents; go.mod declares Go 1.20 and frida-go 1.0.0.

On first run the binary writes its embedded TypeScript agent and package files to a gxpc folder in the system temp directory, runs npm install for frida-objc-bridge and compiles the agent with Frida’s compiler, so Node.js, npm and network access are needed at least once; the compiled agent is then reused. The analyst picks the target by PID, process name or a file to spawn, on a local device (-i local), a USB device (the default) or a remote Frida server; the README documents no device setup or tested OS versions.

Outgoing messages come from hooks on the public libxpc send, reply and notification functions, and new connections from xpc_connection_create_mach_service and xpc_connection_set_event_handler. Incoming messages rely on the private _xpc_connection_call_event_handler and __CFBinaryPlistCreate15, which the agent resolves from debug symbols and caches as offsets per machine and OS build in gxpc.conf in the user’s home directory (or a file given with -c). bplist16 payloads are decoded through an external jlutil executable when one is installed on the host, otherwise by the agent’s own parser or as base64. In the reviewed main.go the --whitelistp option reads the --whitelist value, so PID allow-listing may not work as documented.
MIT. frida-go, the Frida devkit and frida-objc-bridge keep their own licenses, and jlutil is a separate third-party tool not shipped with gxpc.

resources.name: Jsxer
resources.description: C++ decompiler for JSXBIN, the binary format of Adobe's legacy ExtendScript, the ECMAScript 3 dialect used to script applications such as Photoshop, InDesign and After Effects. It reads a JSXBIN 1.0, 2.0 or 2.1 literal, parses it into a syntax tree and prints JavaScript source with a header naming the format version. An experimental --unblind option renames symbols obfuscated by JsxBlind, and the same decompiler is exposed as a shared library with a ctypes-based Python binding.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.7.4, published 2025-03-31 with macOS arm64, macOS x86 and Windows archives. The reviewed master commit, from 2025-04-22, is one commit later and only makes the README's notice more visible: it says the project is being rewritten in Rust on a separate rust-rewrite branch, whose latest commit is from 2025-03-11.

Input is a file holding only the JSXBIN literal, usually beginning with @JSXBIN@; the README warns that other content around it must be removed first. The CLI writes a .jsx file next to the input unless -o names another path; input that fails the JSXBIN signature check yields an error message and no decompiled code.

Source builds need CMake 3.26+ and a C++17 compiler; configuring fetches fmt 9.1.0, plog 1.1.9 and CLI11 2.3.2 from GitHub. The README documents only the macOS build, while CMakeLists.txt also has Windows and Linux branches and builds a static library and a shared library, the latter loaded by bindings/python/decompiler.py from the build directory.

ctest builds four small programs that decompile embedded array, object, member-expression and for-statement samples and print the result; they report the decompiler's status code but do not compare output with the original source, and CI runs them on macOS and Windows for pull requests. TODO.md lists open problems with function argument order, comma-expression declarations, number printing and some XML nodes producing improper code.

AGPL-3.0. The README says Jsxer was made for source code recovery and security research and asks users not to use it to pirate scripts from their authors; it credits Andrin Meier's format research and jsxbin-to-jsx-converter, whose original repository it says was removed after an Adobe DMCA takedown. Decompiled scripts keep their authors' rights.

resources.name: jni_helper
resources.description: Static helper by evilpan for reverse engineering Android JNI code. Its extract_jni.py script parses an APK's DEX files with Androguard, finds methods declared native, derives each one's mangled Java_ symbol name and C prototype, including overloaded methods, and saves them with the exported Java_ and JNI_OnLoad functions of the APK's arm64-v8a native libraries as a JSON signature file. Scripts for Ghidra, IDA Pro and Binary Ninja load that file and apply the prototypes and JNI types to the matching functions; a radare2 script is a work in progress.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.6, published 2024-10-23, whose only asset is the demo APK built by CI; the reviewed master commit of 2025-02-24 only updates a README link. CI builds the demo app with JDK 17 and runs extract_jni.py on it as its only test, without checking the output or exercising the disassembler scripts.

extract_jni.py needs Python 3 with androguard, rich and pyelftools from requirements.txt and takes an APK the analyst already has; it reads native libraries only from lib/arm64-v8a. Methods bound at run time through RegisterNatives are not covered, which the README lists as an open TODO, and the disassembler scripts find functions only by their mangled Java_ symbol names.

The Ghidra script is installed by a Makefile into the ghidra_scripts folder in the user's home directory, together with the bundled jni.h.gdt data-type archive; the IDA plugin has separate versions for IDA Pro before 7.4 and for 7.4 and later; the Binary Ninja script runs from File > Run Script and parses the bundled headers/jni.h. Supported versions of Ghidra, Binary Ninja and radare2 are not stated.

No license file, and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms for the scripts are unstated. Bundled headers keep their own notices: headers/jni.h is Oracle's GPL-2.0 file with the Classpath exception, while r2/jni.h and headers/art_method.h are Android Open Source Project files under Apache-2.0. The demo_apk folder holds the source of the author's test app.

resources.name: Manticore
resources.description: Trail of Bits' now-archived symbolic execution tool for Linux ELF binaries on x86, x86-64, AArch64 and ARMv7, Ethereum smart contracts as EVM bytecode, and WebAssembly modules. It runs a program on symbolic inputs to explore the states it can reach, generates concrete inputs that lead to a chosen state and detects crashes and other failures, solving constraints with an external Yices, Z3 or CVC4 solver. The manticore CLI writes generated test cases to an mcore_ workspace, while the Python API adds instruction hooks, event callbacks and custom initial states; manticore-verifier checks contract properties written in the contract's own language.
requirements: Archived and unmaintained: the README states that the project is no longer internally developed and maintained, and GitHub marks the repository archived. The reviewed master commit, from 2026-06-24, only changes that status; the last change under manticore/ dates from 2022-08-07. The latest release is 0.3.7 on GitHub and PyPI (2022-02-17), and PyPI's nightly 0.3.8.dev builds end on 2024-02-27.

Requires Python 3.7 or later. pip install manticore covers EVM and WASM, manticore[native] adds the pinned capstone 5.0.0rc2 and unicorn 2.x needed for native binaries, and a trailofbits/manticore Docker image is offered. The README names the latest Ubuntu LTS on GitHub Actions as the supported platform, gives macOS experimental EVM and WASM support but no native-binary support, and recommends a larger stack limit; CI at the reviewed commit still runs Python 3.7 on ubuntu-20.04.

Inputs are the user's own ELF binaries, Solidity or Vyper sources or EVM bytecode, or WASM modules. Contract analysis needs solc on PATH and compiles through crytic-compile; the README says EVM Istanbul semantics are not fully implemented, so some opcodes may be unsupported. Whole-program CLI runs are prone to state explosion, which the README suggests limiting by tailoring the initial state through the API.

CI runs ethereum, native, WASM, examples and other test suites after downloading Yices 2.6.2 and solc 0.4.24. tests/native/binaries and examples/linux/binaries hold small prebuilt Linux test programs for amd64 and ARMv7, some with their C sources; larger examples, including CTF problems, live in the separate manticore-examples repository, and server/ holds an unpublished gRPC wrapper for the Manticore UI.
AGPL-3.0; the README says Trail of Bits can be contacted for an exception to its terms. The ASE 2019 paper (arXiv 1907.03890) describes the tool.

resources.name: Awesome Executable Packing
resources.description: A single-README list of resources on executable packing, meaning the bundling, compression, encryption, mutation, protection or virtualization of PE, ELF and other executables, including Android apps, and on detecting and unpacking packed files. About 770 entries are grouped into documentation, dated scientific papers, sample datasets, packers sorted by era from before 2000 to after 2010, and tools for packer identification, unpacking and binary analysis.
requirements: The reviewed README, committed 2026-10-10, has 768 list rows: 94 documentation links and 328 scientific publications under Literature, 37 datasets, 190 packers (90 after 2010, 41 from 2000 to 2010 and 59 before 2000) and 119 tools. All but one publication give a month and year; Literature rows carry emoji type markers and 110 publications carry a star, neither of which the README explains. One documentation row links to the list itself.

Rows give a name, a link and usually a one-line description, with no license, maintenance or platform fields, and many packers and tools are specific to Windows PE files. Packer rows point to vendor sites, SourceForge, GitHub projects, blog analyses and 30 Internet Archive copies of old pages or download archives.

The Datasets section lists public malware repositories and feeds next to packed and benign PE and ELF sample sets and benchmark datasets such as EMBER and SOREL-20M. Samples obtained through them can be live malicious software and fall under each provider's access terms.

CC0-1.0 for the list; CONTRIBUTING.md asks for alphabetically sorted rows and one commit per suggestion. Linked papers, packers, tools and datasets keep their own licenses. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: fiano
resources.description: LinuxBoot's Go tools and libraries for parsing and modifying UEFI firmware images. Its utk command shows an image's firmware volumes and files as a table or JSON, finds, dumps, inserts, removes or replaces files, and extracts an image into a directory that can be reassembled, with a DXE cleaner for deleting unneeded DXE drivers. Further commands cover flash maps (fmap), coreboot CBFS, Intel FIT tables, FSP headers, microcode and LZMA data, and its Go packages also parse Intel ME regions, Boot Guard and CBnT manifests and AMD firmware structures.
requirements: No GitHub releases; the newest tags, v7.0.2 and v6.0.1, both point to commits from 2021-12-01, while main keeps receiving fixes, documentation and dependency updates, the reviewed commit being from 2026-05-14. The README installs utk and fmap with go install at @latest and still says Go 1.13 is required, whereas go.mod declares Go 1.21 and CircleCI uses Go 1.22.

Pure-Go command-line tools; go install places the executables in the go/bin folder of the user's home directory. Input is a firmware image the analyst already has, such as a full flash ROM, and fspinfo supports only FSP 2.0 files. CI checks formatting, runs ineffassign and the unit and race tests, and the Go tests include an extract, reassemble and extract round trip and a JSON regression check on a bundled OVMF image.

BSD-3-Clause, copyright LinuxBoot. Test fixtures include an OVMF.rom built from EDK2's open-source vUDK2018 tag, coreboot ROMs, compression samples and manifest samples, plus two Intel binaries kept under Intel's own redistribution terms with their license files: the Apollo Lake FSP blob Fsp.fd under the FSP License, and the Purley ME Ignition firmware MeRegion.bin for Cascade Lake servers, whose binary-only license forbids reverse engineering that image.
Modification commands rewrite firmware images; the README does not discuss flashing or recovery.

resources.name: Deluder
resources.description: Frida-based interceptor for the traffic of proxy-unaware applications. JavaScript hook scripts on the send and receive functions of WinSock, Linux libc sockets, OpenSSL, GnuTLS and SChannel pass plaintext buffers to Python interceptor modules, which log them or forward them to a proxy for inspection. It spawns or attaches to a process, optionally through a remote frida-server, and was designed mainly as the backend for the author's PETEP proxy; a proxifier interceptor works with other proxy tools, and new scripts and interceptors can be added.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.2.1, published 2025-11-14; the reviewed main commit is identical to that tag. The changelog adds remote frida-server support in 1.1 and GnuTLS and Linux sockets in 1.2. The README lists the hooked functions for each library and their Windows, Linux and macOS module names; other libraries need custom Frida scripts.

Python 3.9+ with the pinned frida 16.4.10, psutil 6.0.0 and argparse 1.4.0. It is installed from a release or clone with setup.py, or run as a module after installing requirements.txt. Analysts choose the process to spawn or attach to by path, PID or name, remote targets need a frida-server for their platform, and child processes are hooked unless that is disabled.

Captured messages go to log, debug, proxifier or PETEP interceptors. PETEP integration uses its own protocol on port 8008 by default, and the proxifier frames data by length prefix, suffix or buffer size. The README warns that dropping intercepted messages is unsupported and breaks interception.

Scripts resolve exported functions in loaded modules whose names match a configurable list, so applications that link these libraries statically or use other TLS stacks need custom scripts. The tests directory has pytest cases for the PETEP and proxifier interceptors and for byte formatting. The reviewed tree has no CI workflow and no automated tests for the Frida hook scripts.
LICENSE.md is GPL-3.0.

resources.name: Pyrrha
resources.description: Quarkslab's firmware cartography tool, which indexes an extracted firmware filesystem into a database browsed with NumbatUI, Quarkslab's fork of the Sourcetrail code explorer. The fs mapper uses LIEF to map ELF and PE files, their imports and exports and the symlinks that point to them; fs-cg disassembles every executable with IDA Pro or Ghidra and links their call graphs across binaries, and decomp indexes one executable's decompiled functions with call cross-references. JSON exports can be post-processed in Python, for example to diff two firmware versions.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.0.3, published to GitHub and PyPI as pyrrha-mapper on 2026-09-21; the reviewed main commit sets the same version. v2.0.0 (2026-07-07) added the Ghidra backend and removed the earlier Quokka dependency. pyproject.toml marks the package Beta and lists Linux and Windows.

Input is a firmware root filesystem that the user has already extracted or mounted, or a single executable for decomp; Pyrrha does not unpack firmware images. The fs quick start uses an OpenWrt x86-64 rootfs downloaded from the OpenWrt project.

pyproject.toml requires Python 3.11+, although the installation page says 3.10. fs needs no disassembler, but fs-cg and decomp need a local IDA Pro 9.1+ or Ghidra 12.0+, found on PATH or through IDADIR or GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR; a Ghidra-based Docker image is published on GitHub's registry, and the IDA CI image is built from the user's own Hex-Rays installer and licence. Results are viewed in NumbatUI or, without newer features such as node renaming, Sourcetrail 2021.4.19.

The GitLab CI file runs pytest unit tests and CLI runs of each mapper, with IDA and Ghidra images for fs-cg and decomp; the GitHub workflows only build documentation and publish releases. tests/test_fw is a small 32-bit ARM Linux fixture holding an OpenSSL 1.1.1n executable built with Buildroot and glibc libraries.
Apache-2.0; NumbatUI is a separate GPL-3.0 project, and IDA Pro is commercial software. The README lists SSTIC, Hack.lu, Pass The SALT and RE//verse talks by the authors.

resources.name: GhidraGPT
resources.description: Ghidra extension that sends one function’s decompiled C to a hosted or local language model the user selects and streams the answer into a GhidraGPT console. Its three actions, offered in the Decompiler and Listing context menus, explain the function; rewrite it by writing recovered function, parameter and variable names, types, the prototype and inline comments back into the program; or audit it for likely security issues. Every action uses only the current function’s decompiler output, and the README calls audit findings leads to verify rather than sound static analysis.
requirements: The reviewed main commit is the v1.4.0 release of 2026-07-22, which attaches GhidraGPT-1.4.0.zip. extension.properties declares Ghidra 12.1.2, and the README requires Ghidra 12.1.x, noting that the extension declares compatibility with the Ghidra version it is built against. Building from source needs JDK 21+, Maven and GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR pointing at a local Ghidra; the zip is then added through Ghidra’s Install Extensions dialog.

Each request sends the function name and its decompiled code, prefixed with instruction addresses for Rewrite together with a list of its variables, to the configured provider: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Cohere, Mistral AI, DeepSeek, Grok, OpenRouter, a local Ollama model or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Hosted providers need the user’s own API key, which the README says is stored in config.properties in a .ghidragpt folder under the user’s home directory with XOR obfuscation that is not encryption; every provider except Ollama needs network access.

Rewrite applies the parsed names, types, prototype and comments in Ghidra transactions without a separate confirmation step. The README states that there is no interprocedural or whole-program analysis, so callers, callees and data flow outside the function are not given to the model.

CI downloads Ghidra 12.1.2, sets up JDK 21 and runs Maven unit tests for configuration handling, prompt building and parsing of model responses and rewrite edits; these do not exercise the Ghidra interface or model output.
Apache-2.0 license; the README names Mohamed Benchikh as author. Ghidra and each model provider keep their own licences and terms.

resources.name: Ghidra Ninja ghidra_scripts
resources.description: Thomas Roth's (Ghidra Ninja) collection of Ghidra Python scripts, which appear under a Ghidra Ninja category in the Script Manager. binwalk.py and yara.py run binwalk or bundled YARA crypto-constant rules over the loaded program and bookmark the findings, YaraSearch.py does the same with a rule file the user chooses, swift_demangler.py demangles Swift function names, golang_renamer.py restores function names in stripped Go binaries from the .gopclntab table, and export_gameboy_rom.py writes a working ROM back out of a Game Boy program imported with GhidraBoy.
requirements: No releases or tags; the last commit is a merge from 2020-10-07. Open issues filed between 2020 and 2025 report problems including golang_renamer data-type errors, a binwalk.py temporary-file error and an out-of-memory failure, with no later commits.

Installed by adding the checked-out repository as a script directory in Ghidra's Script Manager. The scripts are Python 2 code for Ghidra's Jython interpreter, and the README names no supported Ghidra version. binwalk.py, yara.py and YaraSearch.py need binwalk or yara on PATH, swift_demangler.py needs the swift toolchain, and export_gameboy_rom.py needs the GhidraBoy extension.

Input is a program the analyst has loaded into Ghidra; export_gameboy_rom.py works on a Game Boy ROM the user imported, and an open issue says it fails for single-page ROMs. golang_renamer.py only searches for the .gopclntab header used before Go 1.16, and an open issue asks for Go 1.16 support. YARA and binwalk hits are signature matches.

GPL-3.0 (LICENSE). The README says the bundled yara-crypto.yar rules are licensed under GPLv2, with an added SHA256 rule credited to @phoul, and credits golang_renamer.py as a port of George Zaytsev's go_renamer.py.

resources.name: BudsPro-Headtracking: streaming Galaxy Buds Pro head tracking over Samsung’s serial protocol
resources.description: Reimplements the Samsung Galaxy Buds Pro’s proprietary spatial-audio messages in a small Python script so that a PC can stream the earbuds’ head-tracking data in real time. It connects to the earbuds’ GEARMANAGER (or FACTORY) RFCOMM serial service, frames packets with start and end markers and a CRC16-CCITT checksum, enables the sensor stream with attach and two-second keep-alive messages, and decodes the rotation quaternion from the data events. A contributed script converts the quaternion to Euler angles and forwards it over local UDP to a Unity receiver; results are shown only as author-provided sample output.
requirements: The reviewed master commit 63b321a (2024-12-30) merges a contributor change that also accepts the FACTORY service name reported for Galaxy Buds2; the README covers only the Galaxy Buds Pro, and the project has no releases, tests or list of tested earbud firmware. Headtracking.py prints the raw x, y, z, w quaternion (four signed 16-bit values divided by 10,000) or, with -b, frame-timing statistics, and reports gyro-bias and stuck-sensor events only in verbose mode.

It needs the user’s own paired Galaxy Buds Pro, addressed by its Bluetooth MAC address; no Samsung app or firmware is used at runtime or included in the repository. The repository does not document how the message IDs and framing were derived; code comments point to the author’s separate Galaxy Buds desktop client for the full parser and quaternion conversion.

Python 3 with PyBluez on Windows or Linux; the README requires PyBluez 0.22 on Windows because 0.23 fails to enumerate Bluetooth devices. buds_to_unity.py also needs NumPy, hardcodes a device address and sends to 127.0.0.1:12562, and getBudsUDP.cs is a Unity MonoBehaviour adapted from a receiver credited to KAIST UVR Lab.

The README shows sample quaternion output, and benchmark mode reports the average, minimum and maximum time between motion frames, but no captures, tests or recorded benchmark results are published. In the reviewed SpatialSensorManager.py the command payloads are built with Python’s bytes(n), which yields n zero bytes rather than the value n, so the bytes sent may differ from what the constant names suggest.
LICENSE grants MIT (2021, Tim Schneeberger); the Unity script carries an attribution to its original author but no separate license. Galaxy Buds and its services belong to Samsung.

resources.name: FindCrypt - Ghidra Edition
resources.description: Ghidra script that ports Ilfak Guilfanov's FindCrypt plugin for IDA, searching a program's memory or the current selection for constants of cryptographic and compression algorithms. Its serialized signature database keeps the original plugin's 79 algorithm constant sets and, by the README's count, holds 122 detectable constants for hash functions, block and stream ciphers, Curve25519 code, Keccak and zlib; when a whole constant is absent, the script also looks for its individual elements and reports partial matches above a detection threshold. Hits become Ghidra bookmarks and a results table from which matching data can be defined.
requirements: The README says the project is discontinued because its author cannot keep it maintained, and points to forks such as TorgoTorgo/ghidra-findcrypt. The reviewed master commit dates from 2021-03-18; the last release, 1.5 of 2020-04-17, attaches FindCrypt.java and database.d3v, and the script and database both report version 7. No supported Ghidra versions are stated; the installation example path names Ghidra 9.0.

Installation is manual: copy FindCrypt.java into Ghidra's Features/BytePatterns/ghidra_scripts directory and the findcrypt_ghidra database folder into the user's home directory, then run the script from the Script Manager on a program already loaded in Ghidra. Headless runs print the results instead of opening the table.

By default each run contacts raw.githubusercontent.com to compare script and database versions with this repository and downloads a newer database.d3v into the home-directory folder; the README describes the __FORCE_NO_DBUPDATE and __FORCE_NO_SCRIPTUPDATE flags in the script that turn this off.

Detection is a byte search for known constants, so hits mark candidate locations, and code that carries no table constants is not found. New signatures are built with the FCExporter Visual Studio project in Utils, which needs Crypto++ for compression.

GPL-3.0, with the Crypto++ license notice included for the exporter. The README credits Ilfak Guilfanov's original plugin, and the database changelog credits contributor Pawlos with its current format.

resources.name: ReArk
resources.description: Desktop reverse-engineering and AI-assisted analysis workbench for HarmonyOS NEXT packages (.hap, .app and .abc), whose binary releases add Android .apk/.aab, iOS .ipa and standalone PE, ELF and Mach-O analysis. The README describes browsing package structure, resources, signatures and metadata, ABC bytecode disassembly and decompilation with strings and cross-references, Java-like Android decompilation, native header, import and mitigation views, and HDC/ADB device workflows for installing apps, reading logs and mirroring screens. Its built-in ReArk Agent answers questions about the open package with OpenAI-compatible or local Ollama models, retrieving package evidence on demand behind approval flows for host and device actions.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.1.1, published 2026-10-15, with a Windows x64 installer and macOS arm64 and x86_64 disk images; the README lists Windows 10+ and macOS 14.0+ and says Linux is coming in the next release. According to the release notes, Android support arrived in v1.0.0, and iOS, PE, ELF and Mach-O analysis with packer detection in v1.1.0.

The published source lags those releases: the v1.0.0, v1.1.0 and v1.1.1 tags point to commits with no source changes after 2026-07-10, VERSION still reads 0.2.0, and the tree holds HarmonyOS and HDC code but no Android, iOS or native-format backends. Building it needs Qt 6, CMake 3.21+ and C++20 plus the author's hyle package, which CMake requires but which is not published; the optional Wuwe agent runtime is a separate Apache-2.0 repository.

Supply the packages or binaries to analyze yourself. For device and signing workflows the repository bundles plugin/hdc/hdc.exe with libusb_shared.dll and the OpenHarmony hap-sign-tool.jar and app_packing_tool.jar. samples/ holds small HarmonyOS packages (Bridge.hap, contacts.hap, EasyHap-default-unsigned.app and fpt-default-signed.app), the shctf.app and shctf.zip CTF sample documented in docs/shctf-analysis-path.md, and 倩倩手机逆向包.rar, an archive of the fpt sample with its app-data files. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES lists only Font Awesome icons.

ReArk Agent needs a configured model provider: an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a provider named in the release notes or a local Ollama model. The README asks users not to send secrets, certificates, user data or trade secrets to remote providers, and limits use to legally authorized reverse engineering, interoperability, malware and security research. The app checks GitHub's latest-release API for updates.

The repository is Apache-2.0; the bundled OpenHarmony tools and icons keep their own licenses, and the release installers contain components absent from the published source. Decompiled output and agent answers still need analyst review.

resources.name: Binary Refinery
resources.description: Large collection of composable Python command-line units for transforming binary data: encodings, compression, encryption, archive and executable-format extraction, carving and pattern search. Each unit reads stdin and writes stdout, so units chain into shell pipelines, while framing, multibin arguments and meta variables let one pipeline process many chunks, and the binref command searches unit help. The author describes it as a command-line take on CyberChef focused on malware triage; the README also points to a separate binref/agent repository of instructions for language-model agents that use refinery.
requirements: Latest release at review: 0.11.2, uploaded to PyPI on 2026-07-14 and requiring Python 3.10+. The reviewed master commit of 2026-10-11 is 1,138 commits past that tag and still reports version 0.11.2, while its changelog already lists breaking 0.11.3 changes, including Python 3.11+ and renamed meta variables. The README says refinery is still in alpha and that units and parameters can be renamed or removed.

Installed with pip as binary-refinery, preferably into its own virtual environment. The default, extended and all extras add progressively more optional dependencies, and units name a missing dependency when run. Installation creates one shell command per unit, optionally with a prefix to avoid name clashes. The README rates Bash and CMD support as good, PowerShell 7.4+ as reasonable, and Zsh and Fish as having minor issues. Several decompression and cipher routines have Cython extensions next to pure-Python versions.

Inputs are the analyst's own files or data piped on stdin. CI runs pytest on Windows, macOS and Ubuntu with Python 3.11 and 3.13. Tests that need real-world inputs fetch encrypted files from the separate binref/refinery-test-data repository. Unit output depends on the parameters chosen and needs analyst validation.

LICENSE.md is the 3-Clause BSD License, which GitHub does not classify. refinery/lib/thirdparty keeps third-party modules under their own licenses, and refinery/lib/seven ports compression code from 7-Zip.

resources.name: ARSCLib
resources.description: Java library, modeled on AOSP's androidfw ResourceTypes.h and meant to replace aapt/aapt2, that reads, writes, modifies and creates Android resource tables (resources.arsc) and binary XML files such as AndroidManifest.xml. It decodes resources to readable JSON, which also handles obfuscated names, or to XML source when names are intact, and builds either form back into binary resources; APK module classes decode, merge and write whole packages. It also has an experimental DEX read/write package, and the APKEditor command-line tool is built on it.
requirements: Latest release at review: V1.4.0, published 2026-07-01 with an attached ARSCLib-1.4.0.jar; the same version is on Maven Central as io.github.reandroid:ARSCLib. The reviewed main commit, from 2026-10-19, is 34 commits ahead, already sets version 1.4.1 in build.gradle and is labeled part 1 of an overhaul of the library core, so its APIs may differ from the release.

Pure Java with no runtime dependencies (JUnit 4.12 for tests); the Gradle build targets Java 8, ./gradlew jar builds the JAR, and CI runs the unit tests and JAR build on JDK 8. The README says it works on Java platforms including Android, Linux, macOS and Windows. It is used as a Maven dependency or a JAR, not as a standalone command-line tool; the README points to APKEditor for that.

Works on APKs and resource files the user supplies. The README says decoding to XML needs un-obfuscated, valid resource names, so obfuscated tables are decoded to JSON instead, and that building validates far less than aapt/aapt2, leaving the user to know which values Android accepts. The dex package's README calls it experimental and not fully implemented.

src/main/resources/frameworks bundles Android framework resource tables for API levels 23 to 37, each a small APK holding only resources.arsc and AndroidManifest.xml, used to resolve framework references; the commit adding API 37 names Google's platform-37.2-beta3 SDK package as its source. The tests include one small type_id_offset.apk fixture.
Apache-2.0.

resources.name: Pithus (bazaar)
resources.description: Self-hostable Django platform behind the Pithus Android analysis service, which its README describes as built for activists, journalists, NGOs and researchers. An uploaded APK is stored under its SHA-256 and queued for static analyses: Androguard attribute and class extraction, APKiD compiler and packer identification, ssdeep and Dexofuzzy similarity, Quark-Engine behavior rules, androcfg call graphs, Exodus tracker signatures, a MobSF static report, APK signing-block metadata and analyst-written YARA rules with retrohunts over stored samples. Results are indexed in Elasticsearch and shown as web reports and through a REST API, optionally enriched with MalwareBazaar, VirusTotal, MISP and Google Play lookups.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.0.1-beta, published 2026-10-12, a bug-fix and dependency update to v1.0.0-beta of 2026-09-21. That release upgraded the 2021 code base, rewrote the API with a separate Python client and is not compatible with earlier Pithus data; its notes say import documentation will follow. The reviewed master commit, from 2026-10-16, is 27 commits later and adds a MISP connector. A hosted beta runs at beta.pithus.org.

The README documents a Linux development stack started with docker-compose -f local.yml and served at localhost:8001, and warns that a missing-index error may appear on first load. The stack runs a Python 3.13 Django 6 app with a django-q worker, PostgreSQL, Redis, Elasticsearch and Kibana 8.19 with a 2 GB Elasticsearch heap, MobSF v4.5.3, RustFS S3-compatible storage and Prometheus; separate compose files cover Apple M1, staging and production.

Input is an APK uploaded through the web interface or API, or fetched from a URL. VirusTotal and MalwareBazaar lookups send the sample's SHA-256 to those services with configured API keys, MISP matching needs a MISP URL and key, Google Play metadata is scraped by package name, tracker signatures are downloaded from Exodus Privacy at analysis time, and an upload_to_mb management command uploads stored samples to MalwareBazaar when an operator runs it.

The analysis tasks are static or lookup-based; no dynamic or sandboxed execution is part of the pipeline, and rule, similarity and reputation results are indicators. The pytest suite mocks Elasticsearch and storage and uses tests/_data/test.apk, a project-built sample app with the package com.pithus.basicapp. The CI pytest job is commented out, so CI lints, runs bandit and builds and pushes Docker images. Quark-Engine is installed from a fork, and quark-rules holds 280 rule files.
AGPL-3.0; the bundled front-end libraries and the analyzers it calls, including MobSF, keep their own licenses.

resources.name: AngryGhidra
resources.description: Ghidra extension that runs angr symbolic execution from a CodeBrowser panel. The analyst marks a destination address, an optional start address and addresses to avoid with hotkeys, and can make program arguments, memory ranges or registers symbolic, write concrete values into memory and registers, hook instructions or apply bytes patched in Ghidra to the angr project. A bundled Python script runs angr's explorer on the program's original file, the listing highlights the instructions along the path it finds, and the panel shows the argument, memory and stdin values that reach the destination.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.1, published 2024-02-13, with prebuilt extension archives for Ghidra 11.0 and 11.0.1; the older 0.1 release carries builds for Ghidra 9.1.2 through 10.3. The reviewed master commit of 2024-07-29 is two commits later, changing the plugin type and the README. Compatibility with newer Ghidra releases is not stated.

Install angr with pip for Python 3 and put python3 on the PATH; the plugin starts the bundled angryghidra.py as an external process and passes the analyst's settings through a temporary angr_options.json file. No angr version is pinned. Building from source uses Gradle with GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR, followed by File → Install Extensions in Ghidra; if no new-plugin prompt appears, enable AngryGhidraPlugin under File → Configure → Miscellaneous.

angr loads the binary from the path Ghidra recorded at import, so the original file must still be there; raw binaries are loaded as blobs with the architecture of the Ghidra language. The analyst supplies the binary and chooses the find, avoid, hook and symbolic-input settings. Path explosion, unmodeled environment behavior and solver limits remain angr's, and a found path gives one satisfying input.
The README demonstrates it on the SecurityFest 2016 fairlight CTF challenge from angr's examples; no other results or tests are published. MIT license.

resources.name: fpicker
resources.description: Frida-based fuzzing suite for closed-source programs, listed here for its in-process instrumentation and coverage layer. A JavaScript harness injected with Frida starts Stalker at an analyst-chosen function and records the basic blocks executed in the target module on each call, feeding either AFL++'s coverage bitmap or fpicker's own standalone mode. Its passive mode works as a tracer: it attaches to a running process without sending inputs and stores each input that reaches the function together with new coverage, on the local host or on USB and network devices running frida-server.
requirements: There are no releases or tags. The reviewed main commit, from 2025-07-24, moves the harness to the Frida 17 APIs, and the Makefile pins frida-core 17.2.14. The README points to a 2021 blog post for background and says fpicker builds on ToothPicker, developed during the author's master's thesis, and was mostly written at ERNW.

make fpicker-macos, fpicker-linux or fpicker-ios builds the C host program; the Makefile downloads the matching frida-core devkit from Frida's GitHub releases, although the README still describes placing the devkit files by hand. iOS builds use Xcode's iPhoneOS SDK on macOS, harness scripts are bundled with frida-compile, and AFL++ is needed only for AFL++ mode, built with USEMMAP on macOS and iOS.

Each target needs a hand-written harness that names the function where instrumentation starts and, for in-process input, how to call it, so that function and its arguments must first be identified in the target. The README warns that coverage becomes unreliable if the function runs more than once per iteration. Shared-memory communication is unavailable for USB-attached devices, and attach mode does not respawn a target that crashes.

Coverage covers basic blocks in the target module during the instrumented call, not a whole-program trace. The examples are small project-written C programs with seed inputs and slides from a WiSec 2021 tutorial; the repository has no automated tests or CI.
MIT; Frida and AFL++ are separate projects with their own licenses.

resources.name: Even G2 protocol: reverse-engineering Even Realities G2 smart-glasses BLE traffic
resources.description: Documents the Bluetooth Low Energy protocol between the Even app and Even Realities G2 smart glasses, worked out from captured traffic: GATT characteristic UUIDs, an 8-byte transport header with sequence, multi-packet and two-byte service-ID fields, a CRC-16/CCITT over the payload, and protobuf payloads with draft .proto definitions. A Python example built on bleak sends the seven-packet session handshake and drives the teleprompter service to show custom text. The README’s status table marks connection, handshake, teleprompter and calendar widget as working, notifications as partial, and Even AI and navigation as still under research.
requirements: The reviewed main commit of 2026-01-03 is a documentation snapshot with no releases or tags. Only the teleprompter has example code, and docs/teleprompter.md is marked work in progress; the .proto header says field numbers and types are inferred from captured packets and may be incomplete or wrong, and several field meanings carry question marks. The README reports the calendar widget working but includes no calendar example or detailed format, and CONTRIBUTING.md labels Even AI “Cracked!” with its request format unclear while the README still lists it as research.

Using the example needs Even G2 glasses and a host with BLE and Python with bleak 0.21+; it scans for device names containing G2 and connects to the left arm’s device, or the right one with --right. The README says the glasses use standard BLE with no special pairing, and the example’s handshake consists of fixed capability messages and the current time, with no keys. The repository contains no Even app or glasses firmware.

CONTRIBUTING.md describes collecting Android Bluetooth HCI snoop logs while using features in the official app, and the repository commits four such raw logs from the author’s sessions; they are not limited to the glasses’ traffic. No tests or verification beyond the README’s status table are provided.

No license file is present and GitHub detects none, so the documentation and code carry no reuse grant. The README calls this an unofficial community project for educational purposes, not affiliated with Even Realities, and credits the Even Realities community with the protocol research.

resources.name: RetroWrite
resources.description: HexHive's static binary rewriter for x64 and aarch64 Linux ELF binaries, which turns a binary into symbolized, reassemblable assembly so instrumentation can be inserted without source code and without heuristics. Bundled passes add a binary-only AddressSanitizer and AFL coverage instrumentation, plus a coarse-grained control-flow-integrity pass on aarch64, and the symbolized assembly can also be edited by hand or by other tools before reassembly. The KRetrowrite variant of the x64 rewriter instruments Linux kernel modules with BASan or kcov for kernel fuzzing.
requirements: There are no releases or tags, and setup.py says 1.0.0. The reviewed master commit, from 2025-04-26, adjusts an x64 pass added four days earlier that randomizes instruction order within functions; before that, the latest commits, from 2023 and 2024, fixed capstone options and executable stacks on older kernels.

Written in Python 3 (the README names 3.6) with pyelftools, capstone 4.0.2 or later, intervaltree and archinfo pinned to 9.1.11752, which the README says to install with pip rather than from distribution packages. x64 output is reassembled with an ordinary compiler such as gcc, linking -lasan for BASan, or with afl-gcc or afl-clang for AFL coverage; on aarch64, retrowrite -a assembles and links. The README's KRetrowrite setup calls a setup.sh that sits in the demo folders rather than at the repository root.

Inputs are the user's own binaries or kernel modules. Per the README feature table, the x64 rewriter needs position-independent, unstripped binaries from standard compilers and has no C++ support, while the aarch64 rewriter also takes stripped and non-PIE binaries but not kernel modules or C++; --ignore-no-pie and --ignore-stripped skip the checks, to be used with caution. The two architectures use different rewriting algorithms: the IEEE S&P 2020 paper describes the x64 version and a separate HexHive thesis the aarch64 version.

CI runs a SPEC CPU benchmark script on a self-hosted runner, and test scripts clone and rewrite coreutils, SQLite and Debian packages. Demos cover userspace, kernel-module and fuzzing setups; the Docker fuzzing demo bundles fuzz seeds and a patched AFL 2.52b archive but also needs a self-built clang 8, a git bundle of the repository and the separately downloaded LAVA-M corpus, and kernel fuzzing setup downloads about 10 GB of syzkaller VM files.
MIT according to the LICENSE file and README, although GitHub does not recognize the license; capstone is included as a submodule under its own license.

resources.name: House
resources.description: NCC Group’s Python and Flask web interface for Frida-based runtime analysis of Android apps, intended to make writing Frida scripts simpler. From a local browser page the analyst can enumerate loaded classes, the classes in a DEX file, class loaders and a class’s methods, then generate and keep tracing scripts for several functions, including ones in dynamically loaded DEX or JAR files. A configurable monitor logs file, HTTP, WebView, SQL, IPC and SharedPreferences calls.
requirements: The reviewed master commit c3641e3 dates from 2020-12-27; the project has no releases or tags. The README says House was tested with Frida 12.8.6 and needs Frida 12.8.3 or later for DEX/JAR hooking, while requirements.txt and the Pipfile leave frida unpinned, so current Frida releases may not work without changes.

Runs from source with Python 3 and pip or pipenv (Flask, Flask-SocketIO 4.3.2, Flask-Login, Jinja2, IPython and frida), serving the interface on 127.0.0.1, port 8000 by default. The README requires a rooted Android device connected over USB with a frida-server matching the local frida-python version, and recommends attaching only one USB device. The Stetho sideload option expects the analyst to place a stetho.jar on the device; it is not bundled.

The repository bundles the README’s demo app test_apk/overloads.apk (package com.ha0k3.overloads) and a small test_apk/dyhello.dex as test fixtures, plus copies of the Ace editor and Bootstrap for the web interface. The monitor’s hook list in scripts/monitor/monitor_hook.json is described as experimental. Intended for apps the analyst is authorized to test.
MIT (NCC Group). Frida and the bundled web libraries keep their own licenses.

resources.name: ABCDE
resources.description: Kotlin toolkit for OpenHarmony reverse engineering that parses Ark bytecode (.abc) files, the format HarmonyOS app packages carry in modules.abc, along with HAP packages and resource index (.index) files. Its Compose desktop viewer browses classes, methods, fields, literal arrays, imports and exports and disassembles methods, showing imported modules and resource references in readable form; an experimental mode translates some methods literally into JavaScript, and a CLI dumps class lists and resource indexes. The parsing core is also published as a JVM library, and the separate abc-decompiler builds on a patched fork of it.
requirements: No releases or tags are published. The README points to GitHub Actions builds, but no workflow artifacts remained available at review, so the jar has to be built locally; the reviewed main commit of 2025-11-28 is also the latest push. Decompilation to JavaScript is labelled experimental: functions containing try/catch and some instructions, such as the async ones, are unsupported, and the output is a literal, unoptimized translation.

Building needs JDK 17+. ./gradlew :abcdecoder:packageReleaseUberJarForCurrentOS produces a desktop uber-jar for the current OS, while CI's -Puniversal build bundles the Compose runtimes for Linux x64/arm64, Windows x64 and macOS x64/arm64; Gradle resolves dependencies through Aliyun Maven mirrors as well as Maven Central and Google. ./gradlew publishToMavenLocal publishes the core modules for use as io.github.yricky.oh:abcde-jvm, and the abclen size-report and findStr string-search examples show library use.

Inputs are .abc, .hap and resources.index files from the user's own OpenHarmony or HarmonyOS app packages; the repository ships no sample apps. The committed isa.json instruction table is generated from OpenHarmony's arkcompiler_runtime_core isa.yaml, which the updateIsaDefine Gradle property fetches again from Gitee.

CI only builds the universal jar. Most JUnit tests read sample .abc, .hap or resources.index files from the author's local paths or an abcPath environment variable, so only a few encoding and checksum tests run from the repository alone, and no disassembly or decompilation accuracy results are reported.
Apache-2.0; the GUI bundles the JetBrains Mono font under the SIL OFL.

resources.name: Interruptor
resources.description: Frida library, taken from the Dexcalibur project, that uses Frida’s Stalker to trace a process’s system calls and print strace-like lines with the calling thread, module and offset, decoded flag values and file paths resolved from descriptors. A trace can be limited to chosen modules and syscalls by name or pattern, started when a given library loads, extended with Interceptor-style per-syscall callbacks, and used to write drcov basic-block coverage files. The README documents Linux and Android on AArch64 and x64; the source also contains AArch32 Linux and macOS arm64 and x64 entry points.
requirements: Latest npm release at review: @reversense/interruptor 1.0.12, published 2023-04-02; the newest GitHub release is v1.0.9 (2023-03-29). The reviewed main commit of 2026-09-23 adds unreleased changes, including refactored arm64 register handling and a preadv2/pwritev2 argument fix, without a version bump, and the README still calls the project a work in progress.

It is used inside the analyst’s own Frida agent: install the npm package, build from source with npm and TypeScript, or load a webpack-bundled per-architecture script. The README says passing a TypeScript agent directly to frida needs Frida 16 or later, and package.json depends on @types/frida-gum ^17.3.0. Android examples attach to a USB device with frida -U; the README warns that the CodeShare quick-start cannot be configured and may fail on obfuscated or multi-threaded apps.

The README’s support list names the Linux syscall API on AArch64 (SVC, with HVC marked work in progress) and x64 (SYSCALL); the AArch32 Linux and macOS factories in the source have no documented status. The agent tracer cannot follow child or multiple processes, and a standalone host-side tracer is marked TODO. Coverage needs an output path the target process can write. CI runs Mocha tests of the Linux AArch32 and arm64 factories on Node 16; no device test results are published. Intended for software the analyst is authorized to inspect.

package.json and the npm metadata declare GPL-3.0-only, but the LICENSE file is x64dbg’s modified GPL-3.0 text, whose added exception concerns x64dbg plugins rather than this project, so GitHub cannot classify it. The README also promotes the separate commercial Dexcalibur Pro.

resources.name: de4js
resources.description: Browser-based JavaScript deobfuscator and unpacker, built as a Jekyll site that also works offline as a progressive web app. It detects or lets the user pick an encoding and reverses Dean Edwards' Packer, eval- and array-based obfuscators, some Obfuscator.IO output, JSFuck, JJencode, AAencode, URL encoding, My Obfuscate and WiseLoop, then beautifies and highlights the result, with options to unescape strings, merge strings, recover object paths and evaluate constant expressions. An optional userscript sends the code to the JS Nice service to rename unreadable identifiers.
requirements: The repository is archived. The last release, v1.12.0, was published 2021-03-28, and the reviewed master commit from 2021-11-12 adds only dependency updates and a fix to how option values are converted to booleans. The README notes that Obfuscator.IO is always up to date and that automatic tools, this one included, usually do not match its latest version. The homepage, lelinhtinh.github.io/de4js, still served the app through a redirect at review.

No installation is needed for the hosted page. Local copies run with docker-compose, or with Ruby 2.1+, Bundler and the GitHub Pages Jekyll gems, at localhost:4000/de4js/; npm run build also needs workbox-cli to generate the offline service worker. The Wise unpackers load from the NotSoWise git submodule, which must be checked out.

Input is pasted code, an opened file or a script fetched from a URL. The Eval, JSFuck, Array, _Number, Obfuscator.IO and AAencode decoders and the expression-evaluation option run all or part of the input with eval inside a Web Worker, so untrusted code executes in the browser's worker context. The JS Nice userscript sends code to jsnice.org over plain HTTP and does not work offline.
package.json defines no tests and the repository has no automated tests or CI. Whether a decoder succeeds depends on the obfuscator and its version, so output should be checked by reading it.
MIT; the bundled js-beautify, highlight.js, clipboard.js, math.js, Workbox and magic-check code and the AAencode and JJencode decoders keep their own notices.

resources.name: Awesome AI Reverse Engineering
resources.description: A single-README, Chinese-language list of AI-assisted reverse-engineering projects, grouped into JavaScript reversing, binary and native analysis, Android and iOS security, and browser automation and traffic analysis. Its entries are mostly MCP servers, agent skills for Claude, Cursor and Codex, and IDE plugins that connect large language models to tools such as IDA Pro, Ghidra, Binary Ninja, JADX and Frida. Each row is a project name, a link and a one-line Chinese blurb.
requirements: The reviewed README, from the commit dated 2026-09-29, lists 35 projects across four sections: 11 under JavaScript reversing, 9 under binary and native analysis, 9 under Android and iOS security, and 6 under browser automation and traffic analysis. The list carries a last-updated 2026-04 badge.

Each entry gives only a name, a link to a third-party repository and a short Chinese description, with no stated completion, accuracy or maintenance status. The list mixes MCP servers, agent skills and IDE plugins, and several entries are dual-use — anti-bot/WAF traffic evasion, anti-detection browsers, and APK ad or bloat removal with repackaging — so each linked project must be reviewed at its own source for scope, rights and lawful, authorized use.

The list links out and bundles no tools or target files of its own; the GhidraMCP server and the SimoneAvogadro Android reverse-engineering skill it points to are already in this catalog. Linked projects and the software they analyze keep their own licenses.

The README shows an MIT license badge, but the repository contains only README.md with no LICENSE file, and GitHub detects no license, so the list itself states no clear reuse terms. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: dyld_cache_extract
resources.description: macOS application and command-line tool that reads a dyld_shared_cache file from macOS or iOS, shows its header, mappings and image list, and copies one library or every library out to a directory. The CLI offers --info, --extract and --extract-all; the GUI presents the same header details and lets users select images to extract. The README marks the project obsolete and points to the author's dyld-cache-dump.
requirements: The README marks the project obsolete and refers users to dyld-cache-dump. The last commits, on 2023-06-12, fix the build for the then-current Xcode and update CI and the README. Releases 0.1.0 (2017-03-06) and 0.1.1 (2017-06-18) each attach a zipped Dyld Cache Extractor app; there is no newer release.

Builds on macOS with Xcode from dyld_cache_extract.xcodeproj, whose schemes cover the CLI tool, the GUI app and the DCE static library; the PIMPL, GitHubUpdates and xcconfig submodules must be initialized. CI builds and analyzes Debug and Release configurations of the CLI and GUI on macos-latest, with tests disabled.

Needs a dyld_shared_cache file from the user's own macOS or iOS system; the repository contains no caches or extracted libraries. The parser reads only the original header fields (magic, mapping and image tables, dyld base address) of a single cache file and copies each image's bytes plus the __LINKEDIT region; the reviewed code has no split sub-cache handling, and support for current macOS or iOS caches is not documented.
MIT license (2016, Jean-David Gadina, XS-Labs).

resources.name: FLARE IDA Pro utilities
resources.description: Archived collection of IDAPython plugins and scripts from Mandiant's FLARE team for malware and native-code analysis in IDA Pro. It searches code for precomputed API-name hashes used by shellcode, recovers strings built on the stack (statically, or by emulation with flare-emu in ironstrings), applies function types to structure fields and indirect calls, annotates imports with MSDN function, argument and constant information, and uses idb2pat to generate pattern files from an IDB's functions for building FLIRT signatures. Other scripts track static arguments to functions such as string decoders, link Objective-C selector references to their implementations in Mach-O files, and graft stub implementations of common Windows API imports so that decoding or unpacking code can run under IDA's Bochs emulation.
requirements: The repository is archived and read-only, with no releases or tags; the reviewed master commit of 2024-10-29 is its last. Nothing is packaged: the README says to copy plugins/ into IDA's plugins folder and python/ into IDA's python folder or onto PYTHONPATH, and scripts such as annotate_IDB_MSDN.py, ironstrings.py and code_grafter.py are run through File → Script file.

Needs IDA Pro with IDAPython; the README gives Windows %PROGRAMFILES% paths and names no supported IDA version. The code spans several IDA generations: apply_callee_type was fixed for IDA 7.6 SP1 and idb2pat was ported to Python 3, while stackstrings, argtracker and the decompiler_scripts still use Python 2 syntax, and the StackStrings plugin warns that it only works under Python 2 because of its vivisect dependency. Dialog-based tools import PyQt5; ironstrings, objc2_analyzer and revil_string_decrypt need flare-emu and Unicorn, the decompiler_scripts need the Hex-Rays decompiler, and code_grafter targets IDA's Bochs IDB emulation mode.

Samples and IDBs come from the analyst. The repository bundles sc_hashes.db, a SQLite database of about 50 MB holding precomputed hashes of export names from Microsoft DLLs, with make_sc_hash_db.py to rebuild it from a DLL directory the user chooses. The MSDN annotator expects an MSDN_data directory that is not shipped; the MSDN_crawler script builds it with Python 2.7 from an extracted copy of the MSDN documentation and IDA's tilib.
There are no tests or CI. Behaviour is documented through the README, per-tool READMEs and linked FireEye and Mandiant blog posts.

Apache-2.0 for the repository, while msdn_crawler.py is a GPL-2.0-or-later derivative of the zynamics msdn-crawler. IDA Pro, the Hex-Rays decompiler and Microsoft DLLs and documentation keep their own terms.

resources.name: Binlex
resources.description: Binary trait-lexer framework that extracts instructions, basic blocks and functions from executables and emits searchable JSON traits for similarity, hunting and signature work. It models code with a genomics-inspired hierarchy and computes features such as MinHash, TLSH, SHA256, entropy and wildcard byte patterns, so samples can be compared, clustered and turned into signatures at scale. It ships a CLI suite, a Rust API, Python bindings and an IDA plugin, can generate YARA rules from its patterns, and runs processors locally or over IPC and HTTP.
requirements: The reviewed master commit declares a Rust 2024-edition workspace at version 2.0.0. The latest stable GitHub release is v1.1.1 (2023-03-04); the v2.0.0 line is still at release candidates, the most recent being v2.0.0-rc2 (2025-01-14), whose prebuilt zips cover Linux (Debian and Arch), macOS (amd64 and aarch64) and Windows, plus an IDA plugin archive and a server archive. The reviewed master is ahead of those tags.

The README lists Linux, macOS and Windows; input formats PE, ELF and Mach-O; and AMD64, I386 and CIL architectures, with disassembly through Capstone 0.12. Build and install with cargo build --release --workspace, build the Python bindings with maturin, package with make zst/deb/wheel, install the IDA plugin with pip and python -m binlex_ida install, and the repository also provides Docker Compose files for its server, web, MCP and Python images.

Supply the binaries to analyze yourself; the repository commits no sample binaries, and its tests are Rust source. Binlex extracts static traits and hashes and generates patterns and YARA rules; it does not run the target, and derived signatures and similarity scores still need analyst validation.
MIT license; contributions require signing the repository's CLA.

resources.name: GhidrAssist
resources.description: Ghidra extension by Jason Tang, who also wrote GhidrAssistMCP, that adds a tabbed GhidrAssist window to CodeBrowser for LLM-assisted analysis of the open program. Its tabs explain decompiled or disassembled functions with a security summary, keep persistent chats with context macros, MCP tool calling and an optional ReAct agent mode, propose function and variable renames, retypes and structures for review before they are applied, and build a semantic knowledge graph of functions, calls and security features with community detection, alongside Lucene retrieval over reference documents the analyst adds. A SymGraph tab imports and publishes names, types, graph data and documents through the hosted symgraph.ai service.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2.2.0, published 2026-05-29 with extension zips for Ghidra 12.0 and 12.1 Public; the reviewed master commit is three commits later and only updates model guidance and max-token handling. The README and getting-started guide state a Ghidra 11.0 minimum, but release zips are built per Ghidra version and recent ones cover only 12.x. Installation goes through File → Install Extensions, after which the plugin is enabled under CodeBrowser's File → Configure → Miscellaneous; source builds use Gradle with GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR.

Analysis needs at least one configured LLM provider. The reviewed provider types cover Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Gemini and xAI APIs, OpenAI and Gemini subscription sign-in through OAuth, the local Claude Code CLI, a LiteLLM proxy, and local Ollama, LM Studio or Open WebUI endpoints; the documentation's provider tables also list an Anthropic OAuth type that the source does not define. Explanations, chats, Actions, agent runs and the graph's Semantic Analysis step send pseudocode or disassembly to the active provider, so only a local or self-hosted endpoint keeps code on the machine, while graph re-indexing and Security Analysis run without the model. Chats, explanations, graph data and feedback are kept in local SQLite databases and a Lucene index whose paths are set in Settings.

Programs come from the user's own Ghidra projects. Actions suggestions are applied only for the rows the user checks. Chats can reach MCP servers over SSE or streamable HTTP or launch them over stdio; built-in tools read the current function and address, apply the Actions edits and query the semantic graph, and the README pairs the plugin with GhidrAssistMCP for decompilation, cross-reference and other Ghidra-specific tools. Calls to tools whose names do not look read-only wait for an allow-once, allow-for-session or deny decision, and this classification relies on tool-name keywords.

The SymGraph tab looks up the program by SHA-256 without a key, but importing, publishing and uploading need a SymGraph API key, and publishing uploads the raw binary itself when the service does not already hold it. The repository has no tests or CI workflows.
MIT, per LICENSE and the README; Ghidra, model providers and SymGraph keep their own terms. The repository moved from jtang613/GhidrAssist.

resources.name: game-and-watch-patch: Nintendo Game & Watch custom firmware
resources.description: Custom firmware for the Mario and Zelda Game & Watch consoles that patches new C code into the user's own stock firmware backups, so the original firmware runs alongside the retro-go emulator. A Python patcher hooks stock function calls, relocates and LZMA-compresses stock code and data to free flash, and can merge both models' firmware into one image. Committed symbol maps, a cross-reference mapper and an analysis-ELF builder support the reverse engineering, and a journal records the author's first firmware-patching work.
requirements: The reviewed main commit (2026-10-19) is 111 commits past the last tag, v0.12 of 2025-02-25, and no release attaches binaries; the relocation, merged-image, analysis tooling and most tests arrived after that tag. The README lists more Mario features (whole firmware in internal flash, removable song and sleep illustrations, timeouts, clock graphics mods) than Zelda ones and says Zelda's external-flash savings are still to come.

Requires the user's own internal and external flash backups of a Mario or Zelda unit, placed as internal_flash_backup_<device>.bin and flash_backup_<device>.bin; the patcher rejects images whose SHA-1 does not match the stock firmware. The repository commits no firmware, ROMs or keys: tools/re/README.md says the .syms files hold only the project's annotations and that ELFs derived from Nintendo's firmware must never be committed, and docs/mario.md says no ROMs or ROM-hack patches are hosted.

Targets the consoles' STM32H7B0 microcontroller. Builds need GNU Make, the arm-none-eabi GCC toolchain and Python 3.6+ with Pillow, NumPy, pycryptodome, pyelftools, capstone and colorama; flashing uses gnwmanager, and the Mario internal-only mode also needs a patched OpenOCD for an undocumented extra 128 KB of internal flash. An Ubuntu 22.04 Dockerfile installs gnwmanager's OpenOCD and Arm toolchain for x86-64 Linux hosts.

tests/test_golden.py rebuilds fixed option sets and compares output SHA-1 hashes with tests/golden.json, recorded for Arm GNU Toolchain 15.2.Rel1; it skips without the stock backups or under another GCC version. Other unit tests cover relocation, Thumb assembly, layout and symbols, and tools/emu runs patched images through menu tests in the GWemu emulator. CI only runs pre-commit lint checks and builds the Docker image.

COPYING is BSD-3-Clause (2020, Konrad Beckmann, Thomas Roth, STMicroelectronics); the vendored ST CMSIS and HAL sources keep their own notices, and the stock firmware and games remain Nintendo's. The repository's CLAUDE.md is guidance for Claude Code.

resources.name: Driver Buddy Reloaded
resources.description: IDA Pro Python plugin for triaging Windows kernel drivers, building on NCC Group's original DriverBuddy. Its auto-analysis identifies the driver model (WDM, KMDF, UMDF, WDF, Mini-Filter, Stream Minidriver, AVStream or PortCls), locates the device-control dispatch routines, labels IRP, IO_STACK_LOCATION and WDF structures and calls, and discovers and decodes IOCTL codes through Hex-Rays ctree, switch-table and immediate-operand scans. It also reports device names, symbolic links and device ACLs, pool tags, flagged APIs and opcodes, name-based call chains and heuristic vulnerability leads with per-IOCTL risk scores, in an IDA findings window, a JSON file and an HTML report.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2.5.1, published 2026-07-08 as a zip; the reviewed main commit of 2026-10-19 is four commits later, adding an IOCTL-recovery fix for issue #41 with a new regression fixture, DriverEntry typing for the MajorFunction annotator and the licence change noted below. The README says it runs on IDA 7.6+, 8.x and 9.0+ with Python 3, with API differences handled by ida_compat.py, and ida-plugin.json lists Windows, Linux and macOS hosts. IDA 9.0+ installs it with hcli plugin install; 7.6 and 8.x need the script and its package folder copied to the top level of the plugins directory.

Analysts load their own Windows kernel driver (.sys) in IDA. The Hex-Rays decompiler is optional but drives the strongest IOCTL scan, with switch-table and immediate-operand scans as fallbacks, and the experimental DispatchDeviceControl search works only for x64 drivers. Each run writes findings.json, report.html, pooltags.txt and an analysis log next to the IDB, and optional stages are toggled in config.py.

tests/test_dbr.py is a pure-Python regression suite that needs no IDA; run_cross_version.ps1 runs the pipeline under IDA 7.6 SP1, 8.4 and Free 9.3, and run_golden.ps1 compares findings on reference drivers with committed golden JSON captured with the IDA 8.4 decompiler. The README reports that decompiler-based scanning raised IOCTL recovery from 7/28 to 28/28 on HEVD and from 4/17 to 17/17 on ALSysIO64 with no false positives. There is no CI, and these results are project-reported.

tests/drivers bundles IDA databases (.i64) and golden findings for eight reference drivers as regression fixtures: ALSysIO64, HEVD, IObitUnlocker, MODAPI, WinRing0x64, amp, beep and zam64 .sys. Those drivers keep their own vendors' terms.

LICENSE was replaced on 2026-07-10 with the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0, which permits only noncommercial purposes, while release 2.5.1 and earlier carry GPL-3.0 and ida-plugin.json still declares GPL-3.0. IDA Pro and Hex-Rays keep their own terms. The README calls its findings heuristic lead generators for manual review rather than confirmed vulnerabilities.

resources.name: FA (Firmware Analysis)
resources.description: Python framework, mainly used as an IDA plugin, that turns the manual steps of locating symbols, such as finding a string, following its cross-reference and taking the function start, into reusable signatures. Hjson SIG files, grouped into per-platform projects, chain commands that search bytes, strings, immediates or Keystone-assembled opcodes, filter by operands and cross-references, and then set names, types, constants, enums and struct members; Python scripts can drive the same interpreter. In IDA it adds an FA menu and toolbar to find all of a project's symbols, draft a temporary signature from the current function and export symbols plus a C header, and a separate loader runs signatures over a raw ELF file without IDA.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.0.11, published 2026-03-25 without attached files; it tags the reviewed master commit, and the same version is on PyPI as fa 1.0.11. The README installs it by cloning the repository and running pip install -e, says the code base is very IDA-oriented and only considers Ghidra, radare2 or other disassemblers for the future.

The README supports IDA 8.0+, and a March 2026 commit added IDA 9.0 support to make-offset. The package requires Python 3.8+; its dependencies, including keystone-engine, capstone, hjson and rpyc, are installed into IDA's Python. IDA can also run the plugin in script mode to write a symbols file, while the ELF loader script imports pyelftools, which is listed only in the testing requirements.

The binaries, IDA databases and signatures come from the analyst: the repository ships only two small test projects under fa/signatures and no signature sets for real firmware. The README groups signatures into projects partly to lower false positives, and the ELF loader reports symbols with several matches instead of choosing one.

CI lints with flake8 and runs pytest on Python 3.8 to 3.12; the tests check find-bytes on mocked memory segments and ELF symbol search on a small ARM ELF built at test time with Keystone and simpleelf, and neither runs IDA. GPL-3.0 license text; pyproject.toml classifies it as GPLv3 or later.

resources.name: DexKit
resources.description: C++ DEX parsing library with Kotlin and Java APIs that loads an APK, DEX bytes or an app’s class loader and finds classes, methods and fields by their characteristics rather than their obfuscated names. Matchers combine package scope, modifiers and raw access flags, field, parameter and return types, annotations, the strings and numeric constants a method uses and the methods it calls, while batch queries locate many targets from strings at once; results expose opcodes, callers, invoked methods and fields used. Its guides centre on keeping Xposed hook points working across obfuscated app versions, and the same queries serve as a fast, scriptable search over an app’s bytecode.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2.3.0, published 2026-09-22 with no attached files, which added numeric-literal reading and raw DEX access-flag matching and optimized caching and string queries. The reviewed master commit of 2026-10-10 is two core fixes ahead of that tag. Packages are published on Maven Central as org.luckypray:dexkit; the artifact ID changed from DexKit with 2.0.

Android projects need JDK 11+, Kotlin 1.5+, AGP 4.2+ and minSdkVersion 21+, with 23+ recommended because libdexkit.so may not load from compressed APK libraries on older settings. Since 1.1.0 it also runs on Windows, Linux and macOS from a source checkout built with gcc or clang, CMake and Ninja or Make, using MSYS2 on Windows, and CI builds the native libraries on all three. The APK, DEX data or class loader to query comes from the user; the repository’s only app is its own demo.

The guides present DexKit as a tool for Xposed module developers, and the README examples run inside an Xposed hook. Matches depend on the conditions the user writes, so they identify candidate classes and members rather than recover original names. Unit tests with smali fixtures are in the repository, but the reviewed workflows only build the native libraries and packages.
