Everything outside Core/ is Apache-2.0, while the native code in Core/ is LGPL-3.0, although the README’s license badge links only to the LGPL. The README credits AOSP’s slicer, ThreadPool and parallel-hashmap as third-party sources. Apps analysed with it keep their own terms.

resources.name: AndroidReverse101
resources.description: A Chinese-language Android reverse-engineering course by Evil0ctal, planned as 100 daily lessons. It starts from number systems, ARM assembly, the Dalvik/ART runtime and APK loading, then covers APK and DEX structure, Smali editing and repackaging, Frida and Xposed hooking, JNI and native-library analysis, traffic analysis, obfuscation and app hardening, with commands and code for tools such as jadx, apktool, readelf, GDB/LLDB, Frida and Burp Suite. A Crackmes folder adds copies of OWASP's UnCrackable and r2pay practice apps, and a community Indonesian translation follows the published lessons.
requirements: Reviewed at commit 9b72d20 (2025-12-31), the merge of a community Indonesian translation; the Chinese lessons and crackmes were committed between 22 and 25 February 2025, and there are no releases. The README outlines 100 days in three phases, but the tree holds 44 lessons (Days 1–41, 60, 70 and 100), and the Indonesian translation covers the same 44, many in shortened form.

No outside target files are needed to begin: the Day 20 lesson supplies crackme source for learners to compile, and the Crackmes folder commits five practice APKs, UnCrackable-Level1.apk, UnCrackable-Level2.apk, UnCrackable-Level3.apk, r2pay-v0.9.apk and r2pay-v1.0.apk, whose Git blobs are identical to the crackmes in OWASP's MASTG repository. Only Level 1 has a written walkthrough; the README's Crackme 2 link points to a file that is not in the tree.

Lessons assume a desktop host with adb and an Android device, and name tools including jadx, apktool, baksmali, readelf, GDB/LLDB, IDA Pro, Ghidra, Frida with frida-server on the device, Burp Suite and Wireshark; the Xposed lesson starts from a device rooted with Magisk.

Many phase-two lessons and the Day 70 and Day 100 exercises are framed around modifying third-party apps, including defeating licence, paid-feature, root-detection, certificate-pinning and anti-debugging checks. The README and lessons carry no note on legal use or authorization.

The repository is MIT-licensed (copyright 2025 Evil0ctal); the crackmes come from OWASP's CC BY-SA 4.0 MASTG repository, and the tools named keep their own terms. The lessons mention AI as a reverse-engineering subject.

resources.name: fuji-cam-wifi-tool: reconstructing Fujifilm X-series Wi-Fi remote control
resources.description: Reimplements the Wi-Fi remote-control protocol of Fujifilm X-series cameras as a C++ library and an interactive command-line client that joins the camera's access point. Its headers name the control, event and JPEG live-view ports, message types and camera property codes, and source comments keep hex traces of exchanges along with what "the app" sends; the client connects, fires the shutter, records video, adjusts exposure settings and focus point, and streams live view, optionally into a Linux webcam device. README calls the tool very limited and mostly undocumented, so the protocol knowledge lives in code and comments rather than a specification.
requirements: Reviewed at master commit c597fc4 of 2021-03-17, the repository's last push; there are no releases or tags. The README describes an attempt to reverse-engineer the protocol, calls the tool very limited and mostly undocumented, and suggests reading the code. Its connection steps name the X-T10 and a source comment mentions focus-point ranges on the X-T100; no compatibility list for other X-series models is given.

Requires the user's own Fujifilm X-series camera with Wi-Fi remote control: the computer joins the camera's access point, the client connects to 192.168.0.1 on ports 55740–55742, and the first connection must be confirmed on the camera, where the tool registers as "HackedClient". The repository contains no camera firmware, Fujifilm app or capture files; the README gives Wireshark display filters for viewing control messages and streamed JPEG frames.

README documents CMake builds on macOS, Linux and Windows (CMake 2.8.11 minimum, C++11). The interactive shell needs the hkr/linenoise-ng submodule initialized, and Windows builds link Winsock. Optional OpenCV support adds stream_cv, which can feed live view into a Linux v4l2loopback device for use as a webcam.
The repository has no tests or CI. Message meanings are inferred in code comments, several of which are marked unknown or TODO, and command behavior on cameras remains contributor-reported.
Released under the Unlicense, a public-domain dedication; AUTHORS.txt lists five contributors. Fujifilm cameras, firmware, apps and trademarks keep their own rights.

resources.name: pyinstxtractor-ng (PyInstaller Extractor Next Generation)
resources.description: Fork of PyInstaller Extractor (pyinstxtractor) by the same author that extracts the bundled CArchive files and PYZ modules from Linux ELF and Windows PE executables built with PyInstaller, writing .pyc files with repaired headers for a separate bytecode decompiler. Unlike the original script, it unmarshals the PYZ archive with the xdis library, so it does not have to run under the Python version that built the executable, and it automatically decrypts PYZ entries that PyInstaller's optional AES encryption protected, using the key module bundled in the same executable. A one-directory mode extracts the PYZ next to the other files so the result can be run directly, and --info prints archive metadata such as versions, entry points and encryption without writing files.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2026.07.03, published 2026-07-03, with a Linux binary and a Windows .exe built by PyInstaller, so those builds need no Python installation; the same version is on PyPI as pyinstxtractor-ng 2026.7.3. The reviewed main commit is two commits ahead of that tag and only relaxes the pycryptodome requirement from exactly 3.17 to 3.19.1 or later below 4.

Running the script needs Python 3.8+, xdis pinned to 6.3.0 and pycryptodome; a leftover Poetry section in pyproject.toml still caps Python below 3.13. Release binaries come from a manually triggered workflow that builds with Python 3.8 and PyInstaller 5.10.1, and the repository has no tests or test executables.

The script header lists PyInstaller 2.0 through 5.10.1 as supported, and the README states no version range. Entries that can be neither decompressed nor decrypted are saved unchanged with an .encrypted suffix.

The PyInstaller executable comes from the user, and turning the recovered bytecode into source needs a separate decompiler. Recovered code remains subject to the rights of the original program’s owner.
GPL-3.0-only.

resources.name: RETracker
resources.description: Python reverse-engineering framework for the Polyend Tracker music device that patches the vendor's stock firmware, replacing an unused USB RAWHID handler with its own command handler. With the patched firmware flashed, a host CLI reads, hex-dumps and disassembles device memory in ARM or Thumb mode, writes memory, runs code at an address, assembles and executes position-independent "Polyp" modules such as a pad text scroller and screen fades, and copies files to the SD card over USB. Its fwtool.py also unpacks and repacks the Intel HEX .ptf firmware images for loading into a disassembler.
requirements: Only Polyend Tracker firmware 1.5.0 is supported; the README says a private 1.6.0 port was not released because Polyend removed the code the patches relied on. The reviewed main commit of 2024-06-19 only announces a discussion thread, the last code change dates from 2022, and there are no releases or tags.

Patching needs the user's own copy of the stock PolyendTracker_1.5.0.ptf image, which the repository does not include, and the patched image is flashed through the device's normal firmware-update menu. The README warns that the update screen behaves differently with patched images, recommends backing up the SD card first and points to the Tracker's emergency update procedure for recovery.

Needs Python 3 with capstone, keystone-engine, pyusb, intelhex and simple-hexdump; the host finds the device over USB by vendor and product ID. The README's reverse-engineering notes treat the hardware as a Teensy 3.6-class MK66FX microcontroller, give the firmware load address and a RAM address used for Polyps, and say IDA Pro, and probably Ghidra or Binary Ninja, can load the Intel HEX image directly.
There are no tests or CI. Behaviour is documented through README examples and a linked demo video.
No license file was found and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms are unstated. Polyend's firmware keeps its own rights, and the README disclaimer places any device damage at the user's risk.

resources.name: CoBRA (Coefficient-Based Reconstruction of Arithmetic)
resources.description: Trail of Bits' C++23 simplifier for Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) expressions, an obfuscation technique that rewrites simple computations as interleaved arithmetic, bitwise and shift operations. Given an expression and a bit width from 1 to 64, cobra-cli returns a simpler equivalent: a worklist scheduler combines signature-vector and change-of-basis techniques, semilinear handling of constant masks, polynomial recovery, decomposition of mixed products and subexpression lifting, and each result is checked on random inputs or, optionally, with a Z3 equivalence proof. The same engine is available as a library and as an optional LLVM pass plugin that simplifies MBA expressions it detects in LLVM IR.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.3.0, published 2026-06-30 without prebuilt binaries. The reviewed master commit is eight commits ahead: README edits, a CI dependency bump, a fix that requires LLVM only when the pass is built, and a fix that lets cobra-core build under MSVC.

Builds from source with CMake 3.20+ and a C++23 compiler (GCC 13+, Clang 17+ or Apple Clang 16+); a dependency superbuild builds Abseil and Highway, and GoogleTest when tests are enabled. The LLVM pass plugin needs LLVM 19 to 22, runs through opt as cobra-simplify, replaces an expression only when the simplified form is cheaper and drops nuw/nsw flags. Z3 checking is compiled in only when CMake finds Z3; otherwise cobra-cli warns that --verify is ignored. CI builds with Clang 22 and LLVM 22 on Ubuntu 24.04 on every run, and with GCC 14 and on macOS 15 only for version tags; Windows is not in CI.

cobra-cli takes the obfuscated expression as text, with at most 16 variables by default, so expressions in a binary must first be recovered with other tools or reach the pass as LLVM IR. The README's known limitations are deeply interleaved mixed-polynomial MBAs that exhaust the worklist budget, a few candidates that are correct only on Boolean inputs and are reported as verify-failed, and no general logic minimization.

The README reports 1,195 tests, and DATASETS.md reports 75,023 of 75,126 parsed expressions from 35 dataset files and seven sources simplified and spot-checked (99.86%). The OSES subsets are disabled for running out of memory or taking minutes per expression, so their figures come from an earlier run; DATASETS.md says the numbers are checked on every CI run, but the reviewed CI workflow excludes the dataset benchmark tests.

Apache-2.0 for CoBRA. The test/datasets files are redistributed from third-party research projects: THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES lists most as effectively GPL-3.0-only, Loki's as AGPL-3.0-only, and the OSES and ObfuscatorX sets with unspecified or unknown licenses.

resources.name: PiCCANTE
resources.description: Raspberry Pi Pico firmware and hardware designs for a low-cost CAN bus interface aimed at exploring and reverse engineering vehicle networks. It runs two CAN 2.0B channels on RP2040 boards or three on RP2350 boards through the PIO-based can2040 library and exposes them over USB as a GVRET device for SavvyCAN and as per-channel SLCAN devices for Linux SocketCAN via can-utils. A configuration shell, a partial ELM327 emulator for OBD-II PID requests with ISO-TP multi-frame replies, and Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and a web interface on Pico W boards complete the firmware, alongside perfboard and KiCad PCB designs with 3D-printable cases for an OBD-II dongle.
requirements: Only release at review: v0.0.1, published 2025-05-03 with UF2 and ELF firmware for Pico, Pico W, Pico 2 and Pico 2 W; a dev-latest pre-release is rebuilt from main and was built from the reviewed commit of 2026-01-26. The README marks the ELM327 emulator as partial, lacking CAN setup, protocol auto-detection and filters, and lists SD-card logging and software CAN filters as planned. CAN FD and CAN XL are not supported.

Hardware is any Raspberry Pi Pico or Pico 2 board with one to three 3.3 V CAN transceivers such as the SN65HVD; the Pico 2 W is recommended for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The README warns that the 120-ohm termination resistor on most transceiver breakout boards must be removed before joining an existing, terminated bus, and urges caution when connecting to vehicle systems. The OBD-II dongle can add a buck converter, an SD card slot and a voltage divider for battery voltage.

Source builds need the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK, CMake 3.13+ and the GCC ARM toolchain, with FreeRTOS-Kernel, a can2040 fork, littlefs, TinyUSB, pico-extras and FreeRTOS-FAT-CLI as submodules; PICO_BOARD defaults to pico2_w, and the web interface is a separate Svelte project in Web/. CI builds firmware for the four Pico boards on pushes to main and on pull requests, and no test suite is documented.

GPL-3.0-or-later per LICENSE.txt and the README notice; the README attributes the CAN 2.0B-only limit to can2040's licensing, and the bundled DHCP server code carries an MIT notice. No separate license is stated for the KiCad, STL and STEP hardware files.

resources.name: Gymnasticon: bridging proprietary exercise-bike data to standard cycling sensors
resources.description: Node.js bridge that reads power and cadence from exercise bikes whose own apps or services are gone or closed, and re-broadcasts them as standard Bluetooth LE Cycling Power and Cycling Speed and Cadence sensors and as an ANT+ bike power profile, so that Zwift, TrainerRoad, bike computers and watches can use the bike. The author's development notes describe working out the Flywheel Home Bike's stats packets on its Bluetooth UART service after the vendor shut its home service down; Peloton support reads the bike's data cable through a USB serial adapter, while the Schwinn IC4 and Keiser M clients parse the standard Fitness Machine Service and Keiser's documented broadcasts. Bike and app compatibility is project-reported.
requirements: Latest GitHub release at review: v1.4.0, published 2021-02-21 with a Raspberry Pi SD card image; npm's latest is 1.4.1 from 2021-03-24, and the reviewed main commit of 2021-04-21, which adds autodetection for all supported bikes, is still the newest on main. The README lists the Flywheel, Peloton (with an additional cable), Schwinn IC4/IC8 aka Bowflex C6 and Keiser M3i, M3i-TBT and M3iX bikes as tested and the LifeFitness IC5 as probably working; a simulated bot bike serves testing.

Needs the user's own supported bike; no vendor app, firmware or account is used. A Raspberry Pi Zero W is recommended, and the tested hosts are Raspbian Buster on Pi Zero W, 3B+ and 4, macOS 10.14+ and Debian Buster on x86-64. BLE bikes need a Bluetooth 4.1+ adapter with multi-role support, or two adapters; ANT+ output needs an ANT+ USB stick, and Peloton bikes need the extra serial cable linked from the README.

The SD card image is the project's own Raspbian Buster build made with pi-gen scripts in deploy/, with the default pi/raspberry account and SSH disabled; on first boot it switches the root filesystem to an overlay with a read-only boot partition and reads gymnasticon.json from the boot partition. Manual installs use Node.js 12.16.1+ from npm, with libudev-dev on Linux and cap_net_raw or a systemd unit for Bluetooth access, and depend on the abandonware noble and bleno libraries, gd-ant-plus and serialport.

CI builds the package and runs tape unit tests on Node.js 12 and 14; they cover the Flywheel, IC4, Keiser and Peloton parsers on sample packets, the simulated bike and utilities, not live bikes or training apps. power-scale and power-offset options let riders correct bikes that report inaccurate power.
MIT. Bike and app names belong to their owners.

resources.name: IW4L: a Rust runtime that plays Modern Warfare 2 from the user’s installed game
resources.description: Implements a standalone runtime for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 (2009) in Rust on Bevy and wgpu, loading maps, models, textures and weapons from the user’s installed game through native FastFile readers and translating its Direct3D 9 shaders to WGSL. Bots, demo recording and replay, and multiplayer over custom UDP with a QUIC master are implemented, while README warns that gameplay remains incomplete, with missing behavior, bugs and desyncs. README states that the whole project is written by an LLM; NOTICE names the community projects consulted and says the original binaries were read with Ghidra.
requirements: Needs the user’s own MW2 Multiplayer installation, which BUILD.md describes as the Windows depot of a Steam copy; Black Ops and MW3 data are optional. The repository and release archives contain no game data, and CONTRIBUTING.md forbids attaching, committing or linking original game files.

Builds with stable Rust through rustup and GNU Make. Linux needs a C/C++ toolchain and X11, Wayland, ALSA, udev and xkbcommon development packages; macOS needs only the Xcode command-line tools. The Windows release is a password-protected iw4l-windows.zip; given a server operator’s .iw4l-server descriptor, iw4l.exe installs SHA-256-verified executable updates from that operator.
Releases are tagged demo builds, v0.1.0-demo.23 at review. APIs, caches and the wire protocol change between commits, so multiplayer peers must run the same build.

No CI workflow or cargo test suite: make publish-check rejects test modules, and the only permanent checks are two owner-approved end-to-end scenarios driving real clients on MW2 maps with the user’s game data. Fidelity to the original game is not measured.
Apache-2.0 source with two bundled OFL fonts; game assets and trademarks remain their owners’.

NOTICE says no third-party source is vendored and names references read during development, including OpenAssetTools, IW4x, KisakCOD and Plutonium’s decompiled Black Ops II scripts. A provenance note records replacing a movement module after reported similarities to GPL code.

resources.name: Skate 3 Rust Engine: a Bevy rewrite built on Skate 3 reverse-engineering research
resources.description: Reimplements Skate 3’s skating, tricks, grinds and offboard movement in a new Rust and Bevy engine that runs on assets converted from the user’s own Xbox 360 copy, adding difficulty settings and a .skate custom-map format. Physics notes cite functions and constants read from the original executable in IDA, and audio research reads traces from a research-hooks branch of a separate Skate 3 static recompilation. README says gameplay parity is still a work in progress, credits dumbad’s years of format research and states that AI coding tools were used to write the rewrite.
requirements: Play needs the user’s Skate 3 Xbox 360 ISO, or an extracted default.xex with its data folder; setup converts the skater, animations, disc maps and HUD assets into a local data folder, and ISO extraction needs internet access. Skate 3 assets are not included; the bundled format-demo map is described as original procedural content.

Runs on Windows: the release ZIP starts skate3rust.exe and needs an SDL3-compatible gamepad. Source builds need Rust with the MSVC toolchain and LLVM, using BUILD.bat and PLAY.bat; the portable package script needs Python 3.13.

tools/recomp-trace reads traces from the research-hooks branch of Hailey-Ross/skate3recomp, which users must build from their own copy of the game; its README warns that the recompilation’s timing and threading differ from the console game.

The Windows release workflow runs Python tests for the updater, setup and asset pipeline, but not the Rust crates’ own tests. tools/regression-checks compares maps, spawns and customiser output with a user-recorded baseline. Parity results are project-reported.

Original code is GPL-3.0-only, copyright dumbad and contributors; the vendored, patched Bevy crates and tools under tools/vendor/ keep their own licenses, and no rights are granted to Electronic Arts’ code, data, assets or trademarks or to third-party maps and mods. Unofficial and unaffiliated with EA.
tools/claude-skills holds Claude Code skills for developing the engine.

resources.name: Rikugan
resources.description: IDA Pro and Binary Ninja plugin that runs its own agent loop inside the disassembler: a model the user chooses streams its answers and calls more than 60 in-process tools for navigation, decompilation, disassembly, cross-references, strings, types, annotations, scripting and host IL or microcode edits. An orchestrator can map a binary and spawn parallel subagents, findings persist in a RIKUGAN.md file beside the database, and experimental commands apply plain-language patches or, on Binary Ninja, remove control-flow flattening and other obfuscation. README says it was vibecoded with Claude Code.
requirements: README requires IDA Pro 9.0+ with the Hex-Rays decompiler or Binary Ninja in UI mode, and Python 3.10+, while pyproject.toml asks for 3.11+; ida-plugin.json lists IDA 9.0 to 9.2 on Windows, Linux and macOS. Windows also needs the latest Visual C++ 2015–2022 x64 redistributable, and the install scripts are piped from raw GitHub.

Needs at least one model provider: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, MiniMax, Codex, local Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Tool results from the open database go to the chosen provider; profiles limit which data the model may read and which tools it may use.

Version 1.4.0 (released 2026-09-25) at review. README says the agent asks permission before running scripts and never executes the target binary; natural-language patching (/modify) and the Binary Ninja /deobfuscation skill are marked experimental.

CI runs Ruff format and lint checks, mypy on the core and provider modules, pytest with an IDA mock and a desloppify score-regression gate. The repository publishes no benchmark; a Synacktiv article of 2026-10-13 compared it with another Binary Ninja agent on two CREBench tasks and attributed most of the gap to a prompt difference.
MIT per LICENSE and both plugin manifests; IDA Pro, Hex-Rays, Binary Ninja and model services keep their own licences and terms.
README calls the project a work in progress whose first version was built in a single night, and the repository carries an AGENTS.md developer guide.

resources.name: ollvm-unflattener
resources.description: Python command-line deobfuscator for the control-flow flattening applied by Obfuscator-LLVM (OLLVM). Given a flattened function's address, it uses Miasm's symbolic execution to track the dispatcher's state variable, records which blocks each state value selects and which state follows it, and writes a copy of the binary in which the function is reassembled with Keystone in its recovered order; an optional mode also follows the function's calls. The README covers 32- and 64-bit x86 Windows and Linux binaries and contrasts this approach with MODeflattener's static one.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.0, published 2025-04-16 without attached binaries; its notes call it most likely the final release, and the reviewed master commit is that tag and the repository's last push. The tool runs from a clone as python unflattener -i <input> -o <output> -t <hex address>, with -a to follow calls; there are no tests or CI.

The README requires Python 3.10+ and Git; requirements.txt lists miasm, graphviz and keystone-engine without version pins. The code handles PE and ELF files for x86_32 and x86_64 and raises an error for other formats or architectures.

The analyst supplies the obfuscated binary and the target function's address. Functions scoring below 0.9 on a dominator-based flattening heuristic are left unchanged, the dispatcher and state variable are located by structural assumptions about OLLVM's layout, and -a only follows calls into the .text section. Output is a patched copy in which the original function bytes are overwritten with int3 padding and the reassembled function is written at its start.

The samples folder bundles small obfuscated test programs for 32- and 64-bit Linux and Windows (CFF.bin, CFF_full.bin, CFF_full_linux64.bin, CFF_win.exe, CFF_win_full.exe, CFF_win64.exe and CFF_win64_full.exe), their deob_* outputs and C/C++ sources for most of them; a comment in CFF_full.c says Claude generated that test program. The README's only reported result is a before/after control-flow graph of target_function in CFF_full.bin, with no check that deobfuscated binaries behave like the originals.
Apache-2.0; the dependencies keep their own licenses, including GPL-2.0-only for Miasm and GPL-2.0 with a FOSS exception for Keystone.

resources.name: javascript-deobfuscator (LostMyCode)
resources.description: Browser-based Vue app that restores the strings Obfuscator.io hides behind string-array lookups in JavaScript. The user pastes the obfuscated script and names its string array or decoder function, such as _0x439c; the tool classifies the calls as plain array indexing, a one-argument decoder or a two-argument RC4-style decoder, runs the script's own decoder to replace each call with its string literal, rewrites bracketed property access as dot notation and beautifies the result. The author hosts a demo at deo.sigr.io.
requirements: Supply the obfuscated script and identify the target function name yourself; a built-in tip shows call shapes such as _0x439c[103], _0x439c('0x4') and _0x439c('0x2','f]Xg'). The README covers only the Vue CLI 4 project commands (npm install, serve, build and lint), and a GitHub Actions workflow builds the site with Node.js 16 and deploys it to GitHub Pages.
Unversioned: package.json reports 0.1.0 and marks the package private, there are no GitHub releases or npm package, and the reviewed master commit of 2024-05-31 is the latest push.

Only these string-array patterns are handled, with a fourth pattern marked experimental, and unrecognized input returns an error. The code has no passes for control-flow flattening, proxy functions, dead code or Obfuscator.io's other transformations, so those remain in the output. Decoding evaluates the pasted script with eval inside a browser web worker, so the input's own code runs; it is not a static AST transformation. The page template also loads js-beautify from cdnjs and a Google Analytics tag.
The repository has no tests, and the README's only result is an example screenshot.
The repository has no license file and GitHub detects no license, so it grants no stated reuse terms.

resources.name: bun-demincer
resources.description: Node.js pipeline that recovers readable JavaScript from Bun-compiled standalone executables. It extracts the embedded module graph and assets, splits the bundle into one file per module, flags npm vendor code with a fingerprint database, and deobfuscates with wakaru, format-preserving renames recovered from export mappings and optional Gemini-suggested names. Dependency-graph clustering, manual or LLM-assisted cluster labels and cross-version artifact transfer then organize and update the output.
requirements: The reviewed master commit of 2026-03-06 is the repository’s ninth, three days after its initial release commit of 2026-03-03; there are no tags or releases. It needs Node.js 18+ and the npm dependencies in package.json, including node-canvas for cluster PNGs; Bun is needed only to run extracted code. The README says Bun stores the code in a __BUN Mach-O section, appended ELF data or a .bun PE section; extract.mjs parses the Mach-O section header and otherwise searches for Bun's trailer.

Input is a Bun-compiled executable; the repository contains no target binaries or recovered code, and .gitignore excludes pipeline output. data/vendor-fingerprints-1000.json (26 MB) holds property-name and string-literal fingerprints for 23,746 files from 1,668 npm packages and can be rebuilt from a local node_modules. The README says steps 1–4 are automated, while cluster labels need manual input or an LLM.

ai-rename.mjs and ai-rename-scoped.mjs send module source to Google's Gemini API with a GEMINI_API_KEY (default model gemini-3-flash-preview); their names are model suggestions. The README's round-trip reassembly calls a build.mjs it marks as part of the user's project, which this repository does not contain.
The reviewed tree has no tests or CI. The README states MIT, but there is no license file and package.json has no license field. Four of the nine commits carry a Claude Opus 4.6 co-author trailer.

resources.name: GolangAnalyzerExtension
resources.description: Ghidra extension whose Golang Analyzer reads the runtime header and module data in Go binaries built with go1.6 through go1.27 to identify the Go version, rename functions, correct their arguments, comment source files and line numbers, add Go types to the Data Type Manager and label Go strings. A plugin window lists the recovered functions, types, source files and strings with links to Go source, and WebAssembly builds are handled when a separate Wasm loader such as ghidra-wasm-plugin is installed. A bundled script also renames functions that decode gobfuscate-style obfuscated strings and comments the decoded text.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.4.0, published 2026-07-21 from the reviewed master commit, with notes stating support for go1.6 through go1.27. It provides prebuilt zips for Ghidra 12.0 through 12.0.4 and for 12.1, 12.1.2, 12.1.3 and 12.1.4, the last two built on 2026-10-14; install the zip matching the Ghidra release through File > Install Extensions and restart Ghidra. Source builds use Gradle with GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR set to a Ghidra installation.

Analysis runs on Go executables the user supplies, and the analyzer is enabled by default. Source has function handlers for x86, ARM, PowerPC and RISC-V; WebAssembly needs a separate Wasm loader. Function disassembly is off by default, and optional PcHeader-address and Go-version settings override detection. Function-name guessing by pattern matching and BSim exists in source, but its option is not registered and stays off.

The repository commits generated name-guessing data: a 4.3 MB list of calling-function names under test resources and a 53 KB H2 BSim database under scripts, with scripts that produce them by compiling a small sample Go program with each listed Go toolchain and running Ghidra headless. The copy under src/main/resources is empty at this commit, and no target binaries are committed. JUnit tests cover version, header, string and name-data parsing; there is no CI workflow.

The MIT license sits in GolangAnalyzerExtension/LICENSE (2021, mooncat-greenpy); it is not at the repository root, so GitHub detects no license. Output annotates the Ghidra program and needs analyst checking; it does not produce Go source.

resources.name: IDA iOS Helper
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin that cleans up Hex-Rays pseudocode and adds navigation helpers for iOS user-mode binaries and the kernelcache, enabling its components according to the loaded file. For Objective-C and Swift code it hides reference-counting calls, selectors and static class arguments, collapses os_log sequences, turns property helpers into plain assignments or field reads, lists cross-references to a method's selector, and adds Swift type declarations and readable stack strings. For kernelcaches it types the results of safeMetaCast and typed operator new, names and types kalloc_type_view globals, fixes this arguments and lists the possible implementations of a virtual call, while shared helpers remove __break calls, rewrite ranged conditions, collapse block initializers and mark outlined functions.
requirements: Requires IDA Pro 9.0+, and most listed features rewrite Hex-Rays pseudocode, so they assume IDA's decompiler is available. Installation uses IDA's own pip to install the ida-ios-helper package, which needs Python 3.10+ and pins the author's idahelper library at 1.0.18, and then copies ida-plugin.json and ida_plugin_stub.py into IDA's plugins folder.

Latest release at review: 1.0.23, published 2026-06-25 with the wheel and source archive that are also on PyPI. The reviewed master commit is six commits ahead, adding an Objective-C fast-enumeration component and Swift type fixes that are not yet released, and its ida-plugin.json still declares version 1.0.19 and pins ida-ios-helper==1.0.19.

The iOS binaries or kernelcaches come from the analyst. Virtual-call navigation needs vtable symbols in the database, and typing typed operator new results first needs the Locate all kalloc_type_view action. A Swift importer added in June 2026 and not described in the README runs the separate ipsw tool's swift-dump command on the input file to name and type Swift class methods.

CI only checks Python 3.10 compatibility with vermin and runs ruff lint and format checks; there are no automated tests. The repository also holds headless idat probing scripts and a Claude Code skill used while developing the plugin. GPL-3.0.

resources.name: MAMBO
resources.description: Dynamic binary modification framework from the University of Manchester that runs unmodified Linux user-space programs on 32-bit Arm (A32/T32), AArch64 and RV64GC RISC-V, translating their code into a code cache as it executes. An event-driven C plugin API registers callbacks on code-scanning and execution events and emits instrumentation; sample plugins count instruction mixes, branches and blocks, trace memory accesses and system calls, find hotspots, simulate caches, check memory errors and detect data races.
requirements: The reviewed master commit of 2025-01-21 updates the HiPEAC 2025 tutorial. There are no versioned releases; GitHub releases 1 and 2 only host talk slides. The README says application compatibility is improved as needed, lists SPEC CPU2006, PARSEC 3.0, GCC, LibreOffice and GIMP among programs that work on Arm, and notes that most development happens in a private tree.

Builds and runs on an Armv7, Armv8 or RV64GC Linux system, physical or virtual, with GCC, libelf development files and Ruby 1.9.1+; the build generates instruction encoders and decoders from the bundled PIE specifications and links dbm statically. The authors use armhf/arm64 Debian, Ubuntu and Arch Linux ARM and Ubuntu 22.04 on RISC-V; for other hosts, a Dockerfile downloads Ubuntu 24.04 preinstalled server images for Arm64 and RISC-V and runs them under QEMU. Plugins are compiled in through the makefile's PLUGINS list.

Known issues listed in the README: SA_SIGINFO handlers receive incorrect siginfo_t data, synchronous-signal handlers cannot sigreturn, code-cache invalidation after munmap or cache flushes only happens in the calling thread, and RISC-V signal handling is incomplete. MAMBO is not designed to protect itself from the program it translates, so the README says it cannot serve as a secure sandbox without hardening.

CI builds MAMBO in Ubuntu 20.04 chroots under QEMU user emulation for arm64, armhf and riscv64 and only runs /bin/ls under it; the instruction, signal and self-modifying-code programs in test/ are not run by CI. The authors ask users to cite their 2016 ACM TACO paper and list later ICPE 2018, CC 2020, VEE 2020 and ISPASS 2023 papers.
Apache-2.0, with the same license in pie/. Programs to instrument are supplied by the user.

resources.name: garmin-ble: a Python client for Garmin's GFDI watch protocol
resources.description: Python library that talks to Garmin watches over their proprietary GFDI V2 Bluetooth LE protocol, with no Garmin Connect, phone or cloud service. It implements the handshake, multi-link routing, COBS framing, CRC16 checks and protobuf service messages, streams typed readings such as heart rate, HRV, SpO2, stress, Body Battery and accelerometer data, and adds a simulator and recorded-session replay for work without hardware. Its acknowledgements credit Gadgetbridge for the protocol logic and schemas, while a published journal shows how the author decoded the accelerometer payload, which Gadgetbridge only logged, from labelled recordings.
requirements: Reviewed at main commit b662032 (2026-09-27), four commits after v0.3.2 of 2026-08-01, which is also the latest PyPI release; those commits add examples and an announcement video. pyproject marks the package Alpha and the CHANGELOG warns that the pre-1.0 API may change. The README roadmap lists BLE transport, live telemetry, the Watch API, simulator and replay as done, protobuf settings and device state as in progress, and notifications, media control and FIT/GPX file transfers as planned.

Requires the user's own Garmin watch and a Bluetooth LE adapter on the computer; the README warns that the watch allows one BLE connection at a time, so it must be disconnected from the phone first. No Garmin Connect, firmware or SDK is used, and the repository's data files are the author's labelled accelerometer recordings. The README gives no list of tested watches; the bundled simulator profiles model a fenix 7 and a Venu 3, and the CHANGELOG notes that GFDI has no capability query, so a metric's support shows only when the watch accepts or declines its service.

Python 3.10+ with bleak and protobuf, installed from PyPI or from source; development extras add pytest, pytest-mock and pytest-asyncio. Compiled protobuf modules are committed next to their .proto sources, and most examples accept --simulate.

CI runs the pytest suite on Ubuntu with Python 3.10–3.13. Tests cover COBS, CRC16, GFDI, MLR and Smart framing, the bleak-backed transport with mocks, frame tracing, capture files and replay, and watch lifecycle, protobuf and telemetry behavior against the simulator. rev_eng.md documents how the 17-byte accelerometer packet was decoded from nine labelled recordings. Behavior on real watches remains author-reported.

AGPL-3.0-only, matching the Gadgetbridge-derived code the README acknowledges, although the README also calls the library clean-room. Garmin watches, apps and trademarks keep their own rights. One commit message calls the tilt game example a test of unsupervised vibe coding.

resources.name: VanBus
resources.description: Arduino library for ESP8266/ESP8285 and ESP32 boards that receives and transmits packets on the VAN (Vehicle Area Network) comfort bus that PSA fitted to Peugeot and Citroën models until about 2009. It decodes the signal from a GPIO pin, wired through a CAN transceiver or a receive-only resistor divider, in software into packets with identifier, command flags, data and a 15-bit CRC that it can check or try to repair by flipping single bits, and reports queue and error statistics. Example sketches dump raw packets, send a packet, and parse comfort-bus traffic into readable fields on the serial port or a live web page.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.5.1, published 2026-05-29, the version library.properties and VanBusVersion.h declare; the single later master commit (2026-08-22) only adds a pin-swap note to two example sketches. The README says the library supports only the 125 kbit/s VAN rate, with other rates such as 62.5 kbit/s still to be added.

Builds in the Arduino IDE (the author uses 1.8.19) with the ESP8266 board package (tested 2.6.3–3.1.2, CPU at 160 MHz) or the ESP32 package (tested 1.0.6, 2.0.17 and 3.3.5, CPU at 240 MHz), installing the library through the Arduino Library Manager. The LiveWebPage example also needs the arduinoWebSockets library and has the browser load jQuery from Google's CDN; dumping packets into a character buffer needs PrintEx.

Live use needs a PSA vehicle with a VAN comfort bus: the README locates it on pins 2 and 3 of ISO block A at the head unit and documents wiring through an MCP2551 transceiver with a 5 V–3.3 V level converter, an SN65HVD230 transceiver, or a receive-only resistor divider that it says works well only with ESP8266 boards. It warns that the transceiver boards' CAN terminator resistors may make other equipment on the bus malfunction, and transmitting puts packets on the car's bus. The only bundled traffic is the author's serial-monitor log, examples/PacketParser/example_log.txt.

CI compiles the example sketches for an ESP8266 D1 mini and for ESP32 board packages 1.0.6, 2.0.17 and the latest, and runs Arduino Lint in strict mode; it does not exercise a bus. PacketParser calls its packet interpretation highly experimental, gathered from various sources and from experiments on the author's own 2003 Peugeot 406, and the README points to external lists of known IDEN values.
MIT.

resources.name: Class Informer
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin that scans Microsoft Visual C++ binaries for virtual function tables (vftables) through their C++ run-time type information (RTTI), names, labels and comments the vftables it finds, defines the RTTI data structures and identifies single, multiple and virtual inheritance in each class hierarchy. It also processes static initializer and terminator tables, and opens a list window of the vftables with their method counts and class hierarchies, where each line jumps to its vftable. Its author notes that IDA 9's built-in RTTI plugin now finds nearly all of this data, so the current version only sets types that IDA missed and serves mainly as a gathering and browsing view.
requirements: Latest release at review: v6.0.3, published 2026-08-04, which tags the reviewed master commit and attaches a zip holding a single Windows plugin DLL; its notes describe it as a fix for IDA 9.4, and a September 2025 commit had updated the plugin for IDA 9.2 and Qt 6. The plugin loads only for x86/x64 (metapc) databases.

The README's IDA 9.4 note says the plugin flags had to change before IDA would recognize the plugin, which broke loading it through plugins.cfg, so the Alt-2 hotkey is now built in and the plugin also runs from Edit > Plugins. The installation steps still name an older Class_Informer.plw file, and the plugins.cfg arguments the README gives for turning off the demoscene-style intro and its music predate that note.

Source builds need Windows and Visual Studio 2022 (v143 toolset) with Qt 6 for MSVC 2022 x64 and the Qt Visual Studio tools, the IDA SDK inside the IDA directory, and the author's separate IDA_Support repository and libxmp, neither of which is in this repository. There is no CI and there are no tests. The analyst supplies the IDA database; the README says the plugin is tailored to MSVC-compiled binaries and results with other compilers may be unpredictable.
The README states the MIT License, but the repository has no separate license file; according to the README, the tracker module in res is used with the permission of its composer, Drax.

resources.name: Bravo: a reverse-engineered Minecraft server
resources.description: Reimplements the server side of Minecraft’s Alpha- and Beta-era multiplayer in Python on Twisted; its documentation calls it a reverse-engineered implementation written from scratch, credits network traffic dumps and says general Minecraft data went to a community wiki. The final 2.0 release speaks the 1.4.x client protocol for login, chunk transfer, entities, server-side inventories, lighting, physics and Anvil saves, while deliberately changing behaviour such as chunk loading and item stacking. A pluggable architecture adds terrain generation, seasons and commands, and small scripts inspect packets, NBT and region files.
requirements: Unmaintained: the GitHub description marks the project UNMAINTAINED, and the reviewed master commit dates from 2014-09-09, 90 commits after the 2.0 tag (2013-01-10, also the latest PyPI release). The 2.0 changelog adds 1.4.x protocol support without server-side encryption, disables broken online authentication and replaces the Alpha and Beta save formats with Anvil; source pins protocol version 78. The introduction says creative games are probably safe but some Survival-Multiplayer elements are missing, and older pages such as the feature list predate these 2.0 changes.

The server needs no original game files; clients connect with the matching Minecraft client the player owns, which the FAQ says Bravo will not replace. The repository commits no game assets or Mojang code: block, item and recipe definitions are written as Python tables, and the documentation says Bravo inherits no code from other Minecraft projects.

Python 2.6 or 2.7 (CPython or PyPy); requirements.txt pins construct 2.0.6 and Pillow 2.4.0 and needs Twisted 11.0+, including Twisted Conch, with Twisted Words or Web for the IRC and web plugins. It runs as the twistd bravo plugin, configured from bravo.ini.example with a world path, creative or survival mode and the anvil serializer; the packet-parser script still imports a pre-2.0 module path.

Travis CI ran trial over the in-tree tests for protocol packets, chunks, inventories, plugins and serializers on Python 2.6, 2.7 and PyPy. MIT/X11 license, with bravo/nbt.py taken from Thomas Woolford’s MIT NBT library; Minecraft and its client keep Mojang’s rights.

resources.name: dex-oracle
resources.description: Pattern-based Dalvik deobfuscator that takes an APK, a DEX file or a Smali directory, disassembles it with baksmali and runs plugins that look for obfuscation patterns in the Smali code. To learn what a matched call returns, such as a decrypted string, it merges a small driver into the app's DEX, pushes it to a connected Android device or emulator and invokes the static method there through reflection; the result replaces the call as a constant before the APK or DEX is reassembled. Plugins cover simple string encryption, indexed string and class lookups, certain DexGuard patterns and some reflection, and the author describes it as the inspiration for Simplify.
requirements: Development is inactive: the latest RubyGems and GitHub release is 1.0.5 of 2016-07-26, while the reviewed master commit of 2018-12-13 already declares an unpublished 1.0.6. It is installed as a Ruby gem or from source with Bundler; the repository pins Ruby 2.5.3 and needs Java, adb, and smali and baksmali on the PATH, with the README's setup snippet using smali 2.2.5.

Input is the user's own APK, DEX or Smali directory, and a running emulator or attached device with Android 5.0 or later is required because matched methods really execute on it. The README prefers an emulator and warns that the executed code may be hostile; its troubleshooting section instead suggests Android 4.4.2 (API level 19, ARM) if the driver crashes. Only static methods can be executed, and plugins can be disabled when a pattern matches code that is not obfuscation.

The res directory ships the prebuilt driver.dex and a copy of the Android SDK's dx.jar, which the tool uses for DEX merging; rebuilding the driver needs Gradle and the SDK's dx tool. The README lists three plugins, while the plugins directory holds six, adding indexed string and class lookups and a bitwise string-decryption pattern.
RSpec tests with tiny hello-world APK and DEX fixtures and Smali pattern samples ran through a Travis CI configuration on Ruby 2.5.3; the repository has no GitHub Actions workflow.
MIT (LICENSE.txt and the gemspec); dx.jar and the smali tools keep their own terms.

resources.name: Ghidra Snippets
resources.description: A single-page collection of 30 commented Python examples for scripting Ghidra, grouped by task: projects, programs, functions and cross-references, basic blocks, instructions, stack variables, decompiler output, comments, P-code emulation and dumps, call graphs and program slices. It starts from the Flat Program, Flat Decompiler and Flat Debugger APIs, then shows where a task needs Ghidra's fuller API; most snippets include an example of their output.
requirements: Everything is in one README, with no script files or releases. The last change, on 2023-07-19, fixed a typo; the one before, on 2022-11-09, added Flat API notes for Ghidra 10.2. Version remarks range from Ghidra 9.1 and 9.2.2 to 10.2, so names and behavior in current Ghidra releases may differ; the README points to Ghidra's built-in API help and to the ghidra.re online docs, which it says may not be up to date.

The examples run in Ghidra's Python scripting environment, which the README calls the Jython console, against a program the user has loaded. Plotting a function AST also needs GraphViz's dot plus networkx and pydot importable from Jython, and the README notes that Python modules with native code do not work there. Compatibility with PyGhidra or Python 3 is not stated.
Released under CC0 1.0. The README calls the snippets a verbose mashup with more than one way to do each task and invites pull requests.

resources.name: minusone
resources.description: Airbus CERT's Rust deobfuscation engine for scripts: it parses PowerShell or JavaScript with tree-sitter, applies rules that infer the values of syntax-tree nodes and prints a simplified script. The PowerShell rules fold arithmetic, string operations, casts, -join, -replace and format operators, Base64 and UTF decoding, predictable variables and loops, and also resolve Gzip or Deflate streams and AES decryption when the data and key are in the script; the newer JavaScript rules cover literals, operators, string and array built-ins, atob and btoa, Buffer calls, predictable function calls and JSFuck constructs. The CLI can list, select or skip rules and export every rewrite step as HTML or JSON, and Python and WebAssembly bindings embed the engine, including in an online version linked from the README.
requirements: No prebuilt CLI binaries: the latest GitHub release, v0.4.2 from 2025-10-01, has no attached files, and the published packages are minusone 0.4.1 on crates.io, pyminusone 0.4.1 on PyPI with Linux x86_64 and Windows wheels, and minusonejs 0.5.0 on npm. The reviewed main commit is 538 commits past v0.4.2 and declares the core library 0.5.0 and minusone-cli 0.6.1.

Build with Cargo; the crates use Rust edition 2024, Cargo.lock is not committed, and the PowerShell grammar comes from an unpinned Git dependency on a tree-sitter-powershell fork. The CLI needs --lang powershell or --lang javascript. The project's devenv/Nix environment uses nightly Rust, the Python bindings build with maturin, and the WebAssembly module targets wasm32-wasip2 and is transpiled to JavaScript with jco.

The README still lists only PowerShell as supported, names basic JavaScript support as a roadmap item and links rule files at older src/ paths; the JavaScript backend dates from March 2026, after the crates.io and PyPI packages and the v0.4.2 release. Rules rewrite the script statically from values they can infer, and the analyst supplies the scripts; the samples folder holds only small JSFuck test files next to their plain sources.

CI runs devenv test, which runs cargo test and the Python binding test script; the core has unit tests for both languages. MIT license; Cargo metadata names Airbus CERT as author, and the LICENSE copyright line names Sylvain Peyrefitte.

resources.name: Kam1n0
resources.description: Server platform from McGill University's Data Mining and Security Lab that indexes collections of disassembled binaries into shared repositories and searches them for cloned assembly functions. Its applications cover subgraph clone search within one instruction-set family (Asm-Clone), cross-architecture semantic search over VEX IR using symbolic and concrete execution (Sym1n0), Asm2Vec representation learning aimed at compiler optimization and obfuscation, and executable classification built on Asm2Vec. An IDA Pro plug-in sends functions to the server and shows flow-graph, text-diff and clone-group views; the README's accuracy and query-time figures come from the authors' own papers.
requirements: Latest stable release at review: 2.2.0, published 2020-11-15, with Windows installers and Linux tarballs for the server and the IDA Pro plug-in; a nightly-action pre-release from 2023-02-27 attaches Windows builds only. The reviewed master2.x commit of the same date is the default branch's latest, and README says repositories and configuration files from versions before 2.0.0 are no longer supported.

The server needs a 64-bit Java 11 runtime (README asks for Oracle's) and, to disassemble uploaded binaries, an IDA Pro installation with IDAPython set in kam1n0.properties; the shipped configuration requests a 12 GB maximum JVM heap and serves the web interface on port 8571. The plug-in needs IDA Pro newer than 6.7 with IDAPython and the CEF Python wheels its installer bundles. Source also contains an undocumented Ghidra disassembly backend.

Users supply the binaries to index and query. The repository commits test and example binaries built from open-source code: zlib and libpng builds for several architectures and optimization levels, a Chromium DLL, and IDA databases for PuTTY and zlib. Windows installer sources commit the Microsoft .NET Framework 4.0 and Visual C++ x64 redistributable installers and CEF Python wheels, and the server resources commit JavaFX SDK 11.0.2 DLLs, a prebuilt LibVEX library (VEXIRBB.dll) and a local Maven repository holding a z3 jar.

Maven builds the Java 11 modules against those pre-compiled LibVEX and z3 binaries; README says LibVEX comes from angr's fork, and z3 is a submodule. The Maven tests drive Chrome through chromedriver and, per the README, take about three hours; CI only builds the Windows distribution and WiX installers. Accuracy and timing figures are taken from the README and the authors' KDD 2016 and IEEE S&P 2019 papers.

Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.txt), copyright McGill University and the researchers. Bundled runtimes, redistributable installers, wheels and test binaries keep their own licenses, and IDA Pro is separately licensed commercial software.

resources.name: bn
resources.description: Agent-oriented command-line interface for the Binary Ninja database already open in the GUI, reached through a companion plugin that listens on a local Unix-domain socket. Agents read decompilation, IL, disassembly, cross-references, callsites, types and data, export multi-function bundles and run unrestricted Python inside Binary Ninja; renames and prototype, structure and type edits can be previewed, are verified after they apply and roll back on failure. Large text output spills to hashed artifact files, and a packaged Codex skill describes the workflow.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.15.0, published on GitHub and PyPI as bn-cli on 2026-09-04; the reviewed master commit is that tag and the repository's last push. It needs Python 3.12+ and installs as a uv tool; bn plugin install links the BN Agent Bridge plugin into Binary Ninja, and bn skill install links the skill into the skills folder of the Codex home directory. The CLI and the loaded plugin must share bridge protocol 2, so Binary Ninja is restarted or its plugins reloaded after upgrades.

Work happens against a database open in the Binary Ninja GUI; the README says the companion works with a personal license and needs no headless license. The bridge socket lives in the user's cache directory, and the README names no supported operating systems or Binary Ninja versions. With several views open, commands need an explicit --target selector instead of silently using the active tab.

The analyst supplies the binary and database; the repository holds no target binaries. bn py runs unrestricted Python with the user's privileges inside Binary Ninja, and its writes bypass the preview, verification and rollback of built-in mutations; the reviewed bridge code adds no authentication beyond access to the socket path. Whole-database text and constant searches stop after a default five-second analysis budget and report incomplete results.

CI runs pytest on Python 3.12 and 3.14 against a stub binaryninja module, checks release metadata and smoke-tests plugin and skill installation from the built wheel, so no real Binary Ninja instance is exercised. Mutations report verified, noop, unsupported or verification_failed, and the README notes that decompiled output can stay stale after type changes until types are read back or analysis is refreshed.
MIT, added to the repository in v0.14.1; Binary Ninja keeps its own license terms.

resources.name: Titan M tools (Quarkslab)
resources.description: Tools Quarkslab published from its research on Google's Titan M security chip in Pixel phones: a Ghidra loader for Titan M (Citadel) firmware files, nosclient for tracing and sending the chip's protobuf-based commands from Android with a black-box fuzzer built on libprotobuf-mutator, a parser for sigrok SPI captures, and scripts that convert firmware images to the rec files of the chip's SPI rescue feature. The repository also holds the Black Hat Europe 2021 white paper and slides, the ROOTS'21 paper and the Black Hat USA 2022 slides, which describe reverse engineering the firmware, sniffing its SPI communication with the application processor, and black-box and emulation-based fuzzing; the authors say the vulnerabilities they found were disclosed to Google.
requirements: A research release with no tags or packages: the last commit, on 2022-08-22, added the Black Hat USA 2022 slides two days after nosclient was updated for that talk. The emulation-based fuzzer those slides describe is not in the repository, and no Titan M firmware images, Boot ROM dumps or keys are committed.

Firmware files must come from the analyst's own Pixel device; the white paper notes that Titan M first shipped with the Pixel 3. Sending commands with nosclient needs root access on the device, as the white paper explains, and the SPI parser expects a sigrok CSV export of the analyst's own capture.

citadelimgloader builds with Gradle against a local Ghidra installation named by GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR; no supported Ghidra version is stated. nosclient builds with CMake for Linux, for Android arm64 with the NDK, or in the provided Debian 10 Docker image with NDK r21e, after the libnos (AOSP), protobuf, libprotobuf-mutator and sqlite submodules are initialized.

The ROOTS'21 paper reports that the black-box fuzzer rediscovered several known vulnerabilities within seconds and found a new one in the then-latest firmware; these are the authors' results on their own devices. The README says the toolkit also contains an exploit for a known vulnerability.

LICENSE is Apache-2.0. The fuzzer bundles a generated libradamsa.c without its own license notice, the client includes protobuf sources generated from the nugget/app message definitions and small KeyMint enum headers, and the presentation PDFs state no license.

resources.name: iblessing
resources.description: Toolkit for analyzing iOS apps and arm64 Mach-O binaries, built on Capstone, Unicorn and Keystone. Its scanners extract app-bundle metadata such as URL schemes and transport-security settings, locate Objective-C class references and NSPredicate uses, detect symbol wrappers, and partially emulate arm64 code with Unicorn to recover objc_msgSend cross-references, including those passed through blocks. Generators turn the reports into IDA Pro scripts that add cross-references and rename wrappers, or into a local query server, and a shared core library with a plug-in interface supports custom tools.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.0.4-beta, published 2021-11-26 and tagged at the reviewed master commit; every release is marked as a pre-release. Each recent release attaches macOS and Linux command-line and all-in-one binaries, framework archives with the shared core library and headers, and a JSON table of Foundation and UIKit method signatures. The README's feature list leaves Swift class parsing, following branches and calls, and Android scanners unfinished.

Users supply an iOS .app bundle for app-info or an arm64 Mach-O binary for the other scanners; README examples analyze commercial third-party apps after restoring symbols with a separate tool, but no app binaries are committed. The class and objc_msgSend cross-reference scanners accept arm64 binaries only, and app-info is unavailable on Linux because it still depends on Cocoa. The README warns that binary scanners reserve 12 GB of virtual memory per Mach-O file, so physical memory or swap must cover that.

Builds on macOS or Linux with CMake 3.5+ and a C++17 compiler after a recursive clone; compile-cmake.sh first builds the pinned Capstone, Unicorn (arm, aarch64 and x86) and Keystone submodules as static libraries. An Xcode project is also included. IDA Pro is needed only to apply the generated scripts.

GitHub Actions builds on Ubuntu and macOS and, on macOS only, scans the bundled sample-app benchmark and runs the built-in objc_msgSend cross-reference test; Travis CI builds and publishes tagged releases. The README notes that objc-msg-xref follows no calls to save time, so its results are partly missing.

GPL-3.0 (LICENSE). The project calls itself an iOS security exploiting toolkit. Analyzed apps and Apple frameworks keep their own terms, and the Capstone, Unicorn and Keystone submodules carry their own licenses.

resources.name: NTRGhidra
resources.description: Ghidra loader and plugin for Nintendo DS programs. It checks the .nds header, maps either the ARM9 or the ARM7 binary at its RAM address together with the console's memory regions and I/O register labels, decompresses SDK-compressed ARM9 code and overlays, and fills the overlays the user selects at import, while an optional overlay-manager plugin swaps overlays in and out afterwards. The repository also keeps a small Ghidra Function ID database of NitroSDK 3.0 routines for function identification.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.5.1, published 2026-03-24 as NTRGhidra-build.zip for Ghidra 12.0.4, and its tag is the reviewed master commit; earlier releases were built for individual Ghidra 10.x and 11.x versions, and the README names 12.0.4 as the latest supported Ghidra version. The zip installs from the Ghidra project window's File → Install Extensions, and the overlay manager is enabled separately under CodeBrowser's File → Configure → Miscellaneous. The README says the project is looking for maintainers and contributors.

Source builds need a Ghidra installation: build.gradle applies Ghidra's buildExtension.gradle from GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR, the README describes an Eclipse build with the GhidraDev extension, and a GitHub Actions workflow builds the zip with Gradle on every push and attaches it to new releases. The repository has no tests; src/test holds only a placeholder README.

Input is a .nds file the user supplies; the repository contains no ROMs or BIOS files. On import the loader rejects files whose header CRC does not match, asks whether the file is a commercial Nintendo SDK title or homebrew, and asks whether to load the ARM9 or the ARM7 code; commercial titles must carry the expected Nintendo logo CRC and have their ARM9 binary decompressed. The overlay manager re-reads overlays only from the original file at its import path, or from a substitute whose MD5 and SHA-256 match it.

The fidb folder holds nitrosdk3.0.fidb, a 2 KB Function ID database that its README describes as hashes of NitroSDK 3.0.0 functions from commercial games, covering crt0 and file-system routines in ARM code but not Thumb; the loader does not apply it automatically. The loader names its format Nintendo DS (NTR) and DSi (TWL), and the source carries DSi register and memory-region lists, but import maps only the DS ARM9 and ARM7 lists, and CRT0 autoload handling is marked as a TODO.
Apache-2.0. The README credits GBATEK for DS technical information and Gericom's Every File Explorer for the original header and ARM9 decompression code.

resources.name: bosectl: reconstructing Bose’s BMAP headphone protocol
resources.description: Controls Bose headphones from Linux and macOS without the Bose app, account or cloud, through Python, Rust and C++ libraries and command-line tools that implement Bose’s BMAP protocol over Bluetooth RFCOMM. The author documents BMAP’s function blocks, operators, payload layouts and error codes in NOTES.md, reportedly worked out by probing RFCOMM channels, capturing Bluetooth traffic while changing settings in the Bose app and testing each operator, and the libraries cover noise cancellation, EQ, spatial audio, button remapping, profiles and device settings. Support is reported per model by the author and contributors.
requirements: The reviewed commit is the v0.5.0 release of 2026-09-28, which ships Linux x86_64 bmapctl binaries built from the Rust and C++ code with SHA256SUMS; the Rust crate is also on crates.io as bose-bmap 0.5.0, while the Python package installs from the repository through its install scripts or pipx. The README’s device table marks six models, led by the QC Ultra Headphones 2, as verified to differing extents and the Ultra Open Earbuds as partial from a device report; other cataloged BMAP products are recognized by product ID but have no tested configuration.

Needs the user’s own paired Bose headphones and a Bluetooth adapter: BlueZ on Linux, or macOS 10.15+, where the Python library uses PyObjC’s IOBluetooth bindings. The Rust crate is Linux-only, and C++ builds on Linux need CMake, a C++17 compiler and the BlueZ development headers. No Bose software or files are needed at runtime.

README reports probing RFCOMM channels, capturing Bluetooth HCI traffic while toggling settings in the Bose app and testing operators on each function block, and NOTES.md cites class names from the Bose Android app. The app, decompiled code and raw HCI or network captures are not in the repository: captures/ holds eight before-and-after setting snapshots from bmap-capture.py with the MAC address, serial number and other identifiers partly masked, and fixtures/ holds a packet used by the tests.

README says the project uses only BMAP operations the headphones accept without authentication, and that no keys are extracted, no encryption is broken and no traffic is replayed; writes that the app performs after cloud-mediated authentication stay out of reach. USB control is not implemented, and NOTES.md treats the USB interface as being for firmware updates.
CI runs the Python, Rust and C++ test targets on Ubuntu and macOS without headphones; integration tests that need a paired device run only when enabled. MIT license.

resources.name: mgbdis
resources.description: Python disassembler that turns a Game Boy or Game Boy Color ROM, including multi-bank ROMs, into RGBDS-compatible assembly plus a Makefile that reassembles it, so the rebuilt ROM can be compared with the input. An optional .sym file beside the ROM supplies labels and marks code, data, text, padding and 1bpp/2bpp tile-image blocks; images are written as PNG files that rgbgfx converts back, text can use custom character maps, and hardware registers get hardware.inc names. The README explains that SM83 instructions vary in length and data is interleaved with code, so marked code blocks keep it from disassembling mid-instruction.
requirements: Latest release at review: v3.0, published 2025-04-22; the reviewed master commit of 2026-07-31 is 15 commits ahead of that tag and still reports version 3.0. It is a single Python script that needs Python 3.6+, and the generated assembly targets RGBDS v0.8.0 or later, whose rgbasm, rgblink, rgbfix and rgbgfx the generated Makefile calls. Options control hexadecimal case, indentation, operand alignment and mnemonic variants, and a --tiny mode handles unbanked 32 KiB ROMs.

The input is a ROM file the user supplies, optionally with a same-named .sym file; the repository ships no game ROMs. It bundles PyPNG's png.py and a copy of gbdev's hardware.inc, and its only test ROM is assembled during testing from the project's own assembly sources. The README suggests generating code-block symbol files with the author's separate Beaten Dying Moon emulator, which records the instructions actually executed.

GitHub Actions installs the latest RGBDS release, builds the test ROM, disassembles it, diffs the output against committed expected files, then reassembles the disassembly and compares it byte for byte with the test ROM. This checks the tool on its own fixture, not on commercial games. The README notes that RGBDS inserts a NOP after STOP, so a STOP not followed by NOP is emitted as a data byte, and calls the tool slow on large ROMs.
MIT license; png.py carries its own MIT notice. mgbdis produces assembly rather than C, and labels and block boundaries come from the analyst's symbol file.

resources.name: SiMBA
resources.description: Research tool from Denuvo that simplifies linear mixed Boolean-arithmetic (MBA) expressions, which combine bitwise and integer operations and are used in code obfuscation. Like MBA-Blast and MBA-Solver it works algebraically, using the fact that a linear MBA is fully determined by its values on inputs of zeros and ones: it evaluates the expression on every such combination and rewrites it as a linear combination of basic bitwise expressions, without first translating it to 1-bit space. Python scripts simplify single expressions or whole datasets, can check that an input is linear and can prove the result equivalent with Z3.
requirements: Accompanies Benjamin Reichenwallner and Peter Meerwald-Stadler's paper at the CheckMATE 2022 workshop, co-located with ACM CCS 2022 (DOI 10.1145/3560831.3564256, arXiv 2209.06335); the repository also holds the paper PDF, slides and a talk video. The reviewed main commit dates from 2022-12-12, and there are no releases or packages: the scripts run directly from src/.

Needs Python 3; Z3's Python bindings are required by simplify_dataset.py and by the -z verification option of simplify.py. Input is expression text, or a file with one complex expression and its simpler equivalent per line, built from variables, constants and the operators ~, unary minus, *, +, -, &, ^ and |; the tool has no disassembler or decompiler integration. Output constants depend on the bit width, 64 by default and set with -b.

Only linear MBAs are handled: the optional -l check rejects nonlinear input such as products of variables, and the README warns that operator precedence follows Python, so parentheses are needed. Result refinement through lookup tables of bitwise expressions covers up to three variables; expressions with more variables keep the generic linear-combination form.

For reproducing part of the paper's experiments, data/ holds generated sets of 1,000 equivalent linear MBAs per target function with 2 to 4 variables, plus 5- and 6-variable sets for x+y; the README also mentions 7 variables, which are not in the tree. The datasets assume 64 bits, and simplify_dataset.py reports how many results Z3 verified or matched exactly and the average runtime. There is no test suite or CI.
GPL-3.0, copyright 2022 Denuvo GmbH.

resources.name: ghidra-allegrex
resources.description: Ghidra processor module for the Allegrex CPU of the PlayStation Portable, derived from Ghidra's MIPS module. It adds Allegrex-specific instructions, VFPU disassembly and basic decompilation, the PSP calling convention, and an ELF loader that detects PSP executables and applies the PSP-specific type A and B relocation sections, with rebasing after import. Bundled scripts import and export PPSSPP .sym function-label files, and an exporter writes kernel modules as relocatable object files for linking.
requirements: Latest release at review: v21.5, published 2026-10-25, built for Ghidra 12.2 and requiring JVM 25; the reviewed master commit is that tag. Each release zip targets one Ghidra version, so v21.4 of 2026-08-25 remains the build for Ghidra 12.1.3 and 12.1.4. Extension v19 and later install through Ghidra's File > Install Extensions; v18 and earlier are unpacked into Ghidra's Processors directory.

Source builds set GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR and run the Gradle wrapper's buildExtension task, compiling Kotlin and Java against the local Ghidra installation with a JVM 25 toolchain. CI builds the extension against Ghidra 12.2 on Ubuntu and uploads the zip; the repository has no automated tests. The two PPSSPP scripts are written in Ghidra's Python 2 (Jython) dialect, and the .sym file comes from the user's own PPSSPP debugging session.

Inputs are PSP executables in ELF/PRX form, kernel modules or raw binaries that the user supplies; the README notes that game executables must already be decrypted, and the repository contains no PSP software or firmware. Raw binaries need the processor and image base set by hand, and some kernel modules need the reboot.bin type B relocation option at import.

The README lists limits: almost every VFPU operation decompiles to a function call such as vadd_q(...), the vpfxs, vpfxt and vpfxd prefix semantics are not modeled, vfim.s shows its half-float operand as an integer, object files cannot be rebased after import, and functions with 64-bit arguments need custom storage because of a Ghidra issue.

Apache-2.0; the README says it is derived from Ghidra's Apache-2.0 MIPS module and that type B relocation parsing is based on prxtool under AFL v2.0. Separately, REA's PSP static ELF guide uses it as a caller-installed extension and pairs v21.4 with Ghidra 12.1.3.

resources.name: Frida Boot: a beginner binary instrumentation workshop
resources.description: A beginner workshop by leonjza on binary instrumentation with Frida, served as offline pages from a Docker container that has gdb with GEF and frida-tools preinstalled. Three chapters move from a small Linux C program, LD_PRELOAD hooks and how library calls resolve through the PLT and GOT, to Frida’s Interceptor for reading arguments and changing return values, NativeFunction for calling a program’s own functions, Python injector tools, RPC exports, TypeScript agents, frida-server and frida-gadget. It deliberately leaves out Frida’s mobile-app uses, and every exercise targets sample programs shipped with the workshop.
requirements: The reviewed master commit dates from 2021-04-28, with no releases or tags; the prebuilt leonjza/frida-boot image on Docker Hub (tag latest, amd64 only) was last updated the same day. The README links a YouTube recording of the workshop and keeps a PDF of the slides in slides/.

Needs a host with Docker. docker.sh pulls or builds the image and starts it with the SYS_PTRACE capability, serving the course at localhost:9999 and mounting a local code folder into the container. The Dockerfile builds on Debian bullseye-slim and downloads frida-server and frida-gadget 12.9.4 for linux-x86_64, but installs frida-tools, GEF and the frida-agent-example project unpinned, so a fresh build will not reproduce the 2021 tool versions.

Exercises compile and instrument the workshop’s own C samples in software/: a random sleep loop, a fake_sleep LD_PRELOAD library and a PIN-check program whose test_pin function the lessons call directly from Frida, with numbered JavaScript, TypeScript and Python snippets for each step. No third-party target binaries are included or needed; the material covers x86_64 Linux user-space processes.
The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none; the bundled docsify scripts and themes keep their own licenses, and Frida, GEF and the base image are fetched under theirs.

resources.name: IDA Pro MCP Server (fdrechsler)
resources.description: An IDA Pro plugin and a TypeScript MCP server by Florian Drechsler: the plugin starts an HTTP server inside IDA on 127.0.0.1:9045, and the stdio MCP server forwards agent requests to it. Its twelve tools run IDAPython scripts passed inline or by file path, list functions, exports and strings, search names, immediate values and byte sequences, return cross-references to and from an address, and disassemble address ranges. It is a separate codebase from the mrexodia and Hex-Rays IDA MCP servers listed here.
requirements: Dormant: its six commits date from 2025-03-24 to 2025-03-26, with no tags, releases or npm package. The README asks for IDA Pro 8.3 or later, Node.js 18+ and TypeScript; the MCP server is built from a clone with npm install and npm run build, and ida_remote_server.py is copied into IDA's plugins directory, where it starts its server when IDA loads. MCP clients launch the built dist/index.js over stdio.

IDA Pro is commercial software installed separately, and the tools act on whatever database the analyst has open; the repository holds only source files and a screenshot. The README documents eight of the twelve tools and an npm test command, but package.json defines no test script and the project has no tests. At the pinned commit index.ts imports llamaindex, which package.json does not declare, and the search_text tool queries a MongoDB strings collection at localhost:27017 instead of IDA, with its IDA call commented out.

Script tools run arbitrary IDAPython inside IDA, and while a script runs the plugin overrides IDA's prompt functions so that dialogs are auto-confirmed or suppressed. The HTTP server has no authentication: the README's security note relies on the localhost-only default bind and warns about the implications of changing DEFAULT_HOST.
The LICENSE file and README state MIT, while package.json declares ISC. IDA Pro, MCP clients and analysed binaries keep their own terms.

resources.name: Ghidra Headless MCP
resources.description: Headless-only MCP server that drives Ghidra through PyGhidra and is meant to share a container with the agent rather than attach to a Ghidra GUI. Its 212 tools in 34 groups cover program and project lifecycle, disassembly, decompilation and P-code, patching and memory edits, symbols, references, types and structure layouts, search and graph extraction, with raw Python, Java-API and script access for anything else. Programs open read-only by default, edits run in transactions with undo and redo, a fake backend lets development and CI run without Ghidra, and a ghidra_cli client exposes the same tools to shells and agents without MCP.
requirements: The reviewed main commit (2026-09-16) reports version 0.1.0, with no tags or releases; the changelog keeps all changes under Unreleased, and RELEASING.md says source releases go to GitHub only, not PyPI, and that no public release tag should be created until a license is chosen. Install from a checkout with pip. The README says the code, tests and documentation are entirely vibe coded.

Python 3.11+ with pyghidra 3.0.2+ and a local Ghidra installation given through GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR or --ghidra-install-dir; the README names no minimum Ghidra release. MCP runs over stdio or TCP, with setup examples for Claude Code, Codex and generic MCP hosts and a sample Kali-based Dockerfile that installs Ghidra beside the agent. Debugger, Version Tracking, FID, BSim and emulator workflows are listed as not exposed.

ghidra.eval, ghidra.call and ghidra.script run arbitrary Python, Java and scripts inside the Ghidra runtime, and both transports are unauthenticated; the TCP server binds 127.0.0.1, and the README limits use to trusted, containerized environments. Read-only sessions protect program state but do not sandbox filesystem or process access.
