The repository bundles a stripped AArch64 GNU coreutils ls executable in samples/ as the feature fuzzer’s default target, and a small compiled hello test fixture with its C source. The README says CI also runs live Ghidra tests and a wheel check, but the reviewed workflow runs only Ruff and the non-live pytest suite on the fake backend.
GitHub detects GPL-2.0 from the LICENSE file added in the initial commit, while the README and RELEASING.md still treat the license as unchosen and pyproject.toml declares none.

resources.name: Binary Ninja Headless MCP
resources.description: A third-party, headless-only MCP server by Ruben Marks (mrphrazer) that gives agents a large Binary Ninja tool surface the project counts as 181 tools across 36 feature groups, including disassembly, intermediate languages, cross-references, types, search, patching with undo/redo transactions, and arbitrary scripting through binja.eval and binja.call. It speaks MCP over stdio or TCP, ships a schema-derived command-line client (binja_cli), and is meant to run in the same container as the agent runtime. A fake-backend mode runs the CLI, tests and a feature fuzzer without a Binary Ninja license, while real analysis needs a headless-capable license.
requirements: Reviewed at main 7fafd75 (2026-09-19); the pyproject declares package version 0.2.0 and there are no tagged releases. The README positions it against GUI-bound or limited Binary Ninja MCP servers as a headless-only, agent-driven alternative with mutation workflows and scripting, and states the whole project, including its code, tests and documentation, is vibe coded.

Needs Python 3.11+. Real analysis requires a Binary Ninja installation with a headless-capable license and the binaryninja Python module importable; the README notes enterprise and debugger APIs are not covered. A fake-backend mode (BINARY_NINJA_HEADLESS_MCP_FAKE_BACKEND=1) runs the CLI, the pytest suite and the feature fuzzer without a license, which is what CI exercises on Python 3.11 with ruff and pytest.

Install with pip from a clone or straight from the repository. Register it with an MCP host such as Claude Code or Codex over stdio (default) or TCP; the recommended deployment runs the agent and this server in one container. The repository bundles a sample binary, samples/ls (a stripped aarch64 GNU coreutils ls), as the fuzzer and verification target, plus small C fixtures.

The README's security model states that stdio and TCP transports are unauthenticated by default and that binja.eval and binja.call expose arbitrary scripting and broad API access, intended only for trusted containerized environments and not to be exposed to untrusted users or networks. Read-only mode is the session default, memory.read is capped at 65536 bytes, and mutations use undo/redo transactions.

The bundled CLI_VERIFICATION.md reports native coverage of all 181 tools on Binary Ninja 6.0.10601 Ultimate (AArch64 Linux host) across both architectures, transports and argument styles, but its evidence links point to files in the authors' analysis environment rather than the shipped package. GPL-2.0. Use it on binaries the operator is authorized to examine.

resources.name: GM8Decompiler
resources.description: Command-line tool that turns games built with GameMaker 8.0 or 8.1 back into editable .gmk or .gm81 project files. It reads the gamedata section that a built executable carries next to the runner and writes its settings, sprites, sounds, backgrounds, paths, scripts, fonts, timelines, objects, rooms, extensions, included files and GML code in the project format matching the game's version. A Rust rewrite on the OpenGMK project's gm8exe library that replaced the team's fork of WastedMeerkat's gm81decompiler, it is now developed in the OpenGMK repository alongside the GM8Emulator runner reimplementation.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.2.0, published 2024-02-12 with i686 and x86_64 Windows MSVC builds. Its tag points at the January 2022 commit that leaves only the README and licence in this repository, because development moved to OpenGMK while releases are still published here. The release notes list a Rust update from 1.59 to 1.76, a fix for executables written by gm82, and support for the 810 and 811 room formats; the OpenGMK gm8decompiler crate is also at 2.2.0, and its later commits only raise the Rust version and update dependencies.

Source builds use the OpenGMK Cargo workspace, cloned with submodules and built with cargo build --release, which also builds GM8Emulator. rust-toolchain.toml pins Rust 1.77 to keep Windows 7 support, and the OpenGMK README says only MSVC targets are supported on Windows and, because releases are rarely updated, recommends building it yourself. The decompiler crate has no tests, and neither repository has CI workflows at the reviewed commits.

Input is a GameMaker 8.0 or 8.1 game executable the user supplies; neither repository includes games. Usage is gm8decompiler FILENAME: -o names the output, which otherwise is the input path with the .gmk or .gm81 extension for the detected version; -l disables data-integrity checks; -s decompiles on one thread to lower memory use; -p keeps broken custom Execute Code actions instead of converting them to standard ones; and -d sets deobfuscation of GML code processed by Schreib's GM Obfuscator, which the default auto mode enables when assets have empty names.

The README reports the Rust loader as over ten times faster than the old gm81decompiler fork, safer, more thorough and able to read more games; these are project claims, and no per-game compatibility list or output check is published. GPL-2.0-only per Cargo.toml, with the GPL v2 text in LICENCE.md. Recovered projects contain the game's own assets and code, which remain subject to the rights of the game's owner.

resources.name: UELib (Unreal-Library)
resources.description: C# library that reads Unreal Engine 1, 2 and 3 package files such as .u, .upk and .udk, auto-detects a matching game build and deserializes their exports, imports and properties. Its main goal is decompiling UnrealScript bytecode back to source by reconstructing classes, states, functions, structs, enums and default properties; it also deserializes fonts, sounds, palettes and textures. The README’s per-game compatibility table runs from Unreal and Deus Ex to Splinter Cell, Mass Effect and the Batman: Arkham games, and the separate UE Explorer GUI is built on it.
requirements: Published on NuGet as Eliot.UELib: the latest stable package at review is 1.13.7, published 2026-07-17, targeting .NET Framework 4.8, .NET Standard 2.0 and 2.1 and .NET 10, while the newest GitHub release page is 1.12.0 from 2025-09-22. Versions come from Nerdbank.GitVersioning, and the reviewed master commit (2026-10-16) is later than both. The repository also holds a small .NET 10 command-line client, a separate decompiler project and a work-in-progress T3D decompiler.

Input is package files from the user’s own game installations. The README warns that opening an unsupported package could crash the system, that production UE3 packages are often compressed and must first be decompressed with a separate tool, and that some games need third-party decompression or extraction. Textures in .tfc caches, models and animations are not supported, and audio and texture output is expected to work for most games but not confirmed.

Compatibility rows are the author’s and contributors’ reports per game and package version, including known problems such as bad output at function starts for X-COM: Alliance, wrong UStruct offsets for Duke Nukem Forever (2001) and bad byte-codes for Medal of Honor (2010); some rows are marked unverified. The MSTest suite reads TestUC1–TestUC3 packages compiled from the project’s own UnrealScript test classes, and some tests point at local Unreal Tournament or UT2004 installations.

MIT license (Eliot van Uytfanghe). Game packages, scripts and assets keep their rights holders’ terms, and decompiled UnrealScript is a reconstruction, not the original source files. The GitHub description also mentions .uasset, but the README’s compatibility table covers only Unreal Engine 1–3 games.

resources.name: Embedded Hacking (mytechnotalent)
resources.description: A free English course by mytechnotalent on developing, debugging and reverse engineering firmware for the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (RP2350, Arm Cortex-M33). A fourteen-week syllabus with slides, Markdown notebooks and a 40-chapter PDF textbook follows a write, debug, then hack pattern from hello-world through variables, data types, constants, operators, conditionals, structures and functions, using GDB with OpenOCD and Ghidra, with Binary Ninja and IDA versions of the notebooks from week 4; an I2C LCD, GPS, LoRa radio, servo and IR remote supply the exercises. Graded CTFs, story-driven classified-brief challenges and a secure-boot custom bootloader ship as author-built binaries alongside their source.
requirements: Reviewed at commit 76fa253 (2026-10-19). The repository dates from October 2023, but its current history restarts with an initial commit on 2026-10-07 and has received commits almost daily since; there are no releases. Weeks 1–7 and 9–11 have slides and notebooks; Week 8 is a midterm built on CTF-02, Weeks 12–13 list only topics, and the two Week 14 final projects are scenario descriptions with no linked files. A supplemental section, which the README places beyond the course, links Rust, Arm-assembly and RISC-V-assembly tutorials, drivers and IoT CTF projects in the author's other repositories.

The README expects intermediate C including pointers, bare-metal assembly basics, a working model of registers and the stack, command-line use and breadboarding. Hardware is a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 with a Raspberry Pi Debug Probe and the listed parts, among them LEDs, a push button, a 1602 I2C LCD, a DHT11 sensor, an SG90 servo, a VS1838B IR receiver with an NEC remote, a u-blox NEO-6M GPS module, two REYAX RYLR998 LoRa modules and an FT232RL USB-serial adapter; Fritzing and wiring diagrams are in hardware/.

Setup is native on Windows x64, Apple-silicon macOS and Linux x64: the VS Code Raspberry Pi Pico extension installs the Pico SDK, Arm GNU Toolchain, picotool and OpenOCD, builds use CMake and Ninja, and the course adds Ghidra with JDK 21, a serial terminal and a licensed Binary Ninja Personal; the IDA notebook variants additionally assume IDA. Root flash and debug-server scripts wrap flashing and the debug server.

No third-party firmware is needed: the exercises target programs the author wrote, and the repository commits their source with build outputs (ELF, BIN, UF2, HEX, disassembly and map files), two Binary Ninja databases, CTF-02's static libraries (its auth module, an mbedTLS subset and the Argon2 reference implementation), the RP2350 SVD file and the custom bootloader's signed images. datasheets/ holds copies of the RP2350 datasheet, the Pico C/C++ SDK book, Arm's Cortex-M33 Technical Reference Manual, the Armv8-M Architecture Reference Manual, AAPCS32 and Application Note 132, which keep their publishers' terms.

Apache-2.0 for the repository. The README's legal disclaimer limits use to educational, research and defensive work on devices the user owns or is explicitly authorized to test. A bundled OpenCode skill only enforces the author's C coding standard.

resources.name: Apple Continuity Reverse Engineering Toolkit
resources.description: Three macOS helpers from SEEMOO Lab that the Open Wireless Link project used to study Apple wireless services such as AirDrop, Wi-Fi Password Sharing, Handoff and Offline Finding from the host side. process_recon summarizes which processes, log categories and subsystems emit log entries matching chosen keywords; keychain_access uses Frida to hook SecItemCopyMatching in a process and exports the keychain items it accesses to JSON; and lldb breakpoint commands print the Handoff and Universal Clipboard messages that the rapportd daemon sends and receives.
requirements: The repository has three commits: the initial release and a paper link on 2021-04-12, and a 2026-08-17 README edit that replaces the former Open Wireless Link website link with a note that the site is no longer associated with the project. There are no releases. The process_recon example was recorded on macOS 11.0 and the breakpoints name private Rapport framework methods; support for current macOS releases is not documented.

Runs on the analyst's own Mac with Python 3 in a virtual environment and Node.js; make install installs the pinned requirements, including frida 14.2.7 and frida-tools 9.1.0 from 2021, plus the prettier dev dependency. continuity_messages needs lldb and SIP's debugging protection turned off, and keychain_access needs SIP fully disabled for system processes; the README warns about the security implications.

Inputs are the analyst's own devices and accounts: the rapportd examples involve an iPhone next to the Mac and keys for the analyst's iCloud devices, so keychain_access output holds real secrets and should be handled accordingly. keychain_access/tests has small Swift and Objective-C hackme programs and a test.sh that stores and then extracts a dummy keychain password; there are no other tests.

The tools watch logs, keychain calls and daemon messages on the host; they do not capture or decode over-the-air Bluetooth LE or AWDL traffic, unlike the separately listed furiousMAC Continuity notes and Wireshark dissector for Continuity advertisements. The README lists the authors' USENIX Security 2021 Continuity and 2019 AWDL papers and a 2020 dissertation as related publications.

resources.name: lib-osmo-ble: DJI Osmo Pocket 3 Bluetooth LE protocol library
resources.description: Reconstructs the DUML-over-BLE protocol that DJI's Mimo app uses with the Osmo Pocket 3 camera as a Node.js library and CLI for scanning, pairing, gimbal commands and roughly 20 Hz position telemetry without the vendor app. The author reports working from a third party's Wireshark captures and dissector of Mimo traffic, a Go client and trial-and-error debugging; PROTOCOL.md documents the frame layout, CRC parameters, BLE characteristic roles and command IDs. A write-up and bundled patch trace seven bugs that kept the earlier node-osmo library from working with the camera, and the author reports that the patched library completed pairing, Wi-Fi setup and RTMP streaming.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-02-21 main head, which is also the last push; package.json declares 1.0.0, and there are no releases or tags. The README says gimbal motor commands are built and parsed correctly but the camera silently ignores them over BLE alone, probably until Wi-Fi streaming is active, while telemetry works. The library itself implements pairing, gimbal control and telemetry only; Wi-Fi setup and streaming were reached with the patched node-osmo.

Requires the user's own DJI Osmo Pocket 3 and a Bluetooth LE host. PROTOCOL.md reports verification on that model only, from macOS, and the patch notes list Apple Silicon macOS Sequoia, Node.js v25.5.0 and @stoprocent/noble 1.18.2; other DJI devices may differ. Pairing sends a client-chosen PIN (love by default in the CLI) that the user approves on the camera. No DJI firmware, app files or the author's own captures are committed.

Plain Node.js ES modules with two runtime dependencies, @stoprocent/noble ^2.3.10 for BLE and crc-full for the CRC8/CRC16 checks, and no build step; npm link installs the dji-osmo CLI. Diagnostic scripts scan for DJI devices, list characteristic properties and decode and CRC-check DUML hex messages. The node-osmo patch applies with git am to a separate clone of datagutt/node-osmo and builds with pnpm and TypeScript.

There are no automated tests; the npm test script is a placeholder that exits with an error. Evidence is the author's write-up, analysis notes on characteristic mapping, byte order, the Node.js buffer-pool bug and a false-positive run, and an experiment index whose raw logs are gitignored. Device behavior remains author-reported.

LICENSE is MIT, although package.json still says ISC. The reference folder copies the CC0-1.0 Wireshark dissector and message notes from xaionaro/reverse-engineering-dji, and node-osmo is MIT. DJI firmware, apps and trademarks keep their own rights.

resources.name: uefi_retool
resources.description: Python command-line tool and IDA Pro plugin for UEFI firmware reverse engineering. uefi_retool.py unpacks a firmware image with uefi-firmware-parser, collects its executable modules and runs IDA in batch mode on each one, writing their boot-service calls and protocol GUIDs to JSON; a separate command lists protocols whose GUIDs are absent from its EDK2, AMI and vendor GUID tables as proprietary. Inside IDA the plugin applies EFI system-table types and names, lists protocols in an explorer window and, from the JSON, shows a dependency browser and graph across the firmware’s modules.
requirements: The repository is archived. Its last commit (2024-12-28) only updates the README, the last code changes date from 2021-08-03, and the only tag, 1.2.0 from 2020-05-07, is eight commits older; there are no GitHub releases. The tree contains an IDA plugin only and no Ghidra component.

Needs a licensed IDA Pro with IDAPython and PyQt5: copy uefi_analyser.py and the uefi_analyser package into IDA’s plugins directory, then set the IDA and IDA64 executable paths and the module, dump and log directories in config.json, whose example points to IDA Pro 7.6 on Windows. The script uses Python with Click, colorama, terminaltables, tqdm and uefi-firmware-parser 1.8, installed from a tarball named in requirements.txt.

Input is a UEFI firmware image the user supplies; README examples name a ThinkPad X1 Carbon 5th-generation image that the repository does not include, and no firmware images are committed. The analyser recognizes x86 and x86-64 instruction patterns and chooses IDA or IDA64 from each image’s machine type. The bundled GUID tables come from EDK2 and EDK, from ida-efiutils for AMI, and from Dell, Lenovo and ASRock lists, and tools/update_edk2_guids.py refreshes the EDK2 table.
MIT license (2018–2021, yeggor). The repository has no tests or CI. Labels and dependency graphs come from GUID matching and instruction patterns, so they need analyst checking.

resources.name: GTIRB
resources.description: GrammaTech's intermediate representation for passing disassembly, analysis and rewriting results between binary tools, modeled on the role LLVM-IR plays for compilers. An IR holds modules for executables or libraries with their sections, byte intervals, code and data blocks, symbols and symbolic operands, plus an inter-procedural CFG and AuxData tables for analysis results, all referenced by UUID; instruction semantics are deliberately left out, so machine code stays as raw bytes for Capstone/Keystone or any other IL. It serializes as protobuf, with C++, Python and Common Lisp APIs and a partial Java API; the separately listed ddisasm produces it.
requirements: PyPI's newest gtirb is 2.3.2, uploaded 2026-06-16 as a pure-Python wheel for Python 3.8+; the changelog says the PyPI package needs protobuf 4.21.1 or newer. The reviewed master commit of the same day bumps version.txt to 2.3.3, which CHANGELOG marks unreleased. GitHub releases stop at v2.0.0 (2023-12-14, no files), and later versions are git tags. The README says ABI compatibility is not yet provided across any version change, and that stable or unstable packages must match the installed ddisasm and gtirb-pprinter.

Prebuilt options are Windows .zip builds and Ubuntu 20.04 (focal) apt packages from GrammaTech's download server, and the grammatech/ddisasm Docker image with GTIRB, ddisasm and gtirb-pprinter; the README warns that apt metapackages for stable gtirb 2.0.0 and older conflict on upgrade. Source builds need a 64-bit C++17 compiler (GCC, Clang or Visual Studio), CMake 3.10+, Protobuf 3.0.0+ and Boost 1.68+; the Common Lisp API needs further manual setup, and the Java API is marked incomplete.

GTIRB is a data structure, not an analyzer: IR comes from a producer such as ddisasm. The schema names file formats including ELF, PE, COFF, XCOFF, Mach-O and raw images, and ISAs from IA-32 and x64 to ARM, MIPS, PowerPC and, from 2.3.2, RISC-V; what a given producer actually supports is up to that tool. Programs in doc/examples walk the C++ API and compute CFG paths, data symbols and functions in several languages.

The GitLab CI configuration builds and tests on Ubuntu 20.04, 22.04 and 24.04 with GCC and Clang, plus static, Java, Common Lisp, Python and coverage jobs; the GitHub Actions workflow only builds and publishes documentation.

LICENSE.txt places GTIRB under MIT (2018, GrammaTech) and appends Apache-2.0 with LLVM Exceptions for included third-party code, which GitHub leaves unclassified; contributors must sign GrammaTech's CLA.

resources.name: Quokka
resources.description: Quarkslab’s binary exporter, inspired by BinExport, saves a disassembler’s analysis to a protobuf .quokka file so functions, basic blocks, data, cross-references, segments and optionally decompiled code can be used later without the disassembler. Its Python bindings load an export together with the original binary, decode instructions at runtime with Capstone, or optionally lift them to P-code with pypcode, and expose programs, functions and control-flow graphs through one API. The main branch adds Ghidra and Binary Ninja exporters beside the IDA Pro plugin, a parallel quokka-cli batch exporter and name and type edits that can be written back to an IDA database.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.6.2, published 2025-12-08 together with quokka-project 0.6.2 on PyPI; its README supports IDA 7.3+, and it ships prebuilt IDA plugins for IDA 7.4 through 9.2 on Windows, Linux and macOS. The reviewed main commit (2026-10-14) is 261 commits later and declares version 1.0.0; the Ghidra and Binary Ninja exporters, quokka-cli and the IDA 9.1+ requirement described here exist only on main, not in a released package.

Exporting needs one disassembler. The main-branch C++ plugin targets IDA Pro 9.1+, installs through hcli on 9.2+ or builds with CMake, which fetches the open-source IDA SDK for 9.2+ and needs a separately obtained SDK for older versions; the Java extension needs Ghidra 12.0.3+ and JDK 21+; the Binary Ninja plugin declares version 4.0 build 4911 as its minimum, and headless use there needs a commercial license. The Python bindings need Python 3.10+ on main, or 3.8+ for 0.6.2, with capstone, networkx, protobuf and python-magic.

Only the LIGHT export mode works: exports hold block-level data, so loading them needs the original binary for Capstone to decode instructions, and the self-contained FULL mode is planned but not implemented. quokka-cli offers decompiled-code export for IDA only. The README warns that Capstone’s disassembly can differ from the disassembler’s.

Test fixtures in tests/dataset are stored with Git LFS: programs built from the included many_types and sig_test sources, a Linux kernel module (nf_nat_pt.ko), a UEFI PEI module (StatusCodeHandlerPei.efi), a puraUpdate executable and their exports; docs/samples adds a qb-crackme sample and its export. Workflows build the IDA plugin, build and test the Ghidra extension, test the Binary Ninja plugin and run the Python tests on Python 3.10–3.13.
Apache-2.0 license; IDA Pro, Ghidra and Binary Ninja keep their own terms.

resources.name: knife
resources.description: Static reverse-engineering toolkit in Rust, installed as the knife command, that parses PE, ELF, Mach-O and WebAssembly files without running them. It triages hashes, sections, mitigations, imports, strings, indicators and crypto constants; recovers functions, call graphs and CFGs through recursive-descent disassembly for x86/x64 and AArch64; and lifts functions to experimental pseudocode. Analysts' names, notes, types and staged patches persist in a per-binary database shared by the CLI, a terminal UI and an MCP server, and further passes rank risky API call sites by argument provenance and summarize Windows driver dispatch and IOCTL surfaces.
requirements: The repository was created on 2026-08-08. Release v1.8.3 (2026-10-11) ships Linux x86_64, macOS arm64/x86_64 and Windows x86_64 archives, while the reknife crate on crates.io stops at 1.8.0 (2026-09-15); the reviewed main commit is 48 commits past v1.8.3, with unreleased changes listed in CHANGELOG. Source builds need Rust 1.88+, and the README says no system libraries are needed beyond the platform default; knife update needs curl.

Input is a binary the analyst supplies, which knife only reads. Disassembly covers x86/x64 and AArch64, the audit data-flow checks are x86/x64 only, and the README says empty reachability results do not prove unreachability because indirect dispatch is outside the direct call graph. WebAssembly gets section, import/export and WAT views without code analysis. The repository contains no target binaries: tests build synthetic PE and ELF fixtures in code, and data/loldrivers.json is a snapshot of the public LOLDrivers list used for SHA-256 matching.

knife mcp speaks MCP over stdio; docs/MCP.md lists 58 tools, four of which write names, notes, prototypes or staged patches to the project database rather than the binary. The optional investigation desk sends prompts and tool results to the model provider the user configures (local Ollama, OpenRouter, OpenAI or another OpenAI-compatible endpoint) and keeps hosted API keys in the OS credential vault. Optional adapters call a separately installed Rizin, and the provider docs also describe Ghidra headless and capa adapters; YARA-X 1.12 is linked in for rule scans, and a GDB runtime exporter is documented but not yet exposed.

CI runs cargo build and test on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS, plus cargo fmt and clippy. The README presents audit hits as call sites whose argument provenance matches a bug pattern, and its 7z.dll, kernel32.dll and CVE-2017-11882 figures are the author's results.

MIT (2026, 0xblack). The LOLDrivers snapshot comes from that project's public API, and Rizin, Ghidra, capa and YARA-X keep their own licenses. The repository's AGENTS.md is contributor guidance for coding agents.

resources.name: Interactive IDA Plugin List
resources.description: A sortable, filterable list of 618 plugins, loaders, processor modules and scripts for Hex-Rays' IDA Pro, published as a GitHub Pages table with a static copy generated into the README. Each entry links to its project, almost always on GitHub, with a short description and, where recorded, its language (C++ or Python), category tags such as decompiler, deobfuscation, loader, debug or integration, and the date the project was last updated. The list grew out of onethawt's idaplugins-list of about 200 plugins.
requirements: The reviewed main commit, of 2024-11-19, refreshed every last-updated date and holds 618 entries in data.js, mirrored in the README. Those dates record each project's latest activity at refresh time, from 2006 to 2024 with 136 in 2024.

Category tags cover 313 entries; the most common are integration (97), decompiler (63), development (51), loader (42) and debug (39). data.js also notes an IDA version for 385 entries, the highest being 8.4, but the table does not show it, and no entry is marked for IDA 9 or later, so compatibility must be checked at each plugin's source.

The list itself is a static page that needs only a browser; tools/gen_readme.py regenerates the README from data.js and depends on demjson. Listed plugins need the user's own IDA installation, and the list records no license, edition or install requirements for them.
LICENSE is MIT, and lib/DEPENDENCIES.md lists the bundled Tabulator 5.1.8, moment.js and jQuery 3.6.0 files as MIT; listed plugins keep their own licenses.

resources.name: IDA-Skill
resources.description: Agent skill that has an AI agent triage malware samples statically in IDA Pro through headless idat. An initialization script builds the IDA database and exports a summary, imports, exports, entry-point decompilation and filtered strings, and an executor runs IDAPython snippets or files against that database. SKILL.md sets a static-only rule, a top-down method and a rule to hand large string dumps to a sub-agent, and bundled scripts add cryptographic-constant detection, an export-size check and REAI, which sends decompiled functions to a configured OpenAI-compatible model to describe them and rename them with an AI_ prefix.
requirements: Reviewed at main commit 4595864 of 2026-10-21; there are no releases or version numbers, and recent commits are titled only "update". The skill is a SKILL.md with name and description front matter for agent clients that load skill folders; the README demonstrates it with the author's Spore multi-agent framework and names no other tested client. Its commands use Windows PowerShell here-strings and paths under skills/IDA-Skill/tools/.

Requires a licensed IDA Pro installation whose idat executable is set in config.json (the README example is IDA Pro 9.0's idat64.exe) and Python on the host to launch it; decompilation calls rely on the Hex-Rays decompiler. Users supply the samples, and SKILL.md forbids debugging or executing them. REAI needs openai 1.0+ and an API key, endpoint and model edited into tools/reai.py, and it sends decompiled pseudocode to that endpoint.

API.md and docs/ hold a Markdown IDAPython API reference whose source and terms are not stated, analysis/ holds short method notes for tasks such as protocol, algorithm, firmware and driver analysis, and movie.mp4 is a 25 MB demo video. TOOLS.md tells the agent to run reai check first and not to run analyze when a call chain exceeds 40 functions.
The repository has no tests or CI and reports no evaluated samples or accuracy. REAI names and descriptions are model output that needs analyst review.

LICENSE holds the AGPL-3.0 text, while both READMEs call the project GPL-3.0 and add an education-and-research-only, no-commercial-use condition that neither license contains, so reuse terms are unclear. IDA Pro and model APIs keep their own terms.

resources.name: Reverse-Engineering a Bluetooth-Enabled Radar Detector
resources.description: Write-up of how the author decoded the Bluetooth RFCOMM protocol of a Cobra iRAD 900 radar detector so that a Raspberry Pi 3 could receive alerts without the iOS or Android app. Traffic was logged on a jailbroken iPhone with BTServer and filtered in Wireshark; the README then documents the detector's half-second status payload and the 9-byte reply whose ACK byte must echo the detector's sequence byte, and replays recorded responses to the initial settings sync instead of decoding it. A short beginner's case study on RFCOMM traffic analysis with a rough proof-of-concept script, not a maintained client.
requirements: Written in 2017 and last expanded on 2017-07-06; the latest commit, from January 2025, only updates the contact email. It covers one detector model. The alert-type values are only partly identified because the author had no radar gun, the initial sync is replayed rather than decoded, and the README expects the replay data would need re-recording after app settings change.

Following the method needs a Cobra iRAD 900 used with its vendor app and a way to log the phone's Bluetooth traffic; the author used BTServer logging on a jailbroken iPhone 5 and Wireshark. The repository commits the author's three .pklg captures, the Wireshark XML export (data.xml) and the processed packetData.dat; no app or device firmware is included.

radar.py is a self-described extremely rough proof of concept that talks RFCOMM through PyBluez, with the author's detector address and service UUID hard-coded; its setup notes install the Python 2 python-bluez package. parseData.py converts data.xml into packetData.dat, which radar.py loads with pickle, so treat that file as executable input.
MIT License. Cobra's detector, app and trademarks keep their own rights.

resources.name: BARF
resources.description: Python binary analysis framework that loads ELF and PE programs, disassembles 32- and 64-bit x86 and 32-bit ARM code with Capstone and translates it into the REIL intermediate language, so its analyses do not depend on the source architecture. Modules recover control-flow and call graphs, emulate REIL and turn code fragments into Z3 or CVC4 formulas for checking constraints on registers and memory; release 0.6.0 added basic symbolic execution. Bundled command-line tools recover CFGs and call graphs, replay x86 execution traces and search, classify and verify ROP gadgets.
requirements: Inactive since 2019: the reviewed master commit, dated 2019-11-24, is tagged v0.6.0 and is the last commit; 0.6.0 is also the newest PyPI release of barf. GitHub does not mark the repository archived, and it has tags but no GitHub release entries, although the README links a v0.6.0 release page. setup.py classifies it as alpha, and the README still calls it under development.

setup.py and the Travis CI configuration target Python 2.7 and 3.6, with Python 3 support added in 0.6.0. The README says all packages were tested on Ubuntu 16.04 x86_64, and the Dockerfile installs it on Ubuntu 18.04 through Python 2 pip. Dependencies include Capstone 3.0.5rc2+, pefile, pyelftools, networkx, pydot and pyparsing, plus at least one of the Z3 or CVC4 solvers; Graphviz is needed for graph output and PyAsmJIT for some tests.

Binaries come from the analyst. The repository bundles small sample binaries built from included C sources under examples/misc/samples and tests, and two challenge binaries for its worked examples: Flare-On 2015 challenge #2 (examples/flareon-2015/2/bin/very_success) and kao's toy project (examples/kaos-toy-project/bin/toyproject.exe). The Sphinx manual is in Spanish and refers to an install.sh script that is not present at the reviewed commit.

BSD 2-Clause license, copyright 2014 Fundación Dr. Manuel Sadosky. The README describes checking instruction translations by running code natively through PyAsmJIT and in the REIL emulator and comparing the final contexts.

resources.name: cbyge: reconstructing the C by GE smart-bulb cloud protocol
resources.description: Reimplements the cloud control path of the C by GE (now Cync) smart-bulb app as a Go library and a small self-hosted web app. The author reports decompiling the Android app with Apktool, finding its JSON HTTP API for login and device lists and a separate raw TCP protocol to the vendor's server, then working out that protocol's type-and-length message framing and packet encodings from proxied traffic and the Smali code. The resulting API lists devices, reads their status and sets power, brightness, color tone and RGB color.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2021-11-09 main commit; there are no releases. The README states that the code was not informed by a protocol specification and may stop working or fail on some networks and devices. Only the author's own lightbulbs were examined, so the outlets, sensors and switches the same app controls were not reverse-engineered.

Requires the user's own C by GE or Cync account with devices already set up in the official app; newer accounts need the email two-factor login, which the web app or the login_2fa command performs. Control goes through the vendor's cloud rather than local Bluetooth or LAN. The Android app, traffic captures and account data are not in the repository; the README quotes only short Smali excerpts and one status packet from the author's devices.

Builds with Go; go.mod declares Go 1.14 and two small dependencies. The server directory serves a browser front end and a JSON API protected by an optional web password, and the repository also keeps the small TCP and HTTP logging proxies used during the investigation.
There are no tests or CI. The README reports that others have used the API successfully in some cases and that the author found it faster and more reliable than the official app.
BSD-2-Clause, copyright 2021 Alexander Nichol. This is an independent client, not recovered vendor source; the vendor's apps, services and trademarks keep their own rights.

resources.name: Shannon Modem Loader for IDA Pro
resources.description: IDA Pro loader and post-processing scripts for Samsung Exynos "Shannon" baseband modem images that carry a TOC header, including crash dumps. The loader maps the TOC entries to aligned segments and entry points; after auto-analysis the post-processor restores debug-trace structures, names functions from strings and debug-log calls, rebuilds the MPU table and memory map, comments MMU-related coprocessor instructions, performs the ARM scatter-load with its decompression, and labels platform-abstraction-layer and task-initialization functions. The README adds the author's notes on ShannonOS, the PAL and the move from Cortex-R to Cortex-A cores.
requirements: Latest release at review: 01.2025, published 2025-01-01; the reviewed main commit of 2025-01-03 only adds IDA Essential 9.0 to the installer's search list. The README calls the code work in progress and reports testing on a larger set of images from older models such as the G8700 and S7 up to the S22 and S24, with task identification working on recent images.

The README reports testing with IDA Pro 9.0, IDA Pro 8.3 to 8.4 SP2 and IDA Home ARM, and says 7.x with the revamped IDAPython API might work. install.sh copies the loader, Python modules and signatures into a Linux IDA installation; on macOS or Windows the files are copied by hand following the README's table.
Users supply a TOC-format Shannon modem image or crash dump; the repository contains no modem firmware. The README reports that a complete analysis takes about 10 minutes on average hardware.

sig/ holds 17 premade FLIRT signature files for ARM Compiler/RVCT runtime functions, from version 3.1 to 5.06u7. The post-processor reads the image's RVCT build string, applies the matching signature, and on Linux offers to use the include directory of a matching legacy ARM compiler installed in the user's home directory. There are no tests or CI.
MIT License. Modem firmware, IDA Pro and ARM compilers keep their own terms.

resources.name: rabbitizer
resources.description: MIPS instruction decoder written in C that never allocates on the heap, with Python, C++ and Rust bindings in the same repository and the stated aim of producing matching assembly. It decodes one instruction word at a time, focusing on MIPS I to III with partial MIPS IV support, and also handles the N64 RSP, the PlayStation's R3000 GTE, the PSP's R4000 Allegrex and the PS2's R5900; it offers validation checks, instruction-grouping queries, configurable pseudo-instructions and register names, and small helpers for building pointer and symbol detection. Matching-decompilation tooling builds on it: splat and spimdisasm both list it as a Python dependency.
requirements: Latest stable release at review: 1.16.2, published 2026-05-29 on GitHub, PyPI and crates.io, which matches the reviewed 1.x commit. A 2.0.0 alpha series (2.0.0-alpha.9, 2026-05-20) is published from a separate Rust branch; splat and spimdisasm both pin versions below 2.0.0.

Install with pip install rabbitizer or cargo add rabbitizer. The README gives Python 3.9 as the minimum, although pyproject.toml still declares >=3.4, and building the Python bindings from source needs the Python development headers. The C and C++ libraries build with make and clang (C11 and C++17), and the Rust crate declares Rust 1.66.0. Instruction tables for every binding are generated from templates in tables/, and CI checks that the generated files are current.

Input is raw 32-bit instruction words, so callers must take code from their own binaries, choose the CPU variant and handle addresses and symbols themselves. Pseudo-instructions that expand to more than one instruction are deliberately unsupported; the README says output should match, reports that RSP output reassembles to matching code with armips, and calls MIPS IV support partial.

GitHub Actions build the C code with warnings as errors on Ubuntu 22.04 and run build-info, logic and instruction checks, and Python unit tests run on Linux, macOS and Windows; tests/asm holds assembly samples for the GTE, Allegrex and R5900. The README's reference list points to third-party CPU manuals and documentation hosted elsewhere.
MIT.

resources.name: EchoMuse: replacement software that turns the Echo Dot 2nd gen into a Home Assistant voice satellite
resources.description: Replaces the software on an unlocked second-generation Amazon Echo Dot (2016, codename biscuit) so it works as a local Home Assistant voice satellite over the ESPHome API: EchoMuse's own Go firmware drives the microphones, speaker, LED ring and buttons, and a controller on the LAN handles wake words, devices and a dashboard. Its default emOS mode swaps Amazon's Android userspace for the project's own init and busybox while keeping the Dot's kernel from the owner's boot image. An engineering journal records how codec routes, the mute key and other hardware behavior were worked out by measuring the device and diffing the mixer and DAPM state while stock FireOS plays a sound.
requirements: Reviewed main commit 4bbf7ff (2026-10-27) is in active development. At review the latest stable device firmware is v2.18.1 (2026-10-15) and emOS 0.10 (2026-10-02), the controller add-on declares 2.26.3, and early-access v2.19.0-ea.2 and emos-v0.11-ea.1 builds followed. Only the Echo Dot 2nd gen is supported; README calls ports to the Echo Dot 3, Echo 2 and Echo Show 8 in progress and lists open issues, including no WPA3 on emOS under FireOS 6.

Needs the user's own Echo Dot 2nd gen, first unlocked with third-party tools (firebreak running R0rt1z2's amonet-biscuit); README says this is done at the user's own risk and can soft-brick the device. The setup wizard keeps a copy of the device's own boot partition and builds the emOS image from its kernel and device trees, and emOS mounts bionic and tinyalsa read-only from the device's /system. The emOS README says no bootable image is published because it would contain Amazon's kernel; releases carry the project's own firmware binary, init and userspace payload, and busybox with its source.

Requires a working Home Assistant with an Assist pipeline, an always-on host for the controller as a Home Assistant add-on or Docker container, and Chrome or Edge for the one-time WebUSB setup. Source builds use the project's Docker compiler image for the Go device firmware, Python 3.12 for the controller, and emos/build.sh, whose release workflow compiles the init with a pinned Android NDK.

CI runs the controller pytest suite with coverage floors, dashboard and Go device tests, dependency audits and image builds, and the journal and acceptance-test reports describe runs on the maintainer's own devices. It does not reproduce Alexa, and no Amazon software or service is recovered.

MIT, with vendored SpeexDSP (BSD-3-Clause), an ONNX Runtime header, aioesphomeapi protocol buffers and a CC BY 4.0 timer sound listed in NOTICE.md; the project states it is not affiliated with Amazon. README says EchoMuse is written largely with Claude, directed by the maintainer, and that more than half the commits carry a Co-Authored-By: Claude line.

resources.name: ghidrecomp
resources.description: Python command-line decompiler that drives Ghidra through pyghidra to decompile every function of a binary into separate C files, or into one C file and header with Ghidra's C++ exporter, keeping the Ghidra project so later runs can reuse the analysis. Options filter functions by regex, apply PDB symbols from a local file or from Microsoft, Chromium, Mozilla, Intel, NVIDIA and AMD symbol servers, apply extra GDT data-type archives, write Mermaid call-graph Markdown, generate BSim function signatures, and scan the decompiled code with Semgrep rules into SARIF reports.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.5.9, published to PyPI and GitHub on 2026-01-06; the reviewed main commit is that tag. setup.cfg requires Python 3.10+ and pyghidra 2.2.1+ and marks the project as alpha; the CodeQL option is a placeholder that only prints a coming-soon message.

Needs a separate Ghidra installation and the Java runtime it requires, found through GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR. The Dockerfile and devcontainer build on the author's ghidra-python image and pin pyghidra 2.2.1 for Ghidra 11; CI runs pytest in that image for the latest Ghidra and for 11.3, 11.3.2 and 11.4.2. SAST scanning needs Semgrep, installed with the sast extra.

Binaries to decompile are the analyst's own; symbol lookups contact the listed public symbol servers unless --skip-symbols is set. The tests bundle tests/data/afd.sys.10.0.22621.1415, a Microsoft Windows driver build also used in the README examples, an AArch64 ls binary and an ntddk_64.gdt data-type archive; these files keep their publishers' terms.

The README presents the output as decompilations for research and analysis and makes no recompilation claim; the tests check function counts, call graphs, one signature after GDT application, BSim and SAST output. GPL-3.0 (LICENSE); Ghidra and Semgrep keep their own licenses.

resources.name: arkdecompiler
resources.description: Decompiler for HarmonyOS NEXT apps, published under the jd-opensource GitHub organization, that turns Panda binary files (.abc Ark bytecode) back into ArkTS source. Its xabc program parses the bytecode, lifts it into the Ark compiler's Panda IR for analysis, rebuilds an ArkTS syntax tree with loop, class, lexical-environment and module-variable reconstruction, and prints that tree as ArkTS code. A cross-platform GUI, built with either Electron or Tauri, adds a file explorer, function and symbol lists, cross-references, search and a hex view; the README links Black Hat Arsenal presentations from 2025 and 2026.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2026-07-23 master commit. The README marks all instructions as supported and a basic GUI as done, while covering enough corner cases from the official compiler and test262 is still in progress. Release v0.1.0 (2026-04-23) attaches Electron and Tauri GUI builds for Linux x86, macOS arm64 and Windows x86; decompilation runs only on Linux and disassembly on all three, and the GUI needs the paths of the command-line tools configured first.

Building xabc is tested on Ubuntu 22.04 inside an OpenHarmony arkcompiler standalone build: scripts/prepare.sh installs the repo tool, syncs the ark-standalone-build manifest from Gitee, downloads its prebuilts and checks out OpenHarmony v6.0.0.1-Release, and the files in patches/ must be applied to arkcompiler runtime_core, ets_frontend and third_party/protobuf before gn and ninja build xabc. The Dockerfile instead uses Ubuntu 20.04 and the OpenHarmony 5.1.0 release.

xabc reads one .abc file and writes ArkTS plus an AST dump, defaulting to demo.abc and arkdemo.ts. The documented workflow compiles the user's own demo.ts with OpenHarmony's es2abc and decompiles the result; any other bytecode must come from the user's own app packages, and the repository ships no apps or .abc samples.

tests/ holds 18 TypeScript samples for features such as classes, loops, generators, async functions and modules. autotests/scantstests.py compiles cases from the test262 and OpenHarmony TypeScript submodules and records whether decompilation exits cleanly, fails, crashes or times out, with a blacklist of skipped cases. No pass rates or semantic-equivalence results are reported, and the repository has no CI workflow.
Apache-2.0; the OpenHarmony components it builds against keep their own licenses.

resources.name: Vivisect
resources.description: Pure-Python reverse-engineering framework that combines the vivisect static analyzer, the vtrace debugging library and the vdb debugger. Vivisect loads PE, ELF, Mach-O, Intel HEX, S-record and raw blob files into workspaces, disassembles and emulates code through envi architecture modules for x86, AMD64, ARM, Thumb, AArch64, MSP430, H8 and Z80, and adds symbolic execution, a Qt GUI and a remote workspace server. vtrace drives processes on Windows, Linux, FreeBSD, macOS and Solaris and has GDB-stub and VMware backends.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.3.2, uploaded to PyPI on 2026-03-31 from tag v1.3.2 (the project publishes no GitHub release pages); it requires Python 3.8+ and pins PyQt5 5.15.7 for the GUI, and AArch64 support arrived in 1.3.0. The reviewed master commit (2026-09-03) is ten commits later and, still labelled 1.3.2, requires Python 3.11+ and PyQt6 6.5+. Install with pip install "vivisect[gui]"; releases before 1.0.0 are Python 2 only, and Python 2 workspaces are typically not loadable in Python 3.

Bundled helper libraries: vtrace/platforms/windll holds Microsoft’s dbghelp.dll and symsrv.dll for amd64 and i386, committed since 2014 and loaded by the Windows vtrace backend for symbol handling, and pyproject.toml packages them into the PyPI distribution. They are Microsoft binaries under Microsoft’s terms, not the project’s Apache-2.0 license, and no Microsoft license or notice accompanies them. The macOS backend ships a prebuilt machhelper.dylib next to its C source and Makefile.

Input is binaries or firmware images the user supplies. CircleCI runs the unittest suite on Python 3.11 against sample binaries from a separately cloned vivtestfiles repository, and a GitHub Actions workflow checks formatting; documentation is on Read the Docs.
Apache-2.0 license (COPYRIGHT names invisigoth, 2014); the Microsoft DLLs keep their own terms.

resources.name: JNIAnalyzer
resources.description: A Ghidra extension by Terry Chia (Ayrx) with scripts for analyzing the native libraries of Android NDK apps. JNIAnalyzer.java uses the bundled JADX decompiler to extract the signatures of all native methods declared in an APK and applies the return types, parameter names and parameter types to the matching functions in the loaded .so. RegisterNatives.java uses Ghidra's P-Code API to find RegisterNatives calls and lay down the JNINativeMethod structures for dynamically registered methods, and TraceRegisterNatives.java applies the output of the author's trace_registernatives tool. A JNI data-type archive sets up the jni.h types.
requirements: Reviewed at master 7170ce6 (2023-01-02); there are no releases and the default branch has had no commits since that date, so treat it as unmaintained and check compatibility with current Ghidra. Build the extension with Gradle against a Ghidra install (gradle -PGHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR=<dir>), then install the produced zip through Ghidra's Install Extensions dialog and restart.

Analysis runs inside Ghidra on an Android native library the analyst has loaded and is authorized to examine. JNIAnalyzer.java reads a supplied APK with JADX to recover native-method signatures; the README warns it overwrites existing function return types and parameter names and types, and that a function annotated JNIAnalyzer:IGNORE is skipped. RegisterNatives.java is marked experimental.

No third-party target files are committed. The repository vendors its Java build dependencies as JARs under JNIAnalyzer/lib/, including JADX, smali/baksmali, dexlib2, dx, apksig, Guava, ANTLR, RxJava, logback and others, each keeping its own open-source license; the committed android-5.1.jar is a 4-entry stub (a single android/R$style class plus JADX resources), not the Android SDK. The Gradle wrapper JAR is also committed, and data/jni_all.gdt is a Ghidra data-type archive of the JNI types.

The repository has no license file, so reuse terms are unstated; the vendored dependency JARs remain under their respective licenses. A Binary Ninja port exists in the author's separate binja-JNIAnalyzer repository.

resources.name: IMSProg
resources.description: Qt desktop programmer that reads, writes, erases and verifies I2C, SPI and MicroWire EEPROMs, FeRAM, DataFlash and SPI NOR/NAND flash chips through low-cost CH341A, CH347T and FT232H USB programmers. It identifies SPI flash by JEDEC ID against an editable chip database, shows SFDP, status and security registers, scans NAND bad blocks, and keeps the chip image in a hex-editor buffer that can save or load parts of the image and import or export Intel HEX. Companion programs edit the chip database and update it from the author's web server.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.9.1, published 2026-09-04 with a Flatpak and a macOS arm64 build; the ChangeLog says it added FT232H v1.2 support. The reviewed main commit is 41 commits ahead, mostly macOS packaging and path fixes. README lists Debian, Fedora, openSUSE, AUR, ALT, ROSA and RED OS packages and an Ubuntu PPA; a Windows build is maintained separately by a third party.

Builds with CMake, g++ or clang, Qt5 or Qt6 with the Linguist tools, libusb 1.0, libftdi, pkg-config and udev on Linux, where README says Debian before 11 and Ubuntu before 20.04 are unsupported, or with Homebrew packages and the Xcode command-line tools on macOS. build_all.sh compiles and installs the programmer, database editor and updater with the udev rules and chip database. CI builds Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 DEB packages, a Fedora 44 RPM checked with rpmlint and a macOS 15 build; no automated tests are published.

Needs one of the supported USB programmers and, per README, adapters for 93xxx MicroWire, 45xxx DataFlash, WSON-8 SPI NAND and 1.8 V chips. CH347 devices do not support MicroWire, and Verify and Check erase do not skip bad blocks on NAND chips. Images come from the user's own chips; the repository holds no firmware dumps, only its IMSProg.Dat chip database, which the updater downloads from the author's antenna-dvb-t2.ru site.

GPL-3.0-or-later per README, with SNANDer-derived parts under GPL-2.0+, QHexEdit2 under LGPL-2.1 and CH347 code under BSD-1-Clause. IMSProg transfers chip contents only; analysing a dump needs other tools.

resources.name: rbasefind
resources.description: Multithreaded Rust command-line tool that brute-forces the load address of a flat 32-bit firmware image, reimplementing mncoppola's basefind.py and rsaxvc's basefind.cpp. It records the offsets of ASCII strings, reads every 32-bit word as a possible pointer, and ranks candidate base addresses by how many strings each one would turn into pointer targets. The README calls it a simple heuristic that works rather well on some ARM (non-Thumb) binaries and will not work miracles.
requirements: Latest tag at review: v0.1.3, on the reviewed master commit of 2020-09-27, with no GitHub release binaries and no crates.io package. Build it from source with Cargo; Cargo.toml declares no edition and Cargo.lock is ignored, so dependencies such as clap 2.33 and regex 1.3 resolve within their version ranges at build time. The README's TODO lists an automatic mode that would detect endianness and narrow the offset around the best match.

Input is a flat 32-bit image supplied by the user, little-endian by default or big-endian with -b; no firmware or samples are included. By default it takes NUL-terminated printable ASCII strings of at least 10 characters, reads 4-byte-aligned words from the start of the file as pointers, and tests candidate bases every 0x1000 bytes across the 32-bit address space, splitting the range across one thread per CPU core. The whole file is loaded into memory.

Results are a ranked list of candidate bases with match counts, 10 by default, that the analyst must confirm. The README's example takes about 41 seconds on 8 threads for one image and shows that raising the minimum string length to 100 cuts the time at some cost in accuracy. Unit tests cover only the address-range split between threads, and there is no CI.
MIT License (2017, Scott Gayou). Analyzed firmware keeps its own terms.

resources.name: Link Pi ENCx encoders (unofficial documentation)
resources.description: A single-README notebook, kept since 2021 by an owner with no ties to the vendor, on the internals of LinkPi ENC-series video encoders and the TBS 2603SE, which share one firmware line; the author's first units use the F3520D board with a HiSilicon Hi3520DV400. It covers the Linux system and PHP web interface, undocumented features and internal pages, intercom and tally interfaces, default accounts and network services with hardening steps, HiSilicon media-pipeline diagnostics, board pinouts including the UART, firmware recovery, and translated release notes for firmware updates from 2020 to 2026.
requirements: The reviewed main commit, of 2026-07-13, added release notes for firmware 5.2.0 (build 20260531). Findings come from the author's and contributors' own devices; several sections are marked outdated, the release notes are machine-translated from Chinese, and the README says TinyENC1 appears to ship different firmware that the author has not examined.

The procedures need the reader's own encoder and shell access to it. Firmware upgrade and full-flash packages come only from LinkPi's official download pages; none are committed. The repository's only other file is v4l2-ctl, a prebuilt ARM uClibc build of the V4L2 control utility added in 2021 without source or a license notice.

The README lists the vendor's default credentials and exposed services as a security warning, says LinkPi did not answer the author's reports, and gives hardening steps. A 2026 update credits AI for in-progress LD_PRELOAD timestamp hooks.
There is no license file, so the notes state no reuse terms; LinkPi firmware, software and documentation keep the vendor's rights.

resources.name: BinAssist
resources.description: Binary Ninja plugin by Jason Tang, who also wrote GhidrAssist and IDAssist, that adds a BinAssist sidebar for LLM-assisted analysis of the open binary. Its tabs explain functions at the LLIL, MLIL and HLIL levels and individual instructions, keep chats with context macros, MCP tool calling and an optional ReAct agent mode, propose function and variable renames, retypes and structures with confidence scores for review before they are applied, and build a semantic graph of functions and calls with community detection and source-to-sink taint paths, alongside retrieval over reference documents the analyst adds. A SymGraph tab imports and publishes names, graph data and documents through the hosted symgraph.ai service.
requirements: Latest release at review: 2.1.0, published 2026-05-25 as a source-only GitHub release without notes; the reviewed master commit is four commits later and adds a default Claude Code CLI path on macOS and updated model guidance. plugin.json requires Binary Ninja build 5000 or later and lists Linux, Windows and macOS, while the README gives both 4000 and 5000 as the minimum; the README names Linux as the primary development platform and calls Windows and macOS less tested. The packages in requirements.txt, including openai, anthropic, mcp 1.23.3 and whoosh, plus pywin32 on Windows, are installed into Binary Ninja's Python, and a separate Windows guide covers installing them into its user site-packages.

Analysis needs at least one configured LLM provider. The provider types cover Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and xAI API keys, OpenAI and Gemini subscription sign-in through OAuth, the local Claude Code CLI, a LiteLLM proxy for services such as AWS Bedrock and Azure, and local Ollama, LM Studio or Open WebUI endpoints; the documentation's provider tables also list an Anthropic OAuth type that the source does not define. Explanations, chats, Actions, agent runs and the graph's Semantic Analysis step send code from the binary to the active provider, so only a local or self-hosted endpoint keeps it on the machine, while the documentation describes re-indexing, Security Analysis and community detection without the model. The settings documentation places the analysis and RLHF feedback SQLite databases and the RAG index in a .binaryninja/binassist folder of the user's home directory, with analysis results keyed by the binary's SHA-256.

Programs come from the user's own Binary Ninja sessions; the plugin supplies no target binaries. Actions suggestions are applied only for the rows the user selects. Chats can reach MCP servers over streamable HTTP or SSE or launch them over stdio, and the documentation recommends the author's separate BinAssistMCP server for Binary Ninja analysis tools. In the Query tab, calls to tools whose names do not look read-only wait for an allow-once, allow-for-session or deny decision unless the chat accepts all tools, and this classification relies on tool-name keywords.

The SymGraph tab looks up the binary by SHA-256 without a key, but importing, publishing and uploading need a SymGraph API key, and publishing uploads the raw binary bytes, not the .bndb database, when the service does not already hold them. The repository has no tests or CI workflows. MIT, per LICENSE and plugin.json; Binary Ninja, model providers and SymGraph keep their own terms. The repository moved from jtang613/BinAssist.

resources.name: Supplementary AST-Based Deobfuscation Materials
resources.description: Companion code for the ReverseJS blog's 2022 series on deobfuscating JavaScript by manipulating abstract syntax trees with Babel. Each folder pairs a small obfuscated sample with a deobfuscator script and its output, covering string concealing (escape sequences, concatenation, string arrays and string encryption), constant folding including JSFuck-style code, substitution of constant variables, bracket-to-dot property access, dead-code removal, proxy functions and sequence expressions. The README presents them as short learning examples rather than a production deobfuscator.
requirements: Reviewed at the 2023-10-20 master commit, whose last change bumped @babel/traverse to 7.23.2. The blog lists seven posts in the series from May and June 2022, and folders such as Proxy Functions and Sequence Expressions have no matching post; the README warns that code not published on the blog is outdated and experimental, may be inaccurate or buggy, will likely not be updated and should not be used in a production deobfuscator.

Needs Node.js and npm install: package.json declares @babel/core and js-beautify, and the lockfile resolves @babel/parser, @babel/traverse and @babel/generator 7.23.x. Each script is run with node from its folder against the bundled sample. The String Encryption example also imports chrome-remote-interface-extra, which package.json does not list.

The samples are short, author-written obfuscations, so applying the techniques to other code needs the analyst's own inputs and checking. The VM-evaluation proxy-function example and the String Encryption example run code from the sample through Node's vm module, which Node.js documents as not a security mechanism. The author's later blog post reports CVE-2023-45133, an arbitrary-code-execution flaw in @babel/traverse before 7.23.2; the reviewed lockfile already resolves 7.23.2.
There are no tests or CI (the npm test script is a placeholder); expected outputs are committed beside each sample.
MIT (LICENSE), although package.json keeps npm's default ISC field.

resources.name: Cabana (standalone openpilot-cabana)
resources.description: Qt desktop CAN and CAN FD analyzer for decoding signals and reverse engineering unknown messages, split out of openpilot's cabana by Dean Lee, a frequent contributor to it, and now maintained on its own. It shows live per-bit change heatmaps, colors bytes by trend such as counters, toggles or noisy data, searches for signals by value or for bits that change together across messages and buses, mutes known bits, plots signals and edits DBC files with undo, while replaying openpilot drives with synchronized camera video. Sources are openpilot routes, Vector ASC, candump and PEAK TRC logs, SocketCAN, comma.ai Panda devices and live streams from a comma device, with a bundled set of opendbc DBC files.
requirements: The repository was created on 2025-12-30; its README says Cabana was originally developed as openpilot's CAN analysis tool and is now maintained independently, while openpilot still carries its own cabana under openpilot/tools/cabana. Latest release at review: v1.1.2, published 2026-03-16 as a Linux x86_64 tarball; the reviewed main commit, of 2026-06-09, is 66 commits ahead of it.

Source builds use SCons, a C++20 compiler and Qt 6 with Charts, SVG, SerialBus and OpenGL, plus capnproto, ZeroMQ, FFmpeg, libusb and the other Ubuntu/Debian packages the README lists, after initializing the openpilot-replay submodule from the same author. The README also names an AUR package for Arch Linux; SConstruct has a macOS arm64 branch, but the release workflow builds only on Ubuntu 22.04.

Analysis needs the user's own CAN data: logs or live buses from their own vehicle and interface, a Panda, or openpilot routes from their own comma device or comma connect account; --demo opens a demo route instead. The tool highlights candidate bits and signals.
MIT (LICENSE, copyright 2025 Dean Lee); the openpilot-replay submodule is also MIT, and data/opendbc holds 93 DBC files from comma.ai's MIT-licensed opendbc.

resources.name: Awesome RE-MCP
resources.description: A single-README list, written in July 2025, of 28 MCP servers for reverse-engineering tools, grouped into disassemblers and decompilers (IDA Pro, Ghidra, Binary Ninja and others), debuggers, static and dynamic analysis, network analysis, Android and security testing, with a one-line note per entry. It also names tools the author found without an MCP server, links four talks and guides, and points to starting material for writing new servers.
requirements: All seven commits were made on 2025-07-26 and the list has not changed since, so its entries, star counts and status remarks are a July 2025 snapshot. Some of its gap lists no longer hold: for example, it reports no WinDbg MCP server.

Rows give a name, link and short description without language, transport, maintenance status or license, although the contribution guidelines ask submitters for implementation status and transport. One debugger row links a PulseMCP directory page rather than a project.
The network and security-testing entries, such as a collection wrapping SQLMap, Nmap and other scanners, are dual-use tools. The list itself has no tests or verification of its entries.
The README says the list is released under the MIT license, but the repository has no license file and GitHub detects none. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: RE list (extremecoders-re)
resources.description: A single-README list of 71 open-source reverse-engineering tools with a focus on binary analysis, kept as one alphabetical list from Amoco to X86isa. Each entry gives the tool's name, a link and a one- to three-sentence description; the entries span binary analysis frameworks, lifters to LLVM and other intermediate representations, symbolic execution and emulation engines, dynamic instrumentation, whole-system and virtual-machine introspection platforms, decompilers, debugger front ends and deobfuscation tools.
requirements: The reviewed README, last changed on 2024-04-16 when Cannoli was added, links 71 entries in one alphabetical list without categories; the repository's 56 commits since October 2017 mostly add one tool at a time. These are list rows.

Entries give only a name, a link and a short description: 56 point to GitHub and 15 to project, university or vendor pages, such as Intel's Pin page and Tetrane's REVEN Free Edition page rather than source repositories. They state no maintenance status, supported platforms, license or date added.
The repository holds only README.md, with no license file or contribution guide, so the list states no reuse terms; linked tools keep their own licenses. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: DJI MIMO BLE artifacts: reconstructing the DJI Osmo control protocol
resources.description: Documents the Bluetooth Low Energy message format that DJI's proprietary MIMO app uses to control DJI Osmo devices, as artifacts produced while building the independent djictl CLI. The author derives the framing — a magic byte, length, protocol version, header CRC8, subsystem and message-id fields, a payload and a message CRC16 — from the author's own Android BLE logs, and ships a Wireshark dissector plus an annotated catalog of message types. Many message types are labelled as guesses or unknown; the author reports reaching working livestreaming on a DJI Osmo Pocket 3 and pausing further analysis.
requirements: Reviewed at the main-branch head of 2025-06-08. The repository is a set of reverse-engineering notes, not a runnable application: the companion tool djictl lives in a separate repository. The README describes a DJI Osmo Pocket 3.

The method uses the user's own Android phone: the README captures a Bluetooth HCI snoop log through an adb bug report, then opens it in Wireshark. No DJI firmware, app binary or account is committed to or required by this repository, and no captured log is included beyond one Wireshark screenshot.

mimo/ble/message_types.md lists annotated sample frames for about two dozen message types, and the Wireshark dissector in mimo/ble/wireshark-dissector/ maps message-type codes to names; many entries are marked with a question mark or as unknown, so the catalog is partial and author-interpreted rather than a complete specification.

Building the dissector needs Wireshark development headers and pkg-config on a system with a C compiler; its Makefile installs a shared-object plugin into the Wireshark 4.2 plugin directory. The notes record protocol observations only.
The repository is licensed CC0-1.0 (public-domain dedication). DJI, MIMO and Osmo remain trademarks of their owners.

resources.name: Reversecore MCP
resources.description: MCP server that puts radare2 with r2ghidra, LIEF, Capstone, YARA, CAPA, Detect It Easy, binwalk, angr, Volatility3, Scapy, Sleuth Kit and other engines behind 177 typed tools for AI clients such as Claude and Cursor. The tools cover disassembly and decompilation, binary parsing, string, IOC and capability extraction, ESIL emulation and symbolic execution, YARA scanning, memory, PCAP and disk forensics, source-code pattern scanning and session reports with MITRE ATT&CK mapping, alongside 22 guided analysis prompts and per-binary MCP resources. File access is confined to a configured sample workspace, and the server runs over stdio or HTTP/SSE, typically from the project's Docker image.
requirements: Latest release at review: v3.0.5, published 2026-09-28 on GitHub with a wheel, sdist, SBOMs and Sigstore bundles, on PyPI as reversecore-mcp and as a GHCR image. The reviewed main commit of 2026-10-17 is 147 commits ahead of that tag, while pyproject.toml still declares 3.0.5. The README's test and coverage figures (3,069 tests, 88%) are hard-coded badges and differ from the older counts in AGENTS.md.

Python 3.10–3.12, with angr installed only on Python 3.12. Local installs need radare2 on the PATH, plus Volatility3, Scapy and Sleuth Kit for forensics; the README recommends the Docker image, which bundles the engines, with x86 and Apple Silicon compose profiles. It lists Linux or macOS hosts or any Docker environment, at least 4 cores, 8 GB RAM and 20 GB storage; Redis backs the task queue and result cache, and an SQLite memory database keeps notes across sessions.

Binaries, memory images, PCAPs and disk images come from the analyst and are mounted into the workspace, where path validation confines tool access. Optional container sandboxing for dynamic-analysis tools is disabled by default, and HTTP mode accepts only loopback clients unless MCP_API_KEY is set. Some tools and prompts target exploit and PoC development.

CI runs linting, type checks, Bandit, pip-audit and CodeQL, unit tests on Python 3.10–3.12 with an 85% coverage gate, security-boundary, integration and MCP client end-to-end suites, and a wheel build-and-install check; ClusterFuzzLite and nightly fuzzing run separately. Test fixtures include small synthetic vulnerable C targets with seeds, proof-of-concept inputs and ASan logs, and scratch/binaries holds only a hello.c source.

MIT; the wrapped engines and the packages in the Docker image keep their own licenses. ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md records a 2026-08-22 brief asking an orchestrating agent to dispatch subagents for transport hardening, prompt expansion and output optimization, so parts of the code were developed with AI agents.

resources.name: r2pipe
resources.description: radare2's official scripting interface, with implementations for more than two dozen languages in one repository. Every binding sends radare2 command strings and returns their text output, the design behind r_core_cmd_str(), and the README recommends asking for JSON output and decoding it into native objects instead of using the C API. Bindings connect through the R2PIPE_IN/R2PIPE_OUT pipes of a script run from inside r2, a spawned r2 -q0 process, TCP, HTTP or radare2's RAP protocol, many offer asynchronous calls, and r2pipe scripts can also implement radare2 plugins such as disassemblers, IO backends or ESIL syscall handlers.
requirements: The newest GitHub release at review is 6.1.2, published 2026-04-20 as source only, and the reviewed master commit is 54 commits ahead of it; each language is also packaged separately. The Python package r2pipe 2.1.0 (Python 3.6+) was uploaded to PyPI on 2026-10-19, matching python/pyproject.toml, while npm's r2pipe was at 2.8.6 from 2024-01-16 and r2pipe-ts at 0.4.0. The Rust crate lives in the separate r2pipe.rs repository, and the README's capability table marks which backends each language supports.

Apart from the WebAssembly variant, every binding talks to a radare2 process, either spawned locally or reached as a TCP, HTTP or RAP server, and command strings and output formats follow the radare2 version in use. CI installs the radare2 6.1.4 Debian packages on Ubuntu 24.04 and tests the Perl, Python, TypeScript, Ruby, Tcl, Vala, Swift and .NET bindings.

python-wasm is a separate r2pipe_wasm package that runs radare2's wasi-api WebAssembly build inside Python through Wasmer's Python SDK 1.1.0, downloading the newest stable release with that asset by default. Its README verifies only CPython 3.9 on Linux x86_64, pins its examples to 6.1.4 and reports that the published 6.2.2 API module traps during startup.

GitHub detects no repository-wide license. The Python, Python WASM, Go, .NET, Haskell and Erlang directories carry MIT license files and the npm packages declare MIT. Binaries to analyze come from the user, and the TypeScript tests bundle one fixture, typescript/tests/fixtures/wasm-api.wasm.

resources.name: Aptio V UEFI Editor
resources.description: Browser-based editor for the setup menus of AMI Aptio V UEFI firmware, offered as an alternative to AMIBCP. From four sections the user takes from their own BIOS image, it rebuilds the setup forms and their references and shows each setting's VarStore, offset, size, options, failsafe and optimal defaults, access level and Suppress If conditions. Changes to top-level menu targets, suppressions, access levels and defaults are written back into the section files with a change log, and a session can be saved as hash-checked JSON; a separate IFR-Formatter.js script condenses IFRExtractor-RS output into a per-setting VarStore and offset listing.
requirements: Reviewed master commit 44e8c9b (2026-03-15, hash-check changes); the previous source change was in April 2025. There are no releases or tags: the app, version 0.1.0 in its source, is served from GitHub Pages by a workflow that builds it with Node 20, npm ci and Vite. Building locally uses the React, Mantine and TypeScript package.json scripts.

Inputs come from the user's own Aptio V UEFI image, found with UEFITool NE: the Setup PE32 image section, its text output from IFRExtractor-RS 1.6.1 (the only version the editor accepts), the AMITSE PE32 image section and the setupdata body. The page reads them in the browser, rejects non-UEFI IFR output, and checks saved JSON against the files' SHA-256 hashes. The repository includes no firmware images or extracted sections, only screenshots of the tools.
README says the modified files are put back with UEFITool 0.28.0 and that setting visibility methods vary between firmware, so either may need trying.
The repository has no license file, and package.json marks the package private, so reuse terms are not stated. No automated tests are published.

resources.name: DiztinGUIsh
resources.description: Windows disassembler for Super NES ROMs in which the user marks bytes as code or data, steps through 65816 code while the tool tracks the M and X flags and the data bank and direct page registers, adds labels and comments, and exports assembly for the asar assembler that the README says compiles back into the original binary. Execution context can come from BizHawk or BSNES trace logs, BSNES usage maps and BizHawk code/data logs, or live capture over a socket from a custom bsnes-plus build. Project files keep the annotations in merge-friendly XML with a link and checksum for the ROM rather than the ROM itself, so several people can work on one disassembly.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.5.1.0, published 2025-12-07 as a self-contained Windows x64 build; the reviewed master commit of 2026-08-09 is 106 commits later and adds, among other changes, Avalonia versions of several dialogs and a second Diz.AvaloniaUI-Beta executable. The WinForms app targets net10.0-windows, and CI builds, tests and publishes it on Windows with the .NET 10 SDK, while contributing.md still asks for Windows 10+ and .NET SDK 8 or higher.

Input is a SNES ROM file the user supplies; the repository includes no ROMs. HELP.md says project files (.diz, which is gzip-compressed XML, or uncompressed .dizraw) store a link to the ROM with its internal name and checksum instead of the ROM, so they can be shared without it. Live trace capture needs the custom bsnes-plus build from binary1230/bsnes-plus, which listens on port 27015, rather than stock BSNES+, and the README suggests an asar fork with a relative-addressing fix.

The test project bundles small .asm samples, a 4 MB binary trace-log fixture (ct-binary-tracelog7.758s-60fps-locked.bin) from a 7.8-second emulator capture that only commented-out performance-test code references, and SuperFamicheck 1.0's superfamicheck.exe as a helper; tools/dizpack holds Python packing scripts and tools/dizpack-game/ct a Chrono Trigger (US) LZSS codec. Disassembly depends on the user's marking and stepping: the README says the program pauses for input whenever it cannot disassemble accurately, and lists SPC700 and SuperFX support as planned. CI runs the repository's xUnit tests, but no per-game results confirm that exported assembly rebuilds the original.

GPL-3.0 per LICENSE.md, with third-party library licenses listed in Diz.App.Winforms/dist/docs. Exported assembly contains the ROM's code and data and remains subject to the rights of the game's owner.

resources.name: awesome-te
resources.description: A public-domain directory, started in June 2026, of hacking projects for Teenage Engineering devices: custom firmware, reverse-engineering notes and protocol documentation, tools, hardware mods, teardown and recovery guides and community hubs for the OP-1, OP-Z, OP-XY, TP-7, SP-1 Stem Player, EP series, Pocket Operators and other gear. One-line entries are grouped by device and task, each with a maintainer-assigned active, dormant or archived marker, and the scope rule admits only released, TE-specific projects.
