requirements: The reviewed README, committed 2026-10-20 and marked as last reviewed that day, has 195 status-marked rows under 11 device sections and a cross-device section, some of them bundling several links: 136 marked active, 56 dormant and 3 archived. Under the contribution guide the marker reflects activity in the past 12 months; the weekly lychee workflow only checks that links resolve.

Entries mix open-source projects, commercial apps and forum, wiki and repair pages, ranging from SysEx, file-transfer and file-format documentation to Ghidra Blackfin support, and include a few AI tools such as an SP-1 reference packaged as a Claude agent skill and an MCP server for the OP-1 field. Several firmware and flashing entries warn that they erase stored data or can brick a device.

A few rows point to unofficial mirrors of OP-1 and OP-1 field firmware and to an OP-1 firmware decryptor; the list itself recommends Teenage Engineering's official downloads. Device firmware keeps its vendor's terms, and each linked project keeps its own license.
The list and its contributions are dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. An independent discovery list.

resources.name: FirmLoader
resources.description: IDA plugin that applies a microcontroller's memory map to a raw firmware image: once the analyst picks an MCU model, it creates RAM and other memory segments, adds peripheral segments with named registers and, where a vector table is described, labels its entries and turns the handlers they point to into functions. The README compares it to IDA's built-in SVD loader, but it uses a simpler JSON description that can be written by hand from public datasheets. The reviewed commit bundles 813 descriptions for Microchip/Atmel, ST, NXP, TI, Silicon Labs and other MCUs.
requirements: The only release is tag 1.0, titled “IDA 8.X” and published 2024-12-05; it points to a February 2024 commit. The reviewed main commit 5c9c1a1, the last change on 2024-12-05, is four commits ahead: a contributed pull request adds IDA 9.0 support and another adds an STM32L4x1 SRAM2 segment.

Installed by copying firmloader.py and the firmloader_data folder into IDA's plugins directory; it needs IDA with IDAPython, and the plugin code uses Python 3.8+ syntax. The analyst loads the image at the base address the processor documentation gives, renames the main code segment to ROM and chooses the model under Edit > FirmLoader; applying it marks the ROM segment for IDA auto-analysis.

Input is a firmware image the analyst has already read out of a microcontroller; the repository contains no firmware, only the plugin, MCU description JSON files, a data_template.json and two README images. Of the 813 descriptions, 812 are 32-bit; the 16-bit ATmega328 one lists no peripherals, and four for SPC5 and AURIX TC27x parts have no vector table; README says that where a series has several memory sizes, every unit was generated with the largest RAM. Other MCUs need a hand-written description.
Apache-2.0. README names SPC560B64x as a purely hand-written description and otherwise presents the files as a supplement to SVD data without documenting how they were generated.

resources.name: Cat Printer BLE: reconstructing the MXW01 thermal printer protocol
resources.description: Replaces the vendor phone app for the MXW01 “cat printer”, a small Bluetooth Low Energy thermal printer, with a Windows command-line client. The author reports starting from the iOS-only Moblin implementation and then reverse-engineering the vendor's phone app further, and the client sends CRC8-checked commands to one GATT service while streaming 384-pixel image lines in 1-bit or 4-bit grayscale. Several command IDs remain marked as unknown, and the author tested only this one printer model.
requirements: Reviewed at the release 1.2.0 commit of 2025-05-22. The tool prints images with Bayer or Floyd–Steinberg dithering, feeds or retracts paper, and reads battery, paper, temperature and state information; README says it is not an editor and that other printer models are not planned because the author has none to test.

Requires the user's own MXW01 printer. The repository contains only original C# source and a photo; the vendor app the author analysed, any decompiled code and any traffic captures are not included, and no account or vendor software is needed at runtime.

Windows only: the project targets .NET 8 for Windows 10 build 19041 or later with native AOT publishing, using the InTheHand.BluetoothLE and SixLabors.ImageSharp packages; the README asks for the .NET 8 Runtime.

CatPrinter.cs names the GATT service and its command, notification and data characteristics and lists the command IDs, with comments marking several as unknown or guessed. The repository has no test suite or CI, so printing behaviour is author-reported.
MIT license.

resources.name: JS-Deobfuscator (0x1Avram)
resources.description: Node.js deobfuscator for JavaScript produced by Timofey Kachalov's javascript-obfuscator, also offered as obfuscator.io. It parses the sample with esprima and runs eleven stages named after the obfuscator's own, which remove injected self-defending and debug-protection code, unwind control-flow flattening and dead-code injection, restore converted literals and object keys, replace string-array calls with the decoded strings, simplify the result and recursively process code passed to eval. String-array code is detected automatically or supplied as separate files, and an Examples folder pairs original, obfuscated and deobfuscated samples.
requirements: Inactive since the reviewed main commit, a README update on 2023-04-17. The last release, 1.0.7 (2022-12-29), attaches binaries.zip with standalone Windows and Linux builds made with pkg, while package.json still reports 1.0.2. The README says it was developed with Node.js 16.15 and worked with obfuscator versions current at the time; output from older obfuscator versions may produce a different AST.

Run from source after npm install (esprima, escodegen, esquery, estraverse, winston and yargs) with node index.js -i input -o output. When automatic detection fails, the string array, its wrappers, the wrapper names and the rotate code are passed as separate files with -s, -w, -n and -r. esprima does not parse all newer JavaScript syntax, so the README suggests transpiling such input with Babel first.

The README warns that the code is not secure and should run only in an isolated environment such as a virtual machine: string-array decoding evaluates code taken from the sample with eval inside the deobfuscator's own Node.js process. The identifier- and property-renaming stages are empty placeholders, so obfuscated names are not recovered.

Supply the obfuscated script yourself. The Examples text files are derived from small snippets, javascript-obfuscator's example script (BSD-2-Clause) and javascript-algorithms (MIT), with both licenses included.
MIT (LICENSE). A different project from ben-sb javascript-deobfuscator, whose npm package is also named js-deobfuscator; this one is used from its repository or release binaries.

resources.name: a0rfid: an open driver for A0-protocol UHF RFID readers
resources.description: Reconstructs the A0 serial protocol of R2000-family 915 MHz UHF RFID desktop readers, which ship with only Windows software and an Android app, from the vendor app's native command encoder rather than its misleading Java SDK. A userspace CH340 driver, a Python CLI and GUI, and a small Android app then talk to the reader directly for inventory and tag-memory reads. docs/PROTOCOL.md records the frame layout, checksum, command table, response formats and the different field orders of READ and WRITE.
requirements: The reviewed main commit of 2026-09-17 is the second of two commits, with no tags or releases. docs/REVERSE.md describes decompiling the vendor APK, finding that the app bypasses its Java codec and calls libnative-lib.so through JNI, reading per-command field layouts from that library's rfid_encode() jump table, and then confirming the frames on hardware. The result is a protocol description and new host software; no reader firmware or vendor app is recovered, and the reader model is not named beyond the R2000 family.

Using the tools requires a compatible A0-protocol reader on its CH340 USB-UART at 115200 8N1, plus tags to test with. Repeating the analysis requires the vendor's own software package and manual, which are not included: REVERSE.md states that the repository contains no vendor code, only frames observed on the wire and code written from them. android/RFID助手.apk is the project's own prebuilt app, built from android/app by android/build.sh.

The Python tools need Python 3 with pyusb and pyserial. --port USB uses the bundled ch340_usb.py userspace driver, which on macOS needs Homebrew libusb; Linux can instead use the stock ch341 kernel driver through /dev/ttyUSB0. The Android app needs Android 7.0+ with USB host; android/build.sh assumes macOS/Homebrew paths, JDK 17, Android SDK platform 34 and build-tools 34.0.0.

test_offline.py runs 17 hardware-free checks of checksums, frame construction and response parsing, several against frames the author recorded from a reader reporting firmware V2.4.1, and docs/ANDROID.md reports 261 offline Android checks against simulated tags. The author reports confirming the read and write paths on one reader and installing and reading with the app on one DJI Smart Controller Enterprise (Android 7.1.2); the app's multi-bank write features were checked only in simulation. The docs also note occasional firmware hangs and a 20 dBm maximum power on the author's unit.
MIT License (2026, a0rfid contributors); the vendor software, SDK and reader firmware keep their own terms. Write, lock and kill commands change real tags.

resources.name: Android Reverse
resources.description: Android app, published only as release APKs, that runs an APK reverse-engineering workflow entirely on the phone, from package extraction and Java decompilation to native analysis, editing and rebuilding. It extracts APK, XAPK and split APKS packages from storage or installed apps, decompiles each class with Jadx (with fallback and IR modes), CFR, Procyon, JD-Core, Krakatau or Vineflower, analyzes native libraries through an embedded radare2 with pseudo-C, assembly, hex, control-flow-graph and call-graph views, and since v20 edits resources, binary XML, the manifest and smali before rebuilding and signing the APK. A built-in MCP server lets MCP clients edit those project files while rebuilding stays a manual step; the README also lists Flutter Dart AOT analysis through Unflutter and Unity il2cpp metadata parsing.
requirements: Latest release at review: v20, published 2026-08-24, with arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and universal APKs; the README's badges name those two architectures and mark the project as in active development. The first release, on 2026-06-17, said editing and repacking were not yet available. Neither the README nor the release notes state a minimum Android version.

At the reviewed commit the repository holds only the README and six screenshots: no app source, build files or license file, and GitHub detects no license, so the app's terms are unstated. The README credits radare2, Sora Editor and the CFR, Procyon, JD-Core, Krakatau, Vineflower and Jadx engines without naming their licenses.

According to the README everything runs on the device, with no PC, ADB or desktop tools. Users supply the packages or installed apps they analyze, and its disclaimer limits use to education and to security research on apps whose authors have given explicit permission.

The MCP server is described only in one README paragraph and the release notes, with no transport, port, tool list or setup steps, and open issue #2 reports edits made through MCP that did not appear in the app. The README does not say how its Smali Explainer produces explanations.

resources.name: eCapture
resources.description: eBPF-based Linux and Android tool that attaches uprobes to TLS libraries such as OpenSSL, BoringSSL, GnuTLS and NSS, and to Go's TLS stack, recording the plaintext a process sends and receives without a proxy or an installed CA certificate, so analysts can inspect an application's encrypted traffic on a host they control. Output modes write plaintext text, NSS key logs, or pcapng files with embedded TLS secrets for Wireshark and tshark, and a text mode can rebuild complete HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 messages from the captured stream. Separate modules audit bash and zsh commands and MySQL and PostgreSQL queries.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.9.0, published 2026-10-24; the reviewed master commit is identical to that tag. Release assets are Linux amd64, arm64 and loong64 archives and .deb packages plus Android amd64 and arm64 archives; the Docker image is Linux only. The README states that Windows and macOS are not supported; the separate eCaptureQ GUI can connect from them to a remote eCapture service.

Needs Linux kernel 4.18+ on x86_64, 5.5+ on aarch64 or 6.6+ on LoongArch64, or Android on x86_64 or aarch64. Loading the eBPF programs requires root or, per the minimum-privileges guide, CAP_BPF, CAP_PERFMON and CAP_SYS_PTRACE on kernel 5.8+ (CAP_SYS_ADMIN on older kernels), plus CAP_NET_ADMIN for pcapng mode. Source builds need Go 1.26+, clang and LLVM 9+, cmake 3.18.4+, libelf and the pinned libpcap submodule; make nocore builds for kernels without BTF.

Analysts choose the library or program to observe: the tls module locates the system OpenSSL through ld.so.conf paths or takes --libssl, which can also name a statically linked program, and gotls takes the Go program's ELF path; pcapng mode also needs a network interface and capture filter. Pcap mode records TLS-protected HTTP/1.x and HTTP/2 over TCP and HTTP/3 over QUIC, while the pcapng text source rebuilds only HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 over TCP. The project documents root-only end-to-end tests per module (make e2e).

Apache-2.0; libpcap is a git submodule and the bin, dist, deps and bytecode directories hold only placeholders. Captured plaintext and keys can contain passwords, tokens and personal data: the project's defense-and-detection guide asks for written authorization before production use, scoping capture to chosen processes with --pid and handling the data under organizational policy, and describes how to detect eBPF capture tools.

resources.name: AutoProber
resources.description: Flying-probe control stack meant to let a coding agent or an operator take a circuit board on a GRBL 3018-style CNC from locating it on the plate, through XYZ-tagged USB-microscope frames and an annotated map of pads, pins and chips, to probing targets the operator has approved. Python wrappers, a Flask dashboard and AGENTS.md safety rules run every move under an oscilloscope-monitored optical endstop that triggers feed hold and a STOP state with no automatic recovery. The published code covers device control, camera-to-motion calibration and map and probe-candidate review; the README presents locating, stitching and annotating the board as agent tasks.
requirements: README calls the reviewed commit ff0e01f ("1st Release", 2026-04-16) a source-available release candidate; pyproject.toml declares version 0.1.0, no releases are published, and the RELEASE_MANIFEST.md the README cites is not in the repository. There have been no commits since.

The tested hardware is a GRBL-compatible 3018-style CNC over USB serial, a UVC USB microscope served by mjpg_streamer, a Siglent oscilloscope over LAN/SCPI (Channel 4 for the optical endstop, Channel 1 for pogo-probe measurement), an optical endstop on an external 5 V supply, an optional Matter power strip controlled through chip-tool, and the 3D-printed toolhead parts in cad/. docs/BOM.md lists the parts.

Runs on a Linux control host with Python 3.8+ via uv; pyproject.toml declares only Flask and pyserial, while the calibration script also imports OpenCV. Lab hosts, ports and paths come from environment variables in the example config. README says calibration must be generated on the machine that moves and the microscope-to-probe offset measured before real probing, and that the dashboard must not be exposed to untrusted networks. No automated tests are published.

Works with whatever agent the operator uses: README has it ingest the project and drive the dashboard or Python scripts, and AGENTS.md sets the safety rules; no MCP server or specific agent is bundled. README limits use to equipment and targets the user is authorized to test.
PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 with a required copyright notice for GainSec; commercial use needs a separate paid license.

resources.name: MCP Reversing Dataset (mrexodia)
resources.description: Three worked examples by mrexodia of a language model reverse-engineering crackme binaries in IDA Pro through his IDA Pro MCP server. Each folder holds the input binary, a README giving its origin, the prompt and the model, the agent's own report and the exported session transcript, so readers can follow every tool call, rename, retype and comment the agent made on the database. The tasks cover a small Linux password check, an obfuscated Linux flag checker and a Windows crackme that, according to the agent's report, routes its checks through vectored exception handling.
requirements: Three tasks, committed between 2025-03-28 and 2025-04-14 and unchanged since. Each folder's README gives the input, the prompt and the model, next to the agent's report.md and an exported task-history.md transcript; crackme03 adds the agent's solve.py and a launcher that runs the ELF through WSL. All three runs used Claude 3.7 Sonnet in Roo Cline or Roo Code with the author's IDA Pro MCP server.

The repository bundles the three challenge binaries it analyzes: VEHMeme.exe, a Windows crackme the README credits to Brit and xenocidewiki from an earlier CTF; crackme03.elf, compiled with GCC 11.4.0 on Ubuntu 22.04 from a NoraCodes crackmes source file; and transformed.elf, described as a modified version of babush's mcp-job-security obfuscation project. They are small CTF-style samples rather than commercial software, but the repository states no redistribution terms for them.

Following a run needs IDA Pro, which is commercial, the IDA Pro MCP server and an MCP client. The prompts ask the model to rename, retype and comment the database and write a report, and the crackme03 prompt forbids brute forcing. The transcripts are single, unscored runs: the crackme03 report records a password confirmed by running the binary, the mcp-job-security report names the flag it extracted, and the VEHMeme report explains the exception-based check without stating a flag. These are author-published results.
There is no license file, so reuse terms for the transcripts and reports are unstated; the README welcomes contributions, but only the original three tasks exist.

resources.name: jsc-decompile-mozjs-34
resources.description: PHP decoder and decompiler for SpiderMonkey 34 JavaScript bytecode, which the README says may handle .jsc files compiled by cocos2d-x. It parses the XDR-serialized scripts with their atoms, constants, objects, regular expressions and try and scope notes, decodes instructions from a SpiderMonkey 34 opcode table and rebuilds approximate JavaScript for each function context, while a second script prints the decoded operations instead. The author describes it as unfinished and as an example of how a JavaScript virtual machine works.
requirements: No releases; the last commit, on 2021-07-27, fixed global-variable and object-initialization opcodes, and the README says the project may no longer be updated and is not complete. It targets SpiderMonkey 34 bytecode: the README notes that opcodes differ between SpiderMonkey versions, lists the magic values for bytecode versions 33 to 47, and says the tool does not check the magic, so files from nearby versions may partly decode.

Runs on PHP 7.0 or later (the README says it still works on 7.4) after composer install, which only generates the autoloader. php run.php prints reconstructed code for each script context, and php scan.php prints atoms, decoded operations, constants and regular expressions for files that do not decompile. Input .jsc files come from the user; the repository holds no sample files or tests, and the source has no decryption or decompression step, so it reads only plain XDR bytecode.

The README reports a fatal bug when decompiling deeply nested contexts and says output is not runnable, with generated names for local variables that the compiler discarded, so results should be checked against the scan.php operations. There is no license file, and composer.json declares the package proprietary, so the repository grants no reuse terms; recovered scripts remain subject to the rights of the application's owner.

resources.name: Andromeda
resources.description: Interactive command-line tool by Lasha Khasaia for first-pass reverse engineering of Android APKs, written in C/C++ for speed. It unpacks an APK, parses AndroidManifest.xml, the signing certificate and the DEX files at the archive root, then opens a shell with tab completion for listing permissions, activities, services, receivers and likely entry points, listing and searching classes, methods and strings, disassembling a method's Dalvik bytecode and listing, hashing or extracting native libraries. Further commands report whether the app is debuggable, a creation date taken from its certificate, URL and email strings, and a guess at whether it was written in Java, Kotlin or Xamarin .NET.
requirements: Inactive early-stage project: the README says the tool is in the early development stage, and its 29 commits run from 2019-09-22 to the reviewed master commit of 2020-03-14, which removes an editor folder. There are no tags or releases, and GitHub does not mark the repository archived. Documenting the tool is still a TODO; the README shows the command list only as a screenshot, and the author notes very limited Android experience.

Built from source with make, which compiles everything with clang++ in C++17 mode (-std=c++1z) and debug flags (-g -O0), linking zlib and OpenSSL's libcrypto; the README's apt commands install clang, libz-dev and libssl-dev. The Makefile adds libstdc++fs on Linux and Homebrew openssl@1.1 paths on macOS; Windows is not covered.

Input is an APK supplied by the user, run as ./bin/andromeda app.apk. The path must end in .apk, and the tool stops if the unpacked archive lacks AndroidManifest.xml or a DEX file at its root, so bare DEX files are not accepted. The repository contains no sample APKs.

Apache-2.0 license. third_party.md lists the bundled libraries with their own licenses: Google's dexter slicer (Apache-2.0), Claud Xiao's AxmlParser, linenoise-cpp, miniz and pugixml; the tree also bundles the digestpp hashing headers.

resources.name: Dex-Editor-Android
resources.description: Work-in-progress Android app for editing DEX files on the device, built on a modified in-tree copy of Google's smali, baksmali and dexlib2. It loads one or more DEX files into a class tree and opens classes as smali in a Sora Editor view with method, field and string lists, label jumps, search and replace, method flow diagrams and Jadx decompilation of a class or method to Java, then deletes classes or recompiles the edited DEX files. The README credits MT Manager for the app's logic and interface ideas.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.0-sora-editor, published 2026-06-09 with one app-release.apk, while the README's sample-app link still points to v1.3_final of 2025-04-29; the reviewed main commit of 2026-07-29 adds later fixes and merged contributor pull requests. The README lists DEX format versions 40 and, partially, 41, and its to-do list still has batch class insertion and extraction and a direct class renamer.

Build with Android Studio, JDK 17 or 21, Gradle 9.5.0 and Android Gradle Plugin 9.2.1; app/build.gradle compiles against SDK 37 with minSdk 24 and targetSdk 28, and the README also mentions Sketchware Pro on Java 11. Dependencies include jadx-core 1.4.7, Sora Editor 0.23.6 and bundled antlr and commons-io JARs. CI builds debug and unsigned release APKs, and the only unit and instrumented tests are the Android Studio examples.

The file picker selects DEX files the user supplies. An AI Explanation screen that the README does not mention sends a smali method picked from the method list, with a default register-usage prompt or a user-edited one, to Google's Gemini 2.0 Flash API using an API key entered in settings; method flow diagrams are drawn locally with a bundled Graphviz viz.js build.

LICENSE is Apache-2.0 (copyright 2024-26 Krushna Chandra), but the README adds that the code may not be used in private projects and that contributions are welcome only in this repository, restrictions Apache-2.0 itself does not contain, so reuse terms are unclear; the in-tree smali code keeps Google's BSD-style notices.

resources.name: GREASE
resources.description: Galois's command-line tool, Ghidra plug-in and Haskell library for checking properties of binaries with under-constrained symbolic execution. It lifts AArch32, PowerPC or x86_64 ELF executables and shared objects, or LLVM bitcode, into a control-flow graph, simulates each function from fully symbolic registers and grows the inferred memory layout after out-of-bounds accesses, then reports likely undefined behavior such as division by zero or invalid memory access together with concretized arguments. Built-in overrides, or user overrides written in Crucible's S-expression language, model external library functions, and the plug-in presents results in Ghidra.
requirements: No tagged releases at review: the installation guide offers a nightly Docker image built from main (ghcr.io/galoisinc/grease:nightly) or a source build, and the same documentation is published at galoisinc.github.io/grease. The reviewed main commit is dated 2026-09-24; Galois introduced the tool in a blog post dated 2025-03-19.

Source builds need GHC 9.6, 9.8 or 9.10, cabal-install 3.6+ and the repository's git submodules, including Galois's macaw, crucible, what4 and elf-edit. A standalone binary also needs one of the SMT solvers bitwuzla, cvc4, cvc5, yices or z3; it defaults to yices, which CI tests at 2.6.5, and the Docker image includes the solvers. The Ghidra plug-in needs Ghidra 11.0+ and a local grease binary.

Supply the ELF binary or LLVM bitcode yourself. By default every known function is analyzed; entry points can instead be chosen by symbol, address or core dump. The limitations page lists single-threaded analysis only, k-bounded data structures, loops and recursion, skipped calls through symbolic function pointers, no stack-buffer-overflow detection or heap-exhaustion modeling, limited string operations and no support for code that runs before main.

The repository commits small test fixtures built from adjacent C or assembly sources: about 200 AArch32, PowerPC and x86_64 ELF executables and shared objects under grease-exe/tests, plus test ELFs under grease-x86/test-data, ghidra-ecfs/src/test/resources/ecfs and the bundled screach reachability tool's test-data directories.
BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE). The README credits DARPA funding and carries Distribution Statement A, approved for public release. Reports depend on the inferred preconditions, bounds and overrides.

resources.name: IFDA (IoT Firmware Deep Analysis)
resources.description: Static analysis pipeline for extracted IoT firmware: pointed at one ELF or an unpacked root filesystem, it disassembles binaries with Capstone for x86, ARM/Thumb-2, AArch64 and MIPS, recovers functions, call graphs and exploit mitigations, and reports candidate issues from dangerous-function calls, call-graph taint paths, CVE correlation through cve-bin-tool, embedded secrets, script injection patterns and filesystem hardening checks. Reports come out as JSON, Markdown and a CycloneDX SBOM. Optional add-ons are Ghidra headless pseudocode, moria-based extraction of raw images and a Go service with a job queue, REST API, bilingual web UI and an LLM agent that triages a finished scan's findings.
requirements: The reviewed main commit 90c11c2 of 2026-09-21 is the 29th since the project began on 2026-06-10. CHANGELOG calls it v4.4, while the latest tag is V4.1, five commits earlier, there are no GitHub releases and pyproject.toml still declares 2.0.0. README describes a first iteration covering binary reverse engineering and vulnerability discovery; emulated or dynamic validation is listed as planned, not built.

The Python 3.10+ core needs capstone, pyelftools, cryptography, Pillow and cve-bin-tool, which README calls required: it keeps a local CVE database of 1 GB or more and needs network access on first use, and without it correlation falls back to a small curated database with a warning. Optional parts are yara-python, Ghidra headless with JDK 17+ for pseudocode, CuPy for GPU chart rendering, the Go 1.22+ service for the REST API and web UI, and the moria submodule, built with CMake and a C++20 compiler, for unpacking raw images. Linux and macOS are supported; Windows only through WSL2.

Input is a single ELF, an extracted firmware tree or, through the service's extract job, a raw image whose filesystem region the analyst chooses. README and the requirements document limit use to firmware the operator owns or is authorized to assess. The repository contains no firmware; its tests build cross-compiled x86_64, MIPS, ARM and AArch64 samples, and README reports 25 passed and 2 skipped with cross-compilers and Ghidra installed.

README calls decompilation-free static analysis heuristic: findings carry confidence scores, and taint results are candidate paths for analyst validation, not proven exploits. The optional AI analysis sends a finished scan to an OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-protocol endpoint the user configures, storing API keys encrypted; the model pulls finding evidence, pseudocode, init scripts and service data through tools. README says these features were tested with Claude models.
Apache-2.0, added on 2026-09-17; cve-bin-tool (GPL-3.0) is only invoked as a subprocess, and moria is MIT.

resources.name: smali/baksmali
resources.description: Assembler and disassembler for the dex format used by Android's Dalvik VM: baksmali turns dex, APK, odex and oat files into smali text, and smali assembles that text back into a dex file. The README says the syntax, loosely based on Jasmin's and dedexer's, supports the full dex format, including annotations and debug and line information. baksmali can also deodex odex and oat files and list a dex file's classes, methods, fields, strings and references, while the dexlib2 library reads and writes dex files from Java.
requirements: GitHub lists the repository as archived; its last push was on 2024-01-17, and the reviewed master head of 2022-03-08 is ten commits past v2.5.2, the last version, published as org.smali artifacts on Maven Central on 2021-03-03. The README still points downloads to the author's Bitbucket page. Google maintains a fork whose README says it exists because the original is not maintained; it renames the namespace to com.android.tools.smali and publishes 3.x releases (3.0.7 at review) on Google Maven.

Java command-line tools and libraries compiled for Java 8 and built with the bundled Gradle 6.8.2 wrapper; scripts/smali and scripts/baksmali are launcher wrappers for the jars. Users supply their own dex, APK, odex or oat files and can set the API level; analyzing or deodexing optimized files needs a matching boot classpath, which for oat files can be the device's boot.oat. dexlib2's version map at this commit stops at dex 039 (API 28) and maps newer ART versions to API 29.

The repository includes small test-fixture dex files under baksmali/src/test/resources and dexlib2/src/test/resources, hand-written smali examples, and deodexerant, a device-side C helper built in an AOSP tree that dumps Dalvik's inline method table for baksmali's -T option. No other dex, APK or system images are committed.

There is no LICENSE file, so GitHub detects none; NOTICE releases Ben Gruver's code and Google-copyrighted changes under BSD-style three-clause licenses and says portions taken from the Android Open Source Project are used under Apache-2.0.

resources.name: HTTP Toolkit
resources.description: Open-source HTTP(S) debugging proxy for Windows, Linux and macOS that sets up interception for browsers, terminals, backend runtimes, Electron apps and Android devices, then shows the full headers and body of every request and response with body decoding, inline header documentation and filtering. Its transparent proxy handles plain HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP/2 and WebSockets on one port; breakpoints rewrite live requests or responses, and a built-in client sends custom requests. This repository is the project's umbrella README and issue tracker, while the UI, server, Mockttp proxy library, Android app and desktop shell live in sibling repositories.
requirements: At the reviewed commit this umbrella repository holds only the README, a security policy and a demo animation, and serves as the project's issue tracker. The product is built from sibling repositories: httptoolkit-ui (TypeScript and React), httptoolkit-server (Node.js, whose interceptor list covers Chromium-based browsers, Firefox, terminals, Electron, Android over ADB, Frida on Android and iOS, JVM processes and Docker containers), the Mockttp proxy library, the Android app and the Electron desktop shell.

Latest desktop release at review: v1.27.3, published 2026-10-20, with a Windows installer and zip, macOS x64 and arm64 DMGs and Linux x64 and arm64 AppImage, deb, rpm and zip builds. The desktop shell bundles the server and opens the UI in Electron; the server can also run standalone as a CLI with the hosted web UI opened in a browser, and both update themselves separately from the desktop executable.

HTTPS inspection needs the client to trust HTTP Toolkit's CA certificate: interceptors launch preconfigured browsers, terminals and apps, and the server's certificate check downloads or installs the certificate where it is not yet trusted. The Android app trusts the certificate and forwards device traffic through a local VPN; its README says a rooted device is not required but widens the real app traffic that can be tested. Inspect only traffic from your own clients and devices or ones you are authorized to test.

The pricing page lists interception of all supported clients, raw inspection, filtering, manual rewriting and manual requests in the free Hobbyist tier, while mock rules and automatic transforms, edit-and-resend, rule and traffic import/export (including HAR), API validation and advanced proxy settings such as TLS passthrough and upstream proxies need a paid Pro account. The README describes the HTTP Toolkit-specific components as AGPL-3.0 and the reusable libraries as Apache-2.0 or MIT; this repository has no license file, and the desktop README offers its binaries under AGPL-3.0 or CC BY-ND 4.0.

resources.name: Awesome UEFI Security
resources.description: A single-README awesome list of UEFI and BIOS security material, which its maintainer describes as a personal and not comprehensive collection. It links UEFI, PI and ACPI specifications, EDK II development resources, firmware analysis tools such as UEFITool, efiXplorer, CHIPSEC and UEFI plugins for Ghidra and Binary Ninja, SMM-themed CTF challenges, analyses of bootkits found in the wild, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, blog posts, papers and training courses.
requirements: The reviewed README was last changed by a pull request merged on 2025-09-04 that fixed the UEFITool link; the last addition, a 2025 arXiv paper, was committed on 2025-02-01. It holds about 230 linked entries in ten sections, including roughly 35 tools, 57 talks, 71 blog posts and 14 papers.
Most tool entries have no description, and no entry states maintenance status, supported firmware, platform or license. The list itself contains no firmware images, SDKs or tools.
Several sections cover offensive material, including bootkit and SMM backdoor repositories, exploit code and a Secure Boot bypass project.
CC0-1.0 for the list; linked works keep their own licenses. CI runs awesome-lint on pull requests.

resources.name: PLASMA
resources.description: Interactive terminal disassembler, formerly named Reverse, for x86 and x86-64 with partial ARM and MIPS/MIPS64 support, reading ELF, PE and raw binaries. Its visual mode shows functions as indented, colored pseudo-code and lets the analyst reshape the flow by inverting conditional jumps, while a Python API runs scripts for strings, cross-reference call graphs, crypto-constant detection and Keystone assembly. Development stopped in 2019, and the repository has no releases.
requirements: Inactive: the last commit on master, ec7df9b, is dated 2019-03-04, and there are no releases or tags; GitHub does not mark the repository archived. The README still describes the project as in heavy development and warns that the database format may break until structures and type definitions are implemented.

Requires Python 3.4+, Capstone (install.sh builds 4.0-alpha5 from source), pyelftools, pefile with python3-future, msgpack-python 0.4.6+, c++filt from binutils and a UTF-8, 256-colour terminal; python-qt4 for the memory map and Keystone for asm.py are optional. The Dockerfile builds on Ubuntu 16.04.

make runs the regression suite, comparing output for the bundled test binaries with expected .rev listings; tests/ holds 96 small compiled test binaries, most next to their C sources. Analysis inputs are the user's own binaries.
GPL-3.0; the relocation definitions taken from angr's cle keep their BSD-style license.

resources.name: mobdevim
resources.description: Derek Selander's macOS command-line utility for inspecting and controlling iOS devices connected over USB or Wi-Fi through Apple's private MobileDevice framework. It lists devices and installed apps with their Info.plist keys and entitlements, streams the device console, fetches crash logs, shows provisioning profiles and developer certificates, copies an app's data container off the device and back where the sandbox allows, and installs, uninstalls and launches apps with arguments and environment variables. With a Developer Disk Image mounted it also lists and kills processes and simulates location, and output can be printed as plist for scripts.
requirements: No releases or tags; the reviewed main commit of 2024-02-01, which says it fixed log grabbing, is the latest push. The README's usage text shows a build compiled on 2023-11-07 and still marks log retrieval as broken on iOS 16.5 and device backup as a to-do. The repository also commits a prebuilt compiled/mobdevim binary, last changed on 2023-11-07.

Build the Xcode project on macOS; it links /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/MobileDevice.framework, sets macOS deployment targets of 10.12 and 10.13, and a build phase copies mobdevim to /usr/local/bin, which must be writable or the build fails. The README states no supported iOS or Xcode versions.

Needs an iOS device connected over USB or paired for Wi-Fi. Process listing and killing, app launching and location simulation need a mounted Developer Disk Image, which the -I option mounts from a signature and .dmg pair the user supplies, for example from Xcode. Copying app data goes through the house_arrest service, so it works only for apps the sandbox exposes.

GitHub detects no license and the repository root has no license file, so the tool's terms are unstated; the process directory carries a 2018 Hex-Rays MIT license for its Instruments client code, and misc/InstrumentsPlugin.h credits codecolorist's FreeTheSandbox.

resources.name: dalvikus
resources.description: Desktop Android reverse-engineering and modification workbench built with Kotlin Compose Multiplatform. It opens APK and DEX files, edits the DEX classes inside an APK as smali without manual unpacking, with syntax highlighting and code completion, and shows decompiled Java from JADX, CFR or Vineflower. It also browses resources and XML through apktool, searches the class tree, string constants and method and field references, re-signs modified APKs with apksig and zipalign, and installs and starts them on a connected device over ADB.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.0.13, published 2025-10-16, with a macOS dmg, Windows exe and msi installers and a Linux amd64 deb. The reviewed master commit (2026-02-16) is one commit ahead, with a drag-and-drop change in the file tree; the README notes that its screenshots may change as the project evolves.

The README requires JDK 11 or later on Windows, Linux or macOS; the release workflow packages with Java 17, and source builds run ./gradlew :composeApp:run. ADB deployment and APK signing need an Android SDK with platform-tools and build-tools, located through ANDROID_HOME or ANDROID_SDK_ROOT or set in the app's settings, and signing uses a keystore supplied by the user.

Inputs are APK or DEX files supplied by the user. The pinned libraries include smali/baksmali 3.0.9, JADX 1.5.2, CFR 0.152, Vineflower 1.11.1, dex2jar 2.4.32, apktool 2.12.0, apksig and ddmlib; the tree commits the Gradle wrapper JAR, ANTLR-generated Java lexer and parser sources and the Monaspace Neon Frozen font files, and the UI is translated into English, German, Chinese and Hindi.
GPL-3.0 license; the README says the tool is intended solely for ethical purposes. No test suite was found, and CI only packages releases.

resources.name: Firmware-Analysis-Papers
resources.description: A single-README reading list of 28 academic security papers on firmware and embedded-system analysis, grouped by year from 2013 to 2021. It covers rehosting and emulation, firmware fuzzing, symbolic execution, Bluetooth and baseband analysis and bug detection in Linux-based and bare-metal firmware. Each entry is a title linked to a PDF or publisher page, with its venue such as USENIX Security, NDSS, IEEE S&P or CCS.
requirements: The reviewed README, last changed 2021-08-30, lists 28 papers: 10 from 2021, 7 from 2020, 4 from 2019, one from 2018 and 6 under “2017 and Before”, the oldest from 2013. The list has not been updated since, so later work such as Fuzzware (USENIX Security 2022) is absent.

Entries give only a title, a link and a venue label, with no summaries, code, artifact or citation details. Most links go to PDFs on conference, author or arXiv sites; the rest go to an IEEE Xplore page, ResearchGate, or ACM Digital Library URLs carrying session tokens, which may stop working. Year labels can differ from publication years: Firmadyne is labeled NDSS 2017, matching its link's 2017 upload folder.
The repository holds only README.md and no license file, so the list states no reuse terms; the papers keep their authors' and publishers' rights. An independent reading list.

resources.name: XPEViewer
resources.description: Qt-based PE file viewer and editor for Windows, Linux and macOS by horsicq, the author of the catalog's Detect It Easy. Its PE view parses the DOS, NT and optional headers, sections, normal, delay-load and bound imports, exports, resources including manifests, version data and string tables, relocations, TLS callbacks, exception, debug and load-configuration data, certificates, the Rich header and .NET metadata tables. Hex, disassembly, strings, entropy, hash, memory-map and extractor views sit beside Detect It Easy, Nauz File Detector and YARA scans and an optional VirusTotal lookup.
requirements: Latest full release at review: 0.05, published 2024-07-02, with a Linux AppImage, Debian 10–12 and Ubuntu 14.04–24.04 .deb packages, macOS x86_64 and Qt 6 arm64 packages, Windows x86, x64 and XP portable zips and a source tarball. Release 0.06 (2025-12-22) is marked as a prerelease with no attached files; the rolling Beta prerelease carries 0.06 Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 packages and Windows portable zips, and release_version.txt on the reviewed master commit reads 0.06.

Source builds need a recursive clone of 56 horsicq submodules, including Detect-It-Easy, signatures and XYara. docs/BUILD.md covers Docker, a Debian package script, autotools, qmake6 with Qt 6, CMake, macOS with Qt 5.15.2, Windows 7–10 with Visual Studio 2019 and Qt 5.15.2, and Windows XP with Visual Studio 2013 and Qt 5.6.3.

Supply the PE file yourself. The main window opens files for writing when it can and falls back to read-only, so editing changes the opened file; work on a copy. The VirusTotal view uses that online service.

MIT (LICENSE). The README itself is brief: download, run and build links, a changelog and screenshots; the parsed structures come from the PE widget source in the pinned FormatWidgets submodule. The main repository commits no sample binaries.

resources.name: Fermion
resources.description: Ruben Boonen's Electron desktop application that wraps frida-node and the Monaco editor into one window for writing, injecting and refining Frida scripts. The editor brings linting, IntelliSense and Frida API type definitions, a device menu reaches local, USB and remote Frida servers to attach to or spawn processes, scripts reload in the target with a keyboard shortcut and their output appears beside the code. A prototype CALL tracer follows every call a thread makes from a chosen pointer or module symbol until it returns and renders the result as a Graphviz SVG graph, and Frida's JavaScript API documentation is built in.
requirements: Latest release at review: v1.9.3, published 2023-04-20 by the repository's CI with zipped Windows, Linux and macOS builds, pinning Electron 21.0.0, Frida 16.0.17 and frida-gum types 18.3.1. Every later commit, up to the reviewed master commit of 2025-03-20, is an automated keepalive commit, and the release workflow builds only when the package version changes, so the app has not followed the Frida 17 series (17.24.3 at review).

Running from source needs Node.js and npm: in the Fermion folder, set npm_config_runtime=electron and npm_config_target=21.0.0, then run npm install and npm start; release packages are built with electron-packager, and the CI uses Node 16. Remote and mobile targets need a reachable Frida server, which the README says is often detected automatically over USB or in emulators such as Genymotion, or can be given as an IP address and port.

On Windows, attaching to SYSTEM processes needs Fermion running as Administrator with SeDebugPrivilege, because the README says running it as SYSTEM has frozen it since Electron 8; on Linux, attaching may need root or a relaxed kernel.yama.ptrace_scope. The README calls the tracer a prototype whose window can lag on large graphs and which can make the traced process unstable.

The repository commits 22 example Frida scripts, most of them hooks on Windows APIs, a Graphviz library compiled to WebAssembly (Fermion/pages/graphvizlib.wasm) for rendering traces, and bundled jQuery, Semantic UI (with Lato fonts), Split.js and Tailwind CSS assets. Users supply their own devices, processes and apps.
BSD-3-Clause (Copyright 2019 Ruben Boonen); bundled frameworks and fonts keep their own licenses.

resources.name: USBPcap
resources.description: Tomasz Moń's open-source USB packet capture for Windows. A filter driver installed in the Windows USB device stack records the USB Request Blocks (URBs) exchanged with devices on each root hub, and USBPcapCMD writes them to pcap files in the LINKTYPE_USBPCAP format, which Wireshark dissects. Since 1.2.0.0 the project has recommended running USBPcapCMD as a Wireshark extcap: each root hub then appears as a capture interface, with options to capture selected, all or newly connected devices and to add the descriptors of devices that are already attached.
requirements: Latest release at review: 1.5.4.0, published 2020-05-22, with a digitally signed USBPcapSetup installer for x86 and x64 Windows 7, 8 and 10 and a source archive that includes debug symbols. The reviewed master commit (2025-01-25) adds two unreleased driver fixes on top of it, one marked critical, for kernel buffer reallocation and the order of read completions. The installer refuses Windows versions older than 7 (1.5.3.0 was the last release for XP and Vista) and Windows To Go, asks Windows 7 users to install a SHA-2 update (KB3033929 or KB4474419) first, and requires a reboot after installation.

Capture runs on the analyst's own Windows machine. Either run USBPcapCMD.exe to choose a root-hub filter instance and an output file, or copy it into Wireshark's global or personal extcap folder; USBPcap support has been in Wireshark since 1.10.0rc1. The README notes that there is no capture engine DLL. The project's tour recommends capturing newly connected devices, or reconnecting a device after capture starts, so that its descriptors appear in the capture for Wireshark's dissectors.

Per the README, source builds use Windows Driver Kit 7.1.0 for the Windows 7 driver, or Visual Studio 2013 with WDK 8.1 Update for the Windows 8 build. Release drivers are attestation-signed through Microsoft's Hardware Dev Center with the author's own, non-public certificate. Self-built drivers are signed with the committed test certificate (certificates/USBPcapTestCert.*) and, as the README explains, load on 64-bit Windows only with test signing enabled. The only other committed binaries are the NSIS SysRestore.dll installer plugin and two public CA cross-certificates.

The project's capture-limitations page says USBPcap records URBs passed between the stack's functional and physical device objects. It therefore does not show bus states, packet IDs, split transactions, wire timing or transfer speed, nor the enumeration that happens before a device has its address; the page says those appear only in a hardware USB sniffer. Interpreting the captured payloads remains the analyst's own protocol work in Wireshark or another dissector.

The README and SPDX headers license the driver under GPL-2.0 and USBPcapCMD under BSD-2-Clause. GitHub detects no license because there is no license file at the repository root; the texts are in nsis/ and wix/.

resources.name: Xiaomi Kettle BLE protocol: reconstructing a smart kettle's control interface
resources.description: Documents the closed Bluetooth Low Energy GATT protocol of the Xiaomi Kettle, which the author reconstructed by decompiling the Mi Home Android app and disassembling its native encryption library. The write-up covers the connection and authentication handshake, the layout of status notifications and the writable settings characteristics, with a small Go reimplementation of the cipher helpers. The author built a kettle-to-MQTT bridge for Home Assistant from it but did not publish that code, and gives no guarantee that the notes work for others.
requirements: Reviewed at the final commit of 2018-11-29; the repository is archived and consists of a README and one Go file. README says the kettle is built on a QN9020 MCU, and it names no specific model or firmware version.

Applying the notes needs the user's own kettle and any BLE library that can read, write and subscribe to characteristics; the author used Go with currantlabs/ble. The Mi Home app, its native library and any decompiled output are not included, and the handshake uses a token the client generates itself, so no vendor key is committed or needed.

README lists device limits it observed: heating cannot be started over BLE unless Keep Warm mode is already active, Keep Warm can only be re-enabled with the physical button, and its time limit tops out at 12 hours.

cipher.go contains only the cipher and byte-mixing helpers, not a client. There are no tests, captures or verification records, so the protocol description is author-reported; the README credits jadx-gui and IDA Pro.
WTFPL version 2 (LICENSE.txt). Xiaomi and Mi Home remain trademarks of their owner.

resources.name: cantools
resources.description: Python 3 library and command-line tool for CAN bus databases that parses DBC, KCD, SYM, ARXML 3/4 and CDD files and encodes and decodes CAN messages, including simple and extended signal multiplexing and diagnostic DIDs. Its CLI decodes candump output against a database, plots decoded signals from candump logs with matplotlib, dumps each message's bit layout, converts between database formats, generates C pack and unpack code, and monitors a live bus in a text interface through python-can.
requirements: Latest release at review: 45.1.0, published 2026-10-20 on GitHub and PyPI; the reviewed master commit is 15 commits ahead of that tag. It installs with pip, and pyproject.toml requires Python 3.10+ with python-can, bitstruct, textparser, crccheck and argparse_addons, plus optional extras for plotting (matplotlib), caching (diskcache) and Windows curses support for the monitor.

Bring a database describing the target network and frames captured from it: decode reads candump output on standard input and plot reads candump log files, while monitor takes python-can bus arguments for a live interface, and the README's scripting example sends and receives frames on a SocketCAN channel. The repository's tests/files directory holds sample DBC, KCD, SYM, ARXML and CDD databases and generated C sources used by the examples and tests.

Decoding covers only what the supplied database defines; cantools applies existing message and signal definitions rather than inferring unknown layouts, and the README notes that generated C code is limited to signals of at most 64 bits. MIT licensed.

resources.name: inspectrum
resources.description: Desktop analyzer for recorded radio signals, primarily captures from software-defined radio receivers, which the README says handles files of 100 GB and more. A zoomable spectrogram with a tunable filter feeds sample, amplitude, frequency, phase and threshold plots, and cursors measure period and symbol rate and extract symbol values to stdout or the clipboard. Selected time spans, filtered samples and demodulated traces can be exported, and SigMF annotations can be displayed over the spectrogram.
requirements: Latest release at review: v0.4.0, published 2025-12-06 as a source-only GitHub release; the reviewed main commit is that tag. Its notes add Qt 6 and SigMF dataset support, raise the CMake minimum to 3.5 and fix a crash on small files. The README points Linux users to distribution packages, macOS users to Homebrew or MacPorts and Windows users to radioconda or conda-forge.

Source builds need CMake 3.5+ (the README still lists 3.1), a C++14 compiler, Qt 6 or, as a fallback, Qt 5 Core, Widgets and Concurrent, FFTW 3, liquid-dsp 1.3.0+ and pkg-config; distribution-specific steps are on the project wiki. CI builds against Qt 5 and Qt 6 on macOS and Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, but the repository defines no automated tests.

It reads recordings only; the source has no SDR device, capture or transmit code. Users supply their own SigMF recordings or raw sample files, from complex cf32, cf64, cs32, cs16, cs8 and cu8 to real f32, f64, s16, s8 and u8, selected by file extension or --format (unknown extensions are read as cf32), and set the sample rate with --rate or in the controls. 64-bit samples are truncated to 32-bit internally.

Symbol timing comes from cursors the analyst places; the tool does not infer modulation, framing or protocol fields. GPL-3.0, with source headers allowing version 3 or later; the repository holds only source code, CMake modules and a screenshot.

resources.name: PULSAR
resources.description: Research prototype by Hugo Gascon and colleagues that learns a model of an unknown network protocol from recorded traffic. Messages extracted from PCAP traces are embedded as token or n-gram vectors, clustered by matrix factorization through the PRISMA R module, and turned into a Markov-chain state model with message templates and rules linking fields to earlier messages, written out as model files and a Graphviz state graph. The same models drive the tool's session simulator and stateful fuzzer, described in the authors' SecureComm 2015 paper; this entry covers only the protocol-learning part.
requirements: Reviewed at master commit 3c61178 (2022-06-07), the last push; the repository has no releases or tags, and the CLI reports itself as v0.1-dev. Contributed changes merged in 2021 converted the code from Python 2 to Python 3 with 2to3. There are no tests or CI configuration.

Learning takes PCAP traces of the protocol under study, or the captures that Cuckoo sandbox stored for analyzed samples. The repository commits one example model, models/itunes-xbmc, with the roughly 3 MB iTunes–XBMC capture it was learned from (itunes-xbmc.pcap, part of the 2015 initial commit) and its intermediate Derrick, Sally and Harry files; it bundles no other target data.

INSTALL.md has users clone the PRISMA R module into pulsar/modules, build Konrad Rieck's Derrick and Sally C tools from their repositories, install R, Wireshark's mergecap and Graphviz, and pip-install pygraphviz, progressBar, NumPy and python-Levenshtein, giving package commands for CentOS only. Dependencies are unpinned; PRISMA was last updated in 2018, and Derrick and Sally in 2019.

The README points to the SecureComm 2015 paper for the method and to an AISec 2012 paper on learning stateful models for network honeypots; results reported there are the authors'. Learned templates and state machines are statistical approximations that need analyst validation.
BSD-3-Clause (Copyright 2014 Hugo Gascon); the bundled pulsar/core/sippy SIP stack keeps its own GPL-2.0-or-later notices.

resources.name: basefind2
resources.description: Python script that estimates the load address of a flat 32-bit little-endian firmware image without brute-forcing every candidate base, building on mncoppola's basefind.py and rbasefind. It searches the gaps between sorted pointer values for a run of consecutive gaps between string offsets, takes each match as a candidate base, and scores it by the share of sampled strings whose rebased address also appears as a pointer. The README's example finds the correct base of one image in about 26 seconds.
requirements: The whole tool is basefind2.py; the reviewed main commit of 2022-05-02 is the last of six commits made between 2022-04-07 and 2022-05-02, and there are no releases, tags or packages. It needs only Python 3 and its standard library.

Input is a flat image supplied by the user; no firmware or samples are included. Pointers are read as little-endian 32-bit words at 4-byte alignment, with no big-endian or 64-bit option. Strings are runs of at least 10 printable ASCII characters, tabs or line breaks (-sl), a match needs 10 consecutive gaps by default (-dl), and scoring samples every 20th string (-s). The whole file is read into memory.

Output lists each candidate base with its sampled match percentage, and the analyst must choose and confirm one. The README's only example raises -dl to 40 and reports the correct base of one image at 81.64% after about 26 seconds. There are no tests or CI, and the README gives no comparison with rbasefind or basefind.py on shared images.
MIT License (2022, soyer). Analyzed firmware keeps its own terms.

resources.name: paranoid-deobfuscator
resources.description: Python command-line tool that recovers the strings hidden by the Paranoid and LSParanoid Android string-obfuscation plugins, so that smali code becomes readable for static analysis. It scans a smali directory for the obfuscator's string-lookup method and encoded chunk array, decodes the chunks with Python ports of the libraries' DeobfuscatorHelper and RandomHelper classes, and rewrites each lookup call in place as a const-string instruction with a marker comment. Helper commands list the recovered strings, save the chunks to a file and decode a single string from saved chunks.
requirements: Latest release at review: v3.0.2, published 2025-02-18 and uploaded to PyPI the same day; install it with pip or pipx. pyproject.toml requires Python 3.10+ with click 8 (8.1.7 or later) and NumPy 2 (2.1.3 or later), and CI runs pytest on Python 3.10 to 3.13 on every push. The reviewed main commit of 2025-03-26 adds only tests and a donation link after that release.

It works on a smali directory decoded from an APK or DEX file the user supplies, which the README pairs with Apktool or smali/baksmali for decoding and rebuilding, and it overwrites the smali files in place. The README supports only apps obfuscated with Paranoid v0.3.0 or later, released 25 January 2020; a commented-out README warning about Windows refers to issue #14, which is closed.

The command stops when it finds more than one candidate string-lookup method or obfuscated string array, which the source says is not supported yet, and logs a warning for lookup calls it cannot follow. It restores string constants only, not names or other obfuscation. Tests cover string encoding, smali parsing, Paranoid decoding and the issue #18 regression.
Apache-2.0 (copyright 2024 Giacomo Ferretti); the decoding modules state that they were converted from Paranoid's and LSParanoid's Java helpers. Analyzed apps keep their own terms.

resources.name: Ghidrathon
resources.description: Mandiant FLARE's Ghidra extension that embeds the user's local CPython 3 interpreter in Ghidra through Jep, as an alternative to Ghidra's Jython-based Python 2.7 scripting. It adds an interactive Python 3 interpreter window, Python 3 scripts in the Script Manager and Python 3 post-scripts in headless analyzeHeadless runs, with GhidraScript state such as currentProgram() and FlatProgramAPI methods available as Python builtins. Because the configured interpreter or virtual environment is used as is, scripts can import installed packages; the README names capa, Unicorn and angr as motivating examples and shows Unicorn emulating ARM code inside Ghidra.
requirements: The repository is archived on GitHub and read-only. Its last commit on main dates from 2024-05-08, and the latest release, v4.0.0 of 2024-02-13, attaches one extension zip that the release workflow builds against Ghidra 11.0 and bundles with the configure script. The archive states no reason; Ghidra's own change history records that 11.3 (February 2025) integrated PyGhidra, a native CPython 3 interface whose module provides a CPython interpreter plugin and a script provider for CPython 3 GhidraScripts.

The README requires Python 3.8+, exactly Jep 4.2.0, Ghidra 10.3.2+ and Java 17+. Setup installs Jep from util/requirements.txt into the chosen interpreter or virtual environment and runs util/ghidrathon_configure.py against the Ghidra install directory, which writes a ghidrathon.save file there or under GHIDRATHON_SAVE_PATH; the zip is then installed through Ghidra's extension manager, whose version-mismatch prompt the README says may be overridden. Source builds need Gradle 7.3+ and the Jep 4.2.0 JAR downloaded into lib/.

CI built and tested only Ghidra 10.3.2 and 11.0 with Python 3.8 and 3.12 on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS, running the repository's Python tests as headless post-scripts. Jep embeds Python in the JVM through JNI, which the README notes Ghidra's developers advise against, and unlike Ghidra's Java and Jython APIs, scripts read GhidraScript state through calls such as currentProgram().

Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.txt). The repository commits Java and Python sources, an example script, Python tests and three README screenshots, and no binaries; the CI tests analyze a demangler executable taken from the downloaded Ghidra distribution.

resources.name: Ford Fiesta MK5 MS-CAN: decoding the dashboard and radio bus
resources.description: Documents the medium-speed CAN bus that links the 6000CD radio and the dashboard of a restyled (post-2006) Ford Fiesta MK5, worked out by tapping the bus at the radio's QuadLock connector with a Seeed CAN-BUS Shield on an Arduino Uno. The README describes 18 partly or fully decoded message IDs on the 125 kbit/s bus, with byte layouts and scaling formulas: radio text sent to the dashboard LCD over ISO-TP, station names, volume, CD track and steering-column mode and seek buttons, as well as broadcast clock, door, lock, reverse-gear, indicator, light, handbrake, airbag-lamp, pedal, RPM, speed, coolant, key-position, battery and partial VIN data. An incomplete Kayak .kcd definition encodes only the clock and gas-pedal/RPM/speed messages.
requirements: Documentation-only project with 25 commits from 2020-08-22 to the reviewed master commit of 2020-09-30, and no releases or tags. It applies to a Fiesta MK5 built after 2006 (the restyled model) with the 2-DIN 6000CD radio; the README notes that the steering-column volume buttons do not appear on MS-CAN, and the decoding of some IDs is partial.

No Ford software or files are needed; reading the bus requires a CAN interface on the CANH and CANL lines at the radio's QuadLock connector, which the README says needs no 120-ohm terminator. The author used a Seeed CAN-BUS Shield V2.0 on an Arduino Uno R3, but the repository holds only the README, the Kayak .kcd file, a connector pinout image and dashboard indicator icons, with no capture logs, sniffer code or Arduino sketch.

Message layouts and formulas such as volume, track time, speed, coolant temperature and battery voltage are author-reported from the author's own car, and the ISO-TP reading of the LCD text messages is credited to a Reddit commenter. The README documents decoding of observed traffic and gives no procedure for sending frames to the car.
The repository has no license file and GitHub detects none.

resources.name: Katalina
resources.description: Python emulator for Dalvik bytecode that its README likens to Unicorn: it parses a DEX file and executes methods one instruction at a time, substituting Python mocks for common Java and Android APIs such as String, StringBuilder, Base64, ArrayList, AES Cipher and part of reflection. Run over Android entry points, methods matching a name or one method with given arguments, it logs the strings that the code builds or decrypts, optionally as JSON, which helps recover obfuscated strings in apps and malware.
requirements: There are no releases or tags. Development ran from May to December 2023; the reviewed main commit f8e27b9 of 2026-10-01 merges a contributed fix that makes the String.valueOf mock follow the called overload's descriptor.

Requires Python 3.10+ with the pinned requirements.txt packages, including kaitaistruct 0.10 and pycryptodome 3.18.0. main.py takes -xe for Android entry points, -xm for methods matching a name, -x for one fully qualified method with arguments, -dl to skip methods whose names contain listed words and -j for JSON output. Entry-point and name-match runs give each method a SIGALRM time limit, so README says Windows support may be broken and recommends WSL.

Input is one classes.dex from an APK the analyst already has. README lists most instructions, same-class and static calls and String and Base64 APIs as working, iterator and array APIs and cross-class instance calls as partial, and MultiDex and I/O as broken. Framework behaviour without a mock is not reproduced, and the AES mock only tries ECB and then CBC with a zero IV, so recovered strings must be checked against the code. The repository has no tests or CI.
MIT. The first commit included DEX samples, many named after Android malware families, that were removed a month later; the reviewed tree holds only the Python sources.

resources.name: diStorm3
resources.description: Lightweight x86/AMD64 disassembler library in C that the README describes as a decomposer: besides formatted text, distorm_decompose returns a binary structure per instruction with its opcode, operands, prefixes, flow-control class and optionally affected CPU flags. It decodes 16-, 32- and 64-bit code, can stop at calls, returns, branches, interrupts or privileged instructions, and its generated instruction tables cover integer, x87, MMX, 3DNow!, SSE through SSE4.2 and SSE4a, AVX, FMA, AES, CLMUL, VMX and SVM sets. The repository includes the distorm3 Python module, plus example Java and .NET wrappers and sample programs for Linux, Win32 and a Windows kernel driver.
requirements: No commits on master since 2021-12-18, the reviewed commit. The latest PyPI release is distorm3 3.5.2, uploaded 2021-03-19 as a source tarball and a Windows 32-bit Python 3.7 wheel; the GitHub release list ends with 3.5.2b (2021-04-03), and setup.py on master already says 3.5.3, which is not on PyPI.

Install the Python module with pip install distorm3, which compiles the C sources, or build the C library with the Makefiles for Linux, macOS and TinyCC or the Visual Studio solution for Windows. setup.py lists Windows, macOS and Linux, and its newest Python classifier is 3.5; CI last targeted Ubuntu 18.04, Windows and macOS with Python 3.x. The README points to the GitHub wiki for API documentation.

Input is raw machine code bytes plus a code offset and decoding mode supplied by the caller; it decodes instructions only and does not parse executable formats, build control-flow graphs or lift code. The disOps scripts generate its instruction tables from the x86sets.py database.

The repository bundles a test helper executable, test-deps/yasm-1.3.0-win64.exe, which the CI workflow copies into place so the Python tests can assemble their instruction samples with yasm on Windows; no other sample binaries are committed.
BSD three-clause license (COPYING; GitHub reports it as unclassified).

resources.name: JTAGulator
resources.description: Joe Grand's open-source hardware tool and Parallax Propeller firmware for locating on-chip debug interfaces among an unfamiliar board's test points, vias, component pads or connectors. Driven from a serial terminal, its 24 level-shifted channels try pin permutations to identify JTAG pinouts by IDCODE or BYPASS scans, SWD pinouts by IDCODE and UART pinouts with their baud rates. With a known JTAG pinout the firmware can also read device IDs, discover instruction and data registers and map a chip's pins to boundary-scan positions with EXTEST, and other modes pass UART traffic through, act as a SUMP-compatible logic analyzer or emulate a Bus Pirate so OpenOCD can use the board as a JTAG adapter.
requirements: Firmware 1.12, tagged 2023-06-05, is the newest version; the repository publishes tags but no GitHub releases, and the README calls master a development branch whose interim commits may be unstable. Later commits, up to the reviewed one of 2026-09-02, update links and the license text and add the Rev. C hardware design files, and since July 2025 the README names EXPLIoT as maintainer and supporter.

Requires JTAGulator hardware, for which the repository commits the Rev. C design files (Altium project, Gerbers, schematic, bill of materials, assembly drawing and test procedure), a serial terminal on the host and physical wiring to the target's candidate pins. The target I/O voltage, 1.4–3.3 V, must be set before scanning, and the firmware warns that use may affect target behavior; it also warns that its front-end circuitry is incompatible with many SWD-based targets and points to hardware modifications described in the wiki.

The firmware is Spin code for the Propeller P8X32A: the README recommends Propeller Tool 1.3.2 for Windows and calls other environments untested and unsupported, while also giving OpenSpin and PropLoader commands for compiling, loading to RAM or writing to EEPROM. The repository commits the compiled image JTAGulator.eeprom (32 KB), last updated for 1.12. The OpenOCD and logic-analyzer modes need OpenOCD's Bus Pirate driver or an Openbench Logic Sniffer client, and both persist across resets and firmware updates until exited manually.

The README distributes the design under CC BY-SA 4.0 and says the JTAGulator name and logo are registered trademarks of Grand Idea Studio that may not be used on derived works without permission; the Spin source headers still state CC BY 3.0 United States, and GitHub detects no license.

resources.name: CanLab
resources.description: PyQt6 desktop workstation and command-line tool for reverse-engineering CAN bus captures offline. It reads SavvyCAN/GVRET CSV, candump, pcap, Vector BLF/ASC, MDF4 and openpilot logs, then suggests counters, checksums and their algorithms, byte roles, flags, multiplexers, entropy-based field boundaries and cross-ID correlations, decodes J1939 and NMEA 2000 PGNs and reassembles multi-frame messages. A cantools-backed DBC builder checks signal definitions against the captured frames and exports DBC, openpilot DBC, CANdb++, ARXML and Wireshark Lua dissectors, and an optional MCP server offers 29 receive-only analysis tools to assistants.
requirements: README calls CanLab a beta, single-author project. The reviewed commit 8aaa6ff (2026-09-23) declares version 2.1.0 in pyproject.toml, while the latest release is v2.0.0 (2026-09-15) with a Linux x86_64 build and demo videos. README stresses that the analysis is heuristic, suggests candidates rather than identifying signals, and has not been validated on many real vehicles.

Python 3.11+ on Linux, macOS or Windows (developed on 3.12), with optional extras for AI, REST, MCP, hardware adapters, MDF4 (asammdf) and openpilot logs (pycapnp); README asks for 4 GB RAM, 8 GB for the machine-learning features. Live capture uses SocketCAN, a comma.ai Panda, GVRET boards or python-can adapters; README reports one physical adapter used, a CANalyst-II, and the others only on a virtual bus.

Inputs are the user's own captures. The bundled sample is a synthetic Hyundai-style capture generated by a script, the test fixtures are a few lines each, and the real-data acceptance runs fetch public SavvyCAN, CSS Electronics and comma.ai recordings instead of committing them. The opendbc matcher downloads the commaai/opendbc index on first use, and the optional AI analysis sends the selected ID's frame statistics to the configured Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq or Ollama provider.

The application also has bench-only transmit functions behind a global ARM TX switch that is off by default and a blocked-ID list; README restricts them to isolated bench setups. The MCP tools cannot transmit.

README's Testing section reports 753 passing pytest tests (its badge still says 578), interoperability tests against can-isotp, udsoncan and can-j1939, and 99 checks over public real-world recordings; diagnostic requests were tested only against scripted responders. MIT; the NMEA 2000 table derives from CANboat (Apache-2.0) and the cereal schema from comma.ai (MIT).

resources.name: Facedancer
resources.description: Python library for implementing USB devices in software, with a hardware peripheral such as Cynthion or GreatFET acting as a remote-controlled USB controller attached to the target host. Its USBProxy mode sits between a real device and a host, forwarding transfers while filters log, decode or modify them for USB protocol analysis; the README notes this suits devices whose software you do not control, such as embedded systems or game consoles. Version 3 is a ground-up rewrite of the emulation core that ships keyboard, mass-storage and FTDI serial device models plus HID and logging proxy filters, and no longer runs legacy 2.9.x scripts.
requirements: Needs a supported board selected with the BACKEND variable: Cynthion (cynthion), GreatFET One and other LPC4330 boards (greatfet), GoodFET-based Facedancers such as the Facedancer21 (goodfet), Raspberry Pi Raspdancer boards (raspdancer) or HydraDancer and HydraUSB3 (hydradancer). The README says MAX3420/MAX3421-based boards cannot emulate more complex devices or act as USBProxy MITM devices, and that HydraDancer boards do not support host mode.

Latest release at review: 3.1.3, published 2026-05-22 on GitHub and PyPI and identical to the reviewed main commit; pyproject.toml requires Python 3.10+ with pyusb, libusb1, pyserial, prompt-toolkit and hid-parser. The README says Facedancer 3.0 does not work on Windows and runs only on GNU/Linux, while the getting-started guide narrows the warning to Windows control hosts with GreatFET and the proxy guide says USBProxy must run as root on macOS to claim the proxied device.

USBProxy needs the real device being proxied, identified by its vendor and product IDs, and the analyst's filters decide what is forwarded, logged or changed; the README calls the proxy feature complete but in need of more documentation. The repository holds Python sources, examples, tests and documentation, with no board firmware. Emulate and proxy only hosts and devices you own or are authorized to test.
BSD-3-Clause licensed.

resources.name: Doldrums
resources.description: Python parser for the Dart AOT snapshots inside libapp.so, the compiled Dart code of an Android Flutter app. It finds the VM and isolate snapshot symbols with pyelftools, deserializes the snapshot clusters and writes a text dump of every class in the isolate snapshot, with fields, method signatures and each method's absolute code offset in libapp.so. It recovers declarations and offsets for further disassembly, not decompiled function bodies.
requirements: Reviewed at main commit 7430196 (2022-05-01), the last push; there are no releases, and the README calls the tool beta and still missing some deserialization routines and class information. main.py accepts only the snapshot hashes of Dart 2.10 and Dart 2.12, rejects Dart 2.13 as work in progress and any other SDK as unsupported, so apps built with newer Dart releases are out of scope.

Input is the libapp.so ELF of an Android Flutter app, with its _kDartVmSnapshot* and _kDartIsolateSnapshot* symbols. The tests directory commits Dart 2.10 libapp.so builds of a small sample counter app (package sandbox_flutter) for arm64-v8a, armv7 and x64, plus text dumps of the arm64 and x64 builds as reference output; there is no test runner.

Runs as python3 src/main.py [-v] libapp.so output with pyelftools as the only dependency; there is no packaging or declared Python version. The README notes that the verbose option works only for Dart 2.12 snapshots, and that darter is a fully tested parser for the older Dart 2.5.
The author's blog post documents the snapshot format the parser follows. No license file is present and GitHub detects none, so reuse terms are unstated.

resources.name: BIOSUtilities
resources.description: Python collection of 16 parsers and extractors for vendor BIOS/UEFI update formats, including AMI BIOS Guard (PFAT) and UCP, Dell PFS, Insyde iFlash/iFdPacker, Phoenix TDK Packer, Award, Fujitsu, Panasonic, Portwell, Toshiba and VAIO packages and several Apple EFI containers. Each utility checks whether an input matches its format and unpacks the firmware components, such as SPI/BIOS/UEFI, EC and ME images, plus bundled utilities into an output folder, optionally reporting structure information; an Apple EFI identifier names images from their IBIOSI tag. A main.py script tries every utility on the given files, and the biosutilities package exposes the same classes to Python.
requirements: Latest version at review: 25.07.01, published on PyPI as 25.7.1 on 2025-07-01. The reviewed main commit adds one later change, from 2026-10-18, that falls back to the system PATH when a tool is missing from the external folder. The README targets Python 3.10 to 3.13 on Windows, Linux and macOS; pyproject requires Python 3.10+ and offers pefile 2023.2.7 and dissect.util 3.20 as pinned extras.

Several utilities call external programs found on PATH or in an external folder next to the package: 7-Zip, UEFIFind and UEFIExtract from UEFITool, TianoCompress from EDK II and ToshibaComExtractor.
