The MCP server (--mcp) exposes 14 tools over streamable HTTP on 127.0.0.1:8765 by default, or over stdio, and a bundled .mcp.json registers it for Claude Code. Family candidates, emulation traces and AI summaries are heuristic findings for analyst review.

resources.name: gr-lora
resources.description: GNU Radio out-of-tree module by Pieter Robyns and co-authors for receiving and decoding LoRa physical-layer frames with a software-defined radio, implementing the modulation features described in patents and blog posts. Its receiver channelizes the input, detects and synchronizes to LoRa chirps with clock-drift correction, and decodes symbols through Gray mapping, deinterleaving, dewhitening and Hamming decoding into header and payload bytes, which a message socket sink can forward over UDP port 40868. The bundled flowgraphs decode recorded traces or live captures, and the README lists HackRF One, USRP B201, RTL-SDR and LimeSDR as tested receivers.
requirements: The newest commit on master, from 2021-12-10, merged a port to GNU Radio 3.9: CMake requests GNU Radio 3.9, the Python bindings use pybind11, and the library links liquid-dsp and log4cpp. The README was not updated for the port and still lists Python 2, SWIG and wx dependencies, and its Docker image installs python2 packages on an unpinned Arch Linux base; the Travis CI configuration builds GNU Radio maint-3.8. A gr3.7 branch keeps the older code.

Input is IQ samples from an SDR or a recorded file. The receiver block takes sample rate, center frequency, channel list, bandwidth, spreading factor, coding rate, implicit-header, CRC and reduced-rate settings that must match the transmission. apps/lora_receive_file_nogui.py offers to download an example 868.1 MHz SF7 trace from the authors' university server, and further traces are in the separate gr-lora-samples repository. The README lists LoPy, Dragino HAT, Adafruit Feather 32u4, Microchip RN2483 and SX1276 boards as tested transmitters.

The README states that payload and header CRCs are not checked and that several channels cannot be decoded at once; its changelog marks version 0.7's downlink, reduced-rate implicit-header and arbitrary-bandwidth support as experimental. The newest version tag is v0.6.2, so 0.7 exists only on master. docs/test-results holds the authors' decoding rates from suites rerun on 2021-12-01 during the port, such as 100% on the short USRP traces, and the author considers LoRa fully reverse engineered as of version 0.6, citing close to 100% accuracy on clear signals; these are author-reported results.
GPL-3.0 (LICENSE). The README asks research users to cite the Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.853201. It covers the LoRa physical layer only.

resources.name: CNNPRE (IEEE Access 2023)
resources.description: Research code and data for CNNPRE, a message-type identification method for protocol reverse engineering by Javad Garshasbi and Mehdi Teimouri, published in IEEE Access in 2023. A single Colab notebook turns each message's padded bit string into a resized grayscale image, extracts features with an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 as transfer learning, adds message direction and length-group encodings, reduces the features with UMAP and clusters messages with agglomerative clustering and HDBSCAN, scoring each clustering against labelled message types. Preprocessed message datasets for twelve protocols, from ARP and DNS to SMTP and GSM, accompany the notebook.
requirements: Paper: Javad Garshasbi and Mehdi Teimouri, “CNNPRE: A CNN-Based Protocol Reverse Engineering Method,” IEEE Access, vol. 11, pp. 116255–116268, 2023, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3325391; Crossref lists it under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The repository was reviewed at its 2026-01-13 head, a README update; the notebook last changed on 2023-07-06, and there are no releases.

The only code is cnnpre.ipynb, written for Google Colab. It pip-installs umap-learn and hdbscan, apt-installs TeX Live and pandoc for a PDF export, and otherwise relies on Colab's preinstalled TensorFlow, scikit-learn, OpenCV, pandas and yellowbrick without pinned versions. It downloads ImageNet ResNet50 weights, reads one hard-coded CSV (GSM5000-hex.csv) with a message count that must be edited for other datasets, and its last cells mount Google Drive to convert the notebook. There is no package, command-line tool or test.

Inputs are message-level CSVs with direction, labelled message type and each message as hex and bit strings. Data/ holds preprocessed CSVs for ARP, DHCP, DNS, FTP, GSM, HTTP, ICMP, NBNS, NTP, POP, SMTP and Syslog, PCAP/ holds the GSM capture 44CON-gsm-uplink-downlink-sim-example.pcap, and the README names the public WRCCDC 2021 regional competition captures as the other source. No PCAP-to-CSV preprocessing script is included, so a new protocol needs its own conversion, and the notebook's evaluation metrics need ground-truth message types.

The notebook covers message-type clustering only, not field, semantic or state-machine inference. Its results labelled K-Means take the cluster count from a K-means elbow search but cluster with agglomerative clustering, and the saved outputs show one GSM run. Accuracy figures are the paper's.

GitHub detects no license and the repository has no license file, so the code and preprocessed datasets state no reuse terms; the paper's license covers the article, not the repository, and the captures keep their sources' terms.

resources.name: termshark
resources.description: Graham Clark's terminal user interface for tshark, inspired by Wireshark and aimed at inspecting captures on a remote machine, for example over SSH, without copying them back to a desktop. It reads pcap files, fifos or standard input, or captures live from one or more interfaces, and shows a packet list filtered with Wireshark display filters next to the dissected packet structure and a hex view. Analysis views reassemble TCP and UDP streams with search and client- or server-only display, list Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, UDP and TCP conversations that can be turned into display filters, and search packet contents; Wireshark-style profiles can reuse a linked Wireshark profile's packet colors.
requirements: Latest release at review: v2.4.0, published 2022-07-11, with builds for Linux (x64, arm64, armv6), macOS (x64, arm64), FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD and Windows x64. The README also lists Arch, Debian, FreeBSD, Homebrew, MacPorts, Kali, NixOS, Snapcraft, Termux and Ubuntu packages. The reviewed master commit (2022-11-01) is 14 commits ahead of that release, including unreleased hex-view navigation changes, and master has had no commits since.

tshark from Wireshark, version 1.10.2 or later, must be on PATH at run time, because termshark relies on it for all packet analysis; protocol coverage is therefore whatever the installed tshark dissects. Live capture uses dumpcap and works only where the user is permitted to capture. By default, captured packets are saved in the user's cache directory (.cache/termshark/pcaps on Linux), or to a file given with -w. Copying packets to the clipboard over SSH needs X11 forwarding or a custom copy command.

Builds as a single Go executable with go install (module github.com/gcla/termshark/v2; go.mod declares Go 1.13). Besides theme files, the repository commits only small test captures (pkg/pcap/testdata and scripts/pcaps/telnet-cooked.pcap).
MIT license. The README notes that tshark has many features termshark does not expose yet.

resources.name: mithril
resources.description: Offline C++ scanner for the contents of firmware and IoT software, pointed at a single file or an already unpacked root filesystem, that reports embedded secrets, a software bill of materials, known CVEs, open-source licenses, boot-security configuration and weak or publicly known keys, each finding with its evidence and a confidence level. Its SBOM also recovers components from ELF version banners, libc filenames and the kernel banner in stripped images and is written as CycloneDX and SPDX, while the CVE pass joins it against a local OSV and NVD mirror annotated with CISA KEV and EPSS. It does not unpack images; the author's companion tool moria handles identification and extraction.
requirements: A young, fast-moving project: the repository was created on 2026-09-07, and v0.4.0, published 2026-10-22, is the latest release at review, with Linux x86_64 and arm64 and macOS arm64 archives plus Debian packages for amd64 and arm64; the reviewed commit is the merge of that release.

Source builds need CMake 3.20+ and a C++20 compiler and link no third-party libraries; flake.nix, package.nix and Debian packaging are included. Input is a firmware file or a directory already extracted by moria or another unpacker; the --boot pass also reads a raw AMI or EDK2 BIOS image to report UEFI Secure Boot posture.

Scans make no network calls. The CVE pass needs a local mirror in .local/share/mithril under the home directory (or $MITHRIL_DB), downloaded once with --fetch-db from the project's weekly rebuilt db-latest release and checked against published SHA-256 sums (needs curl), or rebuilt from OSV.dev, NVD, CISA KEV, EPSS and the optional kernel.org feed with --update-db. README notes that the kernel checklist is curated rather than exhaustive, so an empty kernel result does not mean the kernel is clean, and that secret findings are well-formed matches, never confirmed live credentials.

The compiled-in key corpora are built from public keys and certificates vendored under data/: the public halves of rapid7 ssh-badkeys, the Vagrant insecure public key, eMudhra intermediate CA certificates, AOSP test-key public halves and the PKfail AMI test Platform Key certificate. THIRD_PARTY.md states that no private-key material is stored, and the key tests generate their keys with openssl at run time.
MIT; the vendored key data keeps its upstream MIT or Apache-2.0 terms, and the mirrored vulnerability feeds belong to their sources.

resources.name: SigDigger
resources.description: Qt graphical digital signal analyzer by Gonzalo José Carracedo Carballal, built on his Suscan and Sigutils libraries; its user manual names reverse engineering of radio signals with unknown parameters as the main use. It receives from SoapySDR-supported SDRs or plays back recorded I/Q and WAV files, shows spectrum and waterfall views, and lets analysts measure captured stretches in a time window with carrier recovery, transforms and symbol sampling. Inspector tabs run user-tunable PSK, FSK and ASK demodulators with parameter estimation and can forward demodulated samples; it also decodes analog video and previews AM, FM and SSB audio.
requirements: Reviewed at master commit 70f688b (2026-02-11); the README says SigDigger, SuWidgets, Suscan and Sigutils all keep their latest working changes on master. The last stable release is v0.3.0 (2022-07-05, with an x86-64 Linux AppImage and a macOS DMG); a rolling pre-release tagged latest, rebuilt on 2025-04-08, provides a 0.3.0 Linux AppImage and a Windows zip. The bundled user manual is version 0.3.0, dated 2022-06-27, and calls itself a draft.

The README targets GNU/Linux and macOS: Linux users can run the AppImage (the manual asks for glibc 2.27 or newer), macOS DMGs are made on request, and the README says reproducible Windows builds with all DLL dependencies are not currently possible, leaving Windows users to build from source. Source builds install Sigutils and Suscan (CMake), then SuWidgets and SigDigger (qmake with Qt 5.9+ or Qt 6), in that order; SigDigger.pro also links FFTW through pkg-config. The README also offers the author's blsd script, which builds everything in a local directory.

Live analysis needs an SDR receiver supported by SoapySDR; without one, recorded RF/IF data can be loaded from WAV or raw complex-float I/Q files. The repository commits no signal recordings. Plugins such as AmateurDSN, APTPlugin, AntSDRPlugin and ZeroMQPlugin live in separate repositories.

LGPL-3.0 (LICENSE); the README says the spectrum widget is Gqrx's plotter with modifications. The manual describes symbol decision as human-guided, so recovered symbols and any protocol interpretation remain the analyst's work.

resources.name: AppMon
resources.description: Frida-based framework by Nishant Das Patnaik, shown at Black Hat Arsenal 2016, for watching the system API calls that native macOS, iOS and Android apps make. Its Sniffer attaches to or spawns an app, loads hook scripts from a bundled library covering areas such as crypto, keychain, files, SQLite, HTTP, IPC and WebView, and records each intercepted call in a per-app SQLite database that a local Flask web interface displays. Further components trace Java classes, methods and argument types in Android apps and repackage IPAs or APKs with Frida Gadget so they can be inspected on non-jailbroken or non-rooted devices.
requirements: The repository is archived on GitHub and read-only. Its last commit on master, from 2022-11-08, changed the Frida release URL in apk_builder/getlibs.sh, and there are no releases. The usage documentation lives in the project wiki, last edited in 2019; the GitHub Pages site only links to it.

requirements.txt pins frida 12.2.6 (September 2018), Flask 1.0.2, Werkzeug 0.15.3 and other packages of that period. The hook scripts rely on Frida's Java and ObjC bridges and on legacy calls such as Module.findExportByName and Memory.readUtf8String, which Frida 17.0.0's release notes (May 2025) say are no longer bundled or have been removed, so current Frida releases are unlikely to work without changes.

The wiki's host setup covers macOS and Ubuntu or Kali Linux, with Android command-line tools on Linux. Jailbroken iOS and rooted Android devices run frida-server. For other devices the IPA Installer injects the committed ipa_installer/release/FridaGadget.dylib (about 14 MB) and re-signs the app with the user's iOS developer provisioning profile, while the APK Builder adds Frida Gadget libraries that getlibs.sh downloads and re-signs the APK with apk_builder/appmon.keystore, a shared key committed with a fixed password. Use these only on apps and devices you are permitted to test.
The README also lists an Intruder component that changes API-call data to alter an app's behavior. Apache-2.0 (LICENSE).

resources.name: img4tool
resources.description: tihmstar's command-line tool and C++ library for Apple's IMG4 firmware container format. It prints the ASN.1 contents of IMG4 files, IM4P payload containers and IM4M signing manifests, including payload types, descriptions and key bags, and extracts IM4P or IM4M parts from IMG4 or SHSH files and payloads from IM4P files, decompressing LZSS or BVX2 (LZFSE) data and decrypting it when given an IV and key. It can also check an IM4M ticket or a signed IMG4 against a BuildManifest, convert IM4M files to SHSH, and build or rename containers for restore tooling.
requirements: Latest release at review: build 218, published 2026-01-29, which provides the CI's macOS and Ubuntu buildroot archives rather than packaged installers. The reviewed master commit (merged 2026-08-20) is two commits ahead of it, merging a fix to the generator argument. The version number is the repository's commit count.

Source builds use autoconf, automake, libtool and pkg-config with a C++11 compiler and require tihmstar's libgeneral. libplist-2.0 (for SHSH reading, verification and conversion) and a crypto backend (OpenSSL, or CommonCrypto on macOS) for decryption and payload hash checks are optional; without one, decryption fails and verification warns that it cannot check payload hashes. BVX2 support needs Apple's libcompression or liblzfse, and an optional libfwkeyfetch build adds a key-lookup option.

Input files are the user's own IMG4, IM4P, IM4M or SHSH files and BuildManifests. The repository is source only and commits no Apple firmware, tickets or keys, and decrypting a payload requires an IV and key that the user supplies. The bundled LZSS decoder (lzssdec.c) is adapted, per its header, from Jonathan Levin's joker code.
LGPL-3.0 license. Container creation, renaming and the IM4R generator option exist for restore workflows.

resources.name: OWL: an open Apple Wireless Direct Link implementation
resources.description: Reimplements Apple Wireless Direct Link (AWDL), the proprietary Wi-Fi ad hoc protocol Apple devices use for peer-to-peer links such as AirDrop, as a user-space C daemon for Linux and macOS; the README calls it the result of reverse engineering by the Open Wireless Link project at TU Darmstadt's SEEMOO lab. OWL runs the master election, synchronises availability windows and the channel sequence, parses and crafts AWDL action and data frames, and provides an awdl0 virtual interface with a link-local IPv6 address, so unmodified IPv6 programs such as SEEMOO's OpenDrop AirDrop client can reach Apple devices. The authors describe the recovered protocol in a MobiCom 2018 paper.
requirements: Archived; the README calls OWL experimental and no longer maintained, says it does not support all AWDL features and may be incompatible with later AWDL versions, and states no affiliation with or endorsement by Apple. The last code change is a January 2022 buffer-overread fix; the 2026-08-17 and 2026-10-12 commits only replaced links to the former owlink website, which the README says is no longer associated with the project. There are no tags or releases.

Needs a Wi-Fi card with active monitor mode and frame injection, used directly: the authors developed and tested with an Atheros AR9280, and virtual machines without USB or PCIe passthrough and WSL are not supported. OWL runs with sudo on one wireless interface, which it then uses only for AWDL, so no access-point connection can run alongside it; channels 6, 44 and 149 are available subject to the local regulatory domain, and OWL can only monitor when it cannot use the chosen channel.

Builds with CMake 3.5+ and a C compiler against libpcap, libev and, on Linux, libnl; on macOS it uses CoreWLAN and needs a tun/tap driver such as tuntaposx. googletest and the radiotap library are git submodules. The workflow on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest builds the code and runs the googletest suite for frame-buffer parsing, election, peers and synchronisation; interoperation with Apple devices is the authors' report.

Nothing from Apple is needed to build it, and the repository holds only source code, tests, build files and an architecture diagram; using it requires nearby Apple devices with AWDL. README lists known gaps: static election metric and counter values, a channel sequence fixed at start-up because adapting it would need a better understanding of Apple's implementation, and no concurrent AP connection. It also cites the group's MobiCom 2018 protocol paper and demo and a USENIX Security 2019 security analysis of AWDL.
GPL-3.0 (COPYING); AWDL and AirDrop remain Apple's proprietary technology.

resources.name: grpc-tools
resources.description: Bradley Kemp's suite of gRPC debugging tools, described as Fiddler or Charles for gRPC. grpc-dump runs as a local HTTP(S) proxy that logs every gRPC and gRPC-Web call an application makes as a JSON stream with service and method names, metadata, any error status and each message both raw and parsed; without the .proto files it decodes messages heuristically. grpc-replay re-sends the recorded requests and checks the server's responses, grpc-fixture answers clients from a saved dump, and the grpc-proxy Go library underlies them.
requirements: Reviewed at master commit 928b1b9 (2023-11-14), the last push. The latest release is v0.2.6 (2020-06-30), and master has six later commits, mostly dependency bumps plus a 64 MB message-size limit. The README calls the tools alpha and warns of breaking changes between releases.

Install through the author's Homebrew tap, the release zips (amd64 builds for Linux, macOS and Windows) or go install; go.mod declares Go 1.13 and requires grpc-go v1.26.0, golang/protobuf v1.4.2 and protoreflect v1.7.0. The application under test must be pointed at the proxy, and the README notes that clients connecting to localhost usually ignore proxy settings; the system_proxy option is documented for macOS.

Clients that expect TLS need a certificate they trust for the intercepted domains; the README recommends mkcert-generated certificates installed on the user's own machine. Supplying .proto roots or descriptors gives exact decoding instead of the heuristic one. The integration tests use a small test.proto and their own recorded dump and fixture files; CircleCI configuration is included.
MIT license. Dumps contain full message contents and metadata, including any credentials in headers, so they should be treated as sensitive.

resources.name: JStillery
resources.description: Minded Security's JavaScript deobfuscator, which Stefano Di Paola forked from esdeobfuscate in 2015, simplifies scripts by partial evaluation on an esprima AST. It folds constant and string expressions, propagates known values through variables and pure function calls, evaluates calls to built-in String, Array and Number methods and atob/btoa, and parses string arguments passed to eval back into code. It runs as a command-line tool on a file or stdin, as an Express server with a web UI and a REST endpoint, or as a browserified library.
requirements: The newest commit on master dates from 2019-04-22, and there are no releases or tags. The 2015 Minded Security blog post that the README links describes JStillery as an internal tool used, among other things, to analyze JavaScript malware samples and normalize scripts for classification. The README also links a hosted REPL at mindedsecurity.github.io/jstillery.

Needs Node.js and npm install; package.json declares no Node.js version and leaves esprima, escodegen and esmangle unpinned, and no lockfile is committed, so each install takes their latest releases. The CLI prints the original and the deobfuscated code. npm run build_server copies the web UI and browserifies the library, and npm run start_server then serves the UI and a /deobfuscate endpoint on port 3001, with server_config.json allowing any origin by default.

Partial evaluation is on by default (the USE_PARTIAL environment variable turns it off only when set to an empty string) and passes selected expressions from the input to Node's vm.runInNewContext. Node's documentation says the vm module is not a security mechanism, so analyze untrusted samples in an isolated environment.

JStillery predates the newer deobfuscators, such as webcrack, javascript-deobfuscator and the Obfuscator.io Deobfuscator, and its documentation does not mention bundle unpacking, string-array decoding or control-flow unflattening. The mocha suite in tests/ compares output for samples including JSFuck, aaencode, jjencode and Dean Edwards' packer with stored expected results, some of which remain only partly simplified.

LICENSE and the README state GPL-3.0, while both package.json files declare ISC; src/jstiller.js keeps the BSD-style notice of esdeobfuscate. The web UI vendors jQuery, Bootstrap, CodeMirror, Font Awesome and js-beautify.

resources.name: Enjarify
resources.description: Pure-Python 3 translator from Dalvik bytecode to equivalent Java bytecode, so Java analysis tools and decompilers can be applied to Android apps: given an APK, with every DEX file of a multidex APK combined into one jar, or a single DEX file, it writes a jar of class files. Its README contrasts it with dex2jar and lists edge cases it handles, such as Unicode class names, constants used as several types, implicit casts, exception handlers that jump into normal control flow, very long methods and classes that reference too many constants. By default it also applies readability optimizations such as copy propagation and unused-value removal.
requirements: Archived. Latest release at review: 1.0.3, published 2016-12-20 with no assets; the last commit is from 2017-01-30. The README says this repository may be out of date and that future development moved to Storyyeller/enjarify, whose master branch is 15 commits ahead, with its last commit on 2020-03-07.

Runs from a clone with Python 3 and no other dependencies. enjarify.sh prefers PyPy3, which the README calls much faster than CPython, and enjarify.bat always calls python3. Input is the analyst's own APK or DEX file; the output defaults to [inputname]-enjarify.jar, -o sets the name, -f allows overwriting and --fast skips the optimizations.

Optional metadata such as source-file attributes, line numbers and annotations is not translated, and the README notes contrived cases that cannot be translated because of Android or Java limits. The output is bytecode, so reading it as source needs a separate Java decompiler. runtests.py translates the bundled fixtures, small classes.dex files with their smali sources and expected outputs in tests/test1 to tests/test7, adds the small Android API stub classes from tests/stubs and runs the result with java.
Apache-2.0; the README states that it is not an official Google product.

resources.name: Yagi
resources.description: Airbus CERT plugin that embeds Ghidra's native decompiler in IDA Pro and IDA Free: pressing F3 on a function shows Ghidra's C output inside IDA, and edits made there, covering global symbols such as function prototypes and the names and types of stack and register variables, are saved to the IDA database. The README lists x86, x86-64, ARM, AArch64, PowerPC, MIPS, SPARC, AVR8, 6502, Z80 and eBPF as supported, while other Ghidra processors such as Dalvik, JVM, RISC-V and 68000 are not yet enabled.
requirements: Inactive since its latest release, v1.5.0 (2022-08-04), which adds eBPF and IDA 7.7 support and ships Windows MSI installers for IDA 7.6, IDA 7.7 and IDA Freeware; the last Linux installers (.sh and .tar.gz for IDA 7.5, 7.6 and Freeware) are in v1.4.0 (2021-12-20). No builds for IDA 8 or later are published. The default branch is main; an older master branch stops in 2021.

Source builds need a recursive clone, whose submodules are Airbus CERT's Ghidra fork on its fix-memory-access-violation branch (pinned at the Ghidra 10.1 release commit), eBPF-for-Ghidra and cylance/eBPF_processor. They also need CMake 3.11+, a C++ compiler (Visual Studio on Windows), flex and bison for the SLEIGH grammar, WiX for the Windows installer, and the Hex-Rays IDA SDK matching the user's IDA version, which the repository does not include.

The workflows build on a self-hosted Windows runner against a locally installed IDA 7.6 SDK. Their googletest unit tests decompile machine-code byte arrays written into the test sources for x86 (16-, 32- and 64-bit), ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC, 6502 and Z80, using mocked IDA loader, symbol and type interfaces. README TODOs include enum types, AArch64 function-end rules and changing constant types.
Apache-2.0; Ghidra's decompiler keeps its own Apache-2.0 terms, and IDA and its SDK are Hex-Rays products under their own licenses.

resources.name: box.js
resources.description: Node.js utility for studying malicious JavaScript that runs a sample inside an emulated Windows JScript environment, with WScript, ActiveX, filesystem, registry, WMI and HTTP objects emulated and source rewriting that exposes eval calls and conditional-compilation code. Each analysis writes a results folder with the URLs requested and those that led to an executable payload, every code snippet executed (JavaScript, cmd.exe and PowerShell), files written with their types and hashes, and a list of IOCs; by default downloads are answered with simulated 404 errors so that fallback sites are revealed. Batch runs, an optional prepended file of browser-object stubs, a Docker image, a REST API and export to VirusTotal or Cuckoo support triage at scale.
requirements: Latest npm release at review: 1.9.29, published 2026-07-02 alongside the reviewed master commit, which adapts the sandbox to the latest vm2 package; RELEASE_NOTES.txt numbers the same releases 1.19.x. Recent development is by Kirk Sayre through pull requests. Installs with npm install box-js --global; package.json declares Node.js 6 or later and depends on vm2 >=3.9.19, jsdom 16, acorn and escodegen, and the READMEs list REMnux and BlackArch packages and Cuckoo, CAPE and IntelOwl integrations.

Input is the analyst's own sample file or folder of samples; the repository ships no malware samples, only emulator code, a generated Windows process list (emulator/processes.json), source-rewriting patches and a mocha test file. Encoded .jse files must first be decoded with the bundled decoder.c, MrBrownstone's 2000–2005 Script Encoder decoder, compiled with a C compiler; VBScript is not parsed as input.

Samples run inside vm2, with a 10-second default timeout; --dangerous-vm switches to Node's vm module, which the README says can be broken. --download makes real requests to the URLs a sample contacts, so leave it off unless the network is isolated. The README recommends a temporary Docker container for further isolation; integrations/docker/Dockerfile is based on node:8-alpine, and the REST API server needs a user who can start Docker containers.

Emulation is incomplete by design: unsupported ActiveX objects or methods stop the analysis until someone implements them, and samples with environment or date checks may show no behaviour. MIT; decoder.c keeps its author's notice.

resources.name: usb-rea
resources.description: Python CLI and stdio MCP server for inferring the USB protocol of a device whose only control software is a vendor app. While the user clicks through the app, it captures traffic with usbmon or USBPcap, takes a label for each action, diffs the packets per action and infers message layouts: constant bytes, rolling counters, scaled 8- to 32-bit values, lookup tables, packed bit fields and sum, XOR or CRC checksums. It also decodes device replies, handshakes with session tokens and image streams sent to device screens, links each inferred field to Wireshark frame numbers in a report, and generates a pyusb driver and a Wireshark Lua dissector.
requirements: Python 3.10+, with pyusb and the MCP SDK as dependencies; version 0.7.7 (released 2026-11-01) is on PyPI. Live capture needs Linux usbmon with dumpcap or tshark, or USBPcap on Windows; offline analysis reads pcap or pcapng files whose actions are marked with timestamps or listed in order with a pause between clicks. The user supplies the device and its vendor app, and the README says the tool only analyzes traffic of devices the user owns.

The README marks the project alpha and lists limits per feature, among them one-byte modes, unsigned 32-bit readings, handshake tokens that must be copied verbatim and image streams of at least three frames. Sending packets to hardware through the replay command or MCP tool requires explicit confirmation.

CI runs pytest on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13, including tshark checks of the generated dissectors. docs/VALIDATION.md uses synthetic devices, captures synthesized from liquidctl's Kraken X and Hydro H100i Platinum drivers and rivalcfg's Rival 100 driver as ground truth, and two Wireshark sample captures downloaded on demand; one user-shared ASUS TUF Gaming LC III LCD capture is stored trimmed, with its image data zeroed. Emulated-gadget tests and real-hardware case studies remain open roadmap items.
MIT per LICENSE and pyproject.toml.
The README expands the name as “Reverse Engineer any USB gadget”.

resources.name: MagiskFrida
resources.description: Magisk, KernelSU and APatch module that installs frida-server on a rooted Android device and starts it at boot, so Frida clients can attach for dynamic instrumentation without starting the server by hand. A daily GitHub Actions job checks for a new Frida release, downloads Frida's official frida-server builds for arm64, arm, x86 and x86_64, and publishes a matching module ZIP with an updater.json for updates from the root manager. The server listens on 127.0.0.1:27042 unless another port is written to a file in the module directory, and the module's action button starts or stops it.
requirements: Needs a rooted Android device with Magisk, KernelSU or APatch on arm64, arm, x86 or x86_64; the README says to install MagiskFrida.zip from the GitHub releases rather than the obsolete Magisk modules repository. The troubleshooting guide asks for a working adb shell, a stable, up-to-date Magisk with MagiskHide disabled and an AOSP-based ROM. Building the ZIP yourself needs uv and Python (CI uses 3.13) and downloads frida-server from Frida's GitHub releases.

Release versions follow the bundled Frida version; at review the latest was 17.25.1-1 (2026-11-01), built the day Frida published 17.25.1. The module only installs and supervises frida-server: instrumentation runs through Frida's own clients and scripts.
The CI workflow builds and publishes the ZIP; the repository has no test suite.

The repository has no license file and GitHub detects no license, so it states no reuse terms for its scripts. The bundled frida-server binaries are Frida's official builds under the wxWindows Library Licence.

resources.name: frida-scripts (0xdea)
resources.description: Marco Ivaldi's (raptor) collection of Frida JavaScript instrumentation scripts for reverse engineering mobile apps and Linux programs. The main Android and iOS tracers hook Java or Objective-C classes and methods selected by name, wildcard or regular expression, plus native functions matched by Frida ApiResolver patterns such as exports:*!open*, and log each call's arguments and return value; they can also print backtraces. Companion scripts enumerate loaded classes and methods, and a Linux pair traces and enumerates functions in an ELF binary and its shared libraries.
requirements: Load a script with Frida's CLI from frida-tools, for example frida -U -f <package> -l raptor_frida_android_trace.js for an app on a USB-connected device, after uncommenting or editing the usage examples at the end of the script. Mobile use needs a device that Frida can instrument; the iOS tracer's header records a jailbroken iPhone 8 on iOS 16.5.

Version 0.2 (2025-10-02) ported the main tracers to Frida 17. Script headers record Frida 17.3.2 on Android 11 and iOS 16.5 and Frida 17.2.1 on Ubuntu, while the android-snippets and ios-snippets directories were tested only with Frida before 17.0.0. The README warns that the iOS and Android scripts may need tweaking and points to Brida as a maintained project that includes some of them.
The repository has no automated tests or CI, and its TODO lists extensive testing with real-world apps.
MIT per LICENSE.

resources.name: Zygisk-Il2CppDumper
resources.description: Zygisk module by Perfare, the Il2CppDumper author, that dumps type metadata from inside a Unity IL2CPP Android app while it runs. Built for one package name, it waits for the app to load libil2cpp.so, resolves the runtime's il2cpp API exports, walks the classes of every loaded assembly and writes dump.cs to the app's files directory, listing namespaces, classes, interfaces and enums with field offsets, properties and method signatures annotated with RVA and virtual addresses. On x86 devices running an ARM build of the app, it loads its ARM library through the Houdini native bridge.
requirements: Needs a rooted Android device with Magisk v24 or later and Zygisk enabled, and an app the user supplies that uses Unity's IL2CPP backend. There are no published releases: the module is built for one package name, either by running the repository's manual Build workflow in a fork with that name or by editing GamePackageName in game.h and running the Gradle task :module:assembleRelease (NDK 25.2.9519653; CI uses Java 11), then installed through Magisk. dump.cs appears under /data/data/<package>/files/ once the app starts.
It writes only dump.cs; unlike the desktop Il2CppDumper, it produces no dummy assemblies or disassembler scripts. The latest master commit is from 2023-05-22, with the module at v1.2.0.
The repository has no tests, and its only CI workflow builds the module on manual dispatch.
MIT per LICENSE, whose copyright line names Rikka; the bundled xDL symbol-lookup library carries its own MIT notice from the HexHacking Team.

resources.name: System Informer
resources.description: Windows process viewer and system inspector, formerly Process Hacker, for examining running programs and the system around them. It gives a highlighted overview of system activity, searches the handles and loaded DLLs of processes to find which one is using a file, shows active network connections and real-time disk access, displays stack traces with kernel-mode, WOW64 and .NET support, and creates, edits and controls services. Version 4.0 adds a Process Monitor that logs process, thread, image, registry, file, handle and silo events from its kernel driver, and plugins add .NET assembly and performance tabs, a window explorer and Hybrid Analysis lookups.
requirements: Windows 10 or later, 32-bit or 64-bit, per the README. Release at review: v4.0.26241.138, published 2026-08-29 as the first 4.0 release; the reviewed master commit is 874 commits ahead of it. Building from source needs Visual Studio 2022 or later and the build_init.cmd and build_release.cmd scripts in build/.

The KSystemInformer kernel driver gives its broader inspection only to verified callers: binaries loaded into System Informer need a .sig from the build's key pair or a Microsoft or anti-malware vendor signature, and loading an unsigned third-party plugin restricts driver access. Builds signed with a developer's own key need debug and test-signing mode, with Secure Boot disabled where applicable.

The Agent Tools plugin is on the master branch only, not in the 4.0 release; its source describes it as exposing System Informer's process data and actions to AI agents over the Model Context Protocol. It is off by default, asks to confirm connections by default and offers stdio setup commands for clients such as Claude Code and Codex CLI. The OnlineChecks plugin's Hybrid Analysis lookups are opt-in with per-service API keys and can optionally submit unknown files.
MIT per LICENSE.txt and the README.

resources.name: CyberChef
resources.description: GCHQ's browser-based workbench for decoding, decrypting, decompressing, parsing and carving data by chaining operations into a recipe, with all processing done client-side. The pinned operation catalogue lists 506 operations, among them XOR brute force, AES, DES and Blowfish decryption, x86 and ARM disassembly, ELF info, file-type detection, file extraction, entropy and strings, YARA rules, Protobuf decoding and Ethernet, IPv4, TCP and UDP header parsing. The Magic operation tries to detect nested encodings automatically, and breakpoints step through a recipe one operation at a time to show the data at each stage.
requirements: Use the hosted app at gchq.github.io/CyberChef, a full copy downloaded from the app, the ghcr.io/gchq/cyberchef Docker image or a Node.js v24 build (npm install, then npm start or npm run build); the README lists Chrome 50+ and Firefox 38+ as supported browsers. Release at review: v11.5.0, published 2026-09-18; the reviewed master commit is newer.

Inputs and recipes stay in the browser and are not sent to the web server. Files of up to about 2 GB load, depending on the browser, and some operations can take a very long time on that much data; Auto Bake can be turned off for large inputs.
Apache-2.0, under Crown Copyright; contributions require signing the GCHQ Contributor Licence Agreement.

resources.name: YARA
resources.description: VirusTotal's pattern-matching tool for identifying and classifying files such as malware samples with rules that combine text, hex and regular-expression strings with a Boolean condition. It scans a file, a folder or a running process from the command line, through the libyara C API or from Python with yara-python. Modules expose parsed structure to rules: pe and elf expose most fields of PE and ELF headers, dotnet adds .NET metadata, math adds calculations such as entropy, and the optional magic and cuckoo modules add libmagic file types and Cuckoo sandbox behavior reports.
requirements: Runs on Windows, Linux and macOS; release at review: v4.6.0, published 2026-10-27. Source builds need automake, libtool, make, gcc and pkg-config. Features that depend on OpenSSL are enabled only when OpenSSL is installed, and the cuckoo (Jansson) and magic (libmagic) modules are compiled only with --enable-cuckoo or --enable-magic; vcpkg also packages YARA.

The README marks YARA as in maintenance mode; the YARA-X README says YARA still receives bug fixes and minor features, while new modules and large features go only into YARA-X. The command-line documentation warns that compiled rules from untrusted sources can lead to the execution of malicious code; since YARA 3.9 they load only with -C.
BSD-3-Clause per COPYING.

resources.name: Cheat Engine
resources.description: Memory scanner, debugger, disassembler and assembler for inspecting and changing running games and other applications; its README calls it a development environment focused on modding games and applications for personal use. The project site lists a memory scanner for finding the variables a game uses, a debugger, disassembler, assembler, speedhack, trainer maker, Direct3D manipulation and system inspection tools, and the README's build notes add Mono, .NET and Java runtime inspection, a VEH debugger interface, Lua and C code in scripts and an optional kernel-mode driver.
requirements: The site's news of 2026-05-29 says Cheat Engine 7.7 was released for Windows, Mac and Linux to Patreon supporters first, followed by a public Windows installer. The newest GitHub release is 7.5 (2023-02-23), which attaches no binaries, and the reviewed master commit dates from 2025-04-19.

Building needs Lazarus 2.2.2 for 64-bit Windows with its i386 cross-compiler for the main project and Visual Studio (usually 2017) for the .sln helper projects, such as the Mono, .NET and Java data collectors. Kernel-mode functions need the DBK driver built without a signature, then booting with unsigned-driver support or signing the driver yourself.

The site describes it as made for modifying single-player games without an internet connection, says it will most likely not work on online games, requires users to be 18 or older, calls it for private and educational purposes and asks users not to violate a game's or application's EULA or terms of service.

The repository has no top-level license file and GitHub detects no license; the site says the source code is visible so that anyone can compile their own version. Bundled components such as tcclib carry their own license files.

resources.name: Noriben
resources.description: Python script that drives Sysinternals Process Monitor to record what a program does while it runs, filters out routine system activity and writes a text report of the processes it created and its file, registry and network activity. It works as a lightweight malware sandbox and can also log events while the analyst runs a sample by hand, with command-line options, user interaction or under a debugger; created files can be scanned with YARA rules and their hashes looked up on VirusTotal. Version 2.1.0 adds DLL-load monitoring, an ASCII process tree and JSON output, and NoribenSandbox.py automates runs inside a guest VM.
requirements: Python 3 and Sysinternals procmon.exe or procmon64.exe on the Windows analysis machine; yara-python is optional for --yara scans and requests for VirusTotal lookups. Release at review: 2.1.0, published 2026-11-03, whose tag is the reviewed main commit.

The README's sandbox workflow runs a sample in a VM, copies the results off and reverts before the next sample. NoribenSandbox.py starts a predefined VM snapshot, copies in the sample, runs Noriben and retrieves a ZIP report and a screenshot; the README says this front end currently runs on macOS hosts.
With a VirusTotal API key it looks up file hashes; uploading every created file to VirusTotal happens only when virustotal_upload is set to True in Noriben.config, which defaults to False.
The 2.1.0 notes add large-scale unit testing, developed with AI assistance; the README runs tests/unit_tester.ps1 through Noriben in a Windows VM with Procmon module loads enabled.
Apache-2.0 per the README and LICENSE.

resources.name: QEMU
resources.description: Machine and user-space emulator that runs code built for one CPU architecture on another through its TCG dynamic translator. System emulation boots a complete emulated machine, such as an ARMv7 board on an x86_64 PC, and user-mode emulation runs Linux or BSD binaries built for another ABI by translating their system calls. For analysis, its gdbstub lets GDB stop the guest, examine registers and memory and set breakpoints and watchpoints, TCG plugins passively instrument execution down to single instructions and memory accesses (bundled examples count instructions, trace system calls and log execution), and system emulation supports deterministic record/replay debugging.
requirements: Builds on modern Linux, macOS, Windows through the Mingw64 toolchain and other Unix hosts (mkdir build, ../configure, make). The upstream repository is gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu; GitHub carries a read-only mirror that asks users to take release tarballs from the QEMU website. The newest tag at review was v11.1.3, on a commit dated 2026-10-28.

User-mode emulation covers only the Linux and BSD system-call interfaces and emulates no hardware, and each guest architecture supports system emulation, user mode or both. TCG plugins observe guest state without changing it, and the bundled syscall plugin works only in user mode. With KVM or Xen, the hypervisor runs the CPU while QEMU provides emulated hardware.
QEMU as a whole is released under GPL-2.0; the LICENSE file gives component details.

resources.name: Hex Fiend
resources.description: Open-source macOS hex editor that inspects and edits binary files of any size without loading them into memory. It supports insertions and deletions, fast search and a data inspector that reads integers and floating-point values as signed or unsigned and big- or little-endian. File > Compare shows the differences between two files while accounting for inserted or deleted bytes, and Tcl binary templates display a file's structure next to its bytes; bundled templates cover COFF, ELF, Mach-O and MS-DOS EXE headers, 6502 disassembly and Commodore 64 PRG files, plus archives, file systems, partition tables and media formats. Its hex and data views are also available as an embeddable framework.
requirements: macOS 10.14.6 or later, required since v2.17. Release at review: v2.18.1, published 2025-03-16; the reviewed master commit is dated 2025-06-29. Custom templates are .tcl files in the app's Templates folder under Application Support.

Binary templates arrived in v2.9 and are written in Tcl, which ships with macOS. Since v2.17 templates can declare file types for automatic selection, but the release notes say most built-in templates do not yet set this information.
BSD-2-Clause per License.txt.

resources.name: ScyllaHide
resources.description: User-mode (ring 3) anti-anti-debug library for 32- and 64-bit Windows programs that hooks system functions so the program being debugged cannot detect the debugger. Its documentation covers options for PEB debug flags such as BeingDebugged, NtGlobalFlag and heap flags, threads hidden with ThreadHideFromDebugger, debugger windows and processes found through window and process-list queries, invalid-handle NtClose checks, input blocking, timing checks, hardware-breakpoint detection and exception-based checks; extra options inject DLLs, prevent thread creation and dump processes started RunPE-style. Plugins integrate it with x64dbg, OllyDbg v1 and v2, IDA and TitanEngine, and the standalone InjectorCLI injects its hook library into a process under any debugger.
requirements: Windows; release at review: v1.4, published 2023-03-24, with the reviewed master commit dated 2023-07-29. Plugins cover x64dbg, OllyDbg v1 and v2, TitanEngine v2 and IDA; the README lists the IDA v6 plugin as not supported and says PE x64 debugging is fully supported with the x64dbg and IDA plugins.

It works only in user mode, and the README points to TitanHide for kernel-mode (ring 0) anti-anti-debug. Each option targets specific anti-debug checks: the documentation advises enabling the timing, hardware-breakpoint, thread-prevention and NtYieldExecution options only when needed, and using the RunPE unpacker, which terminates and dumps newly created processes, only inside a virtual machine.
GPL-3.0. The project is a fork of the original ScyllaHide repository on Bitbucket; the full manual is a PDF attached to the docs-2019-05-17 release, and its LaTeX source is in Documentation/.

resources.name: YARA-X
resources.description: VirusTotal's Rust rewrite of YARA for identifying and classifying files with pattern-matching rules. It is meant to replace YARA, with more detailed error reports, faster regular-expression and hex-pattern matching and a more capable command line. Rules keep YARA's syntax of text, hex and regular-expression patterns joined by a Boolean condition, and modules parse PE, ELF, Mach-O, .NET, Android DEX, Chrome CRX and Windows LNK files; the CLI can also print a module's parsed output as JSON or YAML without any rule, which makes it usable as a file-dissection tool. Rust, C, Go and Python APIs, a rule formatter and a language server with a Visual Studio Code extension are included.
requirements: Pre-built binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows come with each release; macOS users can install it with Homebrew and Python users with pip install yara-x. Building needs a recent Rust toolchain (cargo install --path cli), and the Go library builds on the C API. Release at review: v1.23.0, published 2026-11-05.

Its comparison page says the C/C++, Python and Go APIs are not compatible with YARA's and that process scanning is not implemented yet; a separate page lists rule-level differences. The README calls YARA-X mature and stable and says VirusTotal runs it in production.
BSD-3-Clause per LICENSE; contributions need Google's Contributor License Agreement.

resources.name: de4dot
resources.description: Open-source .NET deobfuscator and unpacker that tries to restore a packed and obfuscated assembly to almost its original form. Depending on the obfuscator, it decrypts strings, constants, methods, resources and embedded assemblies statically or dynamically, removes proxy methods, junk classes and tamper-detection and anti-debug code, devirtualizes virtualized code, deobfuscates control flow and renames symbols to readable names; it can also just detect which obfuscator was used. The README lists 19 supported obfuscators and packers, among them Dotfuscator, .NET Reactor, Eazfuscator.NET and SmartAssembly.
requirements: The repository was archived on GitHub after its last commit on 2020-08-29 and has no GitHub releases; the README points to CI builds for binaries. Source builds use the .NET Framework or .NET Core solution and need dnlib, which de4dot uses to read and write assemblies.

Original symbol names usually cannot be restored, and XAML is not renamed, so WPF or Silverlight assemblies may need --dont-rename. The README offers no support and says newer obfuscator versions may require updating de4dot yourself.
For some obfuscators, and for dynamic string decryption, it loads the assembly and its dependencies into memory and executes them, so the README advises a safe sandbox for suspected malware.
GPL-3.0 (COPYING); bundled libraries such as dnlib, SharpZipLib, QuickLZ and LZMA keep their own license files.

resources.name: ReClass.NET
resources.description: Memory structure editor for reconstructing the classes and data structures of a running x86 or x64 process, a .NET port of ReClass with many additions. Users lay out memory as typed nodes, such as integers, floats, vectors and matrices, text, pointers, arrays, unions, virtual tables and function pointers, with automatic node dissection, highlighting of changed memory, types from PDB debug symbols and RTTI class names, then generate C++ or C# code from the result. It also offers a memory viewer and scanner, a module and section dumper, a debugger that finds what writes to or accesses an address, and plugins that can supply other memory-access methods or game-specific class information, such as for Frostbite games.
requirements: Releases ship x86 and x64 builds with a launcher that picks between them, and the README lists Linux support tested on Ubuntu 18.04. Release at review: v1.2, published 2019-04-15; the reviewed master commit dates from 2023-07-03. Compiling needs Visual Studio 2019, and the Linux native core library needs WSL, plus g++-multilib for cross-platform builds.
It imports ReClass 2007–2016, ReClass QT, Cheat Engine and CrySearch files. Plugins are installed by copying them into the Plugins folder; the README says the Unreal plugin is no longer available.
MIT per LICENSE.

resources.name: ClassyShark
resources.description: Google's standalone browser for Android executables and libraries that shows class interfaces and members, dex counts and dependencies. It opens .dex, .aar and .so libraries, .apk, .jar and .class executables and Android binary XML files such as AndroidManifest, resources and layouts, and it can export what it shows as text.
requirements: Runs as a JAR (java -jar ClassyShark.jar) on a Java runtime; Arch Linux users can install a prebuilt JAR from the AUR. The latest release is 8.2, published 2018-07-25, and the repository was archived on GitHub after its last commit on 2023-05-19.
The README marks its API finder as work in progress; a command-line reference ships as CommandLine.pdf in the repository.
Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.txt and the README.

resources.name: RPISEC Malware Analysis course (CSCI 4976)
resources.description: Materials from the student-run Malware Analysis course that RPISEC taught at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Fall 2015, built around the book Practical Malware Analysis. Twelve lectures run from basic static and dynamic analysis, x86 and IDA through Windows internals, malware behavior, data encoding, covert launching, anti-disassembly, anti-VM and anti-debugging, and packing and unpacking to the Windows kernel and rootkit techniques, with ten labs and four projects that include runtime process manipulation, unpacking automation and an APT sample analysis.
requirements: The course expected working C/C++ and some assembly experience, and students read the matching book chapters before each lecture. It used a Windows 7 32-bit analysis VM, which is not distributed; the v1.0_release (2016-01-14) packages installers for the free tools used, such as IDA Free, OllyDbg, WinDbg, the Sysinternals Suite, PEiD, Regshot and Wireshark.

Most lab and project samples are real malware, stored in ZIP archives encrypted with the password infected; the README says to keep them inside a proper analysis environment. Lectures were not recorded, and slides covering book material are outlines.
The repository has no license file and GitHub detects no license; the reviewed master commit dates from 2017-05-11.

resources.name: Corkami pics
resources.description: Collection of posters and diagrams that dissect file formats byte by byte, published as PNG and PDF images. The binary posters cover executables (ELF, DOS COM and EXE, NE, LE, PE, Mach-O and fat Mach-O, Java class, Dalvik DEX, Python bytecode, SWF, GameCube/Wii DOL and Switch NRO) along with image, video, archive, document, sound and serialization formats, x86 and x64 opcode charts and Dalvik, JVM and .NET opcode tables. The more detailed 101 series explains PE, ELF, Mach-O, ZIP, Java class, PDF, COM and WAV files and includes Inkscape sources and proof-of-concept files.
requirements: Images and PDFs to view in a browser or image viewer; nothing needs installing. The repository has no releases, and the reviewed master commit dates from 2024-02-18.
Besides the file-format posters, the repository holds general posters, tracings and outlines that are not about file formats.
The repository has no license file and GitHub detects no license, so reuse terms are not stated.

resources.name: Keypatch
resources.description: IDA Pro plugin built on the Keystone assembler engine that patches a binary from typed assembly, fills an address range with instructions or raw bytes and searches the loaded binary for assembly instructions. It assembles Arm, Arm64, Hexagon, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC, SystemZ and 16-, 32- and 64-bit x86 code, shows the encoding while you type, can pad with NOPs up to the next instruction boundary, keeps the original instruction in an IDA comment and can undo the last patch.
requirements: Needs IDA Pro on Windows, macOS or Linux with the Keystone engine and its Python binding plus the six module; keypatch.py is copied into IDA's plugins folder. The README confirms IDA Pro 6.4 to 7.5, and the reviewed master commit (2024-09-06) adds IDA 9.0 API changes. The latest tagged release is 2.1 (2017-01-17), while the code reports version 2.2.
Patches change only the IDA database until Edit | Patch program | Apply patches to input file writes them to the original binary.
GPL-2.0 per COPYING.

resources.name: edb-debugger
resources.description: Qt-based graphical debugger for AArch32, x86 and x86-64 programs, inspired by OllyDbg, with Linux as its only officially supported platform. Its interface docks disassembly, register, stack and data views, adds a memory-regions window, process attaching, symbols, an expression syntax and an analysis bar similar to IDA Pro's, and its default plugins include Analyzer, Assembler, BinarySearcher, BreakpointManager, FunctionFinder, HardwareBreakpoints, HeapAnalyzer, OpcodeSearcher, ROPTool and SymbolViewer.
requirements: Linux is the only officially supported platform; FreeBSD, OpenBSD, macOS and Windows ports are underway with varying functionality. Building needs a C++17 GCC or Clang, Qt 5.15+ or 6.8+, Capstone 3.0+ and optionally Graphviz 2.38+, using CMake on a recursive clone so that the submodules are fetched.

Release at review: 1.5.0, published 2024-03-22 and the last version to support Linux kernels older than 3.0; new development targets kernel 3.0 and newer and will be released as 2.0.0. The reviewed master commit is dated 2026-10-27.
GPL-2.0 per COPYING.

resources.name: BinNavi
resources.description: Google's open-sourced binary analysis IDE for inspecting, navigating, editing and annotating the control-flow graphs and call graphs of disassembled code. It also collects and combines execution traces and keeps track of analysis results among a group of analysts. Disassemblies come from IDA Pro through a bundled export plugin that writes the PostgreSQL database BinNavi uses for disassemblies, comments and traces; the README notes that no exporter exists yet for other disassemblers.
requirements: Needs Java 11 or later, a reachable PostgreSQL database and IDA Pro to import disassemblies. It builds from source with Maven and Ant (mvn dependency:copy-dependencies, then ant build-binnavi-fat-jar); the Gradle build is experimental. GitHub releases include BinNavi 6.1 (2016-03-17) and a historical 1.2 version published in 2017.

The README says the project is no longer under active development, and the repository was archived on GitHub after its last commit on 2020-10-23. Graph display uses the commercial yFiles library: the repository ships a pre-built, obfuscated yfileswrap JAR, and changing the yfileswrap packages needs a yFiles license.
Apache-2.0, apart from the yFiles dependency.

resources.name: flare-emu
resources.description: Mandiant FLARE Python library that pairs IDA Pro, Rizin or Radare2 with the Unicorn emulator so analysts can script emulation of the binary they are analyzing, for 32- and 64-bit x86, ARM and ARM64. Its interfaces emulate an instruction range or function with chosen register and stack values, force execution down the branches needed to reach target addresses or every cross-reference to a function, walk all paths through a function, run a standalone byte blob, or emulate from an address until nothing is left, with hooks on instructions and calls. A common use in its README is decrypting malware strings by emulating the decryption routine at each call site and commenting the results.
requirements: Needs Unicorn and its Python bindings plus IDA Pro 7.x or later (older IDA APIs are not supported), Rizin with rzpipe, or Radare2 with r2pipe; the README also shows use through IDA's idalib. Installation means copying flare_emu.py, the framework module and flare_emu_hooks.py into IDA's python directory or onto Python's import path.
The repository was archived on GitHub after a final release tagged 2025-08-14, which has no notes. With Rizin it runs as a command-line script or in a Python shell.
Apache-2.0 per LICENSE-APACHE.TXT.

resources.name: IDA Pro
resources.description: Hex-Rays' commercial interactive disassembler, decompiler and debugger, which turns compiled code for more than 70 processor families into annotated, cross-referenced assembly and decompiled pseudocode. Its 15 decompilers cover 32- and 64-bit x86, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC and RISC-V as well as ARC, V850, TriCore, Hexagon and Android DEX; the Dalvik decompiler, new in IDA 9.5 alongside TriCore and Hexagon, renders DEX bytecode as Java pseudocode. Documented loaders include PE, ELF and Mach-O with Apple dyld shared caches and kernelcaches, DEX, UEFI firmware images, WebAssembly modules and console formats such as Xbox XBE, N64, SNES ROM and PlayStation PSX executables, and the processor list names console CPUs from the NES and Game Boy to the PlayStation 3 Cell, Xbox 360 Xenon and PSP Allegrex. The debugger runs locally or through remote debug servers for Windows, Linux, macOS and Android, and analysis can be scripted with IDAPython, IDC and the C++ SDK, run without a GUI through the idalib library, or driven from MCP clients through IDA MCP.
requirements: Release at review: IDA 9.5 (build 9.5.261026), announced 2026-10-26. Hosts: macOS 12+ (x64 or ARM64); x64 Windows 10 1607+ for the GUI, Windows 7+ for text-mode or headless use; 64-bit Linux, where the installation guide names CentOS 7 or Ubuntu 16.04 and the IDA Free page glibc 2.28 (Debian 10, Ubuntu 18.10, RHEL 8) on x86-64 or ARM64. IDAPython needs Python 3.11+.

Commercial, sold only as yearly subscriptions; perpetual licenses ended on 2024-09-30, and those bought earlier keep working for the version purchased. IDA Pro Essential has two cloud decompilers from one family, Expert two, four or six local ones and Ultimate all local ones, on Named, Computer or Floating licenses; IDA Pro Headless is an OEM license for servers, CI and embedding in products.

IDA Free and IDA Home are Named licenses for non-commercial use only. Free disassembles only x86 and x86-64, decompiles them in the cloud and debugs locally on x86/x64; Home has 70+ disassemblers, 11 cloud decompilers (32- and 64-bit x86, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC and RISC-V, plus Android DEX) and local or GDB-server debugging. Cloud decompilers need an Internet connection.

The IDA 9.5 release notes say the Dalvik decompiler does not rebuild try-with-resources, can emit output that is not valid Java and gives obfuscated files no special treatment, and that the new UEFI plugin focuses on the DXE environment and is still being refined.

resources.name: Binary Ninja
resources.description: Vector 35's commercial interactive disassembler, decompiler and debugger, whose decompiler is built on the BNIL family of intermediate languages and shows either C or BNIL for every officially supported architecture. Depending on the edition it decompiles x86/x86-64, ARMv7/Thumb2, AArch64, PowerPC, MIPS, RISC-V, MSP430, 6502, nanoMIPS, TriCore, C-SKY, M·CORE, Hexagon, NDS32 and TMS320C6x, and it loads raw binaries and PE/COFF, ELF, Mach-O, TE, Intel HEX, Motorola S-Record, TI-TXT, MD1ROM and VxWorks files. C++, Python and Rust APIs automate analysis inside or outside the UI; the open-source debugger runs locally or remotely on Windows, Linux and macOS and also connects to GDB, LLDB and iOS debugserver targets; patches can be made by editing assembly, in the hex editor or with the bundled SCC compiler; and 6.0 added an MCP server. Ultimate adds Firmware Ninja for embedded firmware, which finds code and data regions by entropy and detects memory-mapped I/O accesses, while the EFI Resolver workflow types protocol usage in UEFI PEI, DXE and SMM modules.
requirements: Stable release at review: 6.0.10905 (6.0 Release 2, 2026-10-20), a bug-fix update to 6.0 (2026-09-03). One license covers Linux, macOS and Windows; tested hosts are Ubuntu 24.04/26.04 and macOS 15/26 (x64 or arm64) and Windows 10/11 (x64); minimums: 2 GHz multi-core CPU, 8 GB RAM, 4 GB disk. Needs Python 3.10+.

Four editions: Free, Non-Commercial (Personal, non-commercial use only), Commercial and Ultimate. Paid licenses include a year of updates; versions released during support keep working after it. Online purchases are named licenses (one person, several machines). Only Commercial and Ultimate run plugins headlessly (import binaryninja without the GUI); Non-Commercial uses the API only from GUI-loaded plugins or the Python console.

By edition, Free decompiles x86, x86-64, ARMv7, Thumb2 and AArch64; Non-Commercial and Commercial add PowerPC, MIPS, RISC-V, MSP430, 6502 and the MD1ROM loader; only Ultimate decompiles nanoMIPS, TriCore, C-SKY, M·CORE, Hexagon, NDS32 and TMS320C6x and has the VxWorks loader, Firmware Ninja, Binary Similarity and Ghidra Export.

Free (non-commercial use or commercial evaluation) has no API or plugins and only disassembly, HLIL and Pseudo C views. The free browser-based Binary Ninja Cloud supports all architectures but requires uploading binaries to Vector 35, reads only PE, Mach-O and ELF, lacks API and plugins and has strict performance limits.

resources.name: Hopper Disassembler
resources.description: Cryptic Apps' commercial disassembler, decompiler and debugger for macOS and Linux, which reads Mach-O (macOS and iOS), PE and ELF executables built for 32- and 64-bit Intel, ARMv6, ARMv7, ARM64 and PowerPC processors. Each procedure can be viewed as assembly, as an interactive control-flow graph that exports to PDF or as C-like pseudocode, with Swift name demangling and extraction of Objective-C selectors and messages, and binaries can be patched through the hex editor, the built-in assembler or Python. Debugging of Mac applications uses LLDB or GDB, Python scripts reach most features, an SDK adds file-format parsers and CPU backends, and Hopper 6 brought a new decompiler and an MCP server for LLM clients.
requirements: Version at review: 6.6.1, released 2026-10-29. The Mac build is a Universal Binary for Intel and Apple Silicon and requires macOS 12.4 or later; 5.19.6 is the last version for macOS 10.13 to 11. The Linux build needs a 64-bit Intel processor and is tested only on Ubuntu 24.04, Fedora 41 and Arch Linux (DEB, RPM and tar.xz packages). There is no Windows version.

Commercial, with a per-user Personal License or a hardware-bound Computer License and no restriction on commercial use. Licenses are permanent and include one year of updates; after the update plan lapses, Hopper is limited to the last version released during it, and another year can be bought from within the application.
The free demo has all analysis features but cannot save or export disassembly or modified binaries, disables the debugger backend and limits sessions to 30 minutes.

Hopper cannot read iOS apps taken from an iTunes library, which are encrypted with FairPlay DRM, until the user removes the DRM. Its pseudocode is usually not directly compilable, and the tutorial warns that code wrongly judged unreachable can drop out of it.

resources.name: JEB Decompiler
resources.description: PNF Software's commercial reverse-engineering platform for Android apps and native code, combining a Dalvik decompiler and Android debuggers with disassemblers and decompilers for x86, ARM, MIPS and RISC-V machine code. For APKs it decompiles multi-dex Dalvik bytecode to Java, reconstructs resources and obfuscated XML, cleans up obfuscated code with optimizers that decrypt content and undo reflection, and debugs Dalvik and native ARM or Intel code in one session, stepping from Dalvik into JNI methods. Modules in JEB Pro also decompile WebAssembly, Ethereum EVM contracts (to Solidity-like code), Siemens S7-300/400 PLC blocks and Nvidia SASS GPU code and analyze PDF documents, and its loaders read PE, ELF, Mach-O, Intel HEX and raw (headless) firmware images. The JEB API lets Java and Python scripts, back-end plugins and custom headless clients automate analysis, and JEB also exposes an MCP server for AI agents.
requirements: Version at review: JEB 5.48, released 2026-10-07. Needs a 64-bit JDK 21+ (JDK 23 at most and Oracle or OpenJDK builds recommended); the GUI client runs on Windows, Linux (GTK) and macOS on x64 or arm64. Packages are per-user zip archives sent by email; license keys derive from machine identifiers.

Time-based commercial licenses only, none perpetual: JEB Android (per user, non-professional users, Android apps only), JEB Pro (per user, all modules), JEB Pro Floating (per seat) and JEB Pro OEM (per server, back-end or SaaS use). After a non-OEM subscription expires, existing JDB2 projects still open but new ones cannot be created; per the buy page, only Pro licenses work offline.

JEB Community Edition is free, with most disassemblers and file analyzers and the x86/x86-64 decompilers, but per the features matrix no Dalvik decompiler or debugger, headless launcher or offline use; the EULA sets separate terms for it. JEB Demo has all modules for evaluation but decompiles only part of the code, cannot save or load projects or use the clipboard, and has time-limited sessions that need an Internet connection.

Stated limits: RISC-V support lacks RV128, RVE, vector/SIMD extensions and floating-point decompilation; the S7 decompiler cannot process all MC7 code or S7-1200/1500 blocks; debugging apps that disallow it works on ARMv7 only; command-line Python scripts need a Pro or CE license.

resources.name: WinDbg
resources.description: Microsoft's WinDbg debugger and the Debugging Tools for Windows, documented on Microsoft Learn, for debugging live user-mode and kernel-mode code, analyzing crash dumps and examining CPU registers and memory. The current app keeps the engine, commands and extensions of WinDbg (Classic) and adds Time Travel Debugging, which records a user-mode process and replays it in both directions, JavaScript and NatVis scripting and Linux ELF dump analysis; since 1.2610.1001.0 it also offers WinDbg MCP for supported AI clients.
requirements: WinDbg installs from Microsoft's installer, the Microsoft Store or winget on x64 or ARM64 Windows 11 or Windows 10 1607 and later, not Windows 10/11 S, and direct and Store installs self-update; the release notes, updated 2026-11-05, list 1.2611.4001.0 as newest.

Debugging Tools for Windows (WinDbg Classic and the KD, NTKD, CDB and NTSD console debuggers) ships with the WDK or Windows SDK or as an SDK-only install, with archived SDKs for older Windows. Kernel debugging typically needs a second machine or VM, local kernel debugging and TTD need elevation, and full analysis needs symbols, which for commercial code depend on the vendor.
Free in the Microsoft Store under Microsoft's proprietary WinDbg license terms (updated 2026-10-08): the software is licensed, not sold, may not be redistributed and may send usage data to Microsoft.

TTD records user-mode processes only, and not protected ones such as PPL; recording is typically 10–20x slower, traces can reach several gigabytes in minutes, with index files about twice as large, and may hold personal or security data; anti-virus software can interfere.

WinDbg MCP officially supports GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot CLI, one client per session; clients may send debugger context to their model service, AI findings are not authoritative, and default secure mode blocks high-risk commands such as .shell.

resources.name: 010 Editor
resources.description: SweetScape Software's commercial hex and text editor whose Binary Templates, C/C++-like struct definitions with control flow and functions, parse binary files into hierarchical, editable structures. Templates can run when a file opens and are shared through an online repository, scripts with C/C++-like syntax automate edits and batch runs, and the tools include a Capstone-based disassembler for x86, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC and other code, byte-by-byte comparison, checksums and hashes, and editing of drives and, on Windows, process memory.
requirements: Version 17.0.1, released 2026-11-04, has 64-bit builds for Windows 11/10, macOS 10.14 to 27 on ARM and Intel, and Ubuntu 18.04 to 26.04, plus 32-bit Windows and Linux builds and a portable Windows build. Version 10 dropped Windows XP, macOS 10.7–10.11 and Ubuntu 10.04–14.04, where older releases still run.

Commercial: the evaluation version works for 30 days, after which a license must be bought. Licenses are per user and perpetual, with a year of free upgrades and support, and come as commercial or lower-priced home/academic licenses; the EULA bars home/academic licenses from commercial use, except for members of registered non-profits, and from government or military organizations.

The disassembler only converts bytes to assembly: the manual says 010 Editor cannot execute the result and points to a separate emulator or debugger. Process editing is Windows-only, and the manual warns that incorrect process edits can make programs misbehave or crash the system.
Only ZIP, BMP and WAV templates ship with the editor; templates in the online repository are written and submitted by other users.

resources.name: pestudio
resources.description: Winitor's Windows tool for initial malware assessment, which statically inspects Windows executable files and reports key indicators such as hard-coded URLs and IP addresses, flagged imports, resources and overlay data. The free basic edition also detects file signatures, debug information and TLS callbacks, computes entropy and imphash, shows the rich header and .NET metadata and looks up VirusTotal scores by hash; pestudio-pro adds MITRE ATT&CK mapping, XML reports and the pestudiox.exe command-line version.
requirements: Version 9.61, whose feature and licensing sheets are dated March 2025, ships as a ZIP that needs no installation; the download page says it is fully portable, does not alter the system it runs on and runs on any Windows system.

The free basic edition may be used only in a private context for occasional malware static analysis, not in a professional or corporate environment. pestudio-pro is sold as a one-year license per user that includes free updates, is not renewed automatically and is delivered as a password-protected ZIP.

VirusTotal lookups send only the file's MD5 hash, never the sample, and an XML switch disables them; searching VirusTotal by imphash needs a VirusTotal Intelligence account. The software is provided as-is without warranty, and its bundled XML files may not be used outside pestudio without the author's permission.

resources.name: OllyDbg
resources.description: 32-bit assembler-level analyzing debugger for Windows that emphasizes binary code analysis for programs without source; its site says development is frozen, and the newest version it lists is 2.01 of 27 September 2013. Its analysis recognizes procedures, loops, API calls, switches, tables, constants and strings and decodes calls to more than 1,900 standard API and 400 C functions; it attaches to running programs, debugs DLLs directly, sets conditional, logging, memory and hardware breakpoints and writes patches back to the executable.
requirements: Version 2.01 (27 September 2013) is the newest the site lists, and 1.10 is offered as the final 1.x version. The requirements page lists Windows 95, 98, NT 4.0 SP2 or later, or Windows 2000 and later, and says debugging on NT or 2000 may need administrative rights; the 2.x notes say version 2 does not run on Windows 95 or 98.
OllyDbg is a 32-bit debugger. The 64-bit version is offered only as incomplete, and its latest progress note, of 5 February 2014, put the debugging engine at 70% and analysis at 15%.

Shareware that may be downloaded and used for free; the FAQ says it is rated shareware for copyright reasons only. The download page's agreement covers only version 1.10 and its Plugin Development Kit: permanent or commercial use needs a free registration, the software comes as is, and copies may be shared only complete, unchanged and without a fee. Disassembler 2.01 is released under GPL v3.

The download page warns that many vendors forbid disassembling, decompiling or reverse engineering their programs, including third-party and system libraries, and suggests asking a lawyer whether fair use applies.

resources.name: Practical Malware Analysis
resources.description: No Starch Press book, published in February 2012, that teaches hands-on malware analysis from basic static and dynamic techniques in virtual machines through x86 disassembly with IDA Pro, debugging with OllyDbg and kernel debugging with WinDbg. Later chapters cover malicious Windows programs, covert launching, data encoding, network signatures, anti-disassembly, anti-debugging and anti-VM techniques, unpacking, shellcode, C++ and 64-bit malware, and hands-on labs with solutions have readers dissect malware samples.
requirements: An 800-page book, sold in print with a free ebook or as a PDF, Mobi and ePub ebook. Chapter 12, the detailed table of contents and the index are free PDFs, and an errata PDF is posted.
Following the book needs a safe virtual analysis environment, which it teaches readers to set up, and the analysis tools it covers, such as IDA Pro, OllyDbg and WinDbg.

The publisher's “Download the labs” link leads to a GitHub repository offering the lab binaries as a self-extracting archive or a password-protected 7-Zip file. Its README warns that the binaries contain malicious code that should not be installed or run without first setting up a safe environment, and that, like real malware, some may crash, leak memory or behave unexpectedly.
The labs target Windows XP: many work on newer Windows but some do not, and a separate archive holds labs rebuilt for Windows 7 whose results differ from the book's answers.

resources.name: UABEA
resources.description: Cross-platform reader and writer for the asset bundles and serialized asset files of Unity games, originally based on, though not a fork of, the archived UABE. Its README presents it as a modding and research tool rather than an extractor and points users who only want to extract assets to AssetRipper or AssetStudio; it opens bundles from Unity's Addressables system, whose CRC checks must be cleared with a separate tool before edited bundles load. It builds on AssetsTools.NET with Cpp2IL and Mono.Cecil, and the repository includes texture, audio-clip, font and text-asset plugins.
requirements: Windows and Linux builds come from the releases or from nightly CI artifacts, and the project targets .NET 8. Release at review: v8, published 2024-11-03; the reviewed master commit dates from 2026-05-11. The README also points to UABEANext, a successor with docking and multi-bundle opening that is still a work in progress.
